chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 1
paragraphs: On an unbearably hot evening in early July, a young man stepped out of the tiny room he rented on S. Place and walked slowly, almost hesitantly, toward K. Bridge.

He had managed to avoid his landlady on the staircase. His room was tucked under the roof of a tall five-story building and was more like a closet than a proper room. The landlady, who provided him with the room, meals, and basic service, lived on the floor below. Every time he went out, he had to pass her kitchen, and the door was always open. Each time he walked by, the young man felt a wave of sickness and dread that made him grimace with shame. He was hopelessly in debt to her and terrified of running into her.

This was not because he was a coward -- far from it. But for some time now he had been in an agitated, irritable state bordering on nervous collapse. He had become so completely wrapped up in himself, so cut off from everyone, that he dreaded encountering not just his landlady but anyone at all. He was crushed by poverty, but lately even that had stopped weighing on him. He had given up dealing with practical matters entirely and had lost all desire to try. Nothing his landlady could actually do truly frightened him. But to be stopped on the stairs, forced to listen to her pointless gossip, her nagging demands for payment, her threats and complaints, to have to scramble for excuses, to dodge and lie -- no, he would rather creep down the stairs like a cat and slip out unseen.
This evening, however, stepping out into the street, he became sharply aware of his fear.

"I want to attempt a thing _like that_ and I'm scared of these little things," he thought with a strange smile. "Hm... yes, everything is in a man's hands, and he lets it all slip away out of cowardice -- that's a given. It would be interesting to know what people are most afraid of. Taking a new step, saying a new word -- that's what terrifies them most.... But I talk too much. I talk because I do nothing. Or maybe I do nothing because I talk. I've learned to talk this past month, lying around for days in my hole thinking... about fairy tales. Why am I going there now? Am I capable of _that_? Is _that_ serious? No, it's not serious at all. It's just a fantasy to entertain myself -- a game! Yes, maybe it's just a game."

The heat on the street was brutal -- the stagnant air, the crowds, the plaster, scaffolding, bricks, and dust everywhere, and that distinctive Petersburg stench so familiar to anyone who can't get out of the city in summer -- it all scraped painfully against the young man's already frayed nerves. The unbearable reek from the bars, which were especially numerous in this part of town, and the drunks he kept running into despite it being a workday, completed the picture of misery. A look of profound disgust flickered across the young man's fine features. He was, as it happened, exceptionally handsome -- taller than average, slim, well-built, with striking dark eyes and dark brown hair. Soon he sank into deep thought, or more accurately into a kind of mental blankness. He walked along without noticing his surroundings and without caring to. From time to time he would mutter something under his breath -- a habit of talking to himself that he had just acknowledged. In these moments he would realize that his thoughts were tangled and that he was very weak. He had barely eaten in two days.

He was so badly dressed that even someone accustomed to looking shabby would have been embarrassed to appear on the street in such rags. In this part of town, though, almost nothing you wore would raise an eyebrow. The proximity of the Hay Market, the abundance of disreputable establishments, and the predominantly working-class population crowded into these streets and alleys in the heart of Petersburg meant that every type of person could be seen here, and no figure, however bizarre, would cause surprise. But so much bitterness and contempt had built up in the young man's heart that, despite all the self-consciousness of youth, his rags bothered him least of all on the street. Running into acquaintances or former classmates was another matter -- he hated that at any time. And yet when a drunk being hauled somewhere in a massive wagon pulled by a heavy draft horse suddenly yelled at him from the road -- "Hey, you! German hat man!" -- bellowing and pointing at him, the young man froze and clutched his hat in a panic. It was a tall round hat from Zimmerman's, but completely worn out, faded with age, full of holes and stains, brimless and bent to one side in the most ridiculous way. It was not shame, however, but something closer to terror that seized him.

"I knew it," he muttered in confusion. "I knew it! That's the worst of all! Some stupid thing like this, the most trivial detail, could ruin the whole plan. Yes, my hat is too noticeable.... It looks ridiculous, and that makes it noticeable.... With these rags I should be wearing a cap, any kind of old flat thing, not this grotesque hat. Nobody wears a hat like this -- you'd spot it a mile away, you'd remember it.... The point is that people would remember it, and that would give them a lead. For this kind of thing you need to be as invisible as possible.... Details, details are what matter! It's always the little things that ruin everything...."

He did not have far to go. He knew exactly how many steps it was from his front gate: seven hundred and thirty. He had counted them once, lost in daydreams. At the time he had not believed in those dreams and was only tormenting himself with their horrifying audacity. Now, a month later, he had begun to see them differently. Despite all his internal monologues mocking his own weakness and indecision, he had unconsciously come to see this "horrifying" dream as something to be attempted -- though he still did not fully admit this to himself. He was going now for a "rehearsal" of his plan, and with every step his agitation grew more intense.

With his heart pounding and his hands trembling, he approached a large building that faced the canal on one side and the street on the other. The building was divided into small apartments and housed all kinds of working people -- tailors, locksmiths, cooks, various Germans, girls scraping together a living however they could, petty clerks, and so on. People were constantly coming and going through the two gates and across the two courtyards. Three or four doormen worked in the building. The young man was relieved not to run into any of them, and immediately slipped unnoticed through the right-hand door and up the staircase. It was a back staircase, dark and narrow, but he already knew it well and liked these surroundings -- in this kind of darkness, even the nosiest eyes were nothing to worry about.

"If I'm this scared now, what would it be like if I were actually going to do it?" he couldn't help thinking as he reached the fourth floor. Some movers blocked his way, carrying furniture out of an apartment. He knew a German civil servant and his family had lived there. So this German was moving out, which meant the fourth floor on this staircase would be empty except for the old woman. "That's a good thing, at least," he thought as he rang the bell of the old woman's apartment. The bell made a faint tinkling sound, as if it were tin rather than copper. The small apartments in buildings like these always have bells that sound like that. He had forgotten the sound of this bell, and now its peculiar tinkling seemed to remind him of something, bringing it sharply into focus.... He flinched -- his nerves were completely shot by now. After a moment, the door opened a crack. The old woman peered at her visitor through the gap with obvious suspicion, and nothing was visible but her small eyes, glinting in the darkness. But when she saw other people on the landing, she grew bolder and opened the door wide. The young man stepped into the dark entryway, which was separated from the tiny kitchen by a partition. The old woman stood before him in silence, studying him with a questioning look. She was a tiny, shriveled woman of about sixty, with sharp, hostile eyes and a sharp little nose. Her colorless, somewhat graying hair was heavily greased with oil, and she wore nothing on her head. Around her thin, long neck -- which looked like a chicken's leg -- she had a flannel rag knotted, and despite the heat, a moth-eaten fur cape, yellowed with age, hung loosely from her shoulders. The old woman coughed and groaned constantly. The young man must have looked at her with an unusual expression, because a flash of suspicion returned to her eyes.
"Raskolnikov, a student. I was here a month ago," the young man said quickly, with a slight bow, remembering he needed to be more polite.
"I remember, sir. I remember your visit perfectly well," the old woman said clearly, keeping her searching eyes fixed on his face.

"And here... I am again, on the same business," Raskolnikov continued, slightly thrown and surprised by the old woman's suspicion. "Maybe she's always like this and I just didn't notice it last time," he thought uneasily.
The old woman paused as if considering, then stepped aside and pointed toward the door of the room, letting her visitor go ahead of her.
"Come in, sir."
The small room the young man entered had yellow wallpaper, geraniums and muslin curtains in the windows, and at that moment was brightly lit by the setting sun.

"So the sun will be shining like this _then_ too!" flashed through Raskolnikov's mind almost involuntarily, and he quickly scanned the room, trying to memorize the layout as thoroughly as possible. But there was nothing remarkable about it. The furniture, all very old and made of yellow wood, consisted of a sofa with a large arched back, an oval table in front of it, a vanity table with a mirror between the windows, chairs along the walls, and two or three cheap prints in yellow frames showing German girls holding birds -- that was all. In the corner, a small lamp burned in front of an icon. Everything was spotlessly clean; the floor and furniture were polished to a shine.
"Lizaveta's doing," the young man thought. There wasn't a speck of dust anywhere in the apartment.

"You find this kind of cleanliness in the homes of bitter old widows," Raskolnikov thought, and he glanced curiously at the cotton curtain over the doorway to the other tiny room, where the old woman's bed and dresser were -- a room he had never looked into before. These two rooms were the entire apartment.
"What do you want?" the old woman said sharply, coming into the room and standing before him as before, so she could look him straight in the face.
"I've brought something to pawn," he said, and pulled from his pocket an old-fashioned flat silver watch with a globe engraved on the back and a steel chain.
"But the term on your last pledge has expired. It was due the day before yesterday."
"I'll bring you the interest for another month. Just wait a little."
"Whether I wait or sell your pledge right now -- that's for me to decide, sir."
"How much will you give me for the watch, Alyona Ivanovna?"
"You bring me such worthless things, sir -- it's barely worth anything. Last time I gave you two rubles for your ring, and you could buy one brand new at a jeweler's for a ruble and a half."
"Give me four rubles for it. I'll redeem it -- it was my father's. I'll have money soon."
"A ruble and a half, interest in advance, take it or leave it!"
"A ruble and a half!" the young man cried.

"Take it or leave it." The old woman held the watch back out to him. The young man took it and was so angry he almost walked out, but caught himself immediately, remembering there was nowhere else to go -- and that he had come here with another purpose as well.
"Hand it over," he said roughly.

The old woman fumbled in her pocket for her keys and disappeared behind the curtain into the other room. Left standing alone in the middle of the room, the young man listened intently, thinking. He could hear her unlocking the dresser.

"Must be the top drawer," he thought. "So she keeps the keys in a pocket on the right side. All on one bunch, on a steel ring.... And there's one key that's three times bigger than the others, with deep notches. That can't be for the dresser... so there must be some other chest or strongbox... That's worth knowing. Strongboxes always have keys like that... But how degrading all this is."
The old woman came back.

"Here you are, sir: at ten kopecks per ruble per month, that's fifteen kopecks from a ruble and a half for the month in advance. And for the two rubles I lent you before, you owe me twenty kopecks on the same terms, in advance. That comes to thirty-five kopecks total. So for the watch I give you one ruble and fifteen kopecks. Here."
"What! Only a ruble and fifteen kopecks now!"
"That's right."

The young man didn't argue and took the money. He looked at the old woman and was in no hurry to leave, as if there were still something he wanted to say or do, though he himself didn't quite know what.
"I might bring you something else in a day or two, Alyona Ivanovna -- something valuable -- silver -- a cigarette case, as soon as I get it back from a friend..." He trailed off awkwardly.
"Well, we'll talk about it then, sir."
"Goodbye -- are you always home alone? Your sister isn't here with you?" he asked as casually as he could, stepping into the hallway.
"What business is she of yours, sir?"
"Oh, nothing special, I was just asking. You jump to conclusions too quickly.... Good day, Alyona Ivanovna."

Raskolnikov left in a state of total confusion. The confusion only deepened as he went. He stopped short on the stairs two or three times, as if struck by a sudden thought. Out on the street he burst out: "Oh God, how disgusting this all is! And can I, can I really.... No, that's insane, that's ridiculous!" he said firmly. "How could such a monstrous idea enter my head? What filth my heart is capable of. Yes, filth above all -- vile, revolting, disgusting! -- and for a whole month I've been...." But no words or exclamations could express his turmoil. The wave of revulsion that had begun building in his chest on the way to the old woman's had now reached such intensity, taken such definite shape, that he didn't know what to do with himself to escape his misery. He stumbled along the sidewalk like a drunk, bumping into people, and only came to his senses on the next street. Looking around, he realized he was standing near a tavern that you entered by going down steps from the sidewalk to a basement. At that moment two drunks came out the door, cursing and propping each other up as they climbed the steps. Without a second thought, Raskolnikov went down the steps. He had never been in a tavern before, but now he felt dizzy and was burning with thirst. He wanted a cold beer and blamed his sudden weakness on not having eaten. He sat down at a sticky little table in a dark, dirty corner, ordered a beer, and gulped down the first glass. He felt better immediately, and his thoughts cleared.

"That's all nonsense," he said with a surge of hope, "there's nothing to worry about! It's just physical weakness. One glass of beer, a piece of dry bread -- and in a second the brain is sharper, the mind is clearer, the will is strong! God, how pathetic all this is!"

Despite this contemptuous dismissal, he was already looking cheerful, as if suddenly freed from a terrible weight, and he glanced around at the other people in the room with something like warmth. But even in that moment, he had a vague sense that this lighter mood was not normal either.

There were only a few people left in the tavern. Besides the two drunks he had passed on the steps, a group of about five men and a girl with an accordion had left at the same time. After they went, the room felt quiet and half-empty. The remaining customers were a man who looked like a tradesman, drunk but not falling down, sitting in front of a mug of beer, and his companion -- a huge, heavyset man with a gray beard wearing a short coat. This one was very drunk and had dozed off on the bench. Every so often, as if in his sleep, he would crack his fingers, arms spread wide, his torso bouncing on the bench, while he hummed some pointless tune, trying to recall words that went something like:
"His wife a year he fondly loved, His wife a -- a year he -- fondly loved."
Or suddenly waking up again:
"Walking along the crowded row, He met the one he used to know."

But nobody shared his amusement. His silent companion watched these outbursts with open hostility and suspicion. There was one other man in the room who looked like a retired government clerk. He sat by himself, taking an occasional sip from his mug and glancing around at the others. He, too, seemed agitated about something.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Raskolnikov was not used to crowds, and as mentioned before, he had been avoiding all human contact, especially lately. But now he suddenly felt a desire to be around other people. Something new seemed to be stirring inside him, and with it came a kind of thirst for company. He was so exhausted after a solid month of concentrated misery and dark agitation that he wanted to escape, if only for a moment, into some other world, any world at all. And despite the filthy surroundings, he was glad to stay in the tavern.

The owner was in another room but kept coming down a few steps into the main area, his flashy tarred boots with red turned-down tops appearing before the rest of him. He wore a long coat and a hideously greasy black satin waistcoat with no tie, and his entire face seemed smeared with oil like a door lock. A boy of about fourteen stood behind the counter, and a younger boy handed out whatever was ordered. On the counter lay sliced cucumber, pieces of dried black bread, and chopped-up fish, all reeking. The air was suffocating, so thick with the fumes of alcohol that five minutes in there could make a person drunk.

Sometimes you meet a stranger who captures your interest from the very first moment, before a single word is spoken. That was the impression made on Raskolnikov by a man sitting a short distance away who looked like a retired clerk. The young man would recall this impression many times afterward, and even attributed it to some kind of premonition. He kept glancing at the clerk, partly because the man was staring persistently at him, clearly eager to start a conversation. The clerk looked at everyone else in the room, including the tavern keeper, as if he were bored with their company and felt a condescending contempt for people beneath his station and education -- people not worth talking to. He was a man past fifty, bald and graying, medium height, heavily built. His face, bloated from constant drinking, had a yellowish, almost greenish tinge, with puffy eyelids from which sharp reddish eyes peered out like narrow slits. But there was something very strange about him -- a light in his eyes suggesting intense feeling, perhaps even thought and intelligence, but also a glint of something like madness. He wore an old and hopelessly tattered black dress coat with every button missing except one, which he kept fastened, clearly clinging to this last shred of respectability. A crumpled shirt front, spotted and stained, stuck out from his canvas waistcoat. Like a proper clerk, he was clean-shaven, but it had been so long since he last shaved that his chin looked like a stiff grayish brush. There was still something respectable, something official, about his manner. But he was restless -- he kept running his fingers through his hair and from time to time would let his head sink into his hands, his tattered elbows resting wearily on the stained, sticky table. Finally he looked straight at Raskolnikov and said loudly and firmly:

"May I venture, honored sir, to engage you in polite conversation? For although your appearance might not command respect, my experience tells me that you are an educated man, not accustomed to drinking. I have always respected education when combined with genuine feeling, and I am, moreover, a titular counselor by rank. Marmeladov -- that is my name; titular counselor. I take the liberty of asking -- have you been in government service?"

"No, I'm a student," the young man answered, somewhat surprised by the man's pompous style and by being addressed so directly. Despite the momentary desire for company he had just been feeling, the instant someone actually spoke to him, he felt his usual irritable, uneasy aversion to any stranger who approached him or tried to.

"A student then, or a former student!" the clerk exclaimed. "Just as I thought! I'm a man of experience, sir, vast experience." He tapped his forehead approvingly. "You've been a student or attended some institute of learning!... But allow me...." He got up, staggered, grabbed his jug and glass, and sat down beside the young man, facing him at a slight angle. He was drunk, but spoke fluently and boldly, only occasionally losing his thread and slurring his words. He latched onto Raskolnikov with the hunger of a man who hadn't spoken to a soul in a month.

"Honored sir," he began with almost ceremonial gravity, "poverty is not a sin -- that's a well-known truth. And I know too that drunkenness is no virtue -- that's even more true. But destitution, honored sir, destitution is a sin. In poverty you can still preserve the nobility of your innate feelings, but in destitution -- never. In destitution, a man isn't driven out of human society with a stick -- he's swept out with a broom, to make it as humiliating as possible. And rightly so! Because in destitution I am the first to degrade myself. Hence the tavern! Honored sir, a month ago Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife, and my wife is a very different person from me! Do you understand? Allow me to ask you one more question, out of simple curiosity: have you ever spent a night on a hay barge on the Neva?"
"No, I haven't," Raskolnikov answered. "What do you mean?"

"Well, I've just come from one, and it's the fifth night I've slept there...." He filled his glass, drained it, and paused. Bits of hay were clinging to his clothes and stuck in his hair. He clearly had not undressed or washed in at least five days. His hands were especially filthy -- plump, red, with black nails.

His monologue seemed to generate a languid, general interest. The boys behind the counter started snickering. The tavern keeper came down from the upper room apparently just to listen to this "entertaining fellow" and sat down a little distance away, yawning lazily but with dignity. Marmeladov was evidently a regular here, and his weakness for grandiose speeches had probably developed from the habit of constantly striking up conversations with all kinds of strangers in taverns. This habit becomes a necessity for certain drunks, especially those who are kept on a tight leash at home. Among fellow drinkers, they try to justify themselves and even win a little respect.
"Entertaining fellow!" the tavern keeper pronounced. "So why don't you work? Why aren't you at your post, if you're in the service?"

"Why am I not at my post, honored sir?" Marmeladov went on, addressing himself exclusively to Raskolnikov, as though it were he who had asked. "Why am I not at my post? Doesn't my heart ache knowing what a useless worm I am? A month ago, when Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife with his own hands, and I lay there drunk -- didn't I suffer? Excuse me, young man, has it ever happened to you... hmm... well, to beg for a loan when you already know it's hopeless?"
"Yes, it has. But what do you mean by hopeless?"

"Hopeless in the fullest sense -- when you know in advance you'll get nothing. You know with absolute certainty that this particular man, this most respectable and upstanding citizen, will under no circumstances give you money. And why should he? He knows I won't pay it back. Out of compassion? But Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who follows all the latest ideas, explained the other day that compassion has been forbidden by science itself, and that's already the practice in England, where they have political economy. Why, I ask you, should he give it to me? And yet, knowing perfectly well that he won't, I set off to see him and..."
"Why do you go?" Raskolnikov asked.

"Well, when you have nobody, when there's nowhere else to go! Every person needs somewhere to go. There are times when you absolutely must go somewhere! When my own daughter first went out with a yellow ticket, I had to go too... (for my daughter holds a yellow passport," he added parenthetically, glancing at the young man with a certain unease.) "Never mind, sir, never mind!" he continued hurriedly and with forced composure when both counter boys burst out laughing and even the tavern keeper smirked. "Never mind, I'm not embarrassed by their mocking! Everyone already knows everything, and all that is hidden shall be revealed. I accept it, not with contempt but with humility. So be it! So be it! 'Behold the man!' Tell me, young man -- no, let me put it more strongly and precisely: not _can_ you, but _dare_ you, looking at me now, say that I am not a pig?"
The young man said nothing.

"Well," the orator resumed stolidly, with even greater dignity, once the laughter in the room had died down. "Well, so be it. I am a pig, but she is a lady! I have the appearance of a beast, but Katerina Ivanovna, my wife, is an educated woman, an officer's daughter. Granted, I am a scoundrel, but she is a woman of noble heart, full of refinement, elevated by her upbringing. And yet... oh, if only she could feel something for me! Honored sir, you see, every person needs at least one place where someone cares about him! But Katerina Ivanovna, though she is generous, she is unjust.... And yet, even though I know that when she pulls my hair it's only out of pity -- for I say it again without shame, she pulls my hair, young man," he declared with renewed dignity, hearing the snickering again, "but God, if she would just once.... But no, no! It's all useless, and there's no point talking! No point! Because more than once my wish did come true, and more than once she did feel sorry for me, but... that is my fate, and I am a beast by nature!"
"You can say that again!" the tavern keeper agreed with a yawn. Marmeladov pounded his fist on the table.

"That is my fate! Do you know, sir, do you know -- I sold her very stockings for drink? Not her shoes, mind you -- that would at least be within the normal order of things -- but her stockings, I sold them for drink! And her mohair shawl too, a gift she'd had for ages, her own property, not mine. And we live in a freezing room, and she caught cold this winter and has started coughing up blood. We have three small children, and Katerina Ivanovna works from morning to night -- scrubbing, cleaning, washing the children -- she was raised to value cleanliness from childhood. But her lungs are weak, she's showing signs of consumption, and I feel it! You think I don't feel it? The more I drink, the more I feel it. That's why I drink -- to find some sympathy and feeling in drink.... I drink so I can suffer twice as much!" And in despair he dropped his head onto the table.

"Young man," he continued, raising his head, "I seem to read some kind of trouble in your face. I noticed it the moment you walked in, and that's why I spoke to you. Because in sharing the story of my life, I don't want to make myself a laughingstock before these idle listeners who know it all already -- I'm looking for a person of feeling and education. Know then that my wife was educated at a prestigious school for noble girls, and upon graduating she performed the shawl dance before the governor and other dignitaries, for which she received a gold medal and a certificate of merit. The medal... well, the medal was sold long ago, hmm... but the certificate is still in her trunk, and not long ago she showed it to our landlady. Even though she's almost always fighting with the landlady, she wanted someone to know about her past honors and happier days. I don't blame her for it, not at all, because the only thing she has left is memories -- everything else has turned to dust and ashes. Yes, yes, she's a proud woman, spirited and determined. She scrubs floors herself and eats nothing but black bread, but she will not tolerate disrespect. That's why she wouldn't stand for Mr. Lebeziatnikov's rudeness, and when he beat her for it, she took to her bed more from the wound to her pride than from the blows. She was a widow when I married her, with three children, each smaller than the last. She had married her first husband, an infantry officer, for love and eloped with him from her father's house. She adored her husband, but he took to cards, got into trouble, and died. He beat her near the end -- though she gave as good as she got, as I have documented proof -- and to this day she speaks of him through tears and throws him in my face. And I'm glad, I'm glad that even if only in her imagination, she can think of herself as having once been happy.... She was left with three children in a remote, godforsaken district where I happened to be at the time, and in such hopeless poverty that, though I've seen my share of hardship, I can't begin to describe it. Her relatives had all abandoned her. And she was proud, fiercely proud.... And then, honored sir, I, a widower at the time with a fourteen-year-old daughter from my first marriage, offered her my hand, because I couldn't bear to see such suffering. You can judge the depth of her desperation -- that she, an educated, cultured woman from a distinguished family, agreed to marry me. But she did! Weeping and wringing her hands, she married me! Because she had absolutely nowhere to turn. Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means to have absolutely nowhere to turn? No, you don't understand that yet.... For a whole year I did my duty faithfully and never touched this" -- he tapped the jug with his finger -- "because I have feelings. But even so, I couldn't please her. And then I lost my position too, through no fault of my own but due to staff changes, and that's when I did touch it!... It will be a year and a half now since we finally landed in this magnificent capital, adorned with countless monuments, after many wanderings and disasters. Here I found a position.... I found it and lost it again. Do you follow? This time it was my own fault -- my weakness got the better of me.... We now rent part of a room from Amalia Fyodorovna Lippewechsel, and what we live on and how we pay our rent, I couldn't tell you. There are many other people living there besides us. It's chaos, absolute bedlam... hmm... yes... And meanwhile my daughter from my first marriage has grown up. What she had to endure from her stepmother while growing up, I won't speak of. Katerina Ivanovna may be full of generous feelings, but she's a spirited woman, irritable and short-tempered.... But there's no use going into that! Sonya, as you can imagine, received no education. I tried four years ago to teach her some geography and world history, but since I wasn't exactly an expert myself and we had no proper textbooks -- and whatever books we had... hmm, well, we don't even have those now -- so all her education came to an end. We stopped at Cyrus of Persia. Since she's come of age, she's read some romantic novels, and recently she read a book she got through Mr. Lebeziatnikov -- Lewes's Physiology -- have you heard of it? -- and even told us about parts of it. That's the entirety of her education. And now, honored sir, I'd like to ask you a private question. How much do you think a decent, impoverished girl can earn through honest work? She can't make fifteen kopecks a day if she's respectable and has no special talent, not even working without pause! And on top of that, Ivan Ivanovich Klopstock, the civil counselor -- have you heard of him? -- still hasn't paid her for the half-dozen linen shirts she made him, and drove her away with shouting and insults, claiming the collars weren't sewn right and were crooked. And the little ones are going hungry.... And Katerina Ivanovna paces the room wringing her hands, with her cheeks flushed red the way they always are with that disease. 'Here you are living with us,' she says, 'eating and drinking and staying warm, and what do you contribute?' As if there's much to eat and drink when the children haven't seen a crust in three days! I was lying there at the time... well, so what! I was lying there drunk, and I heard my Sonya answer -- she has a gentle spirit, a soft little voice... fair hair, such a pale, thin little face -- she said: 'Katerina Ivanovna, am I really supposed to do something like that?' Now, Darya Frantsovna, a woman of evil reputation well known to the police, had tried two or three times to get to Sonya through the landlady. 'And why not?' Katerina Ivanovna sneered. 'What are you, some kind of treasure that needs protecting?' But don't blame her, don't blame her, honored sir! She wasn't herself when she said it -- she was out of her mind with illness and the children crying from hunger. And she said it more to wound than anything else.... That's Katerina Ivanovna's nature -- when children cry, even from hunger, she starts hitting them. At six o'clock I watched Sonya get up, put on her headscarf and her cape, and leave the apartment. Around nine she came back. She walked straight up to Katerina Ivanovna and laid thirty rubles on the table in front of her, in silence. Not a word, not even a glance -- she just picked up our big green _drap de dames_ shawl, covered her head and face with it, and lay down on the bed facing the wall. Only her small shoulders and body kept shuddering.... And I lay there, same as before.... And then I saw, young man, I saw Katerina Ivanovna, in the same silence, go over to Sonya's little bed. She knelt there all evening, kissing Sonya's feet, and would not get up. And then they both fell asleep in each other's arms... together... yes... and I... lay there drunk."
Marmeladov broke off, as though his voice had given out. Then he hurriedly filled his glass, drank it down, and cleared his throat.

"Since then, sir," he continued after a brief pause, "since then, owing to an unfortunate incident and information supplied by malicious people -- in which Darya Frantsovna played a leading role, claiming she had been treated disrespectfully -- since then my daughter Sofya Semyonovna has been required to carry a yellow ticket, and because of that she can no longer live with us. Our landlady, Amalia Fyodorovna, wouldn't allow it -- though she herself had been in league with Darya Frantsovna before -- and Mr. Lebeziatnikov too... hmm.... All the trouble between him and Katerina Ivanovna was because of Sonya. At first he had tried to court Sonya himself, but then suddenly got on his high horse: 'How,' he said, 'can a man of my education live under the same roof as a girl like that?' And Katerina Ivanovna stood up for her, wouldn't let it go... and that's how things ended up. Sonya visits us now, mostly after dark. She comforts Katerina Ivanovna and gives her everything she can.... She has a room at the Kapernaumovs' -- they're tailors. Kapernaumov is a lame man with a cleft palate, and his entire large family has cleft palates too. His wife as well. They all live in one room, but Sonya has her own, partitioned off.... Hmm... yes... very poor people, all with cleft palates... yes. So I got up the next morning, put on my rags, raised my hands to heaven, and went to see his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich. Do you know his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich? No? Then you don't know a man of God. He is wax... wax before the face of the Lord, even as wax melts!... His eyes were moist when he heard my story. 'Marmeladov, once already you have disappointed my expectations... I'll take you back one more time, on my own responsibility,' he said. 'Remember that,' he said. 'Now you may go.' I kissed the dust at his feet -- in my thoughts only, because in reality he would never have allowed it, being a statesman and a man of modern, progressive, enlightened views. I went home, and when I announced that I'd been taken back into service and would be receiving a salary again -- my God, what a celebration there was!..."

Marmeladov paused again, overwhelmed with emotion. Just then a whole group of revelers, already drunk, came in from the street, and the sound of a hired accordion and the cracked piping voice of a seven-year-old singing "The Village" drifted in from the entrance. The room filled with noise. The tavern keeper and boys busied themselves with the newcomers. Marmeladov, paying no attention to the arrivals, continued his story. He seemed extremely weak by now, but the drunker he got, the more talkative he became. The memory of his recent success in getting the job seemed to revive him, and it actually showed as a kind of glow on his face. Raskolnikov listened closely.

"That was five weeks ago, sir. Yes.... As soon as Katerina Ivanovna and Sonya heard the news -- Lord have mercy, it was as if I'd entered the kingdom of heaven. Before, I could lie around like an animal and get nothing but abuse. Now they were tiptoeing around, shushing the children: 'Semyon Zakharovich is tired from his work at the office, he's resting -- shh!' They made me coffee before work and heated real cream for me! Real cream, do you hear? And how they scraped together the money for a decent set of clothes -- eleven rubles and fifty kopecks -- I can't imagine. Boots, cotton shirt fronts, a uniform -- magnificent, all of it, for eleven and a half rubles. The first morning I came home from the office, Katerina Ivanovna had cooked a two-course dinner: soup and salted beef with horseradish. We'd never dreamed of anything like it. She didn't own any dresses, not a single one, but she made herself up as if she were going visiting -- and with nothing to work with, she managed to look quite presentable. She'd done her hair nicely, put on some kind of clean collar and cuffs, and there she was, a completely different person -- younger, prettier. Sonya, my darling, had only helped with money: 'For the time being,' she said, 'it's better if I don't visit too often. Maybe after dark, when no one can see.' Do you hear that? I lay down for a nap after dinner, and would you believe it -- even though Katerina Ivanovna had quarreled bitterly with our landlady Amalia Fyodorovna just a week before, she couldn't resist inviting her in for coffee. For two hours they sat there whispering. 'Semyon Zakharovich is back in service now, drawing a salary,' she told her, 'and he went to see his excellency in person, and his excellency himself came out to meet him, made everyone else wait, and led Semyon Zakharovich by the hand into his private office.' Do you hear? 'Of course,' he said, 'Semyon Zakharovich, remembering your past services,' he said, 'and despite your unfortunate weakness, since you now give your word and since we've managed poorly without you' -- do you hear? -- 'I am relying on your word as a gentleman.' And all of that, let me tell you, she made up herself, and not just to show off -- no, she actually believes it, she entertains herself with her own fantasies, I swear she does! And I don't blame her, I don't!... Six days ago, when I brought home my first full paycheck -- twenty-three rubles and forty kopecks -- she called me her darling. 'Darling,' she said, 'my little darling.' And when we were alone, you understand? You wouldn't exactly call me a handsome man, and I'm hardly an ideal husband, would you?... Well, she pinched my cheek and said, 'My little darling.'"

Marmeladov broke off. He tried to smile, but his chin suddenly began to tremble. He managed to control himself. The tavern, the degraded appearance of the man, five nights on a hay barge, a jug of spirits, and yet this piercing love for his wife and children -- it left the listener bewildered. Raskolnikov was listening intently but with a feeling of nausea. He regretted having come in here.

"Honored sir, honored sir!" Marmeladov cried, pulling himself together. "Oh, sir, perhaps all this seems laughable to you, as it does to everyone else, and perhaps I'm just annoying you with the stupid details of my wretched home life. But to me it is no laughing matter. Because I feel it all.... And that whole heavenly day, that whole evening, I spent in blissful dreams -- of how I would arrange everything, dress all the children properly, give her some peace, and rescue my own daughter from dishonor and bring her back to her family.... And much more besides.... Perfectly understandable, sir. Well then, sir" -- Marmeladov suddenly gave a sort of jolt, raised his head, and stared intently at his listener -- "well, on the very next day after all those dreams, exactly five days ago, in the evening, through a cunning trick, like a thief in the night, I stole the key to Katerina Ivanovna's box, took out whatever was left of my pay -- how much exactly I've forgotten -- and now look at me, all of you! It's the fifth day since I left home. They're looking for me there, and my job is finished, and my uniform is lying in a tavern by the Egyptian Bridge -- I traded it for these clothes I'm wearing... and it's the end of everything!"

Marmeladov struck his forehead with his fist, clenched his teeth, shut his eyes, and leaned heavily on the table. But a minute later his expression suddenly changed, and with a certain practiced slyness and show of bravado, he looked at Raskolnikov, laughed, and said:
"This morning I went to see Sonya -- went to ask her for some hair of the dog! Ha ha ha!"
"She didn't actually give it to you?" shouted one of the newcomers, then burst into a roar of laughter.

"This very bottle was bought with her money," Marmeladov declared, still addressing only Raskolnikov. "Thirty kopecks she gave me from her own hand, her last kopecks, everything she had -- I could see it.... She said nothing, just looked at me without a word.... That's not something that happens on earth, but up there... up there they grieve over people, they weep, but they don't blame. They don't blame! And that hurts more, it hurts more when they don't blame! Thirty kopecks, yes! And she probably needs them herself now, don't you think? She has to keep up appearances, after all. It costs money, that kind of smartness -- that special kind, you know? Do you understand? She needs pomade, too, petticoats, starched ones, fancy little shoes to show off her foot when she steps over a puddle. Do you understand, sir, do you understand what all that smartness costs? And here I am, her own father, and I took thirty kopecks of that money for a drink! And I'm drinking it! And I've already drunk it! So who's going to feel sorry for a man like me, eh? Do you feel sorry for me, sir, or not? Tell me! Do you feel sorry or not? Ha ha ha!"
He tried to fill his glass, but there was nothing left. The jug was empty.
"What is there to feel sorry about?" the tavern keeper shouted from nearby.

Laughter and curses followed. The laughter and curses came from those who had been listening and also from those who hadn't heard a word but were simply looking at the spectacle of the fired government clerk.
"Feel sorry? Why should anyone feel sorry for me?" Marmeladov suddenly declaimed, rising to his feet with his arm outstretched, as if he had been waiting for exactly that question.

"Why feel sorry for me, you ask? Yes! There's nothing to feel sorry about! I should be crucified, crucified on a cross, not pitied! Crucify me, judge, crucify me -- but pity me while you do it! And then I'll go to be crucified of my own free will, because it's not pleasure I'm after but tears and suffering!... Do you think, you who sell drink, that this bottle has been sweet to me? It was suffering I sought at the bottom of it, tears and suffering, and I found them, I tasted them. But He will have pity on us -- He who had pity on all mankind, who understood every person and everything. He is the One, He is the judge. He will come on that day and He will ask: 'Where is the daughter who sacrificed herself for her sick, consumptive stepmother and for the small children of another? Where is the daughter who had pity on the wretched drunkard, her earthly father, undaunted by his degradation?' And He will say: 'Come to me! I have already forgiven you once.... I have forgiven you once.... Your sins, which are many, are forgiven, for you have loved much....' And He will forgive my Sonya -- He will forgive her, I know it... I felt it in my heart when I was with her just now! And He will judge and forgive everyone -- the good and the wicked, the wise and the humble.... And when He has finished with all of them, He will call out to us: 'You, too, come forward!' He will say. 'Come forward, you drunkards! Come forward, you weaklings! Come forward, you children of shame!' And we will all come forward, without shame, and we will stand before Him. And He will say: 'You are swine, made in the image of the Beast and bearing his mark. But come, even you!' And the wise ones and the clever ones will say: 'Lord, why do you receive these people?' And He will say: 'I receive them, oh wise ones, I receive them, oh clever ones, because not one of them ever believed himself worthy of this.' And He will stretch out His hands to us, and we will fall down before Him... and we will weep... and we will understand everything! Then we will understand everything!... And everyone will understand -- Katerina Ivanovna, too... she will understand.... Lord, Thy kingdom come!" And he collapsed onto the bench, exhausted and helpless, looking at no one, lost in deep thought. His words had made a certain impression. There was a moment of silence, but then the laughter and cursing started up again.
"That's what he thinks!"
"Talked himself into a stupor!"
"Fine government clerk!"
And so on.
"Let's go, sir," Marmeladov said suddenly, raising his head to address Raskolnikov. "Come with me... Kozel's house, through the courtyard. Time I went home to Katerina Ivanovna."

Raskolnikov had been wanting to leave for some time and had already planned to help him. Marmeladov was far unsteadier on his feet than in his speech and leaned heavily on the young man. It was only two or three hundred steps. The closer they got to the house, the more the drunk man was overtaken by fear and confusion.

"It's not Katerina Ivanovna I'm afraid of now," he muttered anxiously, "and not that she'll start pulling my hair. Who cares about my hair! Forget my hair! That's what I say! It's actually better if she does pull it -- that's not what scares me... it's her eyes I'm afraid of... yes, her eyes... the redness in her cheeks frightens me too... and the way she breathes.... Have you noticed how people with that disease breathe when they're worked up? I'm scared of the children crying, too.... Because if Sonya hasn't brought them food... I don't know what's happened! I don't know! But the blows I'm not afraid of.... Know this, sir: those blows are not painful to me -- they're actually a pleasure. I can't do without them, in fact.... It's better this way. Let her hit me -- it eases her heart... it's better.... There's the building. Kozel's building, the cabinetmaker's. A German, well-off. Lead the way!"

They entered through the courtyard and climbed to the fourth floor. The staircase grew darker as they went up. It was nearly eleven o'clock, and though in summer there is no true night in Petersburg, it was very dark at the top of the stairs.

A grimy little door at the very top of the staircase stood ajar. A feeble candle stub lit up a very poor room about ten paces long, all of it visible from the doorway. Everything was in disarray, littered with rags of every kind, mostly children's clothes. A tattered sheet was strung across the far corner -- behind it was probably the bed. The room contained nothing but two chairs and a sofa upholstered in American leather, full of holes, in front of which stood a plain, unpainted, uncovered kitchen table. A sputtering tallow candle in an iron holder stood on the edge of the table. The family apparently had a room to themselves rather than a partitioned space, but their room was essentially a hallway. The door to the other rooms -- or rather the closet-sized compartments into which Amalia Lippewechsel's apartment was divided -- stood half open, and from behind it came shouting, uproar, and laughter. People were apparently playing cards and drinking tea. Profanities of the coarsest kind flew out periodically.

Raskolnikov recognized Katerina Ivanovna at once. She was a fairly tall, slim, graceful woman, terrifyingly thin, with magnificent dark brown hair and a hectic flush on her cheeks. She was pacing back and forth in her tiny room, pressing her hands to her chest; her lips were cracked, her breathing came in ragged, broken gasps. Her eyes burned feverishly and darted around with a harsh, unblinking stare. The consumptive, feverish face, flickering in the last light of the dying candle, made a sickening impression. She looked to Raskolnikov like she was about thirty -- certainly a strange wife for Marmeladov.... She hadn't heard them or noticed them come in. She seemed lost in thought, seeing and hearing nothing. The room was stuffy, but the window was not open; a stench rose from the staircase, but the door to the stairs was not shut. Clouds of tobacco smoke drifted in from the inner rooms. She kept coughing but did not close the door. The youngest child, a girl of about six, was asleep on the floor, curled up with her head on the sofa. A boy a year older stood trembling and crying in the corner -- he had obviously just been beaten. Beside him stood a nine-year-old girl, tall and thin, wearing a threadbare shift and an ancient cashmere shawl draped over her bare shoulders, long outgrown and barely reaching her knees. Her arm, thin as a stick, was wrapped around her brother's neck. She was whispering to him, trying to calm him down, doing everything she could to stop him from whimpering. At the same time, her large dark eyes -- made even larger by the thinness of her terrified face -- were watching her mother with dread. Marmeladov did not step through the door but dropped to his knees right there in the doorway, pushing Raskolnikov ahead of him. The woman, noticing a stranger, paused and faced him with an indifferent stare, coming to her senses for a moment and apparently trying to figure out what he was doing here. She seemed to decide he was heading for the rooms beyond, since he had to pass through hers to get there. Having dismissed him, she walked toward the front door to close it -- and let out a sudden scream when she saw her husband on his knees in the doorway.

"Ah!" she screamed in a frenzy. "He's back! The criminal! The monster!... And where is the money? What's in your pocket? Show me! And your clothes are different! Where are your clothes? Where is the money? Speak!"
She threw herself at him and started searching his pockets. Marmeladov submissively raised both arms to make the search easier. There was not a single kopeck.

"Where is the money?" she shrieked. "Oh, God -- has he drunk it all? There were twelve silver rubles left in the chest!" In a fury she grabbed him by the hair and dragged him into the room. Marmeladov aided her efforts by obediently crawling on his knees.

"And this is a comfort to me! This doesn't hurt at all, it's a genuine com-fort, ho-nored sir!" he called out, his head jerking back and forth in her grip, his forehead even striking the floor once. The child sleeping on the floor woke up and started crying. The boy in the corner lost all control, trembling and screaming, and rushed to his sister in sheer terror, nearly having a fit. The oldest girl stood shaking like a leaf.

"He's drunk it! He's drunk it all!" the poor woman wailed in despair. "And his clothes are gone! And they're hungry, they're hungry!" She wrung her hands and pointed at the children. "Oh, this cursed life! And you -- aren't you ashamed?" She suddenly rounded on Raskolnikov. "From the tavern! You've been drinking with him! You've been drinking with him too! Get out!"

The young man hurried toward the door without a word. The inner door had swung wide open, and curious faces were peering through it. Coarse, laughing faces with pipes and cigarettes, heads wearing caps, crowded the doorway. Further back you could see figures in open dressing gowns and various states of undress, some holding cards. They were especially entertained when Marmeladov, being dragged around by his hair, shouted that it was a comfort to him. Some even started filing into the room. Finally a harsh, shrill screech rang out -- it was Amalia Lippewechsel herself, pushing her way through the crowd, trying to restore order in her own fashion, threatening the poor woman for the hundredth time with eviction the next day. As he left, Raskolnikov managed to reach into his pocket, grab the copper coins he had gotten as change for his ruble in the tavern, and set them on the windowsill unnoticed. Then, on the stairs, he changed his mind and nearly went back.

"What a stupid thing I've done," he thought. "They have Sonya, and I need the money myself." But realizing it would be impossible to take it back now, and that he wouldn't have taken it back anyway, he shrugged it off and headed to his lodgings. "Sonya needs pomade too," he said as he walked, laughing bitterly. "This kind of smartness costs money.... Hmm! And maybe Sonya herself will go bankrupt today, because there's always a risk in it -- hunting big game, panning for gold.... Then they'd all be without a crust tomorrow if it weren't for my money. Good for Sonya! What a gold mine they've dug there! And they're certainly making the most of it! Oh yes, they are! They've cried about it and gotten used to it. People get used to anything, the scoundrels!"
He fell into thought.

"And what if I'm wrong?" he suddenly cried after a moment's reflection. "What if people aren't really scoundrels -- people in general, the whole human race? Then all the rest is just prejudice, invented fears, and there are no real barriers, and everything is exactly as it should be."

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He woke up late the next day after a fitful sleep, but the sleep had done nothing for him. He woke up irritable, bad-tempered, and full of bile, and looked around his room with loathing. It was a tiny closet of a room, about six paces long. It looked wretched with its dusty yellow wallpaper peeling from the walls, and the ceiling was so low that anyone taller than average felt uncomfortable, constantly afraid of bumping their head. The furniture matched the room: three old chairs, wobbly at best; a painted table in the corner piled with a few notebooks and books, the thick dust on them proving they hadn't been touched in ages. A large, unwieldy sofa took up almost an entire wall and half the floor. It had once been upholstered in chintz but was now in tatters and served as Raskolnikov's bed. He often slept on it fully dressed, without sheets, wrapped in his old student's overcoat, his head on a single small pillow under which he piled all his linen -- clean and dirty -- as a makeshift bolster. A small table stood in front of the sofa.

It would have been hard to sink to a worse state of disorder, but in Raskolnikov's current frame of mind, the squalor actually suited him. He had completely withdrawn from everyone, like a turtle in its shell, and even the sight of the maid who occasionally came in to check on his room made him twitch with irritation. He was in the grip of a fixation so total that everything else had fallen away. His landlady had stopped sending him meals two weeks ago, and he hadn't bothered to argue about it, even though he went without dinner. Nastasya, the cook and only servant, was rather pleased with her lodger's mood and had given up cleaning his room altogether -- only once a week or so she would wander in with a broom. She was the one who woke him that day.
"Get up! Why are you still asleep?" she called to him. "It's past nine. I brought you some tea -- want a cup? You must be half-starved by now."
Raskolnikov opened his eyes, started, and recognized Nastasya.
"Is this from the landlady?" he asked, slowly sitting up on the sofa with a sickly expression.
"From the landlady -- sure!"
She set her own cracked teapot in front of him, full of weak, stale tea, and placed two yellowish lumps of sugar beside it.

"Here, Nastasya, take this," he said, fumbling in his pocket -- he had slept in his clothes -- and pulling out a handful of coppers. "Go buy me a loaf of bread. And get me a little sausage from the butcher's -- the cheapest one."
"I'll get you the bread right now. But wouldn't you rather have some cabbage soup instead of sausage? Good soup, from yesterday. I saved it for you, but you came home late. It's perfectly fine."
When the soup arrived and he began eating, Nastasya sat down beside him on the sofa and started chatting. She was a country girl and very talkative.
"Praskovya Pavlovna is planning to report you to the police," she said.
He scowled.
"The police? What for?"
"You don't pay her and you won't move out. That's what she wants, obviously."
"Damn it, that's all I need," he muttered through clenched teeth. "No, that won't do... not right now. She's a fool," he added aloud. "I'll go talk to her today."

"She's a fool, no doubt about it, just like me. But if you're so clever, why are you just lying around with nothing to show for it? You used to go out and teach children, you said. So why aren't you doing anything now?"
"I am doing something..." Raskolnikov began sullenly and reluctantly.
"What are you doing?"
"Work..."
"What kind of work?"
"I'm thinking," he answered seriously, after a pause.
Nastasya doubled over with laughter. She was the type who laughed silently, her whole body quivering and shaking until she felt sick.
"And how much money have you made from your thinking?" she finally managed to say.
"You can't give lessons without boots. And I'm sick of it anyway."
"Don't bite the hand that feeds you."
"They pay so little for lessons. What good are a few kopecks?" he replied reluctantly, as if answering his own thoughts.
"And you want a fortune handed to you all at once?"
He looked at her strangely.
"Yes, I want a fortune," he said firmly after a brief pause.
"Easy now -- you're scaring me! Should I get you the bread or not?"
"Whatever you like."
"Oh, I forgot! A letter came for you yesterday while you were out."
"A letter? For me? From whom?"
"I don't know. I paid the postman three kopecks of my own money for it. Will you pay me back?"
"Then bring it, for God's sake, bring it!" Raskolnikov cried, suddenly agitated. "Good God!"

A minute later the letter was in his hands. It was from his mother, from the province of R-----. He went pale as he took it. It had been a long time since he'd received any letter, but something else also stabbed at his heart.
"Nastasya, please leave me alone. Here are your three kopecks. Just go, please!"

The letter trembled in his hand. He didn't want to open it with her there -- he needed to be _alone_ with it. When Nastasya had gone, he raised the letter quickly to his lips and kissed it. Then he stared at the address, at the small, slanting handwriting, so dear and familiar, of the mother who had once taught him to read and write. He hesitated, almost afraid. Finally he opened it. It was thick and heavy, over two ounces -- two large sheets of notepaper covered with very small writing.

"My dear Rodya," his mother wrote. "It's been two months since I last wrote to you, and that has caused me pain and even kept me awake at night. But I'm sure you won't blame me for the silence -- it couldn't be helped. You know how much I love you. You are everything to Dunya and me -- our only hope, our only anchor. What grief it was for me to learn that you had left the university some months ago because you couldn't support yourself, and that you had lost your tutoring work and other income! How could I help you on my hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension? The fifteen rubles I sent you four months ago were borrowed, as you know, against my pension from Vasily Ivanovich Vakhrushin, a merchant here in town. He's a kindhearted man and was a friend of your father's. But having given him the right to collect my pension, I had to wait until the debt was repaid, which has only just happened. That's why I haven't been able to send you anything. But now, thank God, I believe I can send you more, and in fact we have reason to congratulate ourselves on a piece of good fortune, which I hasten to tell you about. First -- would you believe it, dear Rodya -- your sister has been living with me these last six weeks, and we won't be separated again. Thank God, her suffering is over. But let me tell you everything in order, so you know exactly what happened and everything we've been hiding from you. When you wrote two months ago that you'd heard Dunya was having a hard time at the Svidrigailovs', and asked me for details -- what could I have written? If I'd told you the whole truth, you would have dropped everything and come to us, even on foot -- I know your character and your feelings, and you would never stand for your sister being mistreated. I was desperate myself, but what could I do? Besides, I didn't know the full truth then. The biggest problem was that Dunya had received a hundred rubles in advance when she took the governess position, on condition that it would be deducted from her monthly salary. So she couldn't leave without repaying the debt. That sum -- now I can explain everything, my precious Rodya -- she had taken mainly to send you the sixty rubles you so desperately needed, which you received from us last year. We lied to you then, saying the money came from Dunya's savings, but it wasn't so. Now I'm telling you the truth because, thank God, things have changed for the better, and so you can see how much Dunya loves you and what kind of heart she has. At first, indeed, Mr. Svidrigailov treated her very rudely, making disrespectful and mocking remarks at the table.... But I don't want to go into all those painful details, since it's all over now. In short, despite the kind and generous behavior of Marfa Petrovna -- Mr. Svidrigailov's wife -- and the rest of the household, Dunya had a very hard time, especially when Mr. Svidrigailov, reverting to his old regimental habits, had been drinking. And how do you think it all turned out? Would you believe that this ridiculous man had been in love with Dunya from the very beginning but had hidden it behind rudeness and contempt? Perhaps he was ashamed of his own hopeless desires, horrified by himself, considering his age and the fact that he was a family man -- and that made him angry at Dunya. Or perhaps he hoped that his rude, sneering behavior would hide the truth from everyone else. But in the end he lost all self-control and had the audacity to make Dunya an open and shameless proposal, promising her all kinds of things, offering to abandon everything and take her to another estate or even abroad. You can imagine what she went through! She couldn't leave at once, not only because of the debt but also to spare Marfa Petrovna's feelings, since suspicions would have been aroused and Dunya would have been blamed for causing a family rift. It would have meant a terrible scandal for Dunya, too -- that was unavoidable. There were other reasons as well that made it impossible for Dunya to escape that awful house for another six weeks. You know Dunya -- you know how smart she is, how strong her will is. She can endure a great deal and even in the most desperate circumstances manages to stay resolute. She didn't even write to me about everything, for fear of upsetting me, though we wrote to each other constantly. It all ended very unexpectedly. Marfa Petrovna accidentally overheard her husband begging Dunya in the garden, and, putting entirely the wrong interpretation on the scene, blamed Dunya for everything. A terrible scene broke out between them right there in the garden. Marfa Petrovna went so far as to hit Dunya, refused to listen to a word, and screamed at her for a solid hour. Then she ordered Dunya packed off to me immediately in a peasant cart, into which they threw all her belongings -- clothes, linens, everything -- in a heap, without folding or packing any of it. And then a heavy rainstorm broke out, and Dunya, humiliated and shamed, had to ride with a peasant in an open cart for all seventeen versts into town. Now imagine what I could have written to you two months ago in response to your letter. I was in despair. I didn't dare write you the truth because you would have been miserable, outraged, and furious -- and what could you have done? You could only have ruined yourself, and Dunya wouldn't have allowed it. Yet how could I fill my letter with trivialities when my heart was so full of grief? For a whole month the town was buzzing with this scandal, and it reached the point where Dunya and I didn't dare go to church because of the contemptuous looks, the whispers, and even the remarks said aloud about us. All our acquaintances avoided us, no one would even greet us in the street, and I heard that some shop clerks were planning to humiliate us by smearing our gates with tar, so that the landlord started telling us we'd have to move. All of this was Marfa Petrovna's doing -- she managed to slander Dunya and drag her name through the mud in every household. She knows everyone in the area, and that whole month she kept coming into town. Being rather talkative and fond of airing her family grievances -- which isn't right -- she spread her version of events not just through the town but across the entire district. It made me ill, but Dunya bore it better than I did. If you could have seen how she endured it all, comforting and cheering me! She's an angel! But by God's mercy, our suffering was cut short. Mr. Svidrigailov came to his senses, repented, and -- probably feeling sorry for Dunya -- presented Marfa Petrovna with complete and undeniable proof of Dunya's innocence in the form of a letter Dunya had been forced to write to him before Marfa Petrovna caught them in the garden. In this letter, which Mr. Svidrigailov had kept after Dunya left, she firmly refused all private meetings and personal explanations he had been begging for, and she reproached him with great passion for the vileness of his behavior toward Marfa Petrovna, reminding him that he was a father and head of a family, and telling him how despicable it was to torment a defenseless girl who was already unhappy enough. The letter, dear Rodya, was written so nobly and movingly that I wept as I read it and cannot read it to this day without tears. Furthermore, the testimony of the servants also cleared Dunya's name -- they had seen and known far more than Mr. Svidrigailov had supposed, as is always the case with servants. Marfa Petrovna was completely stunned, 'crushed again,' as she told us herself. But she was entirely convinced of Dunya's innocence. The very next day, a Sunday, she went straight to the cathedral, knelt down, and prayed with tears for the strength to bear this new trial and to do her duty. Then she came directly from the cathedral to us, told us the whole story, wept bitterly, and in full repentance embraced Dunya and begged her forgiveness. That same morning, without any delay, she went around to every house in town, and everywhere, shedding tears, she declared in the most flattering terms Dunya's innocence and the nobility of her feelings and conduct. She even showed and read aloud to everyone the letter Dunya had written to Mr. Svidrigailov, and allowed people to make copies of it -- which I must say strikes me as excessive. She spent several days this way, driving around the whole town, because some people had taken offense at not being visited first, so everyone had to take turns. In every house she was expected before she arrived, and people gathered for each reading, even those who had already heard it multiple times in their own homes and others'. A great deal of this was unnecessary, in my opinion, but that is Marfa Petrovna's character. In any case, she succeeded in completely restoring Dunya's reputation, and all the shame of the affair fell squarely on her husband as the sole guilty party -- so much so that I actually began to feel sorry for him. The poor madman was treated rather harshly. Dunya was immediately asked to give lessons in several families but refused. All at once, everyone started treating her with marked respect. All of this helped bring about the event that has, one might say, transformed our entire fortunes. You must know, dear Rodya, that Dunya has a suitor and has already agreed to marry him. I'm hurrying to tell you everything about it, and though it was arranged without your consent, I don't think you'll hold it against me or your sister -- you'll see that we couldn't wait to hear from you first. And you couldn't have judged the situation properly without being here. This is how it happened. He already holds the rank of counselor -- Pyotr Petrovich Luzhin -- and is a distant relative of Marfa Petrovna, who played an active role in arranging the match. It began with him expressing through her a desire to meet us. He was properly received, had coffee with us, and the very next day sent us a letter in which he very courteously proposed and asked for a prompt answer. He is a very busy man and in a great hurry to get to Petersburg, so every moment matters to him. Of course we were surprised at first -- it had all happened so fast and unexpectedly. We spent the whole day thinking and talking it over. He's a man of means, reliable, with two government positions and an established fortune. It's true he's forty-five, but he's fairly presentable in appearance and might still be considered attractive to women -- altogether a very respectable and proper man, though perhaps a bit gloomy and somewhat conceited. But that may just be the first impression. And please, dear Rodya, when he arrives in Petersburg shortly, don't judge him too hastily or harshly, as you tend to do, if something about him doesn't appeal to you right away. I say this even though I'm sure he'll make a good impression on you. Besides, to truly understand any person, you must be patient and careful, and avoid forming hasty opinions that are hard to correct later. From many signs, Pyotr Petrovich seems to be a thoroughly estimable man. At his first visit he told us he was a practical man but still shared, as he put it, many of the convictions of 'our most progressive generation' and opposed all prejudices. He said a good deal more -- he seems a bit conceited and likes an audience -- but this is hardly a serious fault. I understood very little of it, of course, but Dunya explained to me that though he isn't a highly educated man, he's intelligent and seems good-natured. You know your sister's character, Rodya. She's resolute, sensible, patient, and generous -- but she also has a passionate heart, as I know well. Of course there's no great love on either side, but Dunya is a smart girl with the heart of an angel, and she will make it her duty to make her husband happy, while he in turn will make her happiness his concern. We have no good reason to doubt that, though it must be admitted the whole thing was arranged rather quickly. He's also a very prudent man, and he'll surely see that his own happiness depends on making Dunya happy. As for certain shortcomings of character, certain habits, and even some differences of opinion -- inevitable in even the happiest marriages -- Dunya says she's confident in herself and sees nothing to worry about, that she can put up with a great deal so long as the relationship is honorable and straightforward. He did strike me at first as somewhat brusque, but that may simply be because he's a blunt man -- and that's probably all it is. For instance, on his second visit, after receiving Dunya's acceptance, he mentioned in conversation that even before meeting Dunya, he had decided to marry a respectable girl without a dowry, and ideally one who had experienced poverty, because, as he explained, a wife should not consider herself her husband's equal but should view him as her benefactor. I should add that he expressed it more politely than I've put it here -- I've forgotten his exact words and only remember the gist. And besides, it clearly wasn't said deliberately but slipped out in the heat of conversation, and he tried to walk it back afterward. Still, it struck me as somewhat rude, and I told Dunya so. But Dunya was annoyed and replied that 'words are not deeds,' which is of course perfectly true. Dunya didn't sleep at all the night before she decided. Thinking I was asleep, she got out of bed and paced the room all night. Finally she knelt before the icon and prayed long and fervently. In the morning she told me she had made up her mind.

"I mentioned already that Pyotr Petrovich is about to leave for Petersburg, where he has a great deal of business and wants to open a law office. He has spent many years handling civil and commercial cases, and just recently won an important one. He needs to be in Petersburg because he has a major case before the Senate. So, dear Rodya, he could be enormously useful to you, in every way, and Dunya and I have agreed that starting right now you could consider your career launched and your future settled. Oh, if only this comes true! It would be such a blessing that we could only see it as Providence. Dunya dreams of nothing else. We've even ventured to mention the subject to Pyotr Petrovich. He answered cautiously, saying that since he needs a secretary, it would be better to pay a salary to a relative than a stranger -- provided the person was qualified (as if there could be any doubt about you!) -- but he wondered whether your university studies would leave you time for office work. The matter was dropped for the moment, but Dunya can think of nothing else. She's been in a kind of fever these past few days and has already drawn up a whole plan for you to eventually become an associate and even a partner in Pyotr Petrovich's practice, which seems perfectly feasible since you're a law student. I completely agree with her, Rodya, and share all her plans and hopes. I think there's every chance of them coming true. Despite Pyotr Petrovich's understandable caution -- he doesn't know you yet -- Dunya is firmly convinced she can achieve everything through her good influence on her future husband. That's what she's counting on. Of course we're careful not to mention these longer-range plans to Pyotr Petrovich, especially the idea of making you his partner. He's a practical man and might dismiss it as pure fantasy. Neither Dunya nor I have said a word about our hope that he'll help with your university expenses -- partly because it will happen naturally in time, and he'll no doubt offer it himself without being asked (how could he refuse Dunya?), especially since you could become his right hand at the office and receive the help not as charity but as an earned salary. Dunya wants to arrange it just this way, and I fully agree. We also haven't raised it for another reason: I particularly wanted you to meet him on equal footing. When Dunya spoke enthusiastically about you, he said you can never judge a person without meeting them in person, and that he looks forward to forming his own opinion when he meets you. You know, my dear Rodya, I think perhaps for certain reasons -- nothing to do with Pyotr Petrovich, just my own personal, perhaps old-womanish ideas -- it might be better for me to go on living by myself rather than with them after the wedding. I'm sure he'll be generous and considerate enough to invite me to stay with my daughter, and if he hasn't mentioned it yet, it's simply been taken for granted. But I'll refuse. I've noticed more than once in life that husbands and mothers-in-law don't always get along smoothly, and I don't want to be even the slightest burden to anyone. For my own sake, too, I'd rather remain independent, as long as I have a crust of bread and children like you and Dunya. If possible, I'd settle somewhere near you. And now for the best news, dear Rodya, which I've saved for last: we may all be together very soon and may embrace each other after a separation of nearly three years! It is _definite_ that Dunya and I are coming to Petersburg -- exactly when I'm not sure, but very soon, possibly within a week. It all depends on Pyotr Petrovich, who will let us know once he's had a chance to get settled in Petersburg. To suit his arrangements, he wants the ceremony to take place as soon as possible, even before the Feast of Our Lady if it can be managed, or if that's too soon, then immediately after. Oh, how happy I'll be to hold you in my arms! Dunya is wild with excitement at the thought of seeing you -- she said in jest the other day that she'd marry Pyotr Petrovich for that alone. She's an angel! She's not writing to you now -- she told me to say that she has so much to tell you that she won't even try to put pen to paper yet, since a few lines would say nothing and would only upset her. She sends you her love and countless kisses. And even though we'll be seeing each other so soon, I'll try to send you some money in the next day or two. Now that everyone knows Dunya is marrying Pyotr Petrovich, my credit has improved, and I'm sure Afanasy Ivanovich will lend me up to seventy-five rubles against my pension, so I may be able to send you twenty-five or even thirty. I'd send more, but I'm worried about our travel costs. Though Pyotr Petrovich has kindly taken on part of the expense -- he's arranged for our bags and large trunk to be shipped through some acquaintances -- we'll still need money when we arrive in Petersburg, where we can't turn up without a kopeck, at least for the first few days. Dunya and I have calculated everything down to the last penny, and the trip won't cost very much. It's only ninety versts to the railway, and we've arranged with a driver we know to be ready. From there, Dunya and I can travel quite comfortably in third class. So I may well be able to send you not twenty-five but thirty rubles. But enough -- I've already filled two sheets and there's no room left. Our whole story -- but so many events have happened! And now, my precious Rodya, I embrace you and send you a mother's blessing until we meet. Love Dunya, your sister, Rodya -- love her as she loves you, and know that she loves you beyond everything, more than herself. She is an angel, and you, Rodya, are everything to us -- our only hope, our only comfort. If only you are happy, we will be happy. Do you still pray, Rodya? Do you still believe in the mercy of our Creator and Redeemer? I'm afraid in my heart that the new spirit of unbelief so widespread today may have touched you. If so, I pray for you. Remember, dear boy, how in your childhood, when your father was alive, you used to lisp your prayers at my knee, and how happy we all were then. Goodbye until we meet. I embrace you warmly, warmly, with so many kisses.
"Yours until death,
"PULCHERIA RASKOLNIKOV."

Almost from the very first line, Raskolnikov's face was wet with tears. But when he finished reading, his face was pale and contorted, and a bitter, angry, malicious smile played on his lips.
