He laid his head on his threadbare, dirty pillow and thought for a long time. His heart was pounding and his mind was in turmoil. Finally the cramped little yellow room -- no bigger than a cupboard, a coffin -- became unbearable. His eyes and his mind craved open space. He grabbed his hat and went out, this time without the fear of running into anyone -- he had forgotten that fear entirely. He headed toward Vasilyevsky Island, walking along Vasilyevsky Prospect as though he had some urgent business. But as usual, he didn't notice where he was going, muttering and even talking aloud to himself, startling passersby. Many of them assumed he was drunk.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 4
paragraphs: His mother's letter had tortured him, but on the central issue he had not hesitated for a single moment, even while reading it. The question was settled, irrevocably settled in his mind: "This marriage will never happen while I'm alive, and Mr. Luzhin can go to hell!" "The whole thing is perfectly clear," he muttered to himself with a vicious smile, savoring his resolve. "No, Mother, no, Dunya -- you won't fool me! And they apologize for not asking my advice, for deciding without me! They think it's all arranged and can't be undone -- we'll see about that! A wonderful excuse: 'Pyotr Petrovich is such a busy man that even his wedding has to be rushed, practically by express mail.' No, Dunya, I see through it all. I know what you want to say to me. I know what you were thinking about when you paced all night, and what your prayers were like before the Holy Mother of Kazan in mother's bedroom. The road to Golgotha is bitter.... Hmm... so it's settled then: you've decided to marry a sensible businessman, Avdotya Romanovna, one who has a fortune (_already_ made his fortune -- so much more solid and impressive), a man with two government posts who shares the views of our most progressive generation, as mother writes, and who _seems_ to be kind, as Dunya herself notes. That _seems_ is everything! And that very Dunya is marrying him for that very '_seems_'! Splendid! Splendid!

"...But why did mother write to me about 'our most progressive generation'? Just as a descriptive detail, or to soften me up toward Mr. Luzhin? Oh, how clever of them! And I'd like to know something else: how open were they with each other that day and night and all this time? Was it all spoken aloud, or did they both understand they were thinking the same thing and there was no need to say it, better not to? Probably something like that. From mother's letter it's obvious: he struck her as somewhat rude, and mother in her simplicity shared her observation with Dunya. And of course Dunya was irritated and 'answered angrily.' Naturally! Who wouldn't be, when the point was perfectly clear without any naive questions, and discussing it was useless? And why does she write 'love Dunya, Rodya -- she loves you more than herself'? Is she secretly pricked by guilt over sacrificing her daughter for her son? 'You are everything to us, our only comfort, our only hope.' Oh, Mother!"
His bitterness grew stronger with every moment. If he had happened to meet Mr. Luzhin just then, he might have killed him.

"Hmm... yes, that's true," he went on, chasing one feverish thought after another. "It's true that 'it takes time and care to know a person,' but there's no mystery about Mr. Luzhin. The main thing is he's 'a practical man and _seems_ kind' -- what a feat, arranging shipment of their bags and trunk! A kind man, obviously! But his _bride_ and her mother are supposed to ride in a peasant cart with a tarp over it. I know those carts -- I've ridden in one. Never mind! It's only ninety versts, and then they can 'travel quite comfortably in third class' for a thousand versts! Quite right. You have to live within your means. But what about you, Mr. Luzhin? She's your bride.... And you must realize that her mother has to borrow against her pension just to make the trip. Sure, it's a business arrangement -- a partnership with equal shares and shared expenses; meals included, but bring your own tobacco. The businessman has gotten the better of them here, too. The luggage will cost less than their fares and probably ship for free. How do neither of them see this? Or do they just not want to? And they're pleased, pleased! And to think this is just the beginning -- the real fruits are yet to come! But what really matters isn't the cheapness, isn't the stinginess -- it's the _tone_ of the whole thing. Because this will be the tone after the marriage. It's a preview. And Mother -- why should she spend so freely? What will she have left by the time she reaches Petersburg? Three silver rubles or two 'paper ones,' as _she_ says... that old woman... hmm. What does she plan to live on in Petersburg afterward? She already has reason to suspect she _won't_ be able to live with Dunya after the wedding, not even for the first few months. The good man has no doubt dropped a hint about that too, though mother would deny it: 'I shall refuse,' she says. So who is she counting on? On what's left of her hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension after Afanasy Ivanovich's debt is paid? She knits woolen shawls and embroiders cuffs, ruining her old eyes. And all her shawls add at most twenty rubles a year to her hundred and twenty -- I know that. So she's pinning all her hopes on Mr. Luzhin's generosity: 'He'll offer it himself, he'll insist.' You may wait a long time for that! That's how it always is with these Schilleresque noble souls: up to the very last moment every goose is a swan, up to the last moment they hope for the best and refuse to see anything wrong. And though they have an inkling of the truth, they won't face it until it's forced on them. The very thought makes them shudder. They push the truth away with both hands until the man they've dressed up in borrowed colors puts a fool's cap on them personally. I wonder if Mr. Luzhin has any medals. I bet he has the Order of St. Anna in his buttonhole and wears it to dinners with merchants and contractors. He'll certainly wear it at his wedding! To hell with him, enough.

"Well... Mother I can understand -- God bless her, that's how she is. But Dunya? Dunya, darling, as if I don't know you! You were almost twenty when I last saw you, and I understood you even then. Mother writes that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' I know that very well. I've known it for two and a half years, and for two and a half years I've been thinking about exactly that -- that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' If she could put up with Mr. Svidrigailov and everything else, she can certainly put up with a great deal. And now mother and she have decided she can also put up with Mr. Luzhin, who expounds his theory that wives rescued from destitution should be forever grateful to their husbands -- and expounds it practically on the first meeting. Granted, he 'let it slip,' though he's supposed to be a sensible man (or maybe it wasn't a slip at all -- maybe he wanted to make his position clear from the start). But Dunya -- Dunya? She sees through the man, of course, but she'll have to live with him. She'd live on black bread and water before she'd sell her soul. She wouldn't trade her moral freedom for comfort. She wouldn't trade it for all of Schleswig-Holstein, let alone Mr. Luzhin's money. No, Dunya was never that sort when I knew her, and... she's still the same, of course! Yes, there's no denying the Svidrigailovs are hard to swallow. Spending your life as a governess in the provinces for two hundred rubles a year is bitter. But I know she'd rather be a slave on a plantation or a serf under a German master than degrade her soul and her moral dignity by binding herself forever to a man she doesn't respect and has nothing in common with -- all for her own advantage. Even if Mr. Luzhin were made of pure gold or were one enormous diamond, she would never have agreed to become his legal concubine. So why is she agreeing? What's the point? What's the answer? It's obvious: for herself, for her own comfort, to save her own life -- she would never sell herself. But for someone else, she'll do it! For someone she loves, someone she adores, she'll sell herself! That's what it comes down to. For her brother, for her mother, she'll sell herself! She'll sell everything! In situations like this, 'we overcome our moral feelings when necessary' -- freedom, peace, conscience, everything gets brought to market. Let my life be ruined, as long as my loved ones are happy! More than that, we become rationalizers, we learn to be Jesuitical, and for a while we can even soothe ourselves, convince ourselves it's our duty for a good cause. That's exactly what's happening here, clear as day. Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov is obviously the central figure in this whole business. Oh yes, she can secure his happiness, keep him at the university, make him a partner in the firm, guarantee his entire future. Maybe he'll even become a rich man someday -- prosperous, respected, perhaps even end his life as a famous man! But what about Mother? It's all about Rodya, precious Rodya, her firstborn! For such a son, who wouldn't sacrifice such a daughter! Oh, loving, biased hearts! Why stop there? For his sake we wouldn't even shrink from Sonya's fate -- Sonya, Sonya Marmeladov, the eternal victim, as long as the world exists. Have you both measured your sacrifice? Really measured it? Is it right? Can you bear it? Is it worth it? Is there any sense in it? Let me tell you, Dunya: Sonya's life is no worse than life with Mr. Luzhin. 'There can be no question of love,' mother writes. But what if there's no question of respect either? What if instead there's only revulsion, contempt, disgust -- what then? So you'll have to 'keep up appearances' too. Do you understand what that means? Do you understand that the Luzhin kind of smartness is exactly the same as Sonya's -- maybe worse, more vile, more degrading -- because in your case, Dunya, it's a bargain for luxuries, while for Sonya it's literally a matter of starvation? It has to be paid for, Dunya, this kind of smartness. And what if later it proves more than you can bear, and you regret it? The bitterness, the misery, the curses, the tears hidden from the whole world -- because you're not Marfa Petrovna! And how will Mother feel then? Even now she's uneasy, worried -- but when she sees it all clearly? And me? What exactly do you take me for? I won't accept your sacrifice, Dunya! I won't accept it, Mother! It will not happen as long as I'm alive! It will not! I refuse!"
He suddenly stopped and stood still.

"It will not happen? But what are you going to do to stop it? Forbid it? And what right do you have? What can you promise them in return that would give you such a right? To devote your whole life to them _after you finish your studies and get a position_? Sure, we've heard that before -- those are just _words_. But what about now? Now something has to be done, right now -- do you understand? And what are you doing now? You're living off them. They borrow against their hundred-ruble pension. They borrow from the Svidrigailovs. How are you going to save them from the Svidrigailovs, from Afanasy Ivanovich Vakhrushin, you future millionaire Zeus who would arrange their lives? In another ten years? In ten years, mother will be blind from knitting shawls -- maybe from crying, too. She'll be worn to a shadow from going hungry. And my sister? Just imagine what might have become of your sister in ten years. What could happen to her in those ten years? Can you picture it?"

He tormented himself with these questions and even found a kind of perverse pleasure in it. None of these questions were new or sudden -- they were old, familiar wounds. It had been a long time since they first started to grip and tear at his heart. Long ago his current anguish had begun. It had grown and gathered strength, ripened and concentrated, until it took the shape of a terrifying, frenzied, fantastic question that gnawed at his heart and mind, demanding an answer. Now his mother's letter had struck like a thunderbolt. It was clear that he could no longer sit passively agonizing over unanswered questions. He had to do something -- do it now, do it fast. He had to make a decision, or else...
"Or give up on life altogether!" he cried suddenly, in a frenzy. "Accept your fate meekly, once and for all, and suffocate everything inside you, giving up every claim to action, to life, to love!"

"Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means when you have absolutely nowhere to turn?" Marmeladov's question suddenly surfaced in his mind. "For every man must have somewhere to turn...."

He started. Another thought -- one he'd had yesterday -- slipped back into his mind. But he didn't start because the thought was returning. He had known, had _felt in advance_, that it would come back. He'd been waiting for it. Besides, it was not just yesterday's thought. The difference was that a month ago, even yesterday, it had been a mere dream. But now... now it appeared as something other than a dream entirely -- it had taken on a new, menacing, completely unfamiliar form, and he suddenly became aware of this.... His head was pounding, and a darkness fell before his eyes.

He looked around urgently, searching for something. He needed to sit down and was looking for a bench. He was walking along K----- Boulevard. There was a bench about a hundred paces ahead. He walked toward it as fast as he could, but on the way he ran into a small incident that absorbed all his attention. While searching for the bench, he had noticed a woman walking about twenty paces ahead, but at first he paid her no more attention than anything else that crossed his path. He had often gone home without noticing his route and was used to walking that way. But there was something so immediately strange about this woman that gradually his attention was drawn to her -- at first reluctantly, almost resentfully, and then more and more intently. He suddenly wanted to understand what was so strange about her. To begin with, she appeared to be very young, and she was walking in the blazing heat bareheaded, without a parasol or gloves, waving her arms in an absurd way. She wore a dress of some thin silky material, but it was put on crookedly, barely fastened, torn open near the waist with a large piece hanging loose. A small scarf was draped around her bare throat but sat crooked, slipping to one side. The girl was also walking unsteadily, stumbling and staggering. She finally captured Raskolnikov's full attention. He caught up with her at the bench, and when she reached it, she collapsed onto it in the corner, let her head fall back, and closed her eyes, apparently in total exhaustion. Looking at her closely, he saw at once that she was completely drunk. It was a strange and disturbing sight. He could barely believe he wasn't mistaken. Before him was the face of a very young girl -- fair-haired, sixteen at most, possibly only fifteen -- a pretty little face, but flushed, heavy-looking, almost swollen. The girl seemed barely aware of what she was doing. She crossed one leg over the other in an indecent way, showing every sign of being oblivious to the fact that she was on a public street.

Raskolnikov didn't sit down, but he couldn't bring himself to leave her, and stood there facing her in confusion. This boulevard was never very busy, and now at two in the afternoon, in the crushing heat, it was completely deserted. Yet on the far side of the boulevard, about fifteen paces away, a gentleman stood at the edge of the sidewalk. He, too, clearly wanted to approach the girl for his own purposes. He, too, had probably noticed her from a distance and followed her, only to find Raskolnikov in his way. He glared at Raskolnikov, though he tried not to be noticed, and waited impatiently for the unwelcome stranger in rags to move on. His intentions were obvious. The gentleman was a plump, stocky man of about thirty, fashionably dressed, with a ruddy complexion, red lips, and a mustache. Raskolnikov was seized with fury -- a sudden urge to insult this fat dandy somehow. He left the girl for a moment and walked toward the man.
"Hey! You, Svidrigailov! What do you want here?" he shouted, clenching his fists and laughing, sputtering with rage.
"What do you mean?" the man asked sternly, scowling with haughty surprise.
"Get away from here. That's what I mean."
"How dare you, you filthy tramp!"

He raised his cane. Raskolnikov lunged at him with his fists, without stopping to consider that this heavyset gentleman was easily a match for two men his size. But at that instant someone grabbed him from behind, and a policeman stepped between them.
"Enough, gentlemen. No fighting in a public place, please. Who are you? What do you want?" he asked Raskolnikov sternly, taking note of his rags.
Raskolnikov studied him closely. He had an honest, sensible, military face with gray mustache and sideburns.

"You're exactly who I need," Raskolnikov cried, grabbing his arm. "I'm a student -- Raskolnikov.... You may as well know that too," he added, turning to the gentleman. "Come with me, I have something to show you."
Taking the policeman by the hand, he led him toward the bench.

"Look -- she's completely drunk. She just came down the boulevard. There's no telling who she is or where she comes from, but she doesn't look like a professional. More likely someone got her drunk and took advantage of her... for the first time... do you follow? And then they put her out on the street like this. Look at how her dress is torn, look at how it was put on. She didn't dress herself -- it was done by someone else, by clumsy hands, a man's hands. That's obvious. Now look over there: that man I was about to fight -- I don't know him, never seen him before -- but he spotted her on the road too, drunk, not knowing what she's doing, and now he's very eager to get his hands on her, to take her somewhere while she's in this state. That's certain, believe me. I saw him watching her, following her, but I got in his way, and now he's just waiting for me to leave. See, he's moved off a bit, pretending to roll a cigarette.... Think about how we can keep her away from him and get her home."

The policeman grasped the situation immediately. The fat gentleman was easy enough to figure out. He turned to examine the girl, bending down for a closer look, and his face showed genuine compassion.

"What a shame!" he said, shaking his head. "She's just a child! She's been tricked -- you can see that at a glance. Listen, miss," he said, addressing her, "where do you live?" The girl opened her weary, glazed eyes, stared blankly at him, and waved her hand.
"Here," said Raskolnikov, reaching into his pocket and finding twenty kopecks. "Take this, call a cab, and have him drive her to her address. If only we could find out where she lives!"
"Miss! Miss!" the policeman began again, taking the money. "I'll get you a cab and take you home myself. Where should I take you? Where do you live?"
"Go away! Leave me alone," the girl mumbled, waving her hand again.
"Oh dear, oh dear! What a disgrace, miss, what a shame!" He shook his head again -- shocked, sympathetic, outraged.
"This is a tricky one," the policeman said to Raskolnikov, giving him another quick once-over. He, too, must have thought Raskolnikov a strange sight -- dressed in rags and handing over money!
"Did you run into her far from here?" he asked.
"I'm telling you, she was walking ahead of me, staggering, right here on the boulevard. She barely made it to the bench before she collapsed."

"The disgraceful things that happen in this world, God have mercy! An innocent creature like this, already drunk! She's been tricked, no doubt about it. Look at how her dress is torn.... The depravity you see nowadays! And she probably comes from a decent family too, maybe poor.... There are plenty like that these days. She looks refined, almost like a lady." And he bent over her again.
Perhaps he had daughters of his own growing up like that -- "looking like ladies, refined," with pretensions to respectability and elegance....
"The main thing," Raskolnikov insisted, "is to keep her out of that scoundrel's hands! Why should she be violated? It's perfectly clear what he wants. Look at the brute -- he's not leaving!"

Raskolnikov spoke loudly and pointed at him. The man heard and seemed about to lose his temper again, but thought better of it and contented himself with a contemptuous look. Then he walked slowly another ten paces away and stopped again.
"We can keep her from him," the policeman said thoughtfully, "if only she'd tell us where to take her. Miss! Hey, miss!" He bent over her once more.

She suddenly opened her eyes wide, looked at him with something like comprehension, got up from the bench, and started walking back the way she had come. "Disgusting people -- they won't leave me alone!" she said, waving her hand again. She walked quickly, though still staggering. The dandy followed her along a different path, keeping his eyes on her.
"Don't worry, I won't let him get to her," the policeman said firmly, and set off after them.
"The depravity you see nowadays!" he repeated aloud with a sigh.
At that moment something seemed to sting Raskolnikov. In an instant, his feelings reversed completely.
"Hey! Wait!" he shouted after the policeman.
The officer turned around.
"Forget it! What's it to you? Let her go! Let him have his fun." He pointed at the dandy. "What business is it of yours?"
The policeman stared at him, bewildered. Raskolnikov laughed.
"Well!" the policeman said with a contemptuous wave, and walked off after the dandy and the girl, probably thinking Raskolnikov was a madman or something worse.

"He took my twenty kopecks," Raskolnikov muttered angrily once he was alone. "Well, let him squeeze some money out of the other one too, for letting him have the girl, and be done with it. Why did I have to interfere? Is it my place to help? Do I have any right to help? Let them eat each other alive -- what's it to me? And how dare I give away twenty kopecks? Were they even mine?"

Despite those strange words, he felt deeply miserable. He sat down on the empty bench. His thoughts drifted aimlessly.... He couldn't fix his mind on anything. He wanted to forget himself entirely, forget everything, and then wake up and start life over....

"Poor girl!" he said, looking at the empty corner where she had sat. "She'll come to her senses and cry, and then her mother will find out.... She'll beat her -- a horrible, shameful beating -- and maybe throw her out. And even if she doesn't, the Darya Frantsovnas will catch wind of it, and the girl will soon be slipping out on the sly here and there. Then the hospital will follow (that's always the fate of those girls from decent families who go wrong on the sly), and then... the hospital again... vodka... taverns... more hospital. In two or three years -- a wreck, dead at eighteen or nineteen.... Haven't I seen cases like that? Every single one of them ended up that way. Ugh! But so what? That's how it should be, they tell us. A certain percentage, they say, has to go that way every year... to the devil, presumably, so the rest can stay pure and unbothered. A percentage! What wonderful words they have -- so scientific, so reassuring.... Once you've said 'percentage,' there's nothing more to worry about. If we used a different word... maybe we'd feel more uneasy.... But what if Dunya ends up as one of the percentage? Part of one, if not another?

"But where am I going?" he thought suddenly. "Strange. I came out for a reason. As soon as I read the letter I rushed out.... I was heading to Vasilyevsky Island, to Razumikhin's. That's right... now I remember. But why? What put the idea of going to Razumikhin into my head just now? That's odd."

He marveled at himself. Razumikhin was one of his old university friends. The remarkable thing was that Raskolnikov had virtually no friends at the university. He kept to himself, saw no one, and didn't welcome visitors -- and soon everyone stopped trying. He took no part in student gatherings, discussions, or amusements. He studied with fierce intensity, sparing himself nothing, and was respected for it, but nobody liked him. He was very poor, and there was something haughty and secretive about him, as though he were hiding something. Some of his classmates felt he looked down on them all like children, as if he were superior in intellect, knowledge, and convictions, as if their interests and beliefs were beneath him.

With Razumikhin, though, he had gotten along -- or at least he was more open and communicative with him than with anyone else. It was impossible not to get along with Razumikhin. He was an exceptionally good-natured and straightforward young man, kindhearted to the point of simplicity, though both depth and dignity lay hidden beneath that simplicity. His better friends understood this, and everyone was fond of him. He was very intelligent, though he could be quite naive at times. He was striking to look at -- tall, thin, black-haired, and always badly shaved. He could be boisterous, and he was reputed to have enormous physical strength. One night, while out celebrating, he had floored a gigantic policeman with a single punch. His capacity for drinking was limitless, but he could also abstain completely. He sometimes went too far with his pranks but was equally capable of doing without them. Another remarkable thing about Razumikhin: no setback discouraged him, and no hardship seemed able to crush him. He could live anywhere and endure extreme cold and hunger. He was very poor, supporting himself entirely by whatever odd jobs he could find. He had endless ways of earning money. He once went an entire winter without heating his room, and claimed he preferred it because you sleep better in the cold. For now, he too had been forced to leave the university, but only temporarily -- he was working with all his might to save enough to go back. Raskolnikov hadn't seen him in four months, and Razumikhin didn't even know his address. About two months ago they had passed each other on the street, but Raskolnikov had turned away and even crossed to the other side to avoid being noticed. Razumikhin had seen him but walked on by, not wanting to bother him.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Of course, I've been meaning to go see Razumikhin, to ask him about work, to get him to find me some tutoring or something..." Raskolnikov thought. "But what can he do for me now? Say he finds me lessons, say he shares his last kopeck with me -- if he has one -- so I can buy boots and make myself presentable enough to give lessons... hmm... and then what? What am I going to do with a few kopecks? That's not what I need now. It's really absurd to be going to Razumikhin...."
The question of why he was heading to Razumikhin's now troubled him more than he realized. He kept searching uneasily for some hidden meaning in this seemingly ordinary action.
"Did I really think I could fix everything, find a way out, just by going to Razumikhin?" he asked himself in confusion.
He thought hard, rubbing his forehead. Then, strangely, after a long stretch of brooding, a thought came to him -- suddenly, as if by accident, as if of its own accord.

"Hmm... to Razumikhin's," he said all at once, calmly, as though he had reached a final decision. "I'll go to Razumikhin's, of course, but... not now. I'll go to him... the day after It, when It is done and everything begins again...."
And suddenly he realized what he was thinking.

"After It!" he shouted, jumping up from the bench. "But is It really going to happen? Is it possible that it actually will?" He left the bench and broke into a near-run. He meant to turn back toward home, but the thought of going home suddenly filled him with violent revulsion. In that hole, in that awful little closet, all of _this_ had been growing inside him for the past month. He walked on aimlessly.

His nervous shuddering had turned into a fever that left him shivering. Despite the heat, he felt cold. With a kind of desperate effort, he began staring at every object he passed, almost unconsciously, driven by some inner need for distraction. But it didn't work, and he kept sinking back into dark thoughts. Whenever he would startle and look up, he immediately forgot what he'd just been thinking and where he was going. In this way he walked all the way across Vasilyevsky Island, came out onto the Lesser Neva, crossed the bridge, and turned toward the islands. At first the greenery and freshness were soothing to his exhausted eyes after the dust of the city and the massive buildings that crowded in on him and weighed him down. There were no taverns here, no suffocating closeness, no stench. But soon even these pleasant new sensations turned into a morbid irritability. Sometimes he stopped in front of a brightly painted summer villa set among green foliage. He would gaze through the fence at elegantly dressed women on verandas and balconies, at children running in the gardens. The flowers especially caught his attention -- he stared at them longer than at anything. He also passed luxurious carriages and men and women on horseback. He watched them with curious eyes but forgot about them before they were out of sight. At one point he stopped and counted his money. He had thirty kopecks. "Twenty to the policeman, three to Nastasya for the letter, so I must have given forty-seven or fifty to the Marmeladovs yesterday," he calculated, for no particular reason, but soon forgot why he had taken the money out at all. He remembered when he passed a tavern, and realized he was hungry.... He went in, drank a glass of vodka, and ate some kind of pie, finishing it as he walked. It had been a long time since he'd had vodka, and it hit him immediately, even though he'd only had one small glass. His legs suddenly grew heavy and a powerful drowsiness came over him. He headed home, but when he reached Petrovsky Island, he stopped, completely spent, turned off the road into the bushes, sank down on the grass, and fell asleep instantly.

In a fevered state, dreams often have a strange realism, a vividness and extraordinary likeness to reality. The images created can be monstrous, yet the setting and the entire picture are so lifelike, so filled with details so subtle, so unexpected yet so artistically perfect, that the dreamer himself, even if he were an artist like Pushkin or Turgenev, could never have invented them while awake. Such feverish dreams stay in the memory for a long time and make a powerful impression on an already strained and destabilized nervous system.

Raskolnikov had a terrible dream. He dreamed he was back in his childhood, in the small town where he was born. He was a boy of about seven, walking through the countryside with his father on the evening of a holiday. It was an overcast, heavy day, and the landscape was exactly as he remembered it -- in fact, he saw it far more vividly in the dream than he ever had in memory. The small town sat on a flat, open plain, bare as the palm of a hand, without even a willow tree nearby. Only in the far distance, a dark smudge of woods showed at the very edge of the horizon. A few steps beyond the last vegetable garden stood a tavern, a large tavern, which had always filled him with aversion, even fear, when he walked past it with his father. There was always a crowd there -- shouting, laughter, cursing, ugly hoarse singing, and often fighting. Drunk, terrifying-looking men hung around outside. He would press close to his father, trembling, whenever he saw them. Near the tavern, the road turned to a dusty track, and the dust was always black. The road wound on, and about a hundred paces further it curved right toward the cemetery. In the middle of the cemetery stood a stone church with a green dome where he used to go to services two or three times a year with his mother and father, for memorial masses for his grandmother, who had died long ago and whom he had never known. On those occasions they would bring a white dish wrapped in a napkin, filled with a special rice pudding with raisins pressed into it in the shape of a cross. He loved that church, with its plain, old-fashioned icons, and the old priest with the trembling head. Near his grandmother's grave, which was marked by a stone, was the tiny grave of his younger brother, who had died at six months old. He didn't remember him at all, but he had been told about his little brother, and every time he visited the cemetery he would cross himself solemnly, bow down, and kiss the small grave. Now he dreamed he was walking with his father past the tavern on the way to the cemetery, holding his father's hand and looking at the tavern with dread. Something unusual was going on. There seemed to be some kind of celebration: a crowd of townspeople in their best clothes, peasant women, their husbands, and riffraff of every sort, all singing and all more or less drunk. Near the entrance to the tavern stood a cart -- but a strange cart. It was one of those large carts usually pulled by heavy draft horses, piled high with wine barrels or other heavy loads. He had always loved watching those massive horses, with their long manes, thick legs, and slow, steady pace, pulling enormous loads with no apparent effort, as though carrying a load were easier for them than going empty. But now, strangely, a thin little sorrel nag had been harnessed to this huge cart. It was one of those peasant horses he had often seen straining desperately under heavy loads of wood or hay, especially when the wheels got stuck in the mud or in a rut. The peasants would beat them so cruelly, sometimes even across the nose and eyes, and he felt so sorry, so sorry for them that he nearly cried, and his mother always pulled him away from the window. Suddenly there was an eruption of shouting, singing, and balalaika music, and a group of large, very drunk peasants came pouring out of the tavern, wearing red and blue shirts with coats slung over their shoulders.
"Get in, everybody get in!" shouted one of them -- a young, thick-necked peasant with a fleshy face as red as a beet. "I'll take you all! Get in!"
But immediately the crowd burst into laughter and jeering.
"Take us all with a horse like that!"
"Mikolka, you're crazy! Hitching a nag like that to a cart like this?"
"That mare's twenty years old if she's a day, boys!"

"Get in! I'll take you all!" Mikolka shouted again, leaping into the cart first, grabbing the reins, and standing up straight at the front. "The bay went off with Matvey," he shouted from the cart, "and this old wreck is breaking my heart -- I feel like I could kill her. She just eats and eats and does nothing. Get in, I said! I'll make her gallop! She'll gallop!" He snatched up the whip, eagerly preparing to flog the little mare.
"Get in! Come on!" The crowd laughed. "You hear that -- she'll gallop!"
"Gallop! She hasn't galloped in ten years!"
"She'll manage a trot!"
"Never mind her, boys -- grab a whip each, get ready!"
"Right! Let her have it!"

They all scrambled into Mikolka's cart, laughing and joking. Six men piled in and there was still room. They hauled in a plump, rosy-cheeked woman dressed in red cotton, wearing a beaded pointed headdress and thick leather shoes. She was cracking nuts and laughing. The crowd around them laughed too -- and how could they not? This wretched nag was supposed to pull the whole cartload of them at a gallop! Two young fellows in the cart had already gotten their whips ready to help Mikolka. With a cry of "Now!" the mare strained with all her might, but far from galloping, she could barely move. She struggled with her legs, panting and flinching under the three whips that rained down on her like hail. The laughter in the cart and the crowd doubled, but Mikolka flew into a rage and beat the mare furiously, as though he actually believed she could gallop.
"Let me in too, boys!" yelled a young man in the crowd, excited by the spectacle.
"Get in, everybody get in!" Mikolka screamed. "She'll pull you all! I'll beat her to death!" And he lashed and lashed at the mare, beside himself with fury.
"Papa, Papa!" the boy cried. "Papa, what are they doing? Papa, they're beating the poor horse!"

"Come along, come along!" his father said. "They're drunk, they're being stupid, they're just fooling around. Come away, don't look!" He tried to pull him away, but the boy tore free from his hand and ran to the horse, beside himself with horror. The poor animal was in a bad way. She was gasping, standing still, then lurching forward again, nearly falling.
"Beat her to death!" Mikolka screamed. "That's what it's come to! I'll finish her!"
"What are you doing? Are you even a Christian, you devil?" an old man in the crowd shouted.
"Who ever heard of a wretched nag like that pulling such a load?" said another.
"You'll kill her!" shouted a third.
"Don't meddle! She's my property! I'll do as I please! Get in, more of you! Everyone get in! I'll make her gallop!..."

Suddenly the crowd roared with laughter, drowning out everything. The mare, stung by the hail of blows, had begun feebly kicking. Even the old man couldn't help smiling. A pathetic little animal like that, trying to kick!
Two boys in the crowd snatched up whips and ran to the mare to beat her ribs -- one on each side.
"Hit her in the face! In the eyes! In the eyes!" Mikolka screamed.
"Give us a song, boys!" someone shouted from the cart, and everyone in it launched into a rowdy song, jingling a tambourine and whistling. The woman went on cracking nuts and laughing.

...The boy ran alongside the mare, ran out in front of her, watched them whipping her across the eyes, right in the eyes! He was crying, choking, tears streaming down his face. One of the men lashed him across the face with a whip. He didn't feel it. Wringing his hands and screaming, he rushed to the gray-haired old man with the gray beard who was shaking his head in disapproval. A woman grabbed the boy by the hand and tried to pull him away, but he tore free and ran back to the mare. She was nearly finished but tried to kick one more time.

"I'll teach you to kick!" Mikolka roared. He threw down the whip, bent forward, and pulled a long, thick wooden shaft from the bottom of the cart. He gripped one end with both hands and, with great effort, swung it over the mare.
"He'll crush her!" voices shouted around him. "He'll kill her!"
"She's my property!" Mikolka screamed, and brought the shaft crashing down. There was the sound of a heavy thud.
"Hit her! Hit her! Why'd you stop?" voices yelled from the crowd.

Mikolka swung the shaft a second time, and it came down again on the spine of the wretched mare. Her hindquarters buckled, but she lurched forward, straining with everything she had -- pulling one way, then the other, trying to move the cart. But six whips were attacking her from every direction, and the shaft rose and fell on her a third time, then a fourth, in heavy, measured blows. Mikolka was in a frenzy because he couldn't kill her with a single blow.
"Tough one!" someone shouted in the crowd.
"She'll go down any second now, boys. She's nearly done," said an admiring spectator.
"Bring an axe! Finish her off!" shouted a third.

"I'll show you! Stand back!" Mikolka screamed. He flung down the shaft, bent into the cart, and pulled out an iron crowbar. "Watch this!" he bellowed, and with all his strength brought it smashing down on the mare. The blow landed. The mare staggered, sank back, tried to pull forward, but the bar came down again in a savage arc across her back and she collapsed to the ground like a felled tree.

"Finish her off!" Mikolka screamed, and leaped out of the cart, wild-eyed. Several young men, also flushed with drink, grabbed whatever they could find -- whips, sticks, poles -- and ran to the dying mare. Mikolka stood to one side, raining random blows with the crowbar. The mare stretched out her head, drew one long breath, and died.
"You butchered her!" someone in the crowd shouted.
"Why wouldn't she gallop, then?"
"My property!" Mikolka yelled, standing with bloodshot eyes, brandishing the crowbar. He looked as though he regretted having nothing left to beat.
"That's no Christian, that's for certain!" many voices were shouting in the crowd.

But the poor boy, beside himself, fought his way through the crowd to the sorrel mare, threw his arms around her bleeding dead head, and kissed it -- kissed her eyes, kissed her lips.... Then he leapt up and flew at Mikolka in a frenzy, swinging his small fists. At that instant his father, who had been chasing after him, snatched him up and carried him out of the crowd.
"Come along, come along! Let's go home," his father said.
"Papa! Why did they... kill... the poor horse!" he sobbed, but his voice broke and the words came in shrieks from his heaving chest.

"They're drunk.... They're brutes... it's not our business!" his father said. The boy threw his arms around his father but felt choked, suffocating. He tried to draw a breath, tried to cry out -- and woke up.
He woke gasping for breath, drenched in sweat, and sat up in terror.
"Thank God, it was only a dream," he said, sitting down under a tree and taking deep breaths. "But what is this? Am I coming down with a fever? What a horrifying dream!"
He felt completely shattered. Darkness and confusion filled his soul. He rested his elbows on his knees and buried his face in his hands.

"My God!" he cried. "Can it be -- can it really be -- that I'm going to take an axe, that I'm going to hit her on the head, split her skull open... that I'm going to step in the warm, sticky blood, break the lock, steal, and tremble -- hide myself, covered in blood... with the axe.... My God, can it be?"
He was shaking like a leaf as he said this.

"But why do I keep going over this?" he continued, sitting up again as if in profound amazement. "I knew I could never bring myself to do it, so why have I been torturing myself all this time? Yesterday, when I went to do that... _experiment_ -- yesterday I realized completely that I could never go through with it.... So why am I going over it again? Why am I still hesitating? Coming down the stairs yesterday, I told myself it was base, loathsome, vile, vile... the very thought of it made me sick, filled me with horror.

"No, I can't do it. I can't! Granted, there is no flaw in the reasoning. Granted, everything I've concluded over the past month is clear as day, true as mathematics.... But my God! I can't bring myself to do it! I can't! So why, why am I still...?"

He rose to his feet, looked around in wonder as though surprised to find himself here, and started walking toward the bridge. He was pale, his eyes were burning, he was exhausted in every limb -- but he suddenly seemed to breathe more easily. He felt he had thrown off the terrible weight that had been pressing down on him for so long. All at once a feeling of relief and peace settled over his soul. "Lord," he prayed, "show me my path. I renounce that cursed... dream."

Crossing the bridge, he gazed quietly and calmly at the Neva, at the blazing red sun setting in the blazing sky. Despite his weakness, he felt no fatigue. It was as though an abscess that had been forming in his heart for a month had suddenly burst. Freedom, freedom! He was free of that spell, that sorcery, that obsession!

Later, when he looked back on that time and everything that happened to him in those days -- minute by minute, point by point -- he was struck by one circumstance with almost superstitious force. Though not extraordinary in itself, it always seemed to him afterward to be the predestined turning point of his fate. He could never understand or explain to himself why, when he was exhausted and it would have been far more convenient to go straight home by the shortest route, he had instead gone through the Hay Market, where he had no reason to go. The detour was obvious and completely unnecessary, though not a long one. True, it had happened to him dozens of times to walk home without noticing which streets he took. But why -- he kept asking himself -- why had such an important, such a decisive, and at the same time such a completely chance encounter happened in the Hay Market (where he had no business being) at the very hour, the very minute of his life when he was in exactly the state of mind and exactly the circumstances in which that encounter could exert the gravest and most decisive influence on his entire destiny? As though it had been lying in wait for him on purpose!

It was about nine o'clock when he crossed the Hay Market. At the tables and stalls, the booths and shops, all the vendors were closing up, clearing away, and packing their goods, and like their customers, heading home. Ragpickers and peddlers of every kind crowded around the taverns in the dirty, stinking courtyards of the Hay Market. Raskolnikov particularly liked this area and the surrounding alleys when he wandered the streets aimlessly. Here his rags drew no contemptuous stares, and you could walk around in any condition without shocking anyone. At the corner of an alley, a peddler and his wife had two tables set up selling ribbon, thread, cotton handkerchiefs, and the like. They had gotten up to leave but were lingering in conversation with a woman who had just approached them. This woman was Lizaveta Ivanovna -- or, as everyone called her, Lizaveta -- the younger sister of the old pawnbroker, Alyona Ivanovna, whom Raskolnikov had visited the day before to pawn his watch and conduct his _experiment_.... He already knew all about Lizaveta, and she knew him slightly too. She was a single woman of about thirty-five, tall, clumsy, timid, meek, and almost simple-minded. She was a complete slave to her sister, who made her work day and night and even beat her. She was standing in front of the peddlers with a bundle, listening earnestly and doubtfully. They were talking about something with particular intensity. The moment Raskolnikov caught sight of her, he was overcome by a strange feeling, something like intense astonishment, though there was nothing especially surprising about the encounter.
"You should make up your own mind, Lizaveta Ivanovna," the peddler was saying loudly. "Come by tomorrow around seven. They'll be there too."
"Tomorrow?" Lizaveta said slowly and thoughtfully, as though unable to decide.

"Honestly, the way you're terrified of Alyona Ivanovna!" the peddler's wife chattered -- a lively little woman. "I look at you and you're like a little child. And she's not even your real sister -- just a half-sister. And the control she has over you!"

"But this time don't say a word to Alyona Ivanovna," her husband cut in. "That's my advice. Just come to us without asking her. It'll be worth your while. Your sister can figure things out for herself later."
"Should I come?"
"Around seven tomorrow. And they'll be here. You can decide for yourself."
"And we'll have a cup of tea," his wife added.
"All right, I'll come," Lizaveta said, still pondering, and slowly started to move away.

Raskolnikov had just passed by and heard every word. He walked on softly, unnoticed, trying not to miss anything. His initial astonishment gave way to a thrill of horror, like a shiver running down his spine. He had learned -- suddenly, completely unexpectedly -- that tomorrow at seven o'clock, Lizaveta, the old woman's sister and only companion, would be away from home, and that therefore at precisely seven o'clock the old woman _would be completely alone_.

He was only a few steps from his lodging. He walked in like a man condemned to death. He thought of nothing and was incapable of thinking. But he felt suddenly, with his whole being, that he no longer had any freedom of thought, any will -- and that everything had been suddenly and irrevocably decided.

Certainly, if he had waited whole years for a suitable opportunity, he could not have hoped for a more certain step toward the success of his plan than the one that had just presented itself. In any case, it would have been difficult to discover beforehand, with such certainty, such precision, and so little risk -- without dangerous inquiries or investigations -- that the next day, at a specific hour, the old woman whose life he was contemplating would be home and entirely alone.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Raskolnikov later found out why the peddler and his wife had invited Lizaveta. It was a perfectly ordinary matter, nothing unusual about it. A family that had recently moved to the city, fallen on hard times, was selling off their household goods and clothes -- mostly women's things. Since the items would fetch little at market, they were looking for a dealer. This was Lizaveta's line of work. She handled these kinds of transactions regularly and had a reputation for honesty, always naming a fair price and sticking to it. She rarely said much and, as already mentioned, was extremely meek and timid.

But Raskolnikov had grown superstitious lately. The traces of superstition lingered in him long afterward and were nearly impossible to shake. In everything that happened, he was always inclined to see something strange and mysterious, as if there were some peculiar force at work, some pattern of meaningful coincidences. The previous winter, a student he knew named Pokorev, who was leaving for Kharkov, had happened to mention in conversation the address of Alyona Ivanovna, the old pawnbroker, in case Raskolnikov ever needed to pawn something. For a long time he didn't go. He had tutoring work and was getting by. Six weeks ago he had remembered the address. He had two things he could pawn: his father's old silver watch and a little gold ring with three red stones, a farewell gift from his sister. He decided to take the ring. From the moment he first laid eyes on the old woman, he felt an overwhelming revulsion for her, though he knew nothing particular about her. He got two rubles from her and stopped at a miserable little tavern on his way home. He ordered tea, sat down, and sank into deep thought. A strange idea was pecking at his brain like a chick in an egg, and it absorbed him completely.

At the next table, almost beside him, sat a student he didn't know and had never seen, along with a young officer. They had just played billiards and were drinking tea. Suddenly he heard the student mention the pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna to the officer and give him her address. This alone seemed strange to Raskolnikov -- he had just come from her, and here was someone mentioning her name. Of course it was coincidence, but he couldn't shake the extraordinary impression, as if someone were speaking specifically for his benefit. The student began telling his friend various details about Alyona Ivanovna.

"She's first-rate," he said. "You can always get money from her. She's rich as a Rothschild -- could give you five thousand rubles at a time, and she doesn't turn down pledges for a single ruble. Lots of our guys have dealt with her. But she's a terrible old witch...."

He went on describing how spiteful and unpredictable she was -- how if your interest payment was even one day late, the pledge was gone; how she gave a quarter of an item's value and charged five, even seven percent a month, and so on. The student chattered away, mentioning that she had a sister, Lizaveta, whom the nasty creature constantly beat and kept in total submission, like a small child, even though Lizaveta was nearly six feet tall.
"Now there's a phenomenon for you," the student said with a laugh.

They started discussing Lizaveta. The student spoke about her with a strange kind of relish, laughing constantly, while the officer listened with interest and asked him to send Lizaveta over to do some mending. Raskolnikov didn't miss a word and learned everything. Lizaveta was younger than the old woman and was her half-sister from a different mother. She was thirty-five. She worked day and night for her sister -- cooking, cleaning, sewing, taking charwoman jobs -- and handed over everything she earned. She didn't dare accept any work without her sister's permission. The old woman had already made her will, and Lizaveta knew about it: she would inherit nothing but some furniture -- chairs and the like. All the money was left to a monastery in N----- province, for prayers to be said for the old woman's soul in perpetuity. Lizaveta was of a lower social rank than her sister, unmarried, and remarkably ungainly in appearance -- very tall, with long feet that seemed to turn outward. She always wore battered goatskin shoes but was clean in her person. What the student found most surprising and amusing was the fact that Lizaveta was constantly pregnant.
"But you said she's ugly?" the officer remarked.

"Yes, she's dark-skinned and looks like a soldier in a dress, but actually she's not ugly at all. She has such a kind face, and kind eyes. Strikingly so. The proof is that plenty of men find her attractive. She's such a soft, gentle creature -- puts up with anything, always willing, ready for anything. And her smile is genuinely sweet."
"Sounds like you find her attractive yourself," the officer laughed.

"It's her oddness. But here's what I wanted to say. I could kill that damn old woman and take her money -- I'm telling you -- without the slightest pang of conscience," the student added with passion. The officer laughed again. Raskolnikov shuddered. How strange this was!

"Listen, I want to ask you a serious question," the student went on, heated. "I was joking, of course, but think about it. On one side you have a stupid, senseless, worthless, spiteful, sick, horrible old woman, not merely useless but actively harmful -- who has no idea why she's even alive, and who'll die in a day or two anyway. You follow? You follow?"
"Yes, yes, I follow," the officer answered, watching his excited friend closely.

"Now listen. On the other side, you have young lives being thrown away by the thousands for lack of help, everywhere you look! A hundred thousand good deeds could be done with that old woman's money -- money that's going to be buried in a monastery! Hundreds, maybe thousands of people could be set on the right path. Dozens of families saved from poverty, ruin, depravity, disease -- all with her money. Kill her, take the money, and devote yourself to serving humanity and the common good. What do you think -- wouldn't one tiny crime be erased by thousands of good deeds? One life for a hundred lives in return -- it's simple math! Besides, what is the life of that sickly, stupid, spiteful old woman worth in the grand scale of things? No more than the life of a louse or a cockroach -- less, actually, because the old woman is doing harm. She's destroying other people's lives. The other day she bit Lizaveta's finger out of sheer spite -- it nearly had to be amputated."
"Of course she doesn't deserve to live," the officer agreed. "But that's just how things are -- it's nature."

"Sure, brother, but we have to correct and redirect nature. Without that, we'd drown in an ocean of prejudice. Without that, there would never have been a single great man. People talk about duty, conscience -- I don't want to say anything against duty and conscience -- but what exactly do we mean by them? Wait, let me ask you another question. Listen!"
"No, wait -- I'll ask you a question. Listen!"
"Go ahead."
"You're making speeches and theorizing, but tell me: would you kill the old woman _yourself_?"
"Of course not! I was just arguing the principle of the thing.... It has nothing to do with me personally...."
"Well, I think if you wouldn't do it yourself, then there's no justice in it at all.... Let's play another game."

Raskolnikov was deeply shaken. Of course, it was all just typical student talk -- the kind of thing he had heard many times before, in different forms and on different topics. But why had he happened to overhear this particular conversation, with these particular ideas, at the precise moment when his own brain was conceiving... _the very same ideas_? And why, at the very moment he had carried away the germ of his idea from the old woman's apartment, had he stumbled upon a conversation about her? This coincidence always struck him as strange. This trivial tavern talk would have an enormous influence on everything that followed -- as though something had been lying in wait, something preordained, some guiding hint....

After returning from the Hay Market, he threw himself on the sofa and sat motionless for a full hour. Meanwhile it grew dark. He had no candle, and it didn't even occur to him to light one. He could never afterward remember whether he had been thinking about anything during that time. At last he felt the familiar fever and chills returning, and realized with relief that he could lie down on the sofa. Soon a heavy, leaden sleep descended on him, crushing him down.

He slept an extraordinarily long time, without dreaming. Nastasya came into his room at ten the next morning and had trouble waking him. She brought tea and bread. The tea was once again the second brewing, served in her own teapot.
"Good grief, how he sleeps!" she cried indignantly. "Always sleeping!"
He got up with effort. His head ached. He stood, paced his tiny room, and collapsed back onto the sofa.
"Going back to sleep?" Nastasya exclaimed. "Are you sick?"
He didn't answer.
"Want some tea?"
"Later," he said with effort, closing his eyes and turning to the wall.
Nastasya stood over him.

"Maybe he really is sick," she said, turned, and left. She came back at two with soup. He was lying in the same position. The tea was untouched. Nastasya felt genuinely offended and began shaking him awake angrily.
"Why are you lying there like a log?" she shouted, looking at him with disgust.
He sat up but said nothing, staring at the floor.
"Are you sick or not?" Nastasya demanded, getting no answer again. "You should go outside and get some air. Are you going to eat this or not?"
"Later," he said weakly. "Go away."
He waved her out.
She lingered a moment, looked at him with pity, and left.
A few minutes later he raised his eyes and stared for a long time at the tea and the soup. Then he picked up the bread, took the spoon, and began to eat.

He ate a little -- three or four spoonfuls, without appetite, mechanically. His headache was better. After eating he lay back on the sofa, but couldn't sleep. He lay still, face down in the pillow, haunted by daydreams -- strange daydreams. In one that kept recurring, he imagined he was in Africa, in Egypt, at some oasis. The caravan was resting. The camels lay peacefully. Palm trees formed a perfect circle around them. Everyone was eating. But he was drinking water from a spring that flowed gurgling nearby. And it was so cool -- wonderful, wonderful -- blue, cold water running over colored stones and over clean sand that glittered like gold.... Suddenly he heard a clock strike. He flinched, roused himself, raised his head, looked out the window, saw how late it was, and sprang up wide awake as though someone had yanked him off the sofa. He crept to the door on tiptoe, opened it silently, and began listening on the staircase. His heart was pounding. But the stairs were quiet -- everyone seemed to be asleep.... It struck him as strange, monstrous, that he could have slept in such oblivion since the day before and had done nothing, prepared nothing.... And it might already have struck six. His drowsiness and confusion gave way to an extraordinary, feverish, almost frantic haste. But there was little to prepare. He focused all his energy on thinking of everything and forgetting nothing, while his heart pounded so hard he could barely breathe. First he had to make a loop and sew it into his overcoat -- a moment's work. He rummaged under his pillow and pulled from the linen stuffed under it an old, worn-out, unwashed shirt. From its rags he tore a long strip, about two inches wide and sixteen inches long. He folded the strip in two, took off his broad, sturdy summer overcoat -- thick cotton, his only outer garment -- and began sewing both ends of the strip to the inside, under the left armhole. His hands trembled as he sewed, but he managed it, and when he put the coat back on, nothing showed from the outside. The needle and thread had been ready for a long time and lay on his table wrapped in paper. As for the loop, it was his own clever design: the loop was meant for the axe. It was impossible to carry an axe through the street in his hands. Hidden under his coat, he would still have to hold it, which would be noticeable. Now he only had to slip the axe head through the loop, and it would hang silently under his arm on the inside. By putting his hand in his coat pocket, he could hold the end of the handle the whole way, keeping it from swinging. And since the coat was very full -- practically a sack -- nobody would be able to tell from the outside that his hand was holding something in the pocket. He had designed this loop two weeks earlier.

When he was finished, he thrust his hand into a small gap between the sofa and the floor, felt around in the left corner, and pulled out the _pledge_ -- prepared long ago and hidden there. This pledge was nothing but a smoothly planed piece of wood, about the size and thickness of a silver cigarette case. He had found it during one of his wanderings, in a courtyard where some kind of workshop was set up. Later he had added a thin, smooth piece of iron that he'd also picked up in the street. Placing the iron -- slightly smaller -- on the piece of wood, he had bound them tightly together, wrapping thread around and around them, then wrapped the whole thing neatly in clean white paper and tied the package so it would be very difficult to undo. This was to distract the old woman for a moment while she struggled with the knot, buying him time. The iron strip was added for weight, so she wouldn't immediately guess the "object" was made of wood. All of this had been stored under his sofa. He had just pulled out the pledge when he heard someone shout in the yard:
"It struck six ages ago."
"Ages ago! My God!"

He rushed to the door, listened, grabbed his hat, and began descending his thirteen steps cautiously, noiselessly, like a cat. The most important thing still remained: stealing the axe from the kitchen. He had decided long ago that the deed must be done with an axe. He also had a folding pocketknife, but he couldn't rely on the knife, and even less on his own strength, so he had settled on the axe. We might note in passing a peculiarity about all his final decisions in this matter: the more definite they became, the more grotesque and absurd they instantly appeared to him. Despite all his agonizing inner struggle, he could never for a single moment truly believe he would carry out his plan.

And indeed, if everything had ever been considered down to the last detail and definitively settled, with no uncertainty remaining, he would probably have abandoned the whole thing as something absurd, monstrous, and impossible. But a whole mass of unsettled points and uncertainties remained. As for getting the axe, this trivial matter caused him no worry, because nothing could be easier. Nastasya was constantly out of the house, especially in the evenings -- running to neighbors or to a shop -- and always left the door open. It was the one thing the landlady was always scolding her about. So when the time came, he would simply have to slip into the kitchen, take the axe, and an hour later -- when everything was over -- go back and replace it. But there were doubts. Suppose he came back an hour later to return it and Nastasya was back and in the kitchen. He would have to walk past and wait for her to leave again. But what if in the meantime she missed the axe, looked for it, raised an alarm -- that would mean suspicion, or at least grounds for it.

But these were all trivial details he hadn't even begun to consider, and had no time for. He was focused on the main thing, putting off minor details until _he could believe in the whole enterprise_. But that seemed utterly impossible. At least it seemed so to him. He couldn't imagine, for instance, that he would someday stop thinking, get up, and simply go there.... Even his recent experiment -- his visit to the old woman's to survey the place -- had been merely an attempt at an experiment, far from the real thing, as if he were saying, "Come on, let's try it out -- why just dream about it!" -- and he had immediately broken down and fled in a fury of self-contempt. Meanwhile, on the moral question, his analysis seemed complete. His reasoning had been honed razor-sharp, and he could find no rational objections within himself. But in the end, he simply stopped believing in himself and stubbornly, slavishly kept groping for arguments in all directions, as though some force were pushing and pulling him toward it.

Long before -- much earlier -- he had been preoccupied with one question: why are almost all crimes so poorly concealed and so easily detected, and why do almost all criminals leave such obvious traces? He had gradually reached many different and curious conclusions. In his view, the main reason lay not so much in the material difficulty of concealing a crime as in the criminal himself. Nearly every criminal experiences a collapse of willpower and reasoning ability -- a childish, phenomenal recklessness -- at the very moment when caution and prudence are most essential. He was convinced that this eclipse of reason and failure of will attacks a person like a disease, develops gradually, reaches its peak just before the crime is committed, continues with equal intensity during the crime itself and for some time afterward -- varying by individual -- and then passes, like any other illness. The question of whether the disease causes the crime, or whether the crime by its very nature always brings something like disease with it, he did not yet feel able to answer.

Having reached these conclusions, he decided that in his own case there would be no such morbid reaction, that his reason and will would remain intact during the execution of his plan, for the simple reason that his plan was "not a crime".... We will skip the process by which he arrived at this last conclusion -- we have gotten too far ahead already.... We will only add that the practical, purely material difficulties occupied a secondary place in his mind. "You just need to keep your willpower and reasoning faculties intact, and you'll deal with all of it when the time comes, once you've thoroughly familiarized yourself with every detail...." But this preparation had never actually begun. His final decisions were what he trusted least, and when the hour struck, everything happened quite differently -- almost accidentally, almost by surprise.

One minor circumstance wrecked his plan before he had even reached the bottom of the staircase. When he reached the landlady's kitchen, its door open as usual, he glanced in cautiously to check whether Nastasya was out and whether the landlady's own door was closed, so she wouldn't peek out when he went in for the axe. But to his astonishment, Nastasya was not only home -- she was right there in the kitchen, pulling laundry from a basket and hanging it on a line. Seeing him, she stopped, turned, and stared at him the whole time he was passing. He looked away and walked past as though he hadn't noticed anything. But it was all over. He didn't have the axe! He was devastated.
"What made me think," he muttered as he passed through the gateway, "what made me think she would definitely be out at that exact moment? Why, why, why was I so sure of it?"
He felt crushed, humiliated. He could have laughed at himself in his rage.... A dull, animal fury boiled inside him.

He stood in the gateway, hesitating. Going out for a walk to keep up appearances was revolting. Going back to his room was even worse. "And what a chance I've lost -- forever!" he muttered, standing aimlessly in the gateway, directly across from the porter's small, dark room, which was also open. Suddenly he froze. From the porter's room, barely two steps away, something shiny under the bench on the right caught his eye.... He looked around -- nobody. He approached the room on tiptoe, went down two steps, and called out weakly for the porter. "Right -- not home. Somewhere nearby though, in the yard, since the door is wide open." He lunged for the axe (it was an axe) and pulled it from under the bench, where it lay between two blocks of wood. Immediately, before stepping out, he fastened it in the loop, shoved both hands in his pockets, and walked out of the room. No one had noticed him. "When reason fails, the devil helps!" he thought with a strange grin. This stroke of luck raised his spirits enormously.

He walked along quietly and steadily, without hurrying, to avoid raising suspicion. He barely looked at the people he passed, trying not to meet anyone's eyes, making himself as inconspicuous as possible. Suddenly he thought of his hat. "For God's sake! I had money the day before yesterday and didn't buy a cap to wear instead!" A curse rose from the depths of his soul.

Glancing into a shop out of the corner of his eye, he saw by a wall clock that it was ten minutes past seven. He had to hurry and at the same time take a roundabout route to approach the building from the other side....

Whenever he had imagined all this beforehand, he had sometimes thought he would be very afraid. But he wasn't very afraid now -- not afraid at all, in fact. His mind was occupied with irrelevant things, though nothing for long. Passing the Yusupov Garden, he found himself absorbed in the idea of building great fountains and how they would cool the air in all the city squares. Gradually he became convinced that if the Summer Garden were extended to the Field of Mars and perhaps connected to the Mikhailovsky Palace garden, it would be a splendid thing, a great benefit to the city. Then he got interested in the question of why, in all great cities, people are not simply forced by necessity but seem somehow peculiarly drawn to live in exactly those parts of town where there are no gardens, no fountains -- where there is the most filth and stench and every kind of squalor. Then his own walks through the Hay Market came to mind, and for a moment he snapped back to reality. "What nonsense!" he thought. "Better not to think about anything at all!"

"People being led to execution probably clutch mentally at every object they pass along the way," flashed through his mind, but only flashed -- like lightning. He pushed the thought away.... And now he was close. Here was the building. Here was the gate. Suddenly a clock struck once somewhere. "What! Can it already be half past seven? Impossible -- it must be fast!"

Luckily, everything went smoothly at the gate again. At that very moment, as if arranged for his benefit, a huge hay cart had just driven in through the gateway, completely screening him as he passed under it. The wagon had barely cleared the entrance into the yard before he had slipped to the right in a flash. On the other side of the wagon he could hear shouting and arguing, but no one noticed him and no one crossed his path. Many windows facing that huge rectangular courtyard were open, but he didn't raise his head -- he didn't have the strength. The staircase leading to the old woman's apartment was right there, just to the right of the gateway. He was already on the stairs....

He drew a breath, pressed his hand to his hammering heart, felt for the axe one more time and adjusted it, then began climbing the stairs softly and cautiously, listening at every step. But the staircase was completely deserted. All the doors were shut. He met no one. One apartment on the first floor was wide open and painters were working inside, but they didn't glance at him. He paused, thought for a moment, and continued. "It would be better if they weren't here, of course, but... they're two floors below."

And there was the fourth floor. There was the door. There was the apartment across the hall -- the empty one. The apartment below the old woman's seemed vacant too: the business card nailed to the door had been torn off -- the tenants had moved away!... He was out of breath. For one instant the thought floated through his mind: "Should I go back?" But he gave himself no answer and began listening at the old woman's door. Dead silence. Then he listened on the staircase -- listened long and hard... then took one last look around, pulled himself together, straightened up, and tested the axe in the loop one more time. "Am I very pale?" he wondered. "Is it obvious I'm agitated? She's suspicious.... Maybe I should wait a bit longer... until my heart stops pounding?"

But his heart wouldn't stop. On the contrary, as if to spite him, it pounded harder and harder. He couldn't stand it any longer. He slowly reached out and rang the bell. Half a minute later, he rang again, louder.

No answer. Ringing further was pointless and would attract attention. The old woman was certainly home, but she was suspicious and alone. He had some knowledge of her habits... and once more he pressed his ear to the door. Either his senses were extraordinarily heightened -- which seems hard to believe -- or the sound was truly very distinct. He suddenly heard something like a hand carefully touching the lock, and the rustle of fabric right at the door. Someone was standing silently pressed against the lock on the other side, secretly listening from within, just as he was doing from without, apparently with her ear to the door.... He shifted slightly on purpose and muttered something aloud so he wouldn't seem to be hiding, then rang a third time -- quietly, calmly, without impatience. Looking back on it later, that moment stood out in his memory with terrifying clarity, forever. He could not understand how he had possessed such cunning, because his mind seemed clouded at moments and he was barely aware of his own body.... An instant later, he heard the latch being unfastened.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 7
paragraphs: The door opened a crack, as before, and once again two sharp, suspicious eyes peered out at him from the darkness. Then Raskolnikov lost his nerve and nearly made a catastrophic mistake.

Afraid the old woman would be frightened at finding them alone together, and not trusting that the sight of him would calm her suspicions, he grabbed the edge of the door and pulled it toward him to prevent her from slamming it shut. She didn't pull back, but she didn't let go of the handle either, so that he nearly dragged her out onto the landing. Seeing that she was blocking the doorway and wouldn't let him pass, he walked straight toward her. She stumbled backward in alarm, tried to speak, but seemed unable to get the words out. She stared at him with wide eyes.

"Good evening, Alyona Ivanovna," he began, trying to sound casual, but his voice wouldn't cooperate -- it cracked and shook. "I've come... I've brought something... but we should step inside... to the light...."
Without waiting for her, he walked straight into the room. The old woman hurried after him, suddenly finding her tongue.
"Good heavens! What is this? Who is it? What do you want?"
"Alyona Ivanovna, you know me... Raskolnikov... here, I brought the pledge I mentioned the other day...." He held out the package.

The old woman glanced briefly at the pledge, then fixed her eyes on her uninvited visitor. She stared at him -- intently, viciously, suspiciously. A minute passed. He even thought he caught something like a sneer in her eyes, as though she had already guessed everything. He felt himself losing control, felt himself growing terrified -- so terrified that if she kept staring at him like that without saying a word for another half minute, he was sure he would bolt.
"Why are you looking at me as if you don't know me?" he said suddenly, with an edge of hostility. "Take it if you want it. If not, I'll go elsewhere. I'm in a hurry."
He hadn't planned to say this at all -- the words had come out on their own. The old woman recovered herself. Her visitor's firm tone apparently restored her confidence.
"But what's the rush, sir? What is it?" she asked, examining the pledge.
"The silver cigarette case -- the one I mentioned last time, remember."
She held out her hand.
"But how pale you are, really... and your hands are trembling! Have you been swimming or something?"
"Fever," he answered abruptly. "You can't help being pale... when you haven't eaten." He could barely get the words out.
His strength was failing again. But his answer sounded plausible, and the old woman took the pledge.
"What is this?" she asked once more, studying Raskolnikov closely and weighing the package in her hand.
"A thing... cigarette case.... Silver.... Look at it."
"Doesn't look much like silver.... How he's wrapped it up!"

Trying to untie the string, she turned toward the window for better light -- all her windows were shut despite the stifling heat -- and stepped away from him entirely, standing with her back to him for several seconds. He unbuttoned his coat and freed the axe from the loop, but didn't pull it all the way out. He held it in his right hand under the coat. His hands were terrifyingly weak -- he could feel them growing more numb and wooden with every second. He was afraid the axe would slip and clatter to the floor.... A wave of dizziness swept over him.
"What's he gone and wrapped this up for?" the old woman cried in irritation, and turned back toward him.

There was not another instant to lose. He pulled the axe completely free, raised it with both hands, barely conscious of himself, and almost effortlessly, almost mechanically, brought the blunt side down on her head. He seemed not to have used his own strength. But the moment the axe struck, his strength returned.

The old woman was bareheaded as always. Her thin, light hair, streaked with gray and heavily greased, was twisted into a rat-tail braid held in place by a broken horn comb that jutted from the back of her neck. Because she was so short, the blow landed squarely on the crown of her skull. She cried out -- but very faintly -- and instantly crumpled to the floor, raising her hands toward her head. In one hand she still clutched "the pledge." He struck her again, and then again, with the blunt side, on the same spot. Blood poured out as from an overturned glass. The body fell backward. He stepped away, let it fall, and immediately bent over her face. She was dead. Her eyes seemed ready to pop from their sockets. Her forehead and whole face were twisted in a convulsive grimace.

He set the axe on the floor beside the body and immediately felt in her pocket -- trying to avoid the spreading blood -- the same right-hand pocket from which she had taken the key during his last visit. He was in full possession of his faculties, free of confusion or dizziness, though his hands were still trembling. He remembered afterward that he had been remarkably collected and careful, trying the whole time not to get blood on himself.... He pulled out the keys at once -- all of them, as before, on a single steel ring. He ran with them into the bedroom. It was a very small room, with an entire wall covered in icons. Against the far wall stood a large bed, very clean, covered with a silk patchwork quilt. Against a third wall was a chest of drawers.
