Strangely, the moment he began fitting the keys into the lock, the moment he heard them jingling, a convulsive shudder passed through him. He suddenly felt tempted to abandon everything and leave. But that lasted only an instant -- it was too late to go back. He actually smiled at himself. Then another terrifying thought struck him. He suddenly imagined that the old woman might still be alive and could regain consciousness. Leaving the keys in the chest, he rushed back to the body, snatched up the axe, and raised it over the old woman again -- but didn't bring it down. There was no doubt she was dead. Bending down for a closer look, he could clearly see that the skull was smashed, even caved in on one side. He started to touch it with his finger but pulled his hand back -- the evidence was clear enough without that. Meanwhile, a large pool of blood had formed. He suddenly noticed a cord around her neck. He tugged at it, but the cord was strong and wouldn't snap, and besides, it was soaked in blood. He tried to pull it out from the front of her dress, but something caught and held it. In his impatience he raised the axe to cut the cord from above, against the body, but didn't dare. With difficulty, getting blood on his hands and the axe, he managed after two minutes of frantic effort to cut the string without touching the body with the blade. He was right -- it was a purse. On the cord hung two crosses, one of cypress wood and one of copper, and a small silver filigree icon, along with a little, greasy chamois leather purse with a steel clasp and ring. The purse was crammed full. Raskolnikov shoved it in his pocket without looking at it, dropped the crosses onto the old woman's body, and rushed back into the bedroom, this time carrying the axe.

He was in a frantic rush. He grabbed the keys and started trying them again, but without success. They wouldn't fit. It wasn't so much that his hands were shaking -- he kept making mistakes. He could see, for instance, that a key wasn't the right one and wouldn't fit, yet he kept trying to force it in. Suddenly he remembered something: the large key with the deep notches, which hung with the smaller ones, couldn't possibly belong to the chest of drawers -- this had occurred to him during his last visit too -- it must be for some kind of strongbox, and that was probably where everything was hidden. He abandoned the chest of drawers and immediately felt under the bed, knowing that old women usually keep boxes under their beds. And there it was: a good-sized box under the bed, at least a yard long, with an arched lid covered in red leather and studded with steel nails. The notched key fit immediately and unlocked it. On top, under a white sheet, lay a red brocade coat lined with hare fur; under that a silk dress, then a shawl -- and below that, nothing but clothes, it seemed. The first thing he did was wipe his bloody hands on the red brocade. "It's red, and blood will be less noticeable on red," the thought passed through his mind. Then he caught himself. "My God, am I losing my mind?" he thought in terror.

But the moment he touched the clothes, a gold watch slid out from under the fur coat. He hurried to turn everything over. Sure enough, scattered among the clothing were various gold items -- probably all unredeemed or not-yet-redeemed pledges -- bracelets, chains, earrings, pins, and the like. Some were in cases, others simply wrapped in newspaper, neatly and precisely folded and tied with string. Without pausing to examine or open the packages and cases, he began stuffing them into the pockets of his trousers and overcoat. But he didn't have time to take many....

Suddenly he heard footsteps in the room where the old woman lay. He froze, motionless as death. But all was quiet -- he must have imagined it. Then he clearly heard a faint cry, as if someone had let out a soft, broken moan. Then silence again for a minute or two. He crouched by the box, holding his breath. Then he leapt to his feet, grabbed the axe, and ran out of the bedroom.

In the middle of the room stood Lizaveta, holding a large bundle. She was staring in stupefaction at her murdered sister, white as a sheet, apparently without the strength to scream. Seeing him burst from the bedroom, she began trembling all over, faintly, like a leaf. A shudder ran across her face. She raised one hand, opened her mouth, but still made no sound. She began backing slowly away from him toward the corner, staring at him steadily, fixedly, but still not making a sound -- as though she couldn't draw enough breath to scream. He rushed at her with the axe. Her mouth twitched pitifully, the way babies' mouths do when they start to get frightened, staring wide-eyed at whatever scares them, on the verge of crying out. This wretched Lizaveta was so simple and so thoroughly crushed and terrified that she didn't even raise a hand to shield her face -- the most necessary, most natural gesture in the world, with the axe poised above her. She only lifted her empty left hand, slowly, not to her face but holding it out in front of her as if pushing him away. The blade of the axe came down directly on her skull and split the entire top of her head in a single blow. She collapsed heavily, instantly. Raskolnikov completely lost his head. He snatched up her bundle, dropped it again, and ran for the door.

Terror seized him more and more powerfully, especially after this second, utterly unexpected murder. He wanted to flee the place as fast as he could. If in that moment he had been capable of clearer thought -- of grasping the full difficulty of his position, its hopelessness, its horror, its absurdity -- of understanding how many obstacles and perhaps how many more crimes he still had to overcome to escape and make it home -- he might well have abandoned everything and gone to turn himself in. And not from fear, but from pure horror and revulsion at what he had done. Revulsion above all surged inside him, growing stronger every minute. Nothing in the world would have made him go back to the strongbox or even into that room.

But a kind of blankness, a dreamlike stupor, was gradually taking hold of him. At moments he forgot himself -- or rather, forgot what was important and latched onto trivialities. Glancing into the kitchen, however, and seeing a bucket half-full of water on a bench, he thought to wash his hands and the axe. His hands were sticky with blood. He dropped the axe blade-first into the water, grabbed a piece of soap from a cracked saucer on the windowsill, and began washing his hands in the bucket. When they were clean, he pulled out the axe, washed the blade, and spent a long time -- about three minutes -- scrubbing the wooden handle where there were bloodstains, rubbing them with soap. Then he wiped everything with a piece of linen hanging on a line in the kitchen, and stood for a long while examining the axe carefully by the window. No trace remained -- only the wood was still damp. He carefully hung the axe back in the loop under his coat. Then, as well as he could in the dim kitchen light, he checked his overcoat, trousers, and boots. At first glance there seemed to be nothing -- only some spots on the boots. He wet the rag and rubbed them. But he knew he wasn't being thorough, that there might be something clearly visible that he was missing. He stood in the middle of the room, lost in thought. Dark, agonizing ideas crowded his mind -- the idea that he was going mad, that at this moment he was incapable of reasoning, of protecting himself, that perhaps he should be doing something entirely different from what he was doing. "My God!" he whispered. "I have to get out of here, get out!" He rushed to the entryway. But there a shock of terror awaited him unlike anything he had ever experienced.

He stood and stared, unable to believe his eyes: the front door -- the outer door to the staircase, where he had stood ringing the bell not long ago -- was open. Standing wide open, at least six inches ajar. No lock, no bolt, the entire time! The old woman hadn't shut it after letting him in -- perhaps as a precaution against being left alone with him. But my God! He had seen Lizaveta come in afterward! And how -- how had he not realized that she must have entered somehow? She couldn't have come through the wall!
He rushed to the door and slid the bolt home.
"No, wrong again! I have to get out, get out...."
He unfastened the bolt, opened the door, and listened on the staircase.

He listened for a long time. Somewhere far below -- maybe at the gate -- two voices were shouting loudly and shrilly, quarreling and cursing. "What's that about?" He waited patiently. At last everything went quiet, as if suddenly cut off. They had gone their separate ways. He was about to step out when suddenly, on the floor below, a door banged open and someone started down the stairs, humming a tune. "Why do they all make so much noise?" flashed through his mind. He closed the door again and waited. Finally everything was still -- not a soul. He had just taken a step toward the staircase when he heard more footsteps.

The steps sounded very far away, at the very bottom of the stairs, but he remembered clearly and distinctly that from the first sound, he began to suspect for some reason that this person was coming _here_ -- to the fourth floor, to the old woman's apartment. Why? Was there something distinctive, something meaningful about the footsteps? They were heavy, steady, unhurried. Now the person had passed the first floor. Now climbing higher -- closer and clearer. He could hear the heavy breathing. Now the third floor.... Coming here! And suddenly it felt as though he had been turned to stone -- like in a dream where you're being chased, nearly caught, about to be killed, and you're rooted to the spot, unable to even move your arms.

At last, when the unknown person was climbing to the fourth floor, Raskolnikov suddenly jerked to life. He managed to slip neatly and quickly back into the apartment and close the door behind him. Then he took the hook and noiselessly fitted it into the catch. Instinct guided him. When it was done, he crouched by the door, holding his breath. The unknown visitor was now at the door too. They stood on opposite sides, just as Raskolnikov had stood with the old woman moments before -- separated by the door, listening.
The visitor drew several heavy breaths. "Must be a big, heavy man," Raskolnikov thought, gripping the axe. It all felt like a dream. The visitor took hold of the bell and rang it loudly.

The instant the tin bell tinkled, Raskolnikov thought he heard something moving in the apartment. For several seconds he listened in dead earnest. The stranger rang again, waited, then suddenly and violently yanked at the door handle. Raskolnikov watched the hook bouncing in its catch with horror, expecting at every moment that it would be torn free. It certainly seemed possible, given how violently the man was shaking it. He was tempted to hold the catch in place, but the man might feel the resistance. Dizziness swept over him. "I'm going to collapse!" flashed through his mind. But the stranger began to speak, and he recovered instantly.

"What the hell? Are they asleep or dead in there? Damn them!" the man bellowed in a thick voice. "Hey, Alyona Ivanovna, you old witch! Lizaveta Ivanovna, you beauty! Open the door! Damn them! Are they asleep or what?"
Enraged, he yanked the bell a dozen more times with all his strength. He was clearly a man of some authority and a close acquaintance.
At that moment quick, light footsteps were heard not far off, on the stairs. Someone else was approaching. Raskolnikov hadn't noticed at first.
"Nobody home? Really?" the newcomer called out in a cheerful, ringing voice, addressing the first visitor, who was still pulling at the bell. "Evening, Koch."
"Must be quite young, judging by the voice," Raskolnikov thought.
"Who the hell knows? I've nearly broken the lock," Koch answered. "But how do you know me?"
"Come on! The day before yesterday I beat you three games straight at billiards, at Gambrinus's."
"Oh!"
"So they're not home? That's weird. Awfully stupid, though. Where would the old woman go? I came here on business."
"I have business with her too."
"Well, what can we do? Go back, I guess. Damn! And I was hoping to get some money!" the young man exclaimed.

"We'll have to give up, of course, but why did she set this time herself? The old witch picked the time! It's out of my way. And where on earth could she have gone? She sits in this apartment year in, year out, the old hag -- her legs are bad -- and all of a sudden she's out for a walk!"
"Should we ask the porter?"
"About what?"
"Where she went and when she'll be back."
"Hmm.... Damn it all.... We could ask.... But she never goes anywhere."
He tugged at the door handle once more.
"Damn it all! Nothing to be done. Let's go."
"Wait!" the young man said suddenly. "Look -- see how the door moves when you pull it?"
"So?"
"That means it's not locked with a key -- it's latched with the hook! Can you hear the hook rattling?"
"So?"

"Don't you see? That proves someone is home. If they were all out, they would have locked the door from the outside with the key, not hooked it from the inside. Listen to the hook rattling! To fasten the hook, someone has to be inside. So they're sitting in there and not opening the door!"
"Right! You're right!" Koch cried, astonished. "What are they doing in there?" He began shaking the door furiously.
"Wait!" the young man said again. "Stop pulling. Something's wrong here.... You've been ringing and banging and they still won't open! Either they've both fainted or..."
"What?"
"Here's what we do. Let's go get the porter and have him wake them up."
"All right."
They started downstairs.
"Wait -- you stay here while I run down for the porter."
"Why?"
"Just trust me."
"All right."
"I'm studying law, you see! It's obvious, ob-vi-ous that something is wrong here!" the young man shouted excitedly, and ran downstairs.

Koch stayed behind. He softly touched the bell, which gave a single tinkle. Then gently, as though thinking it over and examining the situation, he began working the door handle -- pulling it and releasing it -- to confirm once more that the door was only latched with a hook. Then, puffing and panting, he bent down and tried to peer through the keyhole. But the key was in the lock on the inside, so nothing was visible.

Raskolnikov stood gripping the axe. He was in something like delirium. He was even prepared to fight them when they came in. While they were knocking and talking, the idea of ending it all flashed through his mind several times -- to fling open the door and shout at them. At moments he wanted to curse them, taunt them, while they still couldn't get in. "Just hurry up!" was the thought that kept racing through his head.
"But what the devil is he doing?..." Time passed. One minute, another -- nobody came. Koch grew restless.
"What the hell!" he suddenly burst out, and abandoning his post in a fit of impatience, he too clattered downstairs, his heavy boots thumping on the steps. The footsteps faded.
"My God! What do I do?"
Raskolnikov unhooked the latch, opened the door -- silence. Without thinking, without any thought at all, he stepped out, pulled the door shut as carefully as he could, and went downstairs.
He had gone down three flights when he suddenly heard a loud commotion below. Where could he go? There was nowhere to hide. He was about to turn back to the apartment.
"Hey! Stop him! Catch him!"
Someone burst out of an apartment below, shouting, and practically fell rather than ran down the stairs, bellowing at the top of his lungs:
"Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Damn him!"

The shout ended in a shriek. The last sounds came from the courtyard. Then silence. But at the same moment several men began noisily climbing the stairs, talking loudly and rapidly. There were three or four of them. He recognized the young man's ringing voice. "Them!"

Filled with despair, he walked straight toward them, thinking: "Whatever happens, happens!" If they stopped him, it was all over. If they let him pass, it was all over too -- they would remember him. They were getting closer. Only one flight separated them. And then -- salvation! A few steps away on the right, an empty apartment stood with its door wide open -- the second-floor apartment where the painters had been working and which, as if arranged for his benefit, they had just left. It must have been them running down the stairs and shouting. The floor had just been painted. In the middle of the room stood a bucket and a cracked pot with paint and brushes. In an instant he had slipped through the open door and hidden behind the wall -- just in time. They had already reached the landing. Then they turned and continued upstairs to the fourth floor, talking loudly. He waited, tiptoed out, and ran down the stairs.
No one was on the staircase. No one was at the gate. He passed quickly through the gateway and turned left into the street.

He knew -- he knew with perfect certainty -- that at this moment they were in the apartment, that they were astonished to find the door unlatched when it had just been hooked, that by now they were looking at the bodies, and that within another minute they would realize the murderer had just been there, had hidden somewhere, slipped past them, and escaped. They would almost certainly guess he had been in the empty apartment while they were going upstairs. And yet he didn't dare walk any faster, though the next turning was still nearly a hundred yards away. "Should I duck into some gateway and wait on an unfamiliar street? No, hopeless! Should I throw away the axe? Take a cab? Hopeless, hopeless!"

At last he reached the corner. He turned down it more dead than alive. Here he was halfway to safety, and he knew it: it was less risky because there was a dense crowd, and he disappeared into it like a grain of sand. But everything he had been through had drained him so completely that he could barely move. Sweat ran down him in drops; his neck was soaked. "That fellow's had quite a workout!" someone called out as he emerged at the canal embankment.

His awareness was fading now, and the farther he went, the worse it got. He did remember, however, that coming out onto the canal bank, he was alarmed at how few people there were -- making him more conspicuous -- and he thought about turning back. Though he was nearly collapsing from exhaustion, he took a long detour to reach home from a completely different direction.

He was barely conscious when he passed through the gateway of his building! He was already on the staircase before he remembered the axe. And yet he faced a very serious problem: returning it while attracting as little attention as possible. He was, of course, incapable of considering that it might be far better not to return the axe at all, but simply to drop it later in someone's yard. But everything worked out fortunately. The porter's door was closed but not locked, which probably meant the porter was home. But he had so completely lost the ability to think that he walked straight to the door and opened it. If the porter had asked, "What do you want?" he might simply have handed him the axe. But once again the porter wasn't there. He managed to put the axe back under the bench, covering it with the block of wood as before. He didn't meet a soul after that, all the way to his room. The landlady's door was shut. When he reached his room, he threw himself on the sofa just as he was. He didn't sleep, but sank into a blank oblivion. If anyone had entered his room then, he would have leapt up screaming. Fragments and scraps of thoughts swarmed in his brain, but he couldn't hold onto any of them, couldn't settle on a single one, no matter how hard he tried....

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 1
paragraphs: He lay there for a very long time. Now and then he seemed to wake, and at those moments noticed that it was deep into the night, but it didn't occur to him to get up. Finally he noticed it was starting to get light. He was lying on his back, still dazed from his stupor. Fearful, desperate shrieks rose from the street -- sounds he heard every night under his window after two o'clock. They woke him now.
"Ah, the drunks are pouring out of the taverns," he thought. "It's past two." And he immediately leapt up, as though someone had yanked him off the sofa.
"What! Past two o'clock!"
He sat down on the sofa -- and instantly remembered everything. All at once, in a single flash, he remembered everything.

For the first moment he thought he was going mad. A terrible chill seized him -- but it was the fever that had started long before, while he slept. Now violent shivering gripped him so hard that his teeth chattered and his whole body shook. He opened the door and listened. The entire building was asleep. He stared in amazement at himself and at everything around the room, wondering how he could have come home the night before without locking the door, thrown himself on the sofa without undressing, without even taking off his hat. It had fallen off and lay on the floor near his pillow.
"If anyone had come in, what would they have thought? That I was drunk, but..."

He rushed to the window. There was enough light, and he frantically began examining himself from head to foot -- all his clothes. Were there traces? But he couldn't do it that way. Shaking with cold, he started stripping off everything and examining each piece again. He went through every thread and scrap, and, not trusting himself, repeated the search three times.

There seemed to be nothing -- no trace -- except in one spot, where thick drops of dried blood clung to the frayed edge of his trousers. He grabbed a large clasp knife and cut off the frayed threads. There seemed to be nothing else.

Suddenly he remembered that the purse and the things he'd taken from the old woman's strongbox were still in his pockets! He hadn't thought until now of taking them out and hiding them! He hadn't even thought about them while checking his clothes! He rushed to pull everything out and throw it on the table. When he'd emptied his pockets and turned them inside out to make sure nothing remained, he carried the whole pile to the corner. The wallpaper had peeled away from the bottom of the wall and hung in tatters. He began stuffing everything into the hole behind the paper. "They're in! Out of sight, purse and all!" he thought with glee, standing up and staring blankly at the hole, which now bulged out more than ever. Suddenly he shuddered with horror. "My God!" he whispered in despair. "What's wrong with me? Is that hidden? Is that any way to hide things?"
He hadn't counted on having trinkets to conceal. He'd only thought about money and hadn't prepared a hiding place.
"What am I even glad about?" he thought. "Is that hiding things? I'm losing my mind -- plain and simple!"

He collapsed onto the sofa in exhaustion, immediately shaken by another unbearable fit of shivering. Mechanically he pulled his old student's winter coat from the chair beside him -- still warm despite being practically in rags -- covered himself with it, and sank again into drowsiness and delirium. He lost consciousness.
No more than five minutes passed before he leapt up again, and in a frenzy pounced on his clothes once more.
"How could I have fallen asleep again with nothing taken care of? Yes, yes -- I didn't remove the loop from the armhole! I forgot -- forgot something like that! A piece of evidence like that!"
He ripped out the loop, hurriedly cut it to pieces, and stuffed the bits among his linen under the pillow.

"Pieces of torn linen can't arouse suspicion, whatever happens. I don't think so, I don't think so, anyway!" he repeated, standing in the middle of the room. With agonizing concentration he began scanning everything around him again -- the floor, every surface -- trying to make sure he'd missed nothing. The growing conviction that all his faculties, even his memory, even the simplest capacity for thought, were failing him, had become an unbearable torment.
"Is it starting already? Is this my punishment? It is!"
The frayed scraps he'd cut from his trousers were lying on the floor in the middle of the room, where anyone walking in would see them!
"What is wrong with me!" he cried again, like a man losing his mind.

Then a strange thought entered his head: perhaps his clothes were covered in blood, perhaps there were stains everywhere, but he couldn't see them, couldn't notice them because his perception was failing, disintegrating... his reason was clouding over.... He suddenly remembered that the purse had blood on it too. "Ah! Then there must be blood on the pocket lining, since I shoved the wet purse in my pocket!"
In a flash he turned the pocket inside out, and -- yes! -- there were traces, stains on the pocket lining!

"So my mind hasn't completely deserted me -- I still have some sense and memory, since I figured this out myself," he thought triumphantly, breathing a deep sigh of relief. "It's just the weakness of fever, a moment's delirium." He ripped the entire lining out of his left trouser pocket. At that instant, sunlight fell on his left boot. On the sock poking out from it, he thought he saw traces! He flung off the boots. "Traces! The tip of the sock was soaked with blood." He must have accidentally stepped in that pool.... "But what do I do with this now? Where do I put the sock, the scraps, the pocket lining?"
He gathered it all in his hands and stood in the middle of the room.

"In the stove? But they'd search the stove first. Burn them? But with what? I don't even have matches. No, better to go out and throw it all away somewhere. Yes, throw it away," he repeated, sinking onto the sofa. "Right now, this instant, without delay..."
But his head dropped onto the pillow instead. The unbearable icy shivering overtook him again. He pulled his coat over himself.

For a long time, for hours, he was tormented by the urge to "go somewhere right now, this second, and get rid of it all, get it out of sight and done with -- right now, right now!" Several times he tried to get up from the sofa but couldn't.
He was finally jolted awake by violent pounding on his door.
"Open up! Are you dead or alive in there? All he does is sleep!" Nastasya shouted, banging with her fist. "Days on end, snoring away like a dog! A dog is what he is! Open up, I said! It's past ten."
"Maybe he's not home," said a man's voice.
"That's the porter's voice.... What does he want?"
He shot upright on the sofa. His heart was hammering painfully.
"Then who latched the door?" Nastasya retorted. "Now he's started bolting himself in! As if anyone would want to steal from him! Open up, you idiot -- wake up!"
"What do they want? Why the porter? It's all been discovered. Resist or open? Whatever happens!..."
He half rose, leaned forward, and unlatched the door.
His room was so small he could reach the latch without getting out of bed. Sure enough -- the porter and Nastasya were standing there.
Nastasya stared at him strangely. He met the porter's gaze with a look that was both defiant and desperate. The porter silently held out a gray folded paper sealed with wax.
"A notice from the office," he announced, handing him the paper.
"What office?"
"A summons to the police station, obviously. You know which office."
"The police?... What for?..."
"How should I know? You're summoned, so go."
The man studied him carefully, glanced around the room, and turned to leave.
"He's seriously ill!" Nastasya observed, not taking her eyes off him. The porter looked back for a moment. "He's had a fever since yesterday," she added.

Raskolnikov said nothing, holding the paper without opening it. "You shouldn't get up, then," Nastasya went on sympathetically, seeing him lower his feet from the sofa. "You're sick, so don't go. There's no rush. What's that you're holding?"

He looked down. In his right hand he was clutching the scraps he'd cut from his trousers, the sock, and the rags of the pocket lining. He had fallen asleep holding them. Thinking about it later, he remembered that half-waking in his fever, he had grabbed all of it tightly and fallen asleep again.
"Look at the rags he's been collecting -- sleeps with them like they're treasure...."
Nastasya dissolved into her hysterical giggling.

He instantly shoved everything under his coat and fixed his eyes intently on her. Incapable as he was of rational thought at that moment, he sensed that nobody would behave this way with a person about to be arrested. "But... the police?"
"You should have some tea! Want some? I'll bring it -- there's some left."
"No... I'm going. I'll go right now," he muttered, getting to his feet.
"You'll never make it downstairs!"
"Yes, I'll go."
"Suit yourself."
She followed the porter out.
He immediately rushed to the light to examine the sock and the scraps.

"There are stains, but barely noticeable -- covered in grime, rubbed, already discolored. Nobody without prior suspicion could make anything of them. Nastasya couldn't have noticed from that distance, thank God!" Then, trembling, he broke the seal on the notice and began reading. It took him a long time to understand. It was an ordinary summons from the district police station, requiring him to appear that day at half past nine at the office of the district superintendent.
"But when has this ever happened? I've never had anything to do with the police! And why today?" he thought in agonized bewilderment. "God, just let it be over quickly!"
He was about to drop to his knees and pray, but burst out laughing instead -- not at the idea of prayer, but at himself.
He began dressing in a hurry. "If I'm done for, I'm done for -- I don't care! Should I put the sock on?" he suddenly wondered. "It'll just get more dirt on it and the traces will disappear."

But the moment he pulled the sock on, he ripped it off again in loathing and horror. He pulled it off, but then, reflecting that he had no other socks, he picked it up and put it back on -- and laughed again.

"It's all just convention, all relative, just a way of looking at things," he thought in a flash, but only on the surface of his mind, while his whole body shuddered. "There -- I got it on! I ended up putting it on after all!"
But the laughter was quickly followed by despair.

"No, this is too much for me..." he thought. His legs were shaking. "From fear," he muttered. His head was spinning and throbbing with fever. "It's a trap! They want to lure me there and trip me up on everything," he thought as he went down the stairs. "The worst part is I'm practically delirious... I might blurt out something stupid..."

On the stairs he remembered that he was leaving everything exactly where it was, in the hole in the wall. "They're probably doing this on purpose -- to search the place while I'm gone," he thought, and stopped short. But such despair possessed him, such a cynicism of misery, that he waved his hand and kept going. "Just get it over with!"

In the street the heat was unbearable again. Not a drop of rain had fallen in all these days. Again dust, bricks, plaster. Again the stench from the shops and taverns, the drunks, the Finnish peddlers, the decrepit cabs. The sun blazed directly in his eyes, making them ache, and his head started spinning -- the way it does for a feverish man stepping into bright sunlight.
When he reached the turning into _that_ street, he looked down it in an agony of dread... at _that_ building... and immediately averted his eyes.
"If they question me, maybe I'll just tell them everything," he thought as he neared the police station.

The station was about a quarter mile away. It had recently moved to new rooms on the fourth floor of a new building. He'd been briefly to the old office once, long ago. Turning through the gateway, he saw a flight of stairs on the right, which a peasant was climbing with a ledger in his hand. "A building porter, most likely -- so the office is up there." He began climbing the stairs, not wanting to ask anyone for directions.
"I'll go in, fall on my knees, and confess everything..." he thought as he reached the fourth floor.

The staircase was steep, narrow, and slippery with dirty water. The apartment kitchens opened onto the stairs and stood open nearly all day, producing a terrible smell and heat. The staircase was crowded with porters going up and down with their ledgers, policemen, and people of every sort and both genders. The office door also stood wide open. Peasants waited inside. The heat in there was stifling too, with a nauseating smell of fresh paint and stale oil from the newly renovated rooms.

After waiting briefly, he decided to move forward into the next room. All the rooms were small with low ceilings. A terrible impatience drove him on. No one paid any attention to him. In the second room, some clerks sat writing, dressed hardly better than he was -- a rather odd-looking bunch. He approached one of them.
"What do you want?"
He held out the notice.
"You're a student?" the man asked, glancing at the paper.
"Yes, a former student."
The clerk looked at him with zero interest. He was a particularly unkempt individual with the glazed look of a man consumed by a single fixed idea.
"I won't get anything out of this one -- he has no interest in anything," Raskolnikov thought.
"Go in there, to the head clerk," the man said, pointing toward the farthest room.

He went into that room -- the fourth in a row -- a small room packed with people who were somewhat better dressed than those in the outer rooms. Among them were two women. One, poorly dressed in mourning, sat at the table across from the head clerk, writing something at his dictation. The other was a very stout, florid woman with a purplish-red, blotchy face, extravagantly overdressed, wearing a brooch on her bosom the size of a saucer. She was standing to one side, apparently waiting. Raskolnikov thrust his notice at the head clerk. The clerk glanced at it, said "One moment," and went back to attending to the woman in mourning.
He breathed more easily. "It can't be about _that_."
Gradually he began to regain his composure, urging himself to stay calm and courageous.

"Some stupid slip, some trivial carelessness, and I could give myself away! Hmm... it's a shame there's no air in here," he added. "So stuffy.... Making my head spin even worse... and my thoughts too..."

He was aware of terrible inner turmoil. He was afraid of losing self-control. He tried to grab onto something, fix his mind on something completely unrelated, but couldn't manage it at all. Yet the head clerk fascinated him -- he kept hoping to read him, to guess something from his face.

He was a very young man, about twenty-two, with a dark, animated face that looked older than his years. He was fashionably and foppishly dressed, with his hair parted in the middle, carefully combed and pomaded. He wore several rings on his well-groomed fingers and a gold chain across his waistcoat. He had even exchanged a couple of words in French with a foreigner in the room, and said them fairly correctly.

"Luise Ivanovna, please sit down," he said casually to the brightly dressed, purple-faced lady, who was still standing as though she didn't dare take a seat, though there was a chair right beside her.

"Ich danke," she replied, and softly, with a rustle of silk, sank into the chair. Her light blue dress trimmed with white lace billowed around the table like a hot-air balloon, filling nearly half the room. She reeked of perfume. But she was clearly embarrassed about taking up so much space and smelling so strongly, and though her smile was simultaneously insolent and servile, it betrayed obvious unease.

The woman in mourning finished up and stood. Suddenly an officer strode in with a jaunty, self-important swagger of his shoulders at each step. He tossed his cockaded cap on the table and dropped into an armchair. The stout little lady practically jumped out of her seat, bobbing in a frenzy of curtsies, but the officer took absolutely no notice of her, and she didn't dare sit down again in his presence. He was the assistant superintendent. He had a reddish mustache sticking out horizontally on each side of his face, and extremely small features that expressed nothing much except a certain arrogance. He shot an irritated sideways glance at Raskolnikov -- who was so badly dressed, and whose bearing, despite his humiliating position, did not match his clothes at all. Raskolnikov had carelessly fixed a long, direct stare on him, and the officer clearly took offense.
"What do you want?" he barked, apparently astounded that such a ragged creature wasn't annihilated by the majesty of his gaze.
"I was summoned... by a notice..." Raskolnikov faltered.

"It's about the recovery of a debt -- from _the student_," the head clerk cut in hurriedly, tearing himself from his papers. "Here!" He flung a document at Raskolnikov and pointed to the relevant section. "Read this!"
"Money? What money?" Raskolnikov thought. "But... then... it's definitely not _that_."
He trembled with joy. A sudden, intense, indescribable relief flooded through him. A weight had been lifted from his shoulders.

"And what time were you instructed to appear, sir?" the assistant superintendent shouted, sounding for some unknown reason more and more aggrieved. "It says nine o'clock, and it's already past twelve!"

"The notice was delivered to me just fifteen minutes ago," Raskolnikov answered loudly over his shoulder. To his own surprise, he suddenly felt angry too, and found a certain pleasure in it. "And it's enough that I came here at all, sick with fever."
"Kindly stop shouting!"
"I'm not shouting -- I'm speaking quite calmly. It's you who's shouting at me. I'm a student, and I don't allow anyone to shout at me."
The assistant superintendent was so furious that for a moment he could only sputter. He leapt from his chair.
"Be silent! You are in a government office! Don't be insolent, sir!"
"You're in a government office too," Raskolnikov fired back, "and you're smoking a cigarette while shouting, so you're the one showing disrespect to everyone here."
He felt an indescribable satisfaction at having said this.
The head clerk looked at him with a smile. The furious assistant superintendent was visibly thrown.

"That's none of your business!" he finally shouted with forced volume. "Just sign the declaration as required. Show him, Alexander Grigorievich. A complaint has been filed against you! You don't pay your debts! A fine specimen you are!"
But Raskolnikov had stopped listening. He had seized the document eagerly, desperate for an explanation. He read it once, twice, and still didn't understand.
"What is this?" he asked the head clerk.

"It's a writ for the recovery of money owed on an IOU. You must either pay the full amount including costs and expenses, or submit a written declaration of when you can pay, along with an undertaking not to leave the city without paying and not to sell or conceal your property. The creditor has the right to sell your property and proceed against you according to the law."
"But I... don't owe anyone anything!"

"That's not our concern. An IOU for one hundred and fifteen rubles, legally attested and overdue, given by you to the widow of Assessor Zarnitsyn nine months ago, and subsequently transferred by the widow to a Mr. Chebarov, has been filed with us for recovery. Hence the summons."
"But she's my landlady!"
"And what of it?"

The head clerk regarded him with a condescending smile of pity, tinged with triumph, like someone watching a novice under fire for the first time -- as if to say, "Well, how do you feel now?" But what did any of this matter now -- an IOU, a debt collection? Was it worth worrying about, worth even a moment's attention? He stood there, reading, listening, answering, even asking questions -- all mechanically. The triumphant feeling of safety, of deliverance from overwhelming danger, filled his entire soul at that moment -- without thought for the future, without analysis, without speculation or doubt. It was an instant of total, direct, purely instinctive joy. But right then, something like a thunderstorm erupted in the office. The assistant superintendent, still shaken by Raskolnikov's disrespect, still fuming and obviously intent on salvaging his wounded dignity, pounced on the unfortunate well-dressed lady, who had been gazing at him since he walked in with an extraordinarily silly smile.

"You shameless creature!" he suddenly roared at the top of his voice. (The woman in mourning had already left.) "What was going on in your house last night? Another disgrace! You're a scandal to the whole street! Fighting and drinking again! Do you want the workhouse? I've warned you ten times that I wouldn't let you off an eleventh. And here you are again!"

The paper fell from Raskolnikov's hands. He stared at the smartly dressed lady being berated so roughly. But he quickly understood what was happening and immediately began to find the scene genuinely entertaining. He listened with pleasure -- he wanted to laugh and laugh.... Every nerve was on edge.
"Ilya Petrovich!" the head clerk began anxiously, but stopped, knowing from experience that the enraged assistant could not be stopped except by force.

As for the well-dressed lady, at first she positively trembled before the onslaught. But strangely, the more numerous and violent the insults became, the more amiable her expression grew, and the more seductive the smiles she directed at the terrible assistant. She shifted uncomfortably and curtsied constantly, waiting impatiently for a chance to get a word in. At last she found it.

"There was no noise and no fighting in my house whatsoever, Mr. Captain," she began, like peas rattling from a pan, speaking Russian confidently but with a strong German accent. "And no scandal whatsoever, and his honor arrived drunk -- this is the whole truth, Mr. Captain -- and I am not to blame.... Mine is an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and honorable behavior, Mr. Captain, and I never, never want any scandal. But he came completely drunk and then ordered three more bottles, and then he lifted one leg and began playing the piano with his foot, and that is not at all proper in an honorable house, and he _ganz_ broke the piano, and that is very bad manners, and I told him so. And he picked up a bottle and began hitting everyone with it. And then I called the porter, and Karl came, and he punched Karl in the eye, and he punched Henriette in the eye too, and slapped me five times across the face. And it was so ungentlemanly in an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and I screamed. And he opened the window onto the canal and stood in the window squealing like a little pig. A disgrace! The idea of squealing like a pig out the window into the street! Shame on him! And Karl dragged him away from the window by his coat, and it's true, Mr. Captain, he tore _sein Rock_. And then he screamed that _man muss_ pay him fifteen rubles in damages. And I paid him, Mr. Captain, five rubles for _sein Rock_. And he is a most ungentlemanly visitor and caused the whole scandal. 'I'll write about you,' he said, 'I can write about you in all the newspapers.'"
"So he was a writer?"
"Yes, Mr. Captain, and such an ungentlemanly visitor in an honorable house...."
"Now then! Enough! I've already told you..."
"Ilya Petrovich!" the head clerk said again, pointedly.
The assistant glanced at him quickly. The head clerk gave a slight shake of his head.

"...So I'm telling you this, most respectable Luise Ivanovna, and I'm telling you for the last time," the assistant went on. "If there is one more scandal in your honorable house, I will have you locked up personally -- as they say in polite society. You hear me? So a literary man, a writer, took five rubles for his coat-tail in an 'honorable house'? A fine lot, these writers!" He shot a contemptuous glance at Raskolnikov. "There was a scene in a restaurant the other day too -- a writer ate dinner and refused to pay. 'I'll write a satire about you,' he says. And there was another one on a steamship last week who used the foulest language in front of a civil counselor's wife and daughter, a respectable family. And another got thrown out of a confectioner's just the other day. That's what they're like -- writers, literary types, students, soapbox orators.... Pfah! Get out! I'll come check on you personally. And you'd better watch yourself! You hear?"

And he cast a contemptuous glance at Raskolnikov. "There was a scandal in a restaurant the other day, too. Some writer had eaten his dinner and refused to pay. 'I'll write a satire about you,' he says. And just last week, another one on a steamer used the most disgraceful language toward a respectable civil councillor's family — his wife and daughter. And the other day one of them was thrown out of a confectioner's shop. That's what they're like, these writers, literary types, students, loudmouths... Pfoo! Now get along! I'll come check on you myself one day. Then you'd better watch out! Do you hear?"

With hurried deference, Luise Ivanovna began curtsying in every direction, and curtsied her way right to the door. But at the door she stumbled backwards into a handsome officer with a fresh, open face and magnificent thick fair whiskers. This was the district superintendent himself, Nikodim Fomitch. Luise Ivanovna hastily curtsied almost to the ground and fluttered out of the office with quick, mincing steps.

"Thunder and lightning again — a hurricane!" said Nikodim Fomitch to Ilya Petrovitch in a friendly, civil tone. "You've got yourself all worked up again, fuming away! I could hear it from the stairs!"

"Well, so what!" Ilya Petrovitch drawled with gentlemanly nonchalance, swaggering over to another table with some papers, his shoulders swinging jauntily at each step. "Here, take a look if you will: this writer, or student — he was one at some point, at least — doesn't pay his debts, has given a promissory note, won't vacate his room, constant complaints are lodged against him, and then he has the nerve to protest about my smoking in his presence! He behaves like a cad himself — and just look at him, please. There's the gentleman, and what a fine sight he is!"

"Poverty is no crime, my friend, but we all know you go off like gunpowder — you can't take even the slightest criticism," continued Nikodim Fomitch, turning warmly to Raskolnikov. "I expect you took offence at something and went too far yourself. But you'd be wrong about him; he's a fine fellow, I assure you, just explosive! Gets heated, flares up, boils over, and there's no stopping him! And then it's all over! And underneath it all, a heart of gold! His nickname in the regiment was the Explosive Lieutenant..."
"And what a regiment it was, too," cried Ilya Petrovitch, quite pleased by this friendly banter, though still somewhat sulky.

Raskolnikov suddenly felt an urge to say something exceptionally pleasant to all of them. "Excuse me, Captain," he began casually, turning to Nikodim Fomitch, "please try to understand my situation... I'm ready to apologize if I've been rude. I'm a poor student, sick and worn down by poverty. I've had to stop studying because I can't support myself right now, but I'll be getting money soon. I have a mother and sister in the province of X. They'll send it, and I'll pay what I owe. My landlady is a kind-hearted woman, but she's so frustrated that I've lost my tutoring work and haven't paid her for the last four months that she won't even send up my dinner anymore. And I don't understand this promissory note at all. She's demanding I pay on this note. But how can I pay? You be the judge!"
"But that's not our concern, you know," the head clerk observed.

"Yes, yes, I completely agree. But let me explain..." Raskolnikov went on, still addressing Nikodim Fomich but doing his best to include Ilya Petrovich as well, though the latter persistently pretended to be rummaging through papers, contemptuously ignoring him. "Let me explain that I've been living there for nearly three years, and at first... at first... why should I hide it? -- at the very beginning I promised to marry her daughter. It was a verbal promise, freely given... she was a girl... I actually liked her, though I wasn't in love with her... a youthful thing, in short... What I mean is, my landlady extended me generous credit in those days, and I led a rather... careless life..."

"Nobody's asking for your personal details, sir. We don't have time for this," Ilya Petrovich cut in roughly, with a note of triumph. But Raskolnikov stopped him with sudden heat, though he found it extremely hard to speak.

"Excuse me, excuse me -- let me explain... how things happened... I agree, it's not strictly necessary, but... A year ago, the girl died of typhus. I stayed on as a lodger. When my landlady moved to her current apartment, she told me -- in a friendly way -- that she had complete trust in me, but would I mind giving her an IOU for one hundred and fifteen rubles, the total I owed her? She said that as long as I gave her this paper, she would extend me credit again, as much as I needed, and would never -- those were her exact words -- never make use of the IOU until I could pay on my own... And now, when I've lost my lessons and have nothing to eat, she goes ahead with legal proceedings. What am I supposed to say to that?"

"All these touching details are no business of ours," Ilya Petrovich interrupted rudely. "You need to submit a written declaration, but as for your love affairs and all these tragic episodes, we have nothing to do with that."
"Now, come... you're being harsh," Nikodim Fomich murmured, sitting down at the table and starting to write. He looked a little embarrassed.
"Write!" the head clerk said to Raskolnikov.
"Write what?" he answered gruffly.
"I'll dictate it to you."

Raskolnikov had the impression the head clerk treated him more casually and dismissively after his little speech. But strangely, he suddenly felt completely indifferent to what anyone thought of him, and this change happened in a flash, in a single instant. If he had cared to reflect, he would have been astonished that he could have spoken to them the way he just had a minute ago, pressing his feelings on them. And where had those feelings come from? Now, even if the room had been filled not with police officials but with his closest, dearest friends, he would not have found a single human word for them -- so empty was his heart. A bleak sensation of agonizing, eternal solitude and disconnection crystallized in his soul. It wasn't the pettiness of his sentimental outburst to Ilya Petrovich, or the pettiness of the latter's triumph over him, that caused this sudden reversal. Oh, what did his own humiliation matter now, or all these petty vanities -- the officers, the German women, the debts, the police station? If he had been sentenced to burn at the stake at that moment, he wouldn't have stirred, would barely have heard the sentence through. Something entirely new, sudden, and unprecedented was happening inside him. It wasn't that he understood it, but he felt with all the force of direct sensation that he could never again appeal to these people at the police station with sentimental outpourings like his recent one, or with anything else at all. And even if they had been his own brothers and sisters instead of police officers, there would have been absolutely no point in appealing to them, under any circumstance. He had never experienced such a strange, terrible sensation. And the most agonizing part was this: it was more a feeling than a thought or idea -- a direct sensation, the most agonizing of any he had known in his entire life.

The head clerk began dictating the standard form of declaration -- that he could not pay, that he undertook to do so at a future date, that he would not leave the city, that he would not sell or conceal his property, and so forth.
"But you can barely write -- you can hardly hold the pen," the head clerk observed, looking at Raskolnikov with curiosity. "Are you ill?"
"Yes. Dizzy. Go on!"
"That's all. Sign it."
The head clerk took the paper and turned to other business.

Raskolnikov returned the pen but instead of standing up and leaving, he put his elbows on the table and pressed his head in his hands. It felt like a nail was being driven into his skull. A strange idea suddenly seized him: to stand up right now, walk over to Nikodim Fomich, and tell him everything that happened yesterday -- then go home with him and show him the things in the hole in the corner. The impulse was so strong he actually rose from his seat to act on it. "Shouldn't I think about this for a moment?" flashed through his mind. "No, better to throw off the burden without thinking." But suddenly he stopped, rooted to the spot. Nikodim Fomich was talking animatedly with Ilya Petrovich, and the words reached him:

"Impossible. They'll both be released. To start with, the whole story contradicts itself. Why would they have called the porter if they'd done it? To inform on themselves? As a ruse? No, that would be too clever! Besides, the student Pestryakov was seen at the gate by both porters and a woman as he went in. He was walking with three friends who left him only at the gate, and he asked the porters for directions in their presence. Now, would he have asked for directions if he'd been going there with that kind of intent? As for Koch, he spent half an hour at the silversmith's downstairs before going up to the old woman, and he left the silversmith's at exactly a quarter to eight. Now just consider..."

"But wait -- how do you explain this contradiction? They themselves state that they knocked and the door was locked, but three minutes later, when they went up with the porter, the door turned out to be unlatched."

"That's exactly the point. The murderer must have been inside, bolted in. And they would have caught him for certain if Koch hadn't been a fool and gone down to look for the porter too. The murderer must have used that interval to get downstairs and slip past them somehow. Koch keeps crossing himself, saying: 'If I'd stayed, he would have jumped out and killed me with the axe.' He's going to have a thanksgiving service -- ha ha!"
"And nobody saw the murderer?"
"How could they? The building is a regular Noah's Ark," the head clerk put in.
"It's clear, perfectly clear," Nikodim Fomich said warmly.
"No, it's anything but clear," Ilya Petrovich maintained.
Raskolnikov picked up his hat and walked toward the door, but he didn't make it....

When he regained consciousness, he found himself sitting in a chair, someone supporting him on the right, someone else standing on the left holding a yellowish glass of yellow water, and Nikodim Fomich standing before him, staring at him. He stood up from the chair.
"What's this? Are you ill?" Nikodim Fomich asked rather sharply.
"He could barely hold the pen while signing," the head clerk said, settling back at his desk and returning to his work.

"Have you been sick long?" cried Ilya Petrovich from his desk, where he too had been examining papers. He had naturally come over to look when the sick man fainted, but withdrew the moment he came to.
"Since yesterday," Raskolnikov muttered.
"Did you go out yesterday?"
"Yes."
"Even though you were ill?"
"Yes."
"At what time?"
"Around seven in the evening."
"And where did you go, if I may ask?"
"Down the street."
"Short and sweet."
Raskolnikov, white as a sheet, had answered sharply and curtly, without dropping his dark, feverish eyes from Ilya Petrovich's stare.
"He can barely stand on his feet. And you..." Nikodim Fomich began.
"No matter," Ilya Petrovich said in a peculiar tone.
Nikodim Fomich was about to say something more, but glancing at the head clerk, who was watching him very intently, he fell silent. There was a sudden, strange pause.
"Very well, then," Ilya Petrovich concluded. "We won't detain you."
Raskolnikov walked out. He caught the sound of animated conversation behind him, and above it rose the questioning voice of Nikodim Fomich. Out in the street, his faintness passed completely.
"A search -- they'll search my place right away," he repeated to himself, hurrying home. "The bastards! They suspect me."
His old terror seized him completely once again.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 2
paragraphs: "What if they've already searched the place? What if I find them in my room?"
But here was his room. Empty. No one had been in it. Even Nastasya hadn't touched anything. But God -- how could he have left all those things in the hole?

He rushed to the corner, slipped his hand behind the wallpaper, pulled the things out, and stuffed them into his pockets. There were eight items in all: two small boxes with earrings or something of the kind -- he barely looked; then four small leather cases. There was also a chain wrapped in newspaper, and something else in newspaper that looked like a medal or decoration.... He distributed them among the pockets of his overcoat and trousers, trying to make them as inconspicuous as possible. He took the purse too. Then he left his room, leaving the door open. He walked quickly and purposefully, and though he felt shattered, his mind was clear. He was afraid of pursuit, afraid that within the next half hour -- the next quarter hour, perhaps -- orders would be issued to track him down. He had to destroy all traces before then. He had to do it while he still had some strength, some capacity for reasoning left.... Where should he go?

That had been decided long ago: "Throw everything in the canal -- all traces gone in the water, end of story." He had decided this during his night of delirium, when he kept feeling the urge to get up and go, to hurry, to get rid of it all. But getting rid of it turned out to be much harder than he'd thought. He wandered along the Yekaterininsky Canal for half an hour or more, eyeing the steps that led down to the water, but he couldn't bring himself to do it. Either there were rafts moored at the steps where women were washing clothes, or boats were tied up and people were swarming everywhere. Besides, he could be seen from the embankments on all sides. It would look suspicious -- a man going down to the water on purpose, stopping, and throwing something in. And what if the boxes floated instead of sinking? They certainly would. As it was, everyone he passed seemed to be staring at him, turning to look, as if they had nothing better to do than watch him. "Why? Or am I imagining it?" he thought.

Finally it occurred to him that it might be better to go to the Neva. There were fewer people there, he'd be less conspicuous, and it would be more practical in every way -- plus it was farther from here. He wondered how he could have spent a good half hour wandering in this dangerous area, anxious and agitated, without thinking of that before. And he had wasted that half hour on an irrational plan simply because he'd conceived it in his delirium! He was becoming extraordinarily absent-minded and forgetful, and he knew it. He definitely had to hurry.

He walked toward the Neva along V----- Prospect, but on the way another idea struck him. "Why the Neva? Wouldn't it be better to go somewhere far off, to the islands again, and hide the things in some secluded spot -- in a forest, under a bush -- and mark the place?" And though he felt incapable of clear judgment, the idea seemed sound. But he was not destined to get there. Coming out of V----- Prospect toward the square, he noticed on the left a passageway leading between two blank walls into a courtyard. On the right, the bare, unplastered wall of a four-story building stretched deep into the yard. On the left, a wooden fence ran parallel to it for about twenty paces before turning sharply left. It was a deserted, fenced-off area littered with rubbish of various kinds. At the far end of the yard, the corner of a low, grimy stone shed peeked out from behind the fence -- probably a coachmaker's or carpenter's workshop. The whole area near the entrance was black with coal dust. "This would be the place to dump it," he thought. Seeing no one in the yard, he slipped in and immediately noticed near the gate a sink, the kind often found in yards with lots of workmen or cab drivers. On the fence above it, someone had scrawled in chalk the familiar wit: "No loitering." All the better -- nothing suspicious about him going in here. "I'll throw it all in a pile and get out!"

Looking around once more, his hand already in his pocket, he noticed a large, rough-hewn stone against the outer wall, between the entrance and the sink, weighing perhaps sixty pounds. On the other side of the wall was the street. He could hear passersby -- always numerous in this neighborhood -- but no one could see him from the entrance, unless someone came in from the street, which could easily happen. He had to be quick.

He bent down, gripped the top of the stone firmly with both hands, and using all his strength rolled it over. Under the stone was a small hollow in the ground. He immediately emptied his pockets into it. The purse sat on top, and the hollow still wasn't full. Then he gripped the stone again and with a single twist rolled it back into position, though it sat slightly higher than before. He scraped some dirt around it and pressed the edges down with his foot. Nothing was visible.

He went out and headed into the square. Once again an intense, almost unbearable joy swept over him for an instant, as it had at the police station. "I've buried my tracks! And who -- who would ever think of looking under that stone? It's probably been lying there since the building was built and will lie there just as many years more. And even if it were found, who would connect it to me? It's over! No evidence!" And he laughed. Yes, he remembered later that he started laughing -- a thin, nervous, silent laugh -- and went on laughing the whole time he was crossing the square. But when he reached K----- Boulevard, where two days earlier he had come upon the girl on the bench, his laughter abruptly stopped. Other thoughts crept in. He suddenly felt it would be revolting to walk past that bench where he'd sat and brooded after the girl left, and equally hateful to run into that mustachioed policeman he'd given twenty kopecks to. "Damn him!"

He walked on, looking around him angrily and distractedly. All his thoughts now seemed to be circling around a single point, and he felt there really was such a point, and that now -- right now -- he was standing face to face with it. For the first time, truly, in the last two months.

"Damn it all!" he thought suddenly, in a fit of uncontrollable rage. "If it's begun, then it's begun. To hell with the new life! God, how stupid it all is!... And the lies I told today! How pathetically I groveled before that miserable Ilya Petrovich! But that's all nonsense! What do I care about any of them, or about my groveling! That's not it at all! Not it at all!"
He stopped suddenly. A new, utterly unexpected, and extremely simple question had struck him, leaving him baffled and bitterly confounded.

"If this whole thing was really done deliberately and not like an idiot, if I really had a definite purpose, then how is it that I never even looked inside the purse and don't know what I got -- what I went through all this agony for, what I deliberately undertook this vile, filthy, degrading act for? And just now I was about to throw the purse into the water along with everything else, without even looking at it... How is that possible?"

Yes, that was how it was. All exactly so. And yet he had known this before -- it wasn't a new question for him -- even when he had decided in the night, without hesitation or deliberation, as though it had to be that way, as though it couldn't be otherwise.... Yes, he had known it all and understood it all. It had surely been settled yesterday, at the very moment he was bending over the strongbox and pulling out the jewel cases.... Yes, exactly so.

"It's because I'm very sick," he finally decided grimly. "I've been tormenting myself, working myself into a frenzy, and I don't know what I'm doing.... Yesterday and the day before and all this time I've been driving myself crazy.... I'll get well and stop worrying.... But what if I don't get well at all? God, I'm so sick of all of it!"

He kept walking without rest. He desperately wanted some kind of distraction but didn't know what to do, what to try. A new, overpowering sensation was taking hold of him more completely with every passing minute: an immeasurable, almost physical revulsion for everything around him -- a stubborn, malignant hatred. Everyone he met disgusted him -- their faces, their movements, their gestures. If anyone had spoken to him, he felt he might have spat in their face or bitten them....

He stopped suddenly as he came out on the bank of the Little Neva, near the bridge to Vasilyevsky Island. "He lives here, in that building," he thought. "So I haven't come to Razumikhin on purpose? It's the same thing again.... Very interesting, though -- did I come here deliberately or did I just wander here by accident? Never mind. I said the day before yesterday that I'd go see him the day _after_ -- well, here I am! Besides, I really can't walk any farther."
He went up to Razumikhin's room on the fifth floor.

Razumikhin was home in his garret, writing at that moment, and opened the door himself. It had been four months since they'd seen each other. Razumikhin was sitting in a tattered dressing gown, slippers on bare feet, uncombed, unshaved, unwashed. His face registered surprise.

"Is that you?" he cried. He looked his friend up and down; then after a brief pause, whistled. "Things that bad? You've outdone even me, brother!" he added, taking in Raskolnikov's rags. "Come on, sit down -- you must be exhausted."
When Raskolnikov sank onto the American leather sofa, which was in even worse shape than his own, Razumikhin immediately saw that his visitor was sick.
"You're seriously ill -- you know that?" He began feeling his pulse. Raskolnikov pulled his hand away.
"Never mind," he said. "I came to... I have no lessons.... I wanted, but... I don't really want lessons...."
"Listen, you're delirious!" Razumikhin said, watching him carefully.
"No, I'm not."

Raskolnikov got up from the sofa. Climbing the stairs to Razumikhin's, he hadn't realized how much he dreaded coming face to face with his friend. Now, in a flash, he understood that what he wanted least in the entire world at this moment was to be face to face with anyone. Bile rose inside him. He nearly choked with rage at himself the instant he crossed Razumikhin's threshold.
"Goodbye," he said abruptly, and walked toward the door.
"Wait, wait! You strange creature."
"I don't want to," the other said, pulling his hand away again.
"Then what the hell did you come for? Are you out of your mind? This is... almost insulting! I'm not letting you go like this."

"Fine, then -- I came because I know no one but you who could help... to start... because you're kinder than anyone -- smarter, I mean -- and can think things through... and now I see I don't need anything. Do you hear? Nothing at all... nobody's help... nobody's sympathy. I'm on my own... alone. Enough. Leave me alone."

"Hold on, you lunatic! You're absolutely raving. Do what you want, for all I care. Listen -- I don't have any teaching work either, and I don't care, but there's a bookseller named Kheruvimov, and he's as good as a whole batch of lessons. I wouldn't trade him for five. He does a kind of publishing -- puts out natural science pamphlets -- and what sales they get! The titles alone are worth the price! You always said I was a fool, but believe me, brother, there are bigger fools than me! Now this Kheruvimov has decided to be progressive -- not that he understands the first thing about it, but I encourage him naturally. Here are two printer's sheets of a German text -- in my opinion, the crudest charlatanism. It discusses the question 'Is Woman a Human Being?' and, of course, triumphantly proves that she is. Kheruvimov is going to publish this as a contribution to the women's question. I'm translating it. He'll stretch the two and a half sheets to six, we'll slap on a gorgeous half-page title, and sell it for fifty kopecks. It'll go! He pays me six rubles a sheet, which comes to about fifteen for the whole thing, and I've already had six in advance. When we finish this, we're starting on a translation about whales, and then some of the most tedious gossip from Part Two of the _Confessions_ -- we've already marked the passages. Somebody told Kheruvimov that Rousseau was a kind of Radishchev. I certainly don't contradict him -- to hell with him! So, do you want to do the second sheet of 'Is Woman a Human Being?' If you do, take the German text, some pens and paper -- they're all provided -- and take three rubles. Since I got six in advance for the whole thing, three of those are yours. When you finish the sheet, there'll be another three rubles. And don't think I'm doing you a favor -- on the contrary, the moment you walked in I saw how you could help me. First, my spelling is terrible, and second, my German sometimes goes completely off the rails, so I mostly just make things up. The only consolation is that it's probably an improvement. Though who knows -- maybe sometimes it's worse. Will you take it?"

Raskolnikov silently took the German pages, took the three rubles, and without a word walked out. Razumikhin stared after him in astonishment. But when Raskolnikov was on the next street, he turned back, climbed the stairs to Razumikhin's again, laid the German article and the three rubles on the table, and left once more, still without a word.
"Have you lost your mind, or what?" Razumikhin shouted, finally furious. "What kind of game is this? You'll drive me crazy too... What did you come here for, damn it?"
"I don't need... any translation," Raskolnikov muttered from the staircase.
"Then what the hell do you need?" Razumikhin yelled from above. Raskolnikov continued descending in silence.
"Hey! Where do you live?"
No answer.
"Then to hell with you!"

But Raskolnikov was already on the street. On the Nikolaevsky Bridge he was jolted back to full consciousness by an unpleasant incident. A coachman, after shouting at him two or three times, gave him a vicious crack across the back with his whip -- he had nearly walked under the horses' hooves. The lash so enraged him that he leapt toward the railing (for some unknown reason he had been walking right down the middle of the bridge, in the thick of traffic). He clenched and ground his teeth in fury. He could hear laughter, of course.
"Serves him right!"
"Pickpocket, I bet."
"Pretending to be drunk, most likely, throwing himself under the wheels on purpose -- and then you're the one who has to answer for it."
"It's a whole profession, that's what it is."

But as he stood at the railing, still angry and bewildered, watching the retreating carriage and rubbing his back, he suddenly felt someone press money into his hand. He looked. It was an elderly woman in a headscarf and goatskin shoes, accompanied by a girl -- probably her daughter -- wearing a hat and carrying a green parasol.
"Take it, my good man, in Christ's name."

He took it and they walked on. It was twenty kopecks. From his clothes and appearance, they had probably taken him for a beggar -- and the gift was no doubt inspired by the lash of the whip, which made them feel sorry for him.

He closed his hand around the twenty kopecks, walked on about ten paces, and turned to face the Neva, looking toward the palace. The sky was cloudless and the water almost bright blue -- a rare sight on the Neva. The cathedral dome, seen at its best from this spot on the bridge about twenty paces from the chapel, glittered in the sunlight, and in the clean air every ornament on it was clearly visible. The sting of the lash faded, and Raskolnikov forgot about it. A single troubled, not quite definable thought now occupied him completely. He stood still and gazed long and intently into the distance. This spot was deeply familiar to him. When he was at the university, he had stood here hundreds of times -- usually on his way home -- staring at this truly magnificent view, almost always marveling at the vague and mysterious feeling it stirred in him. It had always left him strangely cold; this gorgeous panorama was somehow blank and lifeless for him. He had always wondered at this dark, enigmatic impression, and, not trusting himself, kept putting off any explanation. Now he vividly recalled those old doubts and perplexities, and it struck him as no accident that he was recalling them now. It seemed strange and grotesque that he should have stopped at the same spot as before, as if he actually imagined he could think the same thoughts, be drawn to the same ideas and images that had occupied him... so short a time ago. He found it almost amusing, and yet it wrung his heart. Deep down, hidden far away out of sight, all of that seemed to belong to the past now -- all of it: his old thoughts, his old questions and theories, his old impressions, that panorama, and he himself, and everything.... He felt as though he were rising into the air and everything were fading from view. Making an unconscious movement with his hand, he suddenly noticed the coin in his fist. He opened his hand, stared at it, and with a sweep of his arm flung it into the water. Then he turned and headed home. He felt as though he had cut himself off from everyone and everything at that moment.

It was evening by the time he got home, so he must have been walking for about six hours. How or by what route he returned, he couldn't remember. He undressed, trembling like an exhausted horse, lay down on the sofa, pulled his overcoat over himself, and immediately sank into oblivion....
He was awakened at dusk by a terrible scream. My God, what a scream! He had never heard such unnatural sounds -- such howling, wailing, grinding, tears, blows, and curses.

He could never have imagined such brutality, such frenzy. He sat up in bed in terror, nearly fainting from anguish. But the fighting, wailing, and cursing grew louder and louder. Then, to his intense amazement, he recognized his landlady's voice. She was howling, shrieking, and wailing -- rapidly, frantically, incoherently -- so that he couldn't make out what she was saying. She was begging, clearly -- begging not to be beaten, for she was being beaten mercilessly on the stairs. Her attacker's voice was so horrible with spite and rage that it was more of a rasp than a voice, but he too was saying something, just as fast and unintelligibly, rushing and sputtering. Suddenly Raskolnikov began to tremble. He recognized the voice -- it was Ilya Petrovich's. Ilya Petrovich was here, beating the landlady! He was kicking her, slamming her head against the steps -- that was clear from the sounds, the cries, the thuds. How could this be? Had the world turned upside down? He could hear people running from every floor and every staircase -- voices, exclamations, knocking, doors slamming. "But why, why -- how is this possible?" he kept repeating, seriously thinking he had gone mad. But no, he could hear it all too clearly! And then they would come for him next. "Because obviously... it's all about _that_... about yesterday.... My God!" He wanted to bolt his door, but he couldn't lift his arm... and besides, it would be pointless. Terror gripped his heart like ice, tortured him, numbed him.... But finally, after about ten minutes, the uproar gradually began to subside. The landlady moaned and groaned; Ilya Petrovich still made threats and cursed.... But at last he too seemed to fall silent, and then he was gone. "Has he really left? Dear God!" Yes, and now the landlady was leaving too, still weeping and moaning... then her door slammed.... The crowd was dispersing from the stairs back to their rooms -- exclaiming, arguing, calling to one another, their voices rising to shouts, dropping to whispers. There must have been a great many of them -- practically everyone in the building. "But, God, how can this be? And why -- why had he come here?"

Raskolnikov sank back onto the sofa, drained, but couldn't close his eyes. He lay there for half an hour in such anguish, such an unbearable sensation of infinite terror, as he had never known before. Suddenly a bright light filled his room. Nastasya came in with a candle and a plate of soup. After looking at him carefully and determining he was not asleep, she set the candle on the table and began laying out what she'd brought -- bread, salt, a plate, a spoon.
"You haven't eaten since yesterday, I'll bet. You've been wandering around all day and you're burning up with fever."
"Nastasya... why were they beating the landlady?"
She looked at him intently.
"Who beat the landlady?"
"Just now... half an hour ago. Ilya Petrovich, the assistant superintendent, on the stairs.... Why was he doing that to her, and... why was he here?"
Nastasya studied him silently, frowning. The scrutiny went on for a long time. He felt uneasy, even frightened by her searching gaze.
"Nastasya, why aren't you saying anything?" he asked timidly at last, in a weak voice.
"It's the blood," she finally answered softly, as though talking to herself.
"Blood? What blood?" he mumbled, going white and turning toward the wall.
Nastasya continued to look at him without speaking.
"Nobody has beaten the landlady," she declared at last, firmly and resolutely.
He stared at her, barely able to breathe.

"I heard it myself.... I wasn't asleep... I was sitting up," he said, even more timidly. "I listened for a long time. The assistant superintendent came.... Everyone ran out onto the stairs from every apartment."
"Nobody's been here. That's the blood crying out in your ears. When it has nowhere to go and starts clotting, you begin seeing things.... Are you going to eat something?"
He didn't answer. Nastasya stood over him, watching.
"Give me something to drink... Nastasya."
She went downstairs and came back with a white ceramic jug of water. He remembered only swallowing one sip of cold water and spilling some on his neck. Then came oblivion.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He was not completely unconscious the entire time he was sick. He was in a feverish state -- sometimes delirious, sometimes half-aware. He remembered a great deal afterward. At times it seemed as though a crowd of people surrounded him, wanting to carry him off somewhere, arguing and fighting about him. Then he would be alone in the room. Everyone had left, afraid of him, opening the door just a crack now and then to peek at him. They threatened him, plotted against him, laughed at him, mocked him. He remembered Nastasya often at his bedside. He could make out another person too -- someone he seemed to know well but couldn't identify, and this tormented him, even brought him to tears. Sometimes he thought he had been lying there for a month; at other times everything seemed like part of a single day. But about _that_ -- about _that_ -- he had no memory at all, though every minute he felt he had forgotten something he desperately needed to remember. He tormented himself trying to recall it, moaned, flew into rages, or sank into horrible, unbearable terror.
