Then he would struggle to get up, try to run away, but someone always held him back by force, and he would collapse again into helplessness and oblivion. At last he returned to full consciousness.

It was ten in the morning. On clear days the sun shone into the room at that hour, casting a stripe of light across the right wall and the corner near the door. Nastasya was standing beside him with another person, a complete stranger, who was examining him with great curiosity. He was a young man with a beard, wearing a short-waisted coat -- he looked like a messenger. The landlady was peering in through the half-open door. Raskolnikov sat up.
"Who is that, Nastasya?" he asked, pointing at the young man.
"Look, he's come around!" she said.
"He's come around," the man echoed.

Concluding that Raskolnikov had regained his senses, the landlady closed the door and vanished. She was always shy and dreaded conversations and confrontations. She was a woman of forty, not bad-looking, plump and full-figured, with dark eyes and eyebrows -- good-natured in the way that plump, lazy people tend to be, and absurdly bashful.
"Who... are you?" he continued, addressing the man. But at that moment the door burst open and Razumikhin came in, ducking slightly because of his height.
"What a cabin this is!" he cried. "I'm always banging my head. You call this a room? So you're conscious, brother? Just heard the news from Pashenka."
"He just came around," Nastasya said.
"Just came around," the man echoed with a smile.

"And who might you be?" Razumikhin asked, suddenly turning to him. "My name is Vrazumikhin, by the way -- not Razumikhin, as everyone calls me -- I'm a student and a gentleman. And he's my friend. So who are you?"
"I'm a messenger from our firm, the merchant Shelopaev's office, and I've come on business."

"Please sit down." Razumikhin seated himself on the other side of the table. "It's great that you've come to, brother," he went on, turning to Raskolnikov. "You've barely eaten or drunk anything for four days. We had to give you tea by the spoonful. I brought Zossimov to see you twice. Remember Zossimov? He examined you thoroughly and said right away it was nothing serious -- something seemed to have gone to your head. Some kind of nervous breakdown from bad nutrition -- he says you haven't had enough beer and horseradish -- but it's nothing much, it'll pass and you'll be fine. Zossimov's a first-rate fellow! He's really making a name for himself. Anyway, I won't keep you," he said, turning back to the messenger. "What's your business? You should know, Rodya, this is the second time they've sent someone from that office. It was a different man last time -- I spoke with him. Who was it?"
"That was the day before yesterday, if you please, sir. That was Alexei Semyonovich. He's from our office too."
"He was more articulate than you, don't you think?"
"Yes indeed, sir, he carries more weight than I do."
"Fair enough. Go on."

"At your mother's request, through Afanasy Ivanovich Vakhrushin -- of whom I presume you've heard more than once -- a remittance has been sent to you from our office," the man began, addressing Raskolnikov. "If you're in a... lucid state, I have thirty-five rubles to deliver, as Semyon Semyonovich has received instructions from Afanasy Ivanovich, at your mother's request, to that effect -- same as on previous occasions. Do you know him, sir?"
"Yes, I remember... Vakhrushin," Raskolnikov said dreamily.
"You hear that? He knows Vakhrushin!" Razumikhin exclaimed. "He's in a 'lucid state'! And I can see you're a sharp fellow yourself. Well, it's always nice to hear words of wisdom."

"That is the gentleman -- Vakhrushin, Afanasy Ivanovich. And at your mother's request, who previously sent you a remittance through him in the same manner, he did not decline this time either, and sent instructions to Semyon Semyonovich some days ago to hand you thirty-five rubles, in the hope of better things to come."
"That 'hoping for better things to come' is the best part, though 'your mother' is nice too. So, what do you say? Is he fully conscious?"
"That seems fine. If he could just sign this little form."
"He can scrawl his name. Do you have the book?"
"Yes, here it is."
"Give it here. Come on, Rodya, sit up. I'll hold you. Take the pen and sign 'Raskolnikov' for him. Because right now, brother, money is sweeter to us than honey."
"I don't want it," Raskolnikov said, pushing the pen away.
"Don't want it?"
"I won't sign."
"How the hell can we manage without your signature?"
"I don't want... the money."

"Don't want money! Come on, brother, that's ridiculous. I'm a witness. Don't worry about it, he's just drifting off again. He does that all the time though.... You're a sensible man -- we'll handle him, or rather, we'll just take his hand and he'll sign. Here."
"I could come back another time."
"No, no, why should we trouble you? You're a sensible man.... Now, Rodya, don't keep your visitor waiting -- he has things to do." And he got ready to hold Raskolnikov's hand himself.
"Stop. I'll do it myself," Raskolnikov said, taking the pen and signing his name.
The messenger took out the money and left.
"Excellent! Now then, brother -- are you hungry?"
"Yes," Raskolnikov answered.
"Is there any soup?"
"Some from yesterday," Nastasya answered, still standing nearby.
"With potatoes and rice?"
"Yes."
"I know it by heart. Bring the soup and make us some tea."
"All right."
Raskolnikov watched all this with deep astonishment and a dull, unreasoning dread. He decided to stay quiet and see what happened. "I don't think I'm delirious. I think this is real," he thought.

In a couple of minutes Nastasya returned with the soup and announced that the tea would be ready shortly. Along with the soup she brought two spoons, two plates, salt, pepper, mustard for the beef, and so on. The table was set as it hadn't been in ages. The cloth was clean.
"It wouldn't hurt, Nastasya, if Praskovya Pavlovna sent up a couple of bottles of beer. We could make short work of them."
"Well, aren't you something!" Nastasya muttered, and went off to fulfill his orders.

Raskolnikov continued to stare in wild bewilderment. Meanwhile Razumikhin sat down on the sofa beside him, clumsy as a bear, put his left arm around Raskolnikov's head -- though the patient could sit up perfectly well on his own -- and with his right hand brought a spoonful of soup to his lips, blowing on it first so it wouldn't burn. But the soup was only lukewarm. Raskolnikov swallowed one spoonful eagerly, then a second, then a third. But after a few more, Razumikhin suddenly stopped and said he should check with Zossimov about whether to give him more.
Nastasya came in with two bottles of beer.
"Want some tea?"
"Yes."

"Run along and bring the tea, Nastasya. I think we can venture tea without the doctor's permission. But here's the beer!" He moved back to his chair, pulled the soup and meat in front of himself, and began eating as though he hadn't touched food in three days.

"I should tell you, Rodya, I eat dinner here like this every day now," he said with his mouth full. "It's all thanks to Pashenka -- your dear little landlady -- she insists on feeding me. I don't ask for it, but naturally I don't refuse either. And here's Nastasya with the tea. Quick work! Nastasya, my dear, want some beer?"
"Oh, get on with you!"
"Cup of tea, then?"
"A cup of tea, maybe."
"Pour it out. Wait, I'll pour it myself. Sit down."

He poured two cups, abandoned his dinner, and sat back down on the sofa. As before, he put his left arm around the sick man's head, propped him up, and fed him tea by the spoonful, blowing on each one steadily and earnestly, as though this procedure were the principal and most effective means of his friend's recovery. Raskolnikov said nothing and offered no resistance, though he felt strong enough to sit up on the sofa without support and could easily have held a cup or spoon himself -- perhaps even walked around. But out of some strange, almost animal cunning, he hit on the idea of concealing his strength and lying low for the time being, pretending if necessary that he still wasn't fully in command of his faculties, while listening to find out what was going on. Yet he couldn't overcome his revulsion. After swallowing a dozen spoonfuls of tea, he suddenly pulled his head free, pushed the spoon away with a petulant gesture, and sank back onto the pillow. There were actual pillows under his head now -- real down pillows in clean cases. He noticed this too, and took note of it.
"Pashenka should send us some raspberry jam today so we can make him raspberry tea," said Razumikhin, returning to his chair and attacking his soup and beer.
"And where's she supposed to get raspberries for you?" Nastasya asked, balancing a saucer on her five spread fingers and sipping tea through a lump of sugar.

"At the shop, my dear. You see, Rodya, all kinds of things happened while you were out of commission. When you bolted like that without leaving your address, I got so angry I decided to track you down and teach you a lesson. I started that very day. The running around I did, the inquiries I made! This apartment of yours -- I'd forgotten it, though in fact I never knew it in the first place. And as for your previous place, I could only remember it was somewhere at Five Corners, in Kharlamov's building. I kept looking for this Kharlamov's building, and it turned out it wasn't Kharlamov's at all, but Bukh's. You know how you muddle up names sometimes! Anyway, I lost my temper and went to the address bureau the next day, just on the off chance. And guess what -- in two minutes they looked you up! Your name's on file."
"My name!"

"Naturally. Though they couldn't find some General Kobelev while I was there. Well, it's a long story. But the moment I tracked down this place, I got to know all your affairs -- all of them, brother, every last one. Nastasya can vouch for that. I met Nikodim Fomich and Ilya Petrovich, and the building porter, and Mr. Zametov -- Alexander Grigorievich, the head clerk at the police station -- and last but not least, Pashenka. Nastasya knows...."
"He charmed her," Nastasya murmured with a sly smile.
"Why don't you put the sugar in your tea, Nastasya Nikiforovna?"
"Oh, you!" Nastasya suddenly burst into giggles. "It's not Nikiforovna, it's Petrovna," she added, recovering from her fit of laughter.

"Duly noted. Well, brother, to make a long story short, I was all set to launch a full-scale offensive here -- to root out all malicious influences in the area. But Pashenka won the day. I hadn't expected, brother, to find her so... appealing. Eh? What do you think?"
Raskolnikov didn't speak, but kept his eyes fixed on Razumikhin, full of anxiety.
"Quite commendable, indeed, in every respect," Razumikhin went on, not the least embarrassed by his silence.
"Oh, the sly fox!" Nastasya shrieked again. This conversation was giving her unspeakable pleasure.

"It's a shame, brother, that you didn't go about things the right way from the start. You should have handled her differently. She's an... unusual character, let's say. But we'll talk about her character later.... How did you let things get so bad that she stopped sending up your dinner? And that IOU? You must have been out of your mind to sign an IOU. And that marriage promise, when her daughter Natalya Yegorovna was still alive?... I know all about it! But I can see it's a sensitive subject and I'm being an idiot. Forgive me. But speaking of foolishness -- do you know that Praskovya Pavlovna isn't nearly as foolish as she seems at first glance?"
"No," Raskolnikov mumbled, looking away, but feeling it was better to keep the conversation going.

"She isn't, right?" Razumikhin cried, delighted to get an answer. "But she's not exactly brilliant either, is she? She's fundamentally an... unpredictable character! I'm completely at a loss with her sometimes, I swear.... She must be forty. She says thirty-six, and of course she has every right. But I swear I judge her purely on an intellectual basis, from a sort of metaphysical standpoint. There's some kind of symbolism that's sprung up between us, a kind of algebra or something! I don't understand it myself! Well, that's all nonsense. The point is, since you're no longer a student and have lost your lessons and your decent clothes, and since the young lady's death means she no longer needs to treat you as family, she suddenly got scared. And since you holed up in your den and cut off all contact with her, she decided to get rid of you. She'd been considering it for a while but hated to lose that IOU, because you'd told her yourself that your mother would pay."
"That was low of me to say.... My mother is practically a beggar herself... and I lied to keep my room... and get fed," Raskolnikov said loudly and clearly.

"Yes, that was sensible enough. But the trouble is, at that point a Mr. Chebarov enters the picture -- a businessman. Pashenka would never have taken action on her own. She's too timid. But the businessman is anything but timid, and the first thing he does is ask: 'Is there any chance of collecting on this IOU?' Answer: yes, because the debtor has a mother who'd save her Rodya with her hundred-and-twenty-five-ruble pension even if she had to starve, and a sister who'd sell herself into bondage for his sake. That's what he was counting on.... Why are you flinching? I know every detail of your affairs now, my dear boy -- it's not for nothing that you were so open with Pashenka when you were her prospective son-in-law. I say all this as a friend.... But here's the thing: an honest, sensitive person opens up, and a businessman 'listens and goes on eating you alive.' So she signed the IOU over to this Chebarov as payment, and he promptly filed a formal demand. When I heard about all this, I wanted to blow him up too, just to clear my conscience. But by then Pashenka and I were on excellent terms, and I arranged to stop the whole thing by guaranteeing you'd pay. I vouched for you, brother. You understand? We called in Chebarov, threw him ten rubles, and got the IOU back. And now I have the honor of presenting it to you. She trusts your word now. Here -- take it. You can see I've already torn it up."
Razumikhin laid the note on the table. Raskolnikov glanced at it and turned to the wall without a word. Even Razumikhin felt a pang.
"I see, brother," he said after a moment, "that I've been playing the fool again. I thought I'd cheer you up with my chatter, but I think I've only irritated you."
"Was it you I couldn't recognize when I was delirious?" Raskolnikov asked after a moment's pause, without turning his head.
"Yes, and you flew into a rage about it, especially when I brought Zametov one day."
"Zametov? The head clerk? What for?" Raskolnikov spun around and fixed his eyes on Razumikhin.

"What's wrong?... What are you so upset about? He wanted to meet you because I'd told him a lot about you.... Who else could I have gotten all my information from? He's a great fellow, brother, first-rate... in his own way, of course. We're friends now -- see each other almost every day. I've moved to this part of town, you know. Just moved. I've been to Luise Ivanovna's once or twice with him.... You remember Luise? Luise Ivanovna?"
"Did I say anything while I was delirious?"
"You certainly did! You were out of your mind."
"What did I rave about?"
"What do you mean, what? What people always rave about.... Well, brother, enough of that -- back to work." He got up from the table and reached for his cap.
"What did I rave about?"

"He won't let it go! Worried you gave away some secret? Don't fret -- you said nothing about any countess. But you went on quite a bit about a bulldog, and about earrings and chains, and about Krestovsky Island, and some porter, and Nikodim Fomich and Ilya Petrovich, the assistant superintendent. And something else you were especially fixated on was your own sock. You kept whining: 'Give me my sock.' Zametov searched your whole room for your socks, and with his own perfumed, ring-covered fingers he handed you the rag. Only then did you calm down, and for the next twenty-four hours you clutched the wretched thing in your fist. We couldn't pry it away from you. It's probably still under your blanket somewhere. And then you kept begging pitifully for some fringe for your trousers. We tried to figure out what kind of fringe, but we couldn't make any sense of it. Well -- to business! Here are the thirty-five rubles. I'm taking ten and will give you a full accounting in an hour or two. I'll let Zossimov know at the same time -- he should have been here already, since it's nearly noon. And you, Nastasya, look in on him fairly often while I'm gone, in case he needs a drink or anything. I'll tell Pashenka what's needed on my way out. Goodbye!"

"He calls her Pashenka! What a smooth talker!" Nastasya said as he left. Then she opened the door and stood listening, but couldn't resist running downstairs after him. She was dying to hear what he'd say to the landlady. She was clearly completely charmed by Razumikhin.

The moment she left the room, the sick man threw off the blankets and leapt out of bed like a madman. He had been waiting with burning, agonized impatience for them to leave so he could get to work. But what work? Now, as if to spite him, it escaped him.

"God, just tell me one thing: do they know yet or not? What if they know and are just pretending, mocking me while I lie here sick -- and then they'll walk in and announce that it was discovered long ago and they've just been... What do I do now? That's what I've forgotten -- forgot it on purpose. I remembered a minute ago...."

He stood in the middle of the room and looked around in miserable bewilderment. He went to the door, opened it, listened -- but that wasn't it. Suddenly, as if remembering something, he rushed to the corner where the hole was behind the wallpaper. He examined it, thrust his hand in, felt around -- but that wasn't it either. He went to the stove, opened it, rummaged through the ashes. The frayed scraps from his trousers and the rags of the pocket lining were lying there, just as he'd thrown them. Nobody had looked! Then he remembered the sock Razumikhin had just been telling him about. Yes, there it was on the sofa under the blanket, but so covered with dust and grime that Zametov couldn't possibly have noticed anything.

"Right, Zametov! The police station! And why was I summoned to the police station? Where's the notice? Wait -- I'm mixing things up. That was before. I examined my sock then too, but now... now I've been sick. But what was Zametov doing here? Why did Razumikhin bring him?" he muttered, sinking helplessly onto the sofa. "What does it mean? Am I still delirious, or is this real? I think it's real.... Ah, I remember -- I have to escape! I have to escape right now! Yes, I must, I must escape! But... where? And where are my clothes? My boots are gone. They've taken them! Hidden them! I see! Ah, here's my coat -- they missed that! And here's money on the table, thank God! And here's the IOU... I'll take the money and go, rent another room. They won't find me!... Yes, but the address bureau? They'll find me. Razumikhin will find me. Better to escape completely... far away... to America, and let them do their worst! And take the IOU... it might be useful there.... What else should I take? They think I'm sick! They don't know I can walk -- ha ha ha! I could tell by their eyes that they know everything! If only I could get downstairs! But what if they've posted a guard -- policemen! What's this, tea? Ah, and here's beer left -- half a bottle, cold!"

He grabbed the bottle, which still held a glassful, and gulped it down with relish, as if putting out a fire in his chest. But within a minute the beer went to his head, and a faint, almost pleasant shiver ran down his spine. He lay down and pulled the blanket over himself. His sick, incoherent thoughts grew increasingly fragmented, and soon a light, pleasant drowsiness came over him. With a feeling of comfort he nestled his head into the pillow, wrapped himself more snugly in the soft, padded quilt that had replaced the old, tattered overcoat, sighed softly, and sank into a deep, sound, restorative sleep.

He woke to the sound of someone coming in. He opened his eyes and saw Razumikhin in the doorway, hesitating about whether to enter. Raskolnikov sat up quickly and stared at him as if trying to remember something.
"Ah, you're awake! Here I am! Nastasya, bring up the parcel!" Razumikhin shouted down the stairs. "I'll give you the full accounting in a moment."
"What time is it?" Raskolnikov asked, looking around anxiously.
"You had a great sleep, brother. It's nearly evening -- must be close to six. You slept more than six hours."
"Good Lord! Did I?"

"And why not? It's good for you. What's the rush? Got a date? We have all the time in the world. I've been waiting three hours for you to wake up. Came up twice and found you asleep. Went to Zossimov's twice -- he wasn't home, imagine that! But never mind, he'll show up. I've also been out on my own business -- moved today, you know, with my uncle. I have an uncle staying with me now. But never mind that -- let's get down to it. Hand me that parcel, Nastasya. Now then... how are you feeling, brother?"
"I'm fine. I'm not sick. Razumikhin, have you been here long?"
"I told you -- three hours, waiting."
"No, before that."
"What do you mean?"
"How long have you been coming here?"
"But I explained everything this morning. Don't you remember?"
Raskolnikov thought about it. The morning seemed like a dream. He couldn't piece it together on his own and looked at Razumikhin questioningly.

"Hmm!" said Razumikhin. "He's forgotten. I suspected at the time you weren't quite yourself. But now you're better after your sleep.... You really do look much better. Excellent! Well, to business. Look at this, my friend."
He began unwrapping a bundle that clearly interested him greatly.

"Believe me, brother, this is a matter close to my heart. We have to make you presentable. Let's start from the top. See this cap?" He pulled from the bundle a fairly decent, though cheap and ordinary, cap. "Let me try it on you."
"Later, not now," Raskolnikov said, waving it away irritably.

"Come on, Rodya, don't fight me -- later will be too late. And I won't sleep tonight, because I bought it by guesswork, without measuring. Perfect!" he cried triumphantly, fitting it on. "Just your size! A proper hat is the first requirement of a wardrobe and a recommendation in itself. My friend Tolstyakov has to take off his absurd pudding-basin hat every time he enters any public place where others are wearing theirs. People think he does it out of servile politeness, but it's simply because he's ashamed of the thing. He's such a vain fellow! Look, Nastasya -- here are two specimens of headgear: this Palmerston" -- he picked up Raskolnikov's old, battered hat from the corner, calling it a "Palmerston" for some unknown reason -- "or this gem! Guess the price, Rodya. What do you think I paid, Nastasya?" He turned to her, seeing that Raskolnikov wasn't responding.
"Twenty kopecks, no more," Nastasya guessed.

"Twenty kopecks! Don't be silly!" he cried, offended. "Nowadays even you would cost more than that -- eighty kopecks! And that's only because it's been worn. Plus there's a guarantee: when it wears out, they give you a new one next year. On my word! Now, let us proceed to the United States of America, as we used to call them in school. I'm actually proud of these trousers." He showed Raskolnikov a pair of light summer trousers in gray wool. "No holes, no stains, and perfectly respectable, though slightly worn. And a matching waistcoat, quite fashionable. And the fact that it's been worn is actually an improvement -- it's softer, smoother.... You see, Rodya, the great secret to getting along in the world is to always stick with the season. If you don't insist on asparagus in January, you keep money in your pocket -- and it's the same principle here. It's summer now, so I bought summer things. Warmer fabrics will be needed for autumn, and you'll have to throw these away by then anyway -- they'll have fallen apart on their own, if not from your elevated standards. So guess the price! What do you say? Two rubles and twenty-five kopecks! And remember the guarantee: wear them out and you get a new pair free! That's how they do business at Fedyaev's. Buy once and you're set for life -- because you'll never voluntarily go back. Now the boots. What do you say? A little worn, sure, but they'll last a couple of months -- foreign craftsmanship, foreign leather. The secretary of the English embassy sold them last week, after only six days of wear -- he was desperately short of cash. Price: one ruble fifty. A bargain?"
"But maybe they won't fit," Nastasya observed.

"Won't fit? Look at this!" He pulled Raskolnikov's old, broken boot from his pocket, caked with dried mud. "I didn't go empty-handed -- they took the measurements from this monstrosity. We all pitched in. And as for your linens -- your landlady took care of that. Here, to start with, are three shirts -- hemp fabric, but with a fashionable front.... So then: eighty kopecks for the cap, two rubles twenty-five for the suit -- total three rubles five kopecks; a ruble fifty for the boots -- really excellent quality, mind you -- that's four rubles fifty-five kopecks; five rubles for the underclothes -- bought as a set -- which makes exactly nine rubles fifty-five kopecks. Forty-five kopecks change in coppers. Want them? So there you go, Rodya -- a complete new outfit, because your overcoat still works and even has a certain style. That's what you get from shopping at Sharmer's! As for socks and such, I'll leave that to you. We still have twenty-five rubles. Don't worry about Pashenka or your rent -- I told you, she'll extend you unlimited credit. Now, brother, let me change your shirt, because I think you might shake off your illness along with it."
"Leave me alone! I don't want to!" Raskolnikov waved him off. He had been listening to Razumikhin's playful account of his purchases with disgust.

"Come on, brother, don't tell me I ran around for nothing," Razumikhin insisted. "Nastasya, don't be shy -- help me. That's it." And despite Raskolnikov's resistance, he changed his shirt. The patient sank back on the pillows and said nothing for a minute or two.
"They'll be a long time getting rid of these people," he thought. "What money was all that bought with?" he finally asked, staring at the wall.
"Money? Why, your own! The messenger from Vakhrushin brought it -- your mother sent it. Have you forgotten that too?"
"I remember now," Raskolnikov said after a long, sullen silence. Razumikhin looked at him with a frown, uneasy.
The door opened and a tall, heavyset man came in -- someone whose appearance struck Raskolnikov as familiar.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Zossimov was a tall, heavyset man with a puffy, pale, clean-shaven face and straight flaxen hair. He wore spectacles and a large gold ring on his thick finger. He was twenty-seven. He had on a light grey, fashionable loose coat and light summer trousers -- everything about him was loose, fashionable, and immaculate. His linen was spotless, his watch chain heavy. His manner was slow and seemingly nonchalant, yet he clearly worked hard at appearing casual. He tried to conceal his self-importance, but it showed through at every moment. Everyone who knew him found him tedious but acknowledged he was good at his job.
"I have been to see you twice today, brother. Look -- he has come around," Razumihin called out.
"I see, I see. And how are we feeling now, eh?" Zossimov asked Raskolnikov, watching him carefully. He sat down at the foot of the sofa and made himself as comfortable as he could.
"He is still down," Razumihin went on. "We just changed his linen and he nearly cried."
"That is perfectly natural. You could have put it off if he did not want it.... His pulse is excellent. Is your head still hurting, eh?"

"I am fine, I am perfectly fine!" Raskolnikov declared firmly and irritably. He sat up on the sofa and looked at them with glittering eyes, but sank back onto the pillow at once and turned toward the wall. Zossimov watched him intently.
"Very good.... Coming along nicely," he said lazily. "Has he eaten anything?"
They told him, and asked what he could have.

"He can have anything... soup, tea... mushrooms and cucumbers, of course, you must not give him. No meat either, and... but you know all that!" Razumihin and Zossimov exchanged a look. "No more medicine or anything. I will check on him again tomorrow. Maybe even today... but never mind."
"Tomorrow evening I am taking him for a walk," said Razumihin. "We are going to the Yusupov Garden and then to the Palais de Cristal."
"I would not disturb him tomorrow at all, but I do not know... a little, maybe... we will see."

"What a nuisance! I am having a housewarming tonight -- it is just a step from here. Could he come? He could lie on the sofa. You are coming?" Razumihin said to Zossimov. "Do not forget, you promised."
"All right, but later. What are you planning?"
"Oh, nothing -- tea, vodka, herring. There will be a pie... just friends."
"And who?"
"All neighbors, almost all new friends, except my old uncle, and he is new here too -- he only arrived in Petersburg yesterday on some business. We see each other once every five years."
"What does he do?"

"He has been stagnating his whole life as a district postmaster. Gets a small pension. He is sixty-five -- not worth talking about.... But I am fond of him. Porfiry Petrovitch, the head of the Investigation Department here... But you know him."
"Is he a relative of yours too?"
"A very distant one. But why are you scowling? Just because you quarreled once, you will not come?"
"I could not care less about him."
"Even better. Well, there will be some students, a teacher, a government clerk, a musician, an officer, and Zametov."
"Tell me, please, what could you or he" -- Zossimov nodded at Raskolnikov -- "possibly have in common with this Zametov?"

"Oh, you and your principles! You run on principles like clockwork -- you will not even turn around on your own. If a man is a good fellow, that is the only principle I need. Zametov is a delightful person."
"Even though he takes bribes."

"Well, he does! So what? I do not care if he takes bribes," Razumihin cried with unnatural irritability. "I am not praising him for taking bribes. I only say he is a decent man in his own way! But if you look at people from every angle -- how many good ones are left? I am sure I myself would not be worth a baked onion... maybe with you thrown in."
"That is too little. I would give two for you."

"And I would not give more than one for you. Enough jokes! Zametov is just a boy. I can ruffle his hair, and the point is to draw him closer, not push him away. You never improve a person by rejecting him, especially a young one. You have to be twice as careful with a young person. Oh, you progressive blockheads! You do not understand. You only hurt yourselves by tearing other people down.... But if you want to know, we actually have something in common."
"I would like to know what."
"It is all about a house painter.... We are getting him out of trouble! Though really there is nothing to worry about now. The thing is completely obvious. We are just pushing it along."
"A painter?"
"Have I not told you about it? I only told you the beginning -- about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman. Well, the painter is mixed up in it..."
"Oh, I heard about that murder before and was rather interested in it... partly... for a certain reason.... I read about it in the papers too...."
"Lizaveta was murdered too," Nastasya blurted out, suddenly addressing Raskolnikov. She had been standing by the door the whole time, listening.
"Lizaveta," murmured Raskolnikov, barely audible.
"Lizaveta, the one who sold old clothes. Did you not know her? She used to come here. She even mended a shirt for you once."

Raskolnikov turned toward the wall where, on the dirty yellow wallpaper, he picked out one clumsy white flower with brown lines on it and began studying how many petals it had, how many scallops on the petals, how many lines on them. His arms and legs felt lifeless, as though they had been cut off. He did not try to move, but stared fixedly at the flower.
"But what about the painter?" Zossimov interrupted Nastasya's chatter with obvious displeasure. She sighed and fell silent.
"He was accused of the murder," Razumihin went on heatedly.
"Was there evidence against him?"

"Evidence! Evidence that was no evidence at all -- and that is exactly what we have to prove. It was the same as when they first latched onto those fellows Koch and Pestryakov. God, how stupidly it is all done -- it makes you sick, even though it is none of your business! Pestryakov may be coming tonight.... By the way, Rodya, you already know about this case. It happened before your illness, the day before you fainted at the police station while they were discussing it."
Zossimov looked curiously at Raskolnikov. He did not stir.
"I must say, Razumihin, you are quite the busybody!" Zossimov observed.

"Maybe I am, but we will get him off anyway," Razumihin shouted, slamming his fist on the table. "What is most infuriating is not their lying -- you can always forgive lying, lying is a wonderful thing because it leads to truth -- what is infuriating is that they lie and then worship their own lies.... I respect Porfiry, but... What tripped them up at first? The door was locked, and when they came back with the porter it was open. Therefore Koch and Pestryakov must be the murderers -- that was their logic!"
"Do not get so worked up. They simply detained them -- they had no choice.... And by the way, I have met that Koch fellow. He used to buy unredeemed pledges from the old woman, did he not?"

"Yes, he is a swindler. Buys up bad debts too. Makes a profession of it. But enough about him! You know what really makes me angry? It is their nauseating, ossified, petrified routine.... And this case could be the means of introducing a new method. The psychological evidence alone should be enough to put them on the right track. 'We have facts,' they say. But facts are not everything -- at least half the battle is how you interpret them!"
"And can you interpret them?"
"The thing is, you cannot keep quiet when you have a feeling, a tangible feeling, that you could actually help if only.... Anyway! Do you know the details of the case?"
"I am waiting to hear about the painter."

"Oh, yes! Here is the story. Early on the third day after the murder, while they were still fussing over Koch and Pestryakov -- though those two had accounted for every step and it was plain as day -- an unexpected fact turned up. A man named Dushkin, who runs a tavern across from the building, brought a jeweler's case containing some gold earrings to the police station and told a long story. 'The day before yesterday, just after eight o'clock' -- mark the day and hour! -- 'a journeyman house painter named Nikolay, who had already been in to see me that day, brought me this case of gold earrings and stones and asked me to give him two rubles for them. When I asked where he got them, he said he picked them up in the street. I did not ask any more questions.' I am telling you Dushkin's story. 'I gave him a one-ruble note, figuring if he did not pawn them with me he would with someone else. It would all end the same way -- he would drink it up, so the goods might as well stay with me. Hide something far away and you will find it close to hand. And if any rumors come up, I will take them to the police.' Of course, that is all nonsense. He lies through his teeth. I know this Dushkin -- he is a pawnbroker and a fence, and he did not cheat Nikolay out of a thirty-ruble trinket just to hand it to the police. He was simply scared. But never mind. Back to Dushkin's story: 'I have known this Nikolay Dementyev since he was a child. He comes from the same province and district of Zaraisk -- we are both Ryazan men. And though Nikolay is not a drunkard, he does drink. I knew he had a job in that building, painting work with Dmitri, who comes from the same village too. As soon as he got the ruble, he changed it, had a couple of glasses, took his change, and left. But I did not see Dmitri with him. The next day I heard that someone had murdered Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna with an axe. I knew them, and I got suspicious about the earrings right away -- I knew the murdered woman lent money on pledges. I went to the building and started making quiet inquiries. First I asked: Is Nikolay here? Dmitri told me Nikolay had gone off on a bender -- came home at dawn, drunk, stayed about ten minutes, and left again. Dmitri had not seen him since and was finishing the job alone. Their job was on the same staircase as the murder, on the second floor. When I heard all that, I said nothing to anyone, but I found out what I could about the murder and went home still suspicious. And at eight this morning' -- that was the third day, you understand -- 'I saw Nikolay come in, not sober, though not exactly very drunk -- he could understand what was said to him. He sat down on the bench and did not speak. There was only one stranger in the bar and a man I knew asleep on a bench, and my two boys. Have you seen Dmitri? I asked. No, I have not, he said. And you have not been here either? Not since the day before yesterday, he said. Where did you sleep last night? In Peski, with the Kolomensky men. And where did you get those earrings? I found them in the street -- and the way he said it was odd. He did not look at me. Did you hear what happened that very evening, at that very hour, on that very staircase? I asked. No, he said, I had not heard -- and the whole time he was listening, his eyes were bulging and he turned white as chalk. I told him everything, and he grabbed his hat and started to get up. Wait, Nikolay, I said, will you not have a drink? And I signaled the boy to block the door, and I came out from behind the bar. But he bolted out and down the street and around the corner at a run. I have not seen him since. That settled my doubts -- it was him, clear as day....'"
"I should think so," said Zossimov.

"Wait! Hear the rest. Of course they searched everywhere for Nikolay. They detained Dushkin and searched his place. Dmitri was arrested too. The Kolomensky men were turned inside out. Then the day before yesterday they arrested Nikolay in a tavern at the edge of town. He had gone there, taken the silver cross from his neck, and asked for a drink in exchange. They gave it to him. A few minutes later, the woman went to the cowshed, and through a crack in the wall she saw him in the adjoining stable -- he had made a noose from his sash on a beam, stood on a block of wood, and was trying to get his neck through it. The woman screamed bloody murder and people came running. 'So that is what you are up to!' 'Take me,' he says, 'to such-and-such a police officer. I will confess everything.' So they brought him in with a proper escort. They asked him this and that -- how old he is, twenty-two, and so on. Question: When you were working with Dmitri, did you see anyone on the staircase at such-and-such a time? Answer: Sure, people may have gone up and down, but I did not notice them. Did you hear anything, any noise? We heard nothing special. Did you hear, Nikolay, that on that same day a widow and her sister were murdered and robbed? I never knew a thing about it. First I heard was from Afanasy Pavlovitch the day before yesterday. Where did you find the earrings? I found them on the pavement. Why did you not go to work with Dmitri the next day? Because I was drinking. Where? Oh, such-and-such a place. Why did you run away from Dushkin's? Because I was terrified. What were you terrified of? That I would be accused. -- Now, Zossimov, believe me or not, that question was asked in exactly those words. I know it for a fact -- it was repeated to me precisely! What do you say to that?"
"Well, anyway, there is evidence."

"I am not talking about the evidence right now. I am talking about that question -- about their whole mentality. So they squeezed and squeezed him, and he confessed: 'I did not find them in the street but in the apartment where I was painting with Dmitri.' 'How so?' 'Dmitri and I were painting all day, and we were just getting ready to leave when Dmitri grabbed a brush and painted my face. He ran off and I chased after him, yelling at the top of my lungs. At the bottom of the stairs I ran right into the porter and some gentlemen -- I do not remember how many. The porter swore at me, and the other porter swore too, and the porter's wife came out and swore at us, and a gentleman came in the entrance with a lady and he swore at us too, because Dmitri and I were sprawled right across the way. I grabbed Dmitri by the hair and knocked him down and started hitting him. And Dmitri grabbed my hair too and hit me back. But it was not out of anger -- it was all in fun, for sport. Then Dmitri broke free and ran into the street, and I ran after him but could not catch him, so I went back to the apartment alone to gather my things. I started packing, waiting for Dmitri, and there in the corridor, in the corner by the door, I stepped on a box. I saw it lying there wrapped in paper. I unwrapped it, saw some little clasps, undid them, and inside were the earrings....'"
"Behind the door? Lying behind the door? Behind the door?" Raskolnikov cried out suddenly, staring at Razumihin with a blank look of terror. He slowly sat up on the sofa, leaning on his hand.
"Yes... why? What is the matter? What is wrong?" Razumihin jumped up from his seat too.
"Nothing," Raskolnikov answered faintly, turning back to the wall. They were all silent for a moment.
"He must have been talking in his sleep," Razumihin said at last, looking questioningly at Zossimov. The latter gave a slight shake of his head.
"Well, go on," said Zossimov. "What happened next?"

"What next? As soon as he saw the earrings, forgetting Dmitri and everything, he grabbed his cap and ran to Dushkin, and as we know, got a ruble for them. He lied about finding them in the street, and went off drinking. He keeps repeating the same thing about the murder: 'I know nothing about it, never heard of it until the day before yesterday.' 'Then why did you not go to the police until now?' 'I was scared.' 'And why did you try to hang yourself?' 'From fear.' 'Fear of what?' 'That I would be blamed.' Well, there you have the whole story. Now what do you suppose they concluded from all that?"
"What is there to suppose? There is a clue, such as it is -- a fact. You would not want your painter set free, would you?"
"They have simply decided he is the murderer. They have not a shadow of doubt."

"That is nonsense. You are getting worked up. But what about the earrings? You must admit that if earrings from the old woman's box ended up in Nikolay's hands on the very same day and hour of the murder, they must have gotten there somehow. That counts for a lot in a case like this."

"How did they get there? How did they get there?" cried Razumihin. "How can you, a doctor -- whose duty is to study people and who has more opportunity than anyone to study human nature -- how can you fail to see the man's character in the whole story? Can you not see at once that the answers he gave in the examination are the honest truth? The earrings came into his hands exactly as he described -- he stepped on the box and picked it up."
"The honest truth! But did he not admit himself that he lied at first?"

"Listen carefully. The porter and Koch and Pestryakov and the other porter and the first porter's wife and the woman sitting in the porter's lodge and a man named Kryukov who had just gotten out of a cab and was coming in with a lady on his arm -- that is eight or ten witnesses -- all agree that Nikolay had Dmitri pinned to the ground, lying on top of him hitting him, while Dmitri pulled his hair and hit him back. They were sprawled right across the way, blocking the passage. People cursed at them from all sides while they -- 'like children,' in the witnesses' exact words -- fell all over each other, squealing, wrestling, and laughing with the most ridiculous expressions, and then chased each other out into the street. Now pay close attention. The bodies upstairs were still warm -- warm when they found them! If they, or even Nikolay alone, had committed the murders and broken open the boxes, or even just participated in the robbery, allow me one question: does their behavior -- the squealing, the childish horseplay at the gate -- fit with axes and bloodshed and diabolical cunning and robbery? They would have just killed them, not five or ten minutes before -- the bodies were still warm -- and immediately, leaving the door wide open, knowing people would come any second, they threw away their loot and rolled around like children, laughing and drawing everyone's attention? And there are a dozen witnesses who will swear to it!"
"Of course it is strange! Impossible, really, but..."

"No, brother, no _buts_. Even if the earrings found in Nikolay's hands on the very day and hour of the murder constitute important circumstantial evidence against him -- though his explanation accounts for it and therefore it does not seriously incriminate him -- one must consider the facts proving his innocence, especially since they _cannot be denied_. And do you think, given how our legal system works, that they will accept, or are even capable of accepting, a fact that rests solely on psychological impossibility -- as irrefutable proof that demolishes the circumstantial evidence? No, they will not, because they found the jewelry case and the man tried to hang himself, 'which he could not have done if he had not felt guilty.' That is the crux, that is what drives me mad -- you must understand!"
"I can see you are fired up! Wait a moment. I forgot to ask -- what proof is there that the box came from the old woman?"
"That has been established," said Razumihin with obvious reluctance, frowning. "Koch recognized the jewelry case and identified the owner, who proved conclusively that it was his."
"That is bad. Now another point. Did anyone actually see Nikolay when Koch and Pestryakov were first going upstairs? Is there any evidence on that?"

"Nobody saw him," Razumihin answered with frustration. "That is the worst of it. Even Koch and Pestryakov did not notice them on their way upstairs, though their testimony would not have been worth much anyway. They said they saw the apartment was open and that work must have been going on, but they paid no particular attention and could not remember whether men were actually working there."
"Hmm!... So the only evidence for the defense is that they were beating each other and laughing. That makes for a strong presumption, but... How do you explain the facts yourself?"

"How do I explain them? What is there to explain? The direction is obvious, and the jewelry case points to it. The real murderer dropped those earrings. He was upstairs, locked in, when Koch and Pestryakov knocked at the door. Koch, like a fool, did not stay at the door, so the murderer slipped out and ran down too -- he had no other way of escape. He hid from Koch, Pestryakov, and the porter in the empty apartment while Nikolay and Dmitri had just run out. He waited there while the porter and others went upstairs, stayed until they were out of earshot, then calmly walked downstairs at the exact moment when Dmitri and Nikolay had run into the street and no one was in the entrance. Maybe someone saw him but did not notice -- plenty of people come and go. He must have dropped the earrings from his pocket while standing behind the door and did not realize it because he had other things on his mind. The jewelry case is conclusive proof that he stood there.... That is my explanation."
"Too clever! No, my friend, that is too clever. That beats everything."
"But why? Why?"
"Because everything fits together too neatly... it is too melodramatic."
"Ha!" Razumihin was exclaiming, but at that moment the door opened and a person walked in who was a stranger to everyone present.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 5
paragraphs: This was a gentleman no longer young, stiff and portly in appearance, with a cautious, sour expression. He began by stopping short in the doorway and staring around with open, offensive astonishment, as though asking himself what kind of place he had come to. With deliberate mistrust, and with an air of being alarmed and almost insulted, he surveyed Raskolnikov's low, cramped little room. With the same amazement he stared at Raskolnikov himself, lying on his wretched dirty sofa, undressed, disheveled, unwashed, looking fixedly back at him. Then with equal deliberation he examined the rough, unkempt figure and unshaven face of Razumihin, who stared him boldly in the eye without getting up. An awkward silence lasted a couple of minutes, and then, as might have been expected, there was a shift in the atmosphere. Judging, probably from certain unmistakable signs, that he would get nowhere in this cramped little room by trying to intimidate them, the gentleman softened slightly. He addressed Zossimov in a polite but stern voice, emphasizing every syllable:
"Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a student, or formerly a student?"
Zossimov shifted slightly, and would have answered, had Razumihin not beaten him to it.
"Here he is, lying on the sofa! What do you want?"
This blunt "what do you want" seemed to cut the ground from under the pompous gentleman's feet. He began turning toward Razumihin, but checked himself in time and turned back to Zossimov.

"This is Raskolnikov," Zossimov mumbled, nodding in his direction. Then he gave a prolonged yawn, opening his mouth as wide as it would go. After that he lazily reached into his waistcoat pocket, pulled out a huge gold pocket watch in a round hunter's case, opened it, glanced at it, and just as slowly and lazily put it back.

Raskolnikov himself lay silent, on his back, staring persistently, though without comprehension, at the stranger. Now that his face was turned away from the strange flower on the wallpaper, it was extremely pale and wore a look of anguish, as though he had just undergone a painful operation or been released from the rack. But the newcomer gradually began to catch his attention, then his curiosity, then his suspicion, and finally his alarm. When Zossimov said "This is Raskolnikov," he quickly sat up on the sofa and in an almost defiant but weak, breaking voice said:
"Yes, I am Raskolnikov! What do you want?"
The visitor studied him and pronounced impressively:
"Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin. I believe I have reason to hope that my name is not entirely unknown to you?"
But Raskolnikov, who had been expecting something completely different, stared at him blankly, as though he were hearing the name Pyotr Petrovitch for the first time.
"Is it possible that you have not yet received any information?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, somewhat put out.

In reply, Raskolnikov sank languidly back onto the pillow, put his hands behind his head, and stared at the ceiling. A look of dismay crossed Luzhin's face. Zossimov and Razumihin studied him with even greater curiosity, and at last he showed unmistakable signs of embarrassment.
"I had assumed and calculated," he faltered, "that a letter posted more than ten days ago, perhaps even two weeks..."

"Look, why are you standing in the doorway?" Razumihin broke in. "If you have something to say, sit down. You and Nastasya are crowding the place. Nastasya, make room. Here is a chair -- thread your way in!"

He pushed his chair back from the table, making a little space between the table and his knees, and waited in a rather cramped position for the visitor to "thread his way in." The moment was chosen so that refusal was impossible, and the visitor squeezed through, hurrying and stumbling. Reaching the chair, he sat down and looked suspiciously at Razumihin.

"No need to be nervous," Razumihin blurted out. "Rodya has been sick for five days, delirious for three, but he is recovering now and has an appetite. This is his doctor, who just examined him. I am a friend of Rodya's, also a former student, and right now I am taking care of him. So do not mind us -- just go on with your business."
"Thank you. But will my presence and conversation not disturb the patient?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, turning to Zossimov.
"N-no," Zossimov mumbled. "You might even entertain him." He yawned again.

"He has been conscious for a while now, since morning," Razumihin continued, whose easy familiarity seemed like such natural good nature that Pyotr Petrovitch began to relax a little -- partly, perhaps, because this shabby, impudent young man had introduced himself as a student.
"Your mother --" Luzhin began.
"Hmm!" Razumihin cleared his throat loudly. Luzhin looked at him inquiringly.
"Never mind, go on."
Luzhin shrugged.

"Your mother had begun a letter to you while I was staying in her area. Upon arriving here, I deliberately waited a few days before visiting, so that I could be entirely certain you had been informed. But now, to my astonishment..."
"I know, I know!" Raskolnikov cried out with sudden impatient irritation. "So you are the _fiance_? I know, and that is enough!"
Pyotr Petrovitch was clearly offended this time, but said nothing. He made a violent effort to understand what was happening. There was a moment's silence.

Meanwhile Raskolnikov, who had half turned toward him when he answered, was now staring at him with marked curiosity, as though he had not gotten a good look at him before, or as though something new had struck him. He even sat up on purpose to study him. There was certainly something peculiar about Pyotr Petrovitch's whole appearance -- something that seemed to justify the title of "fiance" so unceremoniously applied to him. First, it was evident -- far too evident -- that Pyotr Petrovitch had made eager use of his days in the capital to spruce himself up in anticipation of his bride -- a perfectly innocent undertaking. Even his own somewhat smug awareness of how much better he looked might have been forgiven under the circumstances, given that he had assumed the role of fiance. All his clothes were fresh from the tailor and perfectly fine, except for being too new and too obviously meant to impress. Even the stylish new round hat carried the same significance. Pyotr Petrovitch treated it with excessive respect, holding it too carefully in his hands. The exquisite pair of lavender gloves -- real Louvain -- told the same story, if only because he did not wear them but carried them for show. Light, youthful colors dominated his outfit. He wore a charming summer jacket in fawn, light trousers, a matching waistcoat, crisp new linen, and a cravat of the lightest cambric with pink stripes -- and the best part was that it all suited him. His fresh, even handsome face looked younger than his forty-five years. His dark mutton-chop whiskers framed both sides nicely, growing thick on his shining, clean-shaven chin. Even his hair, touched here and there with grey and curled at a barber's, did not look ridiculous as curled hair usually does by making a man resemble a German at his own wedding. If there was something unpleasant and repulsive in his rather good-looking, imposing face, it came from entirely different causes. After this unceremonious inspection, Raskolnikov smiled maliciously, sank back onto the pillow, and stared at the ceiling as before.
But Mr. Luzhin steeled himself and seemed to decide to ignore their peculiarities.

"I am deeply sorry to find you in this condition," he began, breaking the silence with an effort. "Had I known of your illness, I would have come sooner. But you know how business is. I also have an important legal matter in the Senate, not to mention other concerns you can probably guess. I am expecting your mother and sister any minute."
Raskolnikov stirred and seemed about to speak; his face showed some excitement. Pyotr Petrovitch paused and waited, but as nothing followed, he went on:
"... Any minute. I have found lodgings for them upon their arrival."
"Where?" asked Raskolnikov weakly.
"Very close by, in Bakaleyev's house."
"That is on Voskresensky," Razumihin put in. "Two floors of rooms, rented out by a merchant named Yushin. I have been there."
"Yes, rooms..."

"A disgusting place -- filthy, stinking, and worse, of dubious reputation. Things have happened there, and all sorts of shady people live there. I went there about some scandalous business. It is cheap, though..."

"I could not, of course, have learned so much about it, being a stranger in Petersburg myself," Pyotr Petrovitch replied stiffly. "However, the two rooms are exceedingly clean, and since it is only for a short time... I have already found a permanent flat -- that is, our future home," he said, addressing Raskolnikov, "and I am having it renovated. Meanwhile, I myself am crammed into lodgings with my friend Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, in Madame Lippevechsel's apartment. It was he who told me about Bakaleyev's house."
"Lebeziatnikov?" said Raskolnikov slowly, as if trying to recall something.
"Yes, Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, a clerk in the Ministry. Do you know him?"
"Yes... no," Raskolnikov answered.

"Excuse me, I thought you did from your question. I was once his guardian.... A very nice young man, quite progressive. I like to meet young people -- one learns new things from them." Luzhin looked around at them all hopefully.
"In what way?" asked Razumihin.

"In the most serious and essential ways," Pyotr Petrovitch replied, as though delighted by the question. "You see, it has been ten years since I visited Petersburg. All the new ideas, reforms, and trends have reached us in the provinces, but to see them clearly one has to be in Petersburg. And it is my view that you learn the most by observing the younger generation. And I must confess, I am delighted..."
"By what?"
"That is a broad question. I may be mistaken, but I think I detect clearer thinking, more -- how shall I put it -- critical rigor, more practicality..."
"That is true," Zossimov remarked offhandedly.

"Nonsense! There is no practicality." Razumihin jumped on him. "Practicality is hard to come by -- it does not drop from the sky. And for the last two hundred years we have been cut off from all practical life. Ideas are fermenting, sure," he said, turning to Pyotr Petrovitch, "and there is a desire for good, though in a childish form. You might even find honesty, despite the swarms of scoundrels. But there is no practicality. Practicality wears sturdy shoes."

"I cannot agree," Pyotr Petrovitch replied with obvious pleasure. "Of course people get carried away and make mistakes, but one must be tolerant. Those mistakes are merely evidence of enthusiasm for the cause and of unfortunate external conditions. If little has been accomplished, the time has been short. Of means I will not speak. But in my personal view, something has already been achieved. New valuable ideas and new valuable works are circulating in place of our old dreamy, romantic authors. Literature is maturing. Many harmful prejudices have been rooted out and ridiculed.... In a word, we have cut ourselves off irrevocably from the past, and that, in my opinion, is a great thing..."
"He has memorized it to show off!" Raskolnikov muttered suddenly.
"What?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, not catching his words, but he got no answer.
"That is all quite true," Zossimov hastened to agree.

"Is it not?" Pyotr Petrovitch continued, glancing affably at Zossimov. "You must admit," he went on, addressing Razumihin with a hint of triumph and condescension -- he nearly added "young man" -- "that there has been progress, or as they say now, advancement in the name of science and economic truth..."
"A cliche."

"No, not a cliche! If, for example, I was told in the past 'love thy neighbor,' what came of it?" Pyotr Petrovitch went on, perhaps with excessive haste. "It came to my tearing my coat in half to share with my neighbor, and we both ended up half-naked. As the Russian proverb says, 'Chase two hares and you will not catch one.' But science now tells us: love yourself above all, for everything in the world rests on self-interest. If you love yourself and manage your own affairs properly, your coat stays whole. Economic truth adds that the more private affairs are properly organized in society -- the more whole coats, so to speak -- the stronger its foundations and the better the common welfare is organized too. So by acquiring wealth solely for myself, I am, in a manner of speaking, acquiring for everyone, and helping to ensure my neighbor gets a bit more than a torn coat -- not through personal charity, but as a natural consequence of general progress. The idea is simple, but unfortunately it has been slow to reach us, blocked by idealism and sentimentality. And yet it would seem to require very little intelligence to grasp..."

"Excuse me, I have very little intelligence myself," Razumihin cut in sharply, "so let us drop it. I started this conversation with a purpose, but I have gotten so sick over the last three years of this chatter for its own sake, this endless stream of cliches, always the same ones, that I blush when other people talk like that. You are naturally eager to display your knowledge, and I do not blame you -- that is perfectly forgivable. I just wanted to find out what sort of man you are, because so many unscrupulous people have latched onto the progressive cause lately and distorted everything they touch for their own benefit that they have dragged the whole cause through the mud. That is enough!"
"Excuse me, sir," Luzhin said, offended, speaking with excessive dignity. "Are you suggesting, so unceremoniously, that I too--"
"Oh, my dear sir... how could I?... Come, that is enough," Razumihin concluded, and he turned abruptly to Zossimov to continue their previous conversation.
Pyotr Petrovitch had the good sense to accept the retraction. He decided to leave in another minute or two.
"I trust our acquaintance," he said, addressing Raskolnikov, "may, upon your recovery and given the circumstances of which you are aware, grow closer... Above all, I wish you a return to health..."
Raskolnikov did not even turn his head. Pyotr Petrovitch began getting up.
"One of her clients must have killed her," Zossimov declared with certainty.
"No doubt about it," agreed Razumihin. "Porfiry is not revealing his own theory, but he is examining everyone who left pledges with her."
"Examining them?" Raskolnikov asked aloud.
"Yes. What of it?"
"Nothing."
"How is he tracking them down?" asked Zossimov.
"Koch supplied some names. Other names were on the pledge wrappers, and some people have come forward on their own."
"It must have been a cunning, experienced criminal! Such boldness! Such nerve!"

"That is exactly what it was not!" Razumihin interjected. "That is what throws everyone off the track. I maintain that he is not cunning, not experienced, and this was probably his first crime! Assume he was a novice and it is obvious that only luck saved him -- and luck can do anything. He probably did not even anticipate the obstacles! And how did he go about it? He grabbed jewelry worth ten or twenty rubles, stuffing his pockets, and rummaged through the old woman's trunks and rags -- yet they found fifteen hundred rubles in cash, plus banknotes, in a box in the top drawer of the chest! He did not know how to rob; he only knew how to kill. It was his first crime, I am telling you -- he panicked. And he escaped not through skill but through sheer luck!"

"You are talking about the murder of the old pawnbroker, I believe?" Pyotr Petrovitch put in, addressing Zossimov. He was standing with hat and gloves in hand, ready to leave, but felt inclined to toss off a few more intellectual remarks. He was clearly eager to make a good impression, and his vanity overrode his prudence.
"Yes. You have heard about it?"
"Oh yes, living in the neighborhood."
"Do you know the details?"

"I cannot say that, but what interests me is a different aspect of the case -- the larger question, so to speak. Setting aside the fact that crime has been rising sharply among the lower classes in the last five years, not to mention the constant robberies and arsons -- what strikes me as strangest is that crime is increasing proportionally in the higher classes too. In one place you hear of a student robbing the mail on the highway. In another, people of good social standing forge banknotes. In Moscow an entire gang was caught forging lottery tickets, and one of the ringleaders was a university lecturer. Then our embassy secretary abroad was murdered for some obscure financial motive.... So if this old pawnbroker was murdered by someone from a higher social class -- since peasants do not pawn gold trinkets -- how do we explain this moral decay among the civilized part of society?"
"There have been many economic changes," Zossimov offered.
"How do we explain it?" Razumihin pounced. "It could be explained by our deep-rooted impracticality."
"What do you mean?"

"What did your Moscow lecturer say when they asked him why he was forging notes? 'Everybody else is getting rich one way or another, so I wanted to get rich quick too.' I do not remember the exact words, but the gist was that he wanted money for nothing, without waiting or working! We have gotten used to having everything handed to us, to walking on crutches, to having our food pre-chewed. And then the great moment came, and everybody showed their true colors."
[*] The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 is meant. --TRANSLATOR'S NOTE.
"But morality? And, so to speak, principles..."
"But why do you worry about it?" Raskolnikov cut in suddenly. "It follows from your own theory!"
"From my theory?"
"Follow your theory to its logical conclusion, and it turns out people may be killed..."
"Good heavens!" cried Luzhin.
"No, that is not right," Zossimov put in.
Raskolnikov lay there with a white face and twitching upper lip, breathing painfully.
"There is a limit to everything," Luzhin went on haughtily. "An economic idea is not an incitement to murder, and one need only suppose..."

"And is it true," Raskolnikov interrupted once more, his voice suddenly quivering with fury and a strange delight in provoking him, "is it true that you told your _fiancee_... within an hour of her acceptance, that what pleased you most... was that she was poor... because it is better to raise a wife from poverty so that you can have total control over her and reproach her for being your benefactress?"

"Good God!" Luzhin cried, furious and flushed with embarrassment. "To twist my words like this! Forgive me, but the report that has reached you -- or rather, been conveyed to you -- has no basis in fact, and I... suspect who... in a word, this arrow... your mother... She seemed to me, in other respects, despite her many excellent qualities, to have a somewhat romantic and exalted way of thinking.... But I was a thousand miles from imagining that she would misunderstand and distort things in such a fantastic way.... And indeed... indeed..."
"I tell you what," cried Raskolnikov, raising himself on the pillow and fixing his piercing, glittering eyes on him. "I tell you what."
"What?" Luzhin stood still, waiting with a defiant and offended expression. Silence lasted for several seconds.
"If you ever again... dare to mention a single word... about my mother... I will throw you down the stairs!"
"What is the matter with you?" cried Razumihin.

"So that is how it is?" Luzhin went pale and bit his lip. "Let me tell you, sir," he began deliberately, making every effort to control himself but breathing hard, "from the very first moment I saw that you were hostile toward me, but I stayed on purpose to learn more. I can forgive a great deal in a sick man and a relative, but after this... never."
"I am not sick," cried Raskolnikov.
"So much the worse..."
"Go to hell!"

But Luzhin was already leaving without finishing, squeezing between the table and chair. Razumihin stood up this time to let him pass. Without glancing at anyone, without even nodding to Zossimov -- who had been signaling him for some time to leave the patient alone -- he walked out, carefully lifting his hat to shoulder height to keep from crushing it as he stooped through the doorway. Even the curve of his spine seemed to express the terrible insult he had received.
"How could you -- how could you!" Razumihin said, shaking his head in bewilderment.

"Leave me alone -- leave me alone, all of you!" Raskolnikov cried in a frenzy. "Will you ever stop tormenting me? I am not afraid of you! I am not afraid of anyone, not anyone now! Get away from me! I want to be alone, alone, alone!"
"Come on," said Zossimov, nodding to Razumihin.
"But we cannot just leave him like this!"
"Come on," Zossimov repeated firmly, and he walked out. Razumihin thought for a moment, then ran after him.
"It could be worse to disobey him," Zossimov said on the stairs. "He must not be agitated."
"What is wrong with him?"

"If only he could get some kind of positive shock -- that is what he needs! At first he was better.... You know, he has something on his mind! Some fixed idea weighing on him.... I am very much afraid of that -- there must be something!"

"Perhaps it is that gentleman, Pyotr Petrovitch. From their conversation it sounds like he is going to marry Raskolnikov's sister, and that Raskolnikov got a letter about it just before falling ill...."

"Yes, damn the man -- he may have made everything worse. But have you noticed? Raskolnikov takes no interest in anything, does not respond to anything, except one subject that seems to agitate him -- the murder."
"Yes, yes," Razumihin agreed. "I noticed that too. He is interested, frightened even. It shook him the day he fell ill at the police station -- he fainted."
"Tell me more about that tonight and I will tell you something afterward. He interests me very much! I will go back and check on him in half an hour.... There will not be any inflammation, though."
"Thanks! And I will wait at Pashenka's in the meantime and keep watch through Nastasya...."
Raskolnikov, left alone, looked with impatience and misery at Nastasya, but she lingered.
"Will you have some tea now?" she asked.
"Later! I am sleepy! Leave me."
He turned sharply to the wall, and Nastasya went out.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 6
paragraphs: But as soon as she left, he got up, latched the door, unwrapped the bundle Razumihin had brought that evening and tied up again, and began dressing. Strangely, he seemed to have become perfectly calm all at once -- not a trace of his recent delirium or the panic that had haunted him lately. It was the first moment of a peculiar, sudden calm. His movements were precise and deliberate; a clear purpose was evident in them. "Today, today," he muttered to himself. He knew he was still weak, but a fierce inner concentration gave him strength and confidence. He hoped he would not collapse in the street. Once he had put on his entirely new clothes, he looked at the money on the table and, after a moment's thought, pocketed it. Twenty-five rubles. He also took the copper change left from the ten rubles Razumihin had spent on the clothes. Then he quietly unlatched the door, slipped out, crept downstairs, and glanced through the open kitchen door. Nastasya was standing with her back to him, stoking the landlady's samovar. She heard nothing. Who would have imagined he would go out? A minute later he was in the street.

It was nearly eight o'clock. The sun was setting. It was as stifling as before, but he drank in the foul, dusty city air eagerly. His head felt slightly dizzy. A savage energy suddenly gleamed in his feverish eyes and his wasted, pale, yellowish face. He did not know or think about where he was going. He had only one thought: "All of _this_ must end today, once and for all, right now. I will not go home without it, because I _will not go on living like this_." How would he end it? With what? He had no idea and did not even want to think about it. He pushed thought away -- thought was torture. All he knew, all he felt, was that everything must change "one way or another," he repeated with desperate, unshakable determination.

Out of old habit he took his usual route toward the Hay Market. A dark-haired young man with a barrel organ stood in the street outside a small general shop, grinding out a sentimental song. He was accompanying a girl of about fifteen who stood on the pavement in front of him. She was dressed in a crinoline, a cloak, and a straw hat with a flame-colored feather -- all old and shabby. In a strong, rather pleasant voice, roughened by street singing, she sang hoping for a coin from the shop. Raskolnikov stopped among the two or three listeners, took out a five-kopeck piece, and placed it in the girl's hand. She broke off abruptly on a sentimental high note, shouted "Come on" to the organ grinder, and they both moved on to the next shop.
"Do you like street music?" Raskolnikov asked, turning to a middle-aged man standing idly beside him. The man looked at him, startled and puzzled.

"I love hearing someone sing to a street organ," said Raskolnikov, and his manner seemed strangely disconnected from the subject. "I like it on cold, dark, damp autumn evenings -- they must be damp -- when all the passersby have pale green, sickly faces. Or better still when wet snow is falling straight down with no wind -- you know what I mean? -- and the streetlamps glow through it..."
"I do not know.... Excuse me..." the stranger muttered, unnerved by both the question and Raskolnikov's strange manner, and he crossed to the other side of the street.

Raskolnikov walked straight on and came to the corner of the Hay Market where the stallholder and his wife had spoken with Lizaveta. But they were not there now. Recognizing the spot, he stopped, looked around, and addressed a young fellow in a red shirt who was lounging outside a grain dealer's shop.
"Is there not a man who keeps a stall here with his wife, at this corner?"
"All sorts of people keep stalls here," the young man answered, looking down at Raskolnikov with condescension.
"What is his name?"
"Whatever he was christened."
"Are you not from Zaraisk yourself? Which province?"
The young man looked at Raskolnikov again.
"It is not a province, your excellency, it is a district. Forgive me graciously, your excellency!"
"Is that a tavern up there?"
"Yes, it is an eating house, and there is a billiard room, and you will find princesses there too.... La-la!"

Raskolnikov crossed the square. In that corner a dense crowd of peasants had gathered. He pushed his way into the thickest part, studying their faces. He felt an inexplicable urge to talk to people. But the peasants ignored him -- they were all shouting in clusters together. He stood there thinking for a moment, then turned right in the direction of V. Prospect.

He had often passed through that little street which angles off from the marketplace toward Sadovy Street. Lately he had often felt drawn to wander around this area whenever he was depressed, so that he might feel even worse.

Now he walked along thinking of nothing. Here there was a huge block of buildings, entirely given over to taverns and eating houses. Women were constantly running in and out -- bareheaded, in their house clothes. They gathered in groups here and there on the pavement, especially around the entrances to various establishments on the ground floor. From one of these came a loud racket -- singing, guitar, and shouts of merriment floating into the street. A crowd of women thronged around the door. Some sat on the steps, others on the pavement, others stood talking. A drunken soldier was staggering along the road nearby, smoking and swearing. He seemed to be trying to find his way somewhere but had forgotten where. One beggar was arguing with another, and a man dead drunk was lying across the road. Raskolnikov joined the group of women, who were talking in hoarse voices. They were bareheaded and wore cotton dresses and goatskin shoes. Some were about forty, others no more than seventeen. Nearly all had blackened eyes.

He felt strangely drawn by the singing and noise from the saloon below.... Someone inside was dancing with wild abandon, stamping his heels to the sounds of a guitar and a thin falsetto voice singing a lively tune. He listened intently, gloomily, dreamily, bending down at the entrance and peering in from the pavement.

"Oh, my handsome soldier,
Don't beat me for nothing,"
trilled the singer's thin voice. Raskolnikov felt a powerful urge to make out the words, as though everything depended on it.
"Should I go in?" he thought. "They are laughing. Drunk. Should I get drunk?"
"Will you not come in?" one of the women asked. Her voice was still musical, less hoarse than the others. She was young and not bad-looking -- the only one in the group.
"Why, she is pretty," he said, straightening up and looking at her.
She smiled, very pleased by the compliment.
"You are not bad looking yourself," she said.
"Is he not thin, though!" another woman observed in a deep voice. "Just come out of the hospital?"
"They all look like generals' daughters, but every one of them has a snub nose," a tipsy peasant in a loose coat chimed in with a sly grin. "Look how jolly they are."
"Get out of here!"
"I am going, sweetheart!"
And he ducked into the saloon below. Raskolnikov moved on.
"Hey, sir!" the girl called after him.
"What?"
She hesitated.
"I would always be happy to spend some time with you, kind sir, but right now I feel shy. Give me six kopecks for a drink, there is a nice young man!"
Raskolnikov gave her whatever came to hand first -- fifteen kopecks.
"Oh, what a generous gentleman!"
"What is your name?"
"Ask for Duclida."
"Well, that is too much," one of the other women remarked, shaking her head at Duclida. "I do not know how you can ask like that. I would die of shame...."

Raskolnikov looked curiously at the speaker. She was a pockmarked woman of about thirty, covered in bruises, with a swollen upper lip. She delivered her criticism quietly and earnestly. "Where is it," thought Raskolnikov, "where have I read about a man condemned to death who says or thinks, an hour before his execution, that if he had to live on some high rock, on such a narrow ledge that there was only room to stand, and all around was the ocean, eternal darkness, eternal solitude, eternal storms -- if he had to remain standing on a square yard of space for the rest of his life, a thousand years, an eternity -- it would still be better to live like that than to die right now! Only to live, to live and live! Life, whatever it may be!... How true that is! My God, how true! Man is a vile creature!... And vile is the one who calls him vile for that," he added a moment later.

He turned into another street. "The Palais de Cristal! Razumihin was just talking about the Palais de Cristal. But what was it I wanted? Yes, the newspapers.... Zossimov said he read about it in the papers. Do you have newspapers?" he asked, entering a fairly spacious and reasonably clean restaurant with several rooms that were, however, rather empty.
