Two or three people were drinking tea, and in a further room four men sat drinking champagne. Raskolnikov thought one of them might be Zametov, but he could not be sure at that distance. "What if it is?" he thought.
"Will you have vodka?" asked the waiter.
"Bring me tea, and the newspapers -- the old ones from the last five days -- and I will tip you."
"Yes, sir. Here is today's. No vodka?"
The old newspapers and tea were brought. Raskolnikov sat down and began scanning them.

"Oh, damn... news items. An accident on a staircase, spontaneous combustion of a shopkeeper from alcohol, a fire in Peski... a fire in the Petersburg district... another fire in the Petersburg district... and another fire in the Petersburg district.... Ah, here it is!" He found what he was looking for and began reading. The lines danced before his eyes, but he read it all and eagerly searched for later updates in the following issues. His hands trembled with nervous impatience as he turned the pages. Suddenly someone sat down at his table. He looked up. It was Zametov, the head clerk, looking just the same -- rings on his fingers, watch chain, curly black hair parted and pomaded, smart waistcoat, rather shabby coat, and somewhat questionable linen. He was in a good mood -- at least he was smiling quite cheerfully and good-naturedly. His dark face was slightly flushed from the champagne.
"What, you here?" he began in surprise, speaking as though they were old friends. "Razumihin told me only yesterday you were unconscious. How strange! And do you know I have been to see you?"
Raskolnikov knew he would come over. He set the papers aside and turned to Zametov. There was a smile on his lips, with a new shade of irritable impatience visible in it.

"I know you have," he answered. "I heard. You looked for my sock.... And you know Razumihin is mad about you? He says you have been with him to Luise Ivanovna's -- you know, the woman you tried to help, the one you winked about to the Lieutenant and he would not understand. Do you remember? How could he fail to understand? It was perfectly obvious."
"What a hothead he is!"
"The Lieutenant?"
"No, your friend Razumihin."
"You must lead a fine life, Mr. Zametov -- free admission to the most agreeable places. Who has been pouring champagne into you?"
"We just had... a drink together.... You talk about pouring!"

"A professional perk! You profit from everything!" Raskolnikov laughed. "It is all right, my dear boy," he added, slapping Zametov on the shoulder. "I am not saying it out of spite -- it is friendly, just for fun, as that workman of yours said when he was scuffling with Dmitri in the old woman case...."
"How do you know about that?"
"Maybe I know more about it than you do."
"How strange you are.... You must still be very ill. You should not have come out."
"Oh, do I seem strange to you?"
"Yes. What are you doing, reading the papers?"
"Yes."
"There is a lot about the fires."

"No, I am not reading about the fires." He looked mysteriously at Zametov, his lips twisting into a mocking smile. "No, I am not reading about the fires," he went on, winking at Zametov. "But confess, my dear fellow, you are dying to know what I am reading about."
"Not in the least. Can I not ask a question? Why do you keep--"
"Listen, you are a man of culture and education, yes?"
"I completed six years of gymnasium," Zametov said with some pride.

"Six years! Oh, my little sparrow! With your parting and your rings -- a man of means. Ha! What a charming boy!" Raskolnikov broke into a nervous laugh right in Zametov's face. Zametov drew back, more baffled than offended.
"How strange you are!" Zametov repeated seriously. "I cannot help thinking you are still delirious."
"Delirious? You are making that up, my little sparrow! So I am strange? You find me curious?"
"Yes, curious."
"Shall I tell you what I was reading, what I was searching for? Look how many papers I had them bring me. Suspicious, is it not?"
"Well, what is it?"
"Pricking up your ears?"
"What do you mean, 'pricking up my ears'?"

"I will explain later. But right now, my boy, I will declare to you... no, better: 'I confess'... No, that is not right either. 'I make a deposition and you take it.' I depose that I was reading, that I was searching -- and I came here specifically for this purpose -- for news about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman," he said in almost a whisper, bringing his face very close to Zametov's. Zametov stared at him, unmoving, without pulling away. What struck Zametov afterward as strangest of all was that the silence that followed lasted exactly a minute, and that they gazed at each other the whole time.
"What if you have been reading about it?" he exclaimed at last, confused and impatient. "What do I care? What of it?"

"The same old woman," Raskolnikov continued in the same whisper, ignoring Zametov's reaction, "the one you were all discussing at the police station, remember, when I fainted. Well, do you understand now?"
"What do you mean? Understand... what?" Zametov asked, almost alarmed.

Raskolnikov's tense, earnest expression was suddenly transformed, and he burst into the same nervous laugh as before, as though utterly unable to control himself. And in a flash he recalled with extraordinary vividness a moment from the recent past -- that moment when he stood behind the door with the axe, the latch trembling, the men outside cursing and shaking it, and he had felt a sudden urge to shout at them, to taunt them, to stick out his tongue, to mock them, to laugh, and laugh, and laugh!
"You are either mad, or..." Zametov began, then stopped, as though stunned by an idea that had suddenly flashed through his mind.
"Or? Or what? Go on, tell me!"
"Nothing," said Zametov, getting angry. "It is all nonsense!"

Both fell silent. After his sudden burst of laughter, Raskolnikov became abruptly thoughtful and melancholy. He put his elbow on the table and rested his head on his hand. He seemed to have completely forgotten about Zametov. The silence lasted some time.
"Why are you not drinking your tea? It is getting cold," said Zametov.

"What? Tea? Oh, yes...." Raskolnikov took a sip, put a morsel of bread in his mouth, and suddenly, looking at Zametov, seemed to remember everything. He pulled himself together. At the same instant his face resumed its original mocking expression. He went on drinking tea.

"There have been a lot of these crimes lately," Zametov said. "Just the other day I read in the Moscow News that a whole gang of counterfeiters was caught in Moscow. An entire organization. They were forging banknotes!"
"Oh, that was ages ago! I read about it a month ago," Raskolnikov answered calmly. "So you would call them criminals?" he added, smiling.
"Of course they are criminals."

"Them? They are children, amateurs, not criminals! Fifty people banding together for such a scheme -- what an idea! Three would be too many, and even then each would have to trust the others more than himself! One person gets drunk and blabs, and the whole thing collapses. Amateurs! They hired strangers to exchange the notes -- imagine entrusting something like that to a random person! And say these amateurs succeed and each makes a million -- then what? Each one depends on all the others for the rest of his life! Better to hang yourself right away! And they could not even exchange the notes properly. The man who went to the bank with five thousand -- his hands were shaking. He counted the first four thousand but did not bother counting the fifth -- he was in such a rush to stuff the money in his pocket and run. Obviously he aroused suspicion. And the whole thing fell apart because of one fool! Is that possible?"
"That his hands were shaking?" Zametov said. "Yes, that is quite possible. I am sure that is possible. Sometimes you just cannot handle the pressure."
"Handle that?"

"Could you handle it? No, I could not. For a hundred rubles, to go through such a terrifying experience? To walk into a bank with forged notes -- where spotting that sort of thing is their whole job? No, I would not have the nerve. Would you?"
Raskolnikov felt an intense urge to stick his tongue out again. Shivers kept running down his spine.

"Here is how I would do it," he began. "This is how I would exchange the notes. I would count the first thousand three or four times, forward and backward, examining each note. Then I would start on the second thousand, count halfway through, then hold up some fifty-ruble note to the light, turn it over, hold it to the light again -- to check if it was genuine. 'I am worried,' I would say, 'a relative of mine lost twenty-five rubles the other day because of a counterfeit note,' and I would tell them the whole story. Then after starting the third thousand, 'No, excuse me,' I would say, 'I think I miscounted the seventh hundred in the second batch,' and I would put down the third and go back to the second, and so on right through to the end. And when I was done, I would pull out a note from the fifth batch and one from the second, hold them to the light again, and ask doubtfully, 'Please exchange these,' and put the clerk in such a state that he would not know how to get rid of me. When I had finally left, I would come back. 'No, excuse me,' I would say, and ask for some clarification. That is how I would do it."

"What terrible things you say!" Zametov said, laughing. "But that is all just talk. In practice you would trip up, I bet. I believe that even a hardened, desperate man cannot always rely on himself, let alone you and me. Take a case close to home -- the old woman murdered in our district. The killer seemed like a desperate man, he risked everything in broad daylight, was saved by a miracle -- but his hands trembled too. He could not manage the robbery, he lost his nerve. That was obvious from the--"
Raskolnikov looked offended.
"Obvious? Then why do you not catch him?" he cried, taunting Zametov maliciously.
"Oh, they will catch him."

"Who? You? You think you could catch him? You have your work cut out! The big test for you people is whether a man is spending money or not. If he had nothing and suddenly starts spending, he must be the man. Any child could outsmart you that way."

"The fact is, that is exactly what they all do," Zametov answered. "A man commits a clever murder at the risk of his life and then goes straight to a tavern to spend the money. That is how they get caught. Not everyone is as clever as you. You would not go to a tavern, of course?"
Raskolnikov frowned and looked hard at Zametov.
"You seem to be enjoying this and would like to know how I would have acted in that case too?" he asked with displeasure.
"I would like to know," Zametov answered firmly and seriously. His words and his look began to take on an almost excessively earnest quality.
"Very much?"
"Very much!"

"All right then. Here is what I would have done," Raskolnikov began, bringing his face close to Zametov's again, staring at him again, speaking in a whisper again -- so that this time Zametov actually shuddered. "Here is what I would have done. I would have taken the money and jewels, walked straight out, and gone to some deserted place surrounded by fences where nobody ever goes -- a kitchen garden or something like that. I would have scouted it out beforehand -- some boulder weighing a hundred pounds or more that had been lying in the corner since the house was built. I would lift that boulder -- there would certainly be a hollow beneath it -- and put the money and jewelry in the hole. Then I would roll the stone back, press it down with my foot, and walk away. And for a year or two, maybe three, I would not touch it. And good luck finding it! Gone without a trace."

"You are a madman," Zametov said, and for some reason he too spoke in a whisper, and drew away from Raskolnikov, whose eyes were glittering. He had gone terribly pale, and his upper lip was trembling and quivering. He leaned as close as possible to Zametov, and his lips began to move without making a sound. This went on for half a minute. He knew what he was doing, but could not stop himself. The terrible word trembled on his lips, like the latch on that door -- another moment and it would break loose, another moment and he would let it go, he would speak.
"And what if it was I who murdered the old woman and Lizaveta?" he said suddenly -- and then realized what he had done.
Zametov stared at him wildly and turned as white as the tablecloth. His face contorted into a forced smile.
"But is that possible?" he managed to say faintly. Raskolnikov glared at him.
"Admit it -- you believed me, did you not?"
"Not at all! I believe it less than ever now," Zametov said hastily.
"Caught you, my little sparrow! So you _did_ believe it before, if now you believe it 'less than ever'?"
"Absolutely not!" cried Zametov, clearly flustered. "Have you been scaring me this whole time just to lead up to that?"

"So you do not believe it? Then what were you all whispering about behind my back when I left the police station? And why did the Lieutenant interrogate me after I fainted? Hey, waiter!" he called, standing up and grabbing his cap. "How much?"
"Thirty kopecks," the waiter replied, hurrying over.

"And here is twenty kopecks for vodka. Look at all this money!" He held out his trembling hand to Zametov, full of banknotes. "Red notes and blue -- twenty-five rubles. Where did I get them? And where did the new clothes come from? You know I did not have a kopeck. You have already cross-examined my landlady, I am sure.... Well, that is enough! _Assez cause!_ Until we meet again!"

He walked out trembling all over with a kind of wild, hysterical sensation that contained an element of unbearable ecstasy. Yet he was gloomy and desperately tired. His face was twisted as though after a seizure. His exhaustion was building rapidly. Any shock or irritation would instantly revive his energy, but his strength collapsed just as quickly once the stimulus was removed.

Zametov, left alone, sat for a long time in the same spot, lost in thought. Raskolnikov had unwittingly triggered a revolution in his brain on a certain point, helping him reach a definitive conclusion.
"Ilya Petrovitch is a blockhead," he decided.

Raskolnikov had barely stepped out of the restaurant when he bumped into Razumihin on the steps. They nearly collided before seeing each other. For a moment they stood staring. Razumihin was greatly taken aback, and then genuine anger blazed fiercely in his eyes.

"So here you are!" he shouted at the top of his voice. "You ran away from your bed! And I have been looking for you under the sofa! We even went up to the attic. I nearly beat Nastasya on your account. And here he is after all! Rodya! What is the meaning of this? Tell me the truth! Confess! Do you hear?"
"It means I am sick to death of all of you and I want to be alone," Raskolnikov answered calmly.
"Alone? When you can barely walk, when your face is white as a sheet and you are gasping for breath? Idiot!... What have you been doing in the Palais de Cristal? Out with it!"
"Let me go!" said Raskolnikov, trying to push past him. This was too much for Razumihin, who grabbed him firmly by the shoulder.
"Let you go? You dare tell me to let you go? Do you know what I will do? I will pick you up, tie you in a bundle, carry you home under my arm, and lock you in!"

"Listen, Razumihin," Raskolnikov began quietly, apparently calm. "Can you not see I do not want your charity? What kind of person takes pleasure in showering kindness on someone who... curses it, who finds it a burden? Why did you come looking for me at the start of my illness? Maybe I was perfectly happy to die. Did I not tell you plainly enough today that you are tormenting me, that I am... sick of you! You seem determined to torture people! I assure you that all of this is seriously hindering my recovery, because it constantly irritates me. You saw that Zossimov left earlier to avoid agitating me. You should leave me alone too, for God's sake! And what right do you have to hold me by force? Can you not see I am in full possession of my faculties? How, how can I convince you to stop persecuting me with your kindness? Call me ungrateful, call me vile -- just let me be, for God's sake, let me be! Let me be!"
He had begun calmly, savoring in advance the poisonous phrases he was about to deliver, but he finished panting and in a frenzy, just as he had been with Luzhin.
Razumihin stood for a moment, thought, and let his hand drop.

"Go to hell, then," he said quietly, almost reflectively. "Wait!" he bellowed, as Raskolnikov started to move. "Listen to me. Let me tell you that every one of you is a babbling, posturing fool! If you have the slightest trouble, you brood over it like a hen on an egg. And you are not even original about it! There is not a spark of independent life in any of you! You are made of candle wax and you have lymph instead of blood. I do not believe in a single one of you! In any situation, the first thing you all do is try to be as unlike a normal human being as possible! Wait!" he shouted with redoubled fury, noticing Raskolnikov was about to leave. "Hear me out! You know I am having a housewarming tonight. They have probably already arrived, but I left my uncle to host them -- I just ran over. And if you were not a fool, a complete and utter fool -- if you were an original instead of a translation... you see, Rodya, I admit you are clever, but you are a fool! -- if you were not a fool, you would come to my place tonight instead of wearing out your shoes in the streets! Since you have already gone out, there is nothing for it. I would give you a comfortable armchair -- my landlady has one... A cup of tea, some company.... Or you could lie on the sofa -- either way, you would be among us.... Zossimov will be there too. Will you come?"
"No."

"Rubbish!" Razumihin shouted, losing patience. "How can you know? You cannot answer for yourself! You do not understand these things.... I have fought and argued with people a thousand times and then gone running back to them.... You feel ashamed and you go back! So remember: Potchinkov's building, third floor...."
"Mr. Razumihin, I do believe you would let anyone beat you up, just out of sheer goodwill."
"Beat me? Who? Me? I would twist his nose off at the very thought! Potchinkov's building, number 47, Babushkin's apartment...."
"I am not coming, Razumihin." Raskolnikov turned and walked away.
"I bet you will!" Razumihin shouted after him. "I refuse to know you if you do not! Wait -- is Zametov in there?"
"Yes."
"Did you see him?"
"Yes."
"Talked to him?"
"Yes."
"What about? Never mind, do not tell me. Potchinkov's building, 47, Babushkin's place -- remember!"
Raskolnikov walked on and turned the corner into Sadovy Street. Razumihin watched him go, then waved his hand and went inside. But halfway up the stairs he stopped.

"Damn it," he muttered, almost aloud. "He sounds rational, and yet... I am a fool! Madmen can sound perfectly rational too! And that was exactly what Zossimov seemed afraid of." He tapped his forehead with his finger. "What if... how could I let him go off alone? He might drown himself.... What a blunder! I cannot allow it." And he ran back to catch Raskolnikov, but there was no sign of him. Cursing, he hurried back to the Palais de Cristal to find Zametov.

Raskolnikov walked straight to the X---- Bridge, stopped in the middle, leaned both elbows on the railing, and stared into the distance. Having parted from Razumihin, he felt so much weaker he could barely make it here. He longed to sit or lie down somewhere right there in the street. Leaning over the water, he gazed mechanically at the last pink flush of sunset, at the row of buildings darkening in the gathering twilight, at one distant attic window on the left bank that blazed as if on fire in the final rays, at the darkening water of the canal. The water seemed to hold his attention. Red circles finally flashed before his eyes; the buildings seemed to move, the passersby, the embankments, the carriages -- everything was spinning. Suddenly he flinched, saved perhaps from fainting by an eerie, horrifying sight. He noticed someone standing to his right. He looked and saw a tall woman in a kerchief, with a long, yellow, wasted face and red, sunken eyes. She was looking straight at him, but clearly saw nothing and recognized no one. Then she leaned her right hand on the railing, lifted her right leg over, then her left, and threw herself into the canal. The filthy water parted and swallowed its victim for a moment, but an instant later the drowning woman floated to the surface, drifting slowly with the current -- head and legs in the water, her skirt billowing over her back like a balloon.
"A woman drowning! A woman drowning!" dozens of voices shouted. People came running. Both banks filled with onlookers. On the bridge, people crowded around Raskolnikov, pressing in behind him.
"Lord have mercy! It is our Afrosinya!" a woman wailed tearfully nearby. "Lord have mercy! Someone save her! Pull her out, good people!"

"A boat! A boat!" came shouts from the crowd. But no boat was needed. A policeman ran down the steps to the canal, threw off his coat and boots, and plunged into the water. The rescue was easy: she had floated within two yards of the steps. He grabbed her clothes with his right hand and with his left seized a pole held out by a comrade. The drowning woman was hauled out immediately. They laid her on the granite pavement of the embankment. She soon regained consciousness, sat up, and began sneezing and coughing, stupidly wiping at her wet dress with her hands. She said nothing.

"She has drunk herself senseless," the same woman's voice wailed beside her. "Senseless. The other day she tried to hang herself and we cut her down. I had just run to the shop, left my girl to watch her -- and now look at this! She is a neighbor, sir, a neighbor -- we live close by, the second house from the end, right there...."

The crowd dispersed. The police remained around the woman. Someone mentioned the police station.... Raskolnikov watched it all with a strange feeling of indifference and detachment. He felt disgusted. "No, that is revolting... water... not good enough," he muttered to himself. "Nothing will come of it," he added. "Nothing to wait for. What about the police station...? And why is Zametov not at the station? It stays open until ten o'clock...." He turned his back to the railing and looked around.

"Very well then!" he said with sudden resolve. He moved away from the bridge and headed toward the police station. His heart felt hollow and empty. He did not want to think. Even his anguish had passed. There was no trace now of the energy with which he had set out "to make an end of it all." Total apathy had taken its place.

"Well, it is a way out," he thought, walking slowly and listlessly along the canal bank. "I will end it, at any rate, because I want to.... But is it a way out? What does it matter! There will be the square yard of space -- ha! But what an ending! Is it really the end? Should I tell them or not? Ah... to hell with it! I am so tired! If only I could sit or lie down somewhere! What I am most ashamed of is how stupid it all is. But I do not even care about that anymore! God, the idiotic ideas that come into one's head."

To reach the police station he had to go straight and take the second left. It was only a few steps away. But at the first corner he stopped, thought for a moment, then turned into a side street and went two blocks out of his way -- perhaps without any reason, or perhaps to delay a minute and buy time. He walked, staring at the ground. Suddenly someone seemed to whisper in his ear. He looked up and saw that he was standing at the very gate of _that_ house. He had not been near it, had not passed it, since _that_ evening. An overwhelming, inexplicable force drew him forward. He went through the gate, through the entrance, then into the first doorway on the right and started climbing the familiar staircase to the fourth floor. The narrow, steep staircase was very dark. He stopped on every landing and looked around curiously. On the first-floor landing the window frame had been removed. "That was not like that before," he thought. Here was the apartment on the second floor where Nikolay and Dmitri had been painting. "Shut up and the door freshly painted. It must be for rent." Then the third floor, and the fourth. "Here!" He was confused to find the door standing wide open. There were men inside; he could hear voices. He had not expected that. After a brief hesitation he climbed the last steps and entered. This apartment too was being renovated; there were workmen inside. This seemed to stun him. He had somehow expected to find everything exactly as he had left it -- perhaps even the corpses in the same positions on the floor. But now -- bare walls, no furniture. It felt wrong. He went to the window and sat on the sill. There were two workmen, both young, one much younger than the other. They were papering the walls with new white paper covered in lilac flowers, replacing the old dirty yellow wallpaper. For some reason, this annoyed Raskolnikov terribly. He glared at the new paper with distaste, as though it grieved him that everything had changed. The workmen had obviously stayed late and were now hurriedly rolling up their paper and preparing to leave. They paid no attention to Raskolnikov. They were talking. He folded his arms and listened.

"She comes to my place in the morning," the older one was telling the younger. "Crack of dawn, all dolled up. 'Why are you preening and primping?' says I. 'I am ready to do anything to please you, Tit Vassilitch!' she says. That is some behavior! And dressed up like a regular fashion magazine!"
"And what is a fashion magazine?" the younger one asked. He obviously looked up to the other as an authority.

"A fashion magazine is a bunch of pictures, colored ones, and they come to the tailors here every Saturday by mail from abroad, showing people how to dress -- men and women both. They are pictures. The men are usually wearing fur coats, and as for the ladies' getups -- well, they are beyond anything you can imagine."
"There is nothing you cannot find in Petersburg," the younger one exclaimed enthusiastically. "Except your mother and father, you can find everything!"
"Except those, you can find everything, my boy," the older one declared sententiously.

Raskolnikov got up and walked into the other room -- the one where the strongbox, the bed, and the chest of drawers had been. Without furniture, the room seemed tiny. The wallpaper was the same. In the corner you could see where the icon case had hung. He looked at the spot and went back to the window. The older workman eyed him sideways.
"What do you want?" he asked suddenly.

Instead of answering, Raskolnikov went out to the landing and pulled the doorbell. The same bell, the same tinny, cracked sound. He rang it a second time, and a third. He listened and remembered. The hideous, agonizing terror he had felt then began coming back with increasing vividness. He shuddered with each ring, and it gave him more and more satisfaction.
"Well, what do you want? Who are you?" the workman shouted, coming out to him. Raskolnikov went back inside.
"I want to rent a flat," he said. "I am looking around."
"People do not come looking at flats at night! And you should come with the building manager."
"They washed the floors -- will they paint them?" Raskolnikov went on. "Is there no blood?"
"What blood?"
"An old woman and her sister were murdered here. There was an enormous pool of it."
"What kind of man are you?" the workman cried, uneasy.
"What kind of man am I?"
"Yes."
"Want to find out? Come to the police station -- I will tell you there."
The workmen stared at him in amazement.
"It is time for us to go, we are late. Come on, Alyoshka. We need to lock up," said the older one.
"Fine, let us go," Raskolnikov said indifferently, and went out first, slowly descending the stairs. "Hey, building manager!" he called out in the gateway.
Several people were standing at the entrance, watching passersby -- the two building managers, a peasant woman, a man in a long coat, and a few others. Raskolnikov walked straight up to them.
"What do you want?" one of the managers asked.
"Have you been to the police station?"
"I was just there. What do you need?"
"Is it open?"
"Of course."
"Is the assistant there?"
"He was, for a while. What do you need?"
Raskolnikov made no reply. He stood among them, lost in thought.
"He came up to look at the apartment," the older workman said, stepping forward.
"Which apartment?"

"The one where we are working. 'Why did you wash away the blood?' he asks. 'There was a murder here,' he says, 'and I have come to rent it.' Then he started ringing the bell -- nearly broke it. 'Come to the police station,' he says, 'I will tell them everything.' Would not leave us alone."
The manager looked at Raskolnikov, frowning and confused.
"Who are you?" he demanded as impressively as he could.

"I am Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a former student. I live in Shil's building, not far from here, apartment number 14. Ask the building manager -- he knows me." Raskolnikov said all this in a lazy, dreamy voice, without turning around, staring intently into the darkening street.
"Why were you up in the apartment?"
"To look at it."
"What is there to look at?"
"Take him straight to the police station," the man in the long coat interjected abruptly.
Raskolnikov looked intently at him over his shoulder and said in the same slow, lazy tone:
"Let us go."
"Yes, take him!" the man continued, more boldly. "Why was he poking around up _there_? What has he got in mind, eh?"
"Not drunk, but God knows what is wrong with him," muttered the workman.
"But what do you want?" the manager shouted again, beginning to get genuinely angry. "Why are you hanging around?"
"Afraid of the police station, are you?" Raskolnikov said mockingly.
"Afraid? Why are you hanging around?"
"He is a crook!" the peasant woman shouted.
"Why waste time talking to him?" cried the other manager, a hulking peasant in an open coat with keys on his belt. "Get out of here! He is a crook, no doubt about it. Get going!"
And seizing Raskolnikov by the shoulder, he flung him into the street. He stumbled forward but caught his balance, looked silently at the spectators, and walked away.
"Strange fellow," the workman remarked.
"Strange people these days," said the woman.
"You should have taken him to the station anyway," the man in the long coat said.
"Better not to get involved," the big manager decided. "A born troublemaker! He _wants_ you to take him in -- once you do, you will never shake him off.... We know the type!"

"Should I go there or not?" thought Raskolnikov, standing in the middle of the road at the crossroads. He looked around, as though expecting someone to give him a decisive answer. But no sound came. Everything was dead and silent, like the stones he walked on -- dead to him, to him alone.... Suddenly, at the far end of the street, two hundred yards away in the gathering darkness, he saw a crowd and heard voices and shouts. In the middle of the crowd stood a carriage.... A light gleamed in the street. "What is it?" Raskolnikov turned right and walked toward the crowd. He seemed to be grasping at anything, and he smiled coldly when he recognized what was happening, for he had fully made up his mind to go to the police station and knew that it would all soon be over.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 7
paragraphs: An elegant carriage stood in the middle of the road, drawn by a pair of spirited grey horses. There was no one inside, and the coachman had climbed down from his seat. The horses were being held by the bridle.... A mass of people had gathered, with the police in front. One officer held a lighted lantern, turning it on something lying near the wheels. Everyone was talking, shouting, exclaiming. The coachman seemed at a loss and kept repeating:
"What a disaster! Good Lord, what a disaster!"

Raskolnikov pushed his way in and finally managed to see what was causing the commotion. On the ground lay a man who had been run over, apparently unconscious and covered in blood. He was very poorly dressed, but not like a laborer. Blood poured from his head and face. His face was crushed, mangled, and disfigured. He was clearly badly hurt.

"Dear God!" the coachman wailed. "What more could I have done? If I had been driving fast, or if I had not shouted at him -- but I was going slowly, not in any hurry. Everyone could see I was driving like everyone else. A drunk cannot walk straight -- we all know that.... I saw him crossing the street, staggering, nearly falling. I shouted again, a second time, a third time, then I reined the horses in, but he fell right under their hooves! Either he did it on purpose or he was too far gone.... The horses are young, easily spooked... they bolted, he screamed... that made it worse. That is how it happened!"
"That is exactly how it was," a voice in the crowd confirmed.
"He shouted, it is true -- he shouted three times," said another voice.
"Three times exactly -- we all heard it," a third voice called out.

But the coachman was not especially distressed or frightened. The carriage clearly belonged to a rich, important person who was waiting for it somewhere. The police were naturally anxious not to upset his plans. All they had to do was get the injured man to the police station and the hospital. No one knew his name.
Meanwhile Raskolnikov had squeezed through and bent closer over him. The lantern suddenly lit up the victim's face. He recognized him.

"I know him! I know him!" he shouted, pushing to the front. "He is a retired government clerk -- Marmeladov. He lives nearby, in Kozel's building.... Get a doctor! I will pay -- look!" He pulled money from his pocket and showed it to the policeman. He was in a state of violent agitation.

The police were glad to learn who the man was. Raskolnikov gave his own name and address, and as earnestly as though it were his own father, he begged the police to carry the unconscious Marmeladov to his lodgings immediately.

"Right here -- three houses away," he said eagerly. "The building belongs to Kozel, a rich German. He was on his way home, no doubt drunk. I know him -- he is a drunkard. He has a family there -- a wife, children. He has a daughter.... It will take too long to get him to the hospital, and there must be a doctor somewhere in the building. I will pay, I will pay! At least he will be looked after at home... they can help him right away. But he will die before you get him to the hospital." He managed to slip something unseen into the policeman's hand. But the matter was straightforward and legitimate, and in any case help was closer here. They lifted the injured man, and people volunteered to carry him.
Kozel's building was thirty yards away. Raskolnikov walked behind, carefully supporting Marmeladov's head and showing the way.
"This way, this way! Head first going up the stairs. Turn him around! I will pay -- I will make it worth your while," he murmured.

Katerina Ivanovna had been doing what she always did in her free moments -- pacing back and forth in her little room from the window to the stove and back, arms folded across her chest, talking to herself and coughing. Lately she had taken to talking more than ever to her eldest daughter, Polenka, a girl of ten, who understood much less than she grasped but knew very well that her mother needed her, and so always watched her with wide, knowing eyes and tried her hardest to look like she understood. This time Polenka was undressing her little brother, who had been sick all day and was going to bed. The boy was waiting for her to take off his shirt, which had to be washed overnight. He sat perfectly still on a chair -- silent, serious, legs straight out in front of him, heels together, toes pointing out.

He was listening to what his mother was telling his sister, sitting motionless with pursed lips and big round eyes -- exactly the way all good little boys are supposed to sit when being undressed for bed. A still younger girl, dressed literally in rags, stood behind the screen waiting her turn. The door to the stairway was open to provide some relief from the clouds of tobacco smoke that drifted in from the other rooms and sent the poor consumptive woman into long, terrible fits of coughing. Katerina Ivanovna seemed to have grown even thinner that week, and the hectic flush on her cheeks was brighter than ever.

"You would not believe, you cannot imagine, Polenka," she said, pacing the room, "what a happy, luxurious life we had in my papa's house, and how this drunkard has brought me to ruin -- and will bring all of you to ruin! Papa was a civil colonel, only a step away from governor. Everyone who visited him said, 'We regard you, Ivan Mihailovitch, as our governor!' When I... when..." she coughed violently, "oh, this cursed life!" she cried, pressing her hands to her chest. "When at my last ball... at the marshal's... Princess Bezzemelny saw me -- the same one who blessed me when your father and I married, Polenka -- she immediately asked: 'Is that not the lovely girl who danced the shawl dance at the graduation ceremony?' (You must mend that tear -- take your needle and darn it the way I showed you, or tomorrow" -- cough, cough, cough -- "he will make the hole bigger," she forced out.) "Prince Schegolskoy, a kammerjunker just arrived from Petersburg... danced the mazurka with me and wanted to propose the next day. But I thanked him with the most flattering expressions and told him my heart had long belonged to another. That other was your father, Polya. Papa was furious.... Is the water ready? Give me the shirt, and the stockings! Lida," she called to the youngest, "you will have to sleep without your chemise tonight... lay your stockings out with it... I will wash them together.... Why does that drunken vagabond not come home? He has worn his shirt until it looks like a dishrag, torn it to shreds! I would do it all together so I would not have to work two nights in a row! Oh, God!" (Cough, cough, cough, cough!) "Again! What is this?" she cried, noticing a crowd in the hallway and men pushing into her room with a burden. "What is it? What are they carrying? Have mercy!"
"Where should we put him?" the policeman asked, looking around after Marmeladov, unconscious and covered in blood, had been carried in.
"On the sofa! Lay him right on the sofa, with his head this way," Raskolnikov directed.
"Run over in the street! Drunk!" someone shouted in the hallway.
Katerina Ivanovna stood frozen, turning white and gasping for breath. The children were terrified. Little Lida screamed, rushed to Polenka, and clung to her, trembling all over.
As soon as they had laid Marmeladov down, Raskolnikov rushed to Katerina Ivanovna.

"For God's sake, stay calm, do not be frightened!" he said quickly. "He was crossing the street and a carriage hit him. Do not be frightened, he will come to. I told them to bring him here... I have been here before, you remember? He will come to. I will pay!"
"This time he has done it!" Katerina Ivanovna cried in despair and rushed to her husband.

Raskolnikov noticed immediately that she was not the kind of woman who faints easily. In an instant she placed a pillow under the unfortunate man's head -- something no one else had thought of -- and began undressing and examining him. She kept her wits about her, forgetting herself, biting her trembling lips and stifling the screams rising in her throat.
Meanwhile, Raskolnikov persuaded someone to run for a doctor. It turned out there was one two doors down.

"I have sent for a doctor," he kept assuring Katerina Ivanovna. "Do not worry, I will pay. Is there water?... And give me a napkin or a towel, anything, quickly.... He is injured but not dead, believe me.... We will see what the doctor says!"

Katerina Ivanovna ran to the window. There, on a broken chair in the corner, a large earthenware basin full of water had been set out, ready for washing the children's and her husband's clothes that night. Katerina Ivanovna did this washing at night at least twice a week, sometimes more. The family had reached such a state that they had practically no change of clothes, and Katerina Ivanovna could not stand uncleanliness. Rather than see dirt in the house, she preferred to work herself to exhaustion at night while everyone slept, hanging the wet clothes on a line to be dry by morning. She picked up the basin at Raskolnikov's request but nearly fell under its weight. But Raskolnikov had already found a towel, wetted it, and begun washing the blood from Marmeladov's face.

Katerina Ivanovna stood nearby, breathing painfully, pressing her hands to her chest. She needed help herself. Raskolnikov was beginning to realize he might have made a mistake in having the injured man brought here. The policeman stood there looking uncertain too.

"Polenka!" Katerina Ivanovna called out. "Run to Sonia -- quickly. If she is not home, leave word that her father has been run over and she must come here at once... as soon as she gets back. Run, Polenka! Here -- put on the shawl."
"Run as fast as you can!" the little boy on the chair cried out suddenly, after which he sank back into the same mute rigidity -- round eyes, heels thrust forward, toes spread apart.

Meanwhile the room had filled with so many people you could not have dropped a pin. The policemen left, all except one who stayed for a while trying to shoo back the crowd pressing in from the stairway. Nearly all of Madame Lippevechsel's lodgers had streamed in from the inner rooms -- first they were packed in the doorway, then they overflowed into the room. Katerina Ivanovna was furious.

"Can you not at least let him die in peace!" she shouted at the crowd. "Is this a show for your entertainment? With your cigarettes!" (Cough, cough, cough!) "You might as well keep your hats on!... And there is one wearing his! Get out! Have some respect for the dead, at least!"

The coughing choked her, but her rebukes had some effect. They clearly had a certain fear of Katerina Ivanovna. The lodgers, one by one, squeezed back into the doorway with that peculiar inner satisfaction that can always be observed among bystanders at a sudden disaster -- a feeling that no living person is exempt from, even among those closest to the victim, and regardless of how sincere their sympathy and compassion may be.
Voices in the hallway could be heard, though, saying the man should be taken to the hospital and that people had no business creating a disturbance here.

"No business dying!" Katerina Ivanovna cried, and she was rushing to the door to unleash her fury on them when she came face to face in the doorway with Madame Lippevechsel, who had only just heard about the accident and had come to restore order. She was an especially quarrelsome and unreasonable German.
"Oh, my God!" she cried, wringing her hands. "Your husband, drunken horses have trampled! To the hospital with him! I am the landlady!"

"Amalia Ludwigovna, I beg you to consider what you are saying," Katerina Ivanovna began in a haughty tone -- she always took a haughty tone with the landlady so that the woman would "remember her place," and even now she could not deny herself this satisfaction. "Amalia Ludwigovna..."
"I have told you once before that you may not dare call me Amalia Ludwigovna. I am Amalia Ivanovna."

"You are not Amalia Ivanovna but Amalia Ludwigovna, and since I am not one of your contemptible flatterers like Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who is laughing behind the door at this very moment" -- indeed, a laugh and the words "they are at it again" were audible from the doorway -- "I shall always call you Amalia Ludwigovna, though I cannot fathom why you dislike the name. You can see for yourself what has happened to Semyon Zaharovitch. He is dying. I ask you to close that door immediately and let no one in. Let him at least die in peace! Otherwise, I promise you, the Governor-General himself will be informed of your behavior tomorrow. The prince knew me as a girl; he remembers Semyon Zaharovitch well and has often been a benefactor to him. Everyone knows Semyon Zaharovitch had many friends and patrons whom he gave up himself, out of honorable pride, knowing his unfortunate weakness. But now" -- she pointed at Raskolnikov -- "a generous young man with means and connections, whom Semyon Zaharovitch has known since childhood, has come to our aid. You may rest assured, Amalia Ludwigovna..."

All this was delivered with extreme rapidity, getting faster and faster, but a coughing fit suddenly cut Katerina Ivanovna short. At that instant the dying man regained consciousness and groaned. She ran to him. The injured man opened his eyes and, without recognition or understanding, stared at Raskolnikov bending over him. He drew deep, slow, painful breaths. Blood seeped from the corners of his mouth and sweat beaded on his forehead. Not recognizing Raskolnikov, he began looking around anxiously. Katerina Ivanovna gazed at him with a sad but stern expression. Tears trickled from her eyes.
"My God! His whole chest is crushed! Look at the blood," she said in despair. "We must get his clothes off. Turn a little, Semyon Zaharovitch, if you can," she called to him.
Marmeladov recognized her.
"A priest," he said hoarsely.
Katerina Ivanovna went to the window, leaned her head against the frame, and cried out in despair:
"Oh, this cursed life!"
"A priest," the dying man said again after a moment's silence.

"They have gone for one!" Katerina Ivanovna shouted. He obeyed her shout and fell silent. With sad, timid eyes he searched for her. She came back and stood by his pillow. He seemed slightly easier, but not for long.
Soon his eyes found little Lida, his favorite, who was shaking in the corner as though having a fit, staring at him with her wide, wondering child's eyes.
"A-ah," he gestured toward her anxiously. He wanted to say something.
"What now?" cried Katerina Ivanovna.
"Barefoot, barefoot!" he muttered, pointing with frantic eyes at the child's bare feet.
"Be quiet," Katerina Ivanovna snapped. "You know perfectly well why she is barefoot."
"Thank God -- the doctor!" Raskolnikov exclaimed with relief.

The doctor came in -- a precise little old man, a German, who looked around mistrustfully. He went up to the sick man, took his pulse, and carefully felt his head. Then, with Katerina Ivanovna's help, he unbuttoned the blood-soaked shirt and exposed the injured man's chest. It was gashed, crushed, and fractured -- several ribs on the right side were broken. On the left, just over the heart, was a large, sinister yellowish-black bruise from a savage kick of the horse's hoof. The doctor frowned. The policeman told him the man had been caught in the wheel and dragged about thirty yards along the road.
"It is remarkable that he regained consciousness at all," the doctor whispered softly to Raskolnikov.
"What do you think?" Raskolnikov asked.
"He will die any minute."
"Is there really no hope?"
"Not the slightest. He is at the very end.... His head is badly injured too.... Hmm... I could bleed him, if you like, but... it would be pointless. He will be dead within five or ten minutes."
"Then bleed him."
"If you wish.... But I warn you it will be perfectly useless."

At that moment more footsteps were heard. The crowd in the hallway parted, and the priest -- a small, grey old man -- appeared in the doorway carrying the sacrament. A policeman had gone for him at the time of the accident. The doctor stepped aside, exchanging glances with him. Raskolnikov asked the doctor to stay a bit longer. He shrugged but remained.

Everyone stepped back. The confession was brief. The dying man probably understood very little; he could only produce broken, indistinct sounds. Katerina Ivanovna took little Lida, lifted the boy from his chair, and knelt in the corner by the stove, making the children kneel before her. The little girl was still trembling, but the boy, kneeling on his small bare knees, rhythmically raised his hand, crossed himself with precision, and bowed down until his forehead touched the floor -- a gesture that seemed to give him particular satisfaction. Katerina Ivanovna bit her lips and held back her tears. She prayed too, occasionally straightening the boy's shirt and managing to drape a kerchief from the chest over the girl's bare shoulders -- all without rising from her knees or pausing in her prayer. Meanwhile the door from the inner rooms cracked open again. In the hallway, the crowd of spectators from every apartment on the staircase grew denser, though no one dared cross the threshold. A single candle stub lit the scene.

At that moment Polenka forced her way through the crowd. She came in breathless from running, pulled off her kerchief, found her mother, went up to her, and said: "She is coming. I met her in the street." Her mother made her kneel beside her.

Timidly and noiselessly, a young girl made her way through the crowd, and her appearance in that room -- amid the poverty, the rags, the death and despair -- was startling. She too was in rags, cheap clothes, but decked out in the garish, unmistakable finery of the streets. Sonia stopped in the doorway and looked around, bewildered, seeming unconscious of everything. She had forgotten her secondhand, gaudy silk dress, so inappropriate here with its absurd long train, and her enormous crinoline that filled the whole doorway, and her light-colored shoes, and the parasol she had brought along though it was useless at night, and her ridiculous round straw hat with its blazing flame-colored feather. Under this rakishly tilted hat was a pale, frightened little face with parted lips and eyes wide with terror. Sonia was a small, thin girl of eighteen with fair hair, rather pretty, with remarkable blue eyes. She stared at the bed and the priest. She too was out of breath from running. At last whispers and a few words from the crowd probably reached her. She looked down and took a step into the room, still staying close to the door.
The service was over. Katerina Ivanovna went back to her husband. The priest stepped aside and turned to offer a few words of consolation to Katerina Ivanovna before leaving.
"And what am I supposed to do with these?" she interrupted sharply and irritably, pointing at the children.
"God is merciful. Look to the Almighty for help," the priest began.
"Ha! He is merciful -- but not to us."
"That is a sin, madam," the priest said, shaking his head.
"And is _that_ not a sin?" cried Katerina Ivanovna, pointing at the dying man.
"Perhaps those who inadvertently caused the accident will agree to compensate you, at least for the loss of his income."

"You do not understand!" Katerina Ivanovna cried angrily, waving her hand. "Why should they compensate me? He was drunk and threw himself under the horses! What income? He brought us nothing but misery. He drank everything away, the drunkard! He robbed us to pay for his drinking, he wasted their lives and mine on drink! And thank God he is dying! One less mouth to feed!"
"You must forgive in the hour of death. Such feelings are a grave sin, madam."

Katerina Ivanovna was busy with the dying man -- giving him water, wiping the blood and sweat from his face, straightening his pillow. She had only turned to speak to the priest for a moment. Now she flew at him almost in a frenzy.

"Oh, Father! Those are just words! Forgive! If he had not been run over, he would have come home tonight drunk, with his only shirt filthy and in rags, and collapsed like a log. And I would have spent the whole night scrubbing and rinsing, washing his rags and the children's, then drying them by the window -- and at daybreak I would have been darning them. That is how I spend my nights!... What is the point of talking about forgiveness? I have already forgiven!"

A terrible, hollow cough cut her short. She pressed a handkerchief to her lips and showed it to the priest, clutching her aching chest with her other hand. The handkerchief was soaked with blood. The priest bowed his head and said nothing.

Marmeladov was in his death agony. He did not take his eyes off Katerina Ivanovna's face as she bent over him again. He kept trying to say something, moving his tongue with difficulty and forming indistinct words. But Katerina Ivanovna, understanding that he wanted to beg forgiveness, cut him off:
"Quiet! No need! I know what you want to say!" And the dying man fell silent. But at that same moment his wandering eyes found the doorway, and he saw Sonia.
Until then he had not noticed her. She was standing in the shadows, in a corner.
"Who is that? Who is that?" he said suddenly, in a thick, gasping voice, in agitation, turning his horrified eyes toward the door where his daughter stood, and struggling to sit up.
"Lie down! Lie _down_!" cried Katerina Ivanovna.

With unnatural strength he had managed to prop himself on his elbow. He stared wildly and fixedly at his daughter for some time, as though not recognizing her. He had never seen her dressed like this before. Suddenly he recognized her -- crushed, ashamed, standing there in her humiliation and garish finery, meekly waiting her turn to say goodbye to her dying father. His face showed intense suffering.

"Sonia! Daughter! Forgive!" he cried, and he tried to reach out to her, but losing his balance, he tumbled off the sofa face-first onto the floor. They rushed to pick him up and put him back, but he was dying. Sonia, with a faint cry, ran to him, threw her arms around him, and held him. He died in her embrace.
"He got what he wanted," Katerina Ivanovna cried, seeing her husband's body. "Well, what now? How am I supposed to bury him? And what will I feed them tomorrow?"
Raskolnikov went up to Katerina Ivanovna.

"Katerina Ivanovna," he began, "last week your husband told me the entire story of his life and circumstances.... Believe me, he spoke of you with passionate reverence. From that evening, when I learned how devoted he was to all of you, and how he loved and respected you especially, Katerina Ivanovna, despite his unfortunate weakness -- from that evening we became friends.... Allow me now... to do something... to repay my debt to my dead friend. Here are twenty rubles -- if that can help at all, then... I... in short, I will come again, I will definitely come again... I may even come tomorrow.... Goodbye!"

And he hurried out of the room, pushing through the crowd to the stairs. But in the crowd he suddenly bumped into Nikodim Fomitch, who had heard about the accident and come to give instructions personally. They had not met since the scene at the police station, but Nikodim Fomitch recognized him instantly.
"Ah, is that you?" he asked.

"He is dead," Raskolnikov answered. "The doctor and the priest have been -- everything was done properly. Do not upset the poor woman too much -- she has consumption as it is. Try to cheer her up if you can... you are a kind man, I know..." he added with a smile, looking straight into his face.
"But you are spattered with blood," Nikodim Fomitch remarked, noticing in the lamplight some fresh stains on Raskolnikov's waistcoat.
"Yes... I am covered in blood," Raskolnikov said with a peculiar expression, then smiled, nodded, and headed downstairs.

He descended slowly and deliberately, feverish but unaware of it, entirely consumed by a new, overwhelming sensation of life and strength that had suddenly surged up within him. This feeling was like that of a condemned man who has just been pardoned. Halfway down the stairs, the priest overtook him on his way home. Raskolnikov let him pass with a silent nod. But as he was descending the final steps, he heard hurried footsteps behind him. Someone was chasing him. It was Polenka. She was running after him, calling: "Wait! Wait!"

He turned around. She was at the bottom of the staircase, stopped one step above him. Dim light came in from the courtyard. Raskolnikov could make out the child's thin but pretty little face, looking at him with a bright, childish smile. She had run after him with a message she was obviously delighted to deliver.
"Tell me, what is your name?... And where do you live?" she asked breathlessly, in a rapid voice.
He placed both hands on her shoulders and looked at her with something like rapture. It gave him such joy to look at her -- he could not have said why.
"Who sent you?"
"Sister Sonia sent me," the girl answered, smiling even more brightly.
"I knew it was Sister Sonia who sent you."
"Mama sent me too... when Sister Sonia was sending me, Mama came over too and said: 'Run fast, Polenka.'"
"Do you love Sister Sonia?"
"I love her more than anyone," Polenka answered with a special earnestness, and her smile grew more serious.
"And will you love me?"

By way of answer, he saw the little girl's face drawing near, her full lips innocently held out to kiss him. Then her thin, stick-like arms held him tightly, her head rested on his shoulder, and she wept softly, pressing her face against him.

"I feel sorry for Papa," she said after a moment, lifting her tear-streaked face and wiping her eyes with her hands. "It is nothing but bad luck now," she added suddenly with the peculiarly solemn air children put on when they are trying to talk like adults.
"Did your father love you?"

"He loved Lida most," she went on very seriously, without smiling, exactly like a grown-up. "He loved her because she is little and because she is sick. And he always used to bring her presents. But he taught us to read, and me grammar and scripture too," she added with dignity. "And Mama never said anything, but we knew she was pleased, and Papa knew it too. And Mama wants to teach me French, because it is time my education began."
"And do you know your prayers?"

"Of course we do! We have known them for a long time. I say mine silently because I am a big girl now, but Kolya and Lida say theirs aloud with Mama. First they say the Hail Mary, and then another prayer: 'Lord, forgive and bless Sister Sonia,' and then: 'Lord, forgive and bless our second father.' Our first father is dead, and this is the other one, but we pray for the first one too."
"Polenka, my name is Rodion. Pray for me too sometimes. 'And Thy servant Rodion' -- nothing more."
"I will pray for you for the rest of my life," the little girl declared passionately, and suddenly smiling again, she threw herself at him and hugged him tightly once more.

Raskolnikov told her his name and address and promised to come the next day without fail. The child went away completely enchanted with him. It was past ten when he stepped into the street. Five minutes later he was standing on the bridge, at the exact spot where the woman had jumped in.

"Enough," he declared, resolutely and triumphantly. "I am done with delusions, imaginary terrors, and phantoms! Life is real! Have I not just lived? My life did not die with that old woman! May the Kingdom of Heaven be hers -- and now enough, old woman, your time is up! Now begins the reign of reason and light... and of will, and of strength... and now we shall see! We shall test our strength!" he added defiantly, as though challenging some invisible power. "And I was ready to accept living on a square yard of space!

"I am very weak right now, but... I believe my illness is over. I knew it would pass when I went out. By the way, Potchinkov's building is just a few steps from here. I should definitely go to Razumihin, even if it were not nearby... let him win his bet! Let us give him some satisfaction too -- it does not matter! Strength -- strength is what you need. You cannot get anything without it, and strength must be won by strength -- that is what they do not understand," he added, proudly and self-assuredly. He walked from the bridge with faltering steps. Pride and self-confidence grew steadily stronger in him. He was becoming a different man with every passing moment. What had happened to work this transformation? He did not know himself. Like a man grasping at a straw, he suddenly felt that he too "could live, that there was still life left for him, that his life had not died with the old woman." Perhaps he was jumping to conclusions too quickly, but he did not stop to think about that.
"But I did ask her to pray for 'Thy servant Rodion,'" the thought struck him. "Well, that was... just in case," he added, and laughed at his own boyish joke. He was in excellent spirits.

He found Razumihin easily. The new tenant was already known at Potchinkov's, and the building manager showed him the way at once. Halfway up the stairs he could hear the noise and animated conversation of a large gathering. The door to the stairway was wide open. He could hear shouts and debate. Razumihin's room was fairly large, and the company numbered about fifteen people. Raskolnikov stopped in the entry, where two of the landlady's servants were busy behind a screen with samovars, bottles, plates, and dishes of pie and snacks brought up from the landlady's kitchen. Raskolnikov sent word in for Razumihin. He came running out, delighted. It was immediately obvious that he had drunk a great deal. Though no amount of liquor could truly make Razumihin drunk, this time the effects were visible.

"Listen," Raskolnikov said quickly, "I only came to tell you that you have won your bet and that no one really knows what may happen to them. I cannot come in -- I am so weak I will fall down any second. So good evening and goodbye! Come see me tomorrow."
"You know what? I will walk you home. If you say you are that weak, you need--"
"And your guests? Who is the curly-haired one who just peeked out?"

"Him? God only knows! Some friend of my uncle's, I expect, or maybe he showed up uninvited... I will leave my uncle with them -- he is an invaluable man. Too bad I cannot introduce you right now. But forget them all! They will not even notice I am gone, and I need some fresh air anyway. You came at just the right moment -- another two minutes and I would have started a fight! They are spouting such insane nonsense... you cannot imagine what people will say! Though actually, why not? Do we not talk nonsense ourselves? And let them... that is how you learn not to!... Wait -- let me get Zossimov."
Zossimov pounced on Raskolnikov almost eagerly and showed a particular interest in him. Soon his face brightened.
"You need to go straight to bed," he said after examining the patient as best he could, "and take something for the night. Will you? I prepared it earlier... a powder."
"Two, if you like," Raskolnikov answered. He took the powder immediately.
"Good that you are seeing him home," Zossimov said to Razumihin. "We will see how he is tomorrow. He is not bad today -- a considerable improvement since this afternoon. Live and learn..."

"Do you know what Zossimov whispered to me as we left?" Razumihin burst out as soon as they were in the street. "I will not tell you everything, brother, because they are such fools. Zossimov told me to talk freely with you on the way and get you to talk freely to me, and afterward I am to report back to him, because he has gotten it into his head that you are... mad, or close to it. Can you imagine! First, you have three times his brains. Second, if you are not mad, you could not care less about his wild theory. And third, that slab of meat whose specialty is surgery has gone off on a tangent about mental illness. And what brought him to this conclusion about you was your conversation today with Zametov."
"Zametov told you everything?"

"Yes, and he was right to. Now I understand it all, and so does Zametov.... The thing is, Rodya... the point is... I am a bit drunk now.... But never mind... the point is that this idea... you understand? was just beginning to hatch in their minds... you understand? That is, nobody dared say it out loud, because the idea is too absurd -- especially since they arrested that painter, the whole thing burst like a bubble. But why are they such fools? I gave Zametov a bit of a beating at the time -- that is between us, brother, do not let on that you know. I have noticed he is touchy about it. It was at Luise Ivanovna's. But today -- today it has all been cleared up. It is mainly that Ilya Petrovitch's doing! He took advantage of your fainting at the station, though he is ashamed of it himself now. I know that for a fact..."
Raskolnikov listened greedily. Razumihin was drunk enough to talk too freely.
"I fainted because it was stuffy and the paint fumes," Raskolnikov said.

"No need to explain that! And it was not just the paint -- the fever had been building for a month. Zossimov will vouch for that! But you should see how crushed that boy Zametov is now -- you would not believe it! 'I am not worth his little finger,' he says. Yours, he means. He has his good moments, brother. But the lesson you gave him today at the Palais de Cristal -- that was priceless! You terrified him at first, you know -- he nearly had convulsions! You practically had him believing all that horrible nonsense again, and then you just -- stuck your tongue out at him! 'There, what do you make of that?' Perfect! He is crushed, destroyed! It was masterful, I swear! Exactly what they deserve! Too bad I was not there! He was hoping to see you desperately. Porfiry wants to meet you too..."
"Ah!... him too... but why did they brand me a madman?"

"Not exactly mad. I must have said too much, brother.... What struck him, you see, was that you seemed interested only in that one subject. Now it is clear why it interested you -- knowing all the circumstances... and how it agitated you and got tangled up with your illness... I am a bit drunk, brother, but to hell with him -- he has some theory of his own... I am telling you, he is obsessed with mental illness. But do not let it bother you..."
For half a minute neither spoke.

"Listen, Razumihin," Raskolnikov began, "I want to tell you something plainly. I have just been at a deathbed -- a clerk who died... I gave them all my money... and besides, I was just kissed by someone who, if I had killed anyone, would still... I mean, I also saw someone else there... with a flame-colored feather... but I am rambling. I am very weak -- hold me up... the stairs are right here..."
"What is it? What is the matter?" Razumihin asked anxiously.
"I am a bit dizzy, but that is not the point. I am so sad, so sad... like a woman. Look -- what is that? Look, look!"
"What?"
"Do you not see? There is a light in my room -- see? Through the crack..."
They were already at the foot of the last flight of stairs, on the level of the landlady's door, and from there they could indeed see that a light was burning in Raskolnikov's garret.
"Strange! Nastasya, perhaps," Razumihin suggested.
"She is never in my room at this hour. She must be in bed by now, but... I do not care! Goodbye!"
"What do you mean? I am coming in with you! We will go in together!"
"I know we are going in together, but I want to shake your hand here and say goodbye to you here. So give me your hand -- goodbye!"
"What is wrong with you, Rodya?"
"Nothing... come on... you will be my witness."
They started up the stairs, and the thought crossed Razumihin's mind that perhaps Zossimov was right after all. "I must have upset him with my chattering!" he muttered to himself.
When they reached the door, they heard voices inside the room.
"What is going on?" cried Razumihin. Raskolnikov was the first to open the door. He flung it wide and stood frozen in the doorway.

His mother and sister were sitting on his sofa, and they had been waiting for an hour and a half. Why had he never expected them, never imagined they might be here -- even though the news of their departure, their journey, their imminent arrival had been told to him repeatedly, just that day? They had spent that hour and a half questioning Nastasya, who stood before them now and had already told them everything. They had been beside themselves with alarm when they learned he had "run off" that day while ill and, as they gathered from Nastasya, delirious. Good God, what had become of him? Both had been weeping, both had been in anguish for that hour and a half.

A cry of joy and ecstasy greeted Raskolnikov's entrance. Both women rushed to him. But he stood like a dead man. A sudden, unbearable sensation struck him like a thunderbolt. He could not lift his arms to embrace them. He could not. His mother and sister hugged him, kissed him, laughed, and wept. He took a step, swayed, and collapsed, unconscious.
Panic, cries of horror, moans... Razumihin, who had been standing in the doorway, flew into the room, scooped up the sick man in his powerful arms, and had him on the sofa in an instant.

"It is nothing, nothing!" he cried to the mother and sister. "It is just a faint, a trifle! The doctor said just now that he is much better, that he is perfectly well! Water! Look -- he is already coming around. It is all right now!"

And seizing Dounia by the arm so hard he nearly dislocated it, he made her lean down to see that "he is all right now." The mother and sister looked at Razumihin with emotion and gratitude, as though he were their guardian angel. They had already heard from Nastasya everything this "very capable young man," as Pulcheria Alexandrovna called him that evening in conversation with Dounia, had done for their Rodya during his illness.

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Raskolnikov sat up on the sofa. He waved weakly at Razumihin to stop the stream of warm, incoherent reassurances he was directing at his mother and sister, took them both by the hand, and for a minute or two gazed from one to the other in silence. His mother was alarmed by his expression. It showed an agonizingly intense emotion and at the same time something rigid, almost unhinged. Pulcheria Alexandrovna began to cry.
Avdotya Romanovna was pale. Her hand trembled in her brother's.
"Go home... with him," he said in a broken voice, pointing to Razumihin. "Goodbye until tomorrow. Tomorrow -- everything.... How long have you been here?"
"We arrived this evening, Rodya," Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered. "The train was terribly late. But, Rodya, nothing could make me leave you now! I will spend the night here, beside you..."
"Do not torture me!" he said with an irritable gesture.
"I will stay with him," Razumihin cried. "I will not leave him for a second. To hell with all my guests! Let them rage all they want! My uncle is running the show up there."
"How can I ever thank you!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, pressing Razumihin's hands again, but Raskolnikov cut her off.
"I cannot stand it! I cannot stand it!" he repeated irritably. "Stop badgering me! Enough -- go away... I cannot take it!"
"Come, Mama, let us step out of the room at least for a moment," Dounia whispered in dismay. "We are clearly upsetting him."
"Can I not even look at him after three years?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna wept.
"Wait," he stopped them again. "You keep interrupting me and my thoughts get muddled.... Have you seen Luzhin?"
"No, Rodya, but he already knows we have arrived. We heard, Rodya, that Pyotr Petrovitch was kind enough to visit you today," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added timidly.
"Yes... he was so kind.... Dounia, I promised Luzhin I would throw him down the stairs and told him to go to hell...."
"Rodya, what are you saying! Surely you do not mean..." Pulcheria Alexandrovna began in alarm, but she stopped, looking at Dounia.

Avdotya Romanovna was watching her brother attentively, waiting for what would come next. Both of them had heard about the quarrel from Nastasya, who had understood and reported what she could, and they were in painful uncertainty and suspense.
"Dounia," Raskolnikov continued with effort, "I do not want this marriage. So tomorrow, at the first opportunity, you must refuse Luzhin. I never want to hear his name again."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Brother, think about what you are saying!" Avdotya Romanovna began sharply, but immediately caught herself. "You are not fit to talk now. Perhaps you are tired," she added gently.

"You think I am delirious? No.... You are marrying Luzhin for _my_ sake. But I will not accept the sacrifice. So write a letter before tomorrow refusing him... let me read it in the morning, and that will be the end of it!"
"I cannot do that!" the girl cried, offended. "What right do you have--"
"Dounia, you are being hasty too. Be quiet -- tomorrow... Do you not see..." the mother intervened anxiously. "We had better go!"

"He is raving," Razumihin declared tipsily. "How else would he dare! Tomorrow all this nonsense will blow over... though today he really did throw him out. That much is true. And Luzhin got angry too.... He showed up here, tried to show off his learning, and left with his tail between his legs...."
"So it is true?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Goodbye until tomorrow, brother," Dounia said with compassion. "Let us go, Mama... Goodbye, Rodya."

"Listen, sister," he called after them, making one last effort. "I am not delirious. This marriage is an abomination. Let me be a scoundrel, but you must not... one scoundrel is enough... and even though I am a scoundrel, I would not claim such a sister. It is me or Luzhin! Go now...."

"You are out of your mind! Tyrant!" Razumihin roared. But Raskolnikov did not answer -- perhaps could not. He lay down on the sofa and turned to the wall, completely spent. Avdotya Romanovna looked at Razumihin with interest. Her dark eyes flashed. Razumihin actually flinched under her gaze.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna stood there, overwhelmed.
"Nothing could make me leave," she whispered desperately to Razumihin. "I will stay somewhere here... Please take Dounia home."

"You will ruin everything," Razumihin whispered back, losing patience. "Come out to the stairs at least. Nastasya, bring a light! I promise you," he went on in a half whisper on the stairs, "he nearly beat up the doctor and me this afternoon! You understand? The doctor himself backed down and left, so as not to provoke him. I stayed downstairs standing guard, but he got dressed and slipped out anyway. And he will do it again if you upset him -- at this hour of night -- and do himself harm...."
"What are you saying?"

"And Avdotya Romanovna certainly cannot be left alone in those lodgings without you. Just think about where you are staying! That scoundrel Pyotr Petrovitch could not find you anything better... But you know I have had a few drinks, that is why I am... cursing. Do not mind it...."
"But I will go to the landlady here," Pulcheria Alexandrovna insisted. "I will beg her to find some corner for Dounia and me for the night. I cannot leave him like this -- I cannot!"

This conversation took place on the landing just outside the landlady's door. Nastasya lit the way from a step below. Razumihin was in a state of extraordinary excitement. Half an hour earlier, walking Raskolnikov home, he had indeed been talking too much and too freely -- and he knew it -- but his head was clear despite the vast amount he had consumed. Now he was in a state bordering on ecstasy, and everything he had drunk seemed to hit him with redoubled force. He stood with the two ladies, gripping both their hands, trying to persuade them and making his case with astonishing directness of speech. At nearly every word, probably to emphasize his points, he squeezed their hands painfully, as in a vise. He stared at Avdotya Romanovna without the slightest regard for propriety. They sometimes pulled their hands free from his huge bony paws, but far from noticing anything wrong, he only pulled them closer. If they had told him to throw himself headfirst down the staircase, he would have done it without a second thought. Pulcheria Alexandrovna felt the young man was a bit too eccentric and pinched her hand too hard, but in her anxiety about Rodya she saw his presence as providential and was unwilling to take notice of his peculiarities. Avdotya Romanovna shared her worry and was not timid by nature, but she could hardly look at the blazing light in his eyes without wonder and almost alarm. Only the boundless trust inspired by Nastasya's account of her brother's odd friend kept her from trying to run away from him or drag her mother along. She also realized that running was probably impossible now. Ten minutes later, however, she felt considerably calmer. It was characteristic of Razumihin that he showed his true nature instantly, whatever mood he was in, so people quickly saw the kind of man they were dealing with.

"You cannot go to the landlady -- that would be absurd!" he cried. "Even if you are his mother, staying here will drive him to a frenzy, and then God knows what will happen! Listen, here is what I will do. Nastasya will sit with him now, and I will escort you both home. You cannot be out on the streets alone -- Petersburg is a terrible place for that.... But never mind! Then I will run straight back here, and in fifteen minutes, on my word of honor, I will bring you a report on how he is, whether he is sleeping, and everything. Then -- listen! -- I will dash home -- I have a houseful of guests, all drunk -- grab Zossimov, that is the doctor who is treating him, he is there too, but he is not drunk, he is never drunk -- and drag him to Rodya, and then straight to you. So you will get two reports within the hour -- one from the doctor, you understand, from the doctor himself, which is a very different thing from my account. If anything is wrong, I swear I will bring you here myself. But if everything is fine, you go to bed. And I will spend the night here in the hallway -- he will not hear me -- and I will have Zossimov sleep at the landlady's, to be on hand. So what is better for him right now -- you or the doctor? The doctor is obviously more useful. So go home! But the landlady is out of the question. It is fine for me, but not for you. She would not take you anyway, because she is... because she is a fool... She would be jealous of me on account of Avdotya Romanovna, and of you too, if you want to know... definitely of Avdotya Romanovna. She is an absolutely, utterly unaccountable character! Though I am a fool too!... Never mind! Come on! Do you trust me? Well, do you trust me or not?"
"Let us go, Mama," said Avdotya Romanovna. "He will certainly do what he has promised. He has already saved Rodya, and if the doctor really will agree to spend the night here, what could be better?"
"You see -- you understand me, because you are an angel!" Razumihin cried in ecstasy. "Let us go! Nastasya! Run upstairs and sit with him -- with a light. I will be back in fifteen minutes."

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was not entirely convinced, but she made no further objection. Razumihin gave each of them an arm and led them down the stairs. He still worried her, though -- he was clearly capable and good-hearted, but was he really in any condition to carry out his promises? He seemed in such a state....

"I see what you are thinking -- that I am in such a state!" Razumihin broke in on her thoughts, guessing them, as he strode along the pavement with enormous steps, so that both ladies could barely keep up -- a fact he did not notice. "Nonsense! That is... I am drunk like a fool, but that is not the point. It is not the wine that has gone to my head. It is seeing you.... But do not mind me! Do not pay attention. I am talking rubbish, I am unworthy of you.... I am utterly unworthy of you!
