The minute I have taken you home, I am going to pour two buckets of water over my head at the gutter, and then I will be fine.... If only you knew how I love you both! Do not laugh, and do not be angry! You can be angry with anyone, but not with me! I am his friend, so I am your friend too. I want to be... I had a feeling... Last year there was a moment... well, it was not really a premonition, because you seem to have fallen from heaven. And I probably will not sleep all night... Zossimov was a little worried earlier that he might go mad... that is why he must not be agitated."
"What did you say?" cried the mother.
"Did the doctor really say that?" asked Avdotya Romanovna, alarmed.

"Yes, but it is not true, not one bit. He gave him some medicine, a powder -- I saw it -- and then your arrival.... It would have been better if you had come tomorrow. It is a good thing we left. And in an hour Zossimov himself will report to you about everything. He is not drunk! And I will not be drunk either.... Why did I get so plastered? Because they dragged me into an argument, damn them! I have sworn off arguing! They talk such garbage! I nearly came to blows! I left my uncle there to preside. Would you believe it -- they insist on the complete elimination of individuality, and that is precisely what delights them! Not to be themselves, to be as unlike themselves as possible. That is what they consider the pinnacle of progress. If only their nonsense were their own -- but it is not..."
"Listen!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna interrupted timidly, but this only added fuel to the flames.

"What do you think?" Razumihin shouted, louder than ever. "You think I am attacking them for talking nonsense? Not at all! I like them to talk nonsense. That is humanity's one privilege over all creation. Through error you come to the truth! I am a man because I err! You never reach any truth without making fourteen mistakes -- and very likely a hundred and fourteen. And that is a fine thing in its way. But we cannot even make mistakes on our own! Talk nonsense, but talk _your own_ nonsense, and I will kiss you for it. To go wrong in your own way is better than to go right in someone else's. In the first case you are a person. In the second you are no better than a bird. Truth will not escape you, but life can be choked. There have been examples. And what are we doing now? In science, development, thought, invention, ideals, ambitions, liberalism, judgment, experience -- in everything, everything, everything -- we are still in the preparatory class. We prefer to live on other people's ideas. It is what we are used to! Am I right? Am I right?" cried Razumihin, squeezing and shaking both ladies' hands.
"Oh, mercy -- I really do not know," poor Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
"Yes, yes... though I do not agree with everything you say," Avdotya Romanovna added sincerely, and then let out a cry as he squeezed her hand so painfully.

"Yes? You say yes? Well, after that you... you..." he cried in rapture, "you are a fountain of goodness, purity, reason... and perfection! Give me your hand... and yours too! I want to kiss your hands, right here, on my knees..." and he dropped to his knees on the pavement, which was fortunately deserted at that hour.
"Stop -- please, what are you doing?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, thoroughly distressed.
"Get up, get up!" Dounia said, laughing despite her own alarm.

"Not until you let me kiss your hands! There! Enough! I am getting up, and we go on! I am a wretched fool, I am unworthy of you, and drunk besides... and I am ashamed.... I am not worthy of loving you, but to pay you homage is the duty of every man who is not an utter beast! And I have paid homage.... Here are your lodgings, and for that alone Rodya was right to throw your Pyotr Petrovitch out! How dare he! How dare he put you in a place like this? It is outrageous! Do you know what kind of people they take in here? And you -- his fiancee! You are his fiancee, yes? Well then, I will tell you -- your _fiance_ is a scoundrel."
"Mr. Razumihin, you are forgetting yourself..." Pulcheria Alexandrovna began.

"Yes, yes, you are right, I did forget myself. I am ashamed of it," Razumihin hastened to apologize. "But... but you cannot be angry with me for speaking this way! Because I am being sincere, and not because... hmm, hmm! That would be disgraceful. In short, not because I... hmm! Let us leave it at that. I do not dare say why. I dare not.... But we all saw today when he walked in that this man is not one of us. Not because he had his hair curled at the barber's, not because he was in such a hurry to show off his intellect -- but because he is a spy, a speculator, a skinflint, and a buffoon. That is obvious. Do you think he is clever? No -- he is a fool. And is he a match for you? Good God! You see, ladies," he stopped suddenly on the way up to their rooms, "my friends back there are all drunk, every one of them, but they are all honest, and even though we do talk rubbish -- including me -- we will eventually talk our way to the truth, because we are on the right path. Pyotr Petrovitch... is not on the right path. Even though I just called them every name in the book, I do respect them all... and though I do not respect Zametov, I like him because he is just a puppy. And I even like that ox Zossimov, because he is honest and knows his craft. But enough -- all said and forgiven. Is it forgiven? Good, let us go on. I know this corridor. I have been here before -- there was a scandal in number three.... Where are you? Which number? Eight? Well, lock yourselves in for the night. Do not let anyone in. I will be back with news in fifteen minutes, and half an hour after that with Zossimov. You will see! Goodbye! I am off!"
"Good heavens, Dounia, what is going to happen?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna said to her daughter, anxious and dismayed.

"Do not worry, Mama," said Dounia, taking off her hat and cape. "God sent this man to help us, even if he has come from a drinking party. We can count on him, I am sure. And everything he has done for Rodya..."

"Oh, Dounia -- who knows if he will even come back! How could I bring myself to leave Rodya?... And how different, how different this was from the meeting I had imagined! He was so sullen, as though he was not even glad to see us...."
Tears came to her eyes.
"No, that is not it, Mama. You did not see clearly -- you were crying the whole time. He is completely unhinged by a serious illness. That is all it is."

"Oh, this illness! What is going to happen? And the way he spoke to you, Dounia!" the mother said, looking timidly at her daughter and trying to read her thoughts, already half-consoled by Dounia's willingness to defend her brother, which meant she had already forgiven him. "I am sure he will think better of it tomorrow," she added, probing further.

"And I am sure he will say exactly the same thing tomorrow... about _that_," Avdotya Romanovna said firmly. And there was nothing more to say, because this was the point Pulcheria Alexandrovna was afraid to discuss. Dounia went to her mother and kissed her. The mother embraced her tightly without a word. Then she sat down to wait anxiously for Razumihin's return, timidly watching her daughter pace the room with folded arms, lost in thought. This pacing while thinking was a habit of Avdotya Romanovna's, and her mother was always afraid to interrupt her at such moments.

Razumihin's sudden, drunken infatuation with Avdotya Romanovna was, of course, ridiculous. But anyone seeing her just then -- walking back and forth, arms folded, pensive and melancholy -- might well have understood it, eccentric state or not. Avdotya Romanovna was remarkably good-looking: tall, strikingly proportioned, strong, and self-assured -- a quality apparent in every gesture, though it in no way detracted from the grace and softness of her movements. In face she resembled her brother, but she could genuinely be called beautiful. Her hair was dark brown, a shade lighter than her brother's. There was a proud light in her nearly black eyes, and yet at times they showed extraordinary kindness. She was pale, but it was a healthy pallor. Her face radiated freshness and vitality. Her mouth was rather small; the full red lower lip protruded slightly, as did her chin -- the only irregularity in her beautiful face, but it gave her a distinctly individual, almost haughty expression. Her face was always more serious and thoughtful than cheerful. But how well laughter suited it -- youthful, lighthearted, carefree laughter! It was natural enough that a warm, open, honest giant like Razumihin, who had never seen anyone like her and was not entirely sober, should lose his head immediately. Besides, as fate would have it, he first saw Dounia transfigured by her love for her brother and her joy at meeting him. Then he watched her lower lip quiver with indignation at her brother's arrogant, cruel, ungrateful words -- and his fate was sealed.

He had spoken the truth, moreover, when he let slip in his drunken rambling on the stairs that the eccentric landlady Praskovya Pavlovna would be jealous of Pulcheria Alexandrovna as well as Avdotya Romanovna on his account. Although Pulcheria Alexandrovna was forty-three, her face still bore traces of its former beauty. She looked much younger than her years, as is almost always the case with women who retain serenity of spirit, warmth of heart, and pure, sincere feeling into old age. We might add in passing that preserving these qualities is the only way to preserve beauty as well. Her hair had begun to turn grey and thin, little crow's-feet had long since appeared around her eyes, and her cheeks were hollow and sunken from worry and grief -- yet it was still a handsome face. She was Dounia over again, twenty years later, minus the protruding lower lip. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was emotional but not sentimental, timid and yielding -- but only up to a point. She could give way and accept a great deal, even things contrary to her convictions, but there was a line defined by honesty, principle, and her deepest beliefs that nothing in the world could make her cross.
Exactly twenty minutes after Razumihin left, there came two soft but hurried knocks at the door: he was back.

"I will not come in -- I do not have time," he said quickly when the door opened. "He is sleeping like a log -- soundly, peacefully. God willing, he will sleep ten hours. Nastasya is with him. I told her not to leave until I return. Now I am off to fetch Zossimov. He will give you his report and then you should turn in. I can see you are too exhausted to do anything..."
And he ran off down the corridor.
"What a very capable and... devoted young man!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, thoroughly delighted.
"He seems like a wonderful person!" Avdotya Romanovna replied with some warmth, resuming her walk around the room.

Nearly an hour later they heard footsteps in the corridor and another knock. Both women waited, this time with complete confidence in Razumihin's promise. He had indeed managed to bring Zossimov. Zossimov had agreed without hesitation to leave the party and see Raskolnikov, but he came to the ladies' door reluctantly and with deep suspicion, not trusting Razumihin's judgment in his exhilarated condition. But his vanity was instantly reassured and flattered: he saw they really were expecting him like an oracle. He stayed exactly ten minutes and succeeded in completely reassuring and comforting Pulcheria Alexandrovna. He spoke with evident sympathy but with the reserve and exaggerated seriousness of a young doctor at an important consultation. He did not utter a word on any other subject and showed no desire whatever to enter into more personal relations with the two ladies. Noting Avdotya Romanovna's dazzling beauty the moment he walked in, he made every effort to ignore her throughout, addressing himself solely to Pulcheria Alexandrovna. All of this gave him enormous inner satisfaction. He declared that in his opinion the patient was currently progressing very satisfactorily. His observations indicated that the illness was due partly to the patient's unfortunate material circumstances over recent months, but also had a moral dimension -- was, so to speak, the product of multiple material and psychological influences, anxieties, fears, worries, certain obsessive ideas, and so forth. Noticing out of the corner of his eye that Avdotya Romanovna was following every word closely, Zossimov allowed himself to expand on this theme. When Pulcheria Alexandrovna anxiously and timidly asked whether there was "any suspicion of insanity," he answered with a calm, candid smile that his words had been exaggerated. The patient certainly showed signs of a fixed idea, something approaching monomania -- he, Zossimov, was particularly studying this fascinating branch of medicine -- but it should be remembered that until today the patient had been delirious, and the arrival of his family would undoubtedly have a beneficial effect on his recovery and provide distraction, "provided all new upsets can be avoided," he added significantly. Then he rose, took his leave with an impressive and gracious bow, and departed amid blessings, warm gratitude, and entreaties. Avdotya Romanovna spontaneously offered him her hand. He left exceedingly pleased with his visit and even more so with himself.
"We will talk tomorrow. Go to bed now!" Razumihin said in parting, following Zossimov out. "I will be back first thing in the morning with my report."
"What a charming girl that Avdotya Romanovna is," Zossimov remarked, practically licking his lips as they stepped into the street.

"Charming? You said charming?" Razumihin roared, and he flew at Zossimov and seized him by the throat. "If you ever dare.... Do you understand? Do you understand?" he shouted, shaking him by the collar and pinning him to the wall. "Do you hear me?"

"Let go, you drunken maniac," Zossimov said, struggling free. When Razumihin released him, Zossimov stared at him for a moment and then burst out laughing. Razumihin stood facing him, brooding and grimly serious.
"Of course I am an ass," he said, dark as a thundercloud. "But still... so are you."
"No, brother, not at all. I am not dreaming of anything foolish."
They walked on in silence, and only when they were nearly at Raskolnikov's building did Razumihin break it, clearly troubled.

"Listen," he said. "You are a good fellow, but among your other faults you are a ladies' man -- I know it -- and a filthy one at that. You are a weak, nervous wreck and a bundle of whims. You are getting fat and lazy and cannot deny yourself anything -- and I call that filthy because it leads straight into the gutter. You have let yourself go so badly that I honestly do not know how you are still a good -- even a dedicated -- doctor. You sleep on a featherbed and get up at night for your patients! In another three or four years you will not bother getting up at all... But to hell with all that, that is not the point.... You are going to spend tonight in the landlady's apartment here. (It took some doing to persuade her!) And I will be in the kitchen. So here is your chance to get to know her better.... It is not what you think! Not a trace of anything like that, brother...!"
"But I do not think anything!"

"Here you have modesty, brother -- silence, bashfulness, fierce virtue... and yet she is melting, simply melting like wax! Save me from her, for the love of God! She is extremely attractive... I will repay you, I will do anything...."
Zossimov laughed harder than ever.
"Well, you are smitten! But what am I supposed to do with her?"

"It will not be any trouble, I promise. Just talk to her -- say whatever you like, as long as you sit next to her and talk. You are a doctor besides -- try treating her for something. I swear you will not regret it. She has a piano, and you know I play a little. I have a song there, a real Russian one: 'I shed hot tears.' She loves the genuine article -- and well, it all started with that song. You are a real performer though, a master, a Rubinstein.... I guarantee you will not regret it!"
"Have you made her some promise? Signed something? A promise of marriage?"
"Nothing, nothing, absolutely nothing of the sort! Besides, she is not that type at all.... Tchebarov tried that approach...."
"Then just drop her!"
"But I cannot just drop her!"
"Why not?"
"Well, I just cannot, that is all! There is an element of... attraction here, brother."
"Then why did you lead her on?"

"I did not lead her on! Maybe I was the one who was led on, in my foolishness. But she will not care whether it is you or me -- as long as somebody sits beside her and sighs.... I cannot explain the situation, brother... Look, you are good at mathematics, and you are working on it now -- start teaching her integral calculus! I am serious, completely serious. It will be all the same to her. She will gaze at you and sigh for a whole year. I talked to her once for two days straight about the Prussian House of Lords -- you have to talk about _something_ -- and she just sighed and sweated! And you must not talk about love -- she is bashful to the point of hysteria -- but make it clear you cannot tear yourself away. That is all it takes. It is incredibly comfortable -- you are completely at home. You can read, sit, lounge around, write. You might even risk a kiss, if you are careful."
"But what do I want with her?"

"Oh, I cannot make you see! Look -- you two are made for each other! I have thought of you many times!... You will end up there eventually! So what difference does it make whether it is sooner or later? There is the featherbed factor, brother -- oh, and not only that! There is a pull here -- here you have the end of the world, a safe harbor, a quiet anchorage, the center of the earth, the three fish that support the world, the essence of pancakes, of rich fish pies, of the evening samovar, of soft sighs and warm shawls, of heated stoves to sleep on -- as cozy as being dead, except you are alive -- the best of both worlds! Well, to hell with it, brother, I am talking rubbish. Time for bed! Listen -- I sometimes wake in the night, so I will go check on him. But there is no need really -- everything is fine. Do not worry yourself. But if you feel like it, you could look in on him once too. If you notice anything -- delirium, fever -- wake me at once. But there should not be anything."

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Razumihin woke the next morning at eight o'clock, troubled and serious. He found himself faced with many new and unexpected complications. He had never imagined he would wake up feeling like this. He remembered every detail of the previous day and knew that something entirely novel had happened to him, that he had experienced an impression unlike anything he had ever known. At the same time he clearly recognized that the dream firing his imagination was hopelessly unattainable -- so unattainable that he was actually ashamed of it and quickly turned his thoughts to the more practical worries and problems left behind by that "thrice-accursed yesterday."

The most awful memory from the day before was how "base and vile" he had shown himself -- not only because he was drunk, but because he had exploited the young woman's situation to abuse her _fiance_ out of jealous stupidity, knowing nothing about their mutual relations and obligations and next to nothing about the man himself. What right did he have to criticize him so hastily and rudely? Who had asked for his opinion? Was it even conceivable that a creature like Avdotya Romanovna would marry an unworthy man for money? So there must be something worthwhile in him. And the lodgings? How could he have known what the rooms were like? After all, the man was furnishing an apartment... God, how contemptible it all was! What kind of excuse was being drunk? That stupid defense was even more degrading! In wine is truth, and the truth had all come out -- "the ugliness of his coarse, jealous heart"! And would such a dream ever be permissible for him, Razumihin? What was he compared to such a woman -- he, the drunken loudmouth from last night? Was such an absurd, cynical comparison even thinkable? Razumihin blushed desperately, and suddenly the memory forced itself upon him of how he had said on the stairs that the landlady would be jealous of Avdotya Romanovna... That was simply unbearable. He slammed his fist down on the kitchen stove, hurt his hand, and sent a brick flying.

"Of course," he muttered to himself a minute later, with a feeling of self-disgust, "of course none of these disgraces can ever be wiped out or made right... so there is no point even thinking about it. I must go to them in silence and do my duty... in silence too... and not ask forgiveness, and say nothing... because all is lost now!"

And yet, as he dressed, he examined his clothes more carefully than usual. He had no other suit -- and if he had, he might have deliberately not worn it. "I would have made a point of not putting it on." Still, he could not remain a cynic and a slob. He had no right to offend other people's feelings, especially when they needed his help and had asked to see him. He brushed his clothes carefully. His linen was always decent; in that respect he was especially clean.

That morning he washed meticulously -- he got soap from Nastasya -- scrubbing his hair, his neck, and especially his hands. When it came to whether or not to shave his stubbled chin (Praskovya Pavlovna had excellent razors left by her late husband), the question was answered furiously in the negative. "Let it stay as it is! What if they think I shaved on purpose to... They would certainly think so! Not a chance!"

"And... the worst of it was that he was so coarse, so dirty, with tavern manners... And even assuming he knew he had some of the basics of a gentleman... what was there to be proud of in that? Everyone ought to be a gentleman, and more than that... And all the same (he remembered) he too had done some things... not exactly dishonest, but still.... And what thoughts he sometimes had; hmm... and to set all that beside Avdotya Romanovna! Well, so be it! He would make a point of being dirty, greasy, tavern-mannered -- and he would not care! He would be even worse!"
He was in the middle of these monologues when Zossimov, who had spent the night in Praskovya Pavlovna's parlor, came in.

He was on his way home and wanted to check on the patient first. Razumihin told him Raskolnikov was sleeping like a log. Zossimov gave orders not to wake him and promised to look in again around eleven.
"If he is still home," he added. "Damn it all! How can you treat patients if you cannot control them? Do you know whether _he_ will go to _them_, or _they_ are coming here?"

"They are coming, I think," Razumihin said, understanding the implied question, "and they will discuss family matters, no doubt. I will clear out. You, as the doctor, have more right to be here than I do."
"But I am not a confessor. I will come, take a look, and leave. I have plenty to do besides looking after them."

"One thing worries me," Razumihin said, frowning. "On the way home last night I talked a lot of drunken nonsense to him... all sorts of things... including that you were afraid he might... go insane."
"You told the ladies too."
"I know -- it was stupid! You can hit me if you want! Did you really think so?"

"Nonsense, I tell you. How could I have seriously thought that? _You_ described him as a monomaniac when you brought me to see him... and then we poured fuel on the fire yesterday -- you did, that is -- with the story about the painter. A fine subject for conversation, when that may have been the very thing he was fixated on! If I had known what happened at the police station, that some wretch... had planted this suspicion in his head! Hmm... I would never have allowed that conversation yesterday. These monomaniacs make mountains out of molehills... they see their fantasies as solid reality.... As far as I recall, Zametov's story cleared up half the puzzle for me. I know of a case where a forty-year-old hypochondriac cut the throat of an eight-year-old boy because he could not stand the boy's daily teasing at dinner! And in this case -- his rags, the rude policeman, the fever, this suspicion! All working on a man half-deranged by hypochondria, with his morbid, exceptional pride! That may well have been what triggered the illness. Well, to hell with it all!... And by the way, that Zametov is actually a nice enough lad, but hmm... he should not have blabbed all that last night. He is an awful chatterbox!"
"But who did he tell? You and me?"
"And Porfiry."
"So what?"
"By the way, do you have any influence on them -- his mother and sister? Tell them to be more careful with him today...."
"They will be fine!" Razumihin replied reluctantly.
"And why is he so set against this Luzhin? A man with money, and she does not seem to dislike him... and they have not got a kopeck themselves, do they?"
"What business is it of yours?" Razumihin snapped with annoyance. "How should I know whether they have a kopeck? Ask them yourself and maybe you will find out...."

"God, what an ass you can be sometimes! Last night's wine has not worn off yet.... Goodbye. Thank your Praskovya Pavlovna for me for the night's lodging. She locked herself in and did not answer my _bonjour_ through the door. She was up at seven -- the samovar was brought to her from the kitchen. I was not granted a personal audience...."

At nine o'clock sharp, Razumihin arrived at the lodgings in Bakaleyev's house. Both ladies were waiting for him with nervous impatience. They had been up since seven or earlier. He walked in looking black as night, bowed awkwardly, and immediately cursed himself for it. He had not reckoned on this: Pulcheria Alexandrovna practically threw herself at him, seized both his hands, and nearly kissed them. He glanced timidly at Avdotya Romanovna, but her proud face wore an expression of such gratitude and warmth, such complete and unexpected respect (instead of the sneering looks and barely concealed contempt he had expected), that it threw him into even greater confusion than insults would have. Fortunately there was a topic ready at hand, and he seized on it eagerly.

Learning that everything was going well and Rodya had not yet woken, Pulcheria Alexandrovna declared she was glad, because "there was something very, very important she needed to discuss beforehand." Then came the question of breakfast and an invitation to share it with them. They had waited to eat with him. Avdotya Romanovna rang the bell. A ragged, dirty waiter appeared, and they ordered tea, which was eventually served in such filthy, chaotic fashion that the ladies were embarrassed. Razumihin launched a vigorous attack on the lodgings but, remembering Luzhin, stopped himself in embarrassment. He was greatly relieved when Pulcheria Alexandrovna's questions came pouring down on him in a steady stream.

He talked for three-quarters of an hour, constantly interrupted by their questions, and managed to describe all the most important facts he knew of Raskolnikov's life over the past year, ending with a detailed account of his illness. He left out a good deal that was better left unmentioned, including the scene at the police station with all its consequences. They listened eagerly, and when he thought he had finished and satisfied his audience, he discovered they felt he had barely started.
"Tell me, tell me! What do you think...? Excuse me, I still do not know your name!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna said hurriedly.
"Dmitri Prokofitch."

"I would very, very much like to know, Dmitri Prokofitch... how he looks at things in general now, that is, how can I put it, what are his likes and dislikes? Is he always this irritable? Tell me, if you can, what his hopes and, so to speak, his dreams are? What influences him now? In a word, I would like..."
"Mama, how can he answer all of that at once?" Dounia observed.
"Good heavens -- I never expected to find him in the least like this, Dmitri Prokofitch!"

"Naturally," Razumihin replied. "I have no mother, but my uncle comes every year and almost every time he can barely recognize me, even just my appearance -- and he is a sharp man. Your three years' separation makes a big difference. What can I tell you? I have known Rodion for a year and a half. He is moody, gloomy, proud, and arrogant -- and lately, perhaps for a long time now, suspicious and prone to dark fancies. He has a noble nature and a kind heart. He does not like showing his feelings and would rather act cruelly than open up. Sometimes, though, he is not morbid at all -- just cold and inhumanly callous, as though two completely different characters were taking turns inside him. Sometimes he is terrifyingly uncommunicative! Everything is a bother, everyone is in the way, and yet he lies on his bed doing nothing. He does not mock things -- not because he lacks the wit, but as though he cannot waste time on trifles. He never listens to what people say. He is never interested in what interests others at any given moment. He thinks very highly of himself, and perhaps he has a right to. Well, what more? I think your arrival will have an extremely positive effect on him."
"God grant it!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, distressed by Razumihin's portrait of her Rodya.

And at last Razumihin ventured to look more openly at Avdotya Romanovna. He had been glancing at her throughout his account, but only for a moment before looking away each time. Avdotya Romanovna had been sitting at the table, listening closely, then had gotten up and resumed her pacing -- arms folded, lips pressed together, occasionally putting in a question without breaking stride. She too had a habit of not fully attending to what was being said. She wore a dress of thin, dark fabric and a white transparent scarf around her neck. Razumihin quickly noticed signs of extreme poverty in their belongings. Had Avdotya Romanovna been dressed like a queen, he would probably not have been afraid of her at all. But perhaps precisely because she was poorly dressed, and because he noticed the shabbiness all around them, his heart filled with dread and he began fearing every word, every gesture -- which was very hard on a man who already felt unsure of himself.

"You have told us a great deal that is interesting about my brother's character... and told it impartially. That is good. I had thought you were too uncritically devoted to him," Avdotya Romanovna observed with a smile. "I think you are right that he needs a woman's care," she added thoughtfully.
"I did not say that exactly, but I daresay you are right, only..."
"What?"
"He loves no one and perhaps never will," Razumihin declared flatly.
"You mean he is incapable of love?"

"You know, Avdotya Romanovna, you are remarkably like your brother -- in everything!" he blurted out, surprising even himself. But then, remembering what he had just said about her brother, he turned red as a lobster and was overcome with confusion. Avdotya Romanovna could not help laughing at the sight of him.

"You may both be wrong about Rodya," Pulcheria Alexandrovna put in, slightly stung. "I am not talking about the present situation, Dounia. What Pyotr Petrovitch writes in this letter and what you and I assumed may be mistaken. But you cannot imagine, Dmitri Prokofitch, how moody and -- what is the word -- unpredictable he is. I could never count on what he would do, even when he was only fifteen. And I am sure he could do something now that nobody else would ever think of doing... For instance, do you know how he stunned me, gave me a shock that nearly killed me, a year and a half ago, when he decided to marry that girl -- what was her name -- his landlady's daughter?"
"Did you hear about that?" Avdotya Romanovna asked.

"Do you suppose," Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on warmly, "that my tears, my pleading, my illness, my possible death from grief, or our poverty would have stopped him? Not at all! He would have calmly stepped over every obstacle. And yet it is not that he does not love us!"

"He never said a word to me about it," Razumihin answered cautiously, "but I did hear something from Praskovya Pavlovna herself -- and she is not one to gossip. What I heard was certainly rather odd."
"And what did you hear?" both ladies asked at once.

"Nothing very extraordinary. I only learned that the marriage -- which fell through only because the girl died -- was not at all to Praskovya Pavlovna's liking. They say the girl was not particularly attractive, even positively plain... and rather sickly... and strange. But she must have had some good qualities, or the whole thing is inexplicable.... She had no money either, and he would not have been influenced by money.... It is always hard to judge in such matters."
"I am sure she was a good person," Avdotya Romanovna said briefly.

"God forgive me, but I was simply relieved when she died. Though I do not know which of them would have caused more misery to the other -- he to her, or she to him," Pulcheria Alexandrovna concluded. Then, tentatively, she began questioning him about the previous day's scene with Luzhin, hesitating and continually glancing at Dounia -- obviously to the latter's annoyance. This episode more than anything else was causing her worry, even alarm. Razumihin went through it all again in detail, but this time he added his own assessment: he openly blamed Raskolnikov for deliberately insulting Pyotr Petrovitch, and did not try to excuse him on grounds of illness.
"He had planned it before his illness," he added.

"I think so too," Pulcheria Alexandrovna agreed with a dejected air. But she was very surprised to hear Razumihin speak so carefully and even respectfully about Pyotr Petrovitch. Avdotya Romanovna was struck by it too.
"So this is your opinion of Pyotr Petrovitch?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna could not resist asking.

"I cannot have any other opinion of your daughter's future husband," Razumihin said firmly and with warmth. "And I do not say it merely out of politeness, but because... simply because Avdotya Romanovna has of her own free will chosen to accept this man. If I spoke rudely about him last night, it was because I was disgustingly drunk and... out of my mind. Yes -- mad, out of my mind, and this morning I am ashamed of it."
He turned crimson and fell silent. Avdotya Romanovna blushed too but did not break the silence. She had not uttered a word from the moment they began discussing Luzhin.
Without her support, Pulcheria Alexandrovna was clearly at a loss. At last, faltering and constantly glancing at her daughter, she confessed that one thing was troubling her terribly.
"You see, Dmitri Prokofitch," she began. "I will be perfectly frank with Dmitri Prokofitch -- shall I, Dounia?"
"Of course, Mama," Avdotya Romanovna said emphatically.

"Here is the thing," she began hastily, as though the permission to discuss her worry lifted a weight from her shoulders. "Very early this morning we received a note from Pyotr Petrovitch, in reply to our letter announcing our arrival. He had promised to meet us at the station, you know, but instead he sent a servant to bring us the address of these lodgings and show us the way. Along with that, he sent word that he would come here himself this morning. But this morning, this note arrived from him. You had better read it. There is one point that greatly concerns me... you will see which one right away... and please tell me your honest opinion, Dmitri Prokofitch! You know Rodya's character better than anyone, and no one can advise us better. I should tell you, Dounia made her decision at once, but I still do not know what to do, and I... I was waiting for your opinion."
Razumihin unfolded the note, which was dated the previous evening, and read as follows:

"Dear Madam, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, I have the honor to inform you that owing to unforeseen obstacles, I was unable to meet you at the railway station. I sent a very capable person in my place. I shall likewise be unable to have the honor of an interview with you tomorrow morning, as I have business in the Senate that cannot be delayed, and also because I do not wish to intrude upon your family circle while you are greeting your son and Avdotya Romanovna her brother. I shall have the honor of visiting and paying my respects at your lodgings no later than tomorrow evening at eight o'clock precisely. Herewith I venture to present my earnest and, I may add, imperative request that Rodion Romanovitch not be present at our meeting, as he offered me a gross and unprecedented insult during my visit to him yesterday, and furthermore, as I wish to obtain from you personally an indispensable and detailed explanation of a certain matter, regarding which I desire to hear your own interpretation. I write in the expectation that Rodion Romanovitch, who seemed so ill during my visit, had suddenly recovered two hours later, and therefore, being well enough to leave the house, may visit you as well. I was confirmed in this belief by the evidence of my own eyes in the lodging of a drunkard who had been run over and subsequently died, to whose daughter, a young woman of notorious character, he gave twenty-five rubles on the pretext of funeral expenses -- which greatly surprised me, knowing the pains it cost you to raise that sum. With particular respect to your estimable daughter, Avdotya Romanovna, I beg you to accept the respectful homage of
"Your humble servant,
"P. LUZHIN."

"What should I do now, Dmitri Prokofitch?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, nearly in tears. "How can I ask Rodya not to come? Yesterday he insisted so forcefully that we refuse Pyotr Petrovitch, and now we are told not to receive Rodya! If he finds out, he will come on purpose, and then... what will happen?"
"Do whatever Avdotya Romanovna decides," Razumihin answered at once, calmly.

"Oh, dear! She says... goodness knows what she says, and she will not explain herself! She says it would be best -- not that it would be best, but that it is absolutely necessary -- for Rodya to make a point of being here at eight o'clock, and that they must meet.... I did not even want to show him the letter. I thought we could somehow prevent him from coming, with your help... because he is so volatile.... Besides, I do not understand the part about the drunkard who died and the daughter, and how he could have given her all the money... which..."
"Which cost you such sacrifice, Mama," Avdotya Romanovna put in.

"He was not himself yesterday," Razumihin said thoughtfully. "If you only knew what he got up to in a restaurant yesterday -- though there was some sense in it too.... Hmm! He did say something as we walked home about a dead man and a girl, but I could not make sense of it.... Though last night I myself..."

"The best thing, Mama, will be for us to go see him ourselves, and I am sure we will immediately see what needs to be done. Besides, it is getting late -- good heavens, it is past ten!" she cried, glancing at a beautiful gold enameled watch that hung around her neck on a thin Venetian chain and was completely out of place with the rest of her outfit. "A gift from her _fiance_," Razumihin thought.
"We must go, Dounia, we must go," her mother said in a flutter. "He will think we are still angry about yesterday, since we are so late. Oh, dear!"

While saying this she was hastily putting on her hat and cloak. Dounia put on hers too. Her gloves, Razumihin noticed, were not merely shabby but had holes in them -- yet this obvious poverty gave both women an air of special dignity, which is always found in people who know how to wear poor clothes well. Razumihin gazed reverently at Dounia and felt proud to be escorting her. "The queen who darned stockings in prison," he thought, "must have looked every inch a queen in that moment, even more than at state banquets."

"My God!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed. "Little did I think I would ever be afraid to see my own son -- my darling, darling Rodya! I am afraid, Dmitri Prokofitch," she added, glancing at him timidly.
"Do not be afraid, Mama," Dounia said, kissing her. "Better to have faith in him."
"Oh, I do have faith in him, but I have not slept all night!" the poor woman cried.
They stepped out into the street.

"You know, Dounia, when I dozed off a little this morning, I dreamed of Marfa Petrovna... she was all in white... she came up to me, took my hand, and shook her head at me -- so sternly, as though she were blaming me.... Is that a good sign? Oh, dear! You do not know, Dmitri Prokofitch -- Marfa Petrovna is dead!"
"No, I did not know. Who is Marfa Petrovna?"
"She died suddenly -- just imagine..."
"Later, Mama," Dounia put in. "He does not know who Marfa Petrovna is."

"Oh, you do not know? And I was thinking you knew all about us. Forgive me, Dmitri Prokofitch -- I have lost track of what I am thinking these last few days. I truly regard you as our guardian angel, and so I assumed you knew everything. I think of you as family.... Do not be angry with me for saying that. Oh dear, what is the matter with your right hand? Did you hurt it?"
"Yes, I bruised it," muttered Razumihin, overjoyed.

"I sometimes speak too much from the heart -- Dounia scolds me for it.... But, dear me, what a closet he lives in! I wonder if he is awake yet? Does this woman, his landlady, really consider that a room? Listen, you say he does not like showing his feelings -- so perhaps I will annoy him with my... weakness? Please advise me, Dmitri Prokofitch. How should I behave with him? I feel completely at a loss, you know."
"Do not question him too much about anything if you see him frown. Do not ask too much about his health -- he does not like that."
"Oh, Dmitri Prokofitch, how hard it is to be a mother! But here are the stairs.... What a dreadful staircase!"
"Mama, you are quite pale. Do not distress yourself, darling," Dounia said, caressing her. Then, with flashing eyes, she added: "He ought to be happy to see you, and you are tormenting yourself."
"Wait -- let me peek in and see if he is awake."

The ladies slowly followed Razumihin, who went ahead. When they reached the landlady's door on the fourth floor, they noticed it was cracked open and two keen black eyes were watching them from the darkness. When their eyes met, the door was suddenly slammed shut with such force that Pulcheria Alexandrovna nearly cried out.

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 3
paragraphs: "He's doing well, quite well!" Zossimov announced cheerfully as they came in.

He had arrived ten minutes earlier and was sitting in his usual spot on the sofa. Raskolnikov sat in the opposite corner, fully dressed and carefully washed and combed for the first time in a while. The room was immediately crowded, but Nastasya managed to follow the visitors in and stayed to listen.

Compared with the day before, Raskolnikov really was almost well, but he was still pale, listless, and gloomy. He looked like a wounded man or someone who had endured terrible physical suffering. His brows were knitted, his lips compressed, his eyes feverish. He spoke little and reluctantly, as though fulfilling a duty, and there was a restlessness in his movements.

All he needed was a sling on his arm or a bandage on his finger to complete the picture of a man with a painful abscess or a broken arm. His pale, gloomy face brightened for a moment when his mother and sister entered, but this only gave it a look of more intense suffering instead of listless dejection. The light quickly faded, but the suffering remained. Zossimov, watching and studying his patient with all the enthusiasm of a young doctor just starting out, noticed no joy at the arrival of his mother and sister, only a kind of bitter, hidden determination to endure another hour or two of unavoidable torture. He later observed that almost every word of the conversation seemed to touch some sore spot and irritate it. At the same time he marvelled at the patient's ability to control himself and hide his feelings, when just the day before he had flown into a frenzy like a madman at the slightest word.

"Yes, I can see myself now that I'm almost well," said Raskolnikov, kissing his mother and sister in welcome, which made Pulcheria Alexandrovna beam at once. "And I don't say this the way I did yesterday," he added, addressing Razumihin with a friendly squeeze of his hand.

"Yes, I'm quite surprised at him today," Zossimov began, clearly delighted by the ladies' entrance, since he hadn't managed to keep up a conversation with his patient for ten minutes. "In another three or four days, if he goes on like this, he'll be just as he was a month or two ago, perhaps even three. This has been building up for a long time, hasn't it? Admit it now, it's perhaps been partly your own fault?" he added with a tentative smile, as though still afraid of irritating him.
"Quite possibly," answered Raskolnikov coldly.

"I would also say," Zossimov continued eagerly, "that your complete recovery depends entirely on you. Now that we can talk, I want to impress upon you that it's essential to address the root causes of your condition. If you do, you'll recover; if not, things will only get worse. I don't know what those causes are, but you must. You're an intelligent man and must have observed yourself. I believe the onset of your illness coincides with your leaving the university. You shouldn't be idle. Work and a clear purpose might do you a great deal of good."
"Yes, yes, you're absolutely right. I'll go back to the university right away, and then everything will be fine..."

Zossimov, who had begun his sage advice partly to impress the ladies, was rather thrown off when he noticed unmistakable mockery on his patient's face. But it lasted only an instant. Pulcheria Alexandrovna immediately began thanking Zossimov, especially for his visit to their lodging the previous night.
"What! He visited you last night?" Raskolnikov asked, as though startled. "So you didn't sleep either after your journey."
"Oh, Rodya, that was only until two o'clock. Dounia and I never go to bed before two at home."

"I don't know how to thank him either," Raskolnikov went on, suddenly frowning and looking down. "Setting aside the question of payment—forgive me for bringing it up"—he turned to Zossimov—"I really don't understand what I've done to deserve such special attention from you. I simply don't understand it, and it weighs on me, precisely because I don't understand. I'm telling you frankly."

"Don't be irritated," Zossimov said, forcing a laugh. "Think of yourself as my first patient. We young doctors love our first patients as if they were our own children, and some practically fall in love with them. And I'm not exactly drowning in patients."
"I'm not even talking about him," Raskolnikov added, pointing to Razumihin, "though he's had nothing from me but insults and trouble."
"What nonsense! You're in a sentimental mood today, are you?" Razumihin shouted.

If he'd been more perceptive, he would have seen that there was no trace of sentimentality in Raskolnikov, but something quite the opposite. Avdotya Romanovna noticed it, though. She was watching her brother intently and uneasily.

"As for you, mother, I don't dare speak," he continued, as though reciting a lesson he'd memorized. "It's only today that I've begun to realize how worried you must have been yesterday, waiting for me to come back."

As he said this, he suddenly held out his hand to his sister, smiling wordlessly. But in that smile there was a flash of real, genuine feeling. Dounia caught it at once and warmly pressed his hand, overjoyed and grateful. It was the first time he had reached out to her since their argument the day before. Their mother's face lit up with radiant happiness at this silent reconciliation. "Yes, that's what I love about him," Razumihin muttered to himself, exaggerating as usual, with a vigorous turn in his chair. "He has these moments."

"And how well he does everything," the mother thought to herself. "What generous impulses, and how simply, how delicately he resolved the misunderstanding with his sister—just by holding out his hand at the right moment and looking at her like that. And what fine eyes, and how handsome his whole face is! He's even better looking than Dounia. But, heavens, what a suit—how terribly he's dressed! Vasya, the errand boy at Afanasy Ivanitch's shop, is better dressed! I could throw myself on him and hug him, cry over him—but I'm afraid. Oh dear, he's so strange! He's speaking kindly, but I'm afraid! What am I afraid of?"

"Oh, Rodya, you wouldn't believe," she began suddenly, rushing to respond, "how unhappy Dounia and I were yesterday! Now that it's all over and we're happy again—I can tell you. We came here practically straight from the train to see you, and that woman—oh, here she is! Good morning, Nastasya! She told us right away that you were delirious with fever and had run away from the doctor, and they were searching the streets for you. You can't imagine how we felt! I kept thinking of the tragic fate of Lieutenant Potanchikov, a friend of your father's—you can't remember him, Rodya—who ran out the same way in a high fever and fell into the well in the courtyard, and they couldn't pull him out till the next day. Of course we were exaggerating. We were about to rush off and find Pyotr Petrovitch to ask for his help, because we were alone, utterly alone," she said plaintively, then stopped short, suddenly remembering that it was still somewhat dangerous to mention Pyotr Petrovitch, even though "we're quite happy again."
"Yes, yes. Of course that's very upsetting," Raskolnikov muttered in reply, but with such a distracted and inattentive air that Dounia stared at him in puzzlement.
"What else was I going to say?" He tried to remember. "Oh, yes—mother, and you too, Dounia, please don't think I wasn't planning to come see you today and was just waiting for you to come first."
"What are you saying, Rodya?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna, equally surprised.
"Is he answering us out of duty?" Dounia wondered. "Being reconciled and asking forgiveness like he's performing a ritual or reciting a lesson?"
"I only just woke up and wanted to come to you, but I was held up because of my clothes. I forgot yesterday to ask her—Nastasya—to wash out the blood. I've only just gotten dressed."
"Blood! What blood?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked in alarm.
"Oh, it's nothing—don't worry. When I was wandering around yesterday, a bit delirious, I came across a man who'd been run over—a clerk..."
"Delirious? But you remember everything!" Razumihin interrupted.
"That's true," Raskolnikov answered with particular care. "I remember everything down to the smallest detail, yet why I did that, why I went there and said what I said—I can't explain clearly now."

"A familiar phenomenon," Zossimov put in. "Actions are sometimes performed in a masterful and most cunning way, while the direction of those actions is deranged, driven by various morbid impulses—rather like a dream."
"Perhaps it's a good thing he thinks I'm practically mad," Raskolnikov thought.
"But perfectly healthy people act the same way too," Dounia observed, glancing uneasily at Zossimov.

"There's some truth in that," the doctor replied. "In that sense, we're all not infrequently a bit like madmen, but with the slight difference that the truly deranged are somewhat more so. We need to draw a line somewhere. A truly normal person barely exists. Among dozens—perhaps hundreds of thousands—you'd hardly find one."
At the word "madman," carelessly dropped by Zossimov while chattering about his favourite subject, everyone frowned.
Raskolnikov sat as if paying no attention, sunk in thought with a strange smile on his pale lips. He was still turning something over in his mind.
"Well, what about the man who was run over? I interrupted you!" Razumihin cried hastily.

"What?" Raskolnikov seemed to wake up. "Oh, I got splattered with blood helping carry him to his lodging. By the way, mother, I did something unforgivable yesterday. I was literally out of my mind. I gave away all the money you sent me to his wife for the funeral. She's a widow now, consumptive, a pitiful creature, three small children, starving, nothing in the house. There's a daughter too. Perhaps you would have given it yourself if you'd seen them. But I had no right to do it, I admit, especially knowing how much you needed that money yourselves. To help others, one must first have the right to do so, otherwise—'Die, dogs, if you're not content!' That's right, isn't it, Dounia?"
"No, it's not," Dounia answered firmly.

"Bah! You too have your ideals," he muttered, looking at her almost with hatred and smiling sarcastically. "I should have thought of that. Well, it's admirable, and better for you. If you reach a certain line and don't cross it, you'll be unhappy; but if you cross it, perhaps you'll be unhappier still. But all that's nonsense," he added irritably, annoyed at having been carried away. "I only meant to say that I beg your forgiveness, mother," he concluded shortly and abruptly.
"That's enough, Rodya. I'm sure everything you do is right," his mother said, delighted.
"Don't be too sure," he answered, twisting his mouth into a smile.
A silence followed. There was a certain awkwardness in everything—the conversation, the silence, the reconciliation, the forgiveness—and everyone felt it.
"It's as though they're afraid of me," Raskolnikov thought, glancing sideways at his mother and sister. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was indeed growing more timid the longer the silence lasted.
"Yet when they weren't here, I seemed to love them so much," flashed through his mind.
"Do you know, Rodya, Marfa Petrovna is dead," Pulcheria Alexandrovna suddenly blurted out.
"What Marfa Petrovna?"
"For heaven's sake—Marfa Petrovna Svidrigaïlov! I wrote you so much about her."
"A-ah! Yes, I remember. So she's dead? Really?" He roused himself suddenly, as if waking up. "What did she die of?"

"Just imagine, completely suddenly," Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered hurriedly, encouraged by his interest. "On the very day I sent you that letter! Would you believe it—that terrible man seems to have been the cause of her death. They say he beat her dreadfully."
"Were they really on such bad terms?" he asked, turning to his sister.

"Not at all. Quite the contrary, in fact. He was always very patient with her, even considerate. For all seven years of their marriage he gave in to her, too much so in many ways. Then all of a sudden, it seems, he lost his patience."
"So he can't have been that terrible if he kept himself in check for seven years? You seem to be defending him, Dounia."
"No, no, he's a terrible man! I can't imagine anyone more terrible!" Dounia answered, almost shuddering, knitting her brows and sinking into thought.

"It happened in the morning," Pulcheria Alexandrovna continued hurriedly. "Right afterward she ordered the horses harnessed to drive to town immediately after dinner. She always went to town in such cases. She ate a very good dinner, so I'm told..."
"After the beating?"

"That was always her habit. And right after dinner, so as not to be late setting off, she went to the bathhouse. You see, she was taking some kind of bathing treatment. They have a cold spring there, and she used to bathe in it every day. No sooner had she gotten into the water than she had a stroke!"
"I should think so," said Zossimov.
"And was the beating severe?"
"What does that matter!" Dounia put in.
"Hmm! I don't really know why you want to tell us this gossip, mother," said Raskolnikov irritably, as though in spite of himself.
"Oh, my dear, I don't know what else to talk about," Pulcheria Alexandrovna let slip.
"Why, are you all afraid of me?" he asked with a strained smile.
"That's certainly true," said Dounia, looking directly and sternly at her brother. "Mother was crossing herself in terror as she came up the stairs."
His face twisted, as though in a spasm.

"Oh, what are you saying, Dounia! Don't be angry, please, Rodya. Why did you say that, Dounia?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, overwhelmed. "You see, coming here, I dreamed the whole way on the train about how we'd meet, how we'd talk everything over together. And I was so happy I didn't notice the journey! But what am I saying? I'm happy now, simply seeing you, Rodya."
"Hush, mother," he muttered in confusion, not looking at her but pressing her hand. "We'll have time to talk freely about everything."

As he said this, he was suddenly overwhelmed by confusion and turned pale. Again that terrible sensation he'd come to know so well lately passed through his soul with a deathly chill. Again it became suddenly, piercingly clear that he had just told a dreadful lie—that he would never be able to speak freely about everything, never again be able to truly speak to anyone about anything. The anguish of this realization was so acute that for a moment he nearly lost himself. He stood up from his seat and, without looking at anyone, walked toward the door.
"What are you doing?" Razumihin cried, grabbing his arm.
He sat down again and began looking around in silence. Everyone stared at him in bewilderment.

"What's wrong with you all—why so glum?" he burst out suddenly and quite unexpectedly. "Say something! What's the point of sitting here like this? Come on, talk! Let's have a conversation. We finally get together and sit in silence. Come on, anything!"
"Thank God! I was afraid the same thing as yesterday was starting again," said Pulcheria Alexandrovna, crossing herself.
"What's the matter, Rodya?" Avdotya Romanovna asked suspiciously.
"Oh, nothing! I just remembered something," he answered, and suddenly laughed.

"Well, if you remembered something, that's fine! I was beginning to think..." Zossimov muttered, getting up from the sofa. "It's time I was off. I'll look in again perhaps, if I can." He bowed and went out.
"What an excellent man!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna observed.

"Yes, excellent, splendid, well-educated, intelligent," Raskolnikov began, suddenly speaking with surprising speed and a liveliness he hadn't shown before. "I can't remember where I met him before my illness. I think I did meet him somewhere. And this one is a good man, too," he nodded at Razumihin. "Do you like him, Dounia?" he asked her, and for some unknown reason burst out laughing.
"Very much," answered Dounia.
"Ugh, what a pig you are!" Razumihin protested, blushing crimson with embarrassment as he got up from his chair. Pulcheria Alexandrovna smiled faintly, but Raskolnikov laughed out loud.
"Where are you going?"
"I have to go."

"You don't have to at all. Stay. Zossimov's gone, so you have to stay. Don't go. What time is it? Is it twelve? What a pretty watch you've got, Dounia. Why are you all silent again? I'm doing all the talking."
"It was a present from Marfa Petrovna," answered Dounia.
"And quite an expensive one!" added Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Ah! It's a big one, hardly ladylike."
"I like that sort," said Dounia.
"So it's not a present from her fiancé," Razumihin thought, unreasonably delighted.
"I thought it was Luzhin's present," Raskolnikov observed.
"No, he hasn't given Dounia any presents yet."
"Ah! And do you remember, mother, I was in love and wanted to get married?" he said suddenly, looking at his mother, who was startled by the abrupt change of subject and the way he spoke of it.
"Oh, yes, my dear."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna exchanged glances with Dounia and Razumihin.

"Hmm, yes. What can I tell you? I don't even remember much. She was such a sickly girl," he went on, growing dreamy and looking down. "Quite an invalid. She liked giving alms to the poor and was always dreaming of entering a convent, and once she burst into tears when she started telling me about it. Yes, yes, I remember very well. She was an ugly little thing. I really don't know what attracted me to her—I think it was because she was always ill. If she'd been lame or hunchbacked, I think I'd have liked her even more," he smiled dreamily. "Yes, it was a sort of spring delirium."
"No, it wasn't only spring delirium," said Dounia with warm feeling.

He fixed a strained, intent look on his sister, but either didn't hear or didn't understand her words. Then, completely lost in thought, he got up, went to his mother, kissed her, went back to his place, and sat down.
"You still love her?" said Pulcheria Alexandrovna, touched.

"Her? Now? Oh, yes. You're asking about her? No, that's all in another world now, and so long ago. And indeed everything happening here seems somehow far away." He looked at them attentively. "You, for instance, I seem to be looking at you from a thousand miles away. But God knows why we're even talking about this! And what's the use of asking?" he added with annoyance, and fell into pensive silence, biting his nails.

"What a wretched room you have, Rodya! It's like a tomb," Pulcheria Alexandrovna said suddenly, breaking the oppressive silence. "I'm sure it's at least half because of this room that you've become so melancholy."
"My room," he answered absently. "Yes, the room had a lot to do with it. I thought that too. But if only you knew, mother, what a strange thing you just said," he added with a peculiar laugh.

A little more and the situation—his mother and sister beside him after three years apart, their intimate tone of conversation in the face of the utter impossibility of truly speaking about anything—would have been more than he could bear. But there was one urgent matter that had to be settled one way or another that day. He'd decided that when he woke up. Now he was glad to remember it as a way out.

"Listen, Dounia," he began gravely and drily, "of course I apologize for yesterday, but I feel it's my duty to tell you again that I'm not backing down from my main point. It's either me or Luzhin. If I'm a scoundrel, you shouldn't be one too. One of us is enough. If you marry Luzhin, I will immediately stop considering you my sister."
"Rodya, Rodya! It's the same as yesterday all over again," Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried mournfully. "And why do you call yourself a scoundrel? I can't bear it. You said the same thing yesterday."

"Brother," Dounia answered firmly and with the same dryness. "You're making a mistake about all this. I thought it over during the night and found where the mistake lies. It's all because you seem to think I'm sacrificing myself for someone. That's not the case at all. I'm simply marrying for my own sake, because things are hard for me. Of course, I'll be glad if I can also be useful to my family. But that's not the main reason for my decision."

"She's lying," he thought, biting his nails vindictively. "Proud creature! She won't admit she wants to do it out of charity! Too proud! Oh, vile natures! They even love as though they hate. Oh, how I hate them all!"

"In fact," Dounia continued, "I'm marrying Pyotr Petrovitch because of two evils I'm choosing the lesser. I intend to fulfill honestly everything he expects of me, so I'm not deceiving him. Why did you just smile?" She flushed too, and there was a flash of anger in her eyes.
"Everything?" he asked with a malicious grin.

"Within certain limits. Both the manner and form of Pyotr Petrovitch's courtship showed me at once what he wanted. He may think too well of himself, but I hope he values me too. Why are you laughing again?"

"And why are you blushing again? You're lying, sister. You're deliberately lying, out of sheer feminine stubbornness, just to hold your own against me. You can't possibly respect Luzhin. I've seen him and spoken with him. So you're selling yourself for money, and in any case you're acting basely. I'm glad at least that you can still blush about it."

"That's not true! I'm not lying!" cried Dounia, losing her composure. "I wouldn't marry him if I weren't convinced he respects me and thinks highly of me. I wouldn't marry him if I weren't firmly certain I can respect him. Fortunately, I'll have convincing proof of that today, and such a marriage isn't a vile thing, as you say! And even if you were right, even if I really had resolved on something vile, isn't it heartless of you to speak to me like that? Why do you demand heroism from me that perhaps you don't have either? That's tyranny! If I ruin anyone, it's only myself. I'm not committing murder! Why are you looking at me like that? Why are you so pale? Rodya, darling, what's wrong?"
"Good heavens! You've made him faint!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.

"No, no, it's nothing. Just a bit of dizziness—not fainting. You have fainting on the brain. Hmm, yes, what was I saying? Oh, yes. How exactly will you get this convincing proof today that you can respect him and that he values you, as you said? I believe you said today?"
"Mother, show Rodya Pyotr Petrovitch's letter," said Dounia.
With trembling hands, Pulcheria Alexandrovna gave him the letter. He took it with great interest, but before opening it, he suddenly looked at Dounia with something like wonder.
"Strange," he said slowly, as though struck by a new idea. "What am I making such a fuss about? What's it all about? Marry whoever you want!"

He seemed to be saying this to himself, but he said it aloud, and looked at his sister for some time, as if puzzled. He finally opened the letter, still with that expression of strange wonder, and read it through twice, slowly and attentively. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was visibly anxious, and indeed everyone expected something significant.

"What surprises me," he began after a short pause, handing the letter back to his mother without addressing anyone in particular, "is that he's a businessman, a lawyer, and his conversation is quite pretentious, yet he writes such an uneducated letter."
They all started. They had expected something quite different.
"But they all write like that, you know," Razumihin observed abruptly.
"You've read it?"
"Yes."
"We showed him, Rodya. We consulted him just now," Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, embarrassed.
"That's just legal jargon," Razumihin put in. "Legal documents are still written that way."
"Legal? Yes, it's exactly that—business language. Not terribly uneducated, not quite educated—business language!"
"Pyotr Petrovitch makes no secret of having had a modest education. He's even proud of being self-made," Avdotya Romanovna observed, somewhat offended by her brother's tone.

"Well, if he's proud of it, he has reason to be—I don't deny it. You seem offended, sister, that I'm making such a trivial criticism of the letter, and you think I'm bringing up petty things just to annoy you. It's quite the opposite. Something about the style struck me that's very relevant to our situation. There's one phrase—'blame yourselves'—put very significantly and plainly, and there's also a threat to leave at once if I'm present. That threat to leave amounts to a threat to abandon you both if you don't obey, to abandon you now, after summoning you to Petersburg. Well, tell me: can you take offense at such a phrase from Luzhin the way you would if it came from him"—he pointed to Razumihin—"or Zossimov, or any of us?"

"N-no," answered Dounia, more animatedly. "I could see clearly that it was too crudely expressed, and that perhaps he simply lacks skill with words. That's a fair observation, brother. I really didn't expect it."

"It's written in legal style and comes across as harsher than he perhaps intended. But I need to disillusion you a bit. There's one passage in the letter, a slander against me, and a rather contemptible one. I gave the money last night to the widow, a woman dying of consumption, crushed by hardship—not 'on the pretext of the funeral,' as he writes, but simply to pay for the funeral. I gave it not to the daughter—a young woman, as he describes, of notorious behaviour, whom I saw for the first time last night—but to the widow. In all this I see an eagerness to slander me and create a rift between us. Again it's expressed in legal language—that is, with too obvious an intent and too naïve an eagerness. He's an intelligent man, but intelligence alone isn't enough to act wisely. It all reveals the man, and I don't think he has much genuine respect for you. I tell you this simply as a warning, because I sincerely wish you well."
Dounia did not reply. Her decision had already been made. She was only waiting for the evening.
"Then what is your decision, Rodya?" asked Pulcheria Alexandrovna, more uneasy than ever at the sudden new business-like tone of his words.
"What decision?"
"You see, Pyotr Petrovitch writes that you shouldn't be with us this evening, and that he'll leave if you come. So will you come?"

"That, of course, is not for me to decide, but for you first—if such a demand doesn't offend you—and secondly, for Dounia, if she's not offended either. I'll do whatever you think best," he added drily.
"Dounia has already decided, and I agree completely," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hastened to say.
"I've decided to ask you, Rodya, to make a point of being with us at this meeting," said Dounia. "Will you come?"
"Yes."
"I'd like to ask you too, to join us at eight," she said, turning to Razumihin. "Mother, I'm inviting him as well."

"Quite right, Dounia. Well, since you've decided," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added, "so be it. I'll feel easier myself. I don't like hiding things and deceiving people. Better to have it all out in the open. Let Pyotr Petrovitch be angry or not!"

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 4
paragraphs: At that moment the door opened softly and a young girl walked into the room, looking timidly around. Everyone turned toward her with surprise and curiosity. At first Raskolnikov didn't recognize her. It was Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov. He had seen her for the first time yesterday, but under such circumstances, in such surroundings and wearing such clothes, that his memory held a very different picture. Now she was a modestly and poorly dressed young girl, very young indeed, almost a child, with a quiet and refined manner and a candid but somewhat frightened-looking face. She wore a very plain house dress and a shabby, old-fashioned hat, but still carried a parasol. Finding the room unexpectedly full of people, she was not so much embarrassed as completely overwhelmed with shyness, like a small child. She was even about to back away. "Oh, it's you!" said Raskolnikov, extremely astonished, and he too was confused. He immediately recalled that his mother and sister knew from Luzhin's letter about "some young woman of notorious behaviour." He had just been protesting against Luzhin's slander and declaring that he had seen the girl for the first time last night, and now here she was. He also remembered that he hadn't protested against the words "of notorious behaviour." All this flashed vaguely and fleetingly through his mind, but looking at her more intently, he saw that this humiliated creature was so humiliated that he suddenly felt sorry for her. When she moved to retreat in terror, it sent a pang through his heart.
"I didn't expect you," he said hurriedly, with a look that made her stop. "Please sit down. You've come from Katerina Ivanovna, no doubt. Not there, please. Sit here."

When Sonia entered, Razumihin, who had been sitting on one of Raskolnikov's three chairs near the door, stood up to let her pass. Raskolnikov first motioned her toward the sofa where Zossimov had been sitting, but then, feeling that the sofa—which served as his bed—was too intimate a place, he hastily directed her to Razumihin's chair.
"You sit here," he said to Razumihin, putting him on the sofa.

Sonia sat down, nearly shaking with nerves, and looked timidly at the two ladies. It was clearly almost inconceivable to her that she could sit beside them. The thought so frightened her that she quickly stood up again and, in utter confusion, addressed Raskolnikov.

"I—I've come for just a minute. Forgive me for disturbing you," she began haltingly. "I come from Katerina Ivanovna, and she had no one else to send. She told me to ask you to be at the service tomorrow morning at Mitrofanievsky, and then to come to us—to her—to do her the honour. She told me to ask you." Sonia stammered and fell silent.

"I'll certainly try, most certainly," Raskolnikov answered. He too had stood up, and he too faltered and couldn't finish his sentence. "Please sit down," he said suddenly. "I want to talk to you. You may be in a hurry, but please spare me two minutes." And he pulled up a chair for her.
Sonia sat down again, and again she cast a timid, frightened glance at the two ladies before dropping her eyes. Raskolnikov's pale face flushed, a shudder ran through him, and his eyes blazed.

"Mother," he said firmly and insistently, "this is Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov, the daughter of that unfortunate Mr. Marmeladov who was run over before my eyes yesterday, and whom I was just telling you about."

Pulcheria Alexandrovna glanced at Sonia and slightly narrowed her eyes. Despite her unease before Rodya's urgent and challenging look, she couldn't deny herself that small satisfaction. Dounia gazed gravely and intently at the poor girl's face, studying her with bewilderment. Sonia, hearing herself introduced, tried to raise her eyes again but was more embarrassed than ever.
"I wanted to ask you," Raskolnikov said hastily, "how things went yesterday. You weren't troubled by the police, for instance?"
"No, that was fine. The cause of death was too obvious. They didn't bother us. Only the other tenants are angry."
"Why?"
"About the body remaining so long. You see, it's hot now. So today they'll carry it to the cemetery chapel until tomorrow. At first Katerina Ivanovna was unwilling, but now she sees it's necessary."
"Today, then?"
"She asks you to do us the honour of attending the church service tomorrow, and then the funeral lunch."
"She's giving a funeral lunch?"
"Yes, a small one. She told me to thank you very much for helping us yesterday. Without you, we would have had nothing for the funeral."
Suddenly her lips and chin began trembling, but she controlled herself with an effort, looking down again.

During the conversation, Raskolnikov studied her carefully. She had a thin, very thin, pale little face, rather irregular and angular, with a sharp little nose and chin. She couldn't have been called pretty, but her blue eyes were so clear, and when they lit up, there was such kindness and simplicity in her expression that you couldn't help being drawn to her. Her face—and her whole figure—had another distinctive quality. Despite her eighteen years, she looked almost like a little girl, almost a child. And in some of her gestures, this childishness seemed almost comical.
"But has Katerina Ivanovna been able to manage on such small means? Does she really plan to have a funeral lunch?" Raskolnikov asked, deliberately keeping the conversation going.

"The coffin will be plain, of course, and everything simple, so it won't cost much. Katerina Ivanovna and I have figured it all out, and there'll be enough left over. She was very anxious that it be done properly. You know how she is."
"I understand, of course. Why are you looking at my room like that? My mother just said it's like a tomb."

"You gave us everything yesterday," Sonia said suddenly in reply, in a loud, rapid whisper, and she looked down again in confusion. Her lips and chin trembled once more. She had been struck at once by Raskolnikov's impoverished surroundings, and the words broke out of her spontaneously. A silence followed. Dounia's eyes softened, and even Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked kindly at Sonia.

"Rodya," she said, getting up, "we'll have dinner together, of course. Come, Dounia. And you, Rodya, should go for a little walk and then rest and lie down before you come to see us. I'm afraid we've worn you out."
"Yes, yes, I'll come," he answered, getting up fussily. "But I have something to attend to."
"But surely you'll have dinner together?" Razumihin cried, looking at Raskolnikov in surprise. "What do you mean?"
"Yes, yes, I'm coming, of course! And you stay a moment. You don't need him right now, do you, mother? Or perhaps I'm keeping him from you?"
"Oh, no, not at all. And will you, Dmitri Prokofitch, do us the favor of dining with us?"
"Please do," added Dounia.
Razumihin bowed, positively beaming. For a moment they were all strangely embarrassed.
"Goodbye, Rodya—that is, until later. I don't like saying goodbye. Goodbye, Nastasya. Oh, I've said goodbye again."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna meant to greet Sonia too, but somehow it didn't come off, and she hurried out of the room in a flutter.

But Avdotya Romanovna seemed to wait her turn, and following her mother, gave Sonia an attentive, courteous bow. Sonia, confused, returned a hurried, frightened curtsy. There was a look of painful discomfort on her face, as though Avdotya Romanovna's courtesy and attention were oppressive and distressing to her.
"Dounia, goodbye!" Raskolnikov called from the hallway. "Give me your hand."
"But I already did. Have you forgotten?" said Dounia, turning to him warmly but awkwardly.
"Never mind, give it to me again." And he squeezed her fingers warmly.
Dounia smiled, blushed, pulled her hand away, and went off quite happy.
"Well, that's wonderful," he said to Sonia, going back in and looking at her brightly. "God give peace to the dead—the living must go on living. Isn't that right?"
Sonia was surprised by the sudden brightness in his face. He looked at her for several moments in silence. The entire story of her dead father floated before his memory in those moments.

"Heavens, Dounia," Pulcheria Alexandrovna began as soon as they were in the street, "I actually feel relieved at leaving—more at ease. How little I imagined yesterday on the train that I could ever be glad of that!"
"I'm telling you again, mother, he's still very ill. Don't you see? Maybe worrying about us upset him. We must be patient. Much can be forgiven."

"Well, you weren't very patient yourself!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna shot back, hotly and jealously. "You know, Dounia, looking at you two—you're his very portrait, not so much in looks as in character. You're both melancholy, both moody and hot-tempered, both proud and both generous. Surely he can't be selfish, Dounia? When I think of what's coming this evening, my heart sinks!"
"Don't worry, mother. What must be, will be."
"Dounia, just think what a position we're in! What if Pyotr Petrovitch breaks it off?" poor Pulcheria Alexandrovna blurted out incautiously.
"He won't be worth much if he does," Dounia answered sharply and contemptuously.

"We did well to leave," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried on. "He was in a hurry about some business. If he goes out for some fresh air—it's so terribly stuffy in his room. But where can you get fresh air here? Even the streets feel like closed rooms. Good heavens, what a city! Watch out—this way—they'll crush you! They're carrying something. Why, it's a piano! How they push! I'm very much afraid of that young woman, too."
"What young woman, mother?"
"Why, that Sofya Semyonovna who was there just now."
"Why?"
"I have a presentiment, Dounia. Believe it or not, the moment she walked in, that very instant, I felt she was the main cause of the trouble."
"Nothing of the sort!" Dounia cried in exasperation. "What nonsense, with your presentiments, mother! He only met her the evening before, and he didn't even recognize her when she came in."

"Well, you'll see! She worries me. But you'll see, you'll see! I was so frightened. She was staring at me with those eyes. I could barely sit still when he started introducing her—remember?
