It seems so strange, but Pyotr Petrovitch writes about her that way, and yet he introduces her to us—to you! So he must think very highly of her."
"People will write anything. We were talked about and written about too. Have you forgotten? I'm sure she's a good girl and that it's all nonsense."
"God grant it!"
"And Pyotr Petrovitch is a contemptible slanderer," Dounia snapped.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was crushed. The conversation died.
"I'll tell you what I need from you," said Raskolnikov, drawing Razumihin to the window.
"Then I'll tell Katerina Ivanovna you're coming," Sonia said hurriedly, preparing to leave.

"One moment, Sofya Semyonovna. We have no secrets. You're not in the way. I want another word or two with you. Listen," he turned suddenly to Razumihin, "you know that—what's his name—Porfiry Petrovitch?"
"Of course! He's a relative. Why?" Razumihin added with interest.
"Isn't he handling that case, you know, the murder? You were talking about it yesterday."
"Yes. What about it?" Razumihin's eyes widened.

"He was asking about people who'd pawned things, and I have some pledges there too—trifles—a ring my sister gave me as a keepsake when I left home, and my father's silver watch. They're only worth five or six roubles altogether, but I value them. What should I do now? I don't want to lose them, especially the watch. I was terrified just now that mother might ask to see it, when we were talking about Dounia's watch. It's the only thing we have left of father's. She'd be sick if it were lost. You know how women are. So tell me what to do. I know I should report to the police station, but wouldn't it be better to go straight to Porfiry? What do you think? I'd like to get it settled quickly. You'll see—mother will ask about it before dinner."

"Definitely not the police station. Definitely Porfiry," Razumihin practically shouted, extraordinarily excited. "I'm so glad! Let's go right now. It's just a couple of steps. We'll be sure to find him."
"All right, let's go."

"He'll be absolutely delighted to meet you. I've told him about you many times. I was talking about you just yesterday. Let's go. So you knew the old woman? That's how it all fits together! Oh, yes, Sofya Ivanovna—"
"Sofya Semyonovna," Raskolnikov corrected. "Sofya Semyonovna, this is my friend Razumihin, and he's a good man."
"If you have to go now," Sonia began, not looking at Razumihin at all and even more embarrassed.
"Let's go," Raskolnikov decided. "I'll come to see you today, Sofya Semyonovna. Just tell me where you live."
He wasn't exactly uneasy, but he seemed hurried and avoided her eyes. Sonia gave her address and blushed as she did so. They all went out together.
"Don't you lock up?" Razumihin asked, following him down the stairs.
"Never," Raskolnikov answered. "I've been meaning to buy a lock for two years. People who don't need locks are fortunate," he said, laughing to Sonia. They stopped in the gateway.

"Do you go to the right, Sofya Semyonovna? By the way, how did you find me?" he added, as though he wanted to say something quite different. He wanted to look into her soft, clear eyes, but couldn't manage it.
"Why, you gave your address to Polenka yesterday."
"Polenka? Oh yes, Polenka—the little girl. She's your sister? Did I give her the address?"
"You'd forgotten?"
"No, I remember."

"I'd heard my father speak of you, only I didn't know your name, and he didn't know it either. And today, when I came, I asked, 'Where does Mr. Raskolnikov live?' I didn't know you only rented a room too. Goodbye—I'll tell Katerina Ivanovna."

She was extremely glad to escape at last. She hurried off, looking down, rushing to get out of sight, to reach the turning on the right twenty steps away and at last be alone—then to walk quickly, looking at no one, noticing nothing, thinking, remembering, turning over every word, every detail. Never, never had she felt anything like this. A whole new world was dimly, unconsciously opening before her. She suddenly remembered that Raskolnikov intended to come to her that very day, perhaps right away!
"Only not today, please, not today!" she kept murmuring with a sinking heart, like a frightened child begging. "Mercy! To me, to that room—he'll see—oh God!"

She was incapable at that moment of noticing an unknown gentleman who was watching her and following at her heels. He had trailed her from the gateway. When Razumihin, Raskolnikov, and she had stood saying goodbye on the pavement, this gentleman, who happened to be passing, had caught Sonia's words: "I asked where Mr. Raskolnikov lived." He cast a quick but attentive glance at all three, particularly at Raskolnikov, to whom Sonia was speaking, then noted the house. All of this was done in an instant, and trying not to betray his interest, he walked on more slowly, as if waiting for something. He was waiting for Sonia. He could see they were parting and that she was heading home.
"Home? Where? I've seen that face somewhere," he thought. "I must find out."

At the corner he crossed the street, looked back, and saw Sonia coming the same way, noticing nothing. She turned the corner. He followed on the opposite side. After about fifty paces he crossed back, caught up with her, and stayed two or three yards behind.

He was a man of about fifty, rather tall and solidly built, with broad, high shoulders that made him look as though he stooped slightly. He wore fine, fashionable clothes and looked like a gentleman of position. He carried a handsome cane, which he tapped on the pavement at each step; his gloves were spotless. He had a broad, rather pleasant face with high cheekbones and fresh color not often seen in Petersburg. His flaxen hair was still thick, with only a touch of gray here and there, and his full, square beard was even lighter than his hair. His eyes were blue, with a cold and thoughtful look; his lips were red. He was remarkably well-preserved and looked much younger than his years.

When Sonia reached the canal embankment, they were the only two people on the pavement. He noticed her dreaminess and distraction. When she reached the house where she lived and turned in at the gate, he followed, looking somewhat surprised. In the courtyard she turned toward the right-hand corner. "Well!" the unknown gentleman muttered, and climbed the stairs behind her. Only then did Sonia notice him. She reached the third floor, turned down the corridor, and rang at No. 9. On the door was inscribed in chalk: "Kapernaumov, Tailor." "Well!" the stranger repeated, wondering at the strange coincidence, and rang next door at No. 8. The two doors were only two or three yards apart.
"You live at Kapernaumov's," he said, looking at Sonia and laughing. "He altered a waistcoat for me yesterday. I'm staying right here, at Madame Resslich's. How odd!" Sonia looked at him attentively.
"We're neighbours," he went on cheerfully. "I only arrived in town the day before yesterday. Well, goodbye for now."
Sonia said nothing. The door opened and she slipped inside. She felt somehow ashamed and uneasy, though she couldn't have said why.
On the way to Porfiry's, Razumihin was obviously excited.
"That's wonderful, brother," he repeated several times, "and I'm glad! I'm glad!"
"What are you so glad about?" Raskolnikov thought to himself.
"I didn't know you'd pawned things with the old woman too. Was it long ago? I mean, how long since you were there?"
"What a simple-hearted fool he is!"

"When was it?" Raskolnikov stopped to think. "Two or three days before her death, it must have been. But I'm not going to redeem the things now," he added with a sort of hurried, conspicuous concern about the items. "I've got no more than a silver rouble left after last night's damned delirium!"
He stressed the word "delirium" deliberately.

"Yes, yes," Razumihin hastened to agree—though it wasn't clear with what. "So that's why you were so affected. Partly, you know, in your delirium you kept mentioning rings and chains! Yes, yes, that makes sense. It's all clear now."

"Listen to that! How that idea must have spread among them. This man would go to the stake for me, and he's delighted that it's been 'cleared up' why I mentioned rings in my delirium! What a hold the idea must have on all of them!"
"Will we find him in?" he asked suddenly.

"Oh yes," Razumihin answered quickly. "He's a nice fellow, you'll see, brother. A bit clumsy—I mean, he's a man of polished manners, but clumsy in a different sense. He's intelligent, very much so, but he has his own way of thinking. He's skeptical, cynical, likes to put people on. Or rather, to make fun of them. He uses the old, methodical approach. But he understands his work thoroughly. Last year he solved a murder case where the police had almost no leads. He's very, very eager to meet you!"
"On what grounds?"

"Oh, it's not exactly—you see, since you've been ill, I happened to mention you several times. So when he heard about you, about your being a law student unable to finish your studies, he said, 'What a pity!' And so I figured, from everything together—not just that. Yesterday, Zametov—you know, Rodya, I said some nonsense on our way home yesterday when I was drunk. I'm worried, brother, that you might exaggerate it—"
"What? That they think I'm a madman? Maybe they're right," he said with a strained smile.
"Yes, yes—that is, no, not at all! But everything I said—and there was other stuff too—it was all drunken nonsense."
"Why are you apologizing? I'm so sick of all this!" Raskolnikov exclaimed with exaggerated irritation, though it was partly an act.
"I know, I know, I understand. Believe me, I understand. It's embarrassing to even talk about."
"Then don't."
Both fell silent. Razumihin was more than ecstatic, and Raskolnikov sensed it with disgust. He was also alarmed by what Razumihin had just said about Porfiry.

"I'll have to put on a performance with him too," he thought, his heart pounding as he turned white, "and make it look natural. But the most natural thing would be to do nothing at all. Carefully do nothing! No, 'carefully' wouldn't be natural either. Well, we'll see how it goes. We'll see soon enough. Is it a good thing I'm going or not? The moth flies to the flame. My heart is pounding—that's what's bad!"
"In this grey building," said Razumihin.

"The most important thing: does Porfiry know I was at the old woman's flat yesterday and asked about the blood? I must find that out instantly, as soon as I walk in—read it from his face. Otherwise I'll find out even if it ruins me."
"Listen, brother," he said suddenly to Razumihin with a sly smile, "I've been noticing all day that you seem strangely excited. Am I right?"
"Excited? Not at all," said Razumihin, stung.

"Yes, brother, I assure you it's noticeable. You sat on your chair in a way you never do—right on the edge, squirming the whole time. You kept jumping up for no reason. One minute you were angry, the next your face turned sweet as candy. You even blushed. Especially when you were invited to dinner—you blushed terribly."
"Nothing of the sort! Nonsense! What are you talking about?"
"Why are you squirming like a schoolboy? Good lord, he's blushing again!"
"What a pig you are!"
"But why are you so embarrassed about it? Romeo! Just wait—I'll tell everyone about you today. Ha-ha-ha! That'll give mother a laugh, and someone else too."
"Listen, listen, this is serious! What next, you devil!" Razumihin was utterly beside himself, going cold with horror. "What will you tell them? Come on, brother—what a pig you are!"

"You're like a summer rose! And if you only knew how well it suits you—a Romeo over six feet tall! And how you've washed today—you even cleaned your nails, I do believe. That's unheard of! And is that pomade in your hair? Bend down."
"Pig!"

Raskolnikov laughed as though he couldn't hold it in. And laughing like that, they entered Porfiry Petrovitch's apartment. This was exactly what Raskolnikov wanted: from inside they could be heard laughing as they came in, still guffawing in the hallway.
"Not a word in here, or I'll brain you!" Razumihin whispered furiously, seizing Raskolnikov by the shoulder.

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Raskolnikov was already entering the room. He came in looking as though he could barely stop himself from bursting into laughter. Behind him Razumihin strode in, gangly and awkward, red as a peony, shamefaced, with an utterly crestfallen and ferocious expression. His face and whole figure really were comical at that moment, and fully justified Raskolnikov's laughter. Raskolnikov, without waiting for an introduction, bowed to Porfiry Petrovitch, who stood in the middle of the room looking at them inquiringly. He held out his hand and shook it, still apparently making desperate efforts to suppress his mirth and say a few words of introduction. But no sooner had he managed a serious expression and mumbled something than he glanced at Razumihin again and lost all control: his stifled laughter burst out all the more irresistibly the harder he tried to hold it back. Razumihin's extraordinary ferocity in response to this "spontaneous" amusement gave the whole scene an appearance of genuine fun and naturalness. Razumihin reinforced this impression as though on purpose.
"Fool! You fiend!" he roared, flailing his arm, which immediately struck a small round table with an empty tea glass on it. Everything went crashing to the floor.
"But why smash chairs, gentlemen? It's a loss to the state," Porfiry Petrovitch quoted cheerfully.

Raskolnikov was still laughing, his hand in Porfiry Petrovitch's, but was careful not to overdo it and waited for the right moment to stop naturally. Razumihin, completely thrown off by knocking over the table and breaking the glass, glared gloomily at the fragments, cursed, and turned sharply to the window where he stood with his back to the room, scowling fiercely and seeing nothing. Porfiry Petrovitch laughed, clearly ready to keep laughing, but was obviously waiting for an explanation. Zametov had been sitting in the corner but rose when the visitors entered and stood waiting with a smile, though he looked at the whole scene and particularly at Raskolnikov with surprise and what seemed like disbelief. Zametov's unexpected presence struck Raskolnikov unpleasantly.
"I need to think about that," he thought. "Excuse me, please," he began, feigning extreme embarrassment. "Raskolnikov."
"Not at all—delighted to meet you. And what a pleasant entrance! Won't he even say hello?" Porfiry Petrovitch nodded toward Razumihin.
"On my honour, I have no idea why he's so furious with me. I only told him on the way over that he looked like Romeo, and proved it. That was all, I think!"
"Pig!" Razumihin ejaculated without turning around.
"There must have been very serious grounds for it, if one little word makes him this angry," Porfiry laughed.

"Oh, you sharp lawyer! Damn you all!" Razumihin snapped, and suddenly, bursting out laughing himself, he walked up to Porfiry with a more cheerful expression as though nothing had happened. "Enough of that! We're all fools. Down to business. This is my friend, Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov. First, he's heard of you and wants to make your acquaintance; second, he has a small matter of business with you. Well! Zametov, what brought you here? Have you two met? Have you known each other long?"
"What does this mean?" Raskolnikov thought uneasily.
Zametov seemed somewhat taken aback, but not very.
"We met at your rooms yesterday," he said casually.
"Well, that saves me the trouble. All last week he was begging me to introduce him to you. You and Porfiry have sniffed each other out without my help. Where's your tobacco?"

Porfiry Petrovitch was wearing a dressing gown, very clean linen, and worn-down slippers. He was a man of about thirty-five, short, stout, even tending to corpulence, and clean-shaven. His hair was cut short and he had a large, round head, particularly prominent at the back. His soft, round, somewhat snub-nosed face had a sickly yellowish tinge but a vigorous and rather ironic expression. It might have looked good-natured except for the eyes, which shone with a watery, crafty light under almost white, blinking lashes. The expression of those eyes was strangely at odds with his somewhat womanish figure and gave it something far more serious than you'd guess at first sight.

As soon as Porfiry Petrovitch heard that his visitor had a small business matter, he invited him to sit at one end of the sofa while seating himself at the other, waiting for the explanation with that attentive and overly serious manner that is at once oppressive and embarrassing, especially for a stranger, especially when what you're discussing seems far too trivial for such solemnity. But Raskolnikov explained his business briefly and clearly, and was pleased enough with himself to even get a good look at Porfiry. Porfiry Petrovitch didn't take his eyes off him once. Razumihin, sitting across the table, listened eagerly and impatiently, looking from one to the other every moment with rather excessive interest.
"Fool," Raskolnikov cursed to himself.

"You need to file a statement with the police," Porfiry replied in a thoroughly businesslike tone, "declaring that having learned of this incident—that is, the murder—you wish to inform the investigating officer that such and such items belong to you and that you wish to redeem them. Or rather, they'll write it up for you."

"The problem is," Raskolnikov did his utmost to feign embarrassment, "at the moment I'm not exactly flush with cash, and even this small amount is beyond me. I only wanted, you see, to declare for now that the things are mine, and that when I have money—"

"That doesn't matter," Porfiry Petrovitch answered, receiving his explanation of his finances coolly. "But if you prefer, you can write directly to me, stating that having been informed of the matter and claiming such and such as your property, you request—"
"On ordinary paper?" Raskolnikov interrupted eagerly, again showing interest in the financial side.

"Oh, the most ordinary." And suddenly Porfiry Petrovitch looked at him with obvious irony, squinting and almost winking at him. But perhaps it was Raskolnikov's imagination, because it lasted only a moment. There was certainly something of the sort. Raskolnikov could have sworn he winked, though God knows why.
"He knows," flashed through his mind like lightning.

"Forgive me for troubling you about such trifles," he went on, slightly flustered. "The things are only worth five roubles, but I treasure them because of who gave them to me, and I must confess I was alarmed when I heard—"
"That's why you were so startled when I mentioned to Zossimov that Porfiry was looking for everyone with pledges!" Razumihin put in with obvious intent.
This was really unbearable. Raskolnikov couldn't help shooting him a look of sharp, vindictive anger, but immediately caught himself.

"You seem to be mocking me, brother," he said to Razumihin with well-feigned irritation. "I'm sure I seem absurdly anxious about such junk. But don't think me selfish or greedy—these two things may not be junk to me. I told you just now that the silver watch, though it's not worth a kopeck, is the only thing left from my father. You can laugh at me, but my mother is here," he turned suddenly to Porfiry, "and if she knew," he turned back hastily to Razumihin, carefully making his voice tremble, "that the watch was lost, she'd be in despair! You know how women are!"
"Not at all! I didn't mean that at all! Quite the contrary!" Razumihin shouted, distressed.
"Was that right? Was it natural? Did I overdo it?" Raskolnikov asked himself in a tremor. "Why did I say that about women?"
"Oh, so your mother is here?" Porfiry Petrovitch inquired.
"Yes."
"When did she arrive?"
"Last night."
Porfiry paused, as though reflecting.
"Your things wouldn't have been lost in any case," he said calmly and coolly. "I've been expecting you for some time."

And as if that were a matter of no importance, he carefully offered the ashtray to Razumihin, who was ruthlessly scattering cigarette ash on the carpet. Raskolnikov shuddered, but Porfiry didn't seem to be looking at him, apparently still preoccupied with Razumihin's cigarette.
"What? Expecting him? Did you know he had pledges there?" Razumihin cried.
Porfiry Petrovitch addressed Raskolnikov directly.
"Your things—the ring and the watch—were wrapped up together, and on the paper your name was written clearly in pencil, along with the date you left them."
"How observant you are!" Raskolnikov smiled awkwardly, making every effort to look him straight in the face, but failing. He suddenly added:
"I only say that because I suppose there were a great many pledges, and it must be hard to remember them all. Yet you remember them all so clearly, and—"
"Stupid! Feeble!" he thought. "Why did I add that?"
"But we know everyone who had pledges, and you're the only one who hasn't come forward," Porfiry answered with barely perceptible irony.
"I haven't been quite well."
"I heard that too. I heard you were in considerable distress. You still look pale."

"I'm not pale at all! No, I'm perfectly well," Raskolnikov snapped rudely and angrily, completely changing his tone. Anger was rising in him and he couldn't hold it back. "And in my anger I'll give myself away," flashed through his mind. "Why are they tormenting me?"

"Not quite well!" Razumihin jumped in. "What next! He was unconscious and delirious all yesterday. Would you believe, Porfiry—as soon as our backs were turned, he got dressed, though he could barely stand, gave us the slip, and went off on some escapade until midnight, delirious the whole time! Can you imagine?"
"Really delirious? You don't say!" Porfiry shook his head in a womanish way.
"Nonsense! Don't believe it! But you don't believe it anyway," Raskolnikov let slip in his anger. But Porfiry Petrovitch didn't seem to catch those reckless words.

"How could you have gone out if you weren't delirious?" Razumihin flared up. "What did you go out for? What was the point? And why on the sly? Were you in your right mind? Now that the danger's passed, I can speak plainly."

"I was sick of them yesterday," Raskolnikov addressed Porfiry suddenly, with a smile of insolent defiance. "I ran away to rent a room where they wouldn't find me, and took a lot of money with me. Mr. Zametov there saw it. Tell me, Mr. Zametov—was I in my right mind yesterday, or delirious? Settle our dispute."
He could have strangled Zametov at that moment, so hateful were his expression and his silence.
"In my opinion, you spoke sensibly and even cleverly, but you were extremely irritable," Zametov said drily.
"And Nikodim Fomitch was telling me today," Porfiry Petrovitch put in, "that he ran into you very late last night at the lodging of a man who'd been run over."

"And there," Razumihin said, "weren't you out of your mind? You gave your last penny to the widow for the funeral. If you wanted to help, give fifteen or twenty, but keep at least three roubles for yourself. Instead you threw away the whole twenty-five!"

"Maybe I found a treasure somewhere that you don't know about. That's why I was so generous yesterday. Mr. Zametov knows I've found a treasure! Forgive us for taking up your time with such trivialities," he said to Porfiry with trembling lips. "We must be boring you."
"Oh no, quite the contrary! If you only knew how much you interest me! It's fascinating to watch and listen. And I'm really glad you've come forward at last."
"How about some tea? My throat's parched," Razumihin cried.
"Excellent idea! Perhaps we'll all join you. Wouldn't you like something stronger before tea?"
"Get out of here!"
Porfiry Petrovitch went out to order tea.
Raskolnikov's thoughts were in turmoil. He was in terrible agitation.

"The worst of it is they don't even bother to disguise it! They don't stand on ceremony! How did you come to discuss me with Nikodim Fomitch if you didn't even know me? They don't care to hide that they're tracking me like a pack of hounds. They simply spit in my face." He was shaking with rage. "Come on then, strike openly—don't play with me like a cat with a mouse. That's hardly polite, Porfiry Petrovitch, and perhaps I won't stand for it! I'll stand up and throw the truth in all your faces, and you'll see how I despise you." He could barely breathe. "But what if it's all in my imagination? What if I'm wrong and just getting angry out of inexperience, not keeping up my wretched act? Maybe it's all unintentional. All the usual phrases, but there's something about them. It could all be said innocently, but there's something. Why did he say 'with her' so bluntly? Why did Zametov add that I spoke 'cleverly'? Why that tone? Yes, the tone. Razumihin is sitting right here—why doesn't he see anything? That innocent blockhead never sees anything! Feverish again! Did Porfiry just wink at me? Of course not—nonsense! Why would he wink? Are they trying to rattle me, or teasing me? Either it's all in my head or they know! Even Zametov is rude. Is Zametov rude? He's changed his mind. I predicted he would. He's at home here; it's my first visit. Porfiry doesn't treat him like a guest—sits with his back to him. They're thick as thieves, no doubt conspiring against me! They were surely talking about me before we came. Do they know about the apartment? If only they'd get on with it! When I said I ran off to rent a flat, he let it pass. I slipped that in cleverly—might be useful later. 'Delirious,' indeed! Ha-ha-ha! He knows all about last night! He didn't know my mother had arrived! The old woman had written the date in pencil! You're wrong—you won't catch me! There are no facts, only guesswork! Show me the facts! Even the flat isn't a fact but delirium. I know what to tell them. Do they know about the flat? I won't leave without finding out. What did I come for? But my anger right now—that might be a fact! Fool, how irritable I am! Maybe that's the right approach—play the sick man. He's probing me. He'll try to trip me up. Why did I come?"
All this flashed through his mind like lightning.
Porfiry Petrovitch returned quickly. He suddenly became more jovial.
"Your party yesterday, brother, has left my head a bit foggy. And I'm out of sorts altogether," he began in a completely different tone, laughing to Razumihin.
"Was it interesting? I left you at the most interesting point. Who won the argument?"
"Oh, nobody, of course. They got onto the eternal questions and floated off into the clouds."
"Just imagine, Rodya, what we got into yesterday. Whether crime really exists. I told you we talked ourselves hoarse."
"What's strange about that? It's an ordinary social question," Raskolnikov answered indifferently.
"The question wasn't framed quite like that," Porfiry observed.

"Not quite, that's true," Razumihin agreed at once, getting heated and hurried as usual. "Listen, Rodion, and tell us your opinion. I want to hear it. I was fighting tooth and nail and wanted your help. I told them you were coming. It started with the socialist doctrine. You know their position: crime is a protest against the abnormality of the social order and nothing more—no other causes are admitted!"
"You're wrong there," cried Porfiry Petrovitch, noticeably animated and laughing as he looked at Razumihin, which made him even more excited.
"Nothing else is admitted!" Razumihin interrupted heatedly.

"I'm not wrong! I'll show you their pamphlets. Everything with them is 'the influence of environment' and nothing else. Their favourite phrase! From which it follows that if society is properly organized, all crime will vanish at once, because there'll be nothing to protest against and everyone will become righteous in an instant. Human nature isn't taken into account—it's excluded, it's not supposed to exist! They don't accept that humanity, developing through a living historical process, will eventually become a normal society. They believe a social system designed by some mathematician's brain will instantly organize all of humanity and make it just and sinless, faster than any living process! That's why they instinctively hate history—'nothing but ugliness and stupidity in it'—and they explain everything as stupidity! That's why they so despise the living process of life. They don't want a living soul! The living soul demands life; it won't obey the rules of mechanics; it's suspicious, it's reactionary! But what they want, even though it smells of death and can be made of rubber, at least isn't alive, has no will, is servile and won't rebel! And in the end it all comes down to building walls and planning rooms and corridors in a commune! The commune is ready, but human nature isn't ready for it—it wants life, it hasn't completed its vital process, it's too early for the graveyard! You can't leap over nature with logic. Logic admits three possibilities, but there are millions! Cut away a million and reduce everything to the question of comfort! That's the easiest solution! Seductively clear—and you don't even have to think! That's the main thing—you mustn't think! The whole secret of life in two pages of print!"

"Now he's off—beating the drum! Grab hold of him!" Porfiry laughed. "Can you imagine," he turned to Raskolnikov, "six people going on like that last night, in one room, with punch to warm things up! No, brother, you're wrong. Environment accounts for a great deal in crime, I can assure you."
"Oh, I know it does. But just tell me this: a man of forty violates a ten-year-old child. Was it environment that drove him to it?"
"Well, strictly speaking, it was," Porfiry observed with noteworthy gravity. "A crime of that nature might well be attributed to the influence of environment."

Razumihin was nearly beside himself. "Oh, if you like," he roared, "I'll prove to you that your white eyelashes can be attributed to the fact that the Ivan the Great bell tower is two hundred and fifty feet tall! I'll prove it clearly, precisely, progressively, and even with a liberal slant! Care to bet?"
"Done! Let's hear how he'll prove it!"

"He's always bluffing, damn him!" cried Razumihin, jumping up and gesticulating. "What's the use of talking to you? He does it all on purpose. You don't know him, Rodion! He took their side yesterday just to make fools of them. And the things he said! And they were thrilled! He can keep it up for two weeks straight. Last year he convinced us he was entering a monastery—he stuck to it for two months. Not long ago he announced he was getting married and had everything ready for the wedding. He even ordered new clothes. We all started congratulating him. There was no bride, nothing—pure fantasy!"
"Wrong! I got the clothes first. It was the new clothes that gave me the idea of fooling you."
"Are you that good a dissembler?" Raskolnikov asked carelessly.

"You'd never have guessed, would you? Just wait—I'll fool you too. Ha-ha-ha! No, I'll tell you the truth. All these questions about crime, environment, children remind me of an article of yours that interested me at the time. 'On Crime,' or something like that—I forget the exact title. I read it with pleasure two months ago in the Periodical Review."
"My article? In the Periodical Review?" Raskolnikov asked in astonishment. "I did write an article about a book six months ago, when I left the university, but I sent it to the Weekly Review."
"But it appeared in the Periodical."
"And the Weekly Review folded, so that's why it wasn't published at the time."
"That's right. But when it folded, the Weekly Review was absorbed into the Periodical, and so your article appeared two months ago. Didn't you know?"
Raskolnikov had not known.
"Why, you could get paid for it! What a strange person you are! You lead such a solitary life that you don't know about things that concern you directly. It's a fact, I assure you."

"Bravo, Rodya! I didn't know either!" cried Razumihin. "I'll run to the reading room today and ask for that issue. Two months ago? What was the date? Doesn't matter—I'll find it. Imagine not telling us!"
"How did you find out the article was mine? It's only signed with an initial."
"I learned quite by chance, the other day, through the editor. I know him. I was very much interested."
"As I recall, I analyzed the psychology of a criminal before and after the crime."

"Yes, and you argued that committing a crime is always accompanied by illness. Very, very original—but that wasn't the part that interested me most. It was an idea at the end of the article that, I'm sorry to say, you only hinted at without fully developing. There's a suggestion that certain people can—not exactly that they're able to, but that they have a perfect right to commit crimes and break moral laws, and that the law doesn't apply to them."
Raskolnikov smiled at the exaggerated and deliberate distortion of his idea.
"What? A right to commit crime? But not because of environmental influence?" Razumihin asked with some alarm.

"No, not exactly," Porfiry answered. "In his article, all people are divided into 'ordinary' and 'extraordinary.' Ordinary people must live in submission and have no right to break the law, because they're ordinary. But extraordinary people have the right to commit any crime and transgress any law, simply because they're extraordinary. That was your idea, if I'm not mistaken?"
"What? That can't be right," Razumihin muttered in bewilderment.
Raskolnikov smiled again. He saw the point at once and knew where they were trying to drive him. He decided to accept the challenge.

"That wasn't quite my argument," he began simply and modestly. "Still, I admit you've stated it almost correctly—perhaps perfectly so." He almost enjoyed admitting this. "The only difference is that I don't claim extraordinary people are always obliged to commit crimes, as you put it. I doubt such an argument could even be published. I simply suggested that an 'extraordinary' person has the right—not an official right but an inner right—to decide in his own conscience to overstep certain obstacles, and only when it's essential for the practical fulfillment of his idea, which may sometimes benefit all of humanity. You say my article is unclear; I'm prepared to make it as clear as I can. Perhaps I'm right in thinking you want me to—very well. I maintain that if the discoveries of Kepler and Newton could not have been made known without sacrificing the lives of one, a dozen, a hundred, or more people, Newton would have had the right—would indeed have been duty-bound—to eliminate that dozen or hundred for the sake of making his discoveries known to all humanity. But it doesn't follow that Newton had a right to murder people randomly or steal at the market every day. Then, I recall, I argue in my article that all legislators and leaders of men—Lycurgus, Solon, Mohammed, Napoleon, and so on—were without exception criminals, since in establishing new laws they violated old ones handed down from their ancestors and held sacred by the people, and they didn't shrink from bloodshed either, if that bloodshed—often of innocent people bravely defending the old ways—served their cause. It's remarkable, in fact, that the majority of these benefactors and leaders of humanity were guilty of terrible carnage. In short, I maintain that all great men, or even those slightly out of the ordinary—anyone capable of saying something new—must by their very nature be criminals, to a greater or lesser degree. Otherwise they can't break out of the common rut, and to remain in it is something they can't accept, again by their very nature, and in my view they shouldn't accept it. You see there's nothing particularly new in all that. The same thing has been printed and read a thousand times before. As for my division of people into ordinary and extraordinary, I admit it's somewhat arbitrary, but I don't insist on exact numbers. I only believe in my central idea: that by a law of nature, people are generally divided into two categories. The first—the inferior, the ordinary—is material that serves only to reproduce its kind. The second category consists of people who have the gift or talent to say a new word. There are, of course, countless subdivisions, but the distinguishing features of both categories are fairly clear. The first category—generally speaking, people conservative by temperament and law-abiding—live in obedience and love being obedient. As I see it, it's their duty to be obedient, because that's their calling and there's nothing humiliating in it. The second category all transgress the law; they are destroyers, or inclined to destruction, according to their abilities. The crimes of these people are of course relative and varied. Most often they seek, in very different ways, the destruction of the present for the sake of something better. But if such a person must, for the sake of his idea, step over a corpse or wade through blood, he can, I maintain, find within himself, in his conscience, a justification for doing so—depending on the idea and its scope, note that. It's only in that sense that I speak of their right to crime in my article—you'll recall it begins with the legal question. There's no need for alarm, though. The masses will almost never grant this right; they punish and hang such people, more or less, thereby quite justly fulfilling their conservative calling. But those same masses, in the next generation, put these criminals on a pedestal and worship them, more or less. The first category is always the person of the present; the second, the person of the future. The first preserves the world and multiplies it; the second moves the world and leads it to its goal. Both have an equal right to exist. In short, for me everyone has equal rights—and vive la guerre éternelle—until the New Jerusalem, of course!"
"Then you do believe in the New Jerusalem?"
"I do," Raskolnikov answered firmly. As he said this, and throughout his entire preceding speech, he kept his eyes fixed on one spot on the carpet.
"And do you believe in God? Forgive my curiosity."
"I do," Raskolnikov repeated, raising his eyes to Porfiry.
"And do you believe in the raising of Lazarus?"
"I do. Why do you ask all this?"
"You believe it literally?"
"Literally."
"I see. I asked out of curiosity. Forgive me. But let's return to the question. They aren't always executed. Some, on the contrary—"
"Triumph in their lifetime? Oh yes, some achieve their ends in this life, and then—"
"They begin executing others?"
"If necessary. In fact, for the most part they do. Your observation is quite witty."

"Thank you. But tell me this: how do you distinguish these extraordinary people from the ordinary ones? Are there signs at birth? I feel there ought to be more precision, some external markers. Forgive the natural concern of a practical, law-abiding citizen, but couldn't they adopt a special uniform, for instance? Wear something distinctive, be branded in some way? Because, you see, if confusion arises and a member of one category imagines he belongs to the other and begins 'eliminating obstacles,' as you so aptly put it, then—"
"Oh, that happens quite often! That remark is wittier than the last."
"Thank you."

"Don't mention it. But note that the mistake can only arise in the first category, among the ordinary people, as I perhaps unfortunately called them. Despite their predisposition to obedience, a great many of them, through some quirk of nature sometimes granted even to a cow, like to imagine themselves advanced thinkers, 'destroyers,' and to push their way into the 'new movement'—quite sincerely, too. Meanwhile, the truly new people are often unnoticed or even scorned as reactionaries. But I don't think there's much danger here. They never go very far. Of course they might get a thrashing now and then to teach them their place, but nothing more. In fact, even that's hardly necessary, since they punish themselves—they're extremely conscientious. Some perform this service for each other, others do it to themselves with their own hands. They'll impose various public acts of penance on themselves, with beautiful and edifying results. In short, you have nothing to worry about. It's a law of nature."

"Well, you've certainly set my mind at rest on that score. But here's another concern. Tell me, please: are there many people who have the right to kill others—these extraordinary people? I'm prepared to bow before them, of course, but you must admit it's alarming if there are a great many of them."

"Oh, you needn't worry about that either," Raskolnikov went on in the same tone. "People with new ideas, people with even the faintest capacity for saying something new, are extraordinarily rare. One thing is clear: the emergence of all these grades and subdivisions must follow some law of nature with unfailing regularity. That law is unknown at present, but I'm convinced it exists and may one day be discovered. The vast mass of humanity is merely raw material, existing only so that by some great effort, some mysterious process, some crossing of races and bloodlines, the world might at last produce one person in a thousand with a spark of independence. Perhaps one in ten thousand is born with still greater independence, one in a hundred thousand with more still. The man of genius is one in millions, and the great geniuses—the crown of humanity—appear perhaps one in many thousand millions. In short, I haven't peered into the crucible where all this takes place. But there certainly is, and must be, a definite law. It can't be a matter of chance."
"Are you two joking?" Razumihin cried at last. "Sitting there making fun of each other? Are you serious, Rodya?"

Raskolnikov raised his pale, almost sorrowful face and gave no reply. The unconcealed, persistent, nervous, and discourteous sarcasm of Porfiry seemed strange to Razumihin set against that quiet, mournful face.

"Well, brother, if you're really serious—you're right, of course, that the idea itself isn't new, that it's like what we've read and heard a thousand times. But what is truly original in all this, what is exclusively your own—and horrifies me—is that you sanction bloodshed in the name of conscience, and, forgive me, with such fanaticism. That, I take it, is the main point of your article. But this sanctioning of bloodshed by conscience is, to my mind, more terrible than the official, legal sanctioning of it."
"You're quite right—it is more terrible," Porfiry agreed.
"Yes, you must have exaggerated! There's some mistake. I'll read it. You can't think that! I'll read it."
"None of that is actually in the article. There's only a hint of it," said Raskolnikov.

"Yes, yes." Porfiry couldn't sit still. "Your attitude toward crime is fairly clear to me now, but forgive my impertinence—I'm truly ashamed to keep bothering you—but there are certain practical possibilities that trouble me. What if some man or youth imagines himself a Lycurgus or a Mohammed—a future one, naturally—and decides to remove all obstacles? He has some grand enterprise before him and needs money for it, and so he tries to get it. Do you see what I mean?"
Zametov gave a sudden guffaw from his corner. Raskolnikov didn't even glance at him.
"I must admit," he went on calmly, "that such cases certainly do arise. The vain and foolish are particularly prone to falling into that trap—young people especially."
"You see? Well, then what?"

"What then?" Raskolnikov smiled. "That's not my fault. It happens and always will. He just said"—he nodded at Razumihin—"that I sanction bloodshed. Society is well enough protected by prisons, exile, investigators, and hard labor. There's no need to worry. You have only to catch the thief."
"And what if we do catch him?"
"Then he gets what he deserves."
"You're certainly logical. But what about his conscience?"
"Why should that concern you?"
"Simple humanity."
"If he has a conscience, he'll suffer for his mistake. That will be his punishment—on top of prison."
"But the real geniuses," Razumihin asked, frowning, "those who have the right to murder? Shouldn't they suffer at all, even for the blood they've shed?"

"Why the word 'should'? It's not a question of permission or prohibition. He will suffer if he's sorry for his victim. Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a great intelligence and a deep heart. The truly great must, I think, experience great sorrow on earth," he added dreamily, no longer in the tone of the conversation.
He raised his eyes, looked at them all thoughtfully, smiled, and picked up his cap. He was too calm compared to how he'd entered, and he felt it. Everyone stood up.

"Well, you can abuse me, be angry with me if you like," Porfiry Petrovitch began again, "but I can't resist. Allow me one more little question—just one small idea I want to express so I don't forget it."
"Very well, tell me your little idea," Raskolnikov stood waiting, pale and grave.

"Well, you see, I really don't know how to put it properly. It's a playful, psychological thought. When you were writing your article, surely you couldn't have helped fancying yourself—just a little—an 'extraordinary' man, someone uttering a new word, in your sense of the term. Isn't that so?"
"Quite possibly," Raskolnikov answered contemptuously.
Razumihin stirred.
"And if so, could you bring yourself—in case of hardship or in service to humanity—to overstep those obstacles? For instance, to rob and murder?"
And again he winked with his left eye and laughed noiselessly, just as before.
"If I did, I certainly wouldn't tell you," Raskolnikov answered with defiant, haughty contempt.
"No, I only asked for the literary interest, in connection with your article."
"How blatant and insulting!" Raskolnikov thought with revulsion.
"Allow me to point out," he answered drily, "that I don't consider myself a Mohammed or a Napoleon, or any figure of that kind, and since I'm not one of them, I can't tell you how I would act."
"Oh come—don't we all think ourselves Napoleons in Russia these days?" Porfiry Petrovitch said with alarming familiarity.
Something peculiar betrayed itself in his very tone of voice.
"Perhaps it was one of these future Napoleons who did for Alyona Ivanovna last week?" Zametov blurted out from the corner.

Raskolnikov said nothing but looked firmly and intently at Porfiry. Razumihin was scowling darkly. He had already begun to notice something. He looked angrily around. A minute of grim silence passed. Raskolnikov turned to leave.

"Going already?" Porfiry said amiably, extending his hand with excessive courtesy. "Very, very glad to have met you. As for your request, have no concerns—write to me as I described, or better yet, come to my office in a day or two—tomorrow, even. I'll be there at eleven, certainly. We'll arrange everything, have a talk. As one of the last people to have been there, you might be able to tell us something," he added with the most good-natured expression.
"You want to question me officially, in proper form?" Raskolnikov asked sharply.

"Why? That's not necessary for now. You misunderstand me. I just never miss an opportunity, and I've spoken with everyone who had pledges. I've taken statements from some of them, and you're the last. Yes, by the way," he cried, as if suddenly struck by a thought, "I just remembered something!" He turned to Razumihin. "You were going on to me about that Nikolay fellow. Of course I know, I know perfectly well," he turned to Raskolnikov, "that he's innocent, but what can one do? We had to bother Dmitri too. Here's the thing: when you went up the stairs that day, it was past seven, wasn't it?"
"Yes," Raskolnikov answered, with the unpleasant feeling that he needn't have said it.

"And when you went up between seven and eight, did you happen to see, on the second floor, in an open apartment—two workmen, or at least one? They were painting in there. Did you notice them? It's very, very important for them."

"Painters? No, I didn't see them," Raskolnikov answered slowly, as though searching his memory, while in reality he was straining every nerve, nearly fainting with anxiety to figure out where the trap lay. "No, I didn't see them, and I don't think I noticed any open apartment on that floor. But on the fourth floor," he said, having now mastered the trap and feeling triumphant, "I remember someone was moving out of the flat across from Alyona Ivanovna's. Some porters were carrying out a sofa and they squeezed me against the wall. But painters—no, I don't recall any painters, and I don't think there was any apartment open. No, there wasn't."
"What do you mean?" Razumihin suddenly shouted, as though something had clicked. "The painters were there on the day of the murder, and he was there three days before! What are you asking about?"

"Ah, I've mixed it up!" Porfiry slapped his forehead. "Damn this case—it's turning my brain!" He addressed Raskolnikov almost apologetically. "It would mean so much to us to find out whether anyone saw them between seven and eight in that apartment. I thought perhaps you could tell us something. I completely mixed up the dates."
"Then you should be more careful," Razumihin remarked grimly.
These last words were spoken in the hallway. Porfiry Petrovitch saw them to the door with excessive politeness.
They walked out into the street, gloomy and silent, and for several steps neither said a word. Raskolnikov drew a deep breath.

chapters.title: Part 3, Chapter 6
paragraphs: "I don't believe it! I can't believe it!" Razumihin kept repeating, trying in bewilderment to refute Raskolnikov's arguments.

They were by now approaching Bakaleyev's lodgings, where Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia had been expecting them for some time. Razumihin kept stopping along the way in the heat of discussion, confused and excited by the very fact that for the first time they were speaking openly about it.
"Then don't believe it," Raskolnikov answered with a cold, careless smile. "As usual, you noticed nothing, but I was weighing every word."

"You're suspicious. That's why you weighed their words. Hmm, certainly, I agree Porfiry's tone was rather odd, and especially that wretch Zametov! You're right, there was something about him—but why? Why?"
"He's changed his mind since last night."
"Quite the contrary! If they had that brainless idea, they'd do their utmost to hide it and conceal their cards, so as to catch you later. But that was all so brazen and careless."

"If they had facts—real facts—or at least some grounds for suspicion, then of course they'd try to hide their game, hoping to get more. They would have searched my room long ago. But they have no facts—not one. It's all a mirage, all ambiguous. A floating idea, nothing more. So they try to throw me off with sheer brazenness. And maybe he was just irritated at having no facts and blurted things out in his annoyance. Or maybe he has a plan. He seems like an intelligent man. Perhaps he wanted to frighten me by letting on that he knows. That's their kind of psychology, brother. But it's sickening to explain it all. Stop!"

"And it's insulting, insulting! I understand you. But since we've started speaking openly now—and it's an excellent thing we have, I'm glad—I'll admit frankly that I've noticed this from them for a while. The merest hint, of course, just an insinuation—but why even an insinuation? How dare they? What possible basis? If you only knew how furious I've been! Think about it: simply because a poor student, unhinged by poverty and depression, on the eve of a severe illness with delirium—note that—suspicious, proud, vain, who hasn't spoken to a soul in six months, dressed in rags and boots with holes in them, has to stand before some wretched policemen and endure their insolence. An unexpected debt shoved in his face, an I.O.U. from Chebarov, fresh paint, thirty degrees of heat, a stifling room, a crowd of people, talk about the murder of someone he'd just visited—and all on an empty stomach! Anyone might faint! And that's what they base everything on! Damn them! I understand how maddening it is, but in your place, Rodya, I'd laugh at them—or better yet, spit in their ugly faces, a dozen times in every direction. I'd lash out neatly and put an end to it. Damn them! Chin up!"
"Still, he put it well," Raskolnikov thought.

"Damn them? But there's another interrogation tomorrow!" he said bitterly. "Do I really have to go explaining myself to them? I'm already disgusted that I lowered myself to talk to Zametov at the restaurant yesterday."
"Damn it! I'll go to Porfiry myself. I'll squeeze it out of him as a relative. He has to tell me the whole story. As for Zametov—"
"He's finally seeing through it," thought Raskolnikov.

"Wait!" cried Razumihin, seizing him by the shoulder. "Wait! You're wrong. I've thought it through. You're wrong! How was that a trap? You say the question about the workmen was a trap. But think: if you had done that, would you have admitted to seeing the painters at the apartment? On the contrary—you'd have seen nothing, even if you had. Who would volunteer evidence against himself?"
"If I had done that thing, I would certainly have said I'd seen the workmen and the apartment," Raskolnikov answered with reluctance and obvious distaste.
"But why speak against yourself?"

"Because only peasants and the greenest novices deny everything flatly under questioning. Any man with the slightest development and experience will certainly try to acknowledge all the external facts that can't be avoided, while seeking other explanations for them—introducing some special, unexpected twist that gives them a different meaning and puts them in a different light. Porfiry could very well have expected me to answer that way—to say I'd seen them, for the sake of plausibility, and then offer some explanation."

"But he would have told you immediately that the workmen couldn't have been there two days before, and that therefore you must have been there on the day of the murder, at eight o'clock. And he'd have caught you on a detail."

"Yes, exactly—he was counting on that. He was counting on me not having time to think it through, and rushing to give the most plausible answer, forgetting that the workmen couldn't have been there two days earlier."
"But how could you forget that?"

"Nothing easier. It's precisely on such simple things that clever people are most easily caught. The more cunning a man is, the less he suspects he'll be tripped up by something obvious. The more cunning the man, the simpler the trap must be. Porfiry is not the fool you think."
"He's a scoundrel, then, if that's the case!"

Raskolnikov couldn't help laughing. But at the same moment he was struck by the strangeness of his own candor and the eagerness with which he'd made this explanation, given that he'd maintained the entire preceding conversation with grim reluctance, obviously with a purpose, out of necessity.

"I'm developing a taste for certain aspects of this," he thought. But almost instantly he became uneasy, as though a sudden and alarming idea had occurred to him. His anxiety kept growing. They had just reached the entrance to Bakaleyev's.
"Go in alone!" Raskolnikov said suddenly. "I'll be right back."
"Where are you going? We're already here!"
"I have to. I'll come in half an hour. Tell them."
"Whatever you say—I'll come with you."

"You want to torture me too!" he screamed, with such bitter irritation, such despair in his eyes, that Razumihin dropped his hands. He stood on the steps for some time, watching gloomily as Raskolnikov strode rapidly away toward his lodging. Finally, gritting his teeth and clenching his fists, he swore to himself he'd squeeze Porfiry like a lemon that very day, and went upstairs to reassure Pulcheria Alexandrovna, who was by now alarmed by their long absence.

When Raskolnikov got home, his hair was soaked with sweat and he was breathing hard. He hurried up the stairs, walked into his unlocked room, and immediately bolted the door. Then, in senseless terror, he rushed to the corner—to the hole in the wallpaper where he had hidden the things. He put his hand in and for several minutes carefully felt through every crack and fold of the paper. Finding nothing, he stood up and drew a deep breath. Walking up to Bakaleyev's steps, he had suddenly imagined that something—a chain, a stud, or even a bit of the wrapping paper with the old woman's handwriting on it—might somehow have slipped out and been lost in some crack, only to turn up later as unexpected, conclusive evidence against him.

He stood as though lost in thought, and a strange, humiliated, half-senseless smile played on his lips. He picked up his cap and quietly left the room. His thoughts were all tangled. He walked dreamily through the gateway.
"Here he is himself!" a loud voice shouted.
He raised his head.

The porter stood at the door of his little room, pointing him out to a short man who looked like a workman—wearing a long coat and a waistcoat and, from a distance, remarkably resembling a woman. He was stooped, and his head in a greasy cap hung forward. From his wrinkled, flabby face, he looked over fifty; his small eyes, buried in fat, stared out grimly, sternly, and with displeasure.
"What is it?" Raskolnikov asked, going up to the porter.
The man stole a look at him from under his brows, studied him attentively and deliberately, then slowly turned and walked out through the gate into the street without a word.
"What was that about?" Raskolnikov cried.
"That fellow was asking if a student lived here—mentioned your name and who you lodge with. Then I saw you coming and pointed you out, and he left. Strange."
The porter seemed somewhat puzzled, but not very. After wondering for a moment, he turned and went back to his room.

Raskolnikov ran after the stranger and immediately spotted him walking along the other side of the street with the same even, deliberate step, eyes fixed on the ground, as though deep in thought. He quickly caught up but walked behind him for some time. At last he drew level and looked at the man's face. The man noticed him at once, glanced at him quickly, then lowered his eyes again. They walked side by side for a minute without saying a word.
"You were asking for me at the porter's?" Raskolnikov said at last, in a strangely quiet voice.
The man gave no answer. He didn't even look at him. Again they walked in silence.
"Why do you come and ask for me and then say nothing? What's the meaning of it?"
Raskolnikov's voice broke; he seemed unable to articulate clearly.
The man raised his eyes and turned a dark, sinister look on Raskolnikov.
"Murderer!" he said suddenly, in a quiet but clear and distinct voice.

Raskolnikov walked on beside him. His legs suddenly went weak, a cold shiver ran down his spine, and his heart seemed to stop for a moment, then began pounding as though it had broken free. They walked like that for about a hundred paces, side by side, in silence.
The man did not look at him.
"What do you mean? What are you—who is a murderer?" Raskolnikov muttered, barely audible.
"You are a murderer," the man answered, still more distinctly and emphatically, with a smile of triumphant hatred, and again looked straight into Raskolnikov's pale face and stricken eyes.

They had reached an intersection. The man turned left without looking back. Raskolnikov stood rooted to the spot, staring after him. He watched the man turn around about fifty paces away and look back at him, still standing there. Raskolnikov couldn't see clearly, but he thought the man was smiling that same smile of cold hatred and triumph.

With slow, faltering steps, knees shaking, Raskolnikov made his way back to his little garret, chilled all over. He took off his cap, put it on the table, and for ten minutes stood without moving. Then he sank exhausted onto the sofa and, with a feeble moan of pain, stretched himself out. He lay there for half an hour.

He thought of nothing. Thoughts or fragments of thoughts, images without order or connection floated through his mind—faces of people he'd seen in childhood or met somewhere and would never have recalled, the bell tower of a church in V., a billiard table in a restaurant with officers playing, the smell of cigars in an underground tobacco shop, a tavern room, a dark back staircase soaked with dirty water and littered with eggshells, and Sunday bells drifting in from somewhere. The images followed one another, spinning like a hurricane. Some he liked and tried to hold onto, but they faded. There was a tightness inside him, but it wasn't crushing—at times it was even pleasant. The slight shivering persisted, but that too was an almost pleasant sensation.

He heard Razumihin's hurried footsteps and closed his eyes, pretending to be asleep. Razumihin opened the door and stood in the doorway for a while, as though hesitating, then stepped softly into the room and went cautiously to the sofa. Raskolnikov heard Nastasya whisper:
"Don't disturb him! Let him sleep. He can eat later."
"Right," Razumihin answered. They both withdrew carefully and closed the door. Another half hour passed. Raskolnikov opened his eyes, turned on his back, and clasped his hands behind his head.

"Who is he? Who is that man who sprang from the earth? Where was he, what did he see? He saw everything, that's clear. Where was he then, and from where did he see? Why has he only now sprung up? And how could he see? Is it possible?" Raskolnikov continued, going cold and shivering. "And the jewel case Nikolay found behind the door—was that possible? A clue? You miss an infinitesimal detail and you can build a whole pyramid of evidence on it! A fly buzzed past and saw it! Is it possible?" He felt with sudden loathing how weak, how physically weak he had become. "I should have known," he thought with a bitter smile. "And how dared I, knowing myself, knowing what I'd be like, take up an axe and shed blood! I should have known beforehand. But I did know!" he whispered in despair. At times he came to a standstill on some thought.

"No, those men aren't made that way. The real Master, to whom all is permitted, storms Toulon, massacres in Paris, forgets an army in Egypt, wastes half a million men in the Moscow campaign, and gets off with a joke at Vilna. And altars are built to him after his death. So all is permitted. No, such men are made not of flesh but of bronze!"

One sudden, irrelevant thought nearly made him laugh. Napoleon, the pyramids, Waterloo—and a miserable, scrawny old woman, a pawnbroker with a red trunk under her bed! A fine hash for Porfiry Petrovitch to digest! How could they? It's too inartistic. "A Napoleon crawling under an old woman's bed!" Ugh, how disgusting!

At moments he felt he was raving. He sank into feverish agitation. "The old woman is beside the point," he thought hotly and incoherently. "The old woman was perhaps a mistake, but she's not what matters! The old woman was only an illness. I was in a hurry to overstep the line. I didn't kill a human being—I killed a principle! I killed the principle, but I didn't overstep—I stopped on this side. All I proved was that I could only kill. And it seems I couldn't even do that. Principle? Why was that fool Razumihin railing against the socialists? They're industrious, commercial people—'the happiness of all' is their cause. No, I only have one life and I won't have another. I don't want to wait for 'the happiness of all.' I want to live myself, or else not live at all. I simply couldn't walk past my mother starving while clutching my rouble, waiting for 'universal happiness.' 'I'm adding my little brick to the happiness of all, and so my heart is at peace.' Ha-ha! Why did you let me slip through? I only live once; I too want— Ugh, I'm nothing but an aesthetic louse!" he added, suddenly laughing like a madman. "Yes, I am definitely a louse," he went on, clutching at the idea, gloating over it, savoring it with vindictive pleasure. "First, because I can reason that I am one; and second, because for a whole month I've been troubling benevolent Providence, calling it to witness that I wasn't acting for selfish pleasure but with a grand and noble purpose—ha-ha! Third, because I aimed at carrying it out as justly as possible, weighing and measuring and calculating. Of all the lice I chose the most useless and proposed to take from her only as much as I needed for the first step, nothing more—the rest would have gone to a monastery, according to her will—ha-ha! And what proves beyond doubt that I am utterly a louse," he added, grinding his teeth, "is that I'm perhaps viler and more loathsome than the louse I killed, and I knew beforehand that I'd tell myself this after killing her. Can anything compare with that horror? The vulgarity! The baseness! I understand the 'prophet' with his sabre on his steed: Allah commands, and trembling creation must obey! The 'prophet' is right—he's right when he plants a cannon across a street and mows down the innocent and guilty alike without deigning to explain! Submit, trembling creature, and don't you dare have desires—that's not for you! I shall never, never forgive the old woman!"
His hair was soaked with sweat; his trembling lips were parched; his eyes stared at the ceiling.

"Mother, sister—how I loved them! Why do I hate them now? Yes, I hate them. I feel a physical hatred for them. I can't bear them near me. I went to my mother and kissed her, I remember. To embrace her and think: if she only knew—should I tell her, then? That's just the sort of thing I might do. She must be like me," he added, straining to think through his delirium. "Oh, how I hate the old woman now! I think I'd kill her again if she came back to life! Poor Lizaveta! Why did she have to come in? It's strange, though—why do I almost never think about her, as if I hadn't killed her? Lizaveta! Sonia! Poor, gentle creatures with gentle eyes. Dear women! Why don't they weep? Why don't they moan? They give up everything. Their eyes are soft and gentle. Sonia, Sonia! Gentle Sonia!"

He lost consciousness. It seemed strange to him that he couldn't remember how he'd gotten into the street. It was late evening. Twilight had fallen and the full moon shone brighter and brighter, but there was a peculiar breathlessness in the air. The streets were crowded—workers and businessmen heading home, others out for a walk. There was a smell of plaster, dust, and stagnant water. Raskolnikov walked along, mournful and anxious. He was distinctly aware of having come out with a purpose, of needing to do something urgently, but he'd forgotten what. Suddenly he stopped and saw a man on the other side of the street, beckoning to him. He crossed over, but at once the man turned and walked away with his head hanging, as though he'd made no sign. "Wait—did he really beckon?" Raskolnikov wondered, but tried to catch up. When he was within ten paces, he recognized the man and was frightened: it was the same stooped man in the long coat. Raskolnikov followed at a distance; his heart was pounding. They turned down a side street; the man still didn't look back. "Does he know I'm following?" Raskolnikov thought. The man entered the gateway of a large house. Raskolnikov hurried to the gate and peered in. In the courtyard, the man turned and again seemed to beckon. Raskolnikov followed at once, but the man had vanished. He must have gone up the first staircase. Raskolnikov rushed after him. He could hear slow, measured footsteps two flights above. The staircase seemed strangely familiar. He reached the window on the first floor; the moon shone through the panes with a melancholy, mysterious light. Then the second floor. This was the apartment where the painters had been working! But how had he not recognized it at once? The footsteps above had died away. "He must have stopped or hidden somewhere." He reached the third floor. Should he go on? The silence was dreadful. But he went on. The sound of his own footsteps frightened him. How dark it was! The man must be hiding in some corner. Then he saw it—the apartment door was standing wide open. He hesitated and went in. The passage was very dark and empty, as though everything had been removed. He crept on tiptoe into the parlour, which was flooded with moonlight. Everything was as before: the chairs, the mirror, the yellow sofa, the pictures in their frames. A huge, round, copper-red moon looked in at the windows. "It's the moon that makes it so still, weaving some mystery," he thought. He stood and waited—waited a long time—and the more silent the moonlight, the harder his heart pounded, until it hurt. And still the same hush. Suddenly there was a momentary sharp crack, like a splinter snapping, and then all was still again. A fly buzzed up and struck the windowpane with a plaintive drone. At that moment he noticed, in the corner between the window and the small cupboard, something like a cloak hanging on the wall. "Why is that cloak here?" he thought. "It wasn't there before." He went up quietly and realized someone was hiding behind it. He carefully moved the cloak aside and saw, sitting in a chair in the corner, the old woman—bent double, her face hidden. He stood over her. "She's afraid," he thought. He stealthily took the axe from the loop and struck her once on the skull, then again. But strangely she didn't stir, as though made of wood. He was frightened. He bent closer, trying to see her face, but she bent her head even lower. He bent down to the ground and peered up at her face from below—and went cold with horror: the old woman was sitting there laughing, shaking with silent laughter, straining with all her might not to let him hear. Suddenly he thought he heard the bedroom door crack open, and there was laughter and whispering inside. Frenzy seized him. He began striking the old woman on the head with all his strength, but with every blow the laughter and whispering from the bedroom grew louder, and the old woman simply shook with mirth. He tried to run, but the passage was packed with people, the apartment doors stood open, and on the landing, on the stairs, everywhere below there were people—rows of heads, all watching, but huddled together in silence, waiting. Something gripped his heart; his legs wouldn't move; they were rooted to the spot. He tried to scream—and woke up.
He drew a deep breath—but his dream seemed strangely to persist: his door was flung open, and a man he had never seen stood in the doorway, watching him intently.
Raskolnikov had barely opened his eyes before he shut them again. He lay on his back, not moving.
"Is it still a dream?" he wondered, and again raised his eyelids the tiniest bit. The stranger was standing in the same place, still watching him.

He stepped carefully into the room, closed the door quietly behind him, went to the table, paused a moment—still keeping his eyes on Raskolnikov—and noiselessly sat down in the chair by the sofa. He placed his hat on the floor beside him and leaned on his cane, chin resting on his hands. It was clear he was prepared to wait indefinitely. As far as Raskolnikov could make out through stolen glances, the man was no longer young, stout, with a full, fair, nearly white beard.

Ten minutes passed. It was still light, but dusk was falling. The room was perfectly still. Not a sound came from the stairs. Only a large fly buzzed and fluttered against the windowpane. The silence became unbearable. Raskolnikov suddenly sat up on the sofa.
"Well, tell me what you want."
"I knew you weren't asleep but only pretending," the stranger answered, laughing calmly. "Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov—allow me to introduce myself."

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 1
paragraphs: "Can this still be a dream?" Raskolnikov thought once more.
He studied the unexpected visitor carefully and suspiciously.
"Svidrigaïlov! Nonsense! It can't be!" he said at last, aloud, in bewilderment.
The visitor didn't seem at all surprised by this exclamation.

"I've come to you for two reasons. First, I wanted to make your personal acquaintance, as I've already heard a great deal about you that's interesting and flattering. Second, I hope you won't refuse to help me in a matter directly concerning the welfare of your sister, Avdotya Romanovna. Without your support, she probably wouldn't let me anywhere near her now, given her prejudice against me. But with your help, I expect—"
"You expect wrong," Raskolnikov interrupted.
"They only arrived yesterday, may I ask?"
Raskolnikov gave no reply.

"It was yesterday, I know. I arrived the day before myself. Well, let me say this, Rodion Romanovitch: I don't consider it necessary to justify myself, but kindly tell me—what was so particularly criminal about my behaviour in all this, speaking without prejudice, with common sense?"
Raskolnikov continued to stare at him in silence.

"That in my own house I persecuted a defenseless girl and 'insulted her with my infamous proposals'—is that it? I'm getting ahead of you, I know. But just suppose that I, too, am a man, et nihil humanum—in a word, that I'm capable of being attracted and falling in love, which is something that doesn't depend on our will. Then everything can be explained in the most natural way. The question is: am I a monster, or am I myself a victim? And what if I am a victim? When I proposed to the object of my passion that we elope to America or Switzerland, I may have felt the deepest respect for her and believed I was promoting our mutual happiness! Reason is the slave of passion, you know. Perhaps I was doing more harm to myself than anyone!"

"But that's not the point," Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust. "Quite simply, whether you're right or wrong, we find you repellent. We want nothing to do with you. We're showing you the door. Get out!"
Svidrigaïlov broke into a sudden laugh.
"There's no getting around you, is there?" he said, laughing in the frankest way. "I hoped to get around you, but you went straight to the heart of it!"
"But you're still trying to get around me!"

"What of it?" Svidrigaïlov cried, laughing openly. "It's what the French call bonne guerre—the most innocent form of deception! But you interrupted me. One way or another, I repeat: there would never have been any unpleasantness if it weren't for what happened in the garden. Marfa Petrovna—"
"You got rid of Marfa Petrovna too, from what they say," Raskolnikov cut in rudely.

"Oh, so you've heard that as well? Naturally. As for your question, I really don't know what to say, though my conscience is perfectly clear on that score. Don't think I'm worried about it. Everything was proper and in order. The medical inquiry diagnosed apoplexy from bathing immediately after a heavy dinner with a bottle of wine, and it couldn't have found anything else. But I'll tell you what I've been thinking about lately, especially on my way here in the train: did I perhaps contribute to the whole catastrophe—morally, somehow, by irritating her or something? But I concluded that was quite impossible too."
Raskolnikov laughed.
"I'm surprised you even bother about it!"

"But what are you laughing at? Consider—I only struck her twice with a switch, and there weren't even any marks. Don't think me a cynic, please. I'm perfectly aware how vile that was and so on. But I also know for certain that Marfa Petrovna was actually rather pleased by my, shall we say, ardor. The scandal over your sister had been squeezed dry; for three days Marfa Petrovna had been stuck at home with nothing to show off in town. And then those two switches fell from heaven! Her very first act was to order the carriage harnessed! Not to mention the fact that there are cases when women are very, very glad to be insulted, whatever indignation they may show. Everyone is like that, in fact; human beings in general love to be insulted—have you noticed? But it's especially true of women. You might almost say it's their only entertainment."
For a moment Raskolnikov thought of getting up and leaving, ending the conversation. But something—a kind of curiosity, even a certain prudence—held him back.
"You enjoy fighting?" he asked carelessly.

"No, not particularly," Svidrigaïlov answered calmly. "Marfa Petrovna and I hardly ever fought. We lived very harmoniously and she was always pleased with me. I only used the whip twice in all our seven years—not counting a third occasion that was rather ambiguous. The first time was two months after our wedding, right after we arrived in the country, and the last was the one we're discussing. You thought I was some kind of monster, a reactionary, a slave driver? Ha ha! By the way, do you remember, Rodion Romanovitch, how a few years ago, in those days of 'beneficent publicity,' a nobleman—I've forgotten his name—was put to shame everywhere, in all the papers, for thrashing a German woman on the train? Remember? It was around that same time, that very year I think, that the 'disgraceful affair of the Age' took place—you know, 'The Egyptian Nights,' that public reading? The dark eyes! Ah, the golden days of youth, where are they? Well, as for the gentleman who thrashed the German, I feel no sympathy for him—after all, why would I? But I must say that sometimes you encounter such provocative 'Germans' that I doubt any progressive could entirely vouch for himself. No one looked at it from that angle then, but it's the truly humane point of view, I assure you."
After saying this, Svidrigaïlov burst into sudden laughter again. Raskolnikov could see clearly that this was a man with a firm purpose in mind, well able to keep it to himself.
"I take it you haven't talked to anyone for several days?" he asked.
"Hardly anyone. I suppose you're wondering how I can be so adaptable?"
"No, I'm wondering why you're too adaptable."

"Because I'm not offended by the rudeness of your questions? Is that it? But why take offense? You asked, and I answered," he replied with a surprising expression of simplicity. "You know, there's hardly anything that interests me," he went on, as though dreamily, "especially now. I've nothing to do. You're perfectly free to think I'm courting you with an ulterior motive, especially since I told you I want to see your sister about something. But I'll confess frankly—I'm terribly bored. These last three days especially, so I'm delighted to have you. Don't be angry, Rodion Romanovitch, but you seem somehow terribly strange yourself. Say what you like, but there's something wrong with you, and now too—not this very minute, I mean, but in general. Well, well, I won't push it. Don't scowl! I'm not such a boor as you think."
Raskolnikov looked at him gloomily.
"You're perhaps not a boor at all," he said. "In fact, I rather think you're a man of good breeding, or at least know how to behave like one on occasion."

"I'm not particularly interested in anyone's opinion," Svidrigaïlov answered drily, with a shade of haughtiness. "So why not be vulgar when it suits? Vulgarity makes such a convenient disguise in our climate—especially if one has a natural inclination that way," he added, laughing again.
"But I've heard you have plenty of connections here. You're, as they say, 'not without resources.' So what do you want with me, unless you have some special purpose?"

"That's true, I do have friends here," Svidrigaïlov admitted, ignoring the main point. "I've already seen some of them. I've been knocking about for three days and either I've seen them or they've seen me. That's natural enough. I'm well dressed, not considered poor. The emancipation of the serfs didn't affect me—my property consists mainly of forests and water meadows, so the income hasn't dropped. But I'm not going to visit them; I was sick of them long ago.
