I've been here three days without calling on a single one. What a city this is! How did it come into being? A city of officials and students of every stripe. Yes, there's a great deal I didn't notice eight years ago, when I was running wild here. My only hope now is in anatomy, by God!"
"Anatomy?"
"But as for those clubs, the Dussauts, the promenades, so-called progress—well, it can all get along without me," he continued, ignoring the question again. "Besides, who wants to be a cardsharp?"
"You were a cardsharp, then?"

"How could I not be? There was a regular set of us, all men of the best society, eight years ago. We had a fine time. And all men of breeding, you know—poets, men of property. And actually, as a rule in Russian society, the best manners are found among those who've been thrashed. Have you noticed? I've gone downhill in the country. Still, I did land in debtors' prison, thanks to a shady Greek from Nezhin. Then Marfa Petrovna turned up, haggled with him, and bought me out for thirty thousand silver. I owed seventy thousand in all. We were united in lawful matrimony, and she spirited me off to the country like a treasure. She was five years older than me, you know. She was very fond of me. For seven years I never left the estate. And note this: my entire life, she held a document over me—that IOU for thirty thousand—so if I ever stirred up trouble, I'd be trapped immediately. And she would have done it! Women see no contradiction in that sort of thing."
"And if it hadn't been for that, would you have bolted?"

"I don't know what to say. It was hardly the document that held me. I didn't want to go anywhere. Marfa Petrovna herself suggested a trip abroad when she saw I was bored, but I'd been abroad before and it always made me feel wretched. For no reason—you look at the sunrise, the Bay of Naples, the sea, and it makes you sad. What's most revolting is that you're genuinely sad! No, it's better at home. At least here you can blame others for everything and make excuses for yourself. I might have gone on an expedition to the North Pole—j'ai le vin mauvais, I can't stand drinking, and there's nothing left but drink. I've tried it. But tell me—I've heard Berg is going up in a great balloon next Sunday from the Yusupov Garden and will take passengers for a fee. Is it true?"
"Would you go up?"
"I—no, not really," Svidrigaïlov muttered, seeming genuinely lost in thought.
"What does he mean? Is he serious?" Raskolnikov wondered.

"No, the document didn't hold me back," Svidrigaïlov went on reflectively. "It was my own doing, staying put. And nearly a year ago, Marfa Petrovna gave me back the document on my name day and threw in a considerable sum of money besides. She had a fortune, you know. 'See how I trust you, Arkady Ivanovitch'—those were her exact words. You don't believe she actually said that? But, you know, I managed the estate quite decently. They know me in the district. I ordered books, too. Marfa Petrovna approved at first, but then worried I was overstudiying."
"You seem to miss Marfa Petrovna a great deal."
"Miss her? Perhaps. Really, perhaps I do. And by the way, do you believe in ghosts?"
"What ghosts?"
"Ordinary ghosts."
"Do you?"
"Perhaps not, pour vous plaire. I wouldn't say no exactly."
"Do you see them, then?"
Svidrigaïlov looked at him rather oddly.
"Marfa Petrovna is kind enough to visit me," he said, twisting his mouth into a strange smile.
"What do you mean, 'kind enough to visit'?"

"She's come three times. I first saw her on the day of the funeral itself, an hour after the burial. It was the day before I left for here. The second time was the day before yesterday, at dawn, at the Malaya Vishera station, on the journey. The third was two hours ago, in the room where I'm staying. I was alone."
"Were you awake?"
"Fully awake. Wide awake every time. She comes, talks to me for a minute, and goes out the door—always the door. I can almost hear her."
"What made me think something like this must be happening to you?" Raskolnikov said suddenly.
At the same moment he was surprised at having said it. He was greatly agitated.
"Really? You thought that?" Svidrigaïlov asked in astonishment. "Did you really? Didn't I say there was something in common between us?"
"You never said that!" Raskolnikov cried sharply and with heat.
"Didn't I?"
"No!"
"I thought I did. When I came in and saw you lying with your eyes shut, pretending, I said to myself at once: 'Here's the man.'"
"What do you mean, 'the man'? What are you talking about?" Raskolnikov cried.
"What do I mean? I really don't know," Svidrigaïlov muttered artlessly, as though he too were puzzled.
For a minute they were silent, staring at each other.
"That's all nonsense!" Raskolnikov shouted in irritation. "What does she say when she comes to you?"

"She? Would you believe it—she talks about the most trivial things, and it makes me angry. Man is a strange creature. The first time she came—I was tired, you know: the funeral service, the burial, the luncheon afterward; finally I was left alone in my study, I lit a cigar and started thinking—she came in through the door. 'You've been so busy today, Arkady Ivanovitch, you forgot to wind the dining-room clock,' she said. I'd wound that clock every week for seven years, and whenever I forgot, she'd always remind me. The next day I was on my way here. I got out at the station at daybreak after sleeping badly, eyes half open, drinking some coffee—and there was Marfa Petrovna suddenly sitting beside me with a pack of cards. 'Shall I tell your fortune for the journey, Arkady Ivanovitch?' She was a great hand at fortune-telling. I'll never forgive myself for not letting her. I ran off in fright, and besides, the bell rang. Then today, sitting in my room after a miserable dinner from a cook-shop, smoking—suddenly Marfa Petrovna again. She came in all dressed up, in a new green silk dress with a long train. 'Good day, Arkady Ivanovitch! How do you like my dress? Aniska can't make like this.' Aniska was a dressmaker in the country, one of our former serf girls who'd trained in Moscow—a pretty thing. She stood there turning in front of me. I looked at the dress, then looked carefully at her face. 'I wonder you trouble to come to me about such trifles, Marfa Petrovna.' 'Good gracious, you won't let one bother you about anything!' To tease her, I said: 'I want to get married, Marfa Petrovna.' 'That's just like you, Arkady Ivanovitch. It doesn't do you much credit to come looking for a bride when you've barely buried your wife. And if you could make a good choice! But I know it won't be for your happiness or hers—you'll only be a laughingstock to everyone.' Then she went out, and her train seemed to rustle. Isn't that nonsense?"
"But perhaps you're lying?" Raskolnikov put in.
"I rarely lie," Svidrigaïlov answered thoughtfully, apparently not noticing the rudeness of the question.
"And before this—had you ever seen ghosts?"

"Y-yes, once in my life, six years ago. I had a serf named Filka. Just after his burial, I called out, forgetting: 'Filka, my pipe!' He came in and went to the cupboard where my pipes were. I sat still and thought: 'He's doing it out of revenge,' because we'd had a violent quarrel just before his death. 'How dare you come in with a hole in your elbow,' I said. 'Get out, you wretch!' He turned and left, and never came again. I didn't tell Marfa Petrovna at the time. I wanted to have a memorial service said for him, but I was ashamed."
"You should see a doctor."

"I know I'm not well without your telling me, though I don't know exactly what's wrong. I'm probably five times as strong as you. I didn't ask whether you believe ghosts can be seen—I asked whether you believe they exist."
"No, I refuse to believe it!" Raskolnikov cried with genuine anger.

"What do people usually say?" Svidrigaïlov murmured, as though talking to himself, looking aside and tilting his head. "They say: 'You're ill, so what you see is only unreal fantasy.' But that's not strictly logical. I agree that ghosts only appear to the sick, but that only proves they can't appear to anyone but the sick—not that they don't exist."
"Of course they don't!" Raskolnikov insisted irritably.

"No? You don't think so?" Svidrigaïlov went on, looking at him steadily. "But what about this argument—help me with it: ghosts are, as it were, shreds and fragments of other worlds, the beginnings of them. A healthy person naturally has no reason to see them, because he is above all a creature of this earth and must, for the sake of wholeness and order, live only in this life. But the moment one falls ill, the moment the normal earthly order of the organism breaks down, one begins to sense the possibility of another world. And the more seriously ill one becomes, the closer the contact with that other world, so that at the moment of death one steps directly into it. I thought about this a long time ago. If you believe in a future life, you could believe this too."
"I don't believe in a future life," said Raskolnikov.
Svidrigaïlov sat lost in thought.
"And what if there are only spiders there, or something of that sort?" he said suddenly.
"He's a madman," thought Raskolnikov.

"We always imagine eternity as something beyond our comprehension, something vast, enormous! But why must it be vast? What if instead of all that, it's just one little room—like a bathhouse in the country, blackened with soot, with spiders in every corner—and that's all eternity is? I sometimes picture it that way."
"Can you really imagine nothing more just and comforting than that?" Raskolnikov cried, with a feeling of anguish.
"More just? Who knows—perhaps that is just. And you know, it's exactly what I would have made it," Svidrigaïlov answered with a vague smile.
This horrible answer sent a cold shiver through Raskolnikov. Svidrigaïlov raised his head, looked at him, and suddenly burst out laughing.

"Just think!" he cried. "Half an hour ago we'd never laid eyes on each other. We considered ourselves enemies. There's an unsettled matter between us. We've tossed it aside and gone sailing off into abstractions! Wasn't I right when I said we were birds of a feather?"
"Allow me," Raskolnikov went on irritably, "to ask you to explain why you've honored me with your visit—and I'm in a hurry, I have no time to waste. I want to go out."
"By all means. Your sister, Avdotya Romanovna, is going to marry Mr. Luzhin, Pyotr Petrovitch?"
"Can you refrain from any question about my sister, from even mentioning her name? I can't understand how you dare utter her name in my presence, if you really are Svidrigaïlov."
"But I've come here precisely to talk about her. How can I avoid mentioning her?"
"Very well. Speak, but be quick."

"I'm sure you've already formed your own opinion of this Mr. Luzhin, a connection of mine through my wife, if you've spent even half an hour with him or heard any facts about him. He's no match for Avdotya Romanovna. I believe she is sacrificing herself, generously and rashly, for the sake of her family. From everything I'd heard about you, I thought you'd be very glad if the match could be broken off without any loss of practical advantage. Now that I know you personally, I'm convinced of it."
"All this is very naïve—excuse me, I should say impudent—on your part," said Raskolnikov.

"You mean I'm pursuing my own interests. Don't worry, Rodion Romanovitch—if I were acting from self-interest, I wouldn't have spoken so openly. I'm not a complete fool. I'll confess something psychologically curious: just now, defending my love for Avdotya Romanovna, I called myself the victim. Well, let me tell you that I feel no love for her now, not the slightest, so that I'm surprised at myself, because I really did feel something—"
"From idleness and depravity," Raskolnikov put in.
"I'm certainly idle and depraved. But your sister has qualities that even I couldn't help being struck by. But that's all nonsense, as I now see."
"Have you seen that for long?"

"I began to be aware of it some time ago, but became fully certain only the day before yesterday, almost at the moment I arrived in Petersburg. In Moscow, though, I still fancied I was coming to win Avdotya Romanovna's hand and cut out Mr. Luzhin."
"Excuse me for interrupting, but please be brief and come to the point. I'm in a hurry, I want to go out."

"With pleasure. On arriving here and deciding on a certain journey, I'd like to make some necessary preliminary arrangements. I left my children with an aunt; they're well provided for and have no need of me personally. And what kind of father would I make? I took only what Marfa Petrovna gave me a year ago. That's enough for me. Forgive me—I'm getting to the point. Before this journey, which may or may not happen, I want to settle the matter of Mr. Luzhin too. It's not that I especially detest him, but it was through him that I quarreled with Marfa Petrovna when I found out she'd cooked up this marriage. I now want to see Avdotya Romanovna through your mediation, and if you like, in your presence, to explain first that she'll gain nothing but harm from Mr. Luzhin. Then, begging her pardon for all past unpleasantness, to offer her a gift of ten thousand roubles and thus help bring about the break with Mr. Luzhin—a break which I believe she herself would welcome, if she could see a way to it."
"You really are mad!" cried Raskolnikov, more astonished than angry. "How dare you talk like that!"

"I knew you'd protest. But first, though I'm not rich, this ten thousand is entirely free. I have absolutely no need of it. If Avdotya Romanovna won't accept it, I'll waste it on something far more foolish. Second, my conscience is perfectly clear—I make the offer with no hidden motive. You may not believe me, but in time both Avdotya Romanovna and you will understand. The point is that I did cause your sister, whom I deeply respect, some trouble and unhappiness, and so, sincerely regretting it, I want—not to compensate or repay her, but simply to do something for her benefit, to show that I'm not privileged to do nothing but harm. If my offer had even the smallest trace of self-interest, I wouldn't have made it so openly, and I wouldn't be offering only ten thousand when five weeks ago I offered more. Besides, I may very soon marry a young lady, which should dispel any suspicion of designs on Avdotya Romanovna. In conclusion, let me point out that in marrying Mr. Luzhin, she'd be taking money just the same—only from a different man. Don't be angry, Rodion Romanovitch. Think it over calmly."
Svidrigaïlov himself was exceedingly calm and composed as he said all this.
"I beg you to say no more," said Raskolnikov. "In any case, this is unpardonable impudence."

"Not at all. Then a man may do nothing but harm in this world, and is prevented from doing the smallest bit of good by trivial social conventions. That's absurd. If I died and left this sum to your sister in my will, surely she wouldn't refuse it?"
"Very likely she would."
"Oh, come. Well, if you refuse, so be it, though ten thousand roubles can be a very useful thing to have. In any case, I ask you to pass on what I've said to Avdotya Romanovna."
"No, I won't."
"In that case, Rodion Romanovitch, I'll be forced to seek a meeting with her myself, which would mean troubling her."
"And if I do pass it on, will you not try to see her?"
"I really don't know what to say. I would very much like to see her once."
"Don't count on it."
"I'm sorry. But you don't know me. Perhaps we'll become better acquainted."
"You think we might?"

"And why not?" Svidrigaïlov said with a smile. He stood up and took his hat. "I didn't really mean to disturb you, and I came without expecting much, though I was very struck by your face this morning."
"Where did you see me this morning?" Raskolnikov asked uneasily.

"I saw you by chance. I kept thinking there's something about you that's like me. But don't worry—I'm not pushy. I got along well with cardsharps; I never bored Prince Svirbey, a great personage and a distant relative; I could write about Raphael's Madonna in Madame Prilukov's album; I never left Marfa Petrovna's side for seven years; and I used to stay at Viazemsky's house in the Haymarket in the old days. And perhaps I'll go up in the balloon with Berg."
"Very well. Are you setting off on your travels soon, may I ask?"
"What travels?"
"Why, that 'journey' you mentioned."

"A journey? Oh yes, I did mention a journey. Well, that's a broad subject. If only you knew what you're asking," he added, and gave a sudden, short laugh. "Perhaps I'll get married instead of traveling. They're arranging a match for me."
"Here?"
"Yes."
"How have you had time for that?"

"But I'm very anxious for an interview with Avdotya Romanovna. I beg you earnestly. Well, goodbye for now. Oh yes! I nearly forgot something. Tell your sister, Rodion Romanovitch, that Marfa Petrovna remembered her in her will and left her three thousand roubles. That's absolutely certain. She arranged it a week before her death, in my presence. Avdotya Romanovna should be able to collect the money in two or three weeks."
"Are you telling the truth?"
"Yes. Tell her. Well, at your service. I'm staying very close to you."
As he went out, Svidrigaïlov bumped into Razumihin in the doorway.

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 2
paragraphs: It was nearly eight o'clock. The two young men hurried to Bakaleyev's to arrive before Luzhin.
"Who was that?" Razumihin asked as soon as they were in the street.

"It was Svidrigaïlov, that landowner in whose house my sister was insulted when she was their governess. He drove her out through his unwanted attentions—Marfa Petrovna, his wife, was behind it. This same Marfa Petrovna later begged Dounia's forgiveness, and now she's suddenly died. We were talking about her this morning. I don't know why, but I'm afraid of that man. He came here straight after his wife's funeral. He's very strange and is determined to do something. We must protect Dounia from him—that's what I wanted to tell you. Do you hear?"
"Protect her! What can he do to Avdotya Romanovna? Thank you for telling me, Rodya. We will, we'll protect her! Where does he live?"
"I don't know."
"Why didn't you ask? What a pity! I'll find out, though."
"Did you see him?" Raskolnikov asked after a pause.
"Yes, I noticed him. I got a good look."
"You really saw him? Saw him clearly?" Raskolnikov pressed.
"Yes, I remember him perfectly. I'd know him among a thousand. I have a good memory for faces."
They walked in silence for a while.
"Hmm, that's good," Raskolnikov muttered. "Because, you know, I thought—I keep thinking it might have been a hallucination."
"What do you mean? I don't follow."
"Well, you all say," Raskolnikov went on, twisting his lips into a smile, "that I'm mad. It occurred to me just now that perhaps I really am mad and only saw a phantom."
"What are you saying?"
"Who can tell? Maybe I really am mad, and everything that's happened these last few days is just my imagination."
"Oh, Rodya, you've been upset again! But what did he say? Why did he come?"
Raskolnikov didn't answer. Razumihin thought for a moment.

"Now let me tell you my story," he began. "I came to you—you were asleep. Then we had dinner, and I went to Porfiry's. Zametov was still there. I tried to get started but couldn't find the right approach. They don't seem to understand and can't understand, but they're not the least bit embarrassed. I took Porfiry aside by the window and tried to talk, but it was still hopeless. He looked away and I looked away. Finally I shook my fist in his ugly face and told him that as his relative I'd smash his skull. He just stared at me. I cursed and left. That was all. Very stupid. To Zametov I said nothing. But you see, I thought I'd made a mess of it. Then on the way downstairs a brilliant idea hit me: why should we care? If you were in any danger, that would be different. But why should you care a fig? You're not connected to any of it. We'll have a laugh at them later. If I were you, I'd baffle them even more. How ashamed they'll be afterward! Hang them! We can give them a thrashing later, but for now let's just laugh at them!"

"To be sure," Raskolnikov answered. "But what will you say tomorrow?" he thought. Strange to say, until that moment it had never occurred to him to wonder what Razumihin would think when he found out. As the thought struck him, Raskolnikov looked at his friend. Razumihin's account of his visit to Porfiry held very little interest for him now. So much had come and gone since then.

In the corridor they ran into Luzhin. He had arrived punctually at eight and was looking for the room number, so all three went in together without greeting or looking at one another. The young men entered first, while Pyotr Petrovitch, with exaggerated propriety, lingered in the passage removing his coat. Pulcheria Alexandrovna came forward at once to greet him in the doorway. Dounia was welcoming her brother. Pyotr Petrovitch walked in and bowed to the ladies quite amiably, though with heightened dignity. He looked rather put out, however, as though he hadn't yet recovered his composure. Pulcheria Alexandrovna, apparently somewhat embarrassed herself, hurriedly seated everyone around the round table where a samovar was boiling. Dounia and Luzhin sat facing each other across the table. Razumihin and Raskolnikov sat opposite Pulcheria Alexandrovna—Razumihin beside Luzhin, Raskolnikov next to his sister.

A moment's silence followed. Pyotr Petrovitch deliberately drew out a cambric handkerchief reeking of perfume and blew his nose with the air of a benevolent man who has been slighted and is firmly resolved to demand an explanation. In the passage it had occurred to him to keep his coat on and leave, thereby giving the two ladies a sharp and emphatic lesson about the gravity of the situation. But he couldn't bring himself to do it. Besides, he didn't like uncertainty, and he wanted answers. If his request had been so openly defied, something lay behind it, and he'd better find out what. He could always punish them later.
"I trust you had a pleasant journey?" he inquired stiffly of Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Oh yes, Pyotr Petrovitch."
"I'm gratified to hear it. And Avdotya Romanovna is not too fatigued?"
"I'm young and strong—I don't tire easily. But it was a great strain for mother," Dounia answered.

"That's inevitable, I'm afraid. Our national railways are terribly long. 'Mother Russia,' as they say, is a vast country. Despite my desire to do so, I was unable to meet you yesterday. But I trust everything went smoothly?"

"Oh no, Pyotr Petrovitch, it was all terribly distressing," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hastened to declare with a particular emphasis. "And if Dmitri Prokofitch hadn't been sent to us, I truly believe, by God Himself, we would have been utterly lost. Here he is! Dmitri Prokofitch Razumihin," she added, introducing him to Luzhin.
"I had the pleasure yesterday," Pyotr Petrovitch muttered, casting a hostile sidelong glance at Razumihin. Then he scowled and fell silent.

Pyotr Petrovitch belonged to that class of persons who appear very polite in society and make a great point of propriety, but who, the moment they're crossed, lose all composure and become more like sacks of flour than elegant men of the world. Again everyone was silent. Raskolnikov remained stubbornly mute; Avdotya Romanovna was unwilling to break the silence prematurely; Razumihin had nothing to say. So Pulcheria Alexandrovna grew anxious again.
"Marfa Petrovna is dead—have you heard?" she began, resorting to her main topic of conversation.

"To be sure, I heard. I was informed immediately, and in fact I've come to let you know that Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov set out for Petersburg in great haste right after his wife's funeral. So at least I have on excellent authority."
"To Petersburg? Here?" Dounia asked in alarm, glancing at her mother.
"Yes, precisely—and no doubt with some design, considering the haste of his departure and all the circumstances preceding it."
"Good heavens! Won't he leave Dounia in peace even here?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.

"I imagine neither you nor Avdotya Romanovna need be alarmed, unless of course you yourselves wish to have some contact with him. For my part, I'm on my guard, and I'm currently tracking down where he's staying."

"Oh, Pyotr Petrovitch, you can't imagine how frightened I am!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on. "I've only seen him twice, but I thought him dreadful, dreadful! I'm convinced he was the cause of Marfa Petrovna's death."

"It's impossible to be certain about that. I have reliable information. I won't deny that he may have hastened the course of events by the moral influence of his affront, so to speak. But as to the general conduct and moral character of that individual, I share your opinion. I don't know whether he's well off now, or exactly what Marfa Petrovna left him—that I'll learn very shortly. But certainly here in Petersburg, if he has any money at all, he'll immediately lapse into his old ways. He's the most depraved and utterly vicious specimen of that class of men. I have good reason to believe that Marfa Petrovna, who was so unfortunate as to fall in love with him and pay off his debts eight years ago, was of service to him in another way as well. Solely through her efforts and sacrifices, a criminal case involving grotesque and homicidal brutality—for which he might easily have been sent to Siberia—was hushed up. That's the sort of man he is, if you care to know."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Raskolnikov listened attentively.
"Are you speaking the truth? Do you have solid evidence for this?" Dounia asked sternly and pointedly.

"I'm only repeating what Marfa Petrovna told me in confidence. I should note that from a legal standpoint the case was far from clear. There was, and I believe still is, a certain woman living here called Resslich, a foreigner, who lent small sums at interest and had other dealings. Svidrigaïlov had longstanding, close, and mysterious relations with this woman. She had a relative—a niece, I believe—living with her, a deaf-mute girl of fifteen or perhaps younger. Resslich hated this girl and grudged her every crust; she beat her mercilessly. One day the girl was found hanging in the attic. The verdict was suicide. After the usual proceedings, the matter was closed. But later, information surfaced that the child had been cruelly violated by Svidrigaïlov. True, this was not established conclusively. The information came from another German woman of loose character whose testimony was unreliable. No formal statement was made to the police, thanks to Marfa Petrovna's money and efforts. It remained gossip. But the story is very significant. You heard, no doubt, Avdotya Romanovna, when you were with them, the story of the servant Philip, who died of ill treatment six years ago, before the abolition of serfdom."
"I heard, on the contrary, that Philip hanged himself."
"Quite so. But what drove him—or perhaps disposed him—to suicide was the systematic persecution and cruelty of Mr. Svidrigaïlov."

"I don't know that," Dounia answered drily. "I only heard a strange story that Philip was a sort of hypochondriac, a 'domestic philosopher,' as the servants put it, who 'read himself silly,' and that he hanged himself partly because of Mr. Svidrigaïlov's mockery rather than his beatings. When I was there, he treated the servants well, and they were actually fond of him, though they did blame him for Philip's death."

"I see, Avdotya Romanovna, that you seem suddenly disposed to defend him," Luzhin observed, twisting his lips into an ambiguous smile. "No doubt he's an astute man, very insinuating with women—of which Marfa Petrovna, who died so strangely, is a terrible example. My only wish has been to be of service to you and your mother with my advice, given the renewed efforts we may certainly expect from him. For my part, I'm firmly convinced he'll end up in debtors' prison again. Marfa Petrovna had no intention of settling anything substantial on him, having her children's interests in mind, and if she left him anything, it would be the barest minimum—something insignificant and short-lived that wouldn't last a year for a man of his habits."
"Pyotr Petrovitch, I beg you," said Dounia, "say no more about Mr. Svidrigaïlov. It makes me miserable."
"He's just been to see me," Raskolnikov said, breaking his silence for the first time.
There were exclamations from everyone, and all eyes turned to him. Even Pyotr Petrovitch was startled.

"An hour and a half ago he came in while I was asleep, woke me, and introduced himself," Raskolnikov continued. "He was fairly cheerful and at ease, and quite expects us to become friends. He's especially anxious for an interview with you, Dounia, and asked me to help arrange it. He has a proposal for you, and he told me what it is. He also told me that a week before her death, Marfa Petrovna left you three thousand roubles in her will, Dounia, and that you can collect the money very soon."
"Thank God!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna, crossing herself. "Pray for her soul, Dounia!"
"It's a fact!" Luzhin blurted out.
"Tell us—what else?" Dounia urged Raskolnikov.
"Then he said he's not rich, that the estate was left to his children who are now with an aunt, that he's staying somewhere not far from me, but where exactly I don't know—I didn't ask."
"But what does he want to propose to Dounia?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna in fright. "Did he tell you?"
"Yes."
"What was it?"
"I'll tell you later."
Raskolnikov stopped talking and turned to his tea.
Pyotr Petrovitch checked his watch.
"I'm afraid I have a business engagement, so I won't be in your way," he said with a slightly piqued air, and began getting up.
"Don't go, Pyotr Petrovitch," said Dounia. "You intended to spend the evening. Besides, you wrote that you wanted to have an explanation with mother."

"Precisely so, Avdotya Romanovna," Pyotr Petrovitch answered impressively, sitting down again but still holding his hat. "I certainly wished for an explanation with you and your honored mother on a very important point. But since your brother cannot speak openly about certain proposals from Mr. Svidrigaïlov in my presence, I too am unwilling to discuss certain matters of the greatest gravity in the presence of others. Moreover, my most important and earnest request has been disregarded."
Assuming an aggrieved air, Luzhin lapsed into dignified silence.

"Your request that my brother not be present was disregarded solely at my insistence," said Dounia. "You wrote that he had insulted you. I think this must be explained immediately and you two must be reconciled. If Rodya really has insulted you, then he should and will apologize."
Pyotr Petrovitch took a harder line.
"There are insults, Avdotya Romanovna, that no amount of goodwill can make one forget. There is a line in everything that it's dangerous to cross, and once crossed, there's no going back."

"That isn't exactly what I was talking about, Pyotr Petrovitch," Dounia interrupted with some impatience. "Please understand: our entire future depends on whether this can be cleared up and set right as quickly as possible. I'm telling you frankly from the start that I can't see it any other way, and if you have the slightest regard for me, this matter must be settled today, however difficult that may be. I repeat: if my brother is at fault, he will ask your forgiveness."

"I'm surprised you put it like that," Luzhin said, growing more and more irritated. "Esteeming and, so to speak, adoring you, I may very well be unable to tolerate certain members of your family. While I aspire to the happiness of your hand, I cannot accept obligations that are incompatible—"

"Oh, don't be so quick to take offense, Pyotr Petrovitch," Dounia interrupted with feeling, "and be the sensible and generous man I've always considered you. I've given you a great promise—I'm your fiancée. Trust me in this, and believe I can judge impartially. My taking on the role of judge is as much a surprise to my brother as to you. When I insisted that he come to today's meeting after receiving your letter, I told him nothing of my intentions. Understand: if you two can't be reconciled, I must choose between you—it's either you or him. That's how it stands on both sides. I mustn't make the wrong choice, and I mustn't. For your sake I'd have to break with my brother; for my brother's sake, with you. Right now I can find out for certain whether he truly is a brother to me, and I want to know. And about you—whether I'm dear to you, whether you value me, whether you're the right husband for me."

"Avdotya Romanovna," Luzhin declared huffily, "your words carry too much weight—indeed they are offensive, considering the position I have the honor to occupy in relation to you. To say nothing of your strange and insulting comparison, putting me on the same level as an insolent boy, you admit the possibility of breaking your promise. You say 'you or he,' thereby showing how little I mean to you. I cannot let this pass, given the relationship and obligations between us."
"What!" Dounia cried, flushing. "I set your interests beside everything I've held most precious in my life, everything that has been my whole life, and you complain that I make too little of you?"

Raskolnikov smiled sarcastically. Razumihin fidgeted. But Pyotr Petrovitch did not accept the rebuke. On the contrary, with every word he grew more obstinate and irritable, as though he was enjoying it.

"Love for the future partner of your life, for your husband, should outweigh your love for your brother," he pronounced solemnly. "And in any case, I refuse to be placed on the same level. Although I said I wouldn't speak openly in your brother's presence, I now intend to ask your honored mother for a necessary explanation on a point that deeply concerns my dignity. Your son," he turned to Pulcheria Alexandrovna, "yesterday, in the presence of Mr. Razudkin—or, I think that's it? Forgive me, I've forgotten your surname"—he bowed politely to Razumihin—"insulted me by distorting something I said to you in private conversation over coffee: namely, that marriage to a poor girl who has experienced hardship is more advantageous from a conjugal standpoint than to one raised in luxury, because it's better for the moral character. Your son deliberately exaggerated the meaning of my words, made them sound ridiculous, and accused me of malicious intent, relying, as far as I could tell, on your letter to him. I shall be happy, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, if you can convince me I'm mistaken and thereby set my mind at ease. Kindly tell me the exact terms in which you repeated my words in your letter to Rodion Romanovitch."
"I don't remember," Pulcheria Alexandrovna faltered. "I wrote them as I understood them. I don't know how Rodya repeated them to you. Perhaps he exaggerated."
"He could not have exaggerated except at your prompting."
"Pyotr Petrovitch," Pulcheria Alexandrovna declared with dignity, "the proof that Dounia and I didn't take your words badly is the fact that we are here."
"Well said, mother," said Dounia approvingly.
"So it's my fault again," Luzhin said, aggrieved.
"Well, Pyotr Petrovitch, you keep blaming Rodion, but you yourself just wrote something false about him," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added, growing bolder.
"I don't recall writing anything false."

"You wrote," Raskolnikov said sharply, not turning toward Luzhin, "that I gave money yesterday not to the widow of the man who was killed, as was actually the case, but to his daughter—whom I'd never seen before yesterday. You wrote this to create a rift between me and my family, and for that purpose added crude remarks about the character of a girl you don't know. All of that is mean slander."

"Excuse me, sir," Luzhin said, trembling with fury. "I elaborated on your qualities and conduct in my letter solely in response to your sister's and mother's inquiries about how I found you and what impression you made on me. As for what you've referred to, kindly point out one word of falsehood—show me that you didn't throw your money away, or that there aren't worthless people in that family, however unfortunate."
"In my opinion, you with all your virtues aren't worth the little finger of that unfortunate girl you're throwing stones at."
"Would you go so far, then, as to let her associate with your mother and sister?"
"I've already done so, if you care to know. I had her sit down today with mother and Dounia."
"Rodya!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Dounia turned crimson. Razumihin knitted his brows. Luzhin smiled with lofty sarcasm.

"You see for yourself, Avdotya Romanovna," he said, "whether agreement between us is possible. I hope this question is now settled once and for all. I shall withdraw, so as not to intrude on the pleasures of family intimacy and the sharing of secrets." He got up and reached for his hat. "But in withdrawing, I venture to request that in the future I be spared such meetings and, so to speak, compromises. I appeal particularly to you, honored Pulcheria Alexandrovna, especially since my letter was addressed to you and to no one else."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was somewhat offended.

"You seem to think we're completely under your authority, Pyotr Petrovitch. Dounia has told you why your wish was disregarded—her intentions were the best. And the tone of your letter was rather like issuing orders. Are we to treat your every wish as a command? Let me tell you, on the contrary: you should be showing us particular consideration right now, because we've given up everything and come here relying on you, so in a sense we're already in your hands."

"That's not quite fair, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, especially at the present moment, when the news of Marfa Petrovna's bequest has arrived—which seems very timely, judging by the new tone you're taking with me," he added sarcastically.
"Judging from that remark, we may certainly conclude you were counting on our helplessness," Dounia observed icily.

"But I certainly cannot count on it now. And in particular, I wouldn't want to interfere with the discussion of the secret proposals of Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov, which he has entrusted to your brother and which, I gather, hold great—and perhaps very agreeable—interest for you."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Razumihin could no longer sit still.
"Aren't you ashamed now, sister?" Raskolnikov asked.
"I am ashamed, Rodya," said Dounia. "Pyotr Petrovitch, go away," she turned to him, white with anger.

Pyotr Petrovitch had clearly not expected this outcome. He had placed too much faith in himself, in his power, and in the helplessness of his victims. He couldn't believe it, even now. He turned pale, and his lips quivered.
"Avdotya Romanovna, if I walk out that door now, after such a dismissal, then you may be sure I will never come back. Think carefully. My word is final."
"What insolence!" Dounia cried, springing from her seat. "I don't want you to come back!"

"What! So that's how it is!" Luzhin exclaimed, unable to believe in the rupture until the very last moment, completely thrown off his calculations. "So that's how it is! But do you realize, Avdotya Romanovna, that I could protest?"

"What right have you to speak to her like that?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna burst out. "What could you possibly protest? What rights do you have? Am I to give my Dounia to a man like you? Go away, leave us alone! We're to blame for agreeing to a bad arrangement, and I most of all!"
"But you bound yourself, Pulcheria Alexandrovna," Luzhin raged, "by your promise, and now you're going back on it! Besides, I was led into expenses on that account—"
This last complaint was so characteristic of Pyotr Petrovitch that Raskolnikov, pale with anger and the effort of containing it, couldn't help laughing. But Pulcheria Alexandrovna was furious.

"Expenses? What expenses? Are you talking about our trunk? But the conductor carried it free, as a favor to you! Mercy, we bound you? Think about it, Pyotr Petrovitch—it was you who bound us hand and foot, not the other way around!"
"Enough, mother, please!" Avdotya Romanovna implored. "Pyotr Petrovitch, please be so kind as to leave."

"I'm going, but one last word," he said, now entirely unable to control himself. "Your mother seems to have completely forgotten that I resolved to take you, so to speak, after the gossip about your reputation had spread all over the district. In disregarding public opinion for your sake and restoring your reputation, I certainly had a right to expect fitting gratitude, even to look for it. And only now have my eyes been opened! I see that I may indeed have acted very, very recklessly in disregarding the general verdict—"
"Does this man want his head bashed in?" Razumihin cried, jumping up.
"You're a mean and spiteful man!" Dounia cried.
"Not a word! Not a move!" Raskolnikov said, holding Razumihin back. Then he walked right up to Luzhin. "Kindly leave this room," he said quietly and distinctly, "and not another word, or—"

Pyotr Petrovitch stared at him for several seconds, his pale face working with rage. Then he turned and walked out. Rarely has any man left a room carrying such vindictive hatred in his heart as he felt toward Raskolnikov. He blamed him, and him alone, for everything. It's worth noting that even as he went down the stairs, he still imagined his case might not be entirely lost, and that, as far as the ladies were concerned, things might 'very well indeed' be set right again.

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fact was that up to the very last moment he had never expected such an outcome. He had been overbearing to the end, never dreaming that two destitute and defenseless women could escape his control. This conviction was reinforced by his vanity and self-regard—a conceit that bordered on delusion. Pyotr Petrovitch, who had risen from nothing, was morbidly prone to self-admiration, had the highest opinion of his intelligence, and sometimes even gloated over his reflection in the mirror. But what he loved and valued above all was the money he had accumulated through hard work and every means available: that money made him the equal of everyone who had once been his superior.

When he had bitterly reminded Dounia that he'd resolved to take her despite evil rumors, Pyotr Petrovitch had spoken with perfect sincerity and had genuinely felt indignant at such 'black ingratitude.' Yet when he first proposed to Dounia, he was fully aware that the gossip was groundless. The story had been contradicted everywhere by Marfa Petrovna and was by then disbelieved by the whole town, which warmly defended Dounia. He would not have denied knowing all this. Yet he still prized his own magnanimity in raising Dounia to his level and considered it something heroic. In speaking of it to Dounia, he had revealed the secret feeling he nursed and admired, and he could not understand why others failed to admire it too. He had called on Raskolnikov with the feelings of a benefactor about to reap the fruits of his good deeds and hear flattering praise. And as he went downstairs now, he felt himself to be a most undeservedly injured and unappreciated man.

Dounia was simply essential to him; giving her up was unthinkable. For years he had entertained voluptuous dreams of marriage while continuing to save money. He brooded with relish, in deepest secrecy, over the image of a girl—virtuous, poor (she must be poor), very young, very pretty, well-born and well-educated, very timid, one who had suffered greatly and was utterly humbled before him, one who would look up to him her whole life as her savior, worship him, admire him, and him alone. How many scenes, how many romantic episodes he had imagined on this seductive theme, when his day's work was done! And now the dream of so many years was nearly realized. The beauty and education of Avdotya Romanovna had impressed him; her helpless situation was powerfully attractive. He had found even more than he'd dreamed of—here was a girl of pride, character, virtue, education, and breeding superior to his own (he felt that), and this creature would be slavishly grateful for his heroic condescension all her life, humbling herself in the dust before him, while he wielded absolute, boundless power over her! Not long before, after much reflection and hesitation, he had also made an important career change and was now entering a wider sphere of business. With this move, his cherished dreams of climbing into a higher social class seemed about to come true. He was determined to try his luck in Petersburg. He knew that women could accomplish a great deal. The charm of a beautiful, virtuous, educated woman might smooth his path enormously, attracting people, creating an aura around him—and now it was all in ruins! This sudden, terrible rupture struck like a thunderbolt; it was like a grotesque joke, an absurdity. He had only been the tiniest bit imperious, hadn't even had time to speak his mind, had merely made a joke, gotten carried away—and it had ended so disastrously. And, of course, he did love Dounia in his way; he already possessed her in his dreams—and all at once! No! The very next day it must all be put right, smoothed over, settled. Above all, that conceited puppy who had caused it all must be crushed. With a sick feeling he also recalled Razumihin, but quickly reassured himself on that score: as though a fellow like that could be compared to him! The one he truly feared was Svidrigaïlov. In short, he had a great deal to attend to.

"No, I'm the most to blame!" said Dounia, kissing and embracing her mother. "I was tempted by his money, but on my honor, brother, I had no idea he was such a despicable man. If I'd seen through him sooner, nothing would have tempted me! Don't blame me, brother!"
"God has delivered us! God has delivered us!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna murmured, half-consciously, as though not fully grasping what had happened.

They were all relieved, and within five minutes they were laughing. Only now and then Dounia went pale and frowned, remembering what had passed. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised to find she was relieved too; only that morning, a break with Luzhin had seemed like a catastrophe. Razumihin was overjoyed. He didn't yet dare express his happiness fully, but he was trembling with excitement, as though a tremendous weight had been lifted from his chest. Now he had the right to devote his life to them, to serve them. Anything might happen now! But he was afraid to think about further possibilities and didn't dare let his imagination run. Raskolnikov, however, sat in the same spot, almost sullen and indifferent. Though he had been the most insistent about getting rid of Luzhin, he now seemed the least affected by what had happened. Dounia couldn't help thinking he was still angry with her, and Pulcheria Alexandrovna watched him anxiously.
"What did Svidrigaïlov say to you?" Dounia asked, coming up to him.
"Yes, yes!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Raskolnikov raised his head.
"He wants to give you ten thousand roubles, and he wishes to see you once, in my presence."
"See her! Out of the question!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. "And how dare he offer her money!"
Raskolnikov then repeated—rather drily—his conversation with Svidrigaïlov, leaving out the account of Marfa Petrovna's ghostly visits, not wanting unnecessary digressions.
"What answer did you give him?" Dounia asked.

"At first I said I wouldn't bring you any message. Then he said he'd do his best to see you on his own, without my help. He assured me his passion for you was a passing fancy and that he no longer has any feelings for you. He doesn't want you to marry Luzhin. His talk was rather muddled on the whole."
"How do you explain him, Rodya? What was your impression?"

"I must confess I don't quite understand him. He offers you ten thousand but says he's not well off. He says he's going away, and ten minutes later forgets he said it. Then he says he's about to get married and already has a bride picked out. He certainly has a motive, probably a bad one. But it's strange how clumsy he is about it, if he really has designs on you. Of course, I refused the money on your behalf, once and for all. Altogether I found him very strange. One might almost think he's mad. But I could be wrong—it might just be a role he's playing. The death of Marfa Petrovna seems to have shaken him deeply."

"God rest her soul," Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed. "I shall always pray for her! Where would we be now, Dounia, without these three thousand? It's as though it fell from heaven! Why, Rodya, this morning we had only three roubles left, and Dounia and I were planning to pawn her watch just to avoid borrowing from that man until he offered help."
Dounia seemed strangely struck by Svidrigaïlov's offer. She stood deep in thought.
"He has some terrible plan," she said in a half-whisper, almost to herself, nearly shuddering.
Raskolnikov noticed her disproportionate alarm.
"I think I'll have to see him again more than once," he said to Dounia.

"We'll keep watch! I'll track him down!" Razumihin cried energetically. "I won't let him out of my sight. Rodya gave me permission himself. He said to me just now: 'Take care of my sister.' Will you give me permission too, Avdotya Romanovna?"
Dounia smiled and held out her hand, but the anxious look didn't leave her face. Pulcheria Alexandrovna watched her timidly, though the three thousand roubles had clearly had a soothing effect.
A quarter of an hour later, they were all engrossed in lively conversation. Even Raskolnikov listened for a while, though he didn't speak. Razumihin held the floor.

"And why, why should you leave?" he rattled on ecstatically. "What would you do in a small town? The important thing is that you're all together and you need each other—you do need each other, believe me! For a while at least. Take me as a partner, and I promise we'll start a wonderful business. I'll explain the whole project in detail—it all came to me this morning, before anything happened. Here's the thing: I have an uncle—I must introduce you to him, a most obliging and respectable old fellow. This uncle has a capital of a thousand roubles, and he lives on his pension and doesn't need the money. For two years he's been pestering me to borrow it from him at six percent interest. I know what that means—he simply wants to help me. Last year I didn't need it, but this year I decided to borrow it as soon as he arrived. You lend me another thousand from your three, and we have enough for a start. So we'll go into partnership—and what are we going to do?"

Then Razumihin laid out his plan. He explained at length that nearly all our publishers and booksellers have no idea what they're selling, which is why they make poor publishers, and that any decent publication generally pays well and sometimes yields a considerable profit. Publishing was what Razumihin had been dreaming of. He'd spent two years working in publishing offices and knew three European languages well, though he'd told Raskolnikov six days earlier that he was 'hopeless' in German—that had been a ploy to get him to take on half a translation and half the payment. He'd been lying, and Raskolnikov knew it.

"Why should we let this chance slip when we have the most important thing—our own capital?" Razumihin cried enthusiastically. "Of course there'll be a lot of work, but we'll work. You, Avdotya Romanovna, Rodion, and I. Some books make excellent profit these days! And the main advantage is that we'll know exactly what needs translating. We'll translate, publish, and learn all at the same time. I can help because I have experience. For nearly two years I've been running around publishers' offices and I know every detail of the trade. You don't have to be a saint to make pots, believe me! And why should we pass up this chance? I know of two or three books where just the idea of translating them is worth a hundred roubles. And I wouldn't take five hundred for the concept of one of them. Yet if I told a publisher, I'm sure he'd hesitate—they're such blockheads! As for the business side—printing, paper, sales—leave that to me. I know my way around. We'll start small and go big. At the very least we'll earn a living and get our investment back."
Dounia's eyes were shining.
"I like what you're saying, Dmitri Prokofitch!" she said.

"I know nothing about it, of course," Pulcheria Alexandrovna put in. "It may be a good idea, but then again, God knows. It's new and untried. Of course, we must stay here at least for a while." She looked at Rodya.
"What do you think, brother?" said Dounia.

"I think it's a very good idea," he answered. "It's too early to dream of a publishing firm, of course, but we could certainly bring out five or six books and be sure of success. I know of one myself that would do well. And as for his being able to manage it, there's no doubt. He knows the business. But we can discuss that later."

"Hurrah!" cried Razumihin. "Now, wait—there's an apartment here in this very building, same landlord. It's separate, doesn't connect with these rooms, it's furnished, and the rent is reasonable—three rooms. Take it for now! I'll pawn the watch tomorrow and bring you the money, and everything can be arranged. You can all live together, with Rodya nearby. But where are you off to, Rodya?"
"What, Rodya, you're leaving already?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked in dismay.
"At a moment like this?" Razumihin cried.
Dounia looked at her brother with incredulous astonishment. He held his cap in his hand, preparing to go.

"Anyone would think you were burying me or saying goodbye forever," he said somewhat oddly. He tried to smile, but it didn't quite come off. "But who knows, perhaps it really is the last time we'll see each other," he let slip accidentally. He had been thinking it, and it simply came out.
"What's wrong with you?" his mother cried.
"Where are you going, Rodya?" Dounia asked strangely.
"I'm obliged to," he answered vaguely, as though hesitating over what to say. But there was a look of sharp determination in his white face.

"I was going to say—on my way here—I meant to tell you, mother, and you, Dounia, that it would be better for us to part for a while. I feel unwell, I'm not at peace. I'll come later—I'll come on my own, when I can. I think of you and I love you. Leave me alone. I decided this before—I'm absolutely resolved on it. Whatever happens to me, whether I'm destroyed or not, I want to be alone. Forget me completely. It's better. Don't ask about me. When I can, I'll come or send for you. Maybe it will all work out. But for now, if you love me, let me go—otherwise I'll start to hate you, I can feel it. Goodbye!"
"Good God!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Both his mother and sister were terribly alarmed. So was Razumihin.
"Rodya, Rodya, make peace with us! Let's be as we were!" his poor mother begged.
He turned slowly to the door and walked out of the room. Dounia caught up with him.
"Brother, what are you doing to mother?" she whispered, her eyes blazing with indignation.
He looked at her dully.
"It doesn't matter—I'll come back. I'm coming," he muttered in an undertone, as though not fully conscious of what he was saying, and went out.
"Heartless, selfish egoist!" Dounia cried.

"He isn't heartless—he's insane! Can't you see? It's you who are heartless, saying that!" Razumihin whispered hotly in her ear, gripping her hand. "I'll be right back!" he shouted to the horror-stricken mother, and ran out.
Raskolnikov was waiting for him at the end of the corridor.
"I knew you'd come after me," he said. "Go back to them—be with them. Be with them tomorrow and always. I—perhaps I'll come, if I can. Goodbye."
And without offering his hand, he walked away.
"But where are you going? What's happening to you? What's wrong? How can you behave like this?" Razumihin muttered, completely at a loss.
Raskolnikov stopped once more.
"Once and for all—never ask me about anything. I have nothing to tell you. Don't come to see me. Maybe I'll come here. Leave me alone, but don't leave them. Do you understand?"

It was dark in the corridor. They stood near a lamp. For a minute they looked at each other in silence. Razumihin remembered that minute for the rest of his life. Raskolnikov's burning, intent eyes grew more penetrating with every second, piercing into his soul, into his consciousness. Suddenly Razumihin started. Something strange passed between them. Some idea, some hint slipped through—something terrible, hideous, and suddenly understood by both. Razumihin went white as a sheet.
"Do you understand now?" Raskolnikov said, his face twitching. "Go back, go to them," he added suddenly, and turning quickly, he walked out of the house.

I shall not try to describe how Razumihin returned to the ladies, how he soothed them, how he insisted that Rodya needed rest during his illness, that Rodya would certainly come back, that he'd come every day, that he was very much upset and mustn't be irritated, that he, Razumihin, would watch over him, find him a doctor—the best doctor—arrange a consultation. In short, from that evening on, Razumihin took his place with them as a son and a brother.

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Raskolnikov went straight to the house on the canal embankment where Sonia lived. It was an old green building of three storeys. He found the porter and obtained vague directions to the rooms of Kapernaumov, the tailor. Having found the entrance to a dark and narrow staircase in a corner of the courtyard, he climbed to the second floor and came out into a gallery that ran around the whole storey over the yard. While he wandered in the darkness, uncertain where to turn for Kapernaumov's door, a door opened three paces away. He mechanically took hold of it.
"Who's there?" a woman's voice asked uneasily.
"It's me—I've come to see you," Raskolnikov answered, and walked into the tiny entrance hall.
On a broken chair stood a candle in a battered copper candlestick.
"It's you! Good heavens!" Sonia cried weakly, and stood rooted to the spot.
"Which is your room? This way?" And Raskolnikov, trying not to look at her, hurried past.

A minute later Sonia came in with the candle, set down the candlestick, and stood before him, completely flustered, beside herself with agitation and apparently frightened by his unexpected visit. Color rushed to her pale face and tears came into her eyes. She felt sick and ashamed—and happy, too. Raskolnikov turned away quickly and sat on a chair by the table. He took in the room at a glance.

It was a large but extremely low-ceilinged room, the only one rented from the Kapernaumovs, whose rooms lay through a closed door in the left wall. On the opposite side, on the right wall, was another door, always locked, leading to the next apartment—a separate lodging. Sonia's room looked like a shed. It was an irregular quadrangle, and this gave it a grotesque appearance. A wall with three windows looking onto the canal ran at an angle, so that one corner was very acute and hard to see into without bright light. The other corner was disproportionately obtuse. There was almost no furniture in the big room: in the right-hand corner stood a bed, with a chair beside it nearest the door. A plain wooden table covered with a blue cloth stood against the same wall, near the door to the other apartment. Two rush-bottomed chairs stood by the table. Against the opposite wall, near the acute corner, was a small plain wooden chest of drawers, looking lost in the emptiness. The yellow, scratched, shabby wallpaper was black in the corners. It must have been damp and full of fumes in winter. Everything spoke of poverty; even the bed had no curtain.

Sonia looked silently at her visitor, who was scrutinizing her room so attentively and unceremoniously, and at last she began to tremble with terror, as though she stood before her judge and the arbiter of her fate.
"I'm late. It's eleven, isn't it?" he asked, still not raising his eyes.
"Yes," Sonia murmured. "Oh, yes it is," she added hastily, as though that offered a way out. "My landlady's clock has just struck—I heard it myself."
"I've come to you for the last time," Raskolnikov went on gloomily, though this was in fact his first visit. "I may not see you again."
"Are you—going away?"
"I don't know. Tomorrow."
"Then you won't come to Katerina Ivanovna's tomorrow?" Sonia's voice shook.
"I don't know. I'll know by morning. Never mind that—I came to say one thing."
He raised his brooding eyes to her and suddenly noticed that he was sitting while she had been standing before him the whole time.
"Why are you standing? Sit down," he said in a changed voice, gentle and friendly.
She sat down. He looked at her kindly, almost with compassion.
"How thin you are! What a hand! Completely transparent, like a dead hand."
He took her hand. Sonia smiled faintly.
"I've always been like this," she said.
"Even when you lived at home?"
"Yes."
"Of course you were," he added abruptly, and the expression of his face and the sound of his voice changed again suddenly.
He looked around the room once more.
"You rent this room from the Kapernaumovs?"
"Yes."
"They live there, through that door?"
"Yes. They have another room like this one."
"All in one room?"
"Yes."
"I'd be afraid in your room at night," he observed darkly.
"They're very good people, very kind," Sonia answered, still seeming dazed, "and all the furniture—everything—is theirs. They're very kind, and the children often come to see me too."
"They all stammer, don't they?"

"Yes. He stammers and he's lame. His wife too—well, not exactly stammers, but she can't speak clearly. She's a very kind woman. He used to be a house serf. And there are seven children—only the eldest stammers; the others are just sickly—they don't stammer. But how did you hear about them?" she added with some surprise.
"Your father told me everything. He told me all about you—how you went out at six and came back at nine, and how Katerina Ivanovna knelt by your bed."
Sonia was embarrassed.
"I thought I saw him today," she whispered hesitantly.
"Whom?"
"Father. I was walking in the street, near the corner, about ten o'clock. He seemed to be walking ahead of me. It looked exactly like him. I wanted to go to Katerina Ivanovna."
"You were out walking in the streets?"
"Yes," Sonia whispered abruptly, again overcome with confusion and looking down.
"Katerina Ivanovna used to beat you, I suppose?"
"Oh no, what are you saying! No!" Sonia looked at him almost with dismay.
"You love her, then?"

"Love her? Of course!" Sonia said with plaintive emphasis, clasping her hands in distress. "Oh, you don't—if you only knew! You see, she's like a child. Her mind has come unhinged, from grief. But how clever she used to be! How generous! How kind! You don't understand—you don't understand!"

Sonia said this in something like despair, wringing her hands in anguish. Her pale cheeks flushed, her eyes held a look of pain. She was clearly stirred to the depths, longing to speak, to advocate, to express something. A kind of insatiable compassion showed in every feature of her face.

"Beat me! How can you say that? Good heavens, beat me! And even if she did—what of it? You know nothing about it. She's so unhappy—oh, so unhappy! And sick. She demands justice; she's pure. She has such faith that there must be justice everywhere, and she expects it. If you tortured her, she wouldn't do wrong. She can't see that it's impossible for people to be perfectly just, and she's angry about it. Like a child! She's good!"
"And what will become of you?"
Sonia looked at him inquiringly.
"They're all on your shoulders, you know. They were before, too. Your father came to you begging for drink money. Well, what happens now?"
"I don't know," Sonia said mournfully.
"Will they stay where they are?"
"I don't know. They're behind on the rent, and the landlady apparently said today that she wants them out. Katerina Ivanovna says she won't stay another minute."
"Where does she get her nerve? She's counting on you?"

"Oh, no, don't talk that way. We're one family; we live as one." Sonia was agitated again, even angry, like a small bird ruffling its feathers. "And what could she do? What could she do?" she went on, growing heated and excited. "How she cried today! Her mind is unhinged—haven't you noticed? One minute she's fussing like a child, making sure everything will be perfect tomorrow for the lunch. The next she's wringing her hands, spitting blood, weeping; then suddenly she starts banging her head against the wall in despair. Then she's comforted again. She's pinning all her hopes on you; she says you'll help her now, and that she'll borrow some money and go back to her hometown with me and open a boarding school for gentlemen's daughters, with me to run it, and we'll start a wonderful new life. She kisses me and hugs me and comforts me—and she has such faith, such faith in these fantasies! You can't contradict her. All day she's been washing, cleaning, mending. She dragged the washtub into the room with her feeble hands and sank onto the bed gasping. We went to the shops this morning to buy shoes for Polenka and Lida—their old ones are worn to nothing. But the money we'd reckoned wasn't enough, not nearly enough. She picked out such dear little boots—she has good taste, you know. And right there in the shop she burst into tears in front of the shopkeepers because she didn't have enough. It was heartbreaking to watch."
"Well, after that I can understand how you live," Raskolnikov said with a bitter smile.

"And don't you feel sorry for them? Don't you?" Sonia flew at him. "I know you gave your last penny, though you hadn't even seen them. If you'd seen everything—oh God! And how many times, how many times I've brought her to tears! Just last week—yes! Only a week before he died. I was cruel! And how often I've done it! I've been wretched thinking about it all day!"
Sonia wrung her hands as she spoke, in the pain of remembering.
"You were cruel?"

"Yes—I! I went to see them," she continued, weeping, "and father said, 'Read to me, Sonia, my head aches—read me something. Here's a book.' He had a book from Andrey Semyonovich Lebeziatnikov, who lives there—he always gets hold of such odd books. And I said, 'I can't stay.' I'd really come to show Katerina Ivanovna some collars. Lizaveta, the peddler, had sold me some collars and cuffs cheap—pretty, new, embroidered ones. Katerina Ivanovna liked them very much. She put them on, looked at herself in the mirror, and was delighted. 'Give them to me, Sonia,' she said, 'please!' She wanted them so much. When would she ever wear them? They just reminded her of her old happy days. She admired herself in the mirror—she has no decent clothes at all, hasn't had for years! And she never asks anyone for anything—she's too proud, she'd sooner give everything away. But these she asked for—she loved them so much. And I didn't want to give them. 'What use are they to you, Katerina Ivanovna?' I said. I actually said that to her! I shouldn't have. She gave me such a look. She was so hurt—so hurt by my refusal. It was painful to see. And she wasn't hurt about the collars, but because I refused. I could see that. If only I could take it all back, change those words! Oh, if I—but none of that matters to you."
"Did you know Lizaveta, the peddler?"
"Yes. Did you?" Sonia asked in some surprise.
"Katerina Ivanovna is consumptive, advanced consumption. She'll die soon," Raskolnikov said after a pause, without answering her question.
"Oh no, no, no!"
And Sonia unconsciously clutched both his hands, as though begging that she should not die.
"But it will be better if she does."
"No, not better! Not at all better!" Sonia echoed in dismay.
"And the children? What can you do then, except take them in yourself?"
"Oh, I don't know!" Sonia cried, almost in despair, putting her hands to her head.
The thought had clearly crossed her mind many times before; he had only stirred it up again.
"And what if even now, while Katerina Ivanovna is still alive, you fall ill and are taken to the hospital—what then?" he pressed, without mercy.
"How can you! That can't happen!"
Sonia's face twisted with terrible fear.

"Can't happen?" Raskolnikov went on with a harsh smile. "You're not insured against it, are you? And then what happens to them? They'll be on the streets, all of them. She'll cough and beg and bang her head against a wall, the way she did today, and the children will cry. She'll collapse, be taken to the police station, then to the hospital—she'll die—and the children—"
"Oh no! God will not let it happen!" burst at last from Sonia's overburdened heart.
She listened, gazing at him imploringly, hands clasped in mute entreaty, as though it all depended on him.
Raskolnikov got up and began pacing the room. A minute passed. Sonia stood with her arms hanging, her head bowed in terrible dejection.
"Can't you save anything? Put something aside for a rainy day?" he asked, stopping suddenly before her.
"No," Sonia whispered.
"Of course not. Have you tried?" he added, almost ironically.
"Yes."
"And it didn't work! Of course not! No need to ask."
He resumed pacing. Another minute passed.
"You don't earn money every day?"
Sonia was more flustered than ever, and color rushed to her face.
"No," she whispered with painful effort.
"It'll be the same with Polenka, no doubt," he said suddenly.
"No! No! It can't be! No!" Sonia cried aloud in desperation, as though she'd been stabbed. "God wouldn't allow anything so terrible!"
"He allows it to happen to others."
"No, no! God will protect her! God!" she repeated, beside herself.
"But perhaps there is no God at all," Raskolnikov answered with a kind of malicious pleasure, laughing as he looked at her.
Sonia's face changed suddenly. A tremor passed over it. She looked at him with unutterable reproach, tried to speak, but couldn't, and broke into bitter, bitter sobbing, hiding her face in her hands.
"You say Katerina Ivanovna's mind is unhinged. Your own mind is unhinged," he said after a short silence.

Five minutes passed. He paced up and down without looking at her. At last he went to her. His eyes glittered. He placed both hands on her shoulders and looked straight into her tearful face. His eyes were hard, feverish, piercing; his lips twitched. Suddenly he dropped to his knees and kissed her foot. Sonia shrank back from him as from a madman. And indeed he looked like one.
"What are you doing?" she whispered, turning pale, and a sudden anguish gripped her heart.
He stood up at once.

"I wasn't bowing to you—I was bowing to all human suffering," he said wildly, and walked to the window. "Listen," he added, turning to her a minute later. "I told a certain insolent man just now that he wasn't worth your little finger—and that I did my sister honor by having her sit beside you."
"Oh, you said that to them! And in front of her?" Sonia cried, frightened. "Sit beside me! An honor! But I'm—dishonorable! Oh, why did you say that?"

"It wasn't because of your dishonor and your sin that I said it, but because of your great suffering. But you are a great sinner, that's true," he added, almost solemnly, "and your worst sin is that you've destroyed and betrayed yourself for nothing. Isn't that terrible? Isn't it terrible that you live in this filth you loathe so, while knowing all along—you need only open your eyes—that you're not helping anyone, not saving anyone from anything? Tell me," he demanded, almost in a frenzy, "how this shame and degradation can exist in you side by side with other, opposite, holy feelings? It would be better, a thousand times better and wiser, to throw yourself into the water and end it all!"
"But what would become of them?" Sonia asked faintly, gazing at him with anguished eyes—but apparently not at all surprised by his suggestion.

Raskolnikov looked at her strangely. He read it all in her face: she had already had that thought, perhaps many times, and in earnest, had considered in her despair how to end it all—so earnestly that now she barely wondered at his words. She hadn't even noticed the cruelty in them. The significance of his reproaches and his peculiar attitude toward her shame she obviously hadn't grasped either—that too was clear to him. But he could see how monstrously the thought of her disgraceful, shameful position had been tormenting her, and for a long time. "What," he thought, "what could have stopped her from putting an end to it?" Only then did he fully realize what those poor little orphans and that pathetic, half-crazed Katerina Ivanovna, banging her head against the wall in her consumption, meant for Sonia.

Nevertheless, it was equally clear that with her character and the education she had somehow received, she could not possibly remain as she was. The question still confronted him: how could she have endured this position for so long without going out of her mind, since she couldn't bring herself to jump into the water? He knew, of course, that Sonia's case was exceptional—though unhappily not unique or even infrequent—but that very uniqueness, her trace of education, her previous life, might have been expected to destroy her at the first step on that revolting path. What sustained her? Surely not depravity. All that degradation had obviously only touched her mechanically; not a drop of true corruption had seeped into her heart. He could see that. He saw through her as she stood before him.
"Three paths lie before her," he thought: "the canal, the madhouse, or finally sinking into the kind of depravity that numbs the mind and turns the heart to stone."
The last seemed most likely to him. But he was a skeptic, he was young, abstract, and therefore cruel, and so he couldn't help believing the final outcome was the most probable.

"But can that really be true?" he exclaimed to himself. "Can this creature, who still preserves the purity of her spirit, be consciously dragged at last into that sink of filth and vice? Has the process already begun? Can it be that she's only endured it so far because vice has begun to seem less loathsome? No, no—that can't be!" he cried, as Sonia had done before. "No, what's kept her from the canal is the idea of sin—and them, the children. And if she hasn't gone out of her mind—but who says she hasn't? Is she in her senses? Can one talk and reason as she does? Can she sit on the edge of the abyss into which she's sliding and refuse to listen when told of the danger? Is she waiting for a miracle? No doubt she is. And isn't that itself a kind of madness?"
He clung stubbornly to that thought. Indeed, he preferred that explanation to any other. He began watching her more intently.
"So you pray to God a great deal, Sonia?" he asked.
Sonia was silent. He stood beside her, waiting for an answer.
"What would I be without God?" she whispered rapidly, forcibly, glancing at him with suddenly blazing eyes and squeezing his hand.
"Ah, so that's how it is!" he thought.
"And what does God do for you?" he asked, probing further.
Sonia was silent for a long time, as though she couldn't answer. Her thin chest heaved with emotion.
"Be quiet! Don't ask! You don't deserve to know!" she cried suddenly, looking at him sternly and wrathfully.
"That's it, that's it," he repeated to himself.
"He does everything," she whispered quickly, looking down again.

"So that's the way out! That's the explanation," he decided, scrutinizing her with eager curiosity and a new, strange, almost morbid feeling. He studied that pale, thin, irregular, angular little face, those soft blue eyes that could flash with such fire, such stern energy, that small body still trembling with indignation and anger—and it all seemed to him more and more strange, almost impossible. "She's a religious fanatic!" he repeated to himself.

There was a book lying on the chest of drawers. He had noticed it each time he paced the room. Now he picked it up and examined it. It was the New Testament, in Russian, bound in leather, old and worn.
"Where did you get this?" he called across the room.
She still stood in the same place, three steps from the table.
"It was brought to me," she answered, reluctantly, without looking at him.
"Who brought it?"
"Lizaveta. I asked her for it."
"Lizaveta! How strange!" he thought.
Everything about Sonia seemed stranger and more extraordinary to him with every passing moment. He carried the book to the candle and began turning the pages.
"Where is the story of Lazarus?" he asked suddenly.
Sonia stared stubbornly at the floor, not answering. She was standing sideways to the table.
"Where is the raising of Lazarus? Find it for me, Sonia."
She stole a glance at him.
"You're not looking in the right place. It's in the fourth gospel," she whispered sternly, without looking at him.
"Find it and read it to me," he said. He sat down with his elbow on the table, leaned his head on his hand, and looked away, bracing himself to listen.
"In three weeks they'll welcome me in the madhouse! I'll probably be there, if I'm not somewhere worse," he muttered to himself.
Sonia approached the table hesitantly, not quite trusting his request. She picked up the book, however.
"Haven't you read it?" she asked, looking across the table at him.
Her voice was growing sterner.
"Long ago. When I was at school. Read!"
"And haven't you heard it in church?"
"I—no. Do you go often?"
"N-no," Sonia whispered.
Raskolnikov smiled.
"I see. And you won't go to your father's funeral tomorrow?"
"Yes, I will. I was at church last week too—I had a requiem service."
"For whom?"
"For Lizaveta. She was killed with an axe."
His nerves tightened further. His head began to spin.
"Were you friends with Lizaveta?"
"Yes. She was good. She used to come—not often—she couldn't. We read together and talked. She will see God."
These last words sounded strange to his ears. And here was something new: the mysterious meetings with Lizaveta, and both of them—religious maniacs.
"I'll become one myself soon! It's contagious!"
"Read!" he cried irritably and insistently.
Sonia still hesitated. Her heart was pounding. She hardly dared read to him. He looked at the "poor lunatic" almost with exasperation.
"Why? You don't believe?" she whispered softly, almost breathlessly.
"Read! I want you to," he insisted. "You used to read to Lizaveta."
Sonia opened the book and found the place. Her hands were shaking; her voice failed her. Twice she tried to begin and couldn't get out the first syllable.
"Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany—" she forced herself to read at last, but on the third word her voice broke like an overstrained string. Her breath caught.

Raskolnikov understood in part why Sonia could not bring herself to read to him, and the more he understood, the more roughly and insistently he demanded it. He understood all too well how painful it was for her to expose and reveal what was her own. He understood that these feelings were truly her secret treasure, perhaps kept for years, perhaps from childhood, while she lived with an unhappy father and a grief-maddened stepmother amid starving children and ugly abuse and reproaches. But at the same time he now knew—knew for certain—that although it filled her with dread and suffering, she had a tormenting desire to read, to read to him, now, whatever might come of it. He read this in her eyes, could see it in her intense emotion. She mastered herself, controlled the spasm in her throat, and continued reading the eleventh chapter of St. John. She reached the nineteenth verse:
