"And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother."
"Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met Him: but Mary sat still in the house."
"Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if Thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
"But I know, that even now, whatsoever Thou wilt ask of God, God will give it Thee."
She stopped again, shamefacedly aware that her voice would quiver and break.
"Jesus said unto her, Thy brother shall rise again."
"Martha saith unto Him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day."
"Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in Me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."
"And whosoever liveth and believeth in Me shall never die. Believest thou this?"
"She saith unto Him,"
(Drawing a painful breath, Sonia read distinctly and forcefully, as though making a public confession of faith:)
"Yea, Lord: I believe that Thou art the Christ, the Son of God, Which should come into the world."
She paused, glanced up at him quickly, but controlled herself and went on reading. Raskolnikov sat without moving, elbows on the table, eyes turned away. She read to the thirty-second verse.
"Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw Him, she fell down at His feet, saying unto Him, Lord, if Thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
"When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, He groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,"
"And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto Him, Lord, come and see."
"Jesus wept."
"Then said the Jews, Behold how He loved him!"
"And some of them said, Could not this Man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?"

Raskolnikov turned and looked at her with emotion. Yes, he had known it! She was trembling in a real physical fever. He had expected it. She was approaching the story of the greatest miracle, and a feeling of immense triumph was overtaking her. Her voice rang like a bell; triumph and joy gave it power. The lines danced before her eyes, but she knew the words by heart. At the last verse—"Could not this Man, which opened the eyes of the blind..."—she dropped her voice and passionately reproduced the doubt, the reproach and censure of the blind, disbelieving Jews, who in another moment would fall at His feet as though struck by thunder, sobbing and believing. "And he—he too is blinded and unbelieving; he too will hear, he too will believe—yes, yes! Now, this very moment!" she dreamed, trembling with joyful anticipation.
"Jesus therefore again groaning in Himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it."
"Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto Him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days."
She emphasized the word four.
"Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?"
"Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up His eyes, and said, Father, I thank Thee that Thou hast heard Me."
"And I knew that Thou hearest Me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that Thou hast sent Me."
"And when He thus had spoken, He cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth."
"And he that was dead came forth."
(She read loudly, cold and trembling with ecstasy, as though she were seeing it before her eyes.)
"Bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."
"Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on Him."
She could read no more. She closed the book and rose quickly from her chair.

"That is all about the raising of Lazarus," she whispered severely and abruptly, and stood motionless, turned away, not daring to raise her eyes to him. She still trembled feverishly. The candle stub flickered in its battered candlestick, dimly lighting the poverty-stricken room where the murderer and the harlot had so strangely come together over the eternal book. Five minutes or more passed.

"I came to talk about something," Raskolnikov said aloud, frowning. He got up and went to Sonia. She raised her eyes to him in silence. His face was particularly stern and held a kind of savage determination.
"I've abandoned my family today," he said, "my mother and sister. I'm not going to see them. I've broken with them completely."
"Why?" Sonia asked, amazed. Her recent meeting with his mother and sister had left a deep impression she could not analyze. She received his news almost with horror.
"I have only you now," he added. "Let us go together. I've come to you. We are both cursed—let us go together!"
His eyes glittered "as though he were mad," Sonia thought.
"Go where?" she asked in alarm, involuntarily stepping back.
"How should I know? I only know it's the same road. I know that for certain, and nothing more. The same goal!"
She looked at him and understood nothing. She knew only that he was terribly, infinitely unhappy.
"None of them will understand if you tell them, but I have understood. I need you—that's why I've come to you."
"I don't understand," Sonia whispered.

"You'll understand later. Haven't you done the same? You too have transgressed—you had the strength to transgress. You took your own life, you destroyed a life—your own. It's all the same! You might have lived in spirit and reason, but you'll end up in the Haymarket. But you won't be able to bear it, and if you stay alone you'll go mad, like me. You're already like a mad creature. So we must go together, on the same road! Let us go!"
"Why? Why are you saying all this?" Sonia said, strangely and violently agitated by his words.

"Why? Because you can't stay like this—that's why! You have to face things squarely at last and stop crying like a child, insisting God won't allow it. What will happen if you're really taken to the hospital tomorrow? She's mad and consumptive; she'll die soon. And the children? Do you mean to tell me Polenka won't come to grief? Haven't you seen children at street corners, sent out by their mothers to beg? I've found out where those mothers live and how they live. Children can't remain children in such places! A seven-year-old is already vicious and a thief. Yet children are the image of Christ: 'Theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' He commanded us to honor and love them. They are the future of humanity."
"What can be done? What can be done?" Sonia repeated, weeping hysterically and wringing her hands.

"What can be done? Smash what must be smashed, once and for all, that's all—and take the suffering upon yourself. What, you don't understand? You'll understand later. Freedom and power—and above all, power! Over all trembling creation, over the whole anthill! That's the goal—remember that! This may be my farewell message. Perhaps it's the last time I'll speak to you. If I don't come tomorrow, you'll hear about everything—and then remember these words. And someday later, in years to come, perhaps you'll understand what they meant. If I do come tomorrow, I'll tell you who killed Lizaveta. Goodbye."
Sonia started with terror.
"Do you know who killed her?" she asked, frozen with horror, staring at him wildly.

"I know, and I'll tell you—you and only you. I've chosen you. I'm not coming to ask your forgiveness—simply to tell you. I chose you long ago for this—when your father talked about you, when Lizaveta was still alive. Goodbye. Don't shake hands. Tomorrow!"
He left. Sonia stared after him as at a madman. But she herself felt like one and knew it. Her head was spinning.

"Good heavens! How does he know who killed Lizaveta? What did those words mean? It's terrifying!" But at the same time the idea did not enter her mind—not for a single moment! "Oh, he must be terribly unhappy! He's abandoned his mother and sister. Why? What happened? What did he have in mind? What did he say to her? He kissed her foot and said—yes, he said it clearly—that he couldn't live without her. Oh, merciful heavens!"

Sonia spent the whole night in fever and delirium. She kept jumping up, weeping, wringing her hands, then sinking back into fitful sleep, dreaming of Polenka, Katerina Ivanovna, Lizaveta, the reading from the Gospel—and him, with his pale face and burning eyes, kissing her feet, weeping.

On the other side of the door on the right, which separated Sonia's room from Madame Resslich's apartment, was a room that had long stood empty. A card was posted on the gate and a notice in the windows overlooking the canal, advertising it for rent. Sonia had long been accustomed to the room being vacant. But all that time, Mr. Svidrigaïlov had been standing at the door of the empty room, listening. When Raskolnikov left, he stood still, thought for a moment, then went on tiptoe to his own room, which adjoined the empty one. He fetched a chair and carried it noiselessly to the door leading to Sonia's room. The conversation had struck him as interesting and remarkable, and he had enjoyed it immensely—so much so that he brought the chair so he wouldn't have to endure the inconvenience in the future, tomorrow for instance, of standing for a whole hour. He could listen in comfort.

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 5
paragraphs: When Raskolnikov arrived at the investigating office at eleven the next morning, as requested, he was surprised at being kept waiting so long—at least ten minutes before he was called in. He had expected them to pounce on him at once. Instead he stood in the waiting room while people who apparently had nothing to do with him passed to and fro. In the next room, which looked like an office, several clerks sat writing, clearly without the slightest notion of who Raskolnikov was. He looked around uneasily and suspiciously for some guard, some watch being kept to prevent his escape. But there was nothing of the sort—only the faces of clerks absorbed in petty paperwork, and other people, none of whom seemed to care about him at all. He could go wherever he liked, for all they cared. The conviction grew stronger that if yesterday's enigmatic man, that phantom sprung from the earth, had truly seen everything, they would not have let him stand here waiting. Would they have sat around until he chose to appear at eleven? Either the man hadn't yet given his information, or he simply knew nothing, had seen nothing—and so everything that had happened yesterday was once again a phantom, inflated by his sick and overstrained imagination. This theory had begun forming the day before, amid all his alarm and despair. Thinking it all over now and preparing for a fresh confrontation, he suddenly realized he was trembling—and a rush of indignation swept over him at the thought that he was trembling with fear at facing that hateful Porfiry Petrovitch. What he dreaded above all was meeting that man again; he hated him with an intense, bottomless hatred and feared that his hatred might betray him. His indignation was so fierce that the trembling stopped at once. He steeled himself to go in with a cold, arrogant bearing and vowed to say as little as possible, to watch and listen, and for once to master his overstrained nerves. At that moment he was called in.

He found Porfiry Petrovitch alone in his study. It was a room of moderate size, furnished with a large writing desk before a sofa upholstered in checkered fabric, a bureau, a bookcase in the corner, and several chairs—all government-issue, polished yellow wood. In the far wall was a closed door, presumably leading to other rooms. When Raskolnikov entered, Porfiry immediately closed the door behind him and they were alone. He greeted his visitor with an apparently warm and good-humored air, though after a few minutes Raskolnikov detected a certain awkwardness, as though Porfiry had been thrown off balance or caught in something private.

"Ah, my dear fellow! Here you are—in our domain!" Porfiry began, extending both hands. "Come, sit down, old man—or maybe you don't like being called 'my dear fellow' and 'old man'—tout court? Please don't think I'm being too familiar. Here, on the sofa."
Raskolnikov sat down, keeping his eyes fixed on him. "In our domain," the apologetic fussing, the French phrase tout court—all characteristic signs.

"He held out both hands but didn't actually give me one—pulled it back in time," Raskolnikov noted suspiciously. They were watching each other, but the instant their eyes met, they looked away quick as lightning.
"I brought you this paper—about the watch. Here it is. Is it all right, or should I copy it again?"

"What? A paper? Yes, yes, don't worry—it's fine," Porfiry said as though in a hurry, and after saying it he took the paper and looked at it. "Yes, perfectly fine. Nothing else needed," he declared with the same rapidity, and set the paper on the table.
A minute later, while talking about something else, he picked it up again and transferred it to his bureau.

"I believe you said yesterday you wanted to question me formally about my acquaintance with the murdered woman?" Raskolnikov began. "Why did I add 'I believe'?" flashed through his mind. "Why am I so uneasy about having said 'I believe'?" came a second flash. And he suddenly felt that his anxiety, from the mere contact with Porfiry, at the first words, at the first glances, had swelled in an instant to monstrous proportions. This was terribly dangerous. His nerves quivered; his agitation mounted. "This is bad! I'll say too much again."

"Yes, yes, yes! There's no hurry, no hurry," Porfiry muttered, pacing around the table without any apparent aim, darting now toward the window, now toward the bureau, now back to the table—at one moment avoiding Raskolnikov's suspicious stare, the next standing still and looking him straight in the face.
His fat, round little figure looked very strange—like a ball rolling from side to side and bouncing back.

"We've plenty of time. Do you smoke? Have you your own? Here—a cigarette!" he offered. "I'm receiving you here, you know, but my quarters are through there—my government quarters. I'm living elsewhere for the time being; some repairs needed doing here. Almost finished now. Government quarters are a wonderful thing, you know. What do you think?"
"Yes, a wonderful thing," Raskolnikov answered, looking at him almost ironically.

"A wonderful thing, a wonderful thing," Porfiry repeated, as though suddenly thinking of something quite different. "Yes, a wonderful thing!" he almost shouted, suddenly fixing his eyes on Raskolnikov and stopping just two steps away.
This stupid repetition was absurdly at odds with the grave, brooding, enigmatic look he turned on his visitor.
But it only spurred Raskolnikov's defiance, and he couldn't resist a reckless, ironic challenge.

"Tell me," he said, looking at Porfiry almost insolently and taking a kind of pleasure in his own boldness, "is it true that there's a sort of legal tradition—a technique in all investigating work—of starting from a distance, with some trivial or irrelevant topic, to encourage the person being questioned, or rather to distract and disarm his caution, and then suddenly to deal him a knockout blow with the real question? Isn't that so? It's supposed to be a sacred tradition, mentioned in all the textbooks of the art."
"Yes, yes. So you think that's why I was going on about government quarters?"

And as he said this, Porfiry screwed up his eyes and winked. A good-humored, crafty look passed over his face. The wrinkles on his forehead smoothed out, his eyes narrowed, his features broadened, and he suddenly broke into prolonged, nervous laughter, shaking all over and looking Raskolnikov straight in the face. Raskolnikov forced himself to laugh too, but when Porfiry, seeing him laugh, erupted into such a guffaw that he turned almost purple, Raskolnikov's disgust overcame all caution. He stopped laughing, scowled, and stared at Porfiry with hatred while the deliberately prolonged laughter continued. The lack of caution was on both sides, however: Porfiry Petrovitch was clearly laughing in his visitor's face and seemed utterly unconcerned by the annoyance it caused. To Raskolnikov, this was highly significant. He realized that Porfiry hadn't been embarrassed before either—that perhaps he, Raskolnikov, had walked into a trap; that something unknown to him lay beneath this, some motive; that perhaps everything was already in place and about to crash down upon him.
He went straight to the point, rose from his seat, and took his cap.

"Porfiry Petrovitch," he began resolutely, though with considerable irritation, "yesterday you expressed a wish that I come here for some inquiries"—he stressed the word "inquiries." "I've come, and if you have questions, ask them. If not, allow me to leave. I have no time to waste—I have to be at the funeral of that man who was run over, whom you also know about," he added, immediately annoyed at the addition, then more irritated at his own irritation. "I'm sick of all this, do you hear? It's partly what made me ill. In short," he practically shouted, feeling that the remark about illness was even more out of place, "in short, either examine me or let me go, immediately. And if you examine me, do it in proper form! I won't have it otherwise. So for now, goodbye—we clearly have nothing more to discuss."

"Good heavens! What do you mean? What should I question you about?" Porfiry cackled, his tone instantly changing as he stopped laughing. "Please don't worry," he began fussing about, making Raskolnikov sit down. "There's no hurry, it's all nonsense. I'm very glad you've come at last. I think of you as a visitor, nothing more. As for my awful laughing, I do apologize, Rodion Romanovitch—that is your name, isn't it? It's my nerves. You tickled me with that witty remark. Sometimes I shake with laughter for half an hour straight, like a rubber ball. I live in fear of a stroke. Do sit down, please—or I'll think you're angry."
Raskolnikov said nothing. He listened and watched, still scowling angrily. He did sit down, but kept hold of his cap.

"I must tell you one thing about myself, dear Rodion Romanovitch," Porfiry continued, moving around the room and again avoiding his visitor's eyes. "I'm a bachelor, you know, an insignificant fellow, unused to society. Besides, I've got nothing ahead of me—I'm set in my ways, going to seed. And have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, that in our Petersburg circles, when two intelligent people meet who aren't close but respect each other—like you and me—it takes them half an hour to find a topic of conversation? They sit there tongue-tied, feeling awkward. Everyone else has things to talk about—ladies, for instance, people of high society always have their subjects, c'est de rigueur. But people of the middle sort like us, thinking people, are always tongue-tied and uneasy. Why is that? Whether it's because we lack public spirit or because we're too honest to deceive each other, I don't know. What do you think? But do put down your cap—it looks as though you're about to leave. It makes me uncomfortable. And I'm so delighted to have you here."
Raskolnikov put down his cap and went on listening silently, with a serious, frowning face, to Porfiry's vague and empty chatter. "Is he really trying to distract me with this drivel?"

"I can't offer you coffee here, but why not spend five minutes with a friend?" Porfiry rattled on. "And these official duties—please don't mind my pacing about, excuse me, dear fellow. I'm terrified of offending you, but exercise is absolutely vital for me. I'm always sitting and glad for any chance to move about for five minutes. Sedentary life, you know. I keep meaning to join a gymnasium—they say officials of all ranks, even privy councillors, skip rope there. Science marches on! But as for my duties here, interrogations and such formalities—you yourself mentioned inquiries just now—I assure you, these sessions are sometimes more embarrassing for the examiner than for the examined. You made that observation yourself, very aptly and wittily." Raskolnikov had made no such observation. "One gets in a muddle! A complete muddle! One keeps harping on the same note, like a drum! There's supposed to be a reform—we'll get a new title, at least, he-he-he! And as for our legal tradition, as you so wittily called it, I thoroughly agree with you. Every suspect, even the most ignorant peasant, knows they start by distracting you with irrelevant questions and then deliver the knockout blow, he-he-he—your apt phrase, he-he! So you really thought my talk about government quarters was meant to—he-he! You're an ironic man. Well, I'll stop! Oh, by the way, yes—one word leads to another. You mentioned formality, about the inquiry. But what's the use of formality? In many cases it's nonsense. A friendly chat sometimes yields far more. One can always fall back on formality later, believe me. And really, what does it amount to? An investigating officer can't be bound by formality at every turn. The work of investigation is, so to speak, a free art in its own way, he-he-he!"

Porfiry paused for breath. He had simply been spouting one empty phrase after another, dropping a few enigmatic words and then reverting to incoherence. He was practically running around the room, moving his fat little legs faster and faster, staring at the ground, right hand behind his back, left hand making gestures that were absurdly out of keeping with his words. Raskolnikov suddenly noticed that as he darted about, Porfiry seemed to pause twice near the door, as though listening.
"Is he expecting something?"

"You're certainly quite right," Porfiry began gaily, looking at Raskolnikov with extraordinary simplicity—which startled him and instantly put him on guard. "Quite right in laughing at our legal methods, he-he! Some of these elaborate psychological techniques are extremely ridiculous, and perhaps useless, if one sticks too rigidly to the forms. Yes. I'm speaking of forms again. Well, if I recognize—or more strictly speaking, suspect—someone of being a criminal in a case entrusted to me, you're reading law, of course, Rodion Romanovitch?"
"I was."

"Well, here's a precedent for the future—not that I'd presume to instruct you, after your published articles on crime! No, I simply state it as a fact: if I consider this man or that one a criminal, why should I trouble him prematurely, even if I have evidence? In one case I may be obliged to arrest immediately, but in another case the situation may be quite different, you see. So why not let the man walk about town for a bit? He-he! I see you don't quite follow, so I'll give you a clearer example. If I lock him up too soon, I may actually give him—so to speak—moral support, he-he! You're laughing?"
Raskolnikov was far from laughing. He sat with compressed lips, his feverish eyes fixed on Porfiry.

"Yet that's exactly how it is, with certain types especially—because people are so different. You say 'evidence.' Well, there may be evidence. But evidence, you know, can usually be read two ways. I'm an investigating officer—a weak man, I confess. I'd like to construct a proof as clear as two times two—a direct, irrefutable demonstration! If I shut him up too soon, even if I'm convinced he's the man, I may actually deprive myself of the means of gathering further evidence against him. How? By giving him, so to speak, a defined position, a fixed status. I set his mind at rest, and he retreats into his shell. They say that at Sevastopol, right after the Battle of Alma, the clever people were terrified the enemy would attack at once and take the city by storm. But when they saw the enemy preferred a regular siege, they were delighted and reassured—it would drag on for two more months at least! You're laughing—you don't believe me? Of course you're right. You're right. These are all special cases, I admit. But note this, dear Rodion Romanovitch: the general case, the case for which all legal forms and rules are designed, doesn't actually exist, because every case, every crime, the moment it occurs, becomes a completely unique case—sometimes unlike anything that's gone before. Truly comic cases of that sort arise. Now, if I leave a certain man entirely alone, don't touch him, don't bother him, but let him know—or at least suspect—every moment that I know everything and am watching him day and night, and if he lives in continual suspicion and terror, he's bound to lose his head. He'll come to me of his own accord, or maybe do something that makes it as plain as two times two—it's delightful. It can happen with a simple peasant, but with someone of our kind—an intelligent, cultivated man, cultivated on a certain side—it's a dead certainty. Because, my dear fellow, it matters enormously to know on which side a man is cultivated. And then there are nerves—nerves, which you've overlooked! They're all sick, nervous, irritable! And how they suffer from spleen! That, I assure you, is a gold mine for us. And it doesn't trouble me at all, his walking around free! Let him, let him walk about for now! I know I've caught him and that he won't escape. Where could he go? He-he! Abroad, maybe? A Pole will escape abroad, but not our man—especially since I'm watching and have taken measures. Into the depths of the country, perhaps? But peasants live there—real, rough Russian peasants. A modern cultivated man would sooner go to prison than live among such strangers. He-he! But that's all trivial, superficial. It's not just that he has nowhere to run—he is psychologically unable to escape me, he-he! What a phrase! By a law of nature, he can't escape, even if he had somewhere to go. Have you seen a moth around a candle? That's how he'll keep circling around me, closer and closer, and then—flop! He'll fly straight into my mouth and I'll swallow him. Very amusing, he-he-he! You don't believe me?"
Raskolnikov made no reply. He sat pale and motionless, still staring into Porfiry's face with the same intensity.

"A good lesson," he thought, going cold. "This is beyond cat and mouse, like yesterday. He can't be showing off his power for no reason, teasing me—he's far too clever for that. He must have another purpose. What is it? It's all bluster, my friend—you're trying to scare me! You have no proof, and the man I saw yesterday doesn't exist. You simply want to rattle me, get me worked up in advance and then crush me. But you're wrong—you won't succeed! But why give me such a broad hint? Is he banking on my shattered nerves? No, my friend, you're wrong. You won't do it, even if you've set some trap. Let's see what you've got."

And he braced himself for a terrible, unknown ordeal. At times he wanted to spring at Porfiry and strangle him. His anger was what he had feared from the start. He felt his parched lips were flecked with foam, his heart pounding. But he was still determined to say nothing until the right moment. He realized this was the best strategy: instead of talking too much, he would irritate his adversary by his silence and perhaps provoke him into speaking too freely. At least, that was what he hoped.

"No, I see you don't believe me—you think I'm playing a harmless joke," Porfiry began again, growing livelier, chuckling constantly and pacing the room once more. "And of course you're right. God gave me a figure that can only provoke comic thoughts in others. A buffoon! But let me tell you, and I repeat, excuse an old man, dear Rodion Romanovitch—you are still a young man, in your first youth, so to speak, and so you prize intellect above all, like all young people. Clever wit and abstract argument fascinate you. That's exactly like the old Austrian Hofkriegsrath, as far as I can judge military matters: on paper they beat Napoleon and took him prisoner, cleverly working it all out in their study—but then General Mack surrendered with his entire army, he-he-he! I see, I see, Rodion Romanovitch, you're laughing at a civilian taking examples from military history! But I can't help it—it's my weakness. I love military science. And I'm terribly fond of all military histories. I've certainly missed my true calling. I should have been in the army! I might not have been a Napoleon, but I could have been a major, he-he! Well, I'll tell you the whole truth, my dear fellow, about this special case: actual reality and a man's temperament are weighty matters, and sometimes they defeat the sharpest calculations! Listen to an old man—I'm speaking seriously, Rodion Romanovitch"—as he said this, the barely thirty-five-year-old Porfiry actually seemed to age; even his voice changed and he seemed to shrink—"moreover, I'm a candid man. Am I candid or not? What do you think? I believe I truly am: I'm telling you these things for nothing, without even expecting a reward, he-he! Well, to continue: wit, in my opinion, is a splendid thing—an ornament of nature and a consolation of life—and the tricks it can play! So that sometimes a poor investigating officer barely knows where he stands, especially when his own imagination runs away with him too—he is only human, after all! But the criminal's temperament saves the day, worse luck for him! But young people, carried away by their own cleverness, don't consider that 'when they overstep all obstacles,' as you put it so wittily yesterday. The man in question—the special case, the incognito—will lie, and lie brilliantly, in the cleverest way. You'd think he'd triumph and enjoy the fruits of his wit—but at the most interesting, the most critical moment, he'll faint! Illness and a stuffy room may play their part, of course, but still! He gave us the idea! He lied incomparably but didn't reckon on his own temperament. That's what betrays him! Or he'll be carried away by his playful wit into mocking the man who suspects him—he'll turn pale, as if deliberately, to mislead, but the pallor will be too natural, too convincing—and again, he's given us an idea! The examiner may be fooled at first, but he'll think differently the next day, if he's not a fool. And it's like that at every step! The man puts himself forward where he's not wanted, talks when he should keep silent, weaves in all sorts of allegories, he-he! Comes and asks: 'Why didn't you arrest me sooner?' He-he-he! And this happens with the cleverest people, the psychologists, the literary men! Temperament reflects everything like a mirror! Look into it and admire what you see! But why are you so pale, Rodion Romanovitch? Is the room stuffy? Shall I open the window?"
"Oh, don't bother, please!" Raskolnikov cried, and suddenly burst out laughing. "Please don't bother!"
Porfiry stopped facing him, paused a moment, and then burst out laughing too. Raskolnikov stood up from the sofa, abruptly cutting short his own hysterical laughter.

"Porfiry Petrovitch," he said loudly and distinctly, though his legs trembled and he could barely stand, "I see clearly at last that you actually suspect me of murdering that old woman and her sister Lizaveta. Let me tell you, for my part, that I'm sick of this. If you believe you have the right to prosecute me, to arrest me—then do it. But I will not be mocked to my face and tormented—"
His lips trembled, his eyes blazed with fury, and his voice broke loose.
"I won't stand for it!" he shouted, bringing his fist down on the table. "Do you hear me, Porfiry Petrovitch? I won't stand for it!"
"Good heavens! What is this?" Porfiry cried, apparently genuinely alarmed. "Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow, what's the matter?"
"I won't stand for it!" Raskolnikov shouted again.
"Hush, dear man! They'll hear—they'll come in! Just think, what could we say to them?" Porfiry whispered in horror, bringing his face close to Raskolnikov's.
"I won't stand for it, I won't stand for it!" Raskolnikov repeated mechanically, but he too had dropped to a sudden whisper.
Porfiry turned quickly and ran to open the window.

"Some fresh air! And you need water, my dear fellow—you're ill!" He was heading for the door to call for some when he found a carafe of water in the corner. "Here, drink a little," he whispered, rushing over with it. "It'll do you good."
Porfiry's alarm and solicitude were so natural that Raskolnikov fell silent and began watching him with wild curiosity. He did not take the water, however.
"Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow, you'll drive yourself out of your mind, I assure you! Drink some water, do!"
He pressed the glass on him. Raskolnikov raised it mechanically to his lips, but set it on the table with disgust.

"Yes, you've had a little episode. You'll bring back your illness this way, dear fellow," Porfiry clucked with sympathetic concern, though he still looked rather shaken. "Good heavens, you must take better care of yourself! Dmitri Prokofitch came to see me yesterday—I know, I know, I have a nasty, ironic temperament, but what they made of it! Good heavens, he came yesterday after you'd left. We had dinner, he talked and talked, and all I could do was throw up my hands. Did he come on your behalf? But do sit down, for mercy's sake!"
"No, not from me. But I knew he went to you, and I know why," Raskolnikov answered sharply.
"You knew?"
"I knew. What of it?"

"Why, this: that I know more about you than just that, Rodion Romanovitch. I know about everything. I know how you went to take a flat that night, when it was dark, and how you rang the bell and asked about blood, so that the workmen and the porter didn't know what to make of it. Yes, I understand your state of mind at that time. But you'll drive yourself mad this way, upon my word! You'll lose your head! You're full of generous indignation at the wrongs you feel you've suffered, first from fate and then from the police, and so you rush from one reckless thing to another, trying to force everyone to speak out and put an end to it, because you're sick of all this suspicion and foolishness. That's right, isn't it? I've guessed how you feel? Only that way you'll lose not just your own head but Razumihin's too—he's too good a man for this situation, you must realize. You're ill, and he's good-hearted, and your illness is contagious. I'll tell you more when you're in a better state. But do sit down, for God's sake! Rest—you look terrible."

Raskolnikov sat down. The shivering had stopped; he burned all over. In amazement he listened with strained attention to Porfiry, who seemed genuinely concerned. But he didn't believe a word, though he felt a strange pull to believe. Porfiry's unexpected revelation about the apartment visit had completely stunned him. "How can it be—he knows about the flat," he thought, "and he tells me himself!"

"Yes, in our legal practice there was a case almost exactly like this—a case of morbid psychology," Porfiry went on quickly. "A man confessed to murder and kept it up! It was a complete hallucination: he produced facts, imposed on everyone—and why? He had been partly, though only partly and accidentally, the cause of a murder, and when he realized he'd given the murderers their opportunity, he sank into despair. It preyed on his mind, turned his brain; he began to imagine things and convinced himself he was the killer. But finally the High Court of Appeal reviewed the case, and the poor man was acquitted and placed in proper care. Thanks to that court! Tut-tut-tut! So, my dear fellow, you'll drive yourself into delirium if you have the urge to act on your nerves—going around ringing bells at night and asking about blood! I've studied all this morbid psychology in my practice. A man is sometimes tempted to jump from a window or a bell tower, and bell-ringing works the same way. It's all illness, Rodion Romanovitch! You've been neglecting your health. You should see an experienced doctor—what good is that fat fellow? You were lightheaded! It was all delirium!"
For an instant everything went spinning before Raskolnikov's eyes.
"Is it possible," flashed through his mind, "that he's still lying? He can't be, he can't be." He pushed the thought away, sensing what fury it could drive him to—fury that might drive him mad.
"I was not delirious! I knew exactly what I was doing!" he cried, straining every faculty to penetrate Porfiry's game. "I was perfectly lucid—do you hear?"

"Yes, I hear and understand. Yesterday too you insisted you weren't delirious—you were particularly emphatic about it! I understand everything you can tell me! But listen, Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow: if you really were a criminal, or somehow mixed up in this damnable business, would you insist that you were not delirious but in full possession of your faculties? And so emphatically and persistently? Would that even be possible? Quite impossible, in my view. If you had anything on your conscience, you'd be far better off insisting you were delirious. That's logical, isn't it?"
There was something sly in that question. Raskolnikov shrank back on the sofa as Porfiry leaned over him, and stared at him in silent bewilderment.
"And another thing, about Razumihin—you ought to have claimed he came on his own initiative, concealing your part in it! But you don't conceal it. You actually stress that he came at your urging."
Raskolnikov had not done so. A chill went down his spine.

"You keep lying," he said slowly and weakly, twisting his lips into a sickly smile. "You're trying again to show that you know my whole game, that you know everything I'll say beforehand," he said, aware that he wasn't weighing his words carefully enough. "You want to frighten me—or you're simply laughing at me."
He continued to stare as he said this, and again his eyes blazed with intense hatred.
"You keep lying," he said. "You know perfectly well that the best strategy for a criminal is to tell the truth as closely as possible—to conceal as little as possible. I don't believe you!"

"What a wily person you are!" Porfiry tittered. "No catching you—you're a perfect monomaniac. So you don't believe me? But you do believe me a quarter of the way already, and I'll soon make you believe the whole, because I have a genuine liking for you and sincerely wish you well."
Raskolnikov's lips trembled.

"Yes, I do wish you well," Porfiry went on, touching Raskolnikov's arm gently. "You must look after your illness. Besides, your mother and sister are here now. You ought to think of them, comfort them—instead, all you do is frighten them."
"What's that to you? How do you know about it? What business is it of yours? You're watching me and want me to know it?"

"Good heavens! I learned it all from you yourself! In your excitement you tell me and everyone else everything. From Razumihin I learned some interesting details yesterday too. No, you interrupted me, but I must point out that for all your cleverness, your suspiciousness makes you lose your common sense. Take the bell-ringing, for example. I, an investigating officer, have handed you this priceless clue—a real fact—and you see nothing in it! If I had the slightest suspicion of you, would I have acted that way? No—I'd first have disarmed your suspicions, kept quiet about what I knew, diverted your attention, and then delivered the blow: 'And what were you doing, sir, at ten or nearly eleven at the murdered woman's flat? Why did you ring the bell? Why did you ask about blood? And why did you invite the porters to go with you to the police station?' That's how I should have acted if I suspected you in the slightest. I should have taken a formal statement, searched your lodging, perhaps arrested you. So clearly I have no suspicion of you, since I've done none of that! But you can't look at it rationally. You see nothing, I say again!"
Raskolnikov flinched so visibly that Porfiry could not fail to notice it.
"You're lying all the time!" he cried. "I don't know your purpose, but you're lying! You didn't talk this way just now, and I can't be mistaken!"

"Lying?" Porfiry repeated, apparently stung, but keeping his good-humored, ironic expression and seeming not the least concerned about Raskolnikov's opinion. "Lying? But how did I treat you just now—I, the investigating officer? Prompting you with every possible defense: illness, delirium, injury, depression, the police officers, all of it! Though, to be sure, all those psychological defenses cut both ways: illness, delirium, 'I don't remember'—that's all very well, but why, my dear sir, in your illness and delirium, were you haunted by precisely those delusions and not others? There might have been different ones, mightn't there? He-he-he!"
Raskolnikov looked at him with haughty contempt.

"In short," he said loudly and imperiously, rising to his feet and pushing Porfiry back slightly as he did so, "in short, I want to know: do you consider me entirely free from suspicion, or not? Tell me, Porfiry Petrovitch, tell me once and for all—and quickly!"

"What a trial you are!" Porfiry cried, with a perfectly good-humored, sly, and composed face. "And why do you want to know? Why do you need to know so much, when no one has even begun to bother you? You're like a child begging for matches! And why are you so anxious? Why do you force yourself on us? He-he-he!"
"I repeat," Raskolnikov cried furiously, "I can't put up with it any longer!"
"With what? The uncertainty?" Porfiry interrupted.
"Don't mock me! I won't have it! I tell you I won't have it. I can't and I won't—do you hear!" he shouted, slamming his fist on the table again.

"Hush! Hush! They'll overhear! I'm warning you seriously—take care of yourself. I'm not joking," Porfiry whispered. But this time his face bore no trace of its usual old-womanish good nature and alarm. Now he was commanding, stern, frowning—for once dropping all pretense.
But this lasted only an instant. Raskolnikov, bewildered, suddenly fell into genuine frenzy—but strangely, he once again obeyed the command to speak quietly, though he was in a paroxysm of fury.

"I will not be tortured," he whispered, instantly recognizing with hatred that he could not help obeying, which drove him to even greater fury. "Arrest me, search me, but act in proper form! Don't play with me! Don't you dare!"
"Don't worry about form," Porfiry interrupted with his old sly smile, gloating, as it were, over Raskolnikov. "I invited you quite informally, in a friendly way."
"I don't want your friendship and I spit on it! Do you hear? Now watch: I'm taking my cap and leaving. What will you say if you mean to arrest me?"
He seized his cap and went to the door.
"But won't you see my little surprise?" Porfiry chuckled, again catching him by the arm and stopping him at the door.
He seemed to grow more playful and good-humored, which drove Raskolnikov wild.
"What surprise?" he asked, standing still and looking at Porfiry in alarm.
"My little surprise—sitting right there, behind the door, he-he-he!" He pointed to the locked door. "I locked him in so he wouldn't escape."
"What is it? Where? What are you—"
Raskolnikov went to the door and tried to open it, but it was locked.
"It's locked. Here's the key!"
And he produced the key from his pocket.
"You're lying!" Raskolnikov roared, losing all restraint. "You lie, you damned Punch!" And he rushed at Porfiry, who retreated to the other door, not at all alarmed.
"I see through it all! You're lying and mocking me so I'll betray myself—"
"Why, you could hardly betray yourself further, dear Rodion Romanovitch. You're beside yourself. Don't shout—I'll call the clerks!"

"You're lying! Call them! You knew I was ill and tried to drive me into a frenzy to make me give myself away—that was your plan! Produce your facts! I see through everything! You have no evidence—nothing but miserable, worthless suspicions, Zametov's guesswork! You knew my character; you wanted to push me to fury and then stun me with priests and deputies! Are you waiting for them? What are you waiting for? Where are they? Bring them out!"

"What deputies, my good man? What an imagination! And it wouldn't even be proper procedure, as you said yourself. You don't know the rules, dear fellow. But procedure can wait, as you see," Porfiry muttered, putting his ear to the door. And indeed, a commotion could be heard on the other side.
"They're coming!" Raskolnikov cried. "You sent for them! You were expecting them! Well, bring them all out—your deputies, your witnesses, whatever you like! I'm ready!"
But at that moment something strange happened—something so utterly unexpected that neither Raskolnikov nor Porfiry Petrovitch could have foreseen such an ending to their interview.

chapters.title: Part 4, Chapter 6
paragraphs: When he remembered the scene afterward, this is how Raskolnikov saw it.
The noise behind the door grew louder, and suddenly the door was pushed open a crack.
"What is it?" Porfiry Petrovitch cried, annoyed. "I gave orders that--"
For a moment there was no answer, but it was clear that several people stood at the door and were apparently pushing someone back.
"What is it?" Porfiry Petrovitch repeated uneasily.
"The prisoner Nikolay has been brought," someone answered.
"He's not wanted! Take him away! Let him wait! What's he doing here? This is completely irregular!" Porfiry shouted, rushing to the door.
"But he--" the same voice began, then suddenly went silent.
Two seconds, no more, were spent in actual struggle, then someone gave a violent shove, and a man, very pale, strode into the room.

The man's appearance was at first glance very strange. He stared straight ahead, as though seeing nothing. There was a look of fierce determination in his eyes, and at the same time a deathly pallor in his face, as though he were being led to the scaffold. His white lips twitched faintly.

He was dressed like a workman and was of medium height, very young, slim, with his hair cut in a round crop and thin, spare features. The man he had shoved aside followed him into the room and managed to grab him by the shoulder -- it was a guard -- but Nikolay pulled his arm free.
Several people crowded curiously into the doorway. Some of them tried to push in. All of this happened almost instantaneously.
"Go away, it's too soon! Wait till you're sent for! Why did you bring him so early?" Porfiry Petrovitch muttered, extremely annoyed, as though thrown completely off his calculations.
But Nikolay suddenly fell to his knees.
"What's this?" Porfiry cried, startled.
"I'm guilty! The sin is mine! I am the murderer," Nikolay declared, somewhat breathless but speaking fairly loudly.
For ten seconds there was silence, as though everyone had been struck dumb. Even the guard stepped back, retreated mechanically to the door, and stood there motionless.
"What did you say?" Porfiry Petrovitch cried, recovering from his momentary shock.
"I... am the murderer," Nikolay repeated after a brief pause.
"What... you... what... whom did you kill?" Porfiry Petrovitch was obviously bewildered.
Nikolay was silent again for a moment.
"Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna. I killed them... with an axe. Everything went dark," he added suddenly, and fell silent again.

He still knelt there. Porfiry Petrovitch stood for some moments as though deep in thought, then suddenly roused himself and waved away the uninvited spectators. They vanished instantly and closed the door. Then he looked toward Raskolnikov, who stood in the corner staring wildly at Nikolay, and started toward him, but stopped short. He looked from Nikolay to Raskolnikov and back again, and then, as though unable to restrain himself, he pounced on Nikolay.
"You're getting ahead of yourself," he shouted at him, almost angrily. "I didn't ask you what came over you. Tell me -- did you kill them?"
"I am the murderer. I want to give a statement," Nikolay pronounced.
"What did you kill them with?"
"An axe. I had it ready."
"He's in a hurry! Did you act alone?"
Nikolay did not understand the question.
"Did you do it alone?"
"Yes, alone. And Mitka is not guilty and had no part in it."
"Don't rush ahead about Mitka! How was it you both ran downstairs at that time? The porters saw you both!"
"It was to throw them off the trail... I ran after Mitka," Nikolay replied hurriedly, as though he had prepared the answer in advance.
"I knew it!" Porfiry cried in vexation. "He's not telling his own story," he muttered, as though to himself, and his eyes suddenly landed on Raskolnikov again.
He had apparently been so absorbed by Nikolay that for a moment he had forgotten Raskolnikov entirely. He caught himself, slightly taken aback.
"My dear Rodion Romanovitch, forgive me!" He rushed up to him. "This won't do. I'm afraid you'll have to leave... it's no good your being here. I will... you see, what a surprise! Goodbye!"
And taking him by the arm, he steered him toward the door.
"I suppose you didn't expect that?" said Raskolnikov, who, though he hadn't yet fully grasped the situation, had regained his nerve.
"You didn't expect it either, my friend. Look how your hand is shaking! Ha-ha!"
"You're shaking too, Porfiry Petrovitch!"
"Yes, I am. I didn't expect it."
They were already at the door. Porfiry was impatient for Raskolnikov to leave.
"And that little surprise of yours -- aren't you going to show it to me?" Raskolnikov asked sarcastically.
"Listen to him -- his teeth are chattering as he asks, ha-ha! You're quite the ironist! Well then, until we meet again!"
"I believe we can say goodbye."
"That's in God's hands," Porfiry murmured with a strained smile.

As he walked through the office, Raskolnikov noticed that many people were staring at him. Among them he spotted the two porters from the house whom he had tried to drag to the police station that night. They stood there waiting. But no sooner had he reached the stairs than he heard Porfiry Petrovitch's voice behind him. Turning around, he saw the investigator running after him, out of breath.
"One word, Rodion Romanovitch. As for the rest, it's in God's hands, but as a matter of procedure there are certain questions I'll need to ask you... so we will meet again, won't we?"
And Porfiry stood facing him with a smile.
"Won't we?" he added.
He seemed to want to say something more, but couldn't get the words out.
"You must forgive me, Porfiry Petrovitch, for what just happened... I lost my temper," Raskolnikov began. He had regained enough composure that he felt an irresistible urge to show off his coolness.

"Don't mention it, don't mention it," Porfiry replied, almost gleefully. "I have a terrible temper myself, I admit it! But we will meet again. If it's God's will, we may see a great deal of one another."
"And get to know each other inside and out?" Raskolnikov added.
"Yes, inside and out," Porfiry Petrovitch agreed, and he narrowed his eyes, studying Raskolnikov intently. "You're off to a birthday party now?"
"To a funeral."
"Of course, the funeral! Take care of yourself and get well."
"I don't know what to wish you," said Raskolnikov, who had started down the stairs but looked back again. "I'd like to wish you success, but your job is such a comical one."
"Why comical?" Porfiry had turned to go, but seemed to prick up his ears at this.

"Well, just think how you must have been tormenting and tormenting that poor Nikolay psychologically, in your usual fashion, until he confessed! Day and night you must have been hammering at him, proving he was the murderer -- and now that he has confessed, you'll start picking him apart again. 'You're lying,' you'll say. 'You're not the murderer! You can't be! This isn't your own story!' You have to admit, it's rather comical."
"Ha-ha-ha! So you noticed that I said to Nikolay just now that he wasn't telling his own story?"
"How could I have missed it!"
"Ha-ha! You're very sharp. You notice everything! You truly have a playful mind! And you always latch onto the comic angle... ha-ha! They say that was Gogol's defining trait, among the writers."
"Yes, Gogol's."
"Yes, Gogol's. I look forward to our next meeting."
"So do I."

Raskolnikov walked straight home. He was so muddled and bewildered that after arriving he sat on the sofa for a quarter of an hour, just trying to collect his thoughts. He didn't even attempt to think about Nikolay -- he was stunned. He felt that the confession was something inexplicable, something beyond his comprehension. But Nikolay's confession was an actual fact. The consequences of that fact were immediately clear: the falsehood would inevitably be discovered, and then they would come after him again. But until then, at least, he was free and had to do something for himself, because the danger was closing in.

But how close was it? His position gradually became clear. Remembering, in rough outline, the main contours of his recent scene with Porfiry, he couldn't help shuddering with horror once more. Of course, he didn't yet know all of Porfiry's aims or see through all his calculations. But he had already shown part of his hand, and nobody knew better than Raskolnikov how dangerous Porfiry's gambit had been. A little more and he might have given himself away completely, with hard evidence. Knowing his nervous temperament, seeing through him from the very first glance, Porfiry had played a bold game -- and was bound to win. Raskolnikov had undeniably compromised himself, but no actual facts had come to light yet; nothing concrete. But was he reading the situation correctly? Wasn't he mistaken? What had Porfiry been driving at? Had he really prepared some kind of surprise? What was it? Had he truly been expecting something, or hadn't he? How would they have parted if Nikolay's unexpected appearance hadn't interrupted them?

Porfiry had shown nearly all his cards -- he had taken a real risk in doing so -- and if he had truly had something up his sleeve (Raskolnikov reflected), he would have shown that too. What was this "surprise"? Was it a joke? Did it mean anything? Could it have concealed anything like a fact, an actual piece of evidence? Yesterday's visitor? What had become of him? Where was he today? If Porfiry really had evidence, it must have something to do with that man...
He sat on the sofa with his elbows on his knees and his face buried in his hands. He was still trembling with nerves. Finally he got up, took his cap, thought for a moment, and went to the door.

He had a vague sense that for today, at least, he could consider himself out of danger. He felt a sudden rush of something almost like joy; he wanted to hurry to Katerina Ivanovna's. He would be too late for the funeral, of course, but he could still make it to the memorial dinner, and there he would see Sonia.
He stood still, thought for a moment, and a suffering smile appeared briefly on his lips.
"Today! Today," he repeated to himself. "Yes, today! So it must be..."

But just as he was about to open the door, it began opening on its own. He flinched and stepped back. The door opened gently and slowly, and there suddenly appeared a figure -- yesterday's visitor from underground.

The man stood in the doorway, looked at Raskolnikov without speaking, and took a step into the room. He looked exactly the same as the day before -- the same build, the same clothes -- but his face had changed dramatically. He looked dejected and sighed deeply. If he had only raised his hand to his cheek and tilted his head to one side, he would have looked exactly like a peasant woman.
"What do you want?" Raskolnikov asked, numb with terror. The man said nothing, but suddenly bowed down almost to the ground, touching it with one finger.
"What is it?" Raskolnikov cried.
"I have sinned," the man said softly.
"How?"
"By evil thoughts."
They looked at each other.

"I was angry. When you came that day, maybe drunk, and told the porters to go to the police station and asked about the blood -- I was angry that they let you go and took you for a drunk. So angry I couldn't sleep. I remembered the address, came here yesterday, and asked for you..."
"Who came?" Raskolnikov interrupted, and instantly a memory began to stir.
"I did. I wronged you."
"So you're from that house?"
"I was standing at the gate with them... don't you remember? We've had our trade in that house for years. We cure and prepare hides, we take work home... What upset me most was--"

And the whole scene from two days earlier in the gateway came flooding back to Raskolnikov's mind. He recalled that there had been several people there besides the porters, women among them. He remembered that one voice had suggested taking him straight to the police station. He couldn't recall the speaker's face, and even now he didn't recognize it, but he remembered turning around and making some kind of reply...

So this was the explanation for yesterday's horror. The most terrifying thought was that he had nearly destroyed himself, had very nearly given everything away, over such a trivial circumstance. So this man could report nothing except his visit to the flat and his questions about the bloodstains. Porfiry, then, had nothing but delirium -- no hard facts -- nothing but this psychology that cuts both ways. So if no new facts came to light (and they must not -- they absolutely must not!), then what could they do to him? How could they convict him, even if they arrested him? And Porfiry had only just learned about the flat -- he hadn't known about it before.
"Was it you who told Porfiry... that I'd been there?" he cried, struck by a sudden idea.
"What Porfiry?"
"The head of the detective department?"
"Yes. The porters wouldn't go, so I went."
"Today?"
"I got there two minutes before you. And I heard everything -- every word of how he tormented you."
"Where? What? When?"
"Right there, in the next room. I was sitting there the entire time."
"What? So you were the surprise? But how is that possible? Good Lord!"

"I saw that the porters didn't want to do what I said," the man began. "'It's too late,' they said, 'and he might be angry we didn't come sooner.' I couldn't sleep, and I started making inquiries. Finding out where to go yesterday, I went today. The first time I went, he wasn't in. When I came back an hour later, he couldn't see me. The third time, they let me in. I told him everything, exactly as it happened, and he started jumping around the room and punching himself in the chest. 'What do you scoundrels mean by this? If I'd known about it, I'd have arrested him!' Then he ran out, called someone over, and talked to him in the corner. Then he turned back to me, scolding and questioning. He scolded me terribly, and I told him everything, including how you didn't dare say a word to me yesterday and how you didn't recognize me. He started running around again, punching himself in the chest, getting angry. And when they announced you, he told me to go into the next room. 'Sit there,' he said. 'Don't move, no matter what you hear.' And he put a chair there for me and locked me in. 'I might call you,' he said. And when Nikolay was brought in, he let me out as soon as you'd gone. 'I'll send for you again and question you further,' he said."
"And did he question Nikolay while you were there?"
"He got rid of me before speaking to Nikolay, just as he'd gotten rid of you."
The man stood still, then suddenly bowed again, touching the ground with his finger.
"Forgive me for my evil thoughts and my slander."
"May God forgive you," Raskolnikov answered.
As he said this, the man bowed once more -- not to the ground this time -- turned slowly, and left the room.
"Everything cuts both ways now," Raskolnikov repeated to himself, and he left more confident than before.
"Now we'll put up a fight," he said with a bitter smile as he descended the stairs. The bitterness was aimed at himself; with shame and contempt he recalled his cowardice.

chapters.title: Part 5, Chapter 1
paragraphs: The morning after the fateful confrontation with Dounia and her mother had a sobering effect on Pyotr Petrovitch. As deeply unpleasant as it was, he was gradually forced to accept as an irreversible fact what had seemed fantastic and unbelievable just the day before. The black snake of wounded vanity had been gnawing at his heart all night. When he got out of bed, Pyotr Petrovitch immediately looked in the mirror. He was afraid he might have jaundice. But his health seemed unimpaired so far, and looking at his noble, fair-skinned face, which had grown somewhat plump lately, Pyotr Petrovitch was briefly comforted by the conviction that he could find another bride -- perhaps even a better one. But returning to reality, he turned aside and spat vigorously, which drew a sarcastic smile from Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, the young friend he was staying with. Pyotr Petrovitch noticed that smile and immediately chalked it up against his young friend. He had been keeping quite a tally of late. His anger doubled when he realized he should never have told Andrey Semyonovitch about the outcome of yesterday's meeting. That was the second mistake he had made in a fit of temper and impulsiveness. Moreover, all morning one annoyance followed another. He even ran into a snag with his legal case at the senate. He was particularly irritated by the landlord of the apartment he had rented in anticipation of his wedding and was having redecorated at his own expense. The landlord, a wealthy German tradesman, refused to consider breaking the freshly signed lease and demanded the full penalty payment, even though Pyotr Petrovitch was returning the place practically renovated. Likewise, the furniture shop refused to return a single ruble of the deposit for items purchased but not yet delivered.

"Am I really to get married just for the sake of the furniture?" Pyotr Petrovitch ground his teeth, and at the same time a flash of desperate hope crossed his mind. "Can it really be so irrevocably over? Is there no point in making one more attempt?" The thought of Dounia sent a sharp pang of desire through his heart. He suffered real anguish at that moment, and if it had been possible to kill Raskolnikov by sheer force of will, Pyotr Petrovitch would have done so on the spot.

"It was my mistake not to have given them money," he thought, making his way gloomily back to Lebeziatnikov's room. "Why on earth was I so stingy? It was false economy! I meant to keep them penniless so they'd turn to me as their savior, and look what happened! If I'd spent fifteen hundred rubles on trousseau and gifts -- trinkets, dressing cases, jewelry, fabrics, all that rubbish from Knopp's and the English shop -- my position would have been stronger. They couldn't have refused me so easily! They're the sort of people who would feel obligated to return money and gifts if they broke it off, and they'd find it hard to do so! Their conscience would prick them: how can we dismiss a man who has been so generous and considerate? I've made a blunder."
And grinding his teeth again, Pyotr Petrovitch called himself a fool -- though not aloud, of course.

He returned home twice as irritated and angry as before. The preparations for the funeral dinner at Katerina Ivanovna's caught his attention as he passed through. He had heard about it the day before; he even had a vague memory of being invited, but he'd been too absorbed in his own troubles to pay attention. Inquiring of Madame Lippevechsel, who was busy laying the table while Katerina Ivanovna was away at the cemetery, he learned that the event was to be quite an affair. All the lodgers had been invited, including some who hadn't known the dead man, and even Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov had been invited despite his previous quarrel with Katerina Ivanovna. He, Pyotr Petrovitch, was not only invited but eagerly expected as the most distinguished of the lodgers. Amalia Ivanovna herself had been invited with great ceremony despite the recent unpleasantness, and she was very busy with preparations, taking obvious pleasure in them. She was dressed to the nines in new black silk and was proud of it. All this gave Pyotr Petrovitch an idea, and he went into his room -- or rather Lebeziatnikov's -- somewhat thoughtfully. He had learned that Raskolnikov was to be one of the guests.

Andrey Semyonovitch had been at home all morning. Pyotr Petrovitch's attitude toward this man was strange, though perhaps natural. He had despised and hated him from the day he moved in, and at the same time seemed somewhat afraid of him. He hadn't come to stay with him in Petersburg simply out of cheapness, though that had been perhaps his main reason. He had heard of Andrey Semyonovitch, who had once been his ward, as a prominent young progressive who played an important role in certain notorious circles whose activities were legendary in the provinces. This had impressed Pyotr Petrovitch. These powerful, all-knowing circles that despised everyone and exposed everyone had long filled him with a peculiar but vague dread. He couldn't, of course, form even an approximate idea of what they actually stood for. Like everyone else, he had heard there were progressives of some sort in Petersburg -- nihilists and the like -- and, like many people, he exaggerated and distorted the meaning of those words to an absurd degree. What he had feared most for many years was being exposed, and this was the chief source of his constant anxiety about moving his affairs to Petersburg. He was frightened of this the way small children are sometimes seized by panic. Some years back, when he was just starting his career, he had encountered two cases in which rather important provincial figures, his patrons, had been cruelly exposed. One case had ended in a great scandal for the person attacked, and the other had very nearly ended in serious trouble. For this reason, Pyotr Petrovitch intended to look into the matter as soon as he reached Petersburg and, if necessary, to get ahead of things by courting favor with "the younger generation." He relied on Andrey Semyonovitch for this, and before his visit to Raskolnikov he had managed to pick up some fashionable phrases. He soon discovered that Andrey Semyonovitch was a commonplace simpleton, but that by no means reassured him. Even if he could be certain that all the progressives were fools like him, it wouldn't have calmed his nerves. He had no real interest in any of the doctrines, ideas, or systems that Andrey Semyonovitch pestered him with. He had his own agenda -- he simply wanted to find out what was happening here. Did these people have any power or not? Did he have anything to fear from them? Would they expose any of his dealings? And what exactly were they going after now? Could he somehow win them over if they really were powerful? Was that the thing to do? In short, hundreds of questions presented themselves.

Andrey Semyonovitch was an anemic, scrofulous little man with strangely flaxen mutton-chop whiskers he was very proud of. He was a clerk and almost always had something wrong with his eyes. He was rather soft-hearted but self-assured, and sometimes extremely pompous in his speech -- which had an absurd effect coming from such a small man. He was one of the lodgers most respected by Amalia Ivanovna, because he didn't get drunk and paid his rent on time. Andrey Semyonovitch really was rather stupid. He had attached himself to the cause of progress and "the younger generation" out of sheer enthusiasm. He was one of that numerous and varied legion of mediocrities, half-formed creatures, and conceited half-educated coxcombs who latch onto whatever idea happens to be most fashionable, only to vulgarize it and turn into a caricature every cause they serve, however sincerely.

Despite his good nature, Lebeziatnikov was also beginning to dislike Pyotr Petrovitch. This happened on both sides without either realizing it. Simple as Andrey Semyonovitch was, he had begun to see that Pyotr Petrovitch was using him and secretly despising him, and that "he was not the right sort of man." He had tried expounding the systems of Fourier and Darwin to him, but lately Pyotr Petrovitch had begun listening too sarcastically and even rudely. The fact was that Pyotr Petrovitch had started to suspect that Lebeziatnikov was not merely a commonplace simpleton but perhaps a liar too, and that he had no connections of any consequence even in his own circles, but had simply picked up ideas thirdhand. Very likely he didn't even know much about his own propaganda work, because he was too muddled. A fine person to expose anyone! It should be noted, by the way, that during those ten days Pyotr Petrovitch had eagerly accepted the strangest flattery from Andrey Semyonovitch. He hadn't objected, for instance, when Andrey Semyonovitch praised him for being ready to contribute to a new "commune," or for agreeing not to christen his future children, or for consenting if Dounia took a lover a month after the wedding. Pyotr Petrovitch so enjoyed having his virtues extolled that he didn't disdain even these when they were attributed to him.

That morning Pyotr Petrovitch had cashed some five-percent bonds, and now he sat at the table counting bundles of banknotes. Andrey Semyonovitch, who almost never had any money, paced the room pretending to regard all those banknotes with indifference and even contempt. Nothing could have convinced Pyotr Petrovitch that Andrey Semyonovitch could really look at the money unmoved, while the latter kept thinking bitterly that Pyotr Petrovitch was perfectly capable of believing this about him and was perhaps even glad of the chance to tease his young friend by reminding him of his inferiority and the vast difference between them.

He found Pyotr Petrovitch incredibly inattentive and irritable that morning, though he, Andrey Semyonovitch, had launched into his favorite subject -- the founding of a special new "commune." The brief remarks that escaped from Pyotr Petrovitch between the clicking of beads on the counting frame betrayed unmistakable and discourteous irony. But the "humane" Andrey Semyonovitch attributed Pyotr Petrovitch's foul mood to his recent break with Dounia, and he was burning with impatience to hold forth on this topic. He had something progressive to say that would console his worthy friend and "could not fail" to advance his development.
"There's some kind of celebration being prepared at that widow's, isn't there?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked suddenly, interrupting Andrey Semyonovitch at the most interesting point.
"Don't you know? I was telling you about it last night, what I think of all such ceremonies. And she invited you too, I heard. You were talking to her yesterday..."

"I never would have expected that penniless fool to spend all the money she got from that other fool Raskolnikov on this feast. I was amazed just now, passing through, at the preparations -- the wines! Quite a few people are invited. It's beyond belief!" continued Pyotr Petrovitch, who seemed to have some purpose in pursuing the conversation. "What? You say I was invited too? When was that? I don't remember. But I won't go. Why should I? I only mentioned to her in passing yesterday the possibility of her obtaining a year's salary as the destitute widow of a civil servant. I suppose she invited me on that account, eh? Ha-ha-ha!"
"I don't intend to go either," said Lebeziatnikov.
"I should think not, after giving her a beating! You might well think twice, ha-ha!"
"Who beat whom?" cried Lebeziatnikov, flustered and blushing.

"You beat Katerina Ivanovna about a month ago. I heard about it yesterday. So that's what your convictions amount to... and the women's rights question wasn't quite sound either, ha-ha-ha!" And Pyotr Petrovitch, as though comforted, went back to clicking his counting beads.

"That's all slander and nonsense!" cried Lebeziatnikov, who was always sensitive about this subject. "It wasn't like that at all, it was completely different. You've heard it wrong -- it's a lie. I was simply defending myself. She came at me first with her nails, she pulled out my entire whiskers. I hope any person has the right to defend himself. I never allow anyone to use violence against me on principle, because it's an act of tyranny. What was I supposed to do? I simply pushed her away."
"Ha-ha-ha!" Luzhin went on laughing spitefully.

"You keep on like that because you're in a bad mood yourself. But that's nonsense and has nothing, absolutely nothing to do with the women's question! You don't understand. I used to think that if women are equal to men in all respects, even in physical strength -- as some now maintain -- then there should be equality in that too. Of course, I realized afterward that such a question really shouldn't arise, because there shouldn't be any fighting, and in the future society fighting is unthinkable. And it would be absurd to seek equality in fighting. I'm not that stupid. Though of course there is fighting now -- there won't be later, but for now there is -- damn it! You get me all confused! It's not because of that that I'm not going. I'm not going on principle, so as not to participate in the revolting convention of memorial dinners -- that's why! Though of course one might go just to laugh at it. A pity there won't be any priests -- I'd certainly go if there were."
"So you'd sit down at someone else's table and insult both it and your hosts, is that it?"

"Certainly not insult -- protest. I'd do it with a worthy purpose. I might indirectly serve the cause of enlightenment and propaganda. It's the duty of every person to work for enlightenment and propaganda, and the more harshly the better, perhaps. I might plant a seed, an idea. Something might grow from that seed. How would I be insulting them? They might be offended at first, but afterward they'd see I'd done them a service. You know, Terebyeva -- who's in the commune now -- was criticized because when she left her family and gave herself to... her cause, she wrote to her father and mother saying she refused to go on living conventionally and was entering a free marriage. People said it was too harsh, that she should have been gentler in her letter. I think that's all nonsense -- there's no need for softness. On the contrary, what's needed is protest. Varents had been married seven years. She left her two children and wrote her husband a straightforward letter: 'I've realized I cannot be happy with you. I can never forgive you for hiding from me that another form of social organization exists through communities. I only recently learned of this from a great-hearted man to whom I have given myself, and with whom I am establishing a community. I speak plainly because I consider it dishonest to deceive you. Do as you see fit. Don't hope to win me back -- it's too late. I hope you will be happy.' That's how such letters should be written!"
"Is that the Terebyeva you said had entered a third free marriage?"

"No, it's only the second, actually! But what if it were the fourth, or the fifteenth -- that's all nonsense! And if I ever regretted the death of my father and mother, it's now. Sometimes I think: if my parents were still alive, what a protest I could have aimed at them! I would have done something deliberate -- shown them, astonished them! I really do wish there were someone to rebel against!"
"To astonish! Ha-ha! Well, have it your way," Pyotr Petrovitch interrupted. "But tell me this: do you know the dead man's daughter, the delicate little one? Is what they say about her true?"

"What of it? In my personal conviction, this is the normal condition of women. Why not? That is -- let me be precise. In our present society it's not altogether normal because it's forced upon them, but in the future society it will be perfectly normal because it will be voluntary. Even as things stand, she was entirely within her rights. She was suffering, and that was her asset, so to speak -- her capital, which she had every right to use as she saw fit. In the future society there will of course be no need for such assets, but her role will have a different significance -- rational and in harmony with her surroundings. As for Sofya Semyonovna personally, I regard her actions as a bold protest against the organization of society, and I deeply respect her for it. I actually rejoice when I look at her!"
"I heard you got her thrown out of these lodgings."
Lebeziatnikov was furious.

"That's more slander!" he yelled. "It wasn't like that at all! That was all Katerina Ivanovna's invention -- she didn't understand! And I never made advances to Sofya Semyonovna! I was simply developing her, entirely unselfishly, trying to awaken her sense of protest. All I wanted was her protest, and besides, Sofya Semyonovna couldn't have stayed here anyway!"
"Have you asked her to join your commune?"

"You keep laughing, and very inappropriately, if you don't mind my saying so. You don't understand! There's no such role in a commune. The commune exists precisely so that there should be no such roles. In a commune, such a role is fundamentally transformed -- what is degrading here becomes perfectly sensible there; what is unnatural under present conditions becomes completely natural in a commune. It all depends on the environment. Everything is environment, and the individual is nothing. And I'm on good terms with Sofya Semyonovna to this day, which proves she never felt wronged by me. I'm trying to draw her into the commune now, but on an entirely different basis. What are you laughing at? We're trying to establish our own commune, a special one, on a broader foundation. We've gone further in our convictions. We reject more! And meanwhile I'm continuing to develop Sofya Semyonovna. She has a wonderful, wonderful character!"
"And you take advantage of her fine character, do you? Ha-ha!"
"No, no! Quite the opposite."
"The opposite! Ha-ha-ha! What a thing to say!"
"Believe me! Why would I hide it? In fact, I find it strange myself how timid, chaste, and modest she is with me!"
"And you, of course, are developing her... ha-ha! Trying to prove to her that all that modesty is nonsense?"

"Not at all! How crudely, how stupidly -- forgive me -- you misunderstand the word development! Good heavens, how crude you still are! We're striving for the freedom of women, and all you can think of is one thing. Setting aside the general question of chastity and feminine modesty as useless in themselves and indeed mere prejudices, I fully accept her chastity toward me, because that's her choice to make. Of course, if she herself were to tell me she wanted me, I'd consider myself very fortunate, because I like the girl very much. But for now, no one has ever treated her more courteously than I have, with more respect for her dignity. I wait in hope -- that's all!"
"You'd do better to give her a present. I bet that never occurred to you."

"You don't understand, as I've already told you! Of course she's in that situation, but it's a different question entirely. You simply look down on her. Observing a fact that you wrongly consider worthy of contempt, you refuse to take a humane view of another person. You don't know what a character she has! I'm only sorry that lately she's completely stopped reading and borrowing books. I used to lend her mine. I'm also sorry that despite all her energy and determination in protest -- which she's already demonstrated once -- she has so little independence, so little self-reliance, so as to break free from certain prejudices and foolish notions. Yet she understands some questions very well -- for instance, about hand-kissing: that it's an insult to a woman for a man to kiss her hand, because it implies inequality. We had a debate about that, and I described it to her. She also listened attentively to an account of French workers' associations.
