Right now I'm explaining the question of entering another person's room in the future society."
"And what's that about?"
"We had a debate recently on the question: does a member of the commune have the right to enter another member's room, man or woman, at any time? And we decided: yes, they do!"
"And what if it's an awkward moment? Ha-ha!"
Lebeziatnikov was genuinely annoyed.

"You always think of something indecent," he cried with disgust. "How frustrated I am that when I was explaining our system, I brought up the question of personal privacy too soon! It's always a stumbling block for people like you -- they turn it into a joke before they understand it. And how pleased with themselves they are! I've always maintained that this question shouldn't be tackled by a beginner until he has firm faith in the system. And tell me, please, what do you find so shameful about cesspools? I'd be the first to volunteer to clean out any cesspool you like. It's not about self-sacrifice -- it's simply work, honorable and useful work, as good as any other and far better than the work of a Raphael or a Pushkin, because it's more useful."
"And more honorable, more honorable! Ha-ha-ha!"

"What do you mean by 'more honorable'? I don't understand such terms when applied to human activity. 'More honorable,' 'nobler' -- those are outdated prejudices that I reject. Everything that is useful to humanity is honorable. I understand only one word: useful! You can snicker all you like, but that's how it is."

Pyotr Petrovitch laughed heartily. He had finished counting the money and was putting it away. But some of the banknotes he left on the table. The "cesspool question" had already been a subject of dispute between them. What was absurd was that it genuinely angered Lebeziatnikov, while it amused Luzhin -- and at that moment he particularly wanted to irritate his young friend.

"It's yesterday's bad luck that makes you so ill-humored and annoying," Lebeziatnikov blurted out. Despite his "independence" and "protests," he still didn't dare stand up to Pyotr Petrovitch and continued to treat him with something of the old deference.

"You'd better tell me this," Pyotr Petrovitch interrupted with haughty displeasure. "Can you -- or rather, are you really on friendly enough terms with that young woman to ask her to step in here for a moment? I think they've all come back from the cemetery. I heard the sound of footsteps. I want to see her, that young woman."
"What for?" Lebeziatnikov asked in surprise.

"I have my reasons. I'm leaving here today or tomorrow, and there's something I wanted to discuss with her. But you may be present during the conversation. In fact, it would be better if you were. Otherwise, God knows what you might imagine."
"I won't imagine anything. I was only asking. If you have something to say to her, nothing could be easier than to call her in. I'll go right now, and you can be sure I won't be in your way."

Five minutes later Lebeziatnikov returned with Sonia. She came in looking very surprised and overcome with her usual shyness. She was always awkward in such situations and always afraid of new people -- she had been that way as a child, and was even more so now. Pyotr Petrovitch greeted her "politely and warmly," but with a certain tone of teasing familiarity which he considered appropriate for a man of his standing when dealing with a creature so young and so interesting as she. He hastened to "put her at ease" and seated her at the table facing him. Sonia sat down, looked around -- at Lebeziatnikov, at the banknotes lying on the table, then back at Pyotr Petrovitch -- and her eyes remained fixed on him. Lebeziatnikov moved toward the door. Pyotr Petrovitch motioned for Sonia to stay seated and stopped Lebeziatnikov.
"Is Raskolnikov in there? Has he arrived?" he asked in a whisper.
"Raskolnikov? Yes. Why? Yes, he's there. I saw him come in just now. Why?"

"Well, I particularly ask you to stay here with us and not leave me alone with this... young woman. I only want a few words with her, but God knows what people might make of it. I wouldn't want Raskolnikov to spread stories. You understand what I mean?"

"I understand!" Lebeziatnikov saw the point. "Yes, you're right. Of course, I'm personally convinced you have no reason to worry, but... still, you're right. Certainly I'll stay. I'll stand by the window and won't be in your way. I think you're right."

Pyotr Petrovitch returned to the sofa, sat down opposite Sonia, looked at her closely, and assumed an extremely dignified, even severe expression, as if to say: "Don't get any ideas, young lady." Sonia was overwhelmed with embarrassment.

"First of all, Sofya Semyonovna, please make my apologies to your respected mother. That is the right way to put it, isn't it? Katerina Ivanovna is like a mother to you?" Pyotr Petrovitch began with great dignity, though affably.
His intentions were clearly friendly.
"Yes, exactly -- like a mother," Sonia answered timidly and hurriedly.
"Then please convey my apologies to her. Due to unavoidable circumstances, I'm forced to be absent and won't be attending the dinner despite your mother's kind invitation."
"Yes... I'll tell her... right away."
And Sonia jumped hastily to her feet.

"Wait, that's not all," Pyotr Petrovitch stopped her, smiling at her simplicity and ignorance of good manners. "You know me poorly, my dear Sofya Semyonovna, if you think I would trouble a person like you over something so trivial, concerning only myself. I have another purpose."

Sonia sat back down quickly. Her eyes flickered again for an instant to the gray-and-rainbow-colored banknotes still on the table, but she quickly looked away and fixed her gaze on Pyotr Petrovitch. She felt it horribly inappropriate, especially for someone like her, to stare at another person's money. She glanced at the gold eyeglass Pyotr Petrovitch held in his left hand and at the massive, extremely handsome ring with a yellow stone on his middle finger. But then she looked away again and, not knowing where to turn, ended up staring straight at Pyotr Petrovitch's face once more. After a pause of even greater solemnity, he continued.
"Yesterday in passing, I happened to exchange a few words with Katerina Ivanovna, poor woman. That was enough for me to determine that she is in a condition that is -- how shall I say -- abnormal."
"Yes... abnormal," Sonia agreed hurriedly.
"Or to put it more simply and clearly: she's ill."
"Yes, more simply and clearly... yes, ill."

"Quite so. And therefore, from a feeling of humanity and -- so to speak -- compassion, I would be glad to help her in any way I can, given her unfortunate position. I believe this entire destitute family now depends entirely on you?"
"May I ask," Sonia said, rising to her feet, "did you say something to her yesterday about the possibility of a pension? Because she told me you had promised to get her one. Is that true?"

"Not in the slightest -- it's absurd! I merely hinted at the possibility of temporary assistance as the widow of a civil servant who had died in the service -- provided she had connections. But apparently your late father hadn't served his full term and hadn't even been in active service recently. In fact, even if there were any hope, it would be extremely slim, because there would be no real claim for aid -- quite the opposite. And she's already dreaming of a pension! Ha-ha-ha! Quite a go-getter, that woman!"

"Yes, she is. She's trusting and good-hearted, and she believes everything because of the goodness of her heart, and... and she's like that... Yes. Please excuse her," said Sonia, and again she stood up to go.
"But you haven't heard what I have to say."
"No, I haven't," murmured Sonia.
"Then sit down." She was dreadfully flustered; she sat down again for the third time.

"Given her situation with her unfortunate little ones, I would be glad, as I've said, to be of service to the extent that I can -- that is, to the extent of my ability, and no more. One might, for instance, organize a subscription for her, or a lottery, something of that sort -- the kind of thing that's always arranged in such cases by friends or even strangers who wish to help. That was what I meant to discuss with you. It could be done."
"Yes, yes... God will reward you for it," Sonia whispered, gazing intently at Pyotr Petrovitch.

"It could be done, but we'll discuss it later. We might begin today -- we'll talk it over this evening and lay the groundwork, so to speak. Come to see me at seven o'clock. Mr. Lebeziatnikov, I hope, will help us. But there is one thing I must warn you about in advance, and it's the reason I've asked you here, Sofya Semyonovna. In my opinion, it would be impossible -- indeed, unsafe -- to put money directly in Katerina Ivanovna's hands. Today's dinner is proof of that. She doesn't have so much as a crust of bread for tomorrow, or a decent pair of shoes, and yet she's bought Jamaica rum, even Madeira I think, and coffee. I saw it as I passed through. Tomorrow you'll all be back to having nothing. It's absurd. So it seems to me that the subscription money should be managed so that the unfortunate widow doesn't know about it -- and that only you, for instance, should handle it. Am I right?"

"I don't know... it's only today, just this once. She was so set on honoring him, on celebrating his memory. And she is very sensible, really... but whatever you think best, and I'd be very, very... they'll all be... and God will reward... and the orphans..."
Sonia burst into tears.

"Very well then, keep it in mind. And now, would you accept this small sum for your relative's benefit, from me personally? I'm very anxious that my name not be mentioned in connection with it. Here... having my own concerns, so to speak, I cannot do more."

And Pyotr Petrovitch held out to Sonia a ten-ruble note, carefully unfolded. Sonia took it, blushed crimson, jumped up, muttered something, and began to take her leave. Pyotr Petrovitch escorted her ceremoniously to the door. She escaped from the room at last, agitated and distressed, and returned to Katerina Ivanovna overwhelmed with confusion.

All this time Lebeziatnikov had been standing by the window or pacing the room, trying not to interrupt the conversation. When Sonia left, he walked up to Pyotr Petrovitch and solemnly held out his hand.

"I heard and saw everything," he said, emphasizing the last word. "That was honorable -- what I mean is, it was humane! You wanted to avoid her gratitude, I could see that! And though I cannot, I confess, sympathize in principle with private charity -- because it not only fails to eliminate evil but actually promotes it -- I must admit that I witnessed your action with pleasure. Yes, yes, I approve."
"That's all nonsense," muttered Pyotr Petrovitch, somewhat disconcerted, looking carefully at Lebeziatnikov.

"No, it's not nonsense! A man who has suffered the distress and humiliation you went through yesterday, and who can still feel for others' misery -- such a man, even if he is making a social error, still deserves respect! I honestly didn't expect it of you, Pyotr Petrovitch, especially given your views. Oh, what a hindrance your views are to you! How upset you are, for instance, by yesterday's bad luck," cried the warmhearted Lebeziatnikov, feeling a renewed surge of affection for Pyotr Petrovitch. "And what do you need with marriage, with legal marriage, my dear, noble Pyotr Petrovitch? Why do you cling to this legality of marriage? You can beat me if you want, but I'm glad -- genuinely glad -- it fell through, that you're free, that you're not entirely lost to humanity! You see, I've spoken my mind!"
"Because I don't want to be made a fool of in your free marriage and raise another man's children -- that's why I prefer legal marriage," Luzhin replied, just to say something.
He seemed preoccupied with something.

"Children? You mentioned children," Lebeziatnikov began like a warhorse at the sound of a trumpet. "Children are a social question of the first importance, I agree, but the question of children has another solution. Some people refuse to have children altogether because they represent the institution of the family. We'll discuss children later, but now, the question of honor -- that's my weak point, I confess. That hateful, militaristic, Pushkin-era word is unthinkable in the vocabulary of the future. What does it even mean? Nonsense! There will be no deception in a free marriage! It's simply a natural consequence of legal marriage, its corrective, so to speak -- a protest. So it's not humiliating at all. And if I ever -- to suppose the absurd -- were legally married, I'd actually be pleased. I'd say to my wife: 'My dear, until now I loved you. Now I respect you, because you've shown you can protest!' You laugh! That's because you can't break free of prejudices. Damn it all! I understand what's unpleasant about being deceived in a legal marriage, but that's simply a despicable consequence of a despicable situation in which both parties are degraded. When the deception is open, as in a free marriage, it ceases to exist -- it's inconceivable. Your wife would simply be proving how much she respects you by considering you incapable of opposing her happiness and avenging yourself on her for her new partner. Damn it all! Sometimes I daydream: if I were to marry -- legally or otherwise, it's all the same -- I'd present my wife with a lover if she hadn't found one herself. 'My dear,' I'd say, 'I love you, but even more than that, I want your respect. See!' Am I not right?"

Pyotr Petrovitch sniggered as he listened, but without much amusement. He was barely listening. He was preoccupied with something else entirely, and even Lebeziatnikov eventually noticed it. Pyotr Petrovitch seemed agitated and kept rubbing his hands. Lebeziatnikov remembered all this and reflected on it afterward.

chapters.title: Part 5, Chapter 2
paragraphs: It would be hard to explain exactly what gave rise to the idea of that senseless dinner in Katerina Ivanovna's disordered mind. Nearly ten of the twenty rubles Raskolnikov had given for Marmeladov's funeral were squandered on it. Perhaps Katerina Ivanovna felt obligated to honor the dead man's memory "properly," so that all the lodgers, and especially Amalia Ivanovna, would see that "he was by no means inferior to them, and perhaps quite their superior," and that no one had the right "to look down on him." Perhaps the main factor was that peculiar poor-man's pride that compels so many destitute people to spend their last savings on some traditional social ritual, simply to be "like everyone else" and not "give anyone reason to despise them." Quite likely, too, Katerina Ivanovna longed to show on this particular occasion -- when she seemed abandoned by everyone -- that those "miserable, contemptible lodgers" should know "she understood how things were done, how to entertain," and that she had been raised "in a genteel, one might almost say an aristocratic colonel's family" and had not been destined for sweeping floors and washing the children's rags at night. Even the poorest, most broken-spirited people are sometimes seized by these fits of pride and vanity that take the form of an irresistible, nervous compulsion. And Katerina Ivanovna was not broken in spirit; circumstances might have killed her, but her spirit could never be crushed -- she could never be intimidated, her will could never be broken. Besides, Sonia had said with good reason that her mind was becoming unhinged. She couldn't exactly be called insane, but for the past year she had been under such relentless pressure that her mind might well have been strained past its limits. The later stages of tuberculosis, doctors say, tend to affect the brain.

The selection of wines was not impressive, and there was no Madeira; but wine there was. There was vodka, rum, and Lisbon wine, all of the cheapest quality but in decent quantities. Besides the traditional rice and honey dish, there were three or four other courses, one of them pancakes, all prepared in Amalia Ivanovna's kitchen. Two samovars were set up so that tea and punch could be offered after dinner. Katerina Ivanovna had done the shopping herself, with the help of one of the lodgers -- a wretched little Pole who had somehow ended up stranded at Madame Lippevechsel's. He had immediately put himself at Katerina Ivanovna's disposal and had spent all the previous day and all that morning running about with his legs barely keeping up, very anxious that everyone should notice his efforts. At every trifle he dashed back to Katerina Ivanovna, even tracking her down at the market, and constantly called her "Pani." By the end she was thoroughly sick of him, though at first she had proclaimed that without this "helpful and generous man" she couldn't have managed at all. It was one of Katerina Ivanovna's traits to paint everyone she met in the most glowing colors. Her praises were so extravagant as to be embarrassing; she would invent flattering details about a new acquaintance and believe them with perfect sincerity. Then just as suddenly she would become disillusioned and rudely, contemptuously cast off the person she had been literally worshiping only hours before. She was by nature cheerful, lively, and peace-loving, but endless failures and misfortunes had made her crave so desperately that everyone live in peace and joy and not dare to disturb it, that the slightest upset, the smallest misfortune, would drive her nearly to frenzy, and in an instant she would plunge from the brightest hopes and fantasies to cursing her fate and raving and banging her head against the wall.

Amalia Ivanovna, too, had suddenly risen enormously in Katerina Ivanovna's estimation and was treated with extraordinary respect -- probably only because she had thrown herself wholeheartedly into the preparations. She had volunteered to lay the table, provide the linens and crockery, and cook the dishes in her kitchen, and Katerina Ivanovna had left everything in her hands and gone off to the cemetery. Everything had turned out quite well: the tablecloth was nearly clean, and although the crockery, knives, forks, and glasses were of every possible shape and pattern, borrowed from various lodgers, the table was properly set by the appointed time. Amalia Ivanovna, feeling she had done her work well, had put on a black silk dress and a cap with new mourning ribbons and greeted the returning party with some pride. This pride, though justified, annoyed Katerina Ivanovna: "As if the table couldn't have been laid without Amalia Ivanovna!" She disliked the cap with its new ribbons too. "Was this stupid German putting on airs because she was the landlady and had agreed as a favor to help her poor lodgers? As a favor! Imagine! Katerina Ivanovna's father, who had been a colonel and practically a governor, sometimes set the table for forty guests, and a person like Amalia Ivanovna -- or rather, Ludwigovna -- wouldn't even have been allowed into the kitchen."

Katerina Ivanovna kept these feelings to herself for the moment, though she resolved that she would certainly have to put Amalia Ivanovna in her place and remind her of her proper station, since God only knew what the woman was starting to imagine. She was also irritated that hardly any of the invited lodgers had come to the funeral -- only the Pole, who had barely made it to the cemetery -- while at the memorial dinner, the most pathetic and insignificant of them had turned up, many not entirely sober. The older, more respectable lodgers had all stayed away, as though by prior agreement. Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, for example, who might be called the most respectable lodger of all, had not appeared, although the evening before, Katerina Ivanovna had told the whole world -- meaning Amalia Ivanovna, Polenka, Sonia, and the Pole -- that he was the most generous, noble-hearted man, with a large fortune and vast connections, who had been a friend of her first husband and a guest in her father's home, and who had promised to use all his influence to obtain her a substantial pension. It should be noted that when Katerina Ivanovna praised someone's connections and fortune, she did it without any ulterior motive, quite disinterestedly, for the sheer pleasure of enhancing the person's stature. Probably "following Luzhin's lead," "that contemptible wretch Lebeziatnikov hadn't shown up either. What did he think he was? He'd only been invited as a courtesy, because he shared a room with Pyotr Petrovitch and was his friend, so it would have been awkward not to ask him."

Among those who failed to appear were "the genteel lady and her spinster daughter," who had been lodgers for only about two weeks but had complained several times about noise and commotion from Katerina Ivanovna's quarters, especially when Marmeladov came home drunk. Katerina Ivanovna had heard this from Amalia Ivanovna, who, during a quarrel, had threatened to throw the whole family out, shouting that they "weren't worth the foot" of the respectable lodgers they were disturbing. Katerina Ivanovna now made it a point to invite this lady and her daughter, "whose foot she wasn't worth," and who had turned away haughtily when they passed her, so they would see that "her thoughts and feelings were more noble" and that "she harbored no malice," and understand that she was not accustomed to living this way. She intended to make this clear through references to her late father's quasi-governorship, while hinting that it was extremely foolish of them to snub her. The stout retired major (actually a discharged low-ranking officer) was also absent, having apparently been "not himself" for the past two days. The actual guests consisted of the little Pole; a pathetic-looking clerk with a pimply face and a greasy coat, who had nothing to say for himself and smelled abominably; a deaf and nearly blind old man who had once worked at the post office and whom someone at Amalia Ivanovna's had been supporting for ages.

A retired clerk from the commissariat department also came -- he was drunk, had a loud and extremely unseemly laugh, and -- can you imagine -- was wearing no waistcoat! One guest sat down at the table without even greeting Katerina Ivanovna. One person, having no proper suit, attempted to come in his dressing gown, but this was too much, and the combined efforts of Amalia Ivanovna and the Pole succeeded in removing him. The Pole, however, brought along two other Poles who didn't live at Amalia Ivanovna's and whom no one had ever seen there before. All of this infuriated Katerina Ivanovna. "Who had she made all these preparations for?" To make room for the guests, the children hadn't even been given places at the table. Instead, the two younger ones sat on a trunk in the far corner, their food set on a box in front of them, while Polenka, as the eldest, was expected to look after them, feed them, and keep their noses wiped "like well-bred children."

In fact, Katerina Ivanovna could hardly help receiving her guests with heightened dignity, even haughtiness. She fixed certain individuals with a severe stare, then loftily invited them to sit down. Having decided for some reason that Amalia Ivanovna must be to blame for the missing guests, she began treating her with extreme disdain, which the landlady immediately noticed and deeply resented. Such a beginning did not bode well for the end. At last everyone was seated.

Raskolnikov arrived at almost the same moment as the group returned from the cemetery. Katerina Ivanovna was delighted to see him, first because he was the one "educated guest, and everyone knew he was two years from becoming a university professor," and second because he immediately and respectfully apologized for having missed the funeral. She pounced on him and seated him at her left (Amalia Ivanovna was on her right). Despite her constant anxiety about the dishes being passed correctly and everyone tasting them, and despite the agonizing cough that interrupted her every minute and seemed to have worsened in recent days, she hastened to pour out in a half-whisper all her pent-up feelings and righteous indignation over the failed dinner, interspersing her complaints with lively, uncontrollable laughter at the expense of her guests and especially her landlady.

"It's all that cuckoo's fault! You know who I mean -- her, her!" Katerina Ivanovna nodded toward the landlady. "Look at her making big eyes -- she can tell we're talking about her but can't understand a word. The owl! Ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.) And what does she think she's doing in that cap? (Cough-cough-cough.) Have you noticed she wants everyone to think she's doing me a favor, gracing us with her presence? I asked her, like a sensible woman, to invite people, especially those who knew my late husband, and look at the collection of fools she's dragged in! The janitors! Look at that one with the pimply face. And those wretched Poles -- ha-ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.) Not one of them has ever set foot in here before. I've never laid eyes on them. What are they doing here, I ask you? There they sit in a row. Hey, pan!" she shouted suddenly at one of them, "have you tried the pancakes? Take some more! Have some beer! Won't you have vodka? Look, he's jumped up and bowing -- they must be half-starved, poor things. Well, let them eat! At least they're quiet. Though I am worried about the landlady's silver spoons... Amalia Ivanovna!" she said suddenly, almost aloud, "if your spoons happen to go missing, I won't be held responsible, I'm warning you! Ha-ha-ha!" She laughed, turning to Raskolnikov and nodding at the landlady again, delighted with her own wit. "She doesn't understand, she doesn't understand again! Look at her sitting there with her mouth hanging open! An owl -- a real owl! An owl in new ribbons, ha-ha-ha!"

Her laugh dissolved into an unbearable coughing fit that lasted five minutes. Drops of sweat stood on her forehead, and her handkerchief was spotted with blood. She silently showed the blood to Raskolnikov and, as soon as she could catch her breath, began whispering to him again with feverish animation, a hectic flush burning in her cheeks.

"You see, I gave her the most delicate instructions -- the most exquisite tact, you might say -- for inviting that lady and her daughter. You know who I mean? It required the utmost finesse, the greatest subtlety, but she handled it so badly that that fool, that conceited nobody, that provincial nonentity -- simply because she's the widow of a major and has come here to pester government offices about a pension and wear out her skirts in waiting rooms -- because at fifty she paints her face (everybody knows it) -- a creature like that didn't see fit to come and hasn't even responded to the invitation, which common decency required! I can't understand why Pyotr Petrovitch hasn't come either. But where's Sonia? Where did she go? Ah, there she is at last! What is it, Sonia -- where have you been? It's odd to be late even to your father's funeral. Rodion Romanovitch, make room for her beside you. That's your place, Sonia... take what you like. Have some of the cold appetizer with aspic -- that's the best. They'll bring the pancakes in a moment. Have the children been served? Polenka, do you have everything? (Cough-cough-cough.) Good. Be a good girl, Lida, and Kolya -- stop fidgeting with your feet. Sit like a little gentleman. What were you saying, Sonia?"

Sonia hastened to relay Pyotr Petrovitch's apologies, trying to speak loudly enough for everyone to hear and carefully using the most respectful phrases, which she attributed to Pyotr Petrovitch himself. She added that he had specifically asked her to say that as soon as possible he would come to discuss business with her privately and to consider what might be done for her, and so on.

Sonia knew this would comfort Katerina Ivanovna, would flatter and gratify her pride. She sat down beside Raskolnikov, gave him a quick bow, and glanced at him with fleeting curiosity. But for the rest of the time she seemed to avoid looking at him or speaking to him. She appeared distracted, though she kept watching Katerina Ivanovna, trying to please her. Neither she nor Katerina Ivanovna had been able to get mourning clothes. Sonia wore dark brown, and Katerina Ivanovna had on her only dress, a dark striped cotton one.

The message from Pyotr Petrovitch was a great success. Listening to Sonia with dignity, Katerina Ivanovna inquired with equal dignity about Pyotr Petrovitch's health, then immediately whispered almost aloud to Raskolnikov that it would certainly have been strange for a man of Pyotr Petrovitch's position and standing to find himself in such "extraordinary company," despite his devotion to her family and his old friendship with her father.

"That's why I'm so grateful to you, Rodion Romanovitch, for not disdaining my hospitality, even in such surroundings," she added, almost aloud. "But I'm sure it was only your special feeling for my poor husband that made you keep your promise."

Then, with renewed pride and dignity, she surveyed her guests and suddenly asked the deaf old man across the table in a loud voice whether he'd like more meat and whether he'd been given wine. The old man didn't answer and for a long time couldn't understand what was being asked, though his neighbors amused themselves by poking and shaking him. He simply stared around with his mouth open, which only increased the general hilarity.

"What an imbecile! Look at him! Why did they bring him? But as for Pyotr Petrovitch, I always had confidence in him," Katerina Ivanovna continued, addressing Amalia Ivanovna in such a sharp, loud voice that the landlady was taken aback, "not like your overdressed trollops, whom my father wouldn't have taken on as kitchen maids, and whom my late husband honored simply by inviting them, out of the goodness of his heart."
"Yes, he was fond of the drink, he was -- he certainly drank!" the commissariat clerk shouted, tossing back his twelfth glass of vodka.

"My late husband certainly had that weakness, and everyone knows it," Katerina Ivanovna pounced at once. "But he was a kind and honorable man who loved and respected his family. The trouble was that his good nature made him trust all sorts of disreputable people, and he drank with fellows who weren't worth the soles of his shoes. Would you believe it, Rodion Romanovitch -- they found a gingerbread rooster in his pocket! He was dead drunk, but he didn't forget the children!"
"A rooster? Did you say a rooster?" the commissariat clerk bellowed.
Katerina Ivanovna did not deign to reply. She sighed, lost in thought.

"No doubt you think, like everyone else, that I was too hard on him," she went on, addressing Raskolnikov. "But that's not true! He respected me -- he respected me deeply! He was kind-hearted! And how I pitied him sometimes! He'd sit in a corner and look at me, and I'd feel such pity for him, such an urge to be gentle -- and then I'd think: 'Be gentle with him and he'll start drinking again.' Strictness was the only thing that kept him in line."
"Yes, he got his hair pulled often enough!" roared the commissariat clerk, downing another glass.
"Some fools could use a good thrashing along with the hair-pulling. And I'm not talking about my late husband now!" Katerina Ivanovna snapped at him.

The flush on her cheeks deepened, her chest heaved. Another minute and she would have caused a scene. Many of the guests were snickering, clearly delighted. They began poking the commissariat clerk and whispering to him, obviously trying to egg him on.
"Allow me -- what exactly are you referring to?" the clerk began. "That is to say, whose -- about whom were you -- but never mind! Nonsense! A widow! I forgive you... I pass!"
And he drained another glass of vodka.

Raskolnikov sat in silence, listening with disgust. He ate only out of politeness, barely tasting the food that Katerina Ivanovna kept heaping on his plate, so as not to hurt her feelings. He watched Sonia intently. But Sonia grew more and more anxious and distressed; she too could see that the dinner would not end peacefully, and she watched Katerina Ivanovna's mounting irritation with dread. She knew that she, Sonia, was the main reason the "genteel" ladies had treated Katerina Ivanovna's invitation with contempt. She had heard from Amalia Ivanovna that the mother had been positively offended and had asked: "How could she seat her daughter next to that young woman?" Sonia sensed that Katerina Ivanovna had already found out about this, and an insult to Sonia meant more to Katerina Ivanovna than an insult to herself, her children, or her father. Sonia knew Katerina Ivanovna would not rest "until she had shown those trollops." To make things worse, someone at the far end of the table passed Sonia a plate with two hearts pierced by an arrow, cut from black bread. Katerina Ivanovna flushed crimson and immediately declared across the table that the sender was "a drunken jackass."

Amalia Ivanovna, sensing something unpleasant in the air and at the same time deeply offended by Katerina Ivanovna's haughtiness, attempted to restore the mood and raise herself in the company's estimation by suddenly, apropos of nothing, telling a story about an acquaintance of hers, "Karl from the chemist's," who was taking a cab one night, and "the cabman wanted him to kill, and Karl very much begged him not to kill, and wept and clasped his hands, and was frightened and from fear his heart was pierced." Although Katerina Ivanovna smiled, she immediately observed that Amalia Ivanovna really shouldn't attempt to tell anecdotes in Russian. The landlady took even greater offense and retorted that her "Vater aus Berlin was a very important man and always walked with his hands in his pockets." Katerina Ivanovna laughed so hard that Amalia Ivanovna nearly lost all patience.

"Listen to the owl!" Katerina Ivanovna whispered, her good humor almost restored. "She meant to say he kept his hands in his pockets, but she said he put his hands in people's pockets. (Cough-cough.) And have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, that all these Petersburg foreigners, especially the Germans, are stupider than us? Can you imagine anyone telling how 'Karl from the chemist's' had 'his heart pierced from fear' -- and that the idiot, instead of punishing the cabman, 'clasped his hands and wept and begged very much'? And she thinks it's terribly touching and doesn't even realize how stupid it is! To my mind, that drunken commissariat clerk is far more clever -- at least you can see he's drunk his brains away. But these foreigners are always so prim and serious... Look at her glaring! She's angry, ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.)"

Her mood restored, Katerina Ivanovna immediately launched into telling Raskolnikov that once she obtained her pension, she intended to open a boarding school for young ladies of good family in her native town of T----. This was the first time she had mentioned the plan to him, and she plunged into the most enchanting details. Somehow the very certificate of honor that Marmeladov had told Raskolnikov about in the tavern -- the one proving that Katerina Ivanovna had danced the shawl dance before the governor and other dignitaries upon finishing school -- suddenly appeared in her hands. This certificate was obviously meant to prove Katerina Ivanovna's right to open a boarding school, but it had been brought out mainly to crush "those two stuck-up trollops" should they appear, proving beyond doubt that Katerina Ivanovna came from "the most noble, one might even say aristocratic family, a colonel's daughter, and was far superior to certain adventuresses who have been so prominent lately." The certificate was immediately passed around among the drunken guests, and Katerina Ivanovna made no effort to hold on to it, since it actually stated in black and white that her father had held the rank of major and was also a companion of an order, making her practically a colonel's daughter.

Warming to her theme, Katerina Ivanovna elaborated on the peaceful, happy life they would lead in T----, on the high school teachers she would hire for her boarding school -- one of them a most respectable old Frenchman named Mangot, who had taught Katerina Ivanovna herself in her youth and was still living in T----, where he would no doubt accept a teaching position on reasonable terms. Next she spoke of Sonia, who would go with her to T---- and assist in all her plans. At this, someone at the far end of the table let out a sudden guffaw.

Though Katerina Ivanovna tried to appear disdainfully unaware of the laughter, she immediately raised her voice and began speaking with conviction about Sonia's undoubted ability to assist her, about "her gentleness, patience, devotion, generosity, and fine education," patting Sonia on the cheek and kissing her warmly twice. Sonia blushed crimson. Katerina Ivanovna suddenly burst into tears, immediately declaring that she was "being silly and emotional, that she was too overwrought, that it was time to stop, and since dinner was over, it was time to serve the tea."

At that moment, Amalia Ivanovna, deeply aggrieved at being excluded from the conversation, made one last effort and, with some trepidation, ventured an extremely weighty observation: that "in the future boarding school she would need to pay particular attention to die Wasche" and that "there certainly must be a good dame to look after the linen," and secondly that "the young ladies must not novels at night read."

Katerina Ivanovna, who was certainly upset and very tired, and thoroughly sick of the dinner, immediately cut her short, saying "she knew nothing about it and was talking nonsense, that it was the laundry maid's business to look after die Wasche, not the directress of a distinguished boarding school, and as for novel-reading, that was simply rude, and she begged her to be quiet." Amalia Ivanovna flared up and, getting angry, declared that she had only "meant her good" and that "she had meant her very good," and that "it was a long time since she had been paid her gold for the lodgings."

Katerina Ivanovna immediately "put her in her place," saying it was a lie that she wished her well, because just yesterday, while her dead husband was lying on the table, she had been hounding her about the rent. To this, Amalia Ivanovna very aptly replied that she had invited those ladies, but "those ladies did not come, because those ladies are ladies and cannot come to a lady who is not a lady." Katerina Ivanovna pointed out that, being a slut, Amalia Ivanovna was hardly in a position to judge what made a real lady. Amalia Ivanovna declared that her "Vater aus Berlin was a very, very important man and both hands in pockets went and always said 'Poof! Poof!'" and she leapt from the table to demonstrate her father, stuffing her hands in her pockets, puffing out her cheeks, and making vague sounds like "poof! poof!" to great laughter from the lodgers, who deliberately encouraged her, hoping for a fight.

But this was too much for Katerina Ivanovna, and she announced in a voice for all to hear that Amalia Ivanovna probably never had a father at all, that she was just some drunken Petersburg Finn who had no doubt once been a cook "and probably something worse." Amalia Ivanovna turned red as a lobster and shrieked that perhaps Katerina Ivanovna never had a father either, "but she had a Vater aus Berlin who wore a long coat and always said poof-poof-poof!"

Katerina Ivanovna remarked contemptuously that her family background was well known and that on that very certificate of honor it was printed that her father had been a colonel, while Amalia Ivanovna's father -- if she even had one -- was probably some Finnish milkman, though more likely she never had a father at all, since it remained unclear whether her name was Amalia Ivanovna or Amalia Ludwigovna.

At this, Amalia Ivanovna, driven to fury, pounded the table with her fist and screamed that she was Amalia Ivanovna, not Ludwigovna, "that her Vater was called Johann and was a burgomaster, and that Katerina Ivanovna's Vater was never at all a burgomaster." Katerina Ivanovna rose from her chair and, in a stern, apparently calm voice -- though she was white-faced and her chest was heaving -- declared that "if she dared for one moment to put her wretched father on the same level as her papa, she, Katerina Ivanovna, would tear the cap off her head and trample it underfoot." Amalia Ivanovna began running around the room, shouting at the top of her lungs that she was the landlady and Katerina Ivanovna must vacate the premises immediately; then she rushed to collect the silver spoons from the table. A tremendous uproar ensued; the children began to wail. Sonia rushed to restrain Katerina Ivanovna, but when Amalia Ivanovna shouted something about "the yellow ticket," Katerina Ivanovna shoved Sonia aside and lunged at the landlady to carry out her threat.
At that very moment the door opened, and Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin appeared on the threshold. He stood surveying the scene with severe, watchful eyes. Katerina Ivanovna rushed toward him.

chapters.title: Part 5, Chapter 3
paragraphs: "Pyotr Petrovitch," she cried, "protect me... you at least! Make this foolish woman understand she can't treat a lady in misfortune like this... There are laws against such things... I'll go to the governor-general himself... She will answer for this... Remembering my father's hospitality, protect these orphans."

"Allow me, madam... allow me." Pyotr Petrovitch waved her off. "As you are well aware, I did not have the honor of knowing your papa" (someone laughed out loud) "and I have no intention of getting involved in your endless squabbles with Amalia Ivanovna... I've come here on my own business... and I need to speak with your stepdaughter, Sofya... Ivanovna, I believe? Let me through."
Pyotr Petrovitch edged past her and went to the opposite corner where Sonia was standing.

Katerina Ivanovna stood frozen in place, as if struck by lightning. She couldn't understand how Pyotr Petrovitch could deny having enjoyed her father's hospitality. Though she'd invented the whole thing herself, she had come to believe it completely. She was also struck by Pyotr Petrovitch's businesslike, dry, and even contemptuous tone. The noise gradually died down as he entered. Not only was this "serious businessman" strikingly out of place at the gathering, but it was clear he had come on some important matter, that something exceptional must have brought him, and that something was about to happen. Raskolnikov, standing beside Sonia, stepped aside to let him pass; Pyotr Petrovitch didn't seem to notice him. A minute later Lebeziatnikov also appeared in the doorway; he didn't come in but stood listening with obvious interest, almost wonder, and seemed confused for a time.

"Forgive me for possibly interrupting, but it's a matter of some importance," Pyotr Petrovitch observed, addressing the company in general. "I'm glad to find other people present. Amalia Ivanovna, I humbly ask you, as mistress of the house, to pay careful attention to what I have to say to Sofya Ivanovna. Sofya Ivanovna," he continued, turning to Sonia, who was very surprised and already alarmed, "immediately after your visit, I found that a hundred-ruble note was missing from my table, in the room of my friend Mr. Lebeziatnikov. If you know in any way where it is now and will tell us, I give you my word of honor, with all present as witnesses, that the matter will end there. Otherwise, I will be forced to take very serious measures, and then... you'll have only yourself to blame."
Complete silence fell over the room. Even the crying children went quiet. Sonia stood deathly pale, staring at Luzhin, unable to say a word. She seemed not to understand. Several seconds passed.
"Well, what's it to be then?" asked Luzhin, looking at her intently.
"I don't know... I know nothing about it," Sonia said faintly at last.

"No, you know nothing?" Luzhin repeated, and paused again for a few seconds. "Think carefully, mademoiselle," he began severely, though still with a tone of admonishment. "Consider. I'm willing to give you time to think it over. Please understand: if I were not absolutely certain, I would never, with my experience, risk accusing you so directly. For such a direct accusation before witnesses, if it turned out to be false or even mistaken, I would bear some responsibility myself. I'm aware of that. This morning I cashed several five-percent bonds for approximately three thousand rubles. The figures are noted in my pocketbook. When I got home, I counted the money — as Mr. Lebeziatnikov will confirm — and after counting two thousand three hundred rubles, I put the rest in my pocketbook in my coat pocket. About five hundred rubles remained on the table, including three hundred-ruble notes. At that moment you came in, at my invitation, and the entire time you were here, you were extremely agitated — three times you jumped up in the middle of our conversation and tried to leave. Mr. Lebeziatnikov can confirm this. You yourself, mademoiselle, will probably not deny that I invited you through Mr. Lebeziatnikov solely to discuss the hopeless and destitute situation of your relative, Katerina Ivanovna, whose dinner I was unable to attend, and the possibility of organizing some kind of subscription or lottery for her benefit. You thanked me and even shed tears. I describe all this exactly as it happened, first to remind you, and second to show that not the slightest detail has escaped my memory. Then I took a ten-ruble note from the table and gave it to you as my initial contribution for your relative's benefit. Mr. Lebeziatnikov saw all of this. Then I walked you to the door — you were still in the same agitated state — after which, left alone with Mr. Lebeziatnikov, I spoke with him for about ten minutes. Then Mr. Lebeziatnikov went out and I returned to the table where the money lay, intending to count it and set it aside as I had planned. To my surprise, one hundred-ruble note had disappeared. Consider the situation carefully. I cannot suspect Mr. Lebeziatnikov — the very idea is beneath me. I cannot have miscounted, because just before you arrived I had finished my accounts and found the total correct. You'll admit that, given your agitation, your eagerness to leave, the fact that your hands were on the table for some time, and considering your social position and the habits associated with it, I was — so to speak, with horror and very much against my will — compelled to form a suspicion: a cruel but justified suspicion! I'll add further that despite my firm conviction, I realize I'm taking a certain risk in making this accusation. But as you can see, I could not let it go. I have taken action, and I'll tell you why: solely, madam, solely because of your black ingratitude! I invite you to help your destitute relative, I give you my donation of ten rubles, and you immediately repay me with such an act. It's outrageous! You need a lesson. Think it over! As a true friend — and you could have no better friend right now — I urge you to consider what you're doing, or I will not relent! Well, what do you say?"
"I took nothing," Sonia whispered in terror. "You gave me ten rubles — here, take it back."
Sonia pulled a handkerchief from her pocket, untied a corner of it, took out the ten-ruble note, and held it out to Luzhin.
"And the hundred rubles — you won't admit to taking those?" he pressed reproachfully, not taking the note.

Sonia looked around. Everyone was staring at her with terrible, stern, mocking, hostile eyes. She looked at Raskolnikov... He stood against the wall with his arms crossed, looking at her with burning eyes.
"Good God!" escaped from Sonia.
"Amalia Ivanovna, we'll need to notify the police, so I humbly ask you to send for the building superintendent in the meantime," Luzhin said softly and almost kindly.
"Gott der Barmherzige! I knew she was the thief!" cried Amalia Ivanovna, throwing up her hands.
"You knew it?" Luzhin seized on this. "Then I take it you had some prior reason for thinking so. I ask you, worthy Amalia Ivanovna, to remember what you just said — you've spoken before witnesses."
A buzz of loud conversation erupted from all sides. Everyone was stirring.
"What!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, suddenly grasping the situation, and she rushed at Luzhin. "What! You're accusing her of stealing? Sonia? You wretches, you wretches!"
She ran to Sonia, threw her wasted arms around her, and held her tight as a vise.
"Sonia! How dare you take ten rubles from him? Foolish girl! Give it to me! Give me the ten rubles right now — here!"

Snatching the note from Sonia, Katerina Ivanovna crumpled it up and flung it straight into Luzhin's face. It hit him in the eye and fell to the floor. Amalia Ivanovna scrambled to pick it up. Pyotr Petrovitch lost his temper.
"Restrain that mad woman!" he shouted.
At that moment several other people appeared in the doorway alongside Lebeziatnikov, including two ladies.

"What! Mad? Am I mad? Idiot!" shrieked Katerina Ivanovna. "You're the idiot, you petty lawyer, you vile man! Sonia, Sonia, take his money! Sonia, a thief! She'd give away her last kopeck!" Katerina Ivanovna broke into hysterical laughter. "Have you ever seen such an idiot?" She turned from side to side. "And you too?" She suddenly spotted the landlady. "You too, sausage-eater! You're calling her a thief, you trashy Prussian hen-leg in a crinoline! She hasn't been out of this room — she came straight from your place and sat down beside me. Everyone saw it. She was sitting right here, next to Rodion Romanovitch. Search her! Since she hasn't left the room, the money would have to be on her! Go ahead, search her! But if you don't find it, then excuse me, my dear fellow, you'll answer for it! I'll go to our Sovereign, to our gracious Tsar himself, and throw myself at his feet — today, this very minute! I'm alone in the world! They'd let me in! You think they wouldn't? You're wrong — I will get in! You counted on her meekness! You relied on that! But I'm not so submissive, let me tell you! You've gone too far. Search her, search her!"
Katerina Ivanovna, frenzied, shook Luzhin and dragged him toward Sonia.

"I'm ready, I'll take responsibility... but please calm down, madam, calm down. I see you're not so submissive after all!... Well, well, but as for the search..." Luzhin stammered, "that should really be done before the police... though there are enough witnesses as it is... I'm willing... But it's rather awkward for a man... given her sex... But with Amalia Ivanovna's help... though of course that's not the proper way to do things... How should we proceed?"

"Anyone who wants can search her!" cried Katerina Ivanovna. "Sonia, turn out your pockets! See! Look, you monster — the pocket's empty! Here was her handkerchief! Here's the other pocket — look! See, you see?"

Katerina Ivanovna turned — or rather yanked — both pockets inside out. But from the right pocket a piece of paper flew out, traced a curve through the air, and landed at Luzhin's feet. Everyone saw it; several cried out. Pyotr Petrovitch bent down, picked up the paper between two fingers, held it up where everyone could see it, and unfolded it. It was a hundred-ruble note folded into eighths. Pyotr Petrovitch displayed it for all to see.
"Thief! Out of my apartment! Police, police!" yelled Amalia Ivanovna. "They must be sent to Siberia! Get out!"

Exclamations rose from all sides. Raskolnikov stayed silent, keeping his eyes fixed on Sonia, with only an occasional quick glance at Luzhin. Sonia stood motionless, as if unconscious. She could barely feel surprise. Suddenly color rushed to her cheeks; she cried out and hid her face in her hands.
"No, it wasn't me! I didn't take it! I know nothing about it!" she cried with a heartrending wail, rushing to Katerina Ivanovna, who clasped her tightly, as though to shield her from the whole world.

"Sonia! Sonia! I don't believe it! You see — I don't believe it!" she cried in the face of the obvious evidence, rocking her in her arms like a baby, kissing her face over and over, then grabbing her hands and kissing them too. "You took it! How stupid these people are! You fools, all of you!" she cried, addressing the entire room. "You don't know, you don't know what a heart she has, what kind of girl she is! Her, steal? She'd sell her last scrap of clothing, she'd go barefoot to help you if you needed it — that's who she is! She has the yellow card because my children were starving — she sold herself for us! Oh, husband, husband! Do you see? Do you see? What a memorial dinner for you! Merciful heavens! Defend her — why are you all just standing there? Rodion Romanovitch, why won't you stand up for her? Do you believe it too? None of you are worth her little finger! God, defend her now!"

The wailing of the poor, consumptive, helpless woman seemed to produce a powerful effect on her audience. The agonized, wasted, consumptive face, the cracked blood-stained lips, the hoarse voice, the tears flowing freely as a child's, the trusting, childlike yet despairing plea for help — it was all so pitiful that everyone seemed to feel for her. Pyotr Petrovitch was at least immediately moved to compassion.

"Madam, madam, this doesn't reflect on you at all!" he cried impressively. "No one would dream of accusing you of being involved or even of being an accomplice, especially since you proved her guilt yourself by turning out her pockets, showing you had no prior knowledge. I'm perfectly ready, perfectly ready to show compassion if poverty, so to speak, drove Sofya Semyonovna to it. But why did you refuse to confess, mademoiselle? Were you afraid of the disgrace? Your first time? You lost your composure, perhaps? Quite understandable... But how could you sink to such an act? Gentlemen," he addressed the whole room, "gentlemen! Feeling compassion for these people, I'm ready to forgive it all even now, despite the personal insult I've received. And may this disgrace serve as a lesson to you in future," he said to Sonia. "I'll take the matter no further. Enough!"

Pyotr Petrovitch stole a glance at Raskolnikov. Their eyes met, and the fire in Raskolnikov's seemed ready to burn him to ashes. Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna appeared to hear nothing. She was kissing and hugging Sonia like a madwoman. The children were also pressing around Sonia from all sides, and Polenka — though she didn't fully understand what was happening — was drowning in tears and shaking with sobs, burying her pretty little face, swollen from crying, against Sonia's shoulder.
"How despicable!" a loud voice suddenly rang out from the doorway.
Pyotr Petrovitch spun around quickly.
"What vileness!" Lebeziatnikov repeated, staring him straight in the face.
Pyotr Petrovitch actually flinched — everyone noticed and remembered it later. Lebeziatnikov strode into the room.
"And you dared to call me as a witness?" he said, walking right up to Pyotr Petrovitch.
"What do you mean? What are you talking about?" Luzhin muttered.
"I mean that you... are a slanderer — that's what my words mean!" Lebeziatnikov said hotly, fixing him with a stern look through his nearsighted eyes.
He was extremely angry. Raskolnikov watched him intently, as though weighing every word. Again there was silence. Pyotr Petrovitch seemed almost struck dumb, at least for the first moment.
"If that's directed at me..." he began, stammering. "But what's wrong with you? Have you lost your mind?"

"I'm perfectly sane, but you're a scoundrel! How despicable! I heard everything. I waited on purpose to make sure I understood, because I'll admit even now the logic isn't entirely clear to me... What you did it all for, I can't grasp."
"What exactly have I done? Stop talking in your ridiculous riddles! Or are you drunk?"

"You might be the drunkard, you vile man, but I'm not! I never touch vodka — it's against my principles. Listen to this, everyone: he himself, with his own hands, gave Sofya Semyonovna that hundred-ruble note! I saw it — I'm a witness, and I'll swear to it! He did it, he did it!" Lebeziatnikov repeated, addressing the whole room.
"Are you out of your mind, you fool?" squealed Luzhin. "She herself just told everyone, right in front of you, that I only gave her ten rubles. How could I have given it to her?"

"I saw it! I saw it!" Lebeziatnikov insisted. "And even though it's against my principles, I'm ready this very minute to swear any oath you want in court, because I saw you slip it into her pocket. Only I was fool enough to think you did it out of kindness! When you were saying goodbye at the door, while you held her hand in one hand, you slipped the note into her pocket with the other — the left one. I saw it!"
Luzhin turned pale.
"What lies!" he cried brazenly. "How could you, standing by the window, have seen the note? You imagined it with your nearsighted eyes. You're raving!"

"No, I didn't imagine it. And even though I was standing some distance away, I saw everything clearly. True, it would have been hard to identify a banknote from the window — you're right about that — but I happened to know it was a hundred-ruble note, because when you were about to give Sofya Semyonovna ten rubles, you picked up a hundred-ruble note from the table. I saw it because I was standing close by at that moment, and an idea immediately struck me, so I didn't forget you had it in your hand. You folded it and kept holding it. I didn't think about it again until you were getting up, when you shifted it from your right hand to your left and nearly dropped it. I noticed because the same idea occurred to me again — that you meant to do her a secret kindness without me seeing. You can imagine how closely I was watching after that, and I saw you succeed in slipping it into her pocket. I saw it! I'll take an oath on it!"

Lebeziatnikov was almost out of breath. Exclamations rose from all sides, mostly expressing astonishment, but some sounding menacing. Everyone crowded around Pyotr Petrovitch. Katerina Ivanovna rushed to Lebeziatnikov.
"I was wrong about you! Protect her! You're the only one defending her! She's an orphan — God has sent you!"
Katerina Ivanovna, barely knowing what she was doing, sank to her knees before him.

"Utter nonsense!" Luzhin roared, furious. "Everything you've said is nonsense! 'An idea struck you, you didn't think, you noticed' — what does any of it prove? So I slipped it to her secretly, on purpose? What for? What reason? What do I have to do with this...?"

"What for? That's what I can't figure out either, but what I'm telling you is a fact — I'm certain of it! Far from being mistaken, you despicable criminal, I remember that a question occurred to me right then, just as I was thanking you and shaking your hand. Why did you put it in her pocket secretly? Why the secrecy? Was it just to hide it from me, knowing my principles oppose private charity as it doesn't achieve any fundamental cure? Well, I decided you must have been ashamed to give such a large sum in front of me. Then I thought maybe you wanted to surprise her — when she'd find a whole hundred-ruble note in her pocket. I know some charitable people love staging their good deeds that way. Then another idea struck me: you wanted to test her, to see if she'd come to thank you when she found it. Then I thought you just wanted to avoid being thanked — as the saying goes, your right hand shouldn't know what your left hand does. I considered so many possibilities that I put off examining it further, though I did feel it would be tactless to show you I knew your secret. But then yet another thought struck me: that Sofya Semyonovna might easily lose the money before she noticed it. That's why I decided to come find her, to tell her you'd put a hundred rubles in her pocket. But on the way I stopped at Madame Kobilatnikov's to drop off the 'General Treatise on the Positive Method,' especially recommending Piderit's article and Wagner's. Then I come here and find — this! Now, could I have had all these thoughts and considerations if I hadn't actually seen you put the hundred-ruble note in her pocket?"

By the time Lebeziatnikov finished his long-winded speech, complete with its logical conclusion, he was quite exhausted, and perspiration was streaming down his face. Unfortunately, he couldn't even express himself properly in Russian, though he knew no other language, so he was completely drained, almost gaunt after this heroic effort. But his speech produced a powerful effect. He'd spoken with such passion, such conviction, that everyone clearly believed him. Pyotr Petrovitch felt that things were going very badly for him.

"What do I care if stupid ideas popped into your head?" he shouted. "That's not evidence. You could have dreamed it all! I'm telling you, you're lying, sir! Lying and slandering me out of spite, simply because I refused to go along with your godless, free-thinking social ideas!"
But this retort did not help Pyotr Petrovitch. Murmurs of disapproval came from all sides.

"Oh, so that's your tack now, is it?" cried Lebeziatnikov. "That's absurd! Call the police — I'll take my oath! There's only one thing I can't understand: what made him risk such a contemptible act. What a pitiful, despicable man!"
"I can explain why he risked it, and if necessary, I'll swear to it too," Raskolnikov said at last in a firm voice, stepping forward.
He appeared calm and composed. Everyone felt clearly, just from looking at him, that he really did know the answer and that the mystery was about to be solved.

"Now I can explain it all," said Raskolnikov, addressing Lebeziatnikov. "From the very beginning, I suspected there was some vile scheme behind this. I began to suspect it based on certain circumstances known only to me, which I'll share with everyone now — they explain everything. Your valuable testimony has made it all clear. I ask everyone to listen. This man" — he pointed at Luzhin — "was recently engaged to my sister, Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikov. But upon arriving in Petersburg, he quarreled with me at our first meeting the day before yesterday, and I threw him out of my room. I have two witnesses to that. He's a very spiteful man... The day before yesterday, I didn't know he was staying here in your room, and so on that very same day — the day we quarreled — he saw me give money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, as a friend of the late Mr. Marmeladov. He immediately wrote to my mother claiming I'd given all my money not to Katerina Ivanovna but to Sofya Semyonovna, making the most contemptible insinuations about my relationship with Sofya Semyonovna. All this was designed to turn my mother and sister against me, by suggesting I was squandering on unworthy things the money they'd sent — their last money. Yesterday evening, in front of my mother, my sister, and Luzhin himself, I stated that I'd given the money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, not to Sofya Semyonovna, and that I had no acquaintance with Sofya Semyonovna and had never even seen her before. I added that Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, with all his fine qualities, wasn't worth Sofya Semyonovna's little finger, despite his speaking so badly of her. When he asked whether I'd seat Sofya Semyonovna next to my sister, I replied that I'd already done so that day. Outraged that my mother and sister refused to quarrel with me based on his insinuations, he grew inexcusably rude to them. A final break occurred and he was thrown out of the house. All of this happened yesterday evening. Now pay special attention to this: if he had succeeded today in proving Sofya Semyonovna was a thief, he would have shown my mother and sister that he was nearly right in his suspicions — that he'd had good reason to be angry at my putting my sister on a level with Sofya Semyonovna — that by attacking me, he'd been protecting my sister's honor. In short, through all this he might even have managed to set my family against me, and he no doubt hoped to be restored to their good graces — to say nothing of his personal revenge on me, since he has reason to believe that Sofya Semyonovna's honor and happiness matter greatly to me. That's what he was scheming. That's the whole explanation, and there can be no other!"

That was roughly how Raskolnikov concluded his speech, which was heard very attentively though frequently interrupted by exclamations from the audience. Despite the interruptions, he spoke clearly, calmly, precisely, and firmly. His decisive voice, his tone of conviction, and his stern expression made a powerful impression on everyone.

"Yes, yes, that's exactly it!" Lebeziatnikov confirmed enthusiastically. "It must be, because he asked me, as soon as Sofya Semyonovna came into our room, whether you were here — whether I'd seen you among Katerina Ivanovna's guests. He called me over to the window and asked me in secret. It was essential for him that you be here! That's it — that's exactly it!"

Luzhin smiled contemptuously and said nothing. But he was very pale. He seemed to be calculating some means of escape. Perhaps he would gladly have simply left, but at that point it was practically impossible — leaving would have been an admission that the accusations against him were true. Besides, the crowd, already worked up by drink, was now far too agitated to let him go. The commissariat clerk, who hadn't fully grasped the situation, was shouting louder than anyone and making suggestions highly unpleasant for Luzhin. But not everyone present was drunk — lodgers had come in from every room. The three Poles were tremendously excited, shouting at him constantly: "The pan is a scoundrel!" and muttering threats in Polish. Sonia had been listening with strained attention, though she too seemed unable to take it all in; she looked as if she were just coming to. She kept her eyes on Raskolnikov, sensing that all her safety lay with him. Katerina Ivanovna was breathing hard and painfully, looking terribly exhausted. Amalia Ivanovna stood there looking more bewildered than anyone, mouth hanging open, unable to make out what had happened. She only understood that Pyotr Petrovitch had somehow come to grief.

Raskolnikov tried to speak again, but they wouldn't let him. Everyone was crowding around Luzhin with threats and shouts of abuse. But Pyotr Petrovitch was not intimidated. Seeing that his accusation of Sonia had completely collapsed, he resorted to brazenness:

"Let me through, gentlemen, let me through! Don't crowd me!" he said, pushing through the mob. "And spare me the threats, please! I assure you they're useless. On the contrary, you'll be held responsible, gentlemen, for violently obstructing justice. The thief has been more than exposed, and I shall prosecute. Our judges are not so blind and... not so drunk, and will not take the word of two notorious troublemakers, atheists, and agitators accusing me out of personal vengeance — which they're foolish enough to admit... Yes, let me through!"

"I don't want to find a single trace of you in my room! Get out at once, and everything between us is finished! When I think of the trouble I've gone to, the way I've been lecturing you... this entire fortnight!"
"I told you myself today I was leaving, when you tried to keep me. I'll simply add that you're a fool. I suggest you see a doctor about your brains and your eyesight. Let me pass, gentlemen!"

He forced his way through. But the commissariat clerk wasn't prepared to let him off so easily: he grabbed a glass from the table, waved it in the air, and hurled it at Pyotr Petrovitch — but it flew straight into Amalia Ivanovna instead. She screamed, and the clerk, losing his balance, crashed heavily under the table. Pyotr Petrovitch made his way to his room and half an hour later had left the building. Sonia, timid by nature, had always known she was more vulnerable to mistreatment than anyone, that she could be wronged with impunity. Until that day she'd believed she might escape misfortune through care, gentleness, and meekness toward everyone. Her disappointment was too great. She could bear almost anything with patience and scarcely a complaint — even this. But in those first moments it was too bitter. Despite her vindication and her triumph — once the initial terror and shock had passed and she could see things clearly — the feeling of helplessness and of the wrong done to her filled her heart with anguish, and she was overcome by hysterical weeping. Finally, unable to endure any more, she rushed from the room and ran home, almost immediately after Luzhin's departure. When the glass flew at Amalia Ivanovna amid loud laughter, it was more than the landlady could stand. She let out a shriek and flew at Katerina Ivanovna like a fury, blaming her for everything.
"Out of my apartment! This instant! Get out!"

She began snatching up everything she could lay hands on that belonged to Katerina Ivanovna and hurling it to the floor. Katerina Ivanovna, pale, almost fainting, gasping for breath, sprang from the bed where she'd collapsed in exhaustion and rushed at Amalia Ivanovna. But the battle was hopelessly one-sided: the landlady swatted her away like a feather.

"What! As if that godless slander weren't enough — this vile creature attacks me! On the day of my husband's funeral, I'm thrown out of my home! After eating my bread and salt, she throws me into the street with my orphans! Where am I supposed to go?" wailed the poor woman, sobbing and gasping. "God!" she cried, her eyes flashing. "Is there no justice on earth? Who should You protect if not us orphans? We'll see! There is law and justice on this earth — there is, and I'll find it! Just wait, you godless creature! Polenka, stay with the children — I'll be back. Wait for me, even if you have to wait in the street. We'll see whether there's any justice left!"

Throwing that green shawl over her head — the one Marmeladov had mentioned to Raskolnikov — Katerina Ivanovna squeezed through the rowdy, drunken crowd of lodgers still filling the room and ran out into the street, wailing and weeping, with some vague intention of immediately going to find justice. Polenka, clutching the two little ones in her arms, crouched terrified on the trunk in the corner, waiting trembling for her mother's return. Amalia Ivanovna stormed around the room, shrieking, wailing, and hurling everything she came across to the floor. The lodgers talked all at once — some commenting on what had happened, others quarreling and swearing, still others breaking into song...
"Now it's time for me to go," Raskolnikov thought. "Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we'll see what you have to say now!"
And he set off toward Sonia's lodgings.

chapters.title: Part 5, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Raskolnikov had been a vigorous champion of Sonia against Luzhin, despite carrying such a weight of horror and anguish in his own heart. But having endured so much that morning, he found a kind of relief in a change of emotions, apart from the strong personal impulse that drove him to defend Sonia. He was also agitated, especially at certain moments, by the thought of his approaching conversation with Sonia: he had to tell her who killed Lizaveta. He knew the terrible suffering it would cause him, and he kept pushing the thought away. So when he cried out on leaving Katerina Ivanovna's, "Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we shall see what you'll say now!" he was still outwardly excited, still energized and defiant from his victory over Luzhin. But strangely, by the time he reached Sonia's lodging, he felt a sudden helplessness and fear. He stopped at the door, asking himself the strange question: "Do I have to tell her who killed Lizaveta?" It was strange because he knew he couldn't help telling her, and couldn't put it off any longer. He didn't yet know why it had to be done — he only felt it — and the agonizing sense of his powerlessness before the inevitable nearly crushed him. To cut short his hesitation and suffering, he quickly opened the door and looked at Sonia from the doorway. She was sitting with her elbows on the table, her face in her hands, but seeing Raskolnikov she got up at once and came toward him as though she had been expecting him.
"What would have become of me without you?" she said quickly, meeting him in the middle of the room.
Clearly she had been desperate to say this to him. It was what she had been waiting for.
Raskolnikov went to the table and sat down in the chair she had just risen from. She stood facing him, two steps away, exactly as she had the day before.
"Well, Sonia?" he said, feeling his voice tremble. "It was all because of 'your social position and the habits associated with it.' Did you understand that just now?"
Her face showed her distress.
"Just don't talk to me the way you did yesterday," she interrupted. "Please don't start. There's enough misery without that."
She hurried to smile, afraid he might not like the reproach.
"It was silly of me to leave. What's happening there now? I wanted to go back right away, but I kept thinking that... you would come."
He told her that Amalia Ivanovna was throwing them out and that Katerina Ivanovna had run off somewhere "to seek justice."
"My God!" cried Sonia. "Let's go at once..."
She snatched up her cape.
"It's always the same with you!" Raskolnikov said irritably. "You have no thought for anyone but them! Stay with me for a while."
"But... Katerina Ivanovna?"
"You won't miss Katerina Ivanovna, don't worry. She'll come to you on her own since she's run out," he added peevishly. "If she doesn't find you here, you'll be blamed for it..."
Sonia sat down in painful suspense. Raskolnikov was silent, staring at the floor, deliberating.

"This time Luzhin didn't want to prosecute you," he began, not looking at Sonia. "But if he had, if it had suited his plans, he would have sent you to prison — if not for Lebeziatnikov and me. Right?"
"Yes," she agreed in a faint voice. "Yes," she repeated, preoccupied and distressed.
"But I might easily not have been there. And Lebeziatnikov showing up was pure accident."
Sonia was silent.
"And if you'd gone to prison — what then? Do you remember what I said yesterday?"
Again she didn't answer. He waited.

"I thought you'd cry out again, 'Don't say it, stop.'" Raskolnikov gave a laugh, though a forced one. "Still silent?" he asked a minute later. "We have to talk about something, you know. I'd actually like to know how you'd resolve a certain 'problem,' as Lebeziatnikov would put it." He was beginning to lose the thread. "No, really, I'm serious. Imagine, Sonia, that you'd known all of Luzhin's intentions beforehand — known for certain that they would ruin Katerina Ivanovna and the children, and you too — since you don't count yourself — Polenka as well, because she'd end up the same way. Well, what if suddenly it all depended on your decision whether he or they would go on living — whether Luzhin should live and keep doing evil, or Katerina Ivanovna should die? How would you decide which of them should die? That's my question."
Sonia looked at him anxiously. There was something peculiar in this halting question — it seemed to be approaching something in a roundabout way.
"I had a feeling you were going to ask something like that," she said, looking at him searchingly.
"I'm sure you did. But how would you answer it?"
"Why do you ask about something that could never happen?" Sonia said reluctantly.
"So it would be better for Luzhin to go on living and doing evil? You haven't even dared to decide that!"

"But I can't know God's will... And why do you ask what can't be answered? What use are such pointless questions? How could it depend on my decision? Who made me a judge over who should live and who should die?"
"Oh, once you bring God into it, nothing can be done," Raskolnikov grumbled darkly.
"Just say straight out what you want!" Sonia cried in distress. "You're leading up to something again... Did you come here just to torture me?"
She couldn't control herself and burst into bitter tears. He looked at her in gloomy misery. Five minutes passed.

"Of course you're right, Sonia," he said softly at last. He was suddenly changed. His tone of assumed arrogance and helpless defiance was gone. Even his voice had suddenly gone weak. "I told you yesterday I wasn't coming to ask forgiveness, and almost the first thing I've done is ask forgiveness... What I said about Luzhin and Providence — that was for my own sake. I was asking forgiveness, Sonia..."
He tried to smile, but there was something helpless and incomplete in his pale smile. He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands.

And suddenly a strange, startling wave of bitter hatred for Sonia passed through his heart. Alarmed and bewildered by this feeling, he lifted his head and looked intently at her; but he met her anxious, painfully worried eyes fixed on him — there was love in them. His hatred vanished like a phantom. It wasn't the real feeling; he had mistaken one emotion for the other. It only meant that the moment had come.
He hid his face in his hands again and bowed his head. Suddenly he went pale, rose from the chair, looked at Sonia, and without a word sat down mechanically on her bed.
That moment felt terrifyingly similar to the one when he had stood over the old woman with the axe in his hand and felt he must not lose another second.
"What's wrong?" asked Sonia, terribly frightened.

He couldn't speak. This was not at all, not at all how he had planned to tell her, and he didn't understand what was happening to him. She went to him softly, sat down on the bed beside him, and waited, not taking her eyes off him. Her heart pounded and sank. It was unbearable. He turned his deathly pale face toward her. His lips moved, straining helplessly to form words. A wave of terror passed through Sonia's heart.
"What's wrong?" she repeated, drawing back slightly.

"Nothing, Sonia, don't be frightened... It's nonsense. Really, it's all nonsense when you think about it," he muttered, like someone delirious. "Why did I come to torture you?" he added suddenly, looking at her. "Honestly, why? I keep asking myself that, Sonia..."
He had perhaps been asking himself that question fifteen minutes ago, but now he spoke helplessly, barely aware of what he was saying, trembling all over.
"Oh, how you're suffering!" she whispered in distress, looking at him intently.
"It's all nonsense... Listen, Sonia." He suddenly smiled — a pale, helpless smile that lasted two seconds. "You remember what I was going to tell you yesterday?"
Sonia waited uneasily.
"I said as I was leaving that I might be saying goodbye forever, but that if I came today, I would tell you who... who killed Lizaveta."
She began trembling all over.
"Well, I've come to tell you."
"Then you really meant it yesterday?" she whispered with difficulty. "How do you know?" she asked quickly, as if suddenly regaining her senses.
Sonia's face grew paler and paler, and she was breathing with difficulty.
"I know."
She paused for a minute.
"Have they found him?" she asked timidly.
"No."
"Then how do you know about it?" she asked again, barely audibly, after another minute's pause.
He turned to her and looked at her very intently.
"Guess," he said, with the same twisted, helpless smile.
A shudder ran through her.
"But you... why are you frightening me like this?" she said, smiling like a child.

"I must be a very close friend of his... since I know," Raskolnikov continued, still gazing into her face as though unable to look away. "He... didn't mean to kill Lizaveta...
