He killed her by accident... He meant to kill the old woman while she was alone, and he went there... and then Lizaveta came in... and he killed her too."
Another terrible moment passed. They still stared at each other.
"You can't guess?" he asked suddenly, feeling as though he were throwing himself off a cliff.
"N-no..." whispered Sonia.
"Take a good look."

The moment he said it, the same familiar sensation froze his heart. He looked at her and suddenly seemed to see Lizaveta's face in hers. He clearly remembered Lizaveta's expression when he had approached her with the axe and she had backed against the wall, stretching out her hand with childlike terror in her face — looking the way small children do when something begins to frighten them, staring fixedly and anxiously at whatever scares them, shrinking back and holding out their little hands, on the verge of tears. Almost the same thing was happening now with Sonia. With the same helplessness and the same terror, she gazed at him for a long time. Then suddenly she put out her left hand, pressed her fingers weakly against his chest, and slowly began to rise from the bed, moving further away while keeping her eyes fixed on him even more intensely. Her terror was contagious. The same fear appeared on his face. He stared back at her in almost the same childlike way.
"Have you guessed?" he whispered at last.
"Good God!" An awful wail tore from her chest.

She collapsed helplessly onto the bed, face in the pillows, but a moment later she sat up, moved quickly toward him, seized both his hands, and gripping them tight with her thin fingers, stared into his face again with that same desperate look. In this last, desperate gaze she tried to search him and find some last shred of hope. But there was no hope; there was no doubt left; it was all true. Later, when she recalled that moment, she found it strange that she had seen it all so clearly at once. She couldn't have said, for instance, that she had foreseen something like this — and yet now, the moment he told her, she felt as if she really had foreseen it all along.
"Stop, Sonia, enough! Don't torture me," he begged miserably.
It was not at all, not at all the way he had imagined telling her — but this was how it happened.

She jumped up, seeming not to know what she was doing, and wringing her hands, walked to the middle of the room. But she quickly went back and sat down beside him again, her shoulder almost touching his. Then all at once she flinched as though stabbed, cried out, and fell to her knees before him, not knowing why.
"What have you done — what have you done to yourself?" she cried in despair. She sprang up, threw her arms around his neck, and held him tight.
Raskolnikov pulled back and looked at her with a mournful smile.
"You're a strange girl, Sonia — you kiss me and embrace me when I tell you about that... You don't realize what you're doing."
"There is no one — no one in the whole world now as unhappy as you!" she cried in a frenzy, not hearing his words, and she broke into violent, hysterical weeping.
A feeling long unfamiliar flooded his heart and softened it at once. He didn't fight it. Two tears rose to his eyes and hung on his lashes.
"Then you won't leave me, Sonia?" he said, looking at her almost with hope.
"No, no, never, nowhere!" cried Sonia. "I'll follow you — I'll follow you everywhere! Oh God! How miserable I am!... Why didn't I know you before? Why didn't you come to me sooner? Oh, God!"
"Here I've come."
"Yes, now! What should we do now?... Together, together!" she repeated as if unconsciously, hugging him again. "I'll follow you to Siberia!"
He recoiled, and the same hostile, almost contemptuous smile appeared on his lips.
"Maybe I don't want to go to Siberia yet, Sonia," he said.
Sonia looked at him quickly.

After her first passionate, agonizing sympathy for the unhappy man, the terrible reality of the murder overwhelmed her again. In his changed tone she seemed to hear the murderer speaking. She stared at him in bewilderment. She still knew nothing — why, how, for what purpose. Now all those questions rushed into her mind at once. And again she couldn't believe it: "He — he is a murderer! Is it possible?"

"What does this mean? Where am I?" she said in utter bewilderment, as though unable to come to her senses. "How could you — you, a man like you... How could you bring yourself to it? What does it mean?"
"Oh, to rob her. Stop, Sonia," he answered wearily, almost with irritation.
Sonia stood as if struck dumb, but suddenly she burst out:
"You were hungry! It was... to help your mother? Yes?"
"No, Sonia, no," he muttered, turning away and hanging his head. "I wasn't that hungry... I did want to help my mother, yes, but... that's not the real reason either... Don't torture me, Sonia."
Sonia clasped her hands.

"Can it really be true? Good God, what a truth! Who could believe it? And how could you give away your last kopeck and yet rob and murder? Oh!" she cried suddenly. "That money you gave Katerina Ivanovna... that money. Could it possibly be..."

"No, Sonia," he broke in quickly. "That money wasn't from the robbery. Don't worry! My mother sent it, and it arrived while I was sick — the day I gave it to you... Razumikhin saw it... he received it for me... That money was mine — my own."
Sonia listened in bewilderment, trying her hardest to comprehend.

"And that money... I don't even really know if there was any money," he added softly, as if thinking aloud. "I took a purse from her neck, made of chamois leather... a purse stuffed full of something... but I didn't look inside; I suppose I didn't have time... And the items — chains and trinkets — I buried them under a stone the next morning, in a courtyard off V— Prospect. They're all still there..."
Sonia strained every nerve to listen.
"Then why... you said you did it to rob her, but you didn't take anything?" she asked quickly, grasping at a straw.

"I don't know... I still haven't decided whether to take that money or not," he said, musing again; then, seeming to wake with a start, he gave a brief, bitter smile. "What stupid nonsense I'm talking, right?"
A thought flashed through Sonia's mind: Was he insane? But she dismissed it at once. No, it was something else. She couldn't make sense of any of it.

"You know, Sonia," he said suddenly with conviction, "let me tell you this: if I'd simply killed because I was hungry" — he stressed every word, looking at her intently yet sincerely — "I would be happy now. You have to believe that! What would it matter to you," he cried a moment later with a kind of despair, "what would it matter if I confessed I'd done wrong? What do you gain by such a pointless victory over me? Oh, Sonia, is that why I've come to you today?"
Again Sonia tried to speak but couldn't.
"I asked you to come with me yesterday because you're all I have left."
"Go where?" Sonia asked timidly.

"Not to steal and not to murder — don't worry," he said with a bitter smile. "We're so different... And you know, Sonia, it's only now, only this very moment, that I understand where I was asking you to go yesterday. Yesterday when I said it, I didn't know myself. I asked you for one thing, I came to you for one thing: don't leave me. You won't leave me, Sonia?"
She squeezed his hand.

"And why, why did I tell her? Why did I let her know?" he cried a minute later in despair, looking at her with infinite anguish. "Here you are, expecting me to explain everything, Sonia — you're sitting there waiting for it, I can see that. But what can I tell you? You won't understand, and you'll only suffer — on my account! So you're crying and embracing me again. Why? Because I couldn't bear my burden and came to dump it on someone else: 'You suffer too, and I'll feel better!' Can you really love such a contemptible wretch?"
"But aren't you suffering too?" cried Sonia.
Again the same wave of feeling surged through his heart and for an instant softened it.

"Sonia, I have a wicked heart — remember that. It may explain a great deal. I've come to you because I'm wicked. There are men who wouldn't have come. But I'm a coward and... a contemptible wretch. But... never mind! None of that matters. I need to talk, but I don't know how to begin."
He paused and sank into thought.
"We're so different!" he cried again. "We're nothing alike. And why, why did I come? I'll never forgive myself for it."
"No, no — it was good that you came," cried Sonia. "It's better that I know — far better!"
He looked at her in anguish.
"What if that really was the reason?" he said, as though reaching a conclusion. "Yes, that's what it was! I wanted to become a Napoleon — that's why I killed her... Do you understand now?"
"N-no," Sonia whispered naively and timidly. "Only keep talking, keep talking — I'll understand, I'll understand it inside myself!" she begged.
"You'll understand? All right, we'll see!" He paused and was lost in thought for some time.

"It was like this: one day I asked myself a question — what if Napoleon, for instance, had been in my place, and if instead of Toulon and Egypt and the crossing of Mont Blanc to launch his career, there had simply been some ridiculous old hag, a pawnbroker, who had to be murdered to get money from her trunk — for his career, you understand. Well, would he have gone through with it if there'd been no other way? Wouldn't he have felt a pang that it was so far from glorious and... sinful, too? Well, I have to tell you that I tormented myself over that question for a terribly long time, and I was deeply ashamed when I finally guessed — all at once, somehow — that not only would it not have given him the slightest pang, it wouldn't even have occurred to him that it wasn't glorious... that he wouldn't have seen anything to hesitate over, and that if there'd been no other way, he'd have strangled her in a second without a thought! So I too... stopped thinking about it... and killed her, following his example. And that's exactly how it was! You think it's funny? Yes, Sonia, the funniest thing of all is that maybe that's precisely how it happened."
Sonia didn't find it funny at all.
"You'd better tell me straight out... without examples," she begged, even more timidly and almost inaudibly.
He turned to her, looked at her sadly, and took her hands.

"You're right again, Sonia. Of course it's all nonsense — practically just talk! You know my mother has almost nothing. My sister happened to get a good education and was condemned to drudgery as a governess. All their hopes rested on me. I was a student, but I couldn't support myself at the university and had to leave for a while. Even if I'd scraped by like that, in ten or twelve years I might, with luck, hope to become some kind of teacher or clerk with a salary of a thousand rubles" — he recited it as though from memory — "and by then my mother would have been worn out with worry and grief, and I still couldn't have kept her comfortable, while my sister... well, my sister might have fared even worse! It's a bitter thing to spend your whole life passing everything by, turning your back on everything, forgetting your mother, and meekly swallowing the insults heaped on your sister. Why should you? Just to bury them and then burden yourself with a wife and children — only to leave them penniless too? So I decided to take the old woman's money and use it for my first years without burdening my mother — to support myself through university and for a little while after — and to do it all on a grand, thorough scale, to build a completely new career and start a new, independent life... Well... of course, killing the old woman was wrong... Well, enough of that."
He dragged himself to the end of his speech in exhaustion and let his head sink.
"Oh, that's not it, that's not it," Sonia cried in distress. "How could anyone... no, that's not right, not right."
"You can see for yourself it's not right. But I've told you the truth — it is the truth."
"As if that could be the truth! God!"
"I only killed a louse, Sonia — a useless, loathsome, harmful creature."
"A human being — a louse!"

"I know she wasn't a louse," he answered, looking at her strangely. "But I'm talking nonsense, Sonia," he added. "I've been talking nonsense for a long time... That's not it — you're right about that. There were completely different reasons for it! I haven't talked to anyone in so long, Sonia... My head aches terribly now."

His eyes burned with feverish brilliance. He was nearly delirious; a restless smile hovered on his lips. His terrible exhaustion showed through his agitation. Sonia could see how he was suffering. Her own head was spinning too. And he spoke so strangely — it seemed almost comprehensible, and yet... "But how? How? God!" She wrung her hands in despair.

"No, Sonia, that's not it," he began again suddenly, lifting his head as though struck by a new and sudden train of thought. "That's not it! Better... imagine — yes, this is definitely better — imagine that I'm vain, envious, malicious, petty, vindictive and... well, perhaps with a tendency toward insanity. Let's get it all out at once! I know they've already been talking about madness — I noticed. I just told you I couldn't support myself at the university. But you know what? Maybe I could have. My mother would have sent me what I needed for the fees, and I could have earned enough for clothes, boots, and food. Tutoring jobs came up at half a ruble each. Razumikhin manages! But I turned sulky and wouldn't do it. Yes, sulky — that's the right word! I sat in my room like a spider. You've been to my room — you've seen it... Do you know, Sonia, that low ceilings and tiny rooms crush the soul and the mind? Oh, how I hated that garret! And yet I refused to leave it — I wouldn't, on principle! I went days without going out, wouldn't work, wouldn't even eat. If Nastasya brought me something, I ate it; if she didn't, I went all day without — I wouldn't ask, out of sheer stubbornness! At night I had no light; I lay in the dark and wouldn't earn money for candles. I should have been studying, but I sold my books; the dust lies an inch thick on the notebooks on my table. I preferred lying still and thinking. And I had dreams all the time — strange dreams of every sort, no need to describe them! But then I began to imagine that... No, that's not it! Again I'm telling it wrong! You see, I kept asking myself: why am I so stupid that when others are stupid — and I know they are — I won't be smarter? Then I understood, Sonia, that if you wait for everyone to get smarter, it'll take too long... Afterward I realized it would never happen — that people won't change, that nobody can change them, and it's not worth the effort. Yes, that's right. That's the law of their nature, Sonia, that's how it is!... And I know now that whoever is strong in mind and spirit will have power over them. Whoever dares the most is the most right in their eyes. Whoever scorns the most will be their lawgiver, and whoever dares the most will be most in the right! That's how it's always been, and that's how it will always be. You'd have to be blind not to see it!"

Though Raskolnikov was looking at Sonia as he said this, he no longer cared whether she understood or not. The fever had taken complete hold of him; he was in a kind of gloomy ecstasy — he really had gone too long without talking to anyone. Sonia sensed that his dark creed had become his faith and his code.

"I realized then, Sonia," he went on eagerly, "that power is given only to the person who dares to stoop down and pick it up. There's only one thing needed: you just have to dare! Then for the first time in my life, an idea took shape that no one had ever thought of before me. No one! I saw as clear as day how strange it is that not a single person in this insane world has ever had the courage to just grab it all and send it to hell! I... I wanted to have that courage... and I killed her. I only wanted to dare, Sonia! That was the whole reason!"
"Oh, stop, stop!" cried Sonia, clasping her hands. "You turned away from God, and God has struck you down — given you over to the devil!"
"So Sonia, when I used to lie there in the dark and all of this became clear to me — was that the devil tempting me?"
"Stop! Don't laugh, blasphemer! You don't understand — you don't understand! Oh God! He won't understand!"

"Quiet, Sonia! I'm not laughing. I know myself that it was the devil leading me. Quiet, Sonia, quiet!" he repeated with grim insistence. "I know all this — I've thought it over and over, whispered it all to myself lying there in the dark... I've argued every point with myself, and I know it all! And how sick I was of going over it again and again! I kept wanting to forget it all and start fresh, Sonia, and stop thinking. And you mustn't suppose I rushed into it like a fool. I went into it like a wise man — and that was precisely my undoing. And you mustn't suppose, for instance, that I didn't know that if I started questioning whether I had the right to seize power, I obviously didn't have it — or that if I asked myself whether a human being is a louse, it proved she wasn't one, at least not for me, though she might be for someone who would go straight to his goal without asking questions... If I agonized all those days over whether Napoleon would have done it or not, I clearly sensed that I wasn't Napoleon. I had to endure the full torment of that battle of ideas, Sonia, and I longed to throw it off: I wanted to murder without theorizing, to murder for my own sake, for myself alone! I didn't want to lie about it even to myself. It wasn't to help my mother that I killed — that's nonsense. I didn't kill to get wealth and power so I could become a benefactor of mankind. Nonsense! I simply did it — I killed for myself, for myself alone, and whether I later became a benefactor to others or spent my life like a spider catching people in my web and sucking the life out of them, I couldn't have cared less at that moment... And it wasn't the money I wanted, Sonia, when I did it. It wasn't so much the money as something else... I understand all of this now... Understand me! Perhaps I'd never have committed another murder. I needed to find out something else; something else was driving me. I needed to find out, and find out quickly, whether I was a louse like everyone else or a man. Whether I could step over the line or not. Whether I dared to stoop down and pick up power, or not. Whether I was a trembling creature, or whether I had the right..."
"The right to kill? The right to kill?" Sonia clasped her hands.

"Oh, Sonia!" he cried irritably, and seemed about to retort, but fell into contemptuous silence. "Don't interrupt me, Sonia. I want to prove just one thing: that the devil led me on, and afterward showed me I had no right to take that path, because I'm just as much a louse as everyone else. He was mocking me, and here I've come to you now! Welcome your guest! If I weren't a louse, would I have come to you? Listen: when I went to the old woman's that day, I only went to try it... You can be sure of that!"
"And you murdered her!"

"But how did I murder her? Is that how people commit murder? Do people go to kill the way I went? Someday I'll tell you how I went! Did I murder the old woman? I murdered myself, not her! I destroyed myself in one blow, once and for all... But it was the devil who killed that old woman — not me. Enough, enough, Sonia! Let me be!" he cried in a sudden spasm of agony. "Let me be!"
He pressed his elbows to his knees and squeezed his head in his hands like a vise.
"What suffering!" A wail of anguish tore from Sonia.
"Well, what should I do now?" he asked, suddenly raising his head and looking at her with a face hideously distorted by despair.

"What should you do?" she cried, jumping up. Her eyes, which had been full of tears, suddenly blazed. "Stand up!" She seized him by the shoulder; he got up, looking at her almost in bewilderment. "Go at once, right now — stand at the crossroads, bow down, and first kiss the earth you've defiled. Then bow down to the whole world, to all four sides, and say out loud to everyone: 'I am a murderer!' Then God will give you life again. Will you go? Will you go?" she asked, trembling all over, seizing both his hands, squeezing them tight, and gazing at him with eyes full of fire.
He was stunned by her sudden fervor.
"You mean Siberia, Sonia? I have to give myself up?" he asked gloomily.
"Accept suffering and redeem yourself through it — that's what you must do."
"No! I'm not going to them, Sonia!"

"But how will you go on living? What will you live for?" cried Sonia. "How is that possible now? How can you face your mother? Oh, what will become of them! But what am I saying? You've already abandoned your mother and sister. You have abandoned them already! Oh God!" she cried. "He knows all this himself. How can he live like this — how? What will become of you?"

"Don't be a child, Sonia," he said softly. "What harm have I done them? Why should I go to the authorities? What would I tell them? It's all a phantom... They destroy millions of people themselves and consider it a virtue. They're rogues and scoundrels, Sonia! I'm not going to them. And what would I say? That I killed her but didn't dare take the money and hid it under a stone?" he added with a bitter smile. "They'd laugh at me and call me a fool for not keeping it. A coward and a fool! They wouldn't understand, and they don't deserve to understand. Why should I go? I won't. Don't be a child, Sonia..."
"You won't be able to bear it — it will be too much!" she repeated, stretching out her hands in desperate supplication.
"Maybe I've been too hard on myself," he observed gloomily, lost in thought. "Maybe after all I am a man and not a louse, and I've been too quick to condemn myself. I'll make another fight for it."
A haughty smile appeared on his lips.
"What a burden to carry! And for your whole life, your whole life!"
"I'll get used to it," he said grimly and thoughtfully. "Listen," he began a minute later. "Stop crying — it's time to talk about facts. I've come to tell you the police are after me, on my trail..."
"Oh!" Sonia cried in terror.

"Why are you crying out? You want me to go to Siberia, yet now you're scared? But listen: I'm not going to turn myself in. I'll fight it, and they won't get anywhere. They have no real evidence. Yesterday I was in grave danger and thought I was lost, but today things look better. Everything they have can be read two ways — I can turn their accusations to my advantage, do you understand? And I will, because I've learned my lesson. But they'll certainly arrest me. If not for something that happened, they would have arrested me today for sure; maybe they still will today... But it doesn't matter, Sonia. They'll let me go again — because they have no real proof, and there won't be any, I give you my word. They can't convict on what they've got. Enough... I just wanted you to know... I'll try to manage things with my mother and sister so they won't be frightened... My sister's future is secure now, I believe... and my mother's should be too... Well, that's all. Be careful, though. Will you come to see me in prison?"
"Oh, I will! I will!"

They sat side by side, mournful and dejected, as though they'd been cast up by a storm, alone on some deserted shore. He looked at Sonia and felt how enormous her love for him was — and strangely, he suddenly felt it as a weight, a pain, to be loved so much. Yes, it was a strange and terrible sensation! On his way to Sonia he had felt that all his hopes rested on her; he had expected to unload at least part of his suffering. But now, when her whole heart turned toward him, he suddenly felt himself immeasurably more unhappy than before.
"Sonia," he said, "maybe you'd better not come to see me in prison."
Sonia didn't answer; she was crying. Several minutes passed.
"Do you have a cross?" she asked, as though suddenly remembering.
At first he didn't understand the question.

"No, of course not. Here, take this one — it's cypress wood. I have another, a copper one that belonged to Lizaveta. I exchanged with Lizaveta: she gave me her cross and I gave her my little icon. I'll wear Lizaveta's now and give you this one. Take it... it's mine! It's mine, you know," she begged. "We'll go to suffer together, and together we'll bear our cross!"
"Give it to me," said Raskolnikov.
He didn't want to hurt her feelings. But he immediately drew back the hand he'd reached out for the cross.
"Not now, Sonia. Later," he added to comfort her.
"Yes, yes, that's better," she repeated with conviction. "When you go to face your suffering, put it on then. You'll come to me, I'll put it on you, we'll pray together, and then we'll go."
At that moment someone knocked three times at the door.
"Sofya Semyonovna, may I come in?" came a very familiar and courteous voice.
Sonia rushed to the door in alarm. The fair-haired head of Mr. Lebeziatnikov appeared in the doorway.

chapters.title: Part 5, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Lebeziatnikov looked agitated.

"I've come to see you, Sofya Semyonovna," he began. "Excuse me... I thought I'd find you here," he said, suddenly turning to Raskolnikov. "That is, I didn't mean anything like... But I just thought... Katerina Ivanovna has gone insane," he blurted out, turning back to Sonia.
Sonia screamed.

"At least it seems that way. But... we don't know what to do, you see! She came back — apparently she'd been thrown out somewhere, maybe beaten... At least that's what it looks like... She'd run to your father's old boss, but he wasn't home — he was dining at some other general's... Just imagine: she rushed off there, to the other general's, and she was so persistent that she got the boss called out from dinner, it seems. You can imagine what happened. She was thrown out, of course; but according to her own account, she screamed abuse at him and threw something at him. It's easy enough to believe... How she wasn't arrested, I can't understand! Now she's telling everyone, including Amalia Ivanovna — though it's hard to understand her; she's screaming and thrashing about... Oh yes, she's shouting that since everyone has abandoned her, she'll take the children into the street with a barrel organ, and the children will sing and dance, and she will too, and they'll collect money, and they'll go every day and stand under the general's window... 'to let everyone see well-born children, whose father was an official, begging in the streets.' She keeps hitting the children and they're all crying. She's teaching Lida to sing 'My Village,' the boy to dance, Polenka the same. She's ripping up all their clothes to make little caps like actors wear; she plans to carry a tin pan and bang on it instead of music... She won't listen to anything... Imagine what it's like! It's beyond anything!"

Lebeziatnikov would have gone on, but Sonia, who had been listening almost breathlessly, snatched up her cloak and hat and ran from the room, dressing as she went. Raskolnikov followed, and Lebeziatnikov came after.

"She's definitely lost her mind!" he said to Raskolnikov as they went into the street. "I didn't want to frighten Sofya Semyonovna, so I said 'it seems like it,' but there's no doubt about it. They say in consumption the tubercles sometimes reach the brain; I wish I knew more about medicine. I tried to reason with her, but she wouldn't listen."
"You talked to her about the tubercles?"

"Not exactly about the tubercles. Besides, she wouldn't have understood! But what I'm saying is, if you convince someone through logic that they have nothing to cry about, they'll stop crying. That's obvious. Don't you agree?"
"Life would be too easy if that were true," Raskolnikov answered.

"Excuse me, but of course it would be rather difficult for Katerina Ivanovna to understand. But did you know that in Paris they've been conducting serious experiments on the possibility of curing the insane through logical argument alone? A professor there — a respected scientist who recently died — believed such treatment was possible. His idea was that there's nothing really wrong with the insane person's body; insanity is, so to speak, a logical mistake, an error of judgment, an incorrect way of seeing things. He would gradually show the patient their error, and — would you believe it? — they say he was successful! But since he also used cold showers, how much of the success was due to the argument is unclear... At least, so it seems."

Raskolnikov had long since stopped listening. Reaching the building where he lived, he nodded to Lebeziatnikov and went in at the gate. Lebeziatnikov snapped out of his monologue, looked around, and hurried on.

Raskolnikov went into his tiny room and stood still in the middle of it. Why had he come back here? He looked at the yellowed, tattered wallpaper, the dust, the sofa... From the courtyard came a loud, persistent hammering — someone seemed to be banging nails. He went to the window, rose on tiptoe, and stared out into the yard for a long time, as if completely absorbed. But the yard was empty, and he couldn't see who was making the noise. In the building to the left, some windows were open; on the sills sat pots of sickly geraniums. Laundry hung from the windows... He knew it all by heart. He turned away and sat down on the sofa.
Never, never had he felt so terrifyingly alone!
Yes, he felt again that he might actually come to hate Sonia, now that he had made her more miserable.
"Why had he gone to her to beg for her tears? Why did he need to poison her life? How contemptible!"
"I'll stay alone," he decided firmly, "and she won't come to the prison!"
Five minutes later he looked up with a strange smile. It was a strange thought.
"Perhaps Siberia really would be better," he thought suddenly.

He couldn't have said how long he sat there, vague thoughts drifting through his mind. Then the door opened and Dunya came in. At first she stood still in the doorway and looked at him, just as he had stood looking at Sonia. Then she came in and sat down across from him, in the same chair as yesterday. He looked at her silently, almost blankly.
"Don't be angry, brother. I've only come for a minute," Dunya said.
Her expression was thoughtful but not severe. Her eyes were bright and soft. He could see she had come to him with love.

"Brother, now I know everything — everything. Dmitri Prokofitch has explained it all. They're harassing and persecuting you based on a stupid, contemptible suspicion... Dmitri Prokofitch told me there's no danger and that you shouldn't look at it with such horror. I don't think so either, and I completely understand how outraged you must be — and I'm afraid this outrage may leave a permanent mark on you. That's what worries me. As for your pulling away from us, I won't judge you — I don't dare — and forgive me for blaming you before. I feel that if I had such a burden, I too would withdraw from everyone. I won't say anything to Mother about this, but I'll talk about you constantly and tell her you'll come soon. Don't worry about her — I'll put her mind at ease. But don't push her too far either — come at least once. Remember, she's your mother. I've come simply to say" — Dunya started to get up — "that if you ever need me, for anything at all... call me, and I'll come. Goodbye!"
She turned sharply and headed for the door.
"Dunya!" Raskolnikov stopped her and walked toward her. "That Razumikhin — Dmitri Prokofitch — is a very good man."
Dunya blushed slightly.
"Well?" she asked, waiting a moment.
"He's capable, hardworking, honest, and capable of real love... Goodbye, Dunya."
Dunya blushed crimson, then suddenly looked alarmed.
"What do you mean, brother? Are we really parting forever — that you're giving me such a farewell message?"
"Never mind... Goodbye."
He turned away and went to the window. She stood there a moment, looked at him anxiously, and left, troubled.

No, he wasn't cold toward her. There had been one moment — the very last — when he had desperately wanted to take her in his arms and say goodbye to her, even to tell her, but he hadn't dared even to touch her hand.
"Afterward she might shudder remembering I embraced her, and feel I stole her kiss."
"And could she endure the truth?" he wondered a few minutes later. "No, she couldn't. Girls like her can't endure things like that! They never can."
And he thought of Sonia.
A breath of fresh air came through the window. The daylight was fading. He picked up his cap and went out.

Of course he couldn't, and wouldn't, consider how sick he was. But all this relentless anxiety and mental torment had to be taking its toll. And if he wasn't actually delirious with fever, it was perhaps only because this constant inner strain was keeping him on his feet and in possession of his faculties. But that artificial energy couldn't last long.

He wandered aimlessly. The sun was setting. A particular kind of misery had begun to weigh on him lately. There was nothing sharp or acute about it; but there was a feeling of permanence about it, of eternity — a foretaste of endless years of this cold, leaden wretchedness, a foretaste of an eternity "on a square yard of space." Toward evening this feeling usually pressed down on him more heavily.

"With this idiotic, purely physical weakness that depends on the sunset or something, you can't help doing something stupid! Next thing you know, you'll go running to Dunya as well as Sonia," he muttered bitterly.
He heard his name called. He turned around. Lebeziatnikov rushed up to him.

"Just imagine — I've been to your room looking for you! She's gone through with her plan and taken the children out! Sofya Semyonovna and I had a terrible time finding them. She's banging on a frying pan and making the children dance. The children are crying. They keep stopping at intersections and in front of shops; a crowd of idiots is running after them. Come on!"
"And Sonia?" Raskolnikov asked anxiously, hurrying after Lebeziatnikov.

"Absolutely frantic. Not Sofya Semyonovna exactly — it's Katerina Ivanovna who's the frantic one, though Sofya Semyonovna is frantic too. But Katerina Ivanovna is completely deranged. I'm telling you, she's totally lost her mind. They'll be taken to the police. You can imagine what that will mean... They're on the canal embankment, near the bridge, not far from Sofya Semyonovna's — quite close."

On the canal embankment, near the bridge and only two houses from where Sonia lived, a crowd had gathered, made up mostly of street children. Katerina Ivanovna's hoarse, broken voice could be heard from the bridge, and it was certainly a strange spectacle likely to attract a street crowd. Katerina Ivanovna, in her old dress with the green shawl, wearing a battered straw hat crushed absurdly to one side, was truly deranged. She was exhausted and gasping for breath. Her wasted, consumptive face looked even more agonized than usual — outdoors, in the sunlight, a consumptive person always looks worse than indoors. But her excitement didn't flag; every minute her agitation grew more intense. She would rush at the children, shout at them, coax them, tell them in front of the crowd how to dance and what to sing, explain why it was necessary, and when they couldn't understand, she'd beat them... Then she'd lunge at the crowd; if she noticed any decently dressed person who stopped to look, she'd immediately appeal to them — look what children "from a genteel, one might say aristocratic, family" had been reduced to. If she heard laughter or jeering, she'd fly at the scoffers and start arguing. Some people laughed, others shook their heads, but everyone was curious at the sight of the madwoman with the terrified children. The frying pan Lebeziatnikov had mentioned wasn't there — at least Raskolnikov didn't see it. Instead of banging on a pan, Katerina Ivanovna clapped her wasted hands whenever she made Lida and Kolya dance and Polenka sing. She tried to sing along herself, but broke off at the second note with a terrible cough, which made her curse in despair and even cry. What enraged her most was the weeping and terror of Kolya and Lida. Some attempt had been made to dress the children up as street performers. The boy wore a turban made of something red and white to look Turkish. There'd been no costume for Lida; she simply wore a red knitted cap — really a nightcap — that had belonged to Marmeladov, decorated with a broken white ostrich feather that had been Katerina Ivanovna's grandmother's and had been kept as a family heirloom. Polenka was in her everyday clothes; she looked at her mother with timid bewilderment and stayed close to her side, hiding her tears. She dimly understood her mother's condition and glanced around uneasily. The street and the crowd terrified her. Sonia followed Katerina Ivanovna, weeping and begging her to come home, but Katerina Ivanovna refused to listen.

"Stop it, Sonia, stop!" she shouted, speaking rapidly, gasping and coughing. "You don't know what you're asking — you're like a child! I've told you I'm not going back to that drunken German. Let everyone in Petersburg see these children begging in the streets, even though their father was an honorable man who served all his life in truth and loyalty, and one might say died in the line of duty." (Katerina Ivanovna had by now invented this fantastic story and thoroughly believed it.) "Let that wretch of a general see! And you're being silly, Sonia — what are we supposed to eat? Tell me that. We've burdened you enough — I won't do it anymore! Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, is that you?" she cried, spotting Raskolnikov and rushing up to him. "Explain to this silly girl that nothing better could be done! Even organ-grinders earn their living, and everyone will see at once that we're different — that we're an honorable, bereaved family reduced to beggary. That general will lose his position, you'll see! We'll perform under his windows every day, and if the Tsar drives by, I'll fall on my knees, push the children forward, and say: 'Protect us, father.' He is the father of the fatherless, he is merciful — he'll protect us, you'll see, and that wretch of a general... Lida, tenez vous droite! Kolya, you'll dance again. Why are you whimpering? Whimpering again! What are you scared of, stupid boy? Lord, what am I to do with them, Rodion Romanovitch? If you only knew how stupid they are! What can you do with such children?"

And she, nearly crying herself — which didn't slow her uninterrupted, rapid torrent of words — pointed at the weeping children. Raskolnikov tried to persuade her to go home, even arguing, hoping to reach her vanity, that it was unseemly for her to wander the streets like an organ-grinder when she was planning to become the headmistress of a boarding school.

"A boarding school! Ha-ha-ha! Castles in the air!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, her laugh dissolving into a cough. "No, Rodion Romanovitch, that dream is over! Everyone has abandoned us!... And that general... You know, Rodion Romanovitch, I threw an inkwell at him — it was sitting in the waiting room by the register where you sign your name. I wrote my name, threw it at him, and ran. Oh, the scoundrels, the scoundrels! But enough of them — now I'll provide for the children myself. I won't grovel before anyone! She's had to bear enough for us!" She pointed at Sonia. "Polenka, how much have we got? Show me! What — only two kopecks? Oh, the miserable wretches! They give us nothing — just chase after us, sticking out their tongues. What's that blockhead laughing at?" She pointed at a man in the crowd. "It's all because Kolya here is so stupid — he drives me mad. What do you want, Polenka? Tell me in French — parlez-moi français! I've taught you, you know some phrases. How else will people see you're from a good family, well-bred children, not like other organ-grinders? We're not putting on a Punch and Judy show in the streets — we're going to sing refined songs... Ah, yes — what shall we sing? You keep distracting me, and we... you see, we've stopped here, Rodion Romanovitch, to find something to sing for money — something Kolya can dance to... Because as you can imagine, our whole performance is improvised... We need to rehearse it properly, and then we'll go to Nevsky Prospect, where there are far more respectable people, and we'll be noticed right away. Lida only knows 'My Village,' and everyone sings that. We need something much more refined... Well, have you thought of anything, Polenka? If only you'd help your mother! My memory's completely gone — otherwise I'd remember something. We certainly can't sing 'A Hussar.' Oh, let's sing something in French — 'Cinq sous.' I've taught it to you. And since it's in French, people will see at once that you're well-born children, and it will be much more touching... We could also sing 'Marlborough s'en va-t-en guerre,' because it's a proper children's song and used as a lullaby in all the best families.

"Marlborough s'en va-t-en guerre, ne sait quand reviendra..." she began singing. "No, better 'Cinq sous.' Now, Kolya — hands on your hips, quickly! And Lida, you keep turning the other way. Polenka and I will sing and clap!
"Cinq sous, cinq sous, pour monter notre ménage."

(Cough-cough-cough!) "Straighten your dress, Polenka — it's slipping off your shoulders," she said, gasping between coughs. "It's especially important now to look nice and genteel, so everyone can see you're well-born children. I said at the time the bodice should be cut longer, two widths wide. It was your doing, Sonia — 'make it shorter,' you said — and now the child looks completely deformed... Why are you all crying again? What's the matter, silly children? Come on, Kolya, start! Hurry up, hurry up! What an insufferable child!
"Cinq sous, cinq sous...
"A policeman again! What do you want?"

A policeman was indeed pushing through the crowd. But at that moment a gentleman in a civilian overcoat — a solid-looking official of about fifty, wearing a medal on his neck (which delighted Katerina Ivanovna and impressed the policeman) — came up and without a word handed her a green three-ruble note. His face wore an expression of genuine sympathy. Katerina Ivanovna accepted it with a polite, even ceremonious bow.

"I thank you, honored sir," she began grandly. "The reasons that have compelled us — take the money, Polenka: you see, there are generous and noble people ready to help a poor gentlewoman in distress. You see, honored sir, these are orphans of a good family — I might even say aristocratic connections — and that wretch of a general sat eating grouse... and stamped his foot when I disturbed him. 'Your Excellency,' I said, 'protect the orphans, for you knew my late husband, Semyon Zakharovitch, and on the very day of his death the vilest scoundrel slandered his only daughter...' That policeman again! Protect me!" she cried to the official. "Why is that policeman coming toward me? We just escaped from one on Meshchanskaya Street. What do you want, you fool?"
"It's not allowed in the streets. You mustn't cause a disturbance."
"It's you who's causing a disturbance! It's the same as if I were playing a barrel organ. What business is it of yours?"
"You need a permit for a barrel organ, and you haven't got one — plus you're collecting a crowd. Where do you live?"
"What — a permit?" wailed Katerina Ivanovna. "I buried my husband today. Why would I need a permit?"
"Please calm down, madam," the official began. "Come along — I'll accompany you... This is no place for you, in the middle of a crowd. You're ill."

"Honored sir, honored sir — you don't know!" screamed Katerina Ivanovna. "We're going to Nevsky Prospect... Sonia! Sonia! Where is she? She's crying too! What's wrong with all of you? Kolya, Lida — where are you going?" she cried in sudden alarm. "Oh, stupid children! Kolya, Lida — where are they running?"

Kolya and Lida, terrified by the crowd and their mother's mad behavior, suddenly seized each other's hands and bolted at the sight of the policeman who wanted to take them somewhere. Weeping and wailing, poor Katerina Ivanovna ran after them. She was a pitiful and awful sight, running along, crying and gasping for breath. Sonia and Polenka chased after them.
"Bring them back, bring them back, Sonia! Oh, stupid, ungrateful children!... Polenka! Catch them!... It's all for your sake..."
She stumbled as she ran and fell.
"She's cut herself — she's bleeding! Oh God!" cried Sonia, bending over her.

Everyone rushed over and crowded around. Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov reached her first, followed quickly by the official, and behind him the policeman, who muttered "Damn!" with a wave of impatience, sensing this was going to be trouble.
"Move along! Move along!" he said to the crowd pressing forward.
"She's dying!" someone shouted.
"She's lost her mind," said another.
"Lord have mercy," said a woman, crossing herself. "Did they catch the little ones? They're bringing them back — the older girl has them... Oh, the little rascals!"
When they looked more carefully at Katerina Ivanovna, they saw she hadn't cut herself on a stone, as Sonia had thought — the blood staining the pavement red was coming from her chest.

"I've seen this before," the official murmured to Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov. "That's consumption. The blood flows and chokes the patient. I saw the same thing with a relative of mine not long ago... nearly half a liter of blood, all at once... What can be done? She's dying."

"This way, this way — to my room!" Sonia begged. "I live here!... That house — the second one. Come to my place, quickly!" She turned frantically from one person to another. "Send for a doctor! Oh God!"

Thanks to the official's efforts, this plan was carried out, with even the policeman helping to carry Katerina Ivanovna. She was brought to Sonia's room nearly unconscious and laid on the bed. The bleeding continued, but she seemed to be coming around. Raskolnikov, Lebeziatnikov, and the official followed Sonia in, along with the policeman, who first drove back the crowd that had followed all the way to the door. Polenka came in leading Kolya and Lida, who were shaking and crying. Several people came in from the Kapernaumovs' apartment too — the landlord himself, a lame, one-eyed man with a wild thatch of hair and whiskers; his wife, a woman with a permanently terrified expression; and several gaping children. Among them, Svidrigailov suddenly appeared. Raskolnikov looked at him in surprise, not understanding where he'd come from — he hadn't noticed him in the crowd. Talk turned to doctors and priests. The official whispered to Raskolnikov that he thought it was too late for a doctor, but ordered one sent for anyway. Kapernaumov ran to find one himself.

Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna had caught her breath. The bleeding stopped for a time. She looked with sick but intent, penetrating eyes at Sonia, who stood pale and trembling, wiping the sweat from her forehead with a handkerchief. At last she asked to be raised up. They propped her into a sitting position on the bed, supporting her on both sides.
"Where are the children?" she asked in a faint voice. "You've brought them, Polenka? Oh, you silly things! Why did you run away... Oh!"
Her parched lips were once more covered with blood. She moved her eyes, looking around the room.
"So this is how you live, Sonia! I've never once been to your room."
She looked at her with suffering.

"We've been your ruin, Sonia. Polenka, Lida, Kolya — come here! Well, here they are, Sonia — take them all! I'm handing them over to you. I've had enough! The party's over." (Cough!) "Lay me down... let me die in peace."
They laid her back on the pillow.
"What — a priest? I don't need one. You don't have a ruble to spare. I have no sins. God must forgive me without that. He knows how I've suffered... And if He won't forgive me, then so be it!"

She sank deeper and deeper into restless delirium. At times she shuddered, turned her eyes from side to side, and recognized everyone for a moment before slipping back into confusion. Her breathing was hoarse and labored; there was a sort of rattle in her throat.

"I said to him, 'Your Excellency...'" she gasped, fighting for every word. "That Amalia Ludwigovna, oh! Lida, Kolya — hands on your hips, quickly! Glissez, glissez! Pas de basque! Tap your heels — be a graceful child!
"Du hast Diamanten und Perlen...
"What next? That's the one to sing.
"Du hast die schönsten Augen, Mädchen, was willst du mehr?
"What an idea! Was willst du mehr? The things this fool invents! Oh yes!
"In the heat of midday, in the vale of Dagestan...

"Oh, how I loved it! I adored that song, Polenka! Your father used to sing it when we were engaged... Oh, those days! Oh, that's what we should sing! How does it go? I've forgotten. Remind me! How did it go?"
She was violently agitated and tried to sit up. At last, in a horribly hoarse, broken voice, she began to sing, shrieking and gasping at every word, with a look of growing terror.
"In the heat of midday!... in the vale!... of Dagestan!... With lead in my breast!..."

"Your Excellency!" she wailed suddenly with a heartrending scream and a flood of tears. "Protect the orphans! You were their father's guest... aristocratic, one might say..." She started, coming back to consciousness, and gazed at everyone with a kind of terror — but immediately recognized Sonia.
"Sonia! Sonia!" she said softly and tenderly, as though surprised to find her there. "Sonia, darling — you're here too?"
They lifted her up again.
"Enough! It's over! Farewell, poor thing! I'm done for! I'm broken!" she cried with bitter despair, and her head fell heavily back on the pillow.

She lost consciousness again, but this time it didn't last long. Her pale, yellow, wasted face fell back, her mouth dropped open, her leg twitched convulsively, she gave one deep, deep sigh — and died.

Sonia fell upon her, threw her arms around her, and lay motionless with her head pressed against the dead woman's wasted chest. Polenka threw herself at her mother's feet, kissing them and weeping violently. Kolya and Lida, though they didn't understand what had happened, sensed something terrible; they clutched each other's little shoulders, stared straight at one another, and simultaneously opened their mouths and began to wail. They were both still in their costumes — one in a turban, the other in the cap with the ostrich feather.
And how had "the certificate of merit" come to be on the bed beside Katerina Ivanovna? It lay there by the pillow; Raskolnikov noticed it.
He walked to the window. Lebeziatnikov hurried over to him.
"She's dead," he said.
"Rodion Romanovitch, I need a word with you," said Svidrigailov, coming up to them.
Lebeziatnikov immediately stepped aside and withdrew discreetly. Svidrigailov drew Raskolnikov further away.

"I'll take care of all the arrangements — the funeral and everything. You know it's a question of money, and as I told you, I have plenty. I'll place those two little ones and Polenka in a good orphanage, and I'll settle fifteen hundred rubles on each of them, to be paid when they come of age — so Sofya Semyonovna won't have to worry about them. And I'll pull her out of the muck too, because she's a good girl, isn't she? So you can tell Avdotya Romanovna that's how I'm spending her ten thousand."
"What's your motive for such generosity?" asked Raskolnikov.

"Oh, you skeptic!" Svidrigailov laughed. "I told you I have no need for that money. Won't you accept that it's simply done out of humanity? After all, she wasn't 'a louse'" — he gestured toward the corner where the dead woman lay — "was she, like some old pawnbroker? Come now, you'll agree — should Luzhin go on living and doing wicked things, or should she die? And if I don't help them, Polenka will end up the same way."

He said this with a kind of playful, sly wink, keeping his eyes fixed on Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov went white and cold, hearing his own words to Sonia thrown back at him. He quickly stepped back and stared wildly at Svidrigailov.
"How do you know?" he whispered, barely able to breathe.
"I lodge here, at Madame Resslich's — right on the other side of the wall. Here's Kapernaumov's place, and next door is Madame Resslich, an old and devoted friend. We're neighbors."
"You?"

"Yes," Svidrigailov continued, shaking with laughter. "I assure you on my honor, dear Rodion Romanovitch, that you've interested me enormously. I told you we'd become friends — I predicted it. Well, here we are. And you'll see what an accommodating person I am. You'll find I'm easy to get along with!"

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 1
paragraphs: A strange period began for Raskolnikov. It was as though a fog had descended on him, wrapping him in a lonely, dreary isolation from which there was no escape. Looking back on it later, he believed his mind had been clouded at times, with occasional lucid intervals, right up until the final catastrophe. He was certain he had been mistaken about many things during this time — about the timing of events, for example. In any case, when he later tried to piece his memories together, much of what he learned about himself came from other people. He had confused incidents, had attributed events to circumstances that existed only in his imagination. At times he was gripped by agonizing, morbid anxiety, sometimes rising to outright panic. But he also remembered moments, hours, perhaps whole days of complete apathy — a reaction to the preceding terror that resembled the abnormal numbness sometimes seen in the dying. In that state he seemed to be deliberately avoiding a full, clear understanding of his situation. Certain essential facts that demanded immediate attention were especially unbearable to him. How gladly he would have freed himself from certain worries — yet neglecting them threatened complete and inevitable ruin.

He was particularly worried about Svidrigailov — one could even say Svidrigailov occupied his thoughts constantly. From the moment of Svidrigailov's all-too-threatening and unmistakable words in Sonia's room, at the time of Katerina Ivanovna's death, the normal workings of his mind seemed to have broken down. Yet although this new fact caused him extreme anxiety, Raskolnikov was in no hurry to confront it. Sometimes, finding himself in some remote, desolate part of the city, in some wretched eating-house, sitting alone and lost in thought, barely knowing how he'd gotten there, he would suddenly think of Svidrigailov. He would recognize with sudden, alarming clarity that he needed to come to terms with that man as soon as possible, to make whatever deal he could. Once, walking outside the city limits, he even convinced himself they had arranged to meet there, that he was waiting for Svidrigailov. Another time he woke before dawn lying on the ground under some bushes, unable to understand how he'd ended up there.

During the two or three days after Katerina Ivanovna's death, he had encountered Svidrigailov two or three times at Sonia's lodgings, where he'd gone aimlessly, just for a moment. They exchanged a few words but never touched on the critical subject, as though they had tacitly agreed to leave it aside for the time being.

Katerina Ivanovna's body was still lying in the coffin. Svidrigailov was busy arranging the funeral. Sonia was very busy too. At their last meeting, Svidrigailov told Raskolnikov he had made arrangements — very satisfactory ones — for Katerina Ivanovna's children. Through certain connections he had managed to reach the right people, and the three orphans could be immediately placed in excellent institutions. The money he had settled on them helped greatly, since it's much easier to place orphans who have some means than destitute ones. He also said something about Sonia and promised to come see Raskolnikov in a day or two, mentioning that "he'd like to discuss something, that there were things they needed to talk about..."

This conversation took place in the hallway on the stairs. Svidrigailov looked intently at Raskolnikov, and after a brief pause, lowered his voice: "What's wrong, Rodion Romanovitch? You don't seem like yourself. You look and listen, but it's as if you don't understand. Pull yourself together! We'll talk things over; I'm just sorry I'm so busy with my own affairs and other people's. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch," he added suddenly, "what every person needs is fresh air — fresh air... more than anything!"

He stepped aside to let the priest and his assistant pass on the stairs. They had come for the requiem service. By Svidrigailov's orders, it was sung twice a day, punctually. Svidrigailov went on his way. Raskolnikov stood still a moment, thought, then followed the priest into Sonia's room. He stood by the door. The service began: quiet, slow, mournful. Since childhood, the thought of death and its presence had always felt oppressive and mysteriously terrible to him; and it had been a long time since he'd last heard a requiem service. There was something else here too — something awful and disturbing. He looked at the children: they were all kneeling by the coffin; Polenka was crying. Behind them, Sonia prayed, weeping softly and — it seemed — timidly.

"She hasn't said a word to me these past two days — she hasn't even glanced at me," Raskolnikov thought. The sunlight was bright in the room; clouds of incense rose; the priest intoned: "Grant rest, O Lord..." Raskolnikov stayed through the entire service. As the priest blessed them and took his leave, he looked around with a strange expression. After the service, Raskolnikov went up to Sonia. She took both his hands and rested her head on his shoulder. This small, friendly gesture puzzled Raskolnikov. It struck him as strange that there was no trace of revulsion, no sign of disgust, no trembling in her hand. It was the ultimate act of self-sacrifice — at least that's how he interpreted it.

Sonia said nothing. Raskolnikov pressed her hand and left. He felt utterly wretched. If he could have escaped to some wilderness, he would have considered himself lucky — even if it meant spending his whole life there. But although he had been almost entirely alone lately, he had never managed to feel truly alone. Sometimes he would walk out of the city onto the highway; once he even reached a small woods. But the lonelier the place, the more aware he became of some uneasy presence nearby. It didn't frighten him, but it annoyed him intensely, so he would hurry back to the city, lose himself in the crowds, duck into restaurants and taverns, walk through the busiest streets. There he felt easier and, paradoxically, more solitary. One evening at dusk he sat for an hour in a tavern listening to songs, and he remembered that he actually enjoyed it. But suddenly the same unease returned, as though his conscience were pricking him. "Here I sit listening to songs — is that what I ought to be doing?" he thought. Yet he immediately sensed that wasn't the only cause; there was something demanding an immediate decision, but he couldn't put it into words or even think it through clearly. It was a hopeless tangle. "No — better to fight again! Better Porfiry again... or Svidrigailov... Better some challenge, some attack. Yes, yes!" he thought. He left the tavern and practically broke into a run. The thought of Dunya and his mother suddenly filled him with something close to panic. That night he woke before dawn among some bushes on Krestovsky Island, shivering with fever. He walked home; it was early morning when he arrived. After a few hours' sleep the fever passed, but he woke up late — two in the afternoon.

He remembered that Katerina Ivanovna's funeral was scheduled for that day, and he was glad he hadn't attended. Nastasya brought him food; he ate and drank eagerly, almost greedily. His head was clearer and he felt calmer than he had in three days. He even felt a passing wonder at his previous attacks of panic.
The door opened and Razumikhin came in.
"Ah — he's eating, so he's not sick," said Razumikhin. He pulled up a chair and sat down across the table from Raskolnikov.
He was troubled and made no attempt to hide it. He spoke with obvious irritation, but without hurrying or raising his voice. He seemed to have some specific, firm purpose in mind.

"Listen," he began decisively. "As far as I'm concerned, you can all go to hell, but from what I can see, it's obvious I can't make head or tail of any of this. Please don't think I've come to interrogate you. I don't want to know — to hell with it! If you start telling me your secrets, I probably won't even stay to listen — I'll just walk out cursing. I've come for one thing only: to find out once and for all whether you're insane. There's a conviction floating around that you're mad or close to it. I'll admit I was leaning that way myself, judging by your stupid, repulsive, and completely inexplicable behavior — and from your recent treatment of your mother and sister. Only a monster or a madman could treat them the way you have. So you must be mad."
"When did you last see them?"

"Just now. Haven't you seen them since? Where have you been? Tell me, please — I've been to your room three times already. Your mother has been seriously ill since yesterday. She was determined to come to you; Avdotya Romanovna tried to stop her, but she wouldn't listen. 'If he's sick, if he's losing his mind, who should look after him if not his mother?' she said. We all came together — we couldn't let her come alone. We begged her to stay calm the whole way. We arrived, and you weren't here. She sat down, waited ten minutes while we stood there in silence. Then she got up and said: 'If he's gone out — meaning he's well enough — and has forgotten his mother, then it's humiliating and improper for his mother to stand at his door begging for kindness.' She went home and took to her bed; now she has a fever. 'I see,' she said, 'that he has time for his girl.' She means Sofya Semyonovna by 'your girl' — your fiancée or your mistress, I don't know which. I went straight to Sofya Semyonovna's myself, wanting to find out what was going on. I looked around — there was the coffin, the children crying, Sofya Semyonovna trying mourning clothes on them. No sign of you. I apologized, left, and reported back to Avdotya Romanovna. So that's all nonsense — you don't have any girl. The likeliest explanation is that you're mad. But here you sit, wolfing down boiled beef as though you haven't eaten in three days. Then again, mad people eat too. But even though you haven't said a word to me... you're not mad! I'd stake anything on it. So you can all go to hell — there's some mystery here, some secret, and I have no intention of racking my brains over your secrets. I've just come to blow off steam," he finished, rising. "To get it off my chest. And now I know what to do."
"What do you intend to do?"
"What business is it of yours?"
"You're going to go on a drinking binge."
"How... how did you know?"
"It's pretty obvious."
Razumikhin paused for a moment.
"You've always been a very rational person, and you've never been mad — never," he said suddenly with warmth. "You're right: I'll drink. Goodbye!"
He started for the door.
"I was talking with my sister about you — the day before yesterday, I think it was — Razumikhin."
"About me! But... where could you have seen her the day before yesterday?" Razumikhin stopped short and even turned slightly pale.
You could see that his heart was pounding — slowly, heavily.
"She came here by herself, sat there, and talked to me."
"She did!"
"Yes."
"What did you say to her... about me, I mean?"
"I told her you were a very good, honest, and hardworking man. I didn't tell her you love her, because she already knows."
"She knows?"

"Of course she does. Wherever I might go, whatever happens to me, you would stay to look after them. I'm entrusting them to your care, so to speak, Razumikhin. I say this because I know perfectly well how you feel about her, and I'm convinced your heart is pure. I also know she may love you too — perhaps she already does. Decide for yourself whether you need that drinking binge or not."

"Rodya! You see... well... damn it! Where are you planning to go? Look, if it's all some secret, fine, never mind... But I... I'll figure out the secret... and I'm sure it's just some ridiculous nonsense you've dreamed up. Anyway, you're a fine fellow — a really fine fellow!"

"What I was about to add — but you interrupted me — was that you made an excellent decision not to try to uncover those secrets. Let time sort it out. Don't worry about it. You'll learn everything when the time comes. Someone said to me yesterday that what a person needs is fresh air — fresh air. I'm about to go see him, to find out exactly what he meant by that."
Razumikhin stood lost in thought and excitement, working something out in silence.
"He's a political conspirator! He must be. And he's on the brink of some desperate step — that's certain. It can only be that! And... Dunya knows," he thought suddenly.

"So Avdotya Romanovna comes to visit you," he said, weighing each syllable, "and you're about to go see a man who says we need more air — and of course that letter... that must be connected somehow," he concluded to himself.
"What letter?"

"She received a letter today. It upset her terribly — far too much. I started talking about you, and she asked me not to. Then... then she said we might have to part very soon. Then she started thanking me warmly for something. Then she went to her room and locked herself in."
"She got a letter?" Raskolnikov asked thoughtfully.
"Yes. You didn't know? Hmm..."
They were both silent.
"Goodbye, Rodion. There was a time, brother, when I... Never mind. Goodbye. You see, there was a time... Well, goodbye! I have to go too. I'm not going to drink. No need now... That's all nonsense!"
He hurried out, but when he had nearly closed the door behind him, he suddenly opened it again and said, looking away:

"Oh, by the way — you know that murder case? Porfiry's case — the old woman? The murderer's been found: he's confessed and given them proof. It's one of those workmen — the house painter, can you imagine? Remember how I defended them here? Would you believe it — the whole scene of fighting and laughing with his co-workers on the stairs while the porter and those two witnesses were on their way up — he staged all of it on purpose, to throw off suspicion. The cunning, the nerve! Hard to believe — but it's his own confession, he admitted everything! What a fool I was to fall for it! But in my opinion he's simply a genius of deception and quick thinking — there's nothing all that surprising about it, I suppose. People like that do exist. And the fact that he couldn't keep it up and confessed actually makes his story more believable. But what a fool I was! I was passionately on their side!"
"Tell me, please — where did you hear this, and why does it interest you so much?" Raskolnikov asked with unmistakable agitation.
"What a question! You ask me why it interests me!... Well, I heard it from Porfiry, among others. In fact, I heard almost everything from him."
"From Porfiry?"
"From Porfiry."
"What... what did he say?" Raskolnikov asked in alarm.
"He gave me an excellent explanation. Psychological — in his usual way."
"He explained it? Explained it himself?"

"Yes, yes. Goodbye! I'll tell you the whole thing another time, but right now I'm busy. There was a time when I thought... But never mind — later! Why would I need to drink now? You've made me drunk without wine. I'm drunk, Rodya! Good-bye — I'm going. I'll come back soon."
He left.

"He's a political conspirator — there's no doubt about it," Razumikhin decided as he slowly descended the stairs. "And he's dragged his sister into it — that's entirely consistent with Avdotya Romanovna's character. They're having meetings!... She hinted as much. So many of her words, her hints — they all point that way! And how else can this whole tangle be explained? Hmm! And I was practically thinking... Good God, what I was thinking! Yes, I lost my mind and wronged him! It was his doing — that day under the lamp in the corridor. Pah! What a crude, vile, nasty idea of mine! Good for Nikolay, confessing... And how clear it all is now! His illness then, all his strange behavior... even before that, back at the university — so gloomy, so morose all the time... But what does that letter mean? Maybe there's something in that, too. Who was it from? I have my suspicions... No, I have to get to the bottom of this!"
He thought of Dunya, and everything he'd heard hit him with full force. His heart pounded, and he suddenly broke into a run.

As soon as Razumikhin left, Raskolnikov got up, went to the window, paced from one corner to the other as if forgetting how small his room was, then sat back down on the sofa. He felt — renewed, somehow. Again there was a fight, a way forward.

"Yes, a way forward had appeared! Things had been too suffocating, too crushing — the weight had been unbearable. A kind of paralysis had set in at times. From the moment of the scene with Nikolay at Porfiry's office, he had felt trapped, penned in without hope of escape. After Nikolay's confession — that very same day — the scene with Sonia had followed. His behavior and his final words had been nothing like what he'd imagined beforehand; he had weakened — instantly, fundamentally! And he had agreed with Sonia at the time, agreed in his heart that he couldn't go on living alone with such a thing on his conscience!

"And Svidrigailov was a riddle... He worried him, true, but somehow on a different level. He might still have a confrontation coming with Svidrigailov. Svidrigailov, too, might be a way out; but Porfiry was a different matter.

"So Porfiry himself had explained it to Razumikhin — had explained it psychologically! He was back to his damned psychology again! Porfiry? But to think that Porfiry could believe, even for a moment, that Nikolay was guilty — after everything that had passed between them before Nikolay's appearance, after that face-to-face conversation that could have only one explanation? During those days Raskolnikov had often replayed passages of that scene with Porfiry in his mind; he couldn't bear to dwell on it. Such words, such looks had been exchanged, things had been said in such a tone, and matters had gone so far that Nikolay — whom Porfiry had seen through from the first word, the first gesture — could not possibly have shaken his conviction.

"And to think that even Razumikhin had started to suspect! The scene in the corridor, under the lamp, had made its impression. He'd gone running to Porfiry... But why had Porfiry received him that way? What had been his purpose in diverting Razumikhin with Nikolay? He must have some plan, some scheme — but what? True, a long time had passed since that morning — too long — and there'd been no sight or sound of Porfiry. Well, that was a bad sign..."

Raskolnikov took his cap and went out, still pondering. It was the first time in a long while that his head had felt clear. "I have to deal with Svidrigailov," he thought, "and as soon as possible. He seems to be waiting for me to come to him on my own." At that moment such a surge of hatred rose in his exhausted heart that he could have killed either of them — Porfiry or Svidrigailov. At the very least, he felt he would be capable of it later, if not now.
"We'll see, we'll see," he repeated to himself.

But no sooner had he opened the door than he ran straight into Porfiry himself in the hallway. Porfiry was coming to see him. For a moment Raskolnikov was dumbfounded — but only for a moment. Strangely, he wasn't very surprised to see Porfiry, and he was barely afraid. He was merely startled, but quickly — instantly — on his guard. "Perhaps this means the end? But how had Porfiry crept up so quietly, like a cat, without making a sound? Could he have been listening at the door?"

"You weren't expecting a visitor, Rodion Romanovitch?" Porfiry explained, laughing. "I've been meaning to look in for a long time. I was passing by and thought — why not stop in for five minutes? Going out? I won't keep you. Just let me have one cigarette."
"Sit down, Porfiry Petrovitch, sit down." Raskolnikov offered his visitor a seat with such a pleased, friendly expression that he would have marveled at himself if he could have seen it.
The last moment had arrived. The final drops had to be drained! Just as a man might endure half an hour of mortal terror with a robber — yet when the knife is finally at his throat, he feels no fear.
Raskolnikov sat down directly facing Porfiry and looked at him without flinching. Porfiry squinted and began lighting a cigarette.
"Speak! Speak!" seemed ready to burst from Raskolnikov's chest. "Well? Why won't you speak?"

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 2
paragraphs: "Ah, these cigarettes!" Porfiry Petrovitch exclaimed at last, having lit one. "They're terrible for you, absolutely terrible, and yet I can't quit! I cough, my throat tickles, I can't breathe properly. You know, I'm a coward — I went to see Dr. B— recently. He gives every patient at least half an hour. He actually laughed when he examined me. He tapped my chest and said: 'Tobacco is bad for you — your lungs are affected.' But how am I supposed to quit? What would I replace it with? I don't drink — that's the problem, he-he-he — that I don't drink. Everything is relative, Rodion Romanovitch — everything is relative!"

"Here he goes with his professional tricks again," Raskolnikov thought with disgust. All the details of their last meeting suddenly came flooding back, along with the same feeling that had overwhelmed him then.

"I actually came to see you the day before yesterday, in the evening — you didn't know?" Porfiry Petrovitch continued, looking around the room. "I came right into this very room. I was passing by, just like today, and I thought I'd return your visit. I walked in — your door was wide open — looked around, waited, and left without giving my name to your servant. Don't you lock your door?"
Raskolnikov's expression grew darker and darker. Porfiry seemed to read his mood.
"I've come to have it out with you, Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow! I owe you an explanation and I must give it to you," he continued with a slight smile, patting Raskolnikov's knee lightly.

But almost at the same instant a serious, careworn look came over his face. To his surprise, Raskolnikov saw a hint of sadness in it. He had never seen or suspected such an expression on Porfiry's face.

"A strange scene took place between us last time, Rodion Romanovitch. Our first meeting was strange too, but then... well, one thing after another! Here's the point: I may have treated you unfairly, and I feel it. Do you remember how we parted? Your nerves were shot, your knees were shaking — and so were mine. And you know, the way we behaved wasn't very civil, wasn't gentlemanly at all. And yet we are gentlemen — above all else, gentlemen. That has to be acknowledged. You remember where things ended up between us?... It was quite improper."
"What is he up to? What does he take me for?" Raskolnikov asked himself in amazement, raising his head and looking straight at Porfiry.

"I've decided that honesty is the best policy between us," Porfiry Petrovitch continued, turning his head away and lowering his eyes, as though unwilling to unsettle his former quarry, as though disdaining his old tricks. "Yes, such suspicions and such scenes can't go on forever. It was Nikolay who put a stop to it — otherwise I don't know where we might have ended up. That damned workman was sitting in the next room the whole time — you can picture that? You know that, of course; and I'm aware he came to see you afterward. But what you believed at the time was wrong: I hadn't sent for anyone, I hadn't made any arrangements. You ask why? Well, what can I say — it all happened so suddenly. I'd barely had time to send for the building porters — you noticed them on your way out, I'm sure. An idea flashed through my mind: I was firmly convinced at the time, you see, Rodion Romanovitch. I thought — even if I let one thing slip for the moment, I'll catch something else. At least I won't lose what matters. You're nervously irritable by temperament, Rodion Romanovitch — out of all proportion to your other qualities of heart and character, which I flatter myself I've partly figured out. Of course, even then I realized that a person doesn't always just stand up and blurt out their whole story. It happens sometimes, if you push someone past the breaking point — but it's rare. I understood that much. What I needed was just one fact, even the smallest concrete detail — something I could hold on to, something tangible, not just psychology. Because if a person is guilty, you should be able to get something solid out of them — you can sometimes get the most astonishing results. I was counting on your temperament, Rodion Romanovitch — on your temperament above all. I had great hopes for you."
"But what are you driving at now?" Raskolnikov finally muttered, asking the question almost without thinking.
"What is he talking about?" he wondered, bewildered. "Does he really believe I'm innocent?"

"What am I driving at? I've come to explain myself — I consider it my duty, so to speak. I want you to understand clearly how the whole business, the whole misunderstanding, developed. I've caused you a great deal of suffering, Rodion Romanovitch. I'm not a monster. I understand what it means for someone who's been through hardship but who is proud, imperious, and above all impatient to endure such treatment! In any case, I regard you as a man of noble character, with elements of genuine magnanimity — though I don't agree with all your views. I wanted to tell you this first, frankly and sincerely, because above all I don't want to deceive you. When I first met you, I felt drawn to you. Perhaps you'll laugh at that. You have every right to. I know you disliked me from the start, and you have no reason to like me. Think what you will — but I want now to do everything I can to erase that impression and show you that I'm a man with a heart and a conscience. I mean it."
Porfiry Petrovitch paused with dignity. Raskolnikov felt a wave of renewed alarm. The idea that Porfiry believed him innocent was starting to make him uneasy.

"There's hardly any need to go through everything in detail," Porfiry Petrovitch went on. "I couldn't, really. To start with, there were rumors. Through whom, how, and when they reached me... and how they implicated you — I don't need to get into all that. My suspicions were triggered by a complete accident, one that might easily never have happened. What was it? Hmm! I think there's no need to go into that either. All those rumors and that accident led me to one idea. I'll admit it openly — I was the first one to fix on you. The old woman's notes about the pledges and so forth — that all came to nothing. Yours was one among a hundred. I also happened to hear about the scene at the police office — someone described it brilliantly, unconsciously recreating the scene with great vividness. It was just one thing after another, Rodion Romanovitch, one thing after another! How could I help arriving at certain conclusions? From a hundred rabbits you can't make a horse; a hundred suspicions don't make a proof — as the English proverb says. But that's pure rationality, and you can't help being partial — a prosecutor is only human, after all.
