I also thought about your article in that journal — remember our first visit when we discussed it? I mocked you then, but that was only to draw you out. I repeat: you're ill, Rodion Romanovitch, and impatient. That you were bold, headstrong, serious, and had felt deeply — I recognized early on. I've felt the same things myself, so your article seemed familiar to me. It was conceived on sleepless nights, with a pounding heart, in ecstasy and suppressed passion. And that proud, suppressed passion in young people — it's dangerous! I mocked you then, but let me tell you: as a literary admirer, I'm very fond of such first efforts, full of youthful fire. There's a haze and a chord vibrating in the mist. Your article is absurd and fantastical, but there's a transparent sincerity in it, a youthful incorruptible pride, and the audacity of despair. It's a dark piece, but that's what makes it powerful. I read it, set it aside, and thought: 'That man won't take the ordinary path.' After such a preamble, how could I not be swept along by what followed? Oh, I'm not saying anything definitive — I'm making no statement now. I simply noted it at the time. 'What's really here?' I asked myself. Nothing! Possibly absolutely nothing. And it's really not proper for a prosecutor to let himself get carried away by notions: here I've got Nikolay on my hands, with real evidence against him — think what you like of it, but it is evidence. He brings his own psychology too; one has to take him into account — it's a matter of life and death. Why am I telling you all this? So you'll understand, and not blame me for my malicious behavior on that occasion. It wasn't malicious, I assure you, he-he! Do you think I didn't search your room at the time? Oh, I did — he-he! I was here while you lay ill in bed — not officially, not in person, but I was here. Your room was searched to the last thread at the first opportunity, but umsonst! I thought: now that man will come — will come to me on his own, and quickly too. If he's guilty, he's bound to come. Someone else wouldn't, but he will. And do you remember how Mr. Razumikhin started discussing the case with you? We arranged that to provoke you — so we deliberately spread rumors, knowing he'd bring them to you. Razumikhin can't restrain his indignation. Mr. Zametov was tremendously struck by your anger and your brazen daring. Think of it — blurting out in a restaurant: 'I killed her!' Too bold, too reckless. I thought at the time: if he's guilty, he'll be a formidable opponent. That's what I was thinking. I was expecting you. And you came! Oh, my heart was pounding. Ah!

"Now — why did you have to come? Your laughter as you entered — do you remember? I saw everything plainly. But if I hadn't been expecting you so keenly, I wouldn't have noticed anything in your laughter. You see the power of mood! And Mr. Razumikhin — ah, that stone, that stone under which the things were hidden! I can picture it somewhere in a kitchen garden. You told Zametov about a kitchen garden, and you repeated it in my office, didn't you? And when we started picking apart your article — how you explained it! Every word could be taken two ways, as though there were a hidden second meaning.

"And so, Rodion Romanovitch, I reached the limit — and smacked my head against a wall. I stopped myself and asked: what am I doing? After all, everything can be explained the other way too, if you want — and in fact more naturally. I had to admit it was more natural. I was tormented! 'No,' I thought, 'I need some concrete detail.' And when I heard about the doorbell-ringing, I held my breath and started trembling. 'Here's my concrete detail!' I thought — and I stopped thinking it over. I would have paid a thousand rubles at that moment to have seen you with my own eyes when you walked a hundred paces beside that workman after he called you a murderer to your face, and you didn't dare ask him a single question the whole way. And then the chills you described? The bell-ringing during your illness, in a half-delirious state?

"So, Rodion Romanovitch — is it any wonder I played those games with you? And what made you show up at that exact moment? It was as if someone had sent you, I swear! And if Nikolay hadn't interrupted us... Remember Nikolay at that moment? Remember him clearly? It was a thunderbolt, a real thunderbolt! And how did I react? I didn't believe the thunderbolt — not for one second. You could see that yourself. And later, when you'd left and Nikolay gave some very plausible answers on certain points — so plausible even I was surprised — even then I didn't believe his story! That's what it means to be firm as a rock! 'No,' I thought, 'not a chance. What has Nikolay got to do with it!'"
"Razumikhin just told me you believe Nikolay's guilty, that you told him so yourself..."

His voice failed him and he broke off. He had been listening in indescribable agitation as this man, who had seen through him completely, now seemed to be retracting everything. He was afraid to believe it and didn't believe it. In those still-ambiguous words he searched desperately for something more definite, more conclusive.

"Mr. Razumikhin!" Porfiry cried, as if delighted by a question from the previously silent Raskolnikov. "He-he-he! I had to get Mr. Razumikhin out of the way — two's company, three's a crowd. Razumikhin is the wrong person for this; besides, he's an outsider. He came running to me, white as a sheet... But never mind him — why bring him into it? Back to Nikolay: would you like to know what kind of man he is, as I understand him? First of all, he's still basically a child — and not exactly a coward, but something like an artist. Really, don't laugh at me for describing him that way. He's innocent, impressionable, and emotional. He has a heart, and he's a dreamer. He sings, dances, tells stories so well that people come from other villages to hear him. He goes to school and laughs until he cries if you hold up a finger at him. He'll drink himself unconscious — not as a vice, but when people treat him. He's like a child in that. And he steals too — without realizing it, because 'how can picking something up be stealing?' And did you know he's an Old Believer? Actually, more of a dissenter. There have been Wanderers in his family, and he spent two years in his village under the spiritual guidance of an elder. I learned all this from Nikolay himself and from people in his village. And what's more — he wanted to flee into the wilderness! He was full of religious fervor, prayed at night, read the old books — the 'true' ones — and read himself nearly out of his mind.
[A religious sect. — Translator's note.]

"Petersburg had a huge effect on him, especially the women and the wine. He's responsive to everything, and he forgot the elder and all that. I learned that an artist here took a liking to him and used to visit him. And then this whole business fell on him.

"Well, he was frightened — he tried to hang himself! He ran away! What can you do about the Russian people's terror of the legal system? The very word 'trial' scares some of them witless. Whose fault is that? We'll see what the new jury system does. God willing, it will help! Well, in prison he apparently remembered the venerable elder; the Bible reappeared too. Do you know, Rodion Romanovitch, what the word 'suffering' means to some of these people? It's not suffering for someone's benefit — it's simply: 'one must suffer.' To accept suffering — and if it comes from the authorities, so much the better. In my time, there was a very meek prisoner who spent an entire year reading his Bible on the stove at night, and he read himself crazy. So crazy that one day, for no reason at all, he grabbed a brick and flung it at the warden — even though the man had never done him any harm. And the way he threw it: deliberately aimed a yard to the side, for fear of actually hurting him. Well, you know what happens to a prisoner who assaults an officer with a weapon. So 'he accepted his suffering.'

"So now I suspect Nikolay wants to 'accept his suffering' — or something like it. I know it for a fact. Only he doesn't know that I know. What — you don't believe such people exist among the peasants? There are plenty. The elder has begun influencing him again, especially after the attempted hanging. But he'll come and tell me everything himself. You think he'll hold out? Just wait — he'll take back his confession. I'm expecting him any hour now to come and recant. I've grown fond of Nikolay and I'm studying him carefully. And you know what? He-he! On some points he answered me very plausibly — clearly he'd gathered some evidence and prepared himself. But on other points he's completely at sea, doesn't know a thing, and doesn't even suspect that he doesn't know!

"No, Rodion Romanovitch, Nikolay has nothing to do with this! This is a fantastical, dark, modern case — an incident of our times, when the human heart is troubled, when people quote the phrase that blood 'renews,' when comfort is preached as the aim of life. Here we have bookish dreams, a mind unhinged by theories. Here is determination in the first stage, but determination of a special kind: he decided to do it like jumping off a cliff or a bell tower, and his legs trembled as he walked to the crime. He forgot to shut the door behind him, yet murdered two people — all for a theory. He committed the murder but couldn't take the money; what he managed to grab, he hid under a stone. Suffering behind the door while they battered at it and rang the bell wasn't enough for him — no, he had to go back to the empty apartment, half-delirious, to relive the bell-ringing, to feel those cold shivers again... All right, we can chalk that up to illness. But consider this: he's a murderer, yet he sees himself as an honest man, despises others, poses as injured innocence. No — that's not the work of a Nikolay, my dear Rodion Romanovitch!"
Everything said before had sounded so much like a retraction that these words hit like a thunderbolt. Raskolnikov shuddered as though he'd been stabbed.
"Then... who then... is the murderer?" he asked in a strangled voice, unable to stop himself.
Porfiry Petrovitch sank back in his chair as though genuinely astonished by the question.
"Who is the murderer?" he repeated, as if unable to believe his ears. "Why, you are, Rodion Romanovitch! You are the murderer," he added, almost in a whisper, in a voice of absolute conviction.
Raskolnikov sprang from the sofa, stood for a few seconds, and sat back down without a word. His face twitched convulsively.

"Your lip is twitching again, just like before," Porfiry observed, almost sympathetically. "You've been misunderstanding me, I think, Rodion Romanovitch," he added after a brief pause. "That's why you're so shocked. I came specifically to tell you everything and deal with you openly."
"It wasn't me — I didn't murder her," Raskolnikov whispered, like a small child caught misbehaving.
"Yes, it was you, Rodion Romanovitch — you and no one else," Porfiry whispered sternly, with conviction.

They were both silent, and the silence lasted a strangely long time — about ten minutes. Raskolnikov put his elbow on the table and ran his fingers through his hair. Porfiry Petrovitch sat quietly, waiting. Finally Raskolnikov looked scornfully at Porfiry.
"You're back to your old tricks, Porfiry Petrovitch! The same old method. Don't you ever get tired of it?"

"Oh, forget all that — what does it matter now? Things would be different if there were witnesses present, but we're whispering alone. You can see for yourself that I haven't come to chase and trap you like a rabbit. Whether you confess or not makes no difference to me at this point. I'm convinced with or without it."
"If that's so, why did you come?" Raskolnikov asked irritably. "I'll ask you the same question again: if you consider me guilty, why don't you arrest me?"
"Well, that's quite a question! I'll answer point by point. First, arresting you outright isn't in my interest."
"How so? If you're convinced, you ought to..."

"Oh, so what if I'm convinced? For now, that's just my theory. Why should I lock you up where you'd be safe? You know that's exactly what it would mean — since you're asking for it yourself. If I put you in a lineup with that workman, for example, and you say to him, 'Were you drunk or not? Who saw me with you? I simply assumed you were drunk, and you were too' — well, what could I say to that? Especially since your version is more plausible than his, because his testimony is backed by nothing but psychology — which is almost indecent, given his ugly mug — while you'd hit the nail on the head, because the man is a notorious, confirmed drunkard. And I've admitted frankly several times already that this psychology business cuts both ways, and the second interpretation is the stronger one, much more convincing. And apart from that, I have nothing against you so far. True, I will arrest you, and I've actually come — quite against protocol — to warn you in advance. But I'm telling you honestly, also against protocol, that it won't be to my advantage. Well, secondly, I've come because..."
"Yes, yes — secondly?" Raskolnikov was listening breathlessly.

"Because, as I just told you, I consider I owe you an explanation. I don't want you to think of me as a monster, since I genuinely like you — believe it or not. And thirdly, I've come with a direct, open proposal: surrender and confess. It will be infinitely better for you — and easier for me too, since my task will be done. Now — is that open enough?"
Raskolnikov thought for a moment.
"Listen, Porfiry Petrovitch. You just said yourself you have nothing but psychology. Yet now you've jumped to mathematics. What if you're the one who's mistaken?"
"No, Rodion Romanovitch, I'm not mistaken. I have a small fact — even then Providence sent it to me."
"What small fact?"

"I won't tell you, Rodion Romanovitch. In any case, I don't have the right to put this off any longer — I must arrest you. So think it over: at this point it makes no difference to me, so I'm speaking purely for your benefit. Believe me — it will be better, Rodion Romanovitch."
Raskolnikov smiled bitterly.
"That's not just ridiculous — it's positively shameless. Even if I were guilty — which I don't admit — what possible reason would I have to confess, when you yourself tell me I'd be safer in prison?"

"Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, don't put too much faith in words. Perhaps prison won't be so restful after all. That's just a theory — my theory — and who am I as an authority? Perhaps I'm hiding something from you even now, he-he! And how can you ask what advantage there'd be? Surely you know how it would reduce your sentence! You'd be confessing at a moment when another man has taken the crime on himself and muddied the entire case. Think about that! I swear before God I'll arrange it so that your confession comes as a complete surprise. We'll sweep away all these psychological points, all the suspicion against you, so that your crime will look like an aberration — because in truth it was an aberration. I'm an honest man, Rodion Romanovitch, and I'll keep my word."
Raskolnikov sat in gloomy silence, his head bowed dejectedly. He thought for a long time and finally smiled again, but this time his smile was sad and gentle.
"No," he said, apparently dropping all pretense with Porfiry. "It's not worth it. I don't care about reducing the sentence."
"That's exactly what I was afraid of!" Porfiry cried with warmth that seemed almost involuntary. "That's precisely what I feared — that you wouldn't care about the reduction."
Raskolnikov looked at him sadly and expressively.
"Don't disdain life!" Porfiry went on. "You have so much of it ahead of you. How can you say you don't want a lighter sentence? You're an impatient man!"
"So much of what ahead of me?"
"Life! What kind of prophet are you? How much do you really know? Seek and you shall find. Perhaps this is God's way of bringing you to Him. And the imprisonment — it isn't forever..."
"The sentence will be reduced," Raskolnikov laughed.
"Is it middle-class disgrace you're afraid of? Maybe you're afraid of it without realizing it, because you're young! But in any case, you of all people shouldn't be afraid to surrender and confess."
"Oh, damn it all!" Raskolnikov whispered with loathing and contempt, as though unwilling to speak aloud.
He stood up again as if meaning to leave, but sank back down in obvious despair.

"Damn it, if you like! You've lost faith and you think I'm just crudely flattering you. But how long have you been alive? How much do you understand? You invented a theory and then were ashamed when it fell apart and turned out not to be at all original! True, it turned out to be something base — but you're not hopelessly base. Not at all! At least you didn't deceive yourself for long: you went straight to the furthest extreme in one leap. How do I see you? I see you as one of those men who could stand there smiling while someone cuts out their entrails — if only they'd found faith or God. Find it, and you'll live. You've needed a change of direction for a long time now. Suffering is a good thing, too. Suffer! Maybe Nikolay is right in wanting to suffer. I know you don't believe it — but don't overthink it. Just throw yourself straight into life, without calculating. Don't be afraid — the current will carry you to shore and set you on your feet. What shore? How would I know? I only believe you have a long life ahead of you. I know you take all my words now for a prepared speech, but perhaps you'll remember them later. They might be useful sometime. That's why I'm saying them. It's lucky you only killed the old woman. If you'd come up with a different theory, you might have done something a thousand times more monstrous. You ought to thank God, perhaps. How do you know — maybe God is saving you for something. Keep your spirits up and be less afraid! Are you frightened by the great atonement ahead? No, it would be shameful to shrink from it. Since you've taken such a step, you must steel yourself. That's justice. Do what justice demands. I know you don't believe it, but truly — life will see you through. In time you'll accept it. What you need right now is fresh air — fresh air — fresh air!"
Raskolnikov actually flinched.
"Who are you? What kind of prophet are you? From what height of serene authority do you pronounce these words of wisdom?"

"Who am I? I'm a man with nothing left to hope for, that's all. A man with perhaps some feeling and sympathy, maybe even some knowledge — but whose day is past. You, though — you're a different matter. There's a life waiting for you. Though who knows — maybe your life will drift away in smoke too. What does it matter that you'll enter a different class of men? It's not comfort you'll miss, not with your heart! What does it matter if no one sees you for a long time? It's not about time — it's about yourself. Be the sun, and everyone will see you. The sun must be the sun, first and foremost. Why are you smiling again — because I'm such a Schiller? I bet you think I'm trying to win you over with flattery. Well, maybe I am, he-he-he! Maybe you'd better not take my word for it — maybe you should never fully believe me. I'm built that way, I confess. But you can judge for yourself how far I'm base and how far I'm honest."
"When do you plan to arrest me?"
"I can give you another day or two to walk around. Think it over, my dear fellow, and pray to God. It's in your interest, believe me."
"And what if I run?" Raskolnikov asked with a strange smile.

"You won't run. A peasant would run; a fashionable follower of someone else's ideology would run — show him the tip of your finger and he'll believe anything for the rest of his life. But you've already stopped believing in your theory. What would you run away with? And what would you do in hiding? It would be hateful, difficult — and what you need more than anything is a definite position, a proper atmosphere. And what atmosphere would you find? If you ran, you'd come back on your own. You can't manage without us. And if I put you in prison — say for a month, two, three — mark my words: you'll confess of your own accord, and you may even surprise yourself. You won't know an hour beforehand that you're about to confess. I'm convinced you'll decide to 'accept your suffering.' You don't believe me now, but you'll come to it. Because suffering, Rodion Romanovitch, is a great thing. Never mind that I've gotten fat — I understand that all the same. Don't laugh at it; there's an idea in suffering. Nikolay is right. No, you won't run, Rodion Romanovitch."
Raskolnikov stood up and took his cap. Porfiry Petrovitch rose as well.
"Going for a walk? The evening should be lovely — if we don't get a storm. Though a storm would clear the air nicely."
He too picked up his cap.

"Porfiry Petrovitch — please don't get the idea that I confessed to you today," Raskolnikov said with sullen insistence. "You're a strange man, and I listened to you out of simple curiosity. But I admitted nothing — remember that!"

"Oh, I know, I'll remember. Look at him — he's trembling! Don't worry, my dear fellow. Have it your way. Take a walk — just don't go too far. One last request, if I may," he added, lowering his voice. "It's an awkward one, but important. If by any chance — though I really don't believe it, and I think you're quite incapable of it — but just in case, during these forty or fifty hours, you were to get the notion of ending things some other way... in some violent fashion — laying hands on yourself..." (It's an absurd idea, but you must forgive me for it.) "Do leave a brief, clear note — just two lines — and mention the stone. It would be more generous. Well then — till we meet! Good thoughts and sound decisions to you!"

Porfiry left, stooping slightly and avoiding Raskolnikov's eyes. Raskolnikov went to the window and waited with irritated impatience until he judged Porfiry had reached the street and moved away. Then he too hurried out of the room.

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He hurried to Svidrigailov. What he hoped to get from the man, he didn't know. But Svidrigailov held some hidden power over him. Having once recognized this, he couldn't rest — and now the time had come.
On the way, one question nagged at him in particular: had Svidrigailov been to see Porfiry?
As far as he could tell, he would have sworn he hadn't. He went over it again and again, reviewed Porfiry's visit in his mind — no, he definitely hadn't gone. Of course not.

But if he hadn't gone yet, would he? For the moment, Raskolnikov felt he wouldn't. Why? He couldn't have explained, and even if he could, he wouldn't have wasted much thought on it just then. It all worried him, yet at the same time he couldn't focus on it. Strangely — no one would have believed it perhaps — he felt only a faint, vague anxiety about his immediate future. A different, far more important concern tormented him: it was about himself, but in a different, more fundamental way. On top of it all, he was conscious of immense moral exhaustion, though his mind was working better that morning than it had recently.

And was it even worth it, after everything that had happened, to keep struggling over these petty details? Was it worth maneuvering to keep Svidrigailov from going to Porfiry? Was it worth investigating, wasting time on someone like Svidrigailov?
Oh, how sick he was of it all!

And yet he was hurrying to Svidrigailov — could he be expecting something new from him? Information? A way out? People will clutch at straws! Was it fate, or some instinct drawing them together? Perhaps it was just exhaustion, despair. Perhaps it wasn't Svidrigailov he needed at all, but someone else, and Svidrigailov had simply presented himself. Sonia? But why would he go to Sonia now? To beg for her tears again? He was afraid of Sonia too. Sonia represented an irrevocable sentence. He had to go his own way or hers. Right now especially, he didn't feel equal to facing her. No — wouldn't it be better to try Svidrigailov? And he couldn't help acknowledging inwardly that for some reason he'd long felt he had to see him.

But what could they possibly have in common? Even their wickedness couldn't be the same kind. The man was deeply unpleasant — clearly depraved, undoubtedly cunning and deceitful, possibly malicious. Such stories circulated about him. True, he was helping Katerina Ivanovna's children, but who knew his motives? The man always had some scheme, some hidden agenda.

There was another thought that had been circling Raskolnikov's mind recently, causing him great distress. It was so painful he made deliberate efforts to push it away. He sometimes thought Svidrigailov was tracking him. Svidrigailov had discovered his secret and had designs on Dunya. What if he still did? Wasn't it practically certain? And what if, having discovered his secret and gained power over him, Svidrigailov intended to use it as a weapon against Dunya?

This idea sometimes tormented even his dreams, but it had never presented itself so vividly as now, on his way to Svidrigailov. The very thought filled him with dark rage. To begin with, it would change everything — even his own situation. He might have to confess his secret to Dunya immediately. Would he have to turn himself in, perhaps, to prevent Dunya from doing something rash? The letter? That morning Dunya had received a letter. Who in Petersburg would be writing to her? Luzhin, maybe? True, Razumikhin was there to protect her, but Razumikhin knew nothing about the situation. Maybe it was his duty to tell Razumikhin? He thought of it with revulsion.

In any case, he had to see Svidrigailov as soon as possible — that much was clear. Thank God, the specifics of their conversation didn't matter much, if only he could get to the heart of the matter. But if Svidrigailov were plotting against Dunya...
Raskolnikov was so drained by everything he'd been through that month that he could only resolve such questions one way: "Then I'll kill him," he thought in cold despair.

A sudden anguish gripped his heart. He stopped in the middle of the street and looked around, trying to get his bearings. He found himself on X— Prospect, thirty or forty paces from the Hay Market, which he'd just come through. The entire second floor of the building to his left was a tavern. All the windows were open; judging by the figures moving behind them, the rooms were packed. Sounds of singing poured out — clarinet, violin, and the boom of a Turkish drum. He could hear women shrieking. He was about to turn back, wondering why he'd come this way, when suddenly, in one of the far windows, he spotted Svidrigailov. He was sitting at a tea table right by the open window, pipe in mouth. Raskolnikov was taken aback, almost terrified. Svidrigailov was watching him silently, studying him — and, what struck Raskolnikov at once, seemed to be on the verge of getting up and slipping away unnoticed. Raskolnikov immediately pretended not to have seen him, gazing absently in another direction while watching him from the corner of his eye. His heart was pounding. And yes — Svidrigailov clearly didn't want to be seen. He took the pipe from his mouth and was about to duck out of sight, but as he stood and pushed back his chair, he apparently realized Raskolnikov had spotted him. What passed between them was much like their first meeting in Raskolnikov's room. A sly smile appeared on Svidrigailov's face, growing wider and wider. Each knew the other had seen him. Finally Svidrigailov burst out laughing.
"Well, come in if you want me — I'm here!" he shouted from the window.

Raskolnikov went up to the tavern. He found Svidrigailov in a tiny back room adjoining the main hall, where merchants, clerks, and all sorts of people were drinking tea to the frantic bellowing of a chorus. The click of billiard balls could be heard in the distance. On the table before Svidrigailov stood an open bottle and a glass half full of champagne. Also in the room were a boy with a small hand organ and a healthy-looking, rosy-cheeked girl of about eighteen in a tucked-up striped skirt and a Tyrolean hat with ribbons. Despite the chorus in the other room, she was singing some servants' hall ditty in a rather husky contralto, accompanied by the organ.

"That's enough," Svidrigailov stopped her as Raskolnikov entered. The girl immediately broke off and stood waiting respectfully. She had been singing her vulgar lyrics with a serious, almost reverential expression.
"Hey, Philip — a glass!" Svidrigailov called out.
"I won't have anything to drink," said Raskolnikov.
"Suit yourself — it wasn't for you anyway. Drink up, Katia! I don't need anything more today — you can go." He poured her a full glass and laid down a yellow banknote.

Katia drank her wine in one long series of gulps, the way women do, without setting down the glass, took the money, kissed Svidrigailov's hand — which he accepted with complete seriousness — and left. The boy trailed out after her with the organ. Both had been picked up from the street. Svidrigailov hadn't been in Petersburg a week, yet everything around him already had a patriarchal quality. The waiter Philip was by now an old friend, thoroughly obsequious.
The door to the main room had a lock on it. Svidrigailov was at home in this little room and probably spent whole days here. The tavern was dirty and wretched — not even second-rate.

"I was on my way to see you and looking for you," Raskolnikov began, "but I don't know what made me turn onto X— Prospect from the Hay Market just now. I never take this route. I usually turn right from the Hay Market. And this isn't the way to your place either. I just turned — and here you are. Strange!"
"Why not just say outright: 'It's a miracle'?"
"Because it might just be coincidence."

"Oh, that's how you people all think!" Svidrigailov laughed. "You won't admit it even when you secretly believe it's miraculous! You just said yourself it 'might' be only coincidence. And what cowards everyone is here about having their own opinion — you can't imagine, Rodion Romanovitch. I don't mean you — you have your own opinions and aren't afraid of them. That's what first attracted my interest."
"Nothing else?"
"Well, that's enough, isn't it?" Svidrigailov was obviously in high spirits, but only slightly so — he'd had no more than half a glass of wine.
"I think you came to see me before you knew I was capable of having what you call opinions of my own," Raskolnikov observed.

"Oh well, that was a different matter. Everyone has their own plans. And speaking of miracles — let me tell you, I think you've been sleeping for the last two or three days. I told you about this tavern myself; there's no miracle in your coming straight here. I described the route, gave you the address, and told you what hours you'd find me. Remember?"
"I don't remember," Raskolnikov answered with surprise.

"I believe you. I told you twice. The address got stamped on your memory mechanically. You turned this way mechanically, following the directions exactly, without being aware of it. When I told you, I hardly thought you'd understood. You give yourself away too easily, Rodion Romanovitch. And another thing: I'm convinced lots of people in Petersburg talk to themselves as they walk. It's a city of half-mad people. If only we had scientists — doctors, lawyers, and philosophers could conduct the most valuable research here, each in their own field. Few places exert so many gloomy, powerful, and strange influences on the human soul as Petersburg. The climate alone does so much. And it's the administrative center of all Russia — its character must radiate across the whole country. But that's neither here nor there. The point is: I've watched you several times. You leave your building holding your head high. Twenty paces from home, you let it drop and fold your hands behind your back. You look around but clearly see nothing in front of you or beside you. Eventually you start moving your lips, talking to yourself — sometimes waving a hand and declaiming — and then you just stop dead in the middle of the road. That's really not a good idea. Someone besides me might be watching, and it won't do you any good. It's really none of my business and I can't cure you, but you understand what I mean."
"Do you know that I'm being followed?" Raskolnikov asked, looking at him searchingly.
"No, I know nothing about that," Svidrigailov replied, seeming surprised.
"Well then, let's leave me out of it," Raskolnikov muttered with a frown.
"Fine, let's leave you out of it."

"Why don't you tell me this: if you come here to drink, and twice directed me to meet you here, why were you just trying to hide and get away when I looked up at the window from the street? I saw you."
"He-he! And why was it that you lay on your sofa with your eyes closed, pretending to be asleep, when you were wide awake the whole time I stood in your doorway? I saw that too."
"I may have had... my reasons. You know that yourself."
"And I may have had mine — though you don't know them."

Raskolnikov dropped his right elbow on the table, rested his chin on his right hand, and stared intently at Svidrigailov. For a full minute he studied that face, which had struck him before. It was a strange face, like a mask: white and ruddy, with bright red lips, a flaxen beard, and still-thick flaxen hair. His eyes were somehow too blue and their expression somehow too heavy and fixed. There was something deeply unsettling about that handsome face, which looked remarkably young for his age. Svidrigailov was smartly dressed in light summer clothes and particularly fastidious about his linen. He wore a massive ring with a precious stone.

"Do I really have to concern myself with you too?" Raskolnikov said suddenly, getting straight to the point with nervous impatience. "Even if you're perhaps the most dangerous man alive and decide to harm me, I'm not going to play games anymore. I'll show you right now that I don't value my own safety as highly as you probably think. I've come to tell you directly: if you persist in your former intentions toward my sister, and if you think you can profit from what's been recently discovered, I will kill you before you can have me locked up. You can count on that. You know I keep my word. And secondly, if there's something you want to tell me — because I keep getting the feeling you have something to say — then say it quickly. Time is short, and soon it may be too late."
"What's the rush?" Svidrigailov asked, studying him with curiosity.
"Everyone has their plans," Raskolnikov answered darkly and impatiently.

"You're the one who just demanded frankness, yet at the first question you refuse to answer," Svidrigailov observed with a smile. "You keep imagining I have hidden motives, so naturally you look at me with suspicion. That's perfectly understandable in your position. Much as I'd like us to be friends, I won't trouble myself trying to prove otherwise. It's not worth the effort, and I had nothing particularly special to discuss with you."
"Then what did you need me for? You're the one who kept hanging around."

"Simply as an interesting subject for study. I liked the fantastical nature of your situation — that's all! Besides, you're the brother of someone who interested me greatly, and I used to hear a great deal about you from that person. I gathered you had quite an influence over her — isn't that enough? Ha-ha-ha! Still, I must admit your question is rather complicated and hard for me to answer. Here, for instance — you came to me not just with a specific purpose but also hoping to hear something new, didn't you? Isn't that right?" Svidrigailov persisted with a sly smile. "Well, can't you imagine that I too, on the train coming here, was counting on you — on you telling me something new, on my getting some profit from you! You see what rich men we are!"
"What profit could you get?"

"How would I know? How could I? You see what kind of tavern I spend my time in — and I enjoy it, or rather, it's not much of an enjoyment, but you have to sit somewhere. That poor Katia just now — did you see her?... If only I were a gourmand, a club gourmet — but look what I eat!"
He pointed to a small table in the corner where the remains of a ghastly-looking beefsteak and potatoes sat on a tin plate.

"Have you eaten, by the way? I've had something and don't want any more. I don't drink at all, for instance — nothing except champagne, and not more than a glass all evening, and even that gives me a headache. I ordered this just now to wind myself up, because I'm heading out somewhere and you find me in a peculiar mood. That's why I tried to hide from you just now, like a schoolboy — I was afraid you'd get in my way. But I think" — he pulled out his watch — "I can spend an hour with you. It's half past four now. If only I were something — a landowner, a father, a cavalry officer, a photographer, a journalist... I'm nothing, no particular occupation, and sometimes I'm positively bored. I honestly thought you'd tell me something new."
"But who are you, really? And why have you come here?"
"Who am I? A gentleman. I served two years in the cavalry, then knocked around Petersburg for a while, then married Marfa Petrovna and lived in the country. There's my biography!"
"You're a gambler, I believe?"
"No — a poor excuse for one. A card-sharp, not a gambler."
"You've been a card-sharp?"
"Yes, I've been a card-sharp too."
"Did you ever get beaten for it?"
"It happened. Why?"
"Well, you could have challenged them to a duel... All in all, it must have been lively."
"I won't argue with you. And besides, I'm no philosopher. I confess I came here mainly for the women."
"Right after burying Marfa Petrovna?"
"Quite so," Svidrigailov smiled with disarming candor. "And? You seem to find something wrong in my talking about women that way."
"You're asking whether I find something wrong with depravity?"

"Depravity! So that's your angle! Well, I'll answer in order — first about women in general, since I do like to talk. Tell me, why should I restrain myself? Why give up women when I have a passion for them? It's an occupation, at least."
"So the only thing you're after here is depravity?"

"Very well — depravity then. You insist on calling it depravity. But at least I appreciate a direct question. In this depravity, at least there's something constant, something rooted in nature rather than dependent on fantasy — something present in the blood like an eternal flame, always burning, not easily extinguished even with the years. You'll agree that's a kind of occupation."
"That's nothing to celebrate. It's a disease — and a dangerous one."

"Oh, is that what you think? I agree it's a disease, like anything taken to excess. And of course, one must practice moderation. But first of all, everyone goes to excess one way or another; and secondly, naturally one should be moderate and sensible, however pathetic it may sound. But what else am I supposed to do? If I didn't have this, I might have to shoot myself. I'm willing to admit that a decent person should endure boredom, but still..."
"And could you actually shoot yourself?"

"Oh, come!" Svidrigailov deflected with disgust. "Please don't talk about that," he added hurriedly, without any of the swagger he'd shown throughout the conversation. His face completely changed. "I'll confess to a shameful weakness — I'm afraid of death, and I don't like hearing it discussed. Did you know I'm something of a mystic?"
"Ah — the apparitions of Marfa Petrovna! Are they still visiting you?"

"Oh, don't talk about them! There haven't been any more in Petersburg, thank God!" he cried irritably. "Let's talk about something else... though... Hmm! I haven't much time and can't stay long with you. Pity! I'd have plenty to tell you."
"What's your engagement — a woman?"
"Yes, a woman — something that came up by chance... No, that's not what I want to discuss."
"And the squalor, the filth of everything around you — doesn't it affect you? Have you lost the strength to stop?"

"You're claiming to have such strength yourself? Ha-ha-ha! You surprise me, Rodion Romanovitch — though I knew you'd say something like that. You preach to me about vice and aesthetics! You — a Schiller, an idealist! Of course, that's all as it should be, and it would be strange if it weren't — yet it does seem odd in practice... Ah, what a shame I have no time. You're a most fascinating character! By the way — are you fond of Schiller? I'm terribly fond of him."
"What a braggart you are," Raskolnikov said with some disgust.

"I swear I'm not!" Svidrigailov laughed. "But I won't argue — let me be a braggart. Why not brag if it hurts no one? I lived seven years in the country with Marfa Petrovna, so when I come across an intelligent person like you — intelligent and highly interesting — I'm simply glad of the conversation. Besides, I've drunk that half-glass of champagne and it's gone slightly to my head. And there's a certain matter that's wound me up considerably — but I'll keep quiet about that... Where are you going?" he asked in alarm.
Raskolnikov had begun to get up. He felt oppressed and stifled, somehow uneasy about having come. He was now convinced that Svidrigailov was the most worthless scoundrel on the face of the earth.

"Wait! Stay a little!" Svidrigailov begged. "At least let them bring you some tea. Sit down — I won't ramble on about myself, I promise. I'll tell you something. Would you like to hear how a woman once tried to 'save' me, as you'd put it? It would actually answer your first question, since the woman in question was your sister. May I? It'll help pass the time."
"Go ahead — but I trust you won't..."
"Oh, don't worry. Besides, even in a worthless, despicable man like me, Avdotya Romanovna can inspire nothing but the deepest respect."

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 4
paragraphs: "You know, perhaps — yes, I told you myself," Svidrigailov began, "that I was in debtors' prison here, for a huge sum, with no prospect of paying it off. There's no need to go into how Marfa Petrovna bought my freedom. Do you know to what insane lengths a woman can sometimes love? She was an honest woman, and very sensible, though completely uneducated. But would you believe that this honest, jealous woman, after many hysterical scenes and reproaches, agreed to enter into a kind of contract with me — one she kept throughout our entire marriage? She was considerably older than me, and besides, she always had a clove or something in her mouth. There was enough swine in my soul — and enough honesty too, of a sort — to tell her straight out that I couldn't be absolutely faithful. This confession drove her into a frenzy, but she seems to have almost liked my brutal frankness. She thought it showed I was unwilling to deceive her by warning her in advance, and for a jealous woman, that's the main thing. After many tears, an unwritten contract was drawn up between us: first, I would never leave Marfa Petrovna and would always be her husband; second, I would never go anywhere without her permission; third, I would never take a permanent mistress; fourth, in return, Marfa Petrovna gave me free rein with the servant girls, but only with her secret knowledge; fifth, God forbid I fall in love with a woman of our own class; sixth, if I were ever visited by a great, serious passion — God forbid — I was obligated to reveal it to Marfa Petrovna. On this last point, however, Marfa Petrovna was fairly relaxed. She was sensible enough, and she couldn't help seeing me as a dissolute wastrel incapable of real love. But a sensible woman and a jealous woman are two very different things, and that's where the trouble came in. To judge some people fairly, though, we have to abandon certain preconceptions and our habitual attitudes toward ordinary people. I have more reason to trust your judgment than anyone's. Perhaps you've already heard plenty that was ridiculous and absurd about Marfa Petrovna. She certainly had some very ridiculous ways, but I tell you frankly: I feel genuine regret for the countless griefs I caused her. Well, I think that's enough by way of a decent funeral oration for the most tender wife of a most tender husband. When we quarreled, I usually held my tongue and didn't provoke her — and that gentlemanly restraint rarely failed. It influenced her, even pleased her; there were times she was positively proud of me. But your sister she could never abide. How she ever risked taking such a beautiful creature into her house as a governess — I can only explain it by saying that Marfa Petrovna was a passionate, impressionable woman who simply fell in love with your sister. Well, who could blame her — look at Avdotya Romanovna! I saw the danger at first glance, and — what do you think? — I resolved not to even look at her. But Avdotya Romanovna herself took the first step — would you believe it? And would you believe that Marfa Petrovna was actually angry with me at first for my stubborn silence about your sister, for my indifferent reception of her endless adoring praise of Avdotya Romanovna? I don't know what she wanted! Of course, Marfa Petrovna told Avdotya Romanovna every detail about me. She had that unfortunate habit of telling literally everyone all our family secrets and constantly complaining about me; how could she not confide in such a wonderful new friend? I expect they talked about nothing else but me, and no doubt Avdotya Romanovna heard all the dark, mysterious rumors about me... I don't mind betting you've heard some of them too?"
"I have. Luzhin accused you of causing the death of a child. Is that true?"
"Please don't bring up those vulgar stories," Svidrigailov said with disgust and irritation. "If you absolutely insist on hearing about all that foolishness, I'll tell you one day, but now..."
"I also heard about some servant of yours in the country whom you mistreated."
"I beg you to drop the subject," Svidrigailov interrupted again with obvious impatience.
"Was that the servant who came to you after death to fill your pipe?... You told me about it yourself." Raskolnikov was growing more and more irritated.
Svidrigailov looked at him closely, and Raskolnikov thought he caught a flash of malicious mockery in that look. But Svidrigailov restrained himself and answered quite civilly:

"Yes, it was. I can see you're extremely curious about all this, and I'll consider it my duty to satisfy your curiosity at the first opportunity. My God — I see I really could pass for a romantic figure with some people. Judge how grateful I must be to Marfa Petrovna for telling Avdotya Romanovna all that mysterious, interesting gossip about me. I can only guess what impression it made, but in any case it worked in my favor. Despite Avdotya Romanovna's natural aversion, and despite my invariably dark and repellent manner — she did come to pity me, pity a lost soul. And once a girl's heart is moved to pity, it's more dangerous than anything. She's bound to want to 'save him,' to bring him to his senses, lift him up, redirect him to nobler aims, restore him to new life and usefulness — well, we all know how far such dreams can go. I saw at once that the bird was flying into the cage on its own. And I prepared accordingly. You're frowning, Rodion Romanovitch? No need. As you know, it all ended in nothing. (Damn, I'm drinking a lot!) You know, I always regretted, from the very beginning, that fate didn't arrange for your sister to be born in the second or third century A.D. as the daughter of a reigning prince or some governor in Asia Minor. She would undoubtedly have been one of those who endured martyrdom with a smile as hot pincers seared her breast. She would have gone to it willingly. And in the fourth or fifth century, she'd have walked off into the Egyptian desert to live for thirty years on roots and ecstasies and visions. She's simply burning to endure some torment for someone, and if she can't find her torment, she'll throw herself out a window. I've heard something about a Mr. Razumikhin — they say he's a sensible fellow; his surname suggests it. He's probably a theology student. Well, he'd better look after your sister! I like to think I understand her, and I'm proud of it. But at the beginning of an acquaintance, as you know, one tends to be more careless and stupid. You don't see clearly. Damn it all — why is she so beautiful? It's not my fault. In short, it began on my side with an irresistible physical desire. Avdotya Romanovna is extraordinarily chaste — incredibly, phenomenally so. Take note: I'm telling you this about your sister as a fact. She is almost morbidly chaste, despite her broad intelligence, and it will stand in her way. There was a girl in the house then, Parasha, a dark-eyed wench I'd never seen before — she'd just arrived from another village — very pretty but incredibly stupid. She burst into tears, wailed so loudly the whole house could hear, and caused a scandal. One day after dinner, Avdotya Romanovna followed me into a garden path and, with blazing eyes, insisted I leave poor Parasha alone. It was nearly our first private conversation. I was naturally delighted to comply, tried to appear flustered and embarrassed — played my part rather well, in short. Then came more meetings, private talks, pleas, entreaties, even tears — would you believe it, even tears? Think what the passion for moral reform can bring some young women to! I, of course, blamed everything on destiny, posed as a man hungering and thirsting for enlightenment, and finally deployed the most powerful weapon for the conquest of a woman's heart — one that never fails. It's the well-known technique: flattery. Nothing in the world is harder than speaking the truth, and nothing easier than flattery. If there's even the slightest false note in speaking the truth, it creates discord, and discord means trouble. But if flattery is false from first note to last, it's still perfectly agreeable, and heard with genuine pleasure. However crude the flattery, at least half of it will seem true. That holds for all levels of education and all classes of society. Even a vestal virgin could be seduced by flattery. I can never think without laughing of how I once seduced a lady devoted to her husband, her children, and her principles. What fun it was, and how little effort! And the lady really did have principles — of her own sort, anyway. My entire strategy consisted of appearing utterly demolished and prostrate before her purity. I flattered her shamelessly, and each time I managed to get a squeeze of the hand or a glance, I'd reproach myself for having stolen it by force, declaring she'd resisted and that I could never have gotten anywhere if I weren't so shameless. I insisted she was so innocent she couldn't have foreseen my treachery, and had yielded unconsciously, without realizing it. In a word, I triumphed, while the lady remained firmly convinced she was innocent, chaste, faithful to all her duties, and had fallen purely by accident. And how angry she was when I finally told her it was my sincere belief she'd been just as eager as I! Poor Marfa Petrovna was terribly susceptible to flattery too; if I'd wanted to, I could have had all her property signed over to me during her lifetime. (I'm drinking far too much wine and talking too much.) I hope you won't be angry if I mention that I was beginning to produce the same effect on Avdotya Romanovna. But I was stupid and impatient and ruined everything. Several times — one time in particular — Avdotya Romanovna was deeply displeased by the expression of my eyes. Would you believe it? There was sometimes a light in them that frightened her, growing stronger and more brazen until it became hateful to her. No need for details, but we parted. Then I did something stupid again. I began mocking all such reforming efforts and attempts to convert me in the crudest way; Parasha returned to the scene, and not just her — in short, there was a huge uproar. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, if you could only see how your sister's eyes can flash sometimes! Never mind that I'm drunk and have had a whole glass of wine — I'm telling you the truth. I assure you, that look haunted my dreams; eventually even the rustle of her dress became more than I could stand. I honestly began to think I might become epileptic. I would never have believed I could be driven to such frenzy. A reconciliation was essential, but by then it was impossible. And imagine what I did! To what depths of stupidity frenzy can drive a man! Never attempt anything in a frenzy, Rodion Romanovitch. I calculated that Avdotya Romanovna was, after all, a pauper (forgive me — that's not the right word, but does it matter if it conveys the meaning?), that she lived by her work, that she had her mother and you to support (you're scowling again), and I decided to offer her all my money — thirty thousand rubles I could have raised at the time — if she'd run away with me to Petersburg. Of course I'd have sworn eternal love, rapture, and the rest. And you know, I was so wild about her that if she'd told me to poison Marfa Petrovna or slit her throat and then marry me — I'd have done it at once! But it ended in the disaster you already know about. You can imagine my fury when I learned Marfa Petrovna had gotten hold of that vile attorney Luzhin and practically arranged a match — which amounted to exactly the same thing I was proposing. Am I right? Am I? I notice you've begun listening very closely... interesting young man..."

Svidrigailov struck the table with his fist impatiently. He was flushed. Raskolnikov saw clearly that the glass or glass and a half of champagne he'd been sipping unconsciously was affecting him — and he decided to take advantage of the opportunity. He was deeply suspicious of Svidrigailov.
"Well, after everything you've said, I'm fully convinced you came to Petersburg with designs on my sister," he said directly, deliberately trying to provoke him.
"Oh, nonsense," Svidrigailov said, seeming to shake himself awake. "I told you... besides, your sister can't stand me."
"I'm certain she can't. But that's not the point."

"Are you so sure she can't?" Svidrigailov screwed up his eyes and smiled mockingly. "You're right — she doesn't love me. But you can never be sure what's passed between a husband and wife, or between a lover and his mistress. There's always a small corner that stays secret from the world, known only to the two people involved. Can you swear that Avdotya Romanovna looked at me with nothing but revulsion?"
"From certain things you've let slip, I gather you still have designs — evil ones, naturally — on Dunya, and that you intend to carry them out without delay."
"What, have I let things slip like that?" Svidrigailov asked in naive dismay, paying absolutely no attention to the word "evil" attached to his designs.
"You're letting them slip right now. Why are you so frightened? What are you so afraid of?"
"Me — afraid? Afraid of you? You're the one who should be afraid of me, cher ami. But what nonsense... I've drunk too much, I can see that. Nearly said too much again. Damn the wine! Hey — water!"
He grabbed the champagne bottle and flung it unceremoniously out the window. Philip brought water.
"That's all nonsense!" Svidrigailov said, wetting a towel and pressing it to his head. "But I can demolish all your suspicions with a single word. Did you know I'm getting married?"
"You told me that before."

"Did I? I've forgotten. But I couldn't have said so definitely, because I hadn't even met my bride then. I only had the idea. But now I actually have a fiancée, and it's all settled. If I didn't have business that can't wait, I'd take you to meet them right now, because I'd like to ask your advice. Oh damn — only ten minutes left! Look at the time. But I must tell you about my marriage — it's an interesting story in its own way. Where are you off to? Leaving again?"
"No, I'm not leaving now."

"Not at all? We'll see. I will take you there — I'll show you my bride — but not now. You'll need to go soon anyway. You'll go right, and I'll go left. Do you know Madame Resslich, the woman I'm lodging with? I know what you're thinking — she's the woman whose girl supposedly drowned herself last winter. Come, are you listening? She arranged the whole thing for me. 'You're bored,' she said, 'you need something to fill your time.' Because, you know, I'm a gloomy, depressive sort. You think I'm lighthearted? No — I'm gloomy. I do no harm, but I sit in a corner for three days without saying a word. And that Resslich is a sly one, I tell you. I know what she has in mind: she thinks I'll get tired of my wife, abandon her, and leave — and then she'll get hold of the girl and make a profit from her, among our class or higher. She told me the father was a broken-down retired official who's been sitting in a wheelchair for three years, paralyzed. The mother, she said, was a sensible woman. There's a son serving in the provinces who never helps, a married daughter who never visits. And they're raising two little nephews on top of their own children, as if they didn't have enough trouble. They pulled their youngest daughter out of school — a girl who'll be sixteen in another month — so she could be married off. She was meant for me. We went to see them. What a comedy! I present myself: a landowner, a widower, from a well-known family, with connections and a fortune. What does it matter that I'm fifty and she's not yet sixteen? Who cares about that? But it is fascinating, isn't it? It's fascinating, ha-ha! You should have seen me talking to the parents. It was priceless. She comes in, curtseys — you can imagine, still in a short dress — an unopened bud! Blushing like a sunset — they'd told her, no doubt. I don't know how you feel about female faces, but in my view, these sixteen years, these childish eyes, this shyness and these bashful tears are lovelier than beauty. And she's a perfect little picture too: fair hair in little curls like a lamb's, plump rosy lips, tiny feet — a charmer!... Well, we became friends. I told them I was in a hurry due to family circumstances, and the very next day — that is, the day before yesterday — we were engaged. Now whenever I visit, I take her on my knee right away and keep her there... She blushes like a sunset, and I kiss her every minute. Her mother naturally impresses on her that this is her husband and this is how it must be. It's delicious! The current betrothed state may actually be better than marriage itself. Here you have what they call la nature et la vérité! Ha-ha! I've talked to her twice; she's far from stupid. Sometimes she sneaks a look at me that positively scorches. Her face is like Raphael's Madonna — you know, the Sistine Madonna has something fantastical in it, something of mournful religious ecstasy. Haven't you noticed? Well, she has something of that look. The day after the engagement, I bought her presents worth fifteen hundred rubles — a diamond set, a pearl set, and a silver dressing case as big as this, full of everything — and even my Madonna's face glowed. I sat her on my knee yesterday, a bit too freely I suppose — she turned crimson and tears appeared, but she tried not to show it. We were left alone, and she suddenly threw her arms around my neck — for the first time, of her own accord — kissed me, and vowed she would be an obedient, faithful, good wife, that she'd make me happy, devote every minute of her life to me, sacrifice everything, everything — and that all she wants in return is my respect, and that she wants 'nothing, nothing more from me — no presents.' You'll agree that to hear such a confession from a sixteen-year-old angel in a muslin dress, with curls and a blush of maidenly modesty and tears of rapture in her eyes — it's rather captivating, isn't it? It's something worth having, isn't it? Well... listen, let's go see my fiancée — only not right now!"
"The fact is, this monstrous difference in age and maturity excites your lust! Will you really go through with such a marriage?"

"Why not? Certainly. Everyone thinks of himself, and the man who's best at deceiving himself lives the most cheerfully. Ha-ha! But why this sudden passion for virtue? Have mercy on me, my friend. I'm a sinful man. Ha-ha-ha!"
"But you've made arrangements for Katerina Ivanovna's children. Though... you had your own reasons for that... I understand everything now."

"I'm very fond of children — always have been," Svidrigailov laughed. "I can tell you a curious example. My first day here, I visited various haunts — after seven years, I simply threw myself at them. You've probably noticed I'm in no rush to reconnect with old friends. I'll manage without them as long as I can. You know, when I was with Marfa Petrovna in the country, the thought of these places, where a man who knows his way around can find plenty, haunted me. Yes, upon my soul! The peasants have vodka, the educated young people shut out from activity waste themselves on impossible dreams and theories; Jews spring up and hoard money; everyone else gives themselves over to debauchery. From the first hour, the city reeked of its familiar smells. I happened into a ghastly den — I like my dens filthy — and there was a so-called dance, with a cancan the likes of which I'd never seen in my day. Yes, there's progress for you. Suddenly I noticed a girl of thirteen, nicely dressed, dancing with a specialist in that line, facing another partner. Her mother was sitting in a chair by the wall. You can't imagine what that cancan was like! The girl felt ashamed, blushed, and finally felt insulted and began to cry. Her partner grabbed her, started spinning her around and performing in front of her; everyone laughed — I like your public, even the cancan public — they laughed and shouted: 'Serves her right! That's what she gets for bringing children!' Well, it's not my concern whether that reasoning was logical or not. I immediately made my plan. I sat down beside the mother and explained that I too was a stranger, that people here were rude and couldn't recognize decent folk or treat them respectfully. I let her understand I had plenty of money, offered to take them home in my carriage. I took them home and got to know them. They were staying in a miserable little hole, having just arrived from the country. She told me she and her daughter could only regard my acquaintance as an honor. I learned they had nothing of their own and had come to the city on some legal matter. I offered my services and money. I found out they'd gone to the dance hall by mistake, thinking it was a real dance school. I offered to help with the girl's education in French and dancing. The offer was accepted with enthusiasm as a great honor — and we're still on friendly terms... If you'd like, we'll go visit them — only not just now."
"Stop! Enough of your vile, disgusting stories, you depraved, loathsome man!"
"Schiller! A true Schiller! O la vertu va-t-elle se nicher? But you know, I'm going to keep telling you these things on purpose, just for the pleasure of hearing your outrage!"
"Of course you are. I can see I'm making a fool of myself," Raskolnikov muttered angrily.
Svidrigailov laughed heartily. Then he called Philip, paid his bill, and started getting up.
"Well, I'm drunk — assez causé," he said. "It's been a pleasure."

"I should think so!" cried Raskolnikov, also rising. "Naturally it's entertaining for a worn-out degenerate to describe such adventures — with some equally monstrous scheme already in mind — especially to a man like me and in circumstances like these... It's stimulating!"

"Well, if you put it that way," Svidrigailov replied, examining Raskolnikov with some surprise, "if you put it that way, you're quite a cynic yourself. You've got the raw material, at any rate. You can understand a great deal... and do a great deal too. But enough. I sincerely regret we haven't talked more, but I won't lose sight of you... Just wait a bit."

Svidrigailov walked out of the restaurant. Raskolnikov followed. Svidrigailov was not, in fact, very drunk — the wine had affected him briefly, but the effect was already passing. He was preoccupied with something important and clearly excited, anxious in anticipation of something. His manner toward Raskolnikov had been changing over the past few minutes, growing ruder and more sneering. Raskolnikov noticed all of this and was uneasy himself. He became deeply suspicious of Svidrigailov and decided to follow him.
They came out onto the sidewalk.
"You go to the right, and I to the left — or the other way around, if you prefer. Only — adieu, mon plaisir. May we meet again."
And he walked off to the right, toward the Hay Market.

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Raskolnikov walked after him.
“What's this?” cried Svidrigailov, turning around. “I thought I said—”
“It means I'm not going to lose sight of you now.”
“What?”
They both stood still and stared at one another, as if measuring each other's strength.

“From all your half-drunk stories,” Raskolnikov observed harshly, “I am absolutely positive that you haven't given up your designs on my sister — you're pursuing them more actively than ever. I've learned that my sister received a letter this morning. You've hardly been able to sit still all this time… You may have dug up a wife along the way, but that means nothing. I'd like to make certain for myself.”
Raskolnikov could hardly have said himself what he wanted or what he wished to make certain of.
“Good heavens! I'll call the police!”
“Go ahead and call them!”

Again they stood for a minute facing each other. At last Svidrigailov's face shifted. Having satisfied himself that Raskolnikov wasn't frightened by his threat, he put on a cheerful, friendly expression.

“What a fellow you are! I deliberately held back from mentioning your affair, though I'm eaten up with curiosity. It's a fantastic business. I had put it off for another time, but you're enough to wake the dead… Well, let's go, but I warn you in advance — I'm only going home for a moment to get some money, then I'll lock up the flat, take a cab, and go spend the evening at the Islands. Now really, are you going to follow me?”
“I'm coming to your lodgings, but not to see you — to see Sofya Semyonovna, to tell her I'm sorry I wasn't at the funeral.”

“Suit yourself, but Sofya Semyonovna isn't at home. She's taken the three children to an elderly lady of high rank, a patroness of some orphan asylums whom I used to know years ago. I charmed the old lady by depositing a sum of money with her to provide for the three children of Katerina Ivanovna, and by subscribing to the institution as well. I also told her Sofya Semyonovna's story in full detail, suppressing nothing. It had an indescribable effect on her. That's why Sofya Semyonovna has been invited to call today at the X. Hotel, where the lady is currently staying.”
“No matter — I'll come all the same.”

“As you please, it makes no difference to me. But I won't come with you. Here we are, we're home. By the way, I'm convinced you regard me with suspicion precisely because I've shown such restraint and haven't troubled you with questions so far… you follow me? It struck you as extraordinary — I'd bet on it. Well, that's what you get for being delicate!”
“And for listening at doors!”

“Ah, so that's it?” Svidrigailov laughed. “Yes, I'd have been surprised if you'd let that slide after everything that's happened. Ha-ha! Though I did grasp something of the pranks you were up to and were telling Sofya Semyonovna about, what was the meaning of it all? Maybe I'm hopelessly behind the times and can't understand. For goodness' sake, explain it to me, my dear boy. Expound the latest theories!”
“You couldn't have heard anything. You're making it all up!”

“But I'm not talking about that (though I did hear something). No, I'm talking about the way you keep sighing and groaning now. The Schiller in you rises up in revolt every other minute, and now you tell me not to listen at doors. If that's how you feel, go inform the police that you had this misfortune — that you made a little mistake in your theory. But if you're convinced that one mustn't listen at doors, yet one may murder old women at one's pleasure, you'd better clear off to America, and quickly too. Run, young man! There may still be time. I mean it sincerely. Are you short of cash? I'll pay your fare.”
“I'm not thinking about any of that,” Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust.

“I understand (but don't put yourself out, don't discuss it if you'd rather not). I understand the questions tormenting you — moral ones, yes? Duties of citizen and man? Set them all aside. They're nothing to you now, ha-ha! You'll say you're still a man and a citizen. If so, you shouldn't have gotten tangled up in this. It's no use taking on a job you're not cut out for. Well — you'd better shoot yourself, or don't you want to?”
“You seem to be trying to enrage me, to make me leave you.”

“What a strange fellow you are! Well, here we are. Welcome to the staircase. You see, that's the way up to Sofya Semyonovna. Look, there's no one home. Don't you believe me? Ask Kapernaumov. She leaves the key with him. Here's Madame Kapernaumov herself. Hey — what? She's rather deaf. Has she gone out? Where? Did you hear that? She's not in and won't be back until late in the evening, probably. Well, come to my room — you wanted to come and see me, didn't you? Here we are. Madame Resslich is out. She's a woman who's always busy, an excellent woman, I assure you… She might have been of use to you if you'd been a little more sensible. Now, look: I take this five-percent bond out of the bureau — see what a pile of them I still have — this one will be turned into cash today. I mustn't waste any more time. The bureau is locked, the flat is locked, and here we are again on the stairs. Shall we take a cab? I'm going to the Islands. Would you like a lift? I'll take this carriage. Ah, you refuse? You've had enough of it! Come for a drive! I think it's going to rain. Never mind, we'll put the hood down…”

Svidrigailov was already in the carriage. Raskolnikov decided that his suspicions were, at least for that moment, unjust. Without answering a word, he turned and walked back toward the Hay Market. If he had only looked back on his way, he might have seen Svidrigailov get out less than a hundred paces off, dismiss the cab, and set off on foot along the pavement. But he had already turned the corner and could see nothing. Intense disgust drew him away from Svidrigailov.
“To think that I could for a single instant have looked for help from that coarse brute, that depraved sensualist and scoundrel!” he cried.

Raskolnikov's judgment had been delivered too lightly and too hastily: there was something about Svidrigailov that lent him a certain original, even mysterious, character. As far as his sister was concerned, Raskolnikov was convinced that Svidrigailov would not leave her in peace. But it was too tiresome and unbearable to keep thinking and thinking about it.

Once alone, he hadn't gone twenty paces before he sank, as usual, into deep thought. On the bridge he stopped by the railing and began staring into the water. And his sister was standing close beside him.

He had met her at the entrance to the bridge, but passed by without seeing her. Dunia had never before encountered him like this in the street, and she was struck with dismay. She stood still, not knowing whether to call out to him or not. Suddenly she saw Svidrigailov coming quickly from the direction of the Hay Market.

He seemed to be approaching cautiously. He didn't step onto the bridge but stopped on the pavement to the side, doing everything he could to keep Raskolnikov from seeing him. He had been watching Dunia for some time and had been making signs to her. She thought he was signaling to beg her not to speak to her brother but to come to him.
That was what Dunia did. She slipped past her brother and went up to Svidrigailov.

“Let's hurry away,” Svidrigailov whispered to her. “I don't want Rodion Romanovitch to know about our meeting. I should tell you I've been sitting with him in the restaurant nearby — he sought me out and I had a devil of a time getting rid of him. He has somehow heard about my letter to you and suspects something. It wasn't you who told him, of course — but if not you, then who?”
“Well, we've turned the corner now,” Dunia interrupted, “and my brother won't see us. I must tell you: I'm going no further with you. Tell me here. You can say it all in the street.”

“In the first place, I can't say it in the street; secondly, you must hear Sofya Semyonovna as well; and thirdly, I'll show you some papers… Look here — if you refuse to come with me, I'll decline to give any explanation and leave at once. But I beg you not to forget that a very curious secret of your beloved brother's rests entirely in my keeping.”
Dunia stood still, hesitating, and fixed her searching eyes on Svidrigailov.
“What are you afraid of?” he observed quietly. “The town isn't the country. And even in the country, you did me more harm than I did you.”
“Have you prepared Sofya Semyonovna?”

“No, I haven't said a word to her, and I'm not even sure she's home now. But most likely she is. She buried her stepmother today — she's not likely to be out paying visits on such a day. For the moment I don't want to speak to anyone about it, and I half regret having spoken to you. The slightest indiscretion is as good as betrayal in a matter like this. I live right there, in that house — we're coming up to it. That's the porter of our building — he knows me very well. You see, he's bowing; he sees I'm coming with a lady, and he's no doubt noticed your face already, which you'll be glad of if you're afraid of me and suspicious. Forgive me for putting it so crudely. I don't have a flat to myself; Sofya Semyonovna's room is right next to mine — she lodges in the next flat over. The whole floor is let out in lodgings. Why are you scared like a child? Am I really so terrible?”

Svidrigailov's lips twisted into a condescending smile, but he was in no mood to smile. His heart was pounding and he could scarcely breathe. He spoke rather loudly to cover his rising agitation. But Dunia didn't notice this peculiar excitement; she was too annoyed by his remark that she was frightened of him like a child and that he was so terrible to her.
“Though I know that you are not a man of honor, I am not in the least afraid of you. Lead the way,” she said with apparent composure, though her face was very pale.
Svidrigailov stopped at Sonia's room.

“Allow me to check whether she's home… She isn't. How unfortunate! But I know she may be back quite soon. If she's gone out, it can only be to see a lady about the orphans. Their mother is dead… I've been meddling and making arrangements for them. If Sofya Semyonovna doesn't come back within ten minutes, I'll send her to you — today, if you like. This is my flat. These are my two rooms. Madame Resslich, my landlady, has the next room. Now, look this way. I'll show you my chief piece of evidence: this door from my bedroom opens into two perfectly empty rooms that are up for rent. Here they are… You should look them over with some attention.”

Svidrigailov occupied two fairly large furnished rooms. Dunia was glancing around mistrustfully, but saw nothing unusual in the furniture or the arrangement of the rooms. Yet there was something to notice — for example, that Svidrigailov's flat sat exactly between two sets of almost uninhabited apartments. His rooms weren't entered directly from the corridor but through the landlady's two nearly empty rooms. Unlocking a door leading out of his bedroom, Svidrigailov showed Dunia the two empty rooms that were up for rent. Dunia stopped in the doorway, not understanding what she was meant to look at, but Svidrigailov hurried to explain.

“Look here, at this second large room. Notice that door — it's locked. Beside the door stands a chair, the only one in the two rooms. I brought it in from my own rooms so I could listen more conveniently. Just on the other side of the door is Sofya Semyonovna's table; that's where she sat talking with Rodion Romanovitch. And I sat here listening, on two consecutive evenings, for two hours each time — and of course I managed to learn something. What do you think?”
“You were listening?”
“Yes, I was. Now come back to my room — we can't sit down out here.”

He led Avdotya Romanovna back into his sitting room and offered her a chair. He sat down at the opposite side of the table, at least seven feet away from her, but probably with the same glow in his eyes that had once frightened Dunia so badly. She shuddered and again looked around distrustfully. It was an involuntary gesture; clearly she didn't want to betray her uneasiness. But the secluded position of Svidrigailov's lodging had suddenly struck her. She wanted to ask whether at least his landlady were home, but pride kept her from asking. Besides, she had another trouble in her heart, incomparably greater than fear for herself. She was in great distress.

“Here is your letter,” she said, laying it on the table. “Can what you write be true? You hint at a crime committed, you say, by my brother. You hint at it too plainly; you daren't deny it now. I must tell you: I'd heard of this stupid story before you wrote, and I don't believe a word of it. It's a disgusting and ridiculous suspicion. I know the story — and why and how it was invented. You can have no proof. You promised to prove it. Speak! But let me warn you — I don't believe you! I don't believe you!”
Dunia said all this hurriedly, and for a moment the color rushed to her face.
“If you didn't believe it, how could you have risked coming to my rooms alone? Why did you come? Simply out of curiosity?”
“Don't torment me. Speak, speak!”

“There's no denying it — you are a brave girl. Upon my word, I thought you'd have asked Mr. Razumihin to escort you here. But he wasn't with you, nor anywhere nearby. I was keeping an eye out. It's spirited of you — it proves you wanted to spare Rodion Romanovitch. But everything about you is divine… About your brother, what can I say to you? You've just seen him yourself. What did you make of him?”
“Surely that can't be the only thing you're building your case on?”

“No, not on that, but on his own words. He came here two evenings in a row to see Sofya Semyonovna. I've shown you where they sat. He made a full confession to her. He is a murderer. He killed an old woman, a pawnbroker, with whom he himself had pawned things. He killed her sister too, a peddler woman called Lizaveta, who happened to come in while he was murdering her sister. He killed them with an axe he had brought with him. He murdered them in order to rob them, and rob them he did. He took money and various items… He told all of this, word for word, to Sofya Semyonovna — the only person who knows his secret. But she has had no part in the murder, by word or deed; she was as horrified by it as you are now. Don't worry, she won't betray him.”
“It cannot be,” Dunia muttered, her lips white. She gasped for breath. “It cannot be. There was not the slightest cause, no sort of reason… It's a lie, a lie!”

“He robbed her — that was the cause. He took money and things. It's true that by his own admission he made no use of the money or the things, but hid them under a stone, where they still are. But that was because he didn't dare make use of them.”
