“But how could he steal, how could he rob? How could he even dream of it?” Dunia cried, jumping up from the chair. “You know him, you've seen him — can he be a thief?”
She seemed to be pleading with Svidrigailov; she had completely forgotten her fear.

“There are thousands and millions of combinations and possibilities, Avdotya Romanovna. A thief steals and knows he's a scoundrel, but I've heard of a gentleman who broke open the mail. Who knows — very likely he thought he was doing a gentlemanly thing! Of course I wouldn't have believed it myself if I'd been told of it the way you're being told now, but I believe my own ears. He explained all the reasons for it to Sofya Semyonovna too. At first she didn't believe her ears, but in the end she believed her own eyes.”
“What… were the reasons?”

“It's a long story, Avdotya Romanovna. Here's… how shall I put it? — a theory of a sort, the same one by which I, for instance, hold that a single misdeed is permissible if the principal aim is good — a solitary wrongdoing and hundreds of good deeds! It's galling too, of course, for a gifted young man of overweening pride to know that if he only had, say, a paltry three thousand, his whole career and his whole future would take a different shape — and yet not to have that three thousand. Add to that the nervous irritation of hunger, of living in a hole, of wearing rags, of a vivid sense of his own social position and that of his sister and mother. Above all, vanity — pride and vanity — though God knows he may have good qualities too… I'm not blaming him, please don't think that; besides, it's none of my business. A special little theory got mixed up in it too — a theory of a sort — dividing humanity, you see, into the ordinary and the superior, meaning persons to whom the law does not apply because of their superiority, persons who make the laws for the rest of mankind — the ordinary, that is. It's fine as a theory, une théorie comme une autre. Napoleon attracted him enormously — that is, what affected him was that so many men of genius have had no hesitation about wrongdoing, have stepped over the law without a second thought. He seems to have imagined that he was a genius too — that is, he was convinced of it for a time. He has suffered a great deal and is still suffering from the idea that he could formulate a theory, but was incapable of boldly stepping over the law — and so he is not a man of genius. And that's humiliating for any proud young man, especially in our day…”
“But remorse? You deny him any moral feeling, then? Is that what he's like?”

“Ah, Avdotya Romanovna, everything is in a muddle now — not that it was ever in particularly good order. Russians in general are broad in their ideas, Avdotya Romanovna, broad like their land and exceedingly inclined toward the fantastic, the chaotic. But it's a misfortune to be broad without a special genius. Do you remember what a lot of talk we had together on this very subject, sitting on the terrace in the evenings after supper? You even used to reproach me with breadth! Who knows — perhaps we were talking at the very time when he was lying here thinking over his plan. We have no sacred traditions in our country, especially in the educated class, Avdotya Romanovna. At best someone will cobble them together out of books or some old chronicle. But those are mostly the scholars and old-fashioned fellows, so much so that it would be almost ill-bred in a man of society. You know my opinions in general, anyway. I blame no one. I do nothing at all, and I persist in that. But we've talked of this more than once before. I was even so happy as to interest you in my opinions… You are very pale, Avdotya Romanovna.”
“I know his theory. I read that article of his about men to whom everything is permitted. Razumihin brought it to me.”
“Mr. Razumihin? Your brother's article? In a magazine? Is there such an article? I didn't know. It must be interesting. But where are you going, Avdotya Romanovna?”
“I want to see Sofya Semyonovna,” Dunia said faintly. “How do I get to her? Perhaps she's come back. I must see her at once. Perhaps she…”
Avdotya Romanovna couldn't finish. Her breath literally failed her.
“Sofya Semyonovna won't be back until night — at least, I don't think she will. She was supposed to be back right away, but if not, then she won't be in until quite late.”
“Ah, then you're lying! I see it now… you were lying… lying all the time… I don't believe you! I don't believe you!” Dunia cried, completely losing her head.
Almost fainting, she sank onto a chair that Svidrigailov hastened to offer her.
“Avdotya Romanovna, what is it? Control yourself! Here is some water. Take a little…”
He sprinkled some water on her. Dunia shuddered and came to herself.

“It has acted violently,” Svidrigailov muttered to himself, frowning. “Avdotya Romanovna, calm yourself! Believe me, he has friends. We'll save him. Would you like me to take him abroad? I have money, I can get a ticket in three days. And as for the murder — he'll yet do all sorts of good deeds to atone for it. Calm yourself. He may become a great man yet. Well, how are you? How do you feel?”
“Cruel man! To be able to mock it! Let me go…”
“Where are you going?”
“To him. Where is he? Do you know? Why is this door locked? We came in through that door, and now it's locked. When did you manage to lock it?”

“We can't exactly be shouting about this all over the flat. I'm not mocking — it's simply that I'm sick of talking like this. But how can you go in such a state? Do you want to betray him? You'll drive him into a fury, and he'll turn himself in. Let me tell you — he is already being watched; they're already on his trail. You'll simply be handing him over. Wait a little: I saw him and was talking to him just now. He can still be saved. Wait a moment, sit down. Let us think it over together. I asked you to come in order to discuss this alone with you and to consider it properly. Please, sit down!”
“How can you save him? Can he really be saved?”
Dunia sat down. Svidrigailov sat down beside her.
“It all depends on you, on you, on you alone,” he began, his eyes glowing, almost in a whisper, barely able to get the words out for emotion.
Dunia drew back from him in alarm. He too was trembling all over.

“You… one word from you, and he is saved. I… I will save him. I have money and friends. I'll send him away at once. I'll get a passport — two passports, one for him and one for me. I have friends… capable people… If you like, I'll get a passport for you… for your mother… What do you want with Razumihin? I love you too… I love you beyond everything… Let me kiss the hem of your dress, let me, let me… The very rustle of it is too much for me. Tell me, ‘Do that,' and I'll do it. I'll do everything. I'll do the impossible. Whatever you believe, I'll believe. I'll do anything — anything! Don't, don't look at me that way. Do you realize you are killing me?…”
He was nearly starting to rave… Something seemed to rush to his head all at once. Dunia jumped up and rushed to the door.
“Open it! Open it!” she called, shaking the door. “Open it! Is there no one out there?”
Svidrigailov got up and came back to himself. His still-trembling lips slowly broke into an angry, mocking smile.
“There is no one at home,” he said quietly and emphatically. “The landlady has gone out, and it's a waste of time to shout like that. You're only exciting yourself for nothing.”
“Where is the key? Open the door at once, at once, you vile man!”
“I've lost the key and can't find it.”
“This is an outrage!” Dunia cried, turning pale as death. She rushed to the farthest corner, where she hurriedly barricaded herself with a little table.
She didn't scream, but she fixed her eyes on her tormentor and watched every movement he made.
Svidrigailov remained standing at the other end of the room, facing her. He was outwardly composed, at least in appearance, but his face was pale as before. The mocking smile did not leave his face.

“You spoke of outrage just now, Avdotya Romanovna. In that case, you can be sure I've taken my precautions. Sofya Semyonovna is not at home. The Kapernaumovs are far away — there are five locked rooms between us. I am at least twice as strong as you are, and I have nothing else to fear either. Because you couldn't complain afterwards. You surely wouldn't really be willing to betray your brother? Besides, no one would believe you. Why would a girl have come alone to visit a solitary man at his lodgings? So that even if you did sacrifice your brother, you could prove nothing. It's very difficult to prove an assault, Avdotya Romanovna.”
“Scoundrel!” Dunia whispered in outrage.

“As you like, but do notice I was only speaking by way of a general proposition. My personal conviction is that you're entirely right — violence is hateful. I only said that to show you that you need feel no remorse even if… you were willing to save your brother of your own free will, as I'm suggesting. You would simply be submitting to circumstances — to violence, in fact, if we must use that word. Think it over. Your brother's fate and your mother's are in your hands. I will be your slave… for the rest of my life… I'll wait right here.”

Svidrigailov sat down on the sofa about eight steps from Dunia. She no longer had the slightest doubt of his unyielding determination. Besides, she knew him. Suddenly she pulled a revolver out of her pocket, cocked it, and laid it in her hand on the table. Svidrigailov jumped up.

“Aha! So that's it, is it?” he cried, surprised but smiling maliciously. “Well, that completely changes the look of things. You've made things wonderfully easier for me, Avdotya Romanovna. But where did you get the revolver? Was it Mr. Razumihin? Why, it's my revolver, an old friend! And how I've hunted for it! The shooting lessons I gave you out in the country have not been wasted.”

“It's not your revolver — it belonged to Marfa Petrovna, whom you killed, wretch! There was nothing of yours in her house. I took it when I began to suspect what you were capable of. If you dare take one step forward, I swear I'll kill you.” She was frantic.
“But your brother? I ask out of curiosity,” said Svidrigailov, still standing where he was.
“Inform on him if you want! Don't move! Don't come any closer! I'll shoot! You poisoned your wife — I know; you are a murderer yourself!” She held the revolver ready.
“Are you so certain I poisoned Marfa Petrovna?”
“You did! You hinted at it yourself; you talked to me about poison… I know you went to get some… you had it ready… It was your doing… It must have been your doing… Scoundrel!”
“Even if that were true, it would have been for your sake… you would have been the cause.”
“You are lying! I have always hated you, always…”

“Oho, Avdotya Romanovna! You seem to have forgotten how you softened toward me in the heat of your reforming zeal. I saw it in your eyes. Do you remember that moonlit night, when the nightingale was singing?”
“That's a lie,” said Dunia, her eyes flashing with fury, “that's a lie and a slander!”
“A lie? Well, if you like, it's a lie. I made it up. Women ought not to be reminded of such things,” he smiled. “I know you'll shoot, you pretty wild creature. Well — shoot away!”

Dunia raised the revolver and, deathly pale, stared at him, measuring the distance and waiting for his first movement. Her lower lip was white and quivering, and her big black eyes flashed like fire. He had never seen her so handsome. The fire glowing in her eyes at the moment she raised the revolver seemed to kindle him, and there was a pang of anguish in his heart. He took a step forward, and a shot rang out. The bullet grazed his hair and flew into the wall behind. He stood still and laughed softly.

“The wasp has stung me. She aimed straight at my head. What's this? Blood?” He pulled out his handkerchief to wipe away the blood, which was running in a thin stream down his right temple. The bullet seemed to have just grazed the skin.
Dunia lowered the revolver and looked at Svidrigailov not so much in terror as in a kind of wild amazement. She seemed not to understand what she was doing or what was happening.
“Well, you missed! Fire again, I'll wait,” Svidrigailov said softly, still smiling, but grimly now. “If you go on like that, I'll have time to grab you before you can cock it again.”
Dunia started, quickly cocked the pistol, and raised it once more.
“Let me be!” she cried in despair. “I swear I'll shoot again. I… I'll kill you.”
“Well… at three paces you can hardly help it. But if you don't… then.” His eyes flashed and he took two steps forward. Dunia pulled the trigger again — it misfired.
“You haven't loaded it properly. Never mind — you still have another charge. Get it ready, I'll wait.”

He stood facing her, two paces away, waiting and gazing at her with wild determination, with feverishly passionate, stubborn, fixed eyes. Dunia saw that he would sooner die than let her go. “And… now, of course, she would kill him, at two paces!” Suddenly she flung the revolver aside.

“She's dropped it!” said Svidrigailov in surprise, and drew a deep breath. A weight seemed to have rolled off his heart — perhaps not only the fear of death; indeed, he may hardly have felt that in the moment. It was deliverance from another feeling, darker and more bitter, which he himself could not have defined.

He went up to Dunia and gently put his arm around her waist. She did not resist, but, trembling like a leaf, looked at him with pleading eyes. He tried to say something, but his lips moved without being able to form a sound.
“Let me go,” Dunia implored. Svidrigailov shuddered. Her voice now was quite different.
“Then you don't love me?” he asked softly. Dunia shook her head.
“And… and you can't? Never?” he whispered in despair.
“Never!”

There followed a moment of terrible, silent struggle in Svidrigailov's heart. He looked at her with an indescribable gaze. Suddenly he withdrew his arm, turned quickly to the window, and stood facing it. Another moment passed.
“Here is the key.”
He took it out of the left pocket of his coat and laid it on the table behind him, without turning or looking at Dunia.
“Take it! Hurry!”
He stared stubbornly out of the window. Dunia went up to the table to take the key.
“Hurry! Hurry!” repeated Svidrigailov, still without turning or moving. But there seemed to be a terrible significance in the tone of that “hurry.”

Dunia understood it, snatched up the key, flew to the door, unlocked it quickly, and rushed out of the room. A minute later, beside herself, she was running along the canal bank in the direction of X. Bridge.

Svidrigailov stood at the window for three minutes. At last he slowly turned, looked around him, and passed his hand across his forehead. A strange smile contorted his face — a pitiful, sad, weak smile, a smile of despair. The blood, already drying, smeared his hand. He looked at it angrily, then dampened a towel and washed his temple. The revolver Dunia had flung away was lying near the door, and it suddenly caught his eye. He picked it up and examined it. It was a little pocket three-barrel revolver of old-fashioned construction. There were still two charges and one cap left in it. It could be fired again. He thought for a moment, put the revolver in his pocket, took his hat, and went out.

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 6
paragraphs: He spent that evening until ten o'clock going from one low haunt to another. Katia turned up again and sang another gutter song about a certain "villain and tyrant" who
"began kissing Katia."

Svidrigailov treated Katia, the organ-grinder, some singers, the waiters, and two little clerks. He was particularly drawn to these clerks by the fact that both had crooked noses — one bent to the left, the other to the right. They eventually took him to a pleasure garden, where he paid their entrance. The garden contained one scraggly three-year-old pine tree and three bushes, plus a "Vauxhall" that was really a drinking establishment where tea was also served, with a few green tables and chairs set around it. A chorus of wretched singers and a drunken but deeply depressed German clown from Munich with a red nose entertained the patrons. The clerks got into a quarrel with some other clerks, and a fight seemed imminent. Svidrigailov was asked to arbitrate. He listened for a quarter of an hour, but they were shouting so loudly that it was impossible to understand them. The only clear fact was that one of them had stolen something and had even managed to sell it on the spot to a Jew, but refused to split the proceeds with his companion. It turned out the stolen item was a teaspoon belonging to the Vauxhall. Once this was discovered, the situation threatened to become serious. Svidrigailov paid for the spoon, got up, and walked out. It was about six o'clock. He hadn't touched a drop of wine the entire time, ordering tea mostly for appearances.

It was a dark, stifling evening. Around ten, threatening storm clouds gathered. There was a clap of thunder and the rain came down like a waterfall — not in drops but in sheets beating against the earth. Lightning flashed every minute, and each flash lasted long enough to count to five.

Soaked to the skin, he went home, locked himself in, opened the bureau, and took out all his money. He tore up two or three papers. Then, putting the money in his pocket, he was about to change his clothes, but looked out the window, listened to the thunder and the rain, and gave up the idea. He took his hat and went out without locking the door. He went straight to Sonia. She was home.

She wasn't alone: the four Kapernaumov children were with her, and she was giving them tea. She received Svidrigailov in respectful silence, looking with wonder at his soaking clothes. The children fled at once in indescribable terror.
Svidrigailov sat down at the table and asked Sonia to sit beside him. She timidly prepared to listen.

"I may be going to America, Sofya Semyonovna," said Svidrigailov, "and since I'm probably seeing you for the last time, I've come to make some arrangements. Well, did you see the lady today? I know what she told you — you don't need to repeat it." Sonia made a movement and blushed. "Those people have their own way of doing things. As for your sisters and your brother, they're truly provided for, and the money assigned to them has been deposited safely — I have the receipts. You'd better keep them yourself, in case anything happens. Here — take them. Well, that's settled. And here are three five-percent bonds worth three thousand rubles. Take these for yourself — entirely for yourself, and let this remain strictly between us. No one else should know, whatever you may hear. You'll need the money, because going on living the old way, Sofya Semyonovna, is wrong — and besides, there's no need for it now."
"I'm so grateful to you, and so are the children and my stepmother," Sonia said hurriedly, "and if I've said so little... please don't think me ungrateful..."
"Enough, enough!"
"As for the money, Arkady Ivanovitch, I'm very grateful, but I don't need it now. I can always earn my own living. Don't think me ungrateful. If you're so charitable, that money..."

"It's for you, Sofya Semyonovna — for you. And please don't waste time arguing. I haven't got time for it. You'll need it. Rodion Romanovitch has two choices: a bullet in the brain, or Siberia." Sonia stared at him wildly and flinched. "Don't be alarmed — I know everything from him personally, and I'm no gossip. I won't tell anyone. You gave him good advice when you told him to turn himself in and confess. It would be far better for him. Well, if it turns out to be Siberia, he'll go — and you'll follow him. That's how it is, isn't it? And if so, you'll need money. You'll need it for him — do you understand? Giving it to you is the same as giving it to him. Besides, you promised Amalia Ivanovna you'd pay what's owed. I heard you. How can you take on such obligations so carelessly, Sofya Semyonovna? It was Katerina Ivanovna's debt, not yours — you should have ignored the German woman. You can't get through the world that way. If anyone ever asks about me — tomorrow or the day after, you'll be asked — don't say anything about my coming here tonight, and don't show the money to anyone or breathe a word about it. Well, goodbye." He rose. "My regards to Rodion Romanovitch. By the way — you'd be wise to keep the money with Mr. Razumikhin for now. You know Mr. Razumikhin? Of course you do. He's a decent fellow. Take it to him tomorrow or... when the time comes. Until then, hide it carefully."
Sonia sprang up from her chair and stared at Svidrigailov in dismay. She desperately wanted to speak, to ask something, but for the first moments she didn't dare and didn't know how to begin.
"How can you... how can you be going out now, in this rain?"

"Well, if I'm heading off to America, should I let a little rain stop me? Ha, ha! Goodbye, Sofya Semyonovna, my dear! Live — and live long. You'll be of use to others. By the way... tell Mr. Razumikhin I send my greetings. Tell him: Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigailov sends his greetings. Be sure you do."
He left, leaving Sonia in a state of bewildered anxiety and vague dread.

It emerged later that the same evening, just after eleven-twenty, he made another very eccentric and unexpected visit. The rain was still coming down. Drenched to the skin, he appeared at the tiny apartment where his fiancée's parents lived, on Third Street in Vasilievsky Island. He had to knock for some time before he was let in, and his visit initially caused great consternation. But Svidrigailov could be very charming when he chose, and the parents' first, quite sensible assumption — that Svidrigailov had drunk so much he didn't know what he was doing — vanished almost immediately. The decrepit father was wheeled in by the tender, sensible mother, who as usual launched the conversation with various roundabout questions. She never asked anything directly: she would begin by smiling and rubbing her hands, then, when she absolutely had to find something out — such as when Svidrigailov would like the wedding — she'd start with eager questions about Paris and court life, only gradually working her way to Third Street. On other occasions this had been quite impressive, but tonight Arkady Ivanovitch seemed unusually impatient and insisted on seeing his fiancée immediately, despite being told she had already gone to bed. The girl appeared, of course.

Svidrigailov informed her at once that urgent business required him to leave Petersburg for a time, and therefore he was bringing her fifteen thousand rubles as a gift, which he'd long intended to give her before the wedding. The logical connection between this gift, his imminent departure, and the absolute necessity of visiting in a downpour at midnight was never made clear. But everything went remarkably smoothly; even the inevitable exclamations of wonder and questions were unusually few and restrained. On the other hand, the gratitude expressed was most effusive, reinforced by tears from the most sensible of mothers. Svidrigailov got up, laughed, kissed his fiancée, patted her cheek, declared he'd return soon, and noticing in her eyes — alongside childish curiosity — a kind of earnest, silent question, he paused and kissed her again, though he felt genuine irritation at the thought that his gift would be immediately locked away by the most sensible of mothers. He left them all in a state of extraordinary excitement, but the tender mama, speaking quietly in a half-whisper, resolved most of their doubts by concluding that Svidrigailov was a great man, a man of great affairs and connections and great wealth — one couldn't tell what he had in his head. He might start a journey and hand out money just as the fancy took him, so there was nothing surprising in it. It was odd that he was so wet, of course, but the English, for instance, were even more eccentric, and people of the upper classes didn't care what others said and didn't stand on ceremony. Perhaps he'd come like that on purpose, to show he wasn't afraid of anyone. Above all, not a word to anyone about it — God knew what might come of it — and the money must be locked up. It was most fortunate that Fedosya the cook hadn't left the kitchen. And above all, not a word to that old cat Madame Resslich. They sat whispering until two in the morning, but the girl went to bed much earlier, amazed and rather sorrowful.

Svidrigailov, meanwhile, at exactly midnight, was crossing the bridge back to the mainland. The rain had stopped and a roaring wind had risen. He began to shiver, and for one moment he stared at the black waters of the Little Neva with a look of special interest, almost inquiry. But he soon decided it was too cold standing by the water; he turned and headed toward Y— Prospect. He walked along that endless street for a long time, nearly half an hour, stumbling more than once in the dark on the wooden pavement, but constantly scanning the right side of the street for something. He'd noticed recently, passing through this area, a wooden hotel of a fair size, and its name — something like the Adrianople — had stuck in his memory. He was right: the hotel was conspicuous enough in that godforsaken place to be visible even in the dark. It was a long, blackened wooden building, and despite the late hour, lights glowed in the windows and there were signs of life inside. He went in and asked a ragged fellow in the corridor for a room. The man looked Svidrigailov up and down, pulled himself together, and led him at once to a cramped, tiny room at the far end of the corridor, under the stairs. There was nothing else — everything was taken. The ragged man looked at him expectantly.
"Is there tea?" Svidrigailov asked.
"Yes, sir."
"What else?"
"Veal, vodka, appetizers."
"Bring me tea and veal."
"You don't want anything else?" the man asked with apparent surprise.
"Nothing."
The ragged man withdrew, completely disillusioned.

"Must be a decent place," Svidrigailov thought. "How is it I didn't know about it? I must look like someone coming from a café chantant who's had some adventure along the way. I wonder who else stays here?"

He lit the candle and examined the room more carefully. It was so low-ceilinged that Svidrigailov could barely stand upright. It had one window; the bed was extremely dirty, and the plain-stained chair and table nearly filled the space. The walls seemed to be made of planks, covered with shabby wallpaper so torn and dusty that the pattern was unrecognizable, though the general color — yellow — could still be made out. One wall was cut short by the sloping ceiling: the room wasn't an attic, but lay directly beneath the stairs.

Svidrigailov set down the candle, sat on the bed, and sank into thought. But a strange, persistent murmur from the next room — sometimes rising to a shout — caught his attention. The murmuring had been going on since he entered. He listened: someone was scolding and almost tearfully berating another person, but only one voice could be heard.

Svidrigailov got up, shaded the candle with his hand, and noticed light seeping through a crack in the wall. He went over and peered through. The neighboring room, somewhat larger than his, had two occupants. One, a very curly-haired man with a red, inflamed face, stood in an orator's pose — coatless, legs spread wide for balance — thumping his own chest. He was reproaching the other man for being a beggar, for having no standing whatsoever, declaring he'd pulled him out of the gutter and could throw him back whenever he pleased, and that only Providence could see the truth of it. The object of this tirade sat in a chair looking like a man who desperately needs to sneeze but can't. He would occasionally turn sheepish, bleary eyes on the speaker but obviously had no idea what was being said and barely heard it. A candle was guttering on the table amid glasses, a nearly empty bottle of vodka, bread and cucumbers, and glasses with dregs of stale tea. After studying this scene, Svidrigailov turned away indifferently and sat back on the bed.

The ragged attendant returned with the tea and couldn't resist asking once more whether the gentleman wanted anything else. Receiving another negative, he withdrew for good. Svidrigailov drank a glass of tea to warm himself but couldn't eat a bite. He was beginning to feel feverish. He took off his coat, wrapped himself in the blanket, and lay down. He was annoyed. "It would have been better to be healthy for the occasion," he thought with a grim smile. The room was stuffy, the candle burned dimly, the wind howled outside, a mouse scratched in the corner, and the whole room smelled of mice and leather. He lay in a kind of half-dream: one thought chased another. He longed to fix his imagination on something. "There must be a garden under the window," he thought. "The sound of trees. How I hate the sound of trees on a stormy night in the dark! They give you a horrible feeling." He remembered disliking it when he'd passed Petrovsky Park earlier. This reminded him of the bridge over the Little Neva, and he felt cold again as he had standing there. "I've never liked water," he thought, "not even in a painting." He suddenly smiled at a strange idea: "You'd think at a time like this, all these questions of taste and comfort shouldn't matter — and yet I've become more particular, like an animal that picks a special spot for... such an occasion. I should have gone to Petrovsky Park! I suppose it seemed too dark, too cold — ha-ha! As if I needed pleasant sensations!... By the way, why haven't I blown out the candle?" He blew it out. "They've gone to bed next door," he thought, seeing no light through the crack. "Well then, Marfa Petrovna — now would be the time for you to appear. It's dark, and the place couldn't be more fitting. But of course, now you won't come!"

He suddenly recalled how, an hour before carrying out his plan with Dunya, he had recommended Raskolnikov to entrust her to Razumikhin's care. "I suppose I really did say it, as Raskolnikov guessed, just to tease myself. But what a rogue that Raskolnikov is! He's been through a lot. He may become a successful rogue in time, once he's gotten over his foolishness. But right now he's too hungry for life. These young men are contemptible on that score. Well, to hell with him! Let him do as he likes. It's nothing to do with me."

He couldn't sleep. Gradually Dunya's image rose before him, and a shudder passed over him. "No, I have to put that aside now," he thought, rousing himself. "I need to think about something else. It's strange and funny: I've never felt great hatred for anyone, never particularly wanted revenge — that's a bad sign, a bad sign. I never liked quarreling and never lost my temper — another bad sign. And those promises I made to her — damn it! But who knows — maybe she could have made a new man of me somehow..."

He ground his teeth and fell silent again. Dunya's image rose once more — exactly as she'd looked after firing the first shot, when she'd lowered the revolver in terror and stared blankly at him, so that he could have seized her twice over without her lifting a hand to defend herself — if only he hadn't reminded her. He remembered how in that instant he had almost felt sorry for her, how something had clutched at his heart...
"Damn! These thoughts again! I have to stop this!"

He was dozing off; the feverish chill had ceased. Suddenly something seemed to scurry over his arm and leg beneath the blanket. He started. "Ugh, damn — must be a mouse," he thought. "It's the veal I left on the table." He hated the idea of throwing off the blanket, getting up, getting cold — but suddenly something unpleasant ran over his leg again. He flung off the blanket and lit the candle. Shaking with feverish chills, he bent down to examine the bed: nothing. He shook the blanket and suddenly a mouse darted out onto the sheet. He tried to catch it, but the mouse zigzagged back and forth without leaving the bed, slipped through his fingers, ran across his hand, and suddenly shot under the pillow. He threw down the pillow, but instantly felt something leap onto his chest and dash across his body and down his back under his shirt. He flinched violently and woke up.
The room was dark. He was lying on the bed, wrapped in the blanket as before. Wind was howling at the window. "How disgusting," he thought with irritation.

He sat up on the edge of the bed with his back to the window. "Better not to sleep at all," he decided. A cold, damp draft seeped from the window. Without getting up, he pulled the blanket over himself and wrapped it tight. He wasn't thinking about anything and didn't want to think. But images rose one after another, incoherent scraps of thought without beginning or end drifted through his mind. He began sinking into drowsiness. Perhaps the cold, or the damp, or the darkness, or the wind howling outside and shaking the trees stirred a persistent craving for the fantastical. He kept dwelling on flowers. He imagined a lovely flower garden, a bright, warm, almost hot day — a holiday, Trinity Sunday. A fine, lavish country house in the English style, overgrown with fragrant flowers, with flower beds running all around it. The porch, twined with climbing plants, was surrounded by beds of roses. A light, cool staircase carpeted with rich rugs was adorned with rare plants in porcelain pots. He noticed especially, in the windows, bouquets of tender white narcissus, heavily fragrant, drooping over their bright green, thick long stems. He was reluctant to move away from them, but he went up the stairs and entered a large, tall drawing room — and again, everywhere, at the windows, by the doors onto the balcony, on the balcony itself — flowers. The floors were strewn with freshly cut, fragrant hay; the windows were open; a fresh, cool, light breeze drifted into the room. Birds chirped outside the window. In the middle of the room, on a table draped in a white satin shroud, stood a coffin. The coffin was covered in white silk with a thick white frill; wreaths of flowers surrounded it on all sides. Among the flowers lay a girl in a white muslin dress, arms crossed and pressed to her breast, as if carved from marble. But her loose fair hair was wet; a wreath of roses circled her head. Her stern, already rigid profile seemed chiseled from marble too, and the smile on her pale lips held an immense, unchildlike sorrow and sorrowful appeal. Svidrigailov knew that girl. No holy icon stood beside the coffin, no candle burned, no prayers were said. The girl had drowned herself. She was only fourteen, but her heart was broken. She had destroyed herself, crushed by an insult that had appalled and stunned her childish soul, had smeared her angel purity with undeserved shame, and torn from her a last cry of despair — unheard, brutally ignored — on a dark night, in the cold and wet, while the wind howled...

Svidrigailov came to himself, rose from the bed, and went to the window. He found the latch and opened it. The wind lashed into the tiny room, stinging his face and chest through his shirt with an icy bite. Under the window there must have been something like a garden — a pleasure garden, apparently. There, too, tea-tables probably stood and songs were sung during the day. Now rain flew in from the trees and bushes; it was as dark as a cellar, and he could barely make out a few dim shapes. Svidrigailov leaned on the windowsill with both elbows and stared into the darkness for five minutes. The boom of a cannon, then another, sounded through the dark night. "The flood signal! The river is rising," he thought. "By morning, the water will be swirling through the streets in the low-lying parts, flooding the basements and cellars. The cellar rats will swim out, and people will curse in the wind and rain as they drag their belongings upstairs. What time is it?" And just as he thought it, a clock somewhere nearby, ticking hurriedly, struck three.

"In another hour it'll be light. Why wait? I'll go now — straight to the park. I'll pick a big bush, one drenched with rain, so that when you brush against it with your shoulder, millions of drops shower down on your head."

He stepped away from the window, closed it, lit the candle, put on his vest, overcoat, and hat, and went out with the candle into the corridor to find the ragged attendant, who would be sleeping somewhere amid candle-stubs and assorted rubbish, to pay for the room and leave. "This is the best moment. I couldn't choose a better one."

He walked for some time through a long, narrow corridor without finding anyone and was about to call out when suddenly, in a dark corner between an old cupboard and the doorframe, he noticed a strange object that seemed to be alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a little girl — no more than five years old — shivering and crying, her clothes as wet as a sopping dishrag. She didn't seem afraid of Svidrigailov but stared at him with blank amazement from her big dark eyes. Now and then she sobbed, the way children do when they've been crying a long time but are beginning to calm down. The child's face was pale and exhausted; she was numb with cold. "How could she have gotten here? She must have hidden and never slept." He began questioning her. The child suddenly came to life, chattering in her baby language about "mommy" and how "mommy would hit her" and about some cup she'd "bwoken." She prattled on without stopping. He could only piece together from her words that she was a neglected child whose mother — probably a drunken cook employed at the hotel — beat and terrorized her. The girl had broken one of her mother's cups and was so frightened that she'd run away the evening before, hidden outside in the rain for ages, finally crept inside, hidden behind the cupboard, and spent the whole night there, crying and shivering in the damp, the dark, and the terror of being beaten. He picked her up, carried her to his room, set her on the bed, and began undressing her. Her torn shoes, on stockingless feet, were as wet as if they'd been standing in a puddle all night. When he'd undressed her, he put her in the bed, covered her up, and wrapped her in the blanket from head to toe. She fell asleep instantly. Then he sank back into gloomy brooding.

"What a fool I am, getting involved," he thought with a sudden feeling of oppressive annoyance. "What idiocy!" In his vexation he picked up the candle, intending to find the ragged attendant and leave at once. "Damn the child!" he thought, reaching for the door — but he turned back to check whether she was sleeping. He carefully lifted the blanket. The child was sleeping soundly and had gotten warm. Her pale cheeks had flushed. But the flush seemed brighter and coarser than a normal rosy glow of childhood. "It's a fever flush," Svidrigailov thought. It looked more like the flush from alcohol — as though she'd been given a full glass of wine. Her crimson lips were hot and burning. But what was this? He suddenly thought her long dark lashes were quivering, as though the lids were lifting and a sly, crafty eye was peeping out with an unchildlike wink — as if the little girl weren't asleep at all but pretending. Yes — that was it. Her lips parted in a smile. The corners of her mouth quivered, as though she were trying to hold it back. But now she gave up all pretense. It was a grin — a broad grin. There was something shameless, provocative in that utterly unchildlike face; it was corruption, the face of a prostitute, the brazen face of a French harlot. Now both eyes were open wide, turning a glowing, shameless stare on him; they laughed, they invited... There was something infinitely hideous and revolting in that laugh, in those eyes, in such depravity in the face of a child. "What? At five years old?" Svidrigailov whispered in genuine horror. "What does this mean?" And now she turned to him, her little face all aglow, reaching out her arms... "Accursed child!" Svidrigailov cried, raising his hand to strike her — but at that moment he woke up.
He was in the same bed, still wrapped in the blanket. The candle had not been lit, and daylight was streaming through the windows.

"Nightmares all night!" He sat up, feeling utterly shattered; his bones ached. A thick fog hung outside, and he could see nothing. It was nearly five. He'd overslept! He got up and put on his still-damp jacket and overcoat. Feeling the revolver in his pocket, he took it out. Then he sat down, pulled a notebook from his pocket, and on the most prominent place on the title page wrote a few lines in large letters. He read them over, then sat thinking with his elbows on the table. The revolver and the notebook lay beside him. Some flies woke and settled on the untouched veal still sitting on the table. He stared at them, then began absently trying to catch one with his free right hand. He kept at it until he was tired, but couldn't catch it. Finally, realizing he was absorbed in this pointless pursuit, he came to himself with a start, got up, and walked resolutely out of the room. A minute later he was in the street.

A thick, milky fog lay over the city. Svidrigailov walked along the slippery, dirty wooden pavement toward the Little Neva. He was picturing the waters of the Little Neva, swollen in the night — Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the wet grass, the wet trees and bushes — and finally, that bush... He began irritably staring at the buildings, trying to think of something else. Not a cab or a soul in the street. The bright yellow little wooden houses looked dirty and dejected with their shutters closed. The cold and damp penetrated his whole body, and he started shivering. Now and then he passed a shop sign and read each one carefully. At last he reached the end of the wooden pavement and came to a large stone building. A dirty, shivering dog crossed his path, tail between its legs. A man in a greatcoat lay face down across the sidewalk, dead drunk. He glanced at him and walked on. A tall tower loomed on his left. "Bah!" he exclaimed. "Here's a good enough place. Why bother with Petrovsky? At least there'll be an official witness."

He almost smiled at this new thought and turned into the street with the large building and the tower. At the great locked gates of the building stood a small man, his shoulder leaning against them, wrapped in a gray soldier's overcoat with a copper Achilles helmet on his head. He cast a drowsy, indifferent look at Svidrigailov. His face wore that perpetual expression of sour dejection so firmly stamped on every face of the Jewish race without exception. The two of them — Svidrigailov and Achilles — stared at each other for several minutes without speaking. Finally it struck Achilles as irregular that a sober man should be standing three steps away, staring at him and saying nothing.
"What do you want here?" he said, without moving or changing position.
"Nothing, brother. Good morning," Svidrigailov answered.
"This isn't the place."
"I'm going to foreign parts, brother."
"Foreign parts?"
"America."
"America."
Svidrigailov took out the revolver and cocked it. Achilles raised his eyebrows.
"I say — this is no place for jokes like that!"
"Why shouldn't it be the place?"
"Because it isn't."
"Well, brother, I don't mind that. It's a perfectly good spot. When they ask you, just say he was going to America."
He raised the revolver to his right temple.
"You can't do that here! This isn't the place!" cried Achilles, suddenly wide awake, his eyes growing bigger and bigger.
Svidrigailov pulled the trigger.

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 7
paragraphs: That same day, around seven in the evening, Raskolnikov was making his way to his mother's and sister's lodgings -- the rooms in Bakaleyev's house that Razumihin had found for them. The staircase led up from the street. Raskolnikov climbed with dragging steps, as though still uncertain whether to go in. But nothing would have turned him back now; his decision was made.
"Besides, it doesn't matter -- they still don't know anything," he thought, "and they're used to thinking of me as eccentric."

He was dressed appallingly: his clothes torn and dirty, soaked from a night in the rain. His face was nearly distorted from exhaustion, exposure, and the inner struggle that had consumed him for twenty-four hours. He had spent the entire previous night alone, God knows where. But he had reached a decision.

He knocked at the door. His mother opened it. Dounia was not home. Even the maid happened to be out. At first Pulcheria Alexandrovna was speechless with joy and surprise; then she took his hand and pulled him into the room.

"Here you are!" she began, faltering with happiness. "Don't be angry with me, Rodya, for greeting you so foolishly with tears. I'm laughing, not crying. Did you think I was crying? No, I'm overjoyed, but I've gotten into this silly habit of weeping. It's been like this ever since your father died -- I cry at everything. Sit down, darling, you must be tired -- I can see you are. Oh, how muddy you are!"
"I was out in the rain yesterday, Mother..." Raskolnikov began.

"No, no," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried to interrupt. "You thought I was going to cross-examine you the way I used to -- don't worry. I understand, I understand everything now. I've learned how things work here, and I truly see that they make more sense. I've decided once and for all: how can I expect to understand your plans or demand that you account for them? God knows what matters you're dealing with, what ideas you're working through. It's not for me to keep nudging your elbow, asking what you're thinking. But my goodness, why am I running around like a fool? I'm reading your article in the journal for the third time, Rodya. Dmitri Prokofitch brought it to me. The moment I saw it, I thought: 'There, you silly woman -- that's what he's been busy with! That's the answer! Scholars are always like this. He has new ideas in his head right now, he's thinking them over, and I just bother and upset him.' I read it, my dear, and of course there was a great deal I didn't understand, but that's only natural -- how could I?"
"Show me, Mother."

Raskolnikov took the journal and glanced at his article. As incongruous as it was with his mood and circumstances, he felt that strange, bittersweet sensation every author experiences the first time he sees himself in print; besides, he was only twenty-three. It lasted only an instant. After reading a few lines, he frowned, and his heart clenched with anguish. All the inner turmoil of the preceding months came flooding back. He flung the article on the table in disgust and anger.

"But however foolish I may be, Rodya, I can see for myself that you'll soon be one of the leading -- if not the leading -- minds in Russian thought. And they dared to think you were mad! You don't know, but they actually believed it. What wretched fools -- how could they fail to recognize genius! Even Dounia nearly believed it -- can you imagine? Your father twice submitted things to journals -- first poems, I have the manuscript and I'll show you -- and then an entire novel. I begged him to let me copy it out, and how we prayed they'd be accepted! They weren't! I was heartbroken, Rodya. But six or seven days ago I was agonizing over your food and clothes and the way you live, and now I see how foolish that was. You can achieve any position you want with your intellect and talent. No doubt you don't care about that now -- you're occupied with far more important things..."
"Dounia's not home, Mother?"

"No, Rodya. I often don't see her; she leaves me alone. Dmitri Prokofitch comes to visit me -- it's very kind of him -- and he always talks about you. He loves and respects you, dear. I'm not saying Dounia is inconsiderate. I'm not complaining. She has her ways and I have mine. She seems to have secrets lately, but I never have any secrets from you two. Of course I'm sure Dounia has far too much sense, and besides, she loves us both... but I don't know where it will all lead. You've made me so happy by coming, Rodya, but she's missed you. When she comes in, I'll tell her: 'Your brother was here while you were out. Where have you been spending your time?' You mustn't spoil me, Rodya. Come when you can, and if you can't, it doesn't matter -- I'll wait. I'll know you love me, and that's enough. I'll read what you write, I'll hear about you from everyone, and sometimes you'll come to see me. What more could I want? Here you are now, come to comfort your mother -- I can see that."
And Pulcheria Alexandrovna began to cry.

"There I go again! Don't mind my foolishness. Goodness, why am I just sitting here?" she cried, jumping up. "There's coffee and I haven't offered you any. That's the selfishness of old age. I'll get it right away!"
"Mother, don't trouble yourself. I'm going in a moment. I haven't come for that. Please listen to me."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna came up to him timidly.

"Mother, whatever happens, whatever you hear about me, whatever anyone tells you -- will you always love me as you do now?" he asked suddenly, from the fullness of his heart, as though not weighing his words.
"Rodya, Rodya, what's wrong? How can you even ask me that? And who would say anything about you? Besides, I wouldn't believe anyone -- I'd refuse to listen."

"I've come to tell you that I've always loved you, and I'm glad we're alone, glad even that Dounia isn't here," he went on with the same impulse. "I've come to say that although you will be unhappy, you must believe that your son loves you now more than himself, and that everything you thought about me -- that I was cruel and didn't care about you -- was all a mistake. I will never stop loving you. Well, that's enough. I felt I had to do this, to begin with this..."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna embraced him in silence, pressing him to her breast and weeping softly.

"I don't know what's wrong with you, Rodya," she said at last. "All this time I've been thinking we were simply boring you, but now I see that some great sorrow is waiting for you, and that's why you're so miserable. I've sensed it for a long time, Rodya. Forgive me for mentioning it. I think about it constantly and lie awake at night. Your sister was talking in her sleep all last night, talking about nothing but you. I caught some words but couldn't make them out. All morning I've had the feeling that something terrible was about to happen, that I was waiting for something -- and now it has come. Rodya, Rodya, where are you going? You're going away somewhere?"
"Yes."

"I knew it! But I could go with you, you know, if you need me. And Dounia too -- she loves you, she loves you so much. And Sofya Semyonovna could come with us, if you'd like. You see, I'm happy to think of her as a daughter now... Dmitri Prokofitch would help us all go together. But... where... where are you going?"
"Goodbye, Mother."
"What -- today?" she cried, as though losing him forever.
"I can't stay. I have to go now..."
"And I can't come with you?"
"No, but kneel down and pray to God for me. Your prayer may reach Him."
"Let me bless you and make the sign of the cross over you. That's right, that's right. Oh God, what is happening to us?"

Yes, he was glad -- very glad -- that no one else was there, that he was alone with his mother. For the first time in all those terrible months, his heart softened. He fell before her, kissed her feet, and they both wept, embracing. And she was not surprised and asked no questions this time. For days now she had sensed that something awful was happening to her son and that a terrible moment had arrived.

"Rodya, my darling, my firstborn," she said through her sobs, "now you're just like when you were small. You used to run to me like this, hug me and kiss me. When your father was alive and we were poor, just being near you was a comfort. And when I buried your father, how often we wept and embraced at his grave, just as we're doing now. And if I've been crying lately, it's because a mother's heart sensed that trouble was coming. The first time I saw you, that evening when we arrived -- I guessed everything from your eyes alone. My heart sank at once. And today, when I opened the door and looked at you, I thought the fatal hour had come. Rodya, Rodya, you're not leaving today, are you?"
"No!"
"You'll come again?"
"Yes... I'll come."
"Rodya, don't be angry -- I don't dare question you. I know I mustn't. Just tell me two words: is it far, where you're going?"
"Very far."
"What's waiting for you there? Some position, some career?"
"Whatever God sends... just pray for me." Raskolnikov moved toward the door, but she clutched at him and gazed despairingly into his eyes. Her face was twisted with fear.
"Enough, Mother," said Raskolnikov, deeply regretting that he had come.
"Not forever? It's not forever yet? You'll come again, you'll come tomorrow?"
"I will, I will. Goodbye." He tore himself away at last.

It was a warm, fresh, bright evening; the weather had cleared in the morning. Raskolnikov hurried to his lodgings. He wanted to finish everything before sunset. He wanted to meet no one until then. Going up the stairs, he noticed Nastasya rush away from the samovar to watch him intently. "Has someone come to see me?" he wondered. He had a sickening vision of Porfiry. But opening his door, he saw Dounia. She was sitting alone, plunged in deep thought, looking as though she had been waiting a long time. He stopped short in the doorway. She rose from the sofa in alarm and stood facing him. Her eyes, fixed on his, showed horror and bottomless grief. And from those eyes alone he saw at once that she knew.
"Should I come in or go away?" he asked uncertainly.
"I've been with Sofya Semyonovna all day. We were both waiting for you. We thought you'd be sure to go there."
Raskolnikov walked into the room and sank exhausted into a chair.
"I feel weak, Dounia. I'm very tired. And right now I'd like more than anything to be in control of myself."
He glanced at her with distrust.
"Where were you all night?"

"I don't remember exactly. You see, sister, I wanted to make up my mind once and for all, and several times I walked along the Neva. I remember that much. I wanted to end it all there, but... I couldn't bring myself to do it," he whispered, looking at her distrustfully again.
"Thank God! That's exactly what we were afraid of, Sofya Semyonovna and I. So you still believe in life? Thank God, thank God!"
Raskolnikov smiled bitterly.
"I don't believe. But I've just been weeping in my mother's arms. I don't believe, but I've just asked her to pray for me. I don't know how that works, Dounia. I don't understand it."
"You went to Mother's? You told her?" Dounia cried in horror. "You didn't!"

"No, I didn't tell her... not in words. But she understood a great deal. She heard you talking in your sleep. I'm certain she already half understands. Maybe I was wrong to go. I don't even know why I went. I'm a contemptible person, Dounia."
"A contemptible person who is ready to embrace suffering! You are ready, aren't you?"

"Yes. Right now. Yes, to escape the disgrace, I thought of drowning myself, Dounia. But as I stared into the water, I told myself that if I've considered myself strong until now, I shouldn't be afraid of disgrace," he said, hurrying on. "It's pride, Dounia."
"Pride, Rodya."
There was a gleam of fire in his dull eyes; he seemed glad to think he was still proud.
"You don't think, sister, that I was simply afraid of the water?" he asked, looking at her with a sinister smile.

"Oh, Rodya, stop!" Dounia cried bitterly. Silence lasted for two minutes. He sat with his eyes fixed on the floor; Dounia stood at the other end of the table, watching him in anguish. Suddenly he stood up.
"It's late. Time to go. I'm going now to turn myself in. But I don't know why I'm doing it."
Large tears rolled down her cheeks.
"You're crying, sister. But can you hold out your hand to me?"
"Did you doubt it?"
She threw her arms around him.
"By going to face your punishment, aren't you already half atoning for your crime?" she cried, holding him tight and kissing him.

"Crime? What crime?" he burst out in sudden fury. "That I killed a vile, harmful creature, a filthy old pawnbroker woman who was no use to anyone? Killing her was atonement for forty sins. She was sucking the life out of the poor. Was that a crime? I'm not thinking about it and I have no intention of atoning for it. And why does everyone keep throwing it in my face? 'A crime! A crime!' Only now do I see the full stupidity of my cowardice, now that I've decided to go through with this pointless disgrace. It's simply because I'm contemptible and have nothing in me that I've decided -- perhaps also for my own advantage, as that... Porfiry... suggested!"
"Brother, brother, what are you saying? You shed blood!" Dounia cried in despair.

"Blood that all men shed," he broke in, almost frantically, "that has flowed in torrents since the beginning of the world, that is poured out like champagne, and for which men are crowned in the Capitol and hailed as benefactors of humanity. Look more closely and you'll understand! I too wanted to do good, and I would have done hundreds, thousands of good deeds to make up for that one act of stupidity -- no, not even stupidity but clumsiness, because the idea wasn't nearly so stupid as it looks now that it's failed. Everything looks stupid when it fails. With that act of clumsiness, I only wanted to establish my independence, to take the first step, to secure the means, and then everything would have been made right by benefits beyond comparison... But I couldn't even carry out the first step, because I'm contemptible -- that's what it comes down to! And yet I refuse to see it your way. If I had succeeded, I'd have been crowned with glory, but now I'm caught in a trap."
"But that's not true, not true at all! Brother, what are you saying?"

"It's not aesthetically pleasing, I admit! I honestly can't understand why bombing people in a proper siege is considered more respectable. Fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence. I've never seen that more clearly than I do right now, and I'm further than ever from considering what I did a crime. I've never been so strong in my convictions as I am at this moment."

Color had rushed to his pale, exhausted face. But as he uttered this last declaration, his eyes happened to meet Dounia's, and he saw such anguish in them that he couldn't help checking himself. He realized that he had, at the very least, made these two poor women miserable, that he was, at the very least, the cause of--

"Dounia, darling, if I'm guilty, forgive me -- though if I am guilty, I can't be forgiven. Goodbye! Let's not argue. It's time -- past time -- to go. Don't follow me, I beg you. There's somewhere else I need to be. But you go now and stay with Mother. I'm begging you! It's my last request. Don't leave her. I left her in a state of anxiety she can't bear -- she'll die or lose her mind. Be with her! Razumihin will be there too. I've spoken to him. Don't cry over me. I'll try to be brave and honorable for the rest of my life, even if I am a murderer. Perhaps someday I'll make a name for myself. I won't disgrace you -- you'll see. I'll prove it yet... But now, goodbye for now," he concluded hastily, noticing a strange expression on Dounia's face. "Why are you crying? Don't cry, don't cry -- we're not parting forever! Oh, wait -- I almost forgot!"

He went to the table, picked up a thick, dusty book, opened it, and took from between the pages a small watercolor portrait on ivory. It was a picture of his landlady's daughter, who had died of fever -- that strange girl who had wanted to become a nun. For a moment he gazed at the delicate, expressive face of his onetime fiancee, kissed the portrait, and handed it to Dounia.

"I used to talk to her about it, a great deal -- to her alone," he said thoughtfully. "I confided much to her heart that has since been so hideously realized. Don't worry," he turned to Dounia, "she was as much against it as you are, and I'm glad she's gone. The main thing is that everything is going to change now, to crack apart," he cried, suddenly returning to his gloom. "Everything, everything -- and am I ready for it? Do I even want it? They say suffering is necessary. What's the point of all this senseless suffering? Will I understand it any better when I'm crushed by hardship and idiocy, enfeebled like an old man after twenty years of hard labor? And what will I have to live for then? Why am I consenting to this? Oh, I knew I was contemptible when I stood looking at the Neva at dawn!"

At last they both went out. It was hard for Dounia, but she loved him. She walked away, but after fifty paces she turned to look at him once more. He was still in sight. At the corner, he too turned, and for the last time their eyes met. But noticing that she was looking at him, he waved her away with impatience, even irritation, and turned the corner sharply.

"I'm cruel, I know," he thought, immediately ashamed of his angry gesture to Dounia. "But why do they love me so much, when I don't deserve it? Oh, if only I were alone and no one loved me and I had never loved anyone! None of this would have happened. But I wonder -- in those fifteen or twenty years, will I really become so meek that I'll grovel before people and whimper at every turn that I'm a criminal? Yes, that's it -- that's exactly it -- that's what they're sending me there for, that's what they want. Look at them all running up and down the streets, every one of them a scoundrel and a criminal at heart, and worse still, an idiot. But try to get me pardoned and they'd howl with righteous indignation. Oh, how I hate them all!"

He fell to wondering by what process it could happen that he would genuinely humble himself before all of them -- humble himself out of conviction. And yet, why not? It had to be so. Wouldn't twenty years of unbroken captivity crush him completely? Water wears away stone. And why, why should he go on living after that? Why should he go now, knowing that was how it would end? It was perhaps the hundredth time he had asked himself that question since the previous evening. But still he went.

chapters.title: Part 6, Chapter 8
paragraphs: When he entered Sonia's room, it was already growing dark. Sonia had been waiting for him all day in terrible anxiety. Dounia had been waiting with her. She had come that morning, remembering Svidrigailov's words that Sonia knew. We will not describe the conversation and tears of the two women, or how quickly they became friends. From that meeting Dounia drew at least one comfort: her brother would not be alone. He had gone to Sonia first with his confession; he had come to her for human connection when he needed it most. Sonia would follow him wherever fate might send him. Dounia did not need to ask -- she knew. She looked at Sonia almost with reverence, which at first nearly embarrassed the girl. Sonia felt herself, on the contrary, hardly worthy of looking at Dounia. The gracious image of Dounia bowing to her so attentively and respectfully at their first meeting in Raskolnikov's room had remained in Sonia's mind as one of the most beautiful visions of her life.

Dounia eventually grew impatient and, leaving Sonia, went to her brother's room to wait for him there. She kept thinking he would come there first. After she left, Sonia was seized by the dread that he might kill himself. Dounia feared the same thing. But all day they had tried to reassure each other that it was impossible, and both were less anxious while together. The moment they parted, each could think of nothing else. Sonia remembered how Svidrigailov had told her the day before that Raskolnikov had two choices -- Siberia or... Besides, she knew his vanity, his pride, his lack of faith.
"Is it possible that only cowardice and fear of death keep him alive?" she wondered in despair.

Meanwhile the sun was setting. Sonia stood by the window, staring out dejectedly, but from her window she could see nothing but the unwhitewashed blank wall of the neighboring building. At last, when she had become nearly certain he was dead -- he walked into the room.
She cried out in joy, but looking carefully into his face, she turned pale.
"Yes," said Raskolnikov, smiling. "I've come for your cross, Sonia. It was you who told me to go to the crossroads. So why are you frightened now that the time has come?"

Sonia stared at him in astonishment. His tone struck her as strange; a cold shiver ran through her, but in an instant she understood that both the tone and the words were a mask. He spoke to her looking away, as though trying to avoid her eyes.

"You see, Sonia, I've decided it will be better this way. There's one particular fact... But it's a long story and there's no point discussing it. Do you know what infuriates me, though? It's that all those stupid, brutish faces will be gaping at me any minute now, bombarding me with their stupid questions, which I'll have to answer -- they'll point their fingers at me... No, I'm not going to Porfiry. I'm sick of him. I'd rather go to my friend, the Explosive Lieutenant -- what a sensation I'll cause! But I need to be calmer; I've become too irritable lately. Can you believe it -- I nearly shook my fist at my sister just now, because she turned around for one last look at me. What a brutal state I'm in! Well then, where are the crosses?"
He seemed barely aware of what he was doing. He couldn't stay still or concentrate his thoughts on anything; his mind raced from one thing to the next; his hands trembled slightly.
Without a word, Sonia took two crosses from the drawer -- one of cypress wood, one of copper. She made the sign of the cross over herself and over him, and hung the wooden cross around his neck.

"It's the symbol of my taking up the cross," he laughed. "As though I haven't suffered enough already! The wooden cross -- the peasant one; the copper one, Lizaveta's -- you'll wear it yourself. Show me! So she wore it... at that moment? I remember two things like these too -- a silver cross and a small icon. I threw them back on the old woman's chest. Those are the ones I should really be wearing now... But I'm talking nonsense and forgetting what matters; I keep losing my train of thought... You see, I came to warn you, Sonia, so you'd know... That's all -- that's all I came for. But I thought I had more to say. You wanted me to go yourself. Well, now I'm going to prison and you'll have your wish. So why are you crying? You too? Don't, stop it! Oh, how I hate all this!"

But his feelings were stirred; his heart ached as he looked at her. "Why is she suffering too?" he thought. "What am I to her? Why does she weep? Why does she look after me, like my mother, like Dounia? She'll end up being my nursemaid."
"Cross yourself. Say at least one prayer," Sonia begged in a timid, broken voice.
"Oh, certainly -- as many as you like! And sincerely, Sonia, sincerely..."
But he wanted to say something entirely different.

He crossed himself several times. Sonia picked up her shawl and draped it over her head. It was the green drap de dames shawl that Marmeladov had once described -- "the family shawl." Raskolnikov remembered and thought of it, but did not ask. He was becoming aware that he was hopelessly distracted and hideously agitated. This frightened him. He was also suddenly struck by the realization that Sonia intended to go with him.

"What are you doing? Where are you going? Stay here, stay! I'll go alone," he cried in cowardly irritation, almost resentful, and moved toward the door. "What's the point of making a procession of it?" he muttered as he went out.
Sonia remained standing in the middle of the room. He hadn't even said goodbye to her; he had already forgotten her. A sharp, rebellious doubt surged through his heart.
"Was this right? Was any of this right?" he thought again as he descended the stairs. "Couldn't he stop and take it all back... and not go?"

But he kept going. He felt suddenly, with absolute finality, that he must stop asking himself questions. Turning into the street, he remembered that he hadn't said goodbye to Sonia, that he had left her standing in the middle of the room in her green shawl, not daring to move after he had shouted at her. He stopped for a moment. In that same instant, another thought hit him, as though it had been lying in wait.

"Why did I go to her just now? I told her it was on business -- what business? I had no business! To tell her I was going? But where was the need? Do I love her? No -- no, I drove her away just now like a dog. Did I really want her crosses? Oh, how low I've sunk! No -- I wanted her tears, I wanted to see her terror, to watch her heart break! I needed something to cling to, something to delay me, a kind face to look at! And I dared to believe in myself, to dream of what I'd become! I'm a pathetic, contemptible wretch -- contemptible!"
He walked along the canal embankment. He didn't have much further to go. But at the bridge he stopped, turned off his path, and walked along it toward the Haymarket.

He looked eagerly left and right, gazing intently at every object, but unable to fix his attention on anything; everything slipped away. "In a week, a month, I'll be crossing this bridge in a prison van. How will I look at the canal then? I should try to remember this," slipped through his mind. "Look at that sign -- how will I read those letters then? It says 'Company' -- there, I should remember that letter 'a,' and look at it again in a month -- how will I see it then? What will I be feeling and thinking then? Good God, how trivial all this must be, what I'm fretting over now! Of course it must all be interesting in its way... Ha-ha-ha! What am I thinking? I'm turning into a child, showing off to myself. Why am I ashamed? Oh! -- that fat man who just shoved me -- a German, must be -- does he have any idea who he just pushed? There's a woman with a baby, begging. It's funny that she considers me more fortunate than herself. I should give her something, just for the absurdity of it. Here's a five-kopeck piece still in my pocket -- where did I get it? Here, here... take it, my good woman!"
"God bless you," the beggar chanted in a tearful voice.

He entered the Haymarket. It was distasteful, deeply distasteful, to be in a crowd, but he walked toward the thickest part of it. He would have given anything to be alone; but he knew that he couldn't have borne being alone for a single moment. A drunk was making a spectacle of himself, trying to dance and falling over. A ring of people had gathered around him. Raskolnikov pushed through the crowd, watched the drunk for several minutes, and gave a short, barking laugh. A minute later he had forgotten the man entirely and no longer saw him, though he was still staring. He drifted on, not remembering where he was, but when he reached the middle of the square, a sudden wave of feeling swept over him, overwhelming him body and soul.

He suddenly recalled Sonia's words: "Go to the crossroads, bow down to the people, kiss the earth -- for you have sinned against it too -- and say aloud to the whole world: 'I am a murderer.'" He trembled as he remembered. The hopeless misery and anxiety of all that time, especially the last hours, had weighed on him so heavily that he clutched at the chance for this new, pure, complete sensation. It came over him like a seizure; a single spark kindled in his soul and spread like fire. Everything in him softened at once, and tears sprang to his eyes. He fell to the earth where he stood...
He knelt in the middle of the square, bowed down to the ground, and kissed the filthy earth with bliss and rapture. He rose and bowed down a second time.
"That one's been drinking," a young man nearby observed.
There was a roar of laughter.

"He's going to Jerusalem, brothers, saying goodbye to his children and his homeland. He's bowing down to all the world and kissing the great city of Saint Petersburg and its pavement," added a slightly drunk workman.
"He's young, too!" someone else noted.
"And a gentleman," someone said in a more serious tone.
"Hard to tell who's a gentleman and who isn't these days."

These remarks and the laughter held Raskolnikov in check, and the words "I am a murderer," which had perhaps been on the tip of his tongue, died away. He endured the comments calmly, however, and without looking back, turned down a street leading toward the police station. Along the way he caught a glimpse of something that did not surprise him -- he had felt it must be so. The second time he had bowed down in the Haymarket, he had spotted Sonia about fifty paces away on his left, hiding behind one of the wooden market stalls. She had followed him on his agonizing journey! In that moment, Raskolnikov felt and knew once and for all that Sonia was with him forever and would follow him to the ends of the earth, wherever fate might take him. His heart was wrung... but he was already approaching the fatal place.

He entered the courtyard with a certain resolve. He had to climb to the third floor. "It'll take me a while to get up there," he thought. The decisive moment still seemed far off, as though he had plenty of time left to reconsider.

The same garbage, the same eggshells on the spiral staircase, the same open apartment doors, the same kitchens belching the same fumes and stench. Raskolnikov had not been here since that day. His legs were numb and buckling under him, but they kept moving forward. He stopped for a moment to catch his breath, to compose himself, to enter like a man. "But why? What for?" he asked himself. "If I must drain this cup, what difference does it make? The more repulsive, the better." He pictured the figure of the "Explosive Lieutenant," Ilya Petrovitch. Was he really going to him? Couldn't he go to someone else? To Nikodim Fomitch? Couldn't he turn around and go straight to Nikodim Fomitch's home? At least it would be done in private... No, no! To the Explosive Lieutenant! If he must drink the cup, drink it down at once.

Feeling cold and barely conscious, he opened the door to the police station. This time there were very few people inside -- just a building porter and a peasant. The doorkeeper didn't even glance out from behind his partition. Raskolnikov walked into the next room. "Maybe I still won't have to say anything," flashed through his mind. A clerk of some sort, not in uniform, was settling in at a desk to write. Another clerk was sitting down in the corner. Zametov was not there. Neither, of course, was Nikodim Fomitch.
"No one in?" Raskolnikov asked, addressing the man at the desk.
"Who are you looking for?"
"Well, well! Not a sound was heard, not a sight was seen, but I smell a Russian... how does that fairy tale go? I've forgotten! At your service!" a familiar voice suddenly cried.
Raskolnikov shuddered. The Explosive Lieutenant stood before him. He had just come in from the third room. "It's the hand of fate," thought Raskolnikov. "Why is he here?"

"Come to see us? What about?" Ilya Petrovitch cried. He was obviously in an excellent mood and perhaps slightly tipsy. "If it's on business, you're a bit early. It's only by chance that I'm here. But I'll do what I can. I must say, I... what is it, what is it? Forgive me..."

The translator's note read: Dostoevsky appears to have forgotten that it is after sunset, and that the last time Raskolnikov visited the police office at two in the afternoon he was reproached for coming too late.
"Raskolnikov."
"Of course -- Raskolnikov. You didn't think I'd forgotten? Don't think me that sort of man... Rodion Ro -- Ro -- Rodionovitch, that's it, isn't it?"
"Rodion Romanovitch."

"Yes, yes, of course, Rodion Romanovitch! I was just getting to it. I've made many inquiries about you. I assure you I've been genuinely sorry since that... since I behaved so badly... It was explained to me afterward that you were a literary man... a scholar of sorts. Mercy me! What literary or scientific man hasn't begun with some eccentricity? My wife and I have the deepest respect for literature -- my wife is a genuine devotee! Literature and art! As long as a man is a gentleman, everything else can be gained through talent, learning, good sense, genius. A hat -- well, what does a hat matter? I can buy a hat as easily as a bun. But what's under the hat, what the hat covers -- that I can't buy! I even meant to come and apologize to you, but I thought maybe... Anyway, is there something you need? I hear your family has arrived?"
"Yes, my mother and sister."

"I've even had the honor and pleasure of meeting your sister -- a highly cultured and charming person. I confess I was sorry about getting so heated with you that time. There it is! And as for my being suspicious about your fainting spell -- that's been thoroughly cleared up! Fanaticism and overwrought nerves! I understand your indignation perfectly. Perhaps you're changing lodgings now that your family has come?"
"No, I just dropped in... I came to ask... I thought I'd find Zametov here."

"Oh yes! Of course -- you two became friends, I heard. Well, no, Zametov is gone. Yes, we've lost Zametov. He left yesterday... quarreled with everybody on the way out, in the rudest way. He's a featherbrained young fool, nothing more; one might have expected something from him, but there -- you know how our brilliant young men are. He wanted to sit for some examination, but it's all just talk and boasting with him -- it never goes anywhere. Of course, it's a very different matter with you, or with your friend Mr. Razumihin. Yours is an intellectual career, and failure won't stop you. For you, one might say, all the pleasures of life amount to nothing -- you are an ascetic, a monk, a hermit! A book, a pen behind your ear, a scholarly paper -- that's where your spirit soars! I'm the same way myself... Have you read Livingstone's Travels?"
"No."
"I have. There are a great many nihilists about nowadays, you know, and it's not surprising, given the times. But we thought... you're not a nihilist, of course? Answer me frankly, frankly!"

"Believe me, you can speak as openly with me as you would with yourself! Official duty is one thing, but... You think I meant to say friendship is something else? No, you're wrong! It's not friendship I mean, but the feeling of a man and a citizen, the feeling of humanity and love for the Almighty. I may be an official, but I must always feel myself a man and a citizen. You were asking about Zametov. Zametov will get himself into some sordid scandal in a house of ill repute, with champagne flying -- that's the sum total of your Zametov! While I, perhaps, am burning with devotion and lofty feelings. Besides, I have rank, position, standing! I am married, have children, fulfill my duties as a man and a citizen. And who is he, may I ask? I appeal to you as a man ennobled by education... Then these midwives have become astonishingly common, too."

Raskolnikov raised his eyebrows. The words of Ilya Petrovitch, who had obviously been at dinner, were mostly a stream of empty sounds to him. But some of them he caught. He looked at the lieutenant inquiringly, not knowing where this was going.

"I mean those short-haired females," the talkative Ilya Petrovitch continued. "'Midwives' is my term for them. I think it's a fine one, ha-ha! They go to the medical academy, study anatomy. If I fall sick, am I supposed to send for some young lady to treat me? Ha-ha!" Ilya Petrovitch laughed, pleased with his own wit.
