"It's an immoderate passion for education, but once you're educated, enough is enough. Why abuse it? Why insult decent people, as that scoundrel Zametov does? And why did he insult me, I ask you? Then look at these suicides -- how common they've become, you can't imagine! People spend their last kopeck and kill themselves. Boys and girls, old men. Just this morning we heard about a gentleman newly arrived in town. Nil Pavlitch -- I say -- what was the name of that gentleman who shot himself?"
"Svidrigailov," someone answered from the other room, in a drowsy, listless voice.
Raskolnikov started.
"Svidrigailov! Svidrigailov shot himself!" he cried.
"What -- you knew Svidrigailov?"
"Yes... I knew him. He hadn't been in town long."

"That's right. He'd recently lost his wife, was a man of reckless habits, and suddenly shot himself -- in the most shocking way. He left a few words in his notebook saying he was dying in full possession of his faculties and that no one was to blame for his death. He had money, they say. How did you come to know him?"
"I... was acquainted with him. My sister was a governess in his family."
"Well, well, well! Then perhaps you can tell us something about him. You had no suspicion?"
"I saw him yesterday. He was... drinking wine. I knew nothing."
Raskolnikov felt as though something had fallen on him and was suffocating him.
"You've gone pale again. It's so stuffy in here..."
"Yes, I should go," Raskolnikov muttered. "Excuse me for troubling you..."
"Not at all! Come as often as you like. It's a pleasure, and I'm glad to say so."
Ilya Petrovitch held out his hand.
"I only wanted... I came to see Zametov."
"I understand, I understand. And it's a pleasure to see you."
"I... am very glad... goodbye," Raskolnikov smiled.

He went out. He was reeling, overcome by dizziness, barely conscious of what he was doing. He started down the stairs, bracing himself with his right hand against the wall. He was vaguely aware of a porter pushing past him on the way up to the station, of a dog barking shrilly on a lower floor, of a woman hurling a rolling pin at it and shouting. He made his way down and out into the courtyard. There, not far from the entrance, stood Sonia, deathly pale and stricken with horror. She looked at him wildly. He stopped before her. There was a look of poignant agony, of despair, on her face. She clasped her hands. An ugly, meaningless smile twisted his lips. He stood there for a moment, grinned, and turned back into the police station.
Ilya Petrovitch had sat down and was rummaging through some papers. Before him stood the same peasant who had jostled past on the stairs.
"Back again! Leave something behind? What's the matter?"
Raskolnikov, his lips white and his eyes staring, walked slowly up to the desk, leaned his hand on it, and tried to speak. But no words came -- only incoherent sounds.
"You're feeling ill! A chair! Here, sit down! Water!"
Raskolnikov collapsed into the chair, but kept his eyes fixed on the face of Ilya Petrovitch, which now showed unpleasant surprise. They stared at each other for a full minute. Someone brought water.
"It was I..." Raskolnikov began.
"Drink some water."
Raskolnikov pushed the water away with his hand and, softly, haltingly, but distinctly, said:
"It was I who killed the old pawnbroker woman and her sister Lizaveta with an axe, and robbed them."
Ilya Petrovitch's mouth fell open. People came running from all directions.
Raskolnikov repeated his statement.

chapters.title: Epilogue, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Siberia. On the banks of a wide, solitary river stands a town, one of Russia's administrative centers. In the town there is a fortress, and in the fortress there is a prison. In the prison, the second-class convict Rodion Raskolnikov has been confined for nine months. Almost a year and a half has passed since his crime.

His trial had proceeded without much difficulty. The prisoner adhered to his statement exactly, firmly, and clearly. He did not confuse or misrepresent the facts, did not soften them in his own favor, did not omit the smallest detail. He explained every aspect of the murder, including the secret of the pledge -- the piece of wood with a strip of metal -- found in the murdered woman's hand. He described in detail how he had taken her keys, what they looked like, the chest and its contents. He explained the mystery of Lizaveta's murder, described how Koch and then the student had knocked, and repeated every word they had said to each other. He told how he had run downstairs and heard Nikolay and Dmitri shouting, how he had hidden in the empty apartment and then gone home. He concluded by identifying the stone in the courtyard off Voznesensky Prospect, under which the purse and trinkets were found. The whole thing was perfectly clear. The lawyers and judges were particularly struck by the fact that he had hidden the trinkets and the purse under a stone without using them, and stranger still, that he couldn't even remember what the trinkets looked like or how many there were. The fact that he had never opened the purse and didn't even know how much was in it seemed incredible. The purse turned out to contain three hundred and seventeen rubles and sixty kopecks. Some of the larger notes on top had been damaged by moisture from lying so long under the stone. The court spent a long time trying to determine why the accused would lie about this one point when he had been truthful and straightforward about everything else. Some lawyers with more psychological insight ultimately conceded that it was possible he truly hadn't looked inside the purse and therefore didn't know what was in it when he hid it. But they immediately drew the conclusion that the crime could only have been committed in a state of temporary mental derangement -- homicidal mania without rational motive or pursuit of gain. This fit the latest fashionable theory of temporary insanity, which was increasingly applied in criminal cases. Moreover, Raskolnikov's depressive condition was confirmed by many witnesses -- Dr. Zossimov, his former classmates, his landlady, and her servant. All of this strongly supported the conclusion that Raskolnikov was not an ordinary murderer and thief, but that something else was at work.

To the intense annoyance of those who held this view, the criminal made almost no effort to defend himself. When asked the decisive question of what had driven him to murder and robbery, he answered with the bluntest frankness that the cause was his wretched circumstances, his poverty and helplessness, and his desire to secure his first steps in life with the three thousand rubles he had expected to find. He had been driven to murder by his shallow and cowardly nature, made worse by deprivation and failure. When asked what had led him to confess, he answered that it was sincere repentance. All of this was almost crudely blunt.

The sentence, however, was more lenient than might have been expected, partly because the criminal had not tried to justify himself but had rather seemed eager to exaggerate his guilt. All the strange and peculiar circumstances of the case were taken into account. There could be no doubt about the criminal's abnormal and poverty-stricken condition at the time. The fact that he had made no use of what he'd stolen was attributed partly to the onset of remorse, partly to his disturbed mental state during the crime. The incidental murder of Lizaveta actually supported the latter theory: a man commits two murders and then forgets that the door is open! Finally, his confession -- coming at the very moment when the case had been hopelessly muddled by Nikolay's false testimony, and when there were no proofs or even suspicions against the real criminal (Porfiry Petrovitch fully kept his word) -- all this did much to soften the sentence. Other circumstances also came to light unexpectedly in the prisoner's favor. Razumihin somehow discovered and proved that while at the university, Raskolnikov had helped support a sick fellow student for six months and, after that student died, had cared for his decrepit old father, eventually placing him in a hospital and paying for his funeral. Raskolnikov's landlady also testified that in their previous lodgings, Raskolnikov had rescued two small children from a burning building and been injured in the process. This was investigated and well confirmed by multiple witnesses. These facts made a favorable impression.
In the end, the criminal was sentenced -- in consideration of extenuating circumstances -- to penal servitude in the second class for a term of only eight years.

At the very start of the trial, Raskolnikov's mother fell ill. Dounia and Razumihin managed to get her out of Petersburg for the duration. Razumihin chose a town on the railway not far from the capital, so he could follow every step of the trial while also seeing Avdotya Romanovna as often as possible. Pulcheria Alexandrovna's illness was a strange nervous condition accompanied by a partial derangement of her mind.

When Dounia returned from her last meeting with her brother, she found their mother already ill, feverish and delirious. That evening she and Razumihin agreed on what they would tell her about Raskolnikov, concocting a complete story about his having to travel to a distant part of Russia on a business assignment that would eventually bring him money and recognition.

But they were struck by the fact that Pulcheria Alexandrovna never questioned them about it -- not then, not later. On the contrary, she had her own version of her son's sudden departure. She told them through tears how he had come to say goodbye, hinting that she alone knew many mysterious and important things, and that Rodya had many powerful enemies who made it necessary for him to go into hiding. As for his future career, she had no doubt it would be brilliant. His article and his obvious literary talent proved it. She read the article constantly, sometimes read it aloud, and practically took it to bed with her -- yet she hardly ever asked where Rodya actually was, even though the others obviously avoided the subject, which should have been enough to arouse her suspicions.

Eventually they grew frightened by Pulcheria Alexandrovna's strange silence on certain topics. She did not, for instance, complain about not receiving letters from him, though in previous years she had lived for nothing else but the hope of his letters. This alarmed Dounia greatly; she began to suspect that their mother sensed something terrible about her son's fate and was afraid to ask, for fear of learning something even worse. In any case, Dounia could see clearly that her mother was not in full possession of her faculties.

Once or twice, however, Pulcheria Alexandrovna steered the conversation in a direction that made it impossible to respond without mentioning where Rodya was, and when she received evasive, suspicious answers, she fell into a gloomy silence that lasted a long time. Dounia finally realized that it was pointless to try to deceive her and concluded that it was better to remain absolutely silent on certain subjects. But it became increasingly obvious that the poor mother suspected something terrible. Dounia remembered that her brother had mentioned their mother overhearing her talk in her sleep the night after the meeting with Svidrigailov, before the day of the confession. Had she understood something from that? Sometimes days and weeks of somber silence and tears would give way to a burst of hysterical excitement, and she would begin talking almost nonstop about her son, about her hopes for his future. Her fantasies were sometimes very strange. They humored her and pretended to agree -- she probably saw through their pretense -- but she kept talking.

Five months after Raskolnikov's confession, he was sentenced. Razumihin and Sonia visited him in prison as often as possible. At last the moment of separation arrived. Dounia swore to her brother that the separation would not be forever; Razumihin said the same. In his youthful fervor, Razumihin had firmly resolved to lay the foundations of a secure livelihood over the next three or four years, save up a certain sum, and emigrate to Siberia -- a land rich in natural resources and in need of workers, enterprising people, and capital. There they would settle in the town where Rodya was, and together they would begin a new life. They all wept at parting.

In the days before his departure, Raskolnikov had been very distracted. He asked often about his mother and was constantly worried about her. He fretted so much that Dounia became alarmed. When he learned of his mother's illness, he grew very somber. He was particularly reserved with Sonia throughout this time. With the help of the money Svidrigailov had left her, Sonia had long since made arrangements to follow the convoy of prisoners being sent to Siberia. Not a word was exchanged between Raskolnikov and her on the subject, but both knew that was how it would be. At the final farewell, he smiled strangely at his sister and Razumihin's passionate plans for their happy future together when he got out of prison. He predicted that their mother's illness would soon prove fatal. Then he and Sonia set off.

Two months later, Dounia married Razumihin. It was a quiet, sorrowful wedding. Porfiry Petrovitch and Zossimov were among those invited. Throughout this whole period, Razumihin wore an air of resolute determination. Dounia had complete faith in his plans, and indeed she could not help believing in him -- he showed a remarkable strength of will. Among other things, he resumed attending university lectures to finish his degree. They were constantly making plans for the future; both counted on settling in Siberia within five years at most. Until then, they placed their hopes on Sonia.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was delighted to bless Dounia's marriage to Razumihin, but after the wedding she grew even more melancholy and anxious. To cheer her, Razumihin told her how Raskolnikov had looked after the sick student and his old father, and how he had been burned rescuing two children from a fire. These two stories excited the disordered imagination of Pulcheria Alexandrovna almost to ecstasy. She talked about them incessantly, even striking up conversations with strangers in the street, though Dounia always accompanied her. In carriages and shops, wherever she could find a listener, she would launch into the story of her son, his article, his care for the student, his injuries from the fire. Dounia didn't know how to restrain her. Apart from the danger of her morbid excitement, there was the risk that someone might recall Raskolnikov's name and mention the recent trial. Pulcheria Alexandrovna managed to find the address of the mother of the two children he had saved and insisted on going to see her.

At last her agitation reached an extreme. She would sometimes burst into tears for no reason and was often ill and feverishly delirious. One morning she declared that by her reckoning, Rodya ought to be home soon -- she remembered that when he said goodbye, he had said to expect him back in nine months. She began preparing for his arrival, tidying up her room, cleaning the furniture, hanging new curtains. Dounia was worried but said nothing and helped. After an exhausting day of joyful daydreams and tears, Pulcheria Alexandrovna fell ill that night. By morning she was feverish and delirious. It was brain fever. She died within two weeks. In her delirium she let slip words that showed she had understood far more about her son's terrible fate than anyone had supposed.

For a long time Raskolnikov did not know of his mother's death, though regular correspondence had been maintained from the time he reached Siberia. The letters were carried on through Sonia, who wrote monthly to the Razumihins and received a reply with unfailing regularity. At first they found Sonia's letters dry and unsatisfying, but eventually they realized that nothing better was possible, for from these letters they received a complete picture of their unfortunate brother's life as a convict. Sonia's letters were filled with the most matter-of-fact detail, the simplest and clearest descriptions of Raskolnikov's surroundings. There was no word of her own hopes, no speculation about the future, no exploration of her feelings. Instead of any attempt to interpret his state of mind or inner life, she gave the plain facts -- his own words, an exact account of his health, what he asked for during their visits, what errands he gave her. All of it was reported with extraordinary precision. The picture of their unhappy brother emerged at last with great clarity. There could be no mistake, because nothing was given but facts.

But Dounia and her husband could draw little comfort from the news, especially at first. Sonia wrote that he was constantly sullen and barely willing to talk; that he showed scarcely any interest in the news from their letters; that he sometimes asked about his mother, and when she finally told him of her death -- seeing that he had already guessed the truth -- she was surprised to find he did not seem greatly affected, at least not outwardly. She reported that although he seemed entirely wrapped up in himself and had, as it were, shut himself off from everyone, he took a very direct and simple view of his new life. He understood his position, expected nothing better for the time being, harbored no ill-founded hopes (so common among prisoners), and seemed almost unsurprised by his surroundings, so different from anything he had known. She wrote that his health was satisfactory; he did his work without shirking or seeking to do more; he was almost indifferent about food, though it was so bad -- except on Sundays and holidays -- that he had eventually been glad to accept money from Sonia for tea every day. He begged her not to fuss about anything else, insisting that all this attention only annoyed him. Sonia added that in prison he shared quarters with the other inmates; she hadn't seen the inside of their barracks but gathered they were crowded, wretched, and unhealthy. He slept on a plank bed with a rug beneath him and refused any better arrangement -- not from any plan or principle, but simply from indifference and inattention.

Sonia wrote simply that at first he had shown no interest in her visits, had been almost angry with her for coming, reluctant to talk, and rude. But in time these visits became a habit and almost a necessity for him, so that he was genuinely upset when she fell ill for several days and couldn't come. She usually saw him on holidays at the prison gates or in the guardroom, where he was brought for a few minutes. On workdays she went to see him at his labor -- either at the workshops, the brick kilns, or the sheds on the banks of the Irtysh.

About herself, Sonia wrote that she had managed to make some acquaintances in the town and was doing sewing. Since there was barely a single dressmaker in the town, she had become practically indispensable in several households. She did not mention that through her efforts the authorities had taken an interest in Raskolnikov, or that his workload had been lightened, and so on.

At last the news came (Dounia had indeed noticed signs of alarm in the preceding letters) that he kept entirely to himself, that his fellow prisoners disliked him, that he went days without speaking, and that he was growing very pale. In her last letter, Sonia wrote that he had fallen seriously ill and had been taken to the prison hospital.

chapters.title: Epilogue, Chapter 2
paragraphs: He was ill for a long time. But it was not the horrors of prison life, the hard labor, the bad food, the shaved head, or the patched clothes that crushed him. What did he care about all those trials and hardships? He was even glad of the hard work -- physically exhausted, he could at least count on a few hours of peaceful sleep. And what was the food to him -- the watery cabbage soup with beetles floating in it? As a student, he had often gone without even that. His clothes were warm and suited to his way of life. He didn't even feel the fetters. Was he ashamed of his shaved head and striped convict's coat? Before whom? Before Sonia? Sonia was afraid of him -- how could he be ashamed before her? And yet he was ashamed, even before Sonia, and he tormented her for it with his contemptuous, rough manner. But it wasn't his shaved head or his chains that shamed him. His pride had been wounded to the core. It was wounded pride that made him ill. Oh, how happy he would have been if he could have blamed himself! He could have borne anything then, even shame and disgrace. But he judged himself harshly, and his embittered conscience found no particularly terrible fault in his past -- only a simple blunder that could happen to anyone. What shamed him was that he, Raskolnikov, had so hopelessly, so stupidly destroyed himself through some blind decree of fate, and now had to submit and accept the "idiocy" of a court's verdict if he was ever to have any peace.

A vague, pointless anxiety in the present, and in the future a ceaseless sacrifice leading to nothing -- that was all that lay before him. And what comfort was it that at the end of eight years he would be only thirty-two and able to start a new life? What was there to live for? What to look forward to? Why should he strive? To live in order to exist? But he had been ready a thousand times before to give up existence for the sake of an idea, a hope, even a fantasy. Mere existence had always been too little for him; he had always wanted more. Perhaps it was precisely the strength of his desires that had made him think he was a man to whom more was permitted than to others.

If only fate had sent him repentance -- burning repentance that would have torn his heart and robbed him of sleep, the kind of repentance whose terrible agony brings visions of the noose or the river! Oh, he would have welcomed it! Tears and torment would at least have been life. But he did not repent of his crime.

At least he might have found relief in raging at his own stupidity, as he had raged at the grotesque blunders that had landed him in prison. But now, in prison, in this new freedom from distraction, he thought over and reexamined all his actions again, and by no means found them as blundering and grotesque as they had seemed at the fatal time.

"In what way," he asked himself, "was my theory stupider than the others that have swarmed and clashed since the beginning of the world? One only has to look at the thing independently, broadly, free from the influence of commonplace ideas, and my theory will by no means seem so... strange. Oh, you skeptics and penny philosophers -- why do you always stop halfway!"

"Why does my act strike them as so horrible?" he said to himself. "Because it was a crime? What does 'crime' mean? My conscience is clear. Yes, it was a legal crime -- the letter of the law was broken and blood was shed. Fine -- punish me for breaking the letter of the law, and leave it at that. Of course, in that case, many of humanity's benefactors who seized power instead of inheriting it should have been punished at their very first step. But those men succeeded, and so they were right -- and I failed, and so I had no right to take that step."
It was only in that -- only in the fact that he had failed and then confessed -- that he recognized his crime.

He also suffered from another question: why hadn't he killed himself? Why had he stood staring at the river and chosen confession instead? Was the will to live really so strong? Was it so hard to overcome? Hadn't Svidrigailov overcome it, even though he feared death?

In his misery, he asked himself this question and could not understand that at the very moment he had stood gazing into the river, he had perhaps already sensed the fundamental falseness in himself and in his convictions. He did not understand that this dim awareness might be the promise of a future crisis, of a new way of seeing life, of his eventual resurrection.

He preferred to attribute it to the dead weight of instinct, which he couldn't overcome -- yet more weakness, more cowardice. He looked at his fellow prisoners and was amazed at how much they all loved life, how much they valued it. It seemed to him they loved and treasured life more in prison than they had in freedom. What terrible agonies and deprivations some of them -- the vagrants, for instance -- had endured! Could they really care so much about a ray of sunshine, a patch of primeval forest, a cold spring hidden away in some remote spot, which a tramp had marked three years ago and longed to see again the way he might long for a sweetheart, dreaming of the green grass around it and the bird singing in the bush? As he looked further, he found even more inexplicable examples.

In prison, of course, there was much he did not see and did not want to see. He lived with his eyes cast down, so to speak. The sight of those around him was repellent and unbearable. But gradually, things began to surprise him, and he started, almost against his will, to notice what he had never suspected before. What surprised him most was the terrible, impassable gulf between himself and everyone else. They seemed to be a different species. He looked at them and they at him with suspicion and hostility. He understood the reasons for his isolation, but he had never imagined until now how deep and strong those reasons were. There were some Polish exiles, political prisoners, among them, who simply looked down on the rest as ignorant peasants. But Raskolnikov couldn't see it that way. He noticed that these "ignorant" men were in many ways far wiser than the Poles. There were also some Russians who were just as contemptuous -- a former officer and two seminary students. Raskolnikov saw their mistake as clearly as anything. He was disliked and avoided by everyone; eventually they began to hate him -- and he couldn't understand why. Men who had been far more guilty despised and laughed at his crime.
"You're a gentleman," they would say. "You shouldn't be hacking people up with an axe. That's not a gentleman's work."

In the second week of Lent, it was his turn to take communion with his group. He went to church and prayed with the others. One day a fight broke out -- he never knew how it started. They all turned on him at once in a fury.
"You're a godless man! You don't believe in God!" they shouted. "You ought to be killed!"

He had never spoken to them about God or his beliefs, but they wanted to kill him as an infidel. He said nothing. One prisoner rushed at him in a blind frenzy. Raskolnikov stood his ground calmly and silently; not a brow twitched, not a muscle of his face moved. The guard managed to get between them just in time, or there would have been bloodshed.

There was another question he couldn't resolve: why did they all love Sonia so much? She didn't try to win their favor and rarely met them, coming only sometimes to visit him at work for a few minutes. Yet everyone knew her. They knew she had followed him here, knew how and where she lived. She never gave them money or did them any particular favors. Only once, at Christmas, she sent them all gifts of pies and rolls. But gradually a closer bond developed between them and Sonia. She wrote letters for them and mailed them to their families. When relatives of the prisoners visited the town, they left presents and money with Sonia at the prisoners' request. Their wives and sweethearts knew her and went to see her. And when she visited Raskolnikov at work, or met a group of prisoners on the road, they all removed their hats. "Dear little mother Sofya Semyonovna -- you are our kind, gentle little mother," these coarse, branded criminals would say to that frail young woman. She would smile and bow to them, and everyone was delighted when she smiled. They admired even the way she walked, and would turn to watch her go. They admired her for being so small, and couldn't decide what they admired most about her. They even came to her when they were ill.

He was in the hospital from the middle of Lent until after Easter. When he recovered, he recalled the dreams he had had during his fever and delirium. He had dreamt that the entire world was doomed by a terrible new plague that had come to Europe from the depths of Asia. Everyone was to perish except a very few chosen ones. Some new kind of microbes had appeared, attacking human bodies, but these microbes were endowed with intelligence and will. People infected by them instantly went mad and violent. But never had people considered themselves so wise, so unshakably in possession of the truth, as these infected victims. Never had they been more confident in their judgments, their scientific conclusions, their moral convictions. Entire villages, entire cities and nations went mad from the infection. Everyone was agitated and no one understood anyone else. Each person believed that he alone possessed the truth, and suffered looking at the others, beating his breast, weeping, wringing his hands. They could not agree on what was evil and what was good, could not decide whom to blame and whom to acquit. They killed one another in a kind of senseless rage. They gathered in armies to march against each other, but even on the march the armies would splinter, the soldiers turning on one another, stabbing, slashing, biting, and devouring each other. Alarm bells rang all day in the cities; people rushed together, but no one knew why they had been summoned or who was summoning them. The most ordinary trades were abandoned, because everyone had his own ideas, his own improvements, and they couldn't agree. The fields were abandoned too. People would meet in groups, agree on something, swear to work together -- then immediately start doing something completely different from what they had planned. They accused one another, fought, and killed. There were fires and famine. Everything and everyone was caught up in destruction. The plague spread further and further. Only a handful of people in the entire world could be saved. They were a pure, chosen people, destined to found a new race and a new life, to renew and purify the earth. But no one had seen these people, no one had heard their words or their voices.

It troubled Raskolnikov that this senseless dream clung to his memory so painfully, that the impression of his feverish delirium lasted so long. The second week after Easter arrived. Warm, bright spring days had come. In the prison ward, the barred windows beneath which the sentinel paced were opened. Sonia had been able to visit him only twice during his illness -- each time she had to get permission, and it was difficult. But she often came to the hospital courtyard, especially in the evening, sometimes just to stand for a moment and look up at the windows of the ward.

One evening, when he was nearly recovered, Raskolnikov fell asleep. Waking, he happened to go to the window, and at once saw Sonia in the distance at the hospital gate. She seemed to be waiting for someone. Something pierced his heart at that instant. He shuddered and stepped away from the window. The next day Sonia didn't come, nor the day after. He noticed that he was waiting for her with growing anxiety. Finally he was discharged. Returning to the prison, he learned from the other convicts that Sofya Semyonovna was ill and confined to her bed.

He was deeply worried and sent someone to ask about her. He soon learned that her illness was not dangerous. When she heard he was anxious about her, Sonia sent him a note written in pencil, telling him she was much better, that she had a slight cold, and that she would soon, very soon come to see him at work. As he read it, his heart ached.

It was another warm, bright day. Early in the morning, around six, he went to work on the riverbank where they ground alabaster, near a kiln in a shed. Only three prisoners had been sent. One went with the guard to the fortress for a tool; the other began preparing firewood and loading the kiln. Raskolnikov came out of the shed onto the riverbank, sat down on a pile of logs, and began gazing at the wide, deserted river. From the high bank, a vast landscape spread before him. From the far bank, the faint sound of singing drifted across the water. Out in the boundless steppe, drenched in sunlight, he could just make out the nomads' tents, like tiny dark specks. There was freedom out there, there lived other people utterly unlike those here; there, time itself seemed to stand still, as if the age of Abraham and his flocks had never passed. Raskolnikov sat gazing, and his thoughts dissolved into daydreams, into pure contemplation. He thought of nothing in particular, but a vague restlessness stirred and troubled him. Suddenly he found Sonia beside him. She had approached soundlessly and sat down next to him. It was still very early; the morning air was still sharp. She wore her old, worn burnous and the green shawl. Her face still showed signs of illness -- it was thinner and paler. She gave him a joyful, welcoming smile, but held out her hand with her usual timidity. She was always timid about offering him her hand, and sometimes didn't offer it at all, as though afraid he would push it away. He always took her hand as though with reluctance, always seemed annoyed to see her, and sometimes sat in stubborn silence throughout her entire visit. There were times she trembled before him and went away in deep grief. But this time their hands did not part. He stole a quick glance at her and looked down at the ground without speaking. They were alone. No one had seen them. The guard had turned away for the moment.

How it happened he could not say. But all at once something seemed to seize him and hurl him at her feet. He wept and threw his arms around her knees. For the first moment she was terrified -- her face went white. She leapt up and looked at him, trembling. But in that same instant she understood, and a light of infinite happiness shone in her eyes. She knew -- she had no doubt -- that he loved her, loved her beyond everything, and that at last the moment had come.

They tried to speak but could not. Tears stood in their eyes. They were both pale and thin; but in those sick, pale faces shone the dawn of a new future, a full resurrection into new life. Love had renewed them; the heart of each held infinite wellsprings of life for the heart of the other.

They resolved to wait and be patient. They still had seven years ahead of them, and what terrible suffering and what boundless happiness lay before them! But he had risen again, and he knew it, felt it with every fiber of his being. And she -- she lived only in his life.

That evening, after the barracks were locked, Raskolnikov lay on his plank bed and thought about her. He had even noticed that day that all the prisoners who had been his enemies seemed to look at him differently. He had even spoken to them, and they had answered in a friendly way. He remembered this now and thought it could not be otherwise. Wasn't everything bound to change now?

He thought of her. He remembered how he had constantly tormented her and wounded her heart. He recalled her pale, thin little face. But these memories scarcely troubled him now; he knew with what infinite love he would repay all her suffering. And what were all, all the agonies of the past! Everything -- even his crime, his sentence, his imprisonment -- seemed to him now, in the first rush of feeling, like some external, alien fact that had nothing to do with him. But he could not think coherently about anything that evening and could not have analyzed anything consciously. He was simply feeling. Life had taken the place of theory, and something entirely different would now work itself out in his mind.

Under his pillow lay the New Testament. He picked it up mechanically. It was Sonia's -- the same book from which she had read him the raising of Lazarus. At first he had been afraid she would pester him about religion, talk about the gospels, and force books on him. But to his great surprise she had never once brought it up and had not even offered him the Testament. He had asked her for it himself, not long before his illness, and she had brought the book without a word. He had not opened it until now.
He did not open it now either, but a thought passed through his mind: "Can her beliefs become mine? Her feelings, her aspirations, at least..."

She too had been deeply shaken that day, and during the night she fell ill again. But she was so happy -- so unexpectedly happy -- that she was almost afraid of her own happiness. Seven years -- only seven years! At the start of their happiness, in certain moments, they were both ready to look at those seven years as though they were seven days. He did not know that this new life would not come to him for nothing, that he would have to pay dearly for it, that it would cost him great effort, great suffering.

But that is the beginning of a new story -- the story of a man's gradual renewal, his gradual regeneration, his passage from one world into another, his initiation into a new and unknown life. That might be the subject of a new tale, but our present story is ended.
